items.title: Hemingway’s Heated—and Entirely One-Sided—Rivalry With a Younger Writer

items.author: Stephen Bates
paragraphs: On June 4, 1952, Ernest Hemingway stood at his typewriter at Finca Vigía, his home outside Havana, and wrote to one of his favorite correspondents, Harvey Breit, of the Times Book Review. The letter wanders from topic to topic: his favorite saint (St. Jude), some has-beens of American literature (John Dos Passos and John Steinbeck), and why he stands while typing. “I write standing up because sitting down broadens the ass,” he says. “I have had a narrow, hard ass all of my life and I keep it and a good left hook as other writers preserve their clippings and I hope to be buried with both of them.”

Hemingway also brings up a thirty-year-old writer and former bullfighter named Barnaby Conrad. Conrad fought bulls in Spain in the mid-nineteen-forties, and published his first novel, “The Innocent Villa,” in 1948. He had sent it to Hemingway, along with a fan letter. “He sounded like a good, straight kid,” Hemingway tells Breit, “and I am pretty sure he did whatever he said he did with bulls.” He says he meant to reply, but wasn’t sure what to say about “not a very good novel.” He clipped Conrad’s letter inside the book and forgot about it.

Now Hemingway has received Conrad’s newly published second novel, “Matador.” It’s bound to be derivative of his own meditation on bullfighting, “Death in the Afternoon,” he tells Breit: “Death” is the ur-text, the book that derives from the art itself, whereas all subsequent books derive from “Death”; and, on the whole, “I am not proud of what it has begotten.” As for “Matador,” “I can’t tell about this book until I read it and I hope the hell it is good.”

Seven days later, on June 11th, Hemingway is back at the typewriter, addressing the same correspondent about the same young novelist. Now that he has read “Matador,” the good, straight kid has become a fraud, a defamer, and, worst of all, a gentleman. The letter is so unhinged that he tells Breit to return it without showing anyone else. He has already written one draft too incautious to send at all.

If Hemingway let off steam in his June 11th letter, it soon built up again. Over the next five years, he bad-mouthed Conrad to his Scribner’s editor Wallace Meyer, his fellow bullfighting aficionado Rupert Bellville, the Chicago Tribune literary editor Fanny Butcher, the New York Post columnist Leonard Lyons, and C. W. Wilcox of Scribner’s Bookstore, in addition to Breit. Conrad, oblivious, continued sending him gushing letters.

As a boy in Hillsborough, California, near San Francisco, Conrad was drawn to what he called the Hemingway model of the intellectual man’s man. While studying art in Mexico City one summer during college, he began attending bullfights. At his third fight, he jumped into the ring, which was illegal but not uncommon, and made rudimentary passes using his Brooks Brothers raincoat as a cape. He got out intact; the raincoat didn’t. A Mexican matador offered to teach him the fundamentals of bullfighting, but during one lesson a bull struck him from behind, smashed his leg—Conrad later said his knee made a sound “like a popping log in a fireplace”—and broke several fingers. Back in the United States, he underwent surgery, and had to wear a brace and walk with a cane. His applications to the V-12 Navy College Training Program and a volunteer ambulance service were both rejected.

After graduating from Yale, Conrad joined the State Department as a code clerk and then got posted to Spain as a vice-consul, in late 1943. There, he befriended two of the towering matadors of the century, Juan Belmonte and Manolete, and began training with them. When Conrad was knocked down at a practice session, Belmonte ran to help him while Manolete lured the animal away. In 1945, billed as Niño de California, Conrad appeared on a program with Belmonte. He ultimately fought about thirty times, ten on programs with Belmonte, and considered resigning from the State Department to become a full-time matador, but another knee injury foreclosed that possibility. When he left Spain, at the end of 1945, Belmonte and Manolete both came to Seville to see him off.

Back in the United States, Conrad turned his adventures in Spain into “The Innocent Villa,” published in 1948 to mixed reviews. He then wrote a novel about a legendary bullfighter on the day of his last fight. Although the book includes a disclaimer that all its characters, apart from a brief appearance by Belmonte, are fictional, its protagonist is transparently based on Manolete, who had been fatally gored in 1947. Published in 1952, “Matador” became a best-seller.

Part of “Matador” ’s appeal grew out of Conrad’s experiences in Spain. Reviewers and feature writers stressed that he had studied under renowned bullfighters, entered the ring, and—the intellectual man’s man—emerged to tell what it was really like.

Not so, according to Hemingway. Conrad is “very skillful,” he tells Breit in the June 11th letter, but “he would never convince the boys.” The “Matador” author photo shows Conrad by a poster for one of his bullfights, and the last line is “Entrada por invitación.” If it was an invitation-only fight, Hemingway says, then “nobody was fighting nothing for money and the bulls were calves.” A calf presented nothing like the mortal danger of a full-grown bull, and killing one in the ring “is the worst form of chickenshit I know.” Hemingway further suggests that Conrad is not just a fraud but a fop, the “Gentleman Calf-Sticker” and the “Dean Acheson of bull fighting,” a reference to the patrician Secretary of State. “Gentleman” was an insult; Hemingway once told the editor Maxwell Perkins that F. Scott Fitzgerald was always a gentleman but “never a man.”

In “Death in the Afternoon,” Hemingway had called bullfighting “the only art in which the artist is in danger of death.” He tells Breit in the June 11th letter that he had fought “the hard way” during Pamplona’s famous bullfighting festival, the Fiesta de San Fermín, entering the ring “six mornings straight” for seven years (a number he would inflate to eleven years in a subsequent letter), facing “every sort of bitch and bastard animal” that had fought “as many as 20 times” in amateur events. (Animals that have fought previously are more dangerous, because they may have figured out that the cape is just a distraction.) This wasn’t calf-sticking, he says: “People got killed for nothing every morning.” Even so, he knew his limits. The matador Maera tried to persuade him to enter the ring with “one famous educated cow” by saying, “Ernesto you son of a bitch you could not be killed by a more distinguished animal.” But, he recalls, “I did not want any part of her.” Some people begged him to stay out of the ring altogether, before it was too late, he says, while others remarked that “if we get killed in July we do not have to be rained on and broke in October.”

As Hemingway acknowledged elsewhere, though, the Pamplona festival was hardly a showplace for grace under pressure. It featured an early-morning melee in which several hundred men would enter the ring. A heifer, a steer, or occasionally a young bull would be released, usually with its horns covered. The men would taunt and tease the animal until it charged, and then either cape it or run. Some men would get knocked down, butted, or trampled. Hemingway’s friend Donald Ogden Stewart broke several ribs in 1924, but “he was in no real danger,” Hemingway would write a few years later, adding, “It was a rough Spanish game but no rougher than boxing or professional football.”

In several descriptions of these amateur events, including some of his own, Hemingway sounds less like a matador than a rodeo clown. When he jumped on the back of one animal, according to his friend Gerald Murphy, it collapsed beneath his weight. In “Death in the Afternoon,” Hemingway claims that, to avoid getting injured, he once grabbed a bull’s horns and rode around the ring on its muzzle while spectators laughed uproariously. In the nineteen-fifties, the Spanish writer José Luis Castillo-Puche asked about his experience in the bullring. Hemingway replied that “even my friends thought it was a laugh riot.”

Hemingway’s prominence in the history of Spanish bullfighting, of course, stems from the page, not the ring. The first year he attended the Pamplona festival, in 1923, he claimed that he and his wife, Hadley, were the only English speakers there. When he wrote about bullfighting that year in the Toronto Star Weekly, he figured that readers needed a pronunciation guide: “ ‘Ole!’—pronounced Oh-Lay!—roared the crowd.” Through his articles, novels, short stories, and “Death in the Afternoon,” he introduced much of the English-speaking world to bullfighting. Everyone who wrote about the topic thereafter toiled in his shadow, and knew it.

Conrad certainly knew it: “Death in the Afternoon” introduced him to bullfighting, as he noted in his letters to Hemingway. But he proceeded to learn a great deal on his own by living in Spain, befriending matadors, and entering the ring. Hemingway followed Spanish bullfighting during visits to Spain between 1923 and 1931. Conrad knew it more intensely for a shorter time, while living there between 1943 and 1945. Though a decade separated their sojourns in Spain, the two men shared friends and acquaintances there. Conrad, accordingly, wasn’t just one more writer working in Hemingway’s shadow. He knew people Hemingway had written about—and Hemingway was aware of it. In “Death in the Afternoon,” Belmonte is the object of sweeping generalizations and grand judgments. Conrad got the impression that Hemingway and Belmonte must have spent extended time together and known each other well; Belmonte, however, said they had met only a few times. Conrad could compare the real Belmonte with the “Death in the Afternoon” “Belmonte.” He might try to do the same with Hemingway and “Hemingway.”

Not that one needed to be a potential fact checker to provoke an unfatherly response from Papa. Throughout his career, Hemingway sniped at other writers—his juniors (Conrad, James Jones), his mentors (Sherwood Anderson, Gertrude Stein), and his contemporaries (Fitzgerald, William Faulkner). He punched up, down, and sidewise. His manly posturing fit a pattern, too. Reviewing “Death in the Afternoon,” in 1933, Max Eastman likened his style to “wearing false hair on the chest.” When they encountered each other a few years later, Hemingway struck Eastman across the face with a book.

Along with being a calf-sticking impostor, Conrad, according to Hemingway, was a malicious defamer. Pacote, the Manolete-like protagonist of “Matador,” is Spain’s greatest bullfighter and plans to retire after one last fight. After his girlfriend calls him a coward, he gets drunk but sobers up before entering the ring and gives the greatest performance of his life. As Pacote delivers the fatal thrust with his sword, the bull raises its head and gores him. He dies in the infirmary.

Hemingway can’t see past the drunkenness. If Manolete was sober as he entered the ring for his final fight, the book is a malicious libel, he tells Breit in the June 11th letter. He tells Butcher, Lyons, and Wilcox the same thing. In a July 15th letter, he urges Breit to write a magazine article about “Matador” ’s slanders and their reception in Spain, given that “the Spanish regard Manolete with practically a religious veneration,” and offers to provide “detailed suggestions how you might build it.” Breit apparently didn’t take him up on it. If “Matador” did provoke any controversy in Spain, Conrad doesn’t mention it in his two memoirs, “Fun While It Lasted” and “Name Dropping,” nor in his autobiographical articles.

Eight years after “Matador,” Hemingway himself issued a harsher indictment against Manolete. In 1960, Life featured his three-part account of the 1959 Spanish bullfighting season, later gathered into a book called “The Dangerous Summer,” which proved to be his last major work published during his lifetime. In it, he blames Manolete, dead since 1947, for debasing bullfighting through vulgar showmanship and outright cheating. Hemingway may have seen his accusation as broadly comparable to the one he saw in “Matador”: dishonor. But there’s a difference between drinking before entering the ring once and corrupting bullfighting for years. There are differences, too, between “Matador,” a work of fiction, and “The Dangerous Summer,” a work of nonfiction; and between Conrad, a novice novelist when he wrote “Matador,” and Hemingway, a Nobel laureate in literature when he wrote “The Dangerous Summer.”

Hemingway’s accusations caused an uproar in Spain and attracted coverage in the United States. Manolete’s friends and admirers defended him from the charge that he had sullied bullfighting—including, in a letter to Life, Barnaby Conrad. After faulting Hemingway for misconstruing Manolete’s style in the ring, he closed on a gracious note: “Mr. Hemingway still writes more interestingly on the bulls than anyone going, whether I agree with him or not.”

Did any of Hemingway’s left hooks even strike their target? Three weeks after Hemingway’s June 11th letter, Breit described Conrad as “young and handsome” in the Times Book Review. In 1956, when Conrad sought permission to quote some Hemingway writings in a bullfighting anthology, Hemingway told Meyer to refuse: “I am predjudiced [sic] against Mr. Conrad.” Scribner’s ignored Hemingway and let Conrad use brief excerpts. Hemingway famously said that “the most essential gift for a good writer is a built-in, shockproof, shit detector.” Perhaps, when reading Hemingway’s denunciations, his correspondents applied their own built-in, shockproof shit detectors.

Though he received no responses from Hemingway, Conrad kept sending him chatty letters. In hopes of expressing his admiration face to face, he once wrote and then phoned to ask if he could visit the Hemingways in Cuba, but Mary Hemingway told him that Ernest was ill. Conrad had no way of knowing that Hemingway was intent on avoiding him. “If I don’t meet him then, at least, I was never his pal,” Hemingway told Leonard Lyons in 1954.

Decades later, long after Hemingway’s death, in 1961, Carlos Baker, Hemingway’s biographer, told Conrad about some of the letters deriding him. After getting copies, Conrad concluded, as he told a reporter in 1991, that Hemingway had been “extremely jealous I had fought bulls and written about it.” Conrad had decorated his beach house in Carpinteria, California, with bullfighting memorabilia: a poster for a fight featuring Niño de California, the mounted head of a bull, his own charcoal sketches of Manolete and Belmonte. To the mix he added framed copies of several Hemingway letters about him originally sent to Meyer at Scribner’s. Conrad apparently didn’t know about the fevered 1952 letters to Breit. It’s a shame. Gentleman Calf-Sticker is hard to beat. ♦

items.title: “Fatherland” Cleans Up the Rough Edges of History
items.description: Paweł Pawlikowski’s “Fatherland” offers an amiable eighty-two minutes of condensed history, centered on the septuagenarian novelist Thomas Mann’s trip, in the summer of 1949, to Germany—West and East—in order to receive each country’s Goethe Prize on the occas
items.author: Richard Brody
paragraphs: Paweł Pawlikowski’s “Fatherland” offers an amiable eighty-two minutes of condensed history, centered on the septuagenarian novelist Thomas Mann’s trip, in the summer of 1949, to Germany—West and East—in order to receive each country’s Goethe Prize on the occasion of that great predecessor’s bicentenary. If Pawlikowski’s aim was to portray Mann (played by Hanns Zischler) as a terminal bore and a pompous ass, he succeeded brilliantly, even if he failed to suggest the reasons for his own animosity. Mann, who has been living in Los Angeles since 1941, is accompanied on the journey by his daughter Erika (Sandra Hüller), who serves as his assistant, even editing his speeches. And he does gives speeches. He gives an impromptu one at a press conference at their first stop, Goethe’s native Frankfurt; he gives a carefully crafted one at the formal prize ceremony there, and he gives another at the East German ceremony in Weimar, Goethe’s longtime home, overtly under Soviet dominion. What’s more, he gives speeches, terse but fusty, in private, to Erika.

For the most part, Mann struts around looking iconic, bearing an air of absurd vanity in his belief that, as an eminent anti-Nazi exile and a Nobel Prize winner who left Germany, in 1933, soon after Hitler came to power, his supra-ideological presence in both Germanies, at a time of Cold War tension, could indeed matter. But Mann most of all strikes an air of formality even in private, even when, in Frankfurt, he gets the grim news of the death of his son Klaus (August Diehl)—Erika’s brother and confidant, who is also a noted author—from a drug overdose. (His death was ruled a suicide.) Most pompous of all are the silences; the most conspicuous of them hollows out one of the major early scenes, when father and daughter, newly arrived in West Germany and travelling by car to Frankfurt, pass through streets of destruction, a country ravaged by war—and remain silent. Yes, awestruck and horrified, no doubt; still, I wondered throughout why silence served Pawlikowski as an optimal mode of expression.

Throughout my viewing, something felt off—in style and in substance—and the first concrete diagnosis came through in my colleague Anthony Lane’s recent New Yorker Profile of Pawlikowski, which I had deliberately delayed reading until after seeing the movie. (History may have no spoilers, but drama does.) That in-depth portrait mentions a fundamental change the filmmaker wrought upon Mann’s real-life 1949 journey: the author was, in fact, accompanied by his wife, Katia, who, in “Fatherland,” is said to be too weak to travel. The character of Erika, a writer and intellectual with her own range of uneasy connections to Germany—she’ll encounter an ex-husband and an ex-lover there—is a screenwriter’s convenience, a walking plot-production machine. Behind closed doors, however, the switch from a spouse to a child, from Mann the husband to Mann the father, is the switch from the intimate to the casual, from uninhibited speech to guardedness.

It took no more than minutes of curiosity to find that the fulcrum of “Fatherland,” the death of Klaus —the first character seen in the movie—occurred not during the Germany trip but some months before it. As for the trip itself, it was far more tumultuous, far more infuriating to Mann, and far more unflattering toward West Germany than the movie lets on. Upon his return to the United States, Mann wrote, for the Times, that, in West Germany, “they live by the slogan: ‘Everything was better under Hitler!’ By virtue of the experiences they claim to have had, they declare triumphantly that democracy has been tried and found wanting. Democracy to them means the Occupation Powers and all who ‘collaborate’ with them.” This isn’t the elegant stuffiness of “Fatherland”; it conjures a Fassbinder-esque film—outspoken, insolent, crude, loud, and brazen. Mann may not have shared his testimony, his vision, his voice with Erika during the tour, but he might have with Katia.

To share that voice in “Fatherland,” Pawlikowski would have to imagine it. But his economy of expression also suggests that the film, which is never at risk of spilling out beyond the confines of its scripted pointedness, depends on an economy of imagination. Its contrivances are less like conveniences or abridgments than like deceptions: the facts and the tone are in service to a style that itself has little room for variety or range. “Fatherland” is a muted, muffled quiet-box of understatement, twisting history less for dramatic effect than for affectlessness. Pawlikowski has developed a felt-lined aesthetic—of black-and-white images, in the traditional nearly square screen dimensions, that leave space around the characters—that bespeaks observational detachment and comes off as culture personified. This forced reserve and mannered dignity create a hermetic atmosphere of refinement (from behind the camera) and of elimination (in front of it). It is a cinema of prefabricated meaning and predetermined moods, in which images limit the very kinds of events that can be depicted.

Here, Pawlikowski further rarefies the style that he developed in “Ida” (2013) and advanced in “Cold War” (2018), but not to advantage. I found myself thinking of other filmmakers who rarefy: Christopher Munch, whose 1991 feature, “The Hours and Times,” about the 1963 Barcelona jaunt of John Lennon and Brian Epstein, has the decency to stick to these characters and not replace Epstein with, say, George Martin; or Hong Sangsoo, whose radical reduction of space and span in his new movie, “The Day She Returns,” creates great cinematic leeway for the uninhibited voice of its actress-protagonist; or Robert Bresson, whose severe restraint served artistically as both microscope and microphone, to experience infinitesimal gestures on a cosmic scale of moment and morality.

In “Fatherland,” such microscopy is reversed. Pawlikowski’s camera reduces the figures and voices, in order to fit them into his own rigidly molded spaces. The characters are petrified like specimens, expressing and embodying only what fits into the film’s design, with no potential for inconvenient loose ends for viewers to follow outside the frame’s borders. It’s a sieve too fine for anything as inconvenient as bodies or as coarse as discourse to get through—an aesthetic of purification, disincarnation, signification, as if the mere fact of keeping voices down and holding thoughts in were itself a mark of urbanity, conferring that cultural virtue upon a dignified audience. The movie sanitizes the past and removes its tang, its pungency, leaving a craving for contact with nature, with raw experience, with incongruities and accidents and anything but what fits, in lieu of such synthetic sophistication. ♦

items.title: The Old-School Ambition of “The Brightness”
items.description: Pella and Irma, two classmates at Westish College, in Wisconsin, are the best of friends. Pella, a newly engaged divorcée and former wild child, has just graduated. Irma, several years younger, is a rising academic star, a scholarship student from a rural Cath
items.author: B D McClay
paragraphs: Pella and Irma, two classmates at Westish College, in Wisconsin, are the best of friends. Pella, a newly engaged divorcée and former wild child, has just graduated. Irma, several years younger, is a rising academic star, a scholarship student from a rural Catholic family, so unhip that her lack of touch is its own form of cool. Together, they’ve been in weekly independent-study sessions, reading authors such as Edith Wharton, for the past three years. But if they’re such good friends—why aren’t they talking? Sure, Pella is planning her friend Owen’s wedding, and Irma is gearing up for her senior year. But that doesn’t explain the sudden distance between them, or why the reclusive Irma made the uncharacteristic decision to go to the big parties that open Westish’s school year without telling Pella.

“The Brightness” (Little, Brown), Chad Harbach’s new novel, clocks in at nearly seven hundred pages, but the bulk of it follows Pella and Irma over the span of a few late-summer days in 2015. At Owen’s wedding, Pella’s engagement falls apart and her friendship with Irma seems to reach a breaking point. At Westish, Irma participates in a prank that is meant to draw awareness to sexual assault on campus. The rest of the book covers the subsequent nine months, in which the two women navigate the fallout of these events, Pella from New York and Irma from Westish, only to be reunited toward the end.

By this point, they have assumed the same aimlessness. Pella isn’t getting married, Irma isn’t going to grad school, and neither of them has a job, let alone a career. Unlike other people they encounter throughout the book—people who have shaped themselves and climbed professional heights—there is something unfinished about Pella and Irma. They’re always becoming, never being. Usually, when people don’t grow up, something has gone awry: they didn’t get to, they didn’t plan to, or they have simply delayed as long as possible. With others, though, resistance to a sleek and defined persona is fundamental. Like curly hair that must be ruthlessly flat-ironed into submission—both our heroines have such hair, though Irma’s is “frizzy,” which means curly but unhappy—these people push back against any form in which they find themselves, even if they chose it.

Readers of Harbach’s first novel, “The Art of Fielding” (2011), will recognize some of these names: Pella, Owen, Westish College. That’s because “The Brightness” is its metafictional sequel, with the premise that the previous book was written by Owen as a roman à clef. This conceit allows Harbach to trace the development of not just his characters but his own work, through the reception of Owen’s book and through the way Westish students discuss his other authorial proxy, Edith Wharton. Irma, for instance, adores Wharton but nonetheless engages in a little trash talk: “Wharton’s world is too narrow. . . . I mean, Wharton is flawless at describing the world she sees—but the world she describes is restricted to what she can see, and see readily. She never gropes around in the darkness—she never reaches toward the numinous.”

Throughout “The Brightness,” characters dismiss ambitious realist novels, whether historical or contemporary in concern, as “not exactly the news about how we live” or as bland, “mashed-potato realism.” The middlebrow realist is a master technician, a superb replicator of experience, but neither more nor less than this. These statements—coming as they do in the pages of a large, enjoyable novel that could be called quasi-historical and even accused of having a “whole boring ‘plot’ ”—begin to suggest a preoccupation with whether such novels are worth anyone’s time. The existence of the book says yes; the characters within it say maybe.

Irma has been avoiding her friend for a simple reason: she’s been busy planning her prank. At the parties that ring in the school year, two of her accomplices apply temporary tattoos that say “RAPE VICTIM” onto passed-out athletes’ foreheads. Then Irma publishes a manifesto in the campus newspaper under the moniker Witches of Westish. Once a video of one of the athletes freaking out goes up online (“I’M A DUDE! I WAS NOT SEXUALLY ASSAULTED!” he screams), what starts as a feminist protest becomes a national story, with one of the victims appearing on a Fox News show hosted by a floppy-haired man named Hunter Stroman.

Perhaps because it avoids a situation in which someone is actually raped, “The Brightness” portrays this particular kind of youthful political action with a touching mixture of the high-mindedness, impishness, bravado, self-aggrandizement, and pointlessness that such events really contain. The Witches of Westish want attention, which they get but are unprepared to handle; the athlete who goes on Fox News wants his pride back but instead swings a national spotlight onto Dahlia, a pranker who is suspended; the college administration just wants this whole problem somehow not to be a problem, which is impossible. Celebrities get involved—Lana Del Rey wears a sweatshirt that says “FREE DAHLIA”—as do feminist media startups (such as the titular Brightness), but, as far as campus-rape prevention goes, nothing is accomplished. Some people make money, some people use the buzz to shore up a brand, and some people get their lives wrecked, but who falls into this last category comes down to bad luck more than to justice.

Irma views both herself and her friends as bystanders to the main issue, campus rape; they are raising awareness but otherwise not involved. As events get out of control, though, Irma realizes that her friend Dahlia wants them to. Whenever offered a chance for rapprochement, Dahlia escalates. Her chosen victim, earnestly seeking to understand why she did what she did, tries to have a conversation with her, but she refuses so that he will take his complaints to the administration. Irma’s slow recognition that Dahlia has something different at stake here, as well as the inevitable reveal of what that “something different” happens to be, is delayed because Irma, for all her intelligence, can’t put together why an upbeat, confident classmate might suddenly become moody and self-destructive. Irma lives in a world in which people are fundamentally kind and good. There are things she cannot see and does not understand. Instead, what she sees when she looks at Dahlia is somebody who is fearless to the point of neglecting herself, and part of their friendship lies in how comforting this lack of comprehension is for Dahlia.

The fictional models Harbach cites, both within the text (such as Wharton’s story “The Pelican”) and in interviews (such as “Anna Karenina”), are attentive to social judgments and situations. They are about just and unjust ostracism, the delicacy of one’s reputation, who gets away with things and who doesn’t. They understand that human relationships and human interiority both exist within a world, and this world constrains not only what people do but what they can even regard as possible. Harbach is a gifted observer of undergraduates, their pathos and their comedy, but his Westish is a gentle and perhaps too-good-natured institution, where even the jocks are nerds. This means that the larger social dynamics created by rape—even the prospect of rape—in small, intimate communities go unconsidered. There is no one genuinely malicious at Westish, and thus none of the moral compromises one finds at an actual college: the friends who take sides, which usually means picking the person who’s less trouble; the real but unspoken feeling that sexual assault may be an inevitable part of freewheeling social life; the surreal experience of being in a class about “Tess of the d’Urbervilles” with someone you know to have hurt other people. The singular strangeness of studying at a small college is striving not to know what you know about somebody else, for the sake of higher learning, or at least for the peace of the classroom. These kinds of forces, which explain why students behave in the self-warping ways that they do, are missing, as is the sense that people are ever constrained by something beyond their own quirks of personality or individual delusions.

Meanwhile, back at Owen’s wedding, old friends and enemies reunite, dance, drink too much, and go to bed with the wrong people. Here, again, Harbach demonstrates a profound gift for observing individuals and their relationships. His depiction of the wedding is replete with the sort of tiny triumphs and failures of these occasions: comparing yourself with an old classmate and feeling like a loser, comparing yourself with a younger person and feeling like you wasted your potential, ending up in a group at the end of the night you’d never have chosen and will never see again. Pella, for her part, spends the night obsessed with proving herself to be a flourishing adult. She helped Owen write his book, and helped him plan this wedding, but knowing that she “had once again played the supportive editorial role” means that she is filled with a sense of resentment. She fawns on an old high-school friend, then steals the attention of a guy the friend likes. She is embarrassed by her fiancé’s physical unself-consciousness—he’s at peace with his balding and weight gain, his sunscreen is applied all wrong—as if this somehow reflects poorly on her. Can she really be impressive if she’s with a man who just wants “a grilled cheese of a woman, salty, filling, and cheap”?

Collapsing relationships are the bread and butter of many an insightful novel. But Harbach also captures a more delicate thing in his depiction of Owen and Pella: the frustration that exists between a successful artist and a less successful friend who feels instrumental to that success. Pella envies Owen and secretly enjoys things like a negative review that compares his book to morphine, even as she lives vicariously through the praise and attention he receives. She knows that Owen hasn’t done her dirty, professionally speaking, but still feels neglected.

Once again, though, there’s a social aspect to the proceedings that Harbach avoids, this time not by leaving things out but by insufficiently considering what he’s put in. As mentioned, “The Art of Fielding” is a real novel in “The Brightness.” Various lines make clear that it should be regarded as nearly identical to Harbach’s book. That means it’s a book about two things: first, Henry Skrimshander, a talented Westish shortstop who gets the yips, and, second, Owen’s love affair with the president of the college (who was also Pella’s father). Owen seems to have made no changes to events as they happened. Nevertheless, his “Art of Fielding,” like Harbach’s, is treated by critics as a “roseate” work of old-fashioned realism.

The problem is that Owen’s book would not be received as comforting and old-fashioned. It would be seen as a work of merciless autofiction in the vein of Karl Ove Knausgaard, and it would be discussed, as his books are, as aggressive, antisocial, and spiteful. Despite almost everyone at the wedding having read Owen’s novel, he faces no social fallout: there is no frustration at his depiction of the school and his peers, and no paranoia about whether he’ll expose them further. More to the point, such a book would simply not be described by critics as full of “comforts,” and “The Brightness” is too concerned elsewhere with the way discourses play out online to ignore the debates a work of barely disguised fiction about sleeping with your closeted college president would create. The only person who responds to it in a way that seems even remotely accurate is, oddly, Hunter Stroman, who calls it a novel about being “groomed for gay sex by the sixty-year-old president of [Owen’s] college.”

“The Brightness” suffers from its own problems with thin disguises. The Times is the Times in this book, Vice is Vice, the TV show “Girls” is the TV show “Girls,” and Lana Del Rey is Lana Del Rey. On the other hand, there are women’s websites named the Termagant and the Napkin, a designer label named Jane and Janet, a publication named the SoHo Review, and, of course, a Fox News host named Hunter Stroman. Every time a new, media-adjacent name appears, it’s unclear whether what you’re encountering is a fictional invention or an inside joke. In a conversation before Owen’s wedding, a character dismisses a forthcoming novel as a “period piece” by quipping, “The characters are always humming old advertising jingles. And the price of everything is repeated ad nauseam: ‘Oh goodness! Three shillings six for a jiggery-joo!’ ” But if such an effect was what Harbach sought to avoid by not saying “Jezebel,” “The Hairpin,” or “Tucker Carlson,” he sacrificed a much more important sense of social reality. The titular Brightness, for instance—a women’s media startup that was founded by an actress, and that publishes a mixture of glossy fashion content, aggregated slop, and barely edited confessional pieces—represents a kind of corporate girl power that the reader, sitting at the lofty vantage point of ten years later, knows isn’t heading anywhere except off a cliff. For the characters, though, it’s just a website, and, as glamorous as the media world it represents seems, neither Pella nor Irma wants to join it. It is neither an aspiration nor a temptation; it is not a friend or an enemy; it is just indistinctly there.

These flaws are all the more frustrating because so much of “The Brightness” is beautiful and perceptive. Irma, in particular—who has abandoned her rural Catholic roots but still appears to others as a confusing aesthetic mix of Fox News and flower child, “starch and eccentricity . . . shrewdness and innocence”—is a wholly convincing portrait of someone who is fiercely loyal to her family and their values (despite being at odds with them) but who also feels alternately freed and imprisoned by her own singularity. She is depicted without a trace of condescension, and her struggles with her identity can’t simply be chalked up to a restrictive childhood. They are existential problems that are represented seriously:

Passages like this one are not only a joy to read—they convey something fundamental about people, who are always in conflict with themselves, managing a jumble of desires that pull in wildly different and sometimes mutually exclusive directions. Irma is not going to resolve her dilemma by having sex or cutting loose, nor by renouncing such pastimes and doubling down on intellect. Her need to be multiple represents the tension that will run through the rest of her life, not something that can be reconciled to create a new, final, and perfect Irma. When she does have sex, she experiences the aftermath, too, as doubled: “a kind of grief-in-love, a losing-in-the-having. . . . A new kind of unloneliness, which now she could never unknow.”

The accusation levelled within “The Brightness” against novels that are stuck in the past, whether formally or through their subject matter, is that they are “not exactly bringing the news.” The proper response to this complaint is that novels do not bring the news; the news brings the news. This is as true of art that is experimental and political as of art that is old-fashioned. While in New York, Pella becomes smitten with the work of a feminist artist named Sylvie, especially a film called “Death of My Husband.” In it, Sylvie talks directly to a man standing behind her camera, who asks, “Would you consider killing one’s husband a revolutionary act?” Sylvie replies, “Revolutions just go round and round. I’ve been trying to become an artist.” At the end of the film, pregnant by a man she despises, Sylvie says simply, “There’s no way out.”

Art like Sylvie’s inherently contains two messages. Even if there’s “no way out,” the film’s existence says, “You’re not alone.” An artist is always becoming an artist, the same way Pella and Irma will always be becoming Pella and Irma. All works of art are addressed in part to people they cannot know, with problems they cannot understand. To prove that an old-fashioned book can be excellent, it isn’t necessary to dramatize arguments about the form. You need only a prose style, an interest in people, and a sense of society. In art as in sports, the best defense is a good offense. ♦

items.title: The Great, Cynical Fun of “The Traitors”
items.description: The reality-competition series “De Verraders” premièred in the Netherlands in 2021. Originally, Marc Pos, the creator, had designs to set the action entirely on a ship. He wanted to strand his contestants at sea as a nod to national lore: the seventeenth-centu
items.author: Doreen St Félix
paragraphs: The reality-competition series “De Verraders” premièred in the Netherlands in 2021. Originally, Marc Pos, the creator, had designs to set the action entirely on a ship. He wanted to strand his contestants at sea as a nod to national lore: the seventeenth-century wreck of the Batavia, a Dutch East India Company ship. In 1629, the ship, carrying roughly three hundred souls, was headed from Amsterdam to its namesake port in Indonesia, when it struck a coral reef not too far from the landmass that would become known by the Europeans as New Holland, or Australia. What followed was the stuff of legend: the survivors were marooned, and the ship’s under-merchant, who had long been plotting a mutiny, orchestrated a series of killings, with everyone guessing who was in on it. Wouldn’t this serve as a juicy reference for Pos’s pop-psychology contest? How about throwing the losers into the sea? But the plan was ultimately too expensive. So production shifted the activity to a castle, all chandelier and shadow, and ordered a set of hooded cloaks for the contestants, setting the aesthetic that informs the now global franchise “The Traitors.”

Recently, Indonesia, in a kind of post-colonial cultural boomerang, announced its own version of “The Traitors.” About forty international adaptations are either airing or have been greenlit, putting the series on par with reality bigwigs such as “Survivor” and “Big Brother.” The premise of “The Traitors” is a gleeful ripoff of the parlor game known as Mafia, in which unwitting players must suss out the secret designated killers among them, not unlike what happened on the Batavia. At the start of the series, a small number of players are tapped to be the “traitors”—literally tapped, by the show’s host, on the shoulder during a blindfolded ceremony. The rest are “faithful.” Each night, the traitors meet in a turret to decide which players to “murder,” or eliminate from the game. By day, the whole group takes on missions, to build up a shared prize pot, with the traitors posing as faithful throughout. Then the group votes on whom to banish from the castle. Ideally, the faithful root out the duplicitous among them; if any traitors are left standing at the game’s fiery end, they can steal the prize money. Paranoia abounds! Did you hear So-and-So mention that there were “three” traitors? How could they possibly know that? Was that a slip? Did he look you in the eyes when he said, “I am one-hundred-per-cent faithful”? The descent into foolish and self-destructive groupthink provides the drama.

We know this game structure well: a group is dropped into a fishbowl environment with a charismatic host, who sets arduous tasks (physical, psychological, or both), and every evening the contestants convene, in a council format, to rant, cry, trade accusations, and, eventually, exile someone, all while a pot of cash sits on the horizon.

But however derivative of competition television “The Traitors” may be, the mood of the series is totally different—it is both quaint and greasy—because it so seamlessly matches our culture of incentivized fraud. Embedded in the production of the show is the feeling of being trapped in a hall of mirrors; scenes are edited flagrantly, drowning the viewer in red herrings. The manipulation tactics of the traitor are what you root for; the faithful exhaust you. “The Traitors,” which has won Emmys, is like “Jeopardy,” in a way. Jeering at the contestants for their naïveté and their shortsightedness, you feel like your brain is working.

The American version of “The Traitors,” which premièred in 2023, is hosted by a Scot, Alan Cumming. He is a scheming ringmaster, his eyes kohl-lined, his body wrapped in couture finery for which there are no descriptive words. He can roll consonants in a way that has not happened before in human speech. He makes a meal of the goth gig. He is too good to be doing this, to be on NBC on a Thursday. But his presence, his apparent delight as adults in scuba suits shoot themselves out of helicopters in pursuit of gold, is part of what makes the show so appealing. Against the singularity of Cumming, who brings the American players to his “home” country, for a game set in a handsome castle in the Scottish Highlands, the group always seems dinky, which is interesting, because it’s largely composed of B- and C-list celebrities.

The U.S. adaptation of “The Traitors,” with its gravestone and haunted-doll ambience, was seemingly lifted wholesale from the U.K. version of the show, which had been greenlit less than a year after the Dutch original. There’s just one critical difference: the U.K. version had cast all regular people, with regular jobs—except for that one magician, in Season 1. (“I’m one of the top magic creators in the world and I can read people; it’s my job,” he insisted, even though his predictions were regularly wrong.)

Initially, American producers tried to split the baby: half nobodies, half stars. But the hybridity didn’t take. The celebrities sucked up a lot of air, and so the show leaned in, switching to all-celebrity casts. The all-civilian versions—in the U.K., Ireland, New Zealand, and, at least at the beginning, Australia—have the thinnest veneer of social consciousness. For viewers, that is the undertow of “The Traitors”: the feel of a social experiment. Certain occupations, such as a teacher, make a contestant seem “smart,” whereas others—say, a lawyer—have an inherent shadiness. Women are suspected quickly. White people last long, etc. Communication is as fragile as glass.

What we have had in America, for the most part, is a social experiment conducted on a very particular population: reality-TV alumni. Instead of teachers and lawyers, the contestants are former “Bachelorettes” and “Biggest Losers”; the two main blocs are the “Gamers” (people who competed on shows like “Big Brother,” “The Amazing Race,” and “The Real World”) and the “Housewives” (self-explanatory). U.S. “Traitors” has been a reality show for reality-show stars, veterans of the genre, which is why it has typically been the least interesting version of the competition. The participants are dressed to the hilt by a surely overworked stylist, and they are only ever fake-indignant. The “Housewives,” such as Lisa Rinna (Beverly Hills) and Dorinda Medley (New York City), find themselves victims of a prejudice, of being seen as vindictive or else less strategically minded than the “gamers,” like Parvati Shallow, or Rob Mariano, a.k.a. Boston Rob, both alumni of “Survivor.” The winner of the last celebrity season was a traitor: Rob Rausch, a snake wrangler from Alabama, and a recent graduate of the romance den of “Love Island.” As a white-boy dreamboat in his overalls, he exploited the “low” reputation of dating shows in the entertainment hierarchy, managing to manipulate the faithful, winning in the end. On “Love Island,” he was seen as a liar, as a cad who, like, led on Leah just to dump her; on “The Traitors,” he committed a much worse betrayal, but to widespread approval and even admiration.

“The Traitors” is evolving. The U.K. is airing two versions this year: the typical civilian one, and its first celebrity spin-off. The Americans, in a twist, are the sole civilians. This season is called “The Traitors: New Blood.” (Celebrity traitors will return next year.) In “New Blood,” the fifth season of the U.S. show, “The Traitors” is now established enough for the cast to get self-referential. As the season opened, Kim Daily, a Black, sharply dressed trial attorney, said in her confessional that she would be telling the group that she is a basketball coach, obscuring her real profession. (Daily, obviously a viewer of the franchise, likely knew, too, that Black and brown players tend to go first.) But she can’t fool the cast, who immediately clock her as an intellectual threat; the traitors, sensing her influence over her fellow-faithful, murder her first. And so “The Traitors” is like a cheery hell for some players, who can’t, for all their suave maneuvering, escape the set rhythm of the show. Bias will win. Lessons are never learned. It’s great, cynical fun.

Joe Vanella, a crimson-cheeked funeral director from Long Island, is currently falling apart this season. He is playing the role of castle dad all while he connives in the turret alongside Tomica Adams, a pilot, and Katie Fites, a marketer. Joe is feeling guilty because he has grown close to Michael Foote, a gay lawyer and a faithful, befriending him by lying to his face. Sexuality and disability are the main “differences” that the production team allows to enter its ambit; the contestants rarely touch the third rail of race. (This past week, the banishment of the “Industry” actress Myha’la from U.K. “Celebrity Traitors” finally brought high-profile attention to the racial-bias question.) So Joe is flubbing missions, nearly blowing his cover, in one profoundly hilarious episode, as he tried to “murder in plain sight,” by tossing someone an apple. Overwhelmed, he eats the apple instead.

I don’t know if teary Joe is going to make it. I watch “The Traitors” with a blank mind, usually. But this week I found myself more alert to its theatre of lies. I think it’s because I’m observing the heated reactions to a film that owes some debt to reality television: “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s portrait of the former Theranos C.E.O. Elizabeth Holmes. One invective accuses the directors of destroying the truth-telling potential of documentary. Put another way, in bringing the footage into the realm of film, and not reality television—his domain—Fielder breached some ethical standard. This is a ridiculous complaint, though it’s rooted in a hunger for veracity that one can instinctively understand. In the film, Fielder installs himself at a beach house with Holmes; her partner, the vexing Billy Evans; and their two children, as she prepares to go to prison for fraud. He gets so close to Holmes, who claims innocence, whose steel opacity makes her his double, that he can no longer see her. And so, in Fielder fashion, after Holmes goes to prison, he restages or re-creates reality in order to try to get to some truth about her. He makes a Rube Goldberg machine of reality. But that doesn’t work. Can we trust him? Can we trust Holmes? Can we trust the relationship between Holmes and Evans? Is she manipulating her documentarian, her husband, or vice versa? If you saw that film expecting to gain an answer about Holmes’s innocence or culpability, then, yes, you came up frustrated. You want to live in a faithful world of councils, discernment, and banishment. But you are in the turret, the hall of mirrors. ♦

items.title: How Macron Destabilized France
items.description: Last weekend, mass riots erupted across France after weeks of protests by lycée students over underfunding and poor conditions in their schools. As the demonstrations grew, they expanded to include other groups, including those upset with the cost of living an
items.author: Isaac Chotiner
paragraphs: Last weekend, mass riots erupted across France after weeks of protests by lycée students over underfunding and poor conditions in their schools. As the demonstrations grew, they expanded to include other groups, including those upset with the cost of living and the Presidency of Emmanuel Macron, and rioters looting property and setting fires around Paris and other French cities. Macron’s second term ends next year, and even before the violence of last weekend, Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right party known as the National Rally, was, according to polls, his most likely successor. That appears to be even more true now, with Le Pen’s final-round opponent now likely to be Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a left-wing politician who has associated himself with the protest movement but who is also radically unpopular in the country at large.

I recently spoke by phone with Julian Jackson, an emeritus professor of modern French history at Queen Mary University of London, and the author of a number of books on French history, including the definitive biography of Charles de Gaulle, about the situation in France. During our conversation, which has been edited for length and clarity, we discussed what the riots mean for the political future of the country, why Macron’s Presidency is ending disastrously, and whether the riots will be understood as a hinge point of French history.
How much are the youth protests important in and of themselves, and how important are they because of what they symbolize about the state of the country?

That is a good way to think about it, because some events become important for what they represent, and these events are important because of what they reveal about a whole mass of anxieties and discontent in France today. But I think their importance has now become qualitatively metamorphosed, or changed, by what happened on Saturday with the rioting. So I think that’s created a qualitative change. We have moved from a protest that is revealing a lot of anxieties of the younger generation—and not just them, but also older generations—into a whole questioning about the functioning of the state or the government. I remember reading something saying that there will be a “before October 17th” and an “after October 17th.” And I think that may be slightly overdoing it, but it certainly transformed the political landscape.
You are referring specifically to the amount of violence that night?

Yes. But not just the violence. There was also the sense that the state was completely taken unawares and just had no control. It was like there was almost a void. There was a similar mood in 1968, actually, when de Gaulle’s No. 2, Édouard Balladur, described how he just had a sense that the state wasn’t able to do anything. And so I think there was that sense of a sort of void on that night, because people do need reassurance that they can be protected—their property and their lives. I was at a dinner party that evening just by chance, in Paris, and they were all, I think, fairly centrist, maybe slightly right of center, but totally not extremist people. And it was striking how one of them in particular was in a state of almost apoplectic fury. It was a bit like the way that some people wrote, after the Paris Commune of 1871, that this was a kind of Saturnalian, orgiastic, obscene uprising. And he talked in the same sort of language, that these people should just be shot. He meant the rioters, not the students, but what it showed me was a sort of class panic, a social panic, that that night created. And everywhere you go in France, people are terribly worried now about what’s going to happen next.

You are suggesting that this could be seen as a hinge moment, and my first thought was that you meant it will be the moment when everyone looks back and says that this was when they knew Le Pen was going to come to power.

And then, when you were just describing that dinner party, I thought to myself, this is also going to be a reason, perhaps in their own minds, for people like that—centrist to right-of-center—to justify taking this giant step and voting for Le Pen.

Whether or not it’s pulled down the last obstacle to a lot of people accepting the idea that they could vote for this party or not, I think you’re right. I still won’t say that Marine Le Pen is definitely going to be elected. They’ve got six months to go, and a lot of things can happen. But obviously if you’re putting money on it, she will be elected, and the chances have obviously increased hugely as a result of what happened, not only because it will frighten people into voting for her but also because the only other person who’s been audible, really, in this moment is Mélenchon, on the extreme left. He had lost a bit of traction over the last two years, I think because of a number of things, partly because of antisemitism and partly just because he did seem to be slightly losing it and slightly a figure of the past. But this has definitely reinvigorated him.

And he obviously can’t defend the pillaging and looting on Saturday night, but he’s very clever. He says when he’s asked, Well, I’m not the government. It’s not for me to make a comment on that. I’m going to say that I think the students are at least legitimate in their demands, and I’m completely with them, and I will demonstrate with them. And it’s not for me to comment on the violence because that’s something the state should deal with. And it’s obviously a completely devious answer.

But what’s very interesting is that what you might call the centrist politicians have almost been completely inaudible over the last few days. They just don’t know what to say. So, yes, I think it is a radicalizing moment, but in both directions. I think it will win Mélenchon new support and win Marine Le Pen new support. So I agree with your skepticism. Who knows whether it’s a turning point, but it sort of feels like that at the moment.

And the way the French election works is that there’s a first round for the Presidential contenders and then the two front-runners go forward. And Le Pen is polling well against the centrist candidates in a possible final round, with small to medium leads. But she beats Mélenchon by over thirty points.

Absolutely. And all I would say about that is that if, and it is an if, a centrist candidate does get to the second round, at that point there’s a chance they could be in a position to actually win six months down the line, but we don’t know how long the impact of what happened on Saturday is going to go on because there are more demonstrations coming up, obviously. I had the sense, talking to people, that they’re living on a volcano and they’re sort of tiptoeing around, knowing that the government’s paralyzed, and it can’t do anything, so they just wait till the Presidential election. And there’s this sort of strange, ghostly expectancy, which is quite weird, a mixture of apprehension and fear.
You said the centrist candidates, from the socialist center-left to the center-right, seem somewhat paralyzed. Why?

Well, Mélenchon has been with the lycée a hundred per cent from Day One, they love him, and Le Pen basically says, We need order. Meanwhile, the centrists are not sure where to situate themselves. If they go too close to the school protesters, they seem to be legitimatizing disorder, but then if they go too close to supporting everything the police does, that is a problem, too. It is the classic problem of centrism when the two extremes are so voluble and actually convincing to their own constituencies, and also some of the centrists were in Macron’s government, so that is also a problem for them, and it is difficult for them to find their voice.

And the reason for that is that the one thing you cannot underestimate at this moment is the cold contempt everyone has for Macron. I have not met a person who has anything good to say about Macron. Actually, I had lunch with one of his ministers the other day who obviously did say good stuff about him. But beyond that, it’s almost impossible. And, of course, the picture people have of Macron at one level is a rather authoritarian figure telling people what to do, a sort of vertical President. But then another, a vertical President who simply has no power. He’s the worst of both worlds.
I was about to say he seems helpless, but people also think he’s a top-down–
They’re right; he is. But unfortunately, without being able to do anything, because there are no levers to pull any longer, which is a very sort of strange situation.
Saying the only person you met who likes him is a minister of his reminds me of the Onion headline, “Dukakis Wins 80 Percent of Dukakis Family Vote.”
Yes, absolutely. I remember that actually.

I remember something people were saying four or five years ago, maybe around the second time that Macron fought off Le Pen, in 2022, that basically Macron has had incredible political success, and he will have been President for ten years, but at the same time, he’s killed off the center right and the center left and not provided any alternative. And so you’ve had this chasm that, when he leaves, is going to exist. I remember political analysts saying that five years ago, and it seems like sometimes political analysts say things that turn out to be true and sometimes it turns out to be not true. But it turned out to be exactly right.

I completely agree. I have written something along those lines myself in various pieces about Macron. And I think I must have written five years ago myself that the tragedy of Macron, really, who did seem to offer something, was that he either seemed indifferent to or incapable of thinking about the succession. If you want to take a contrast with a President who he resembles, Valéry Giscard d’Estaing, who was also a centrist liberal, but who really did make efforts to build a center party between the Gaullists and the left. And Macron simply has either not bothered to do it or failed to do it. I don’t think he’s particularly bothered to do it. And what’s so striking is that whenever he’s had a prime minister, he immediately sets out to undermine that person who should be a credible successor.

Macronism was always going to be strange because it does move from the center left to the center right. Some of the people under the Macron umbrella are really very far right, and the people on the left are not very far left, but they’re certainly not far from the Socialists. So he had succeeded, but he only succeeded in bringing over individuals. He was never interested enough in a structure. You know what people jokingly said about how his movement was originally called En Marche? And people said, typically, that the initials of the movement were his own initials.

I think Macron both profited from the weakness of the political parties, first the Socialists and then the Gaullists on the right, and also hastened it, as it were. And he created no alternative future. He also really did show too much contempt in the early days for what the French call intermediary organizations. He sort of thought it was just him and the people. So, trade unions, local mayors, local associations—he was terribly dismissive of those sort of civil-society organisms that can actually make it possible to get things done. Admittedly, I started off as an admirer, and I had great hope, like so many people. I think he’s politically been brilliant at exploiting the possibilities of coming to power and then disastrous at knowing what to do with it.

We have talked a lot about Macron, and almost all of the things you’ve said about his failures are essentially character flaws or political errors based upon his character flaws. How would you define what his agenda was, and to what degree his policies were failures or not failures, too? Because France is obviously facing what a lot of people think is a pretty calamitous budget situation going forward. And you do hear some people blaming him for it. You say other people say, No, he tried his best; he raised the retirement age. But I’m curious how much you think his failures were, in fact, mostly personal and how much they were also policy-based.

Well, I think it seems to me incontrovertibly the case that the French need to deal with their issue of the pensions and that he was absolutely right in what he wanted to do. I think he was a liberal, he was a left liberal, a liberal in the European rather than the American sense, and he wanted a degree of deregulation, but with slightly leftist social rhetoric. It was a kind of Blairism, you might almost say. So there was something attractive and plausible in the agenda. But the Yellow Vest movement started after a gasoline-tax increase. And then it was done for good.

He had framed the gasoline-tax increase as an environmental policy. But of course, he wasn’t prepared for the reaction in any kind of way. And what he never thought of was that the people who were going to be most hit were not the sort of urbanites who believe in environmental protection in Paris but people living in deprived areas who desperately needed their cars to get to work. And so it’s almost as if he has this sense of detachment from what France really was. I also think he made a very big error at the very, very beginning. He said, Well, it’s going to be a regime. I’m going to encourage entrepreneurialism and a “startup nation,” all that kind of thing. But one of his first measures was to abolish a redistributive tax, and that was a really bad symbol that announced, I’m the President of the rich.

And it was so badly judged because it wasn’t going to liberate the economy. It was a handout, really, to the richer segment of the population. And so I think he had some perfectly good ideas. People of the socialist left would not agree with that, but I, as a centrist Social Democrat, think that he had perfectly good ideas. But the problem isn’t the ideas. The problem is his disconnectedness. Remember, he had never been elected to anything before becoming President. He didn’t have that feel for France. I don’t know whether you saw, but he made a very revealing comment to the French writer Emmanuel Carrère a bit of time ago. He said, “I was never a teenager,” which is an extraordinarily revealing comment, actually.
Also slightly disturbing given his romantic history, but we can leave that alone.

I want to ask you about de Gaulle because you wrote a really astonishing biography of him. There are obviously a lot of differences, but there are a lot of similarities: rising above the established parties; coming to power as this figure above politics, in some way; staying for ten years in Macron’s case, eleven in de Gaulle’s case; student uprisings at the ten-year mark. So anyone can come up with the similarities. But what struck me especially from your book is that de Gaulle was also just a very strange figure who would try to make these, in the Macron phrase, Jupiterian decisions. De Gaulle could be almost dictatorial. He could be authoritarian. He would sometimes remove himself from politics in strange ways and make decisions that no one could understand. And it almost felt to me, after reading your book and watching Macron, that Macron was sort of self-consciously trying to do this, but it just didn’t work in his case.

I think you’re right. I think that is how he pitched himself. Each President has an official photograph of themselves, and Macron’s has him with de Gaulle’s war memoirs in the back. Macron came after the failed Presidency of François Hollande, who said he wanted to be a normal President. And in a way, the problem is the Fifth Republic doesn’t really quite allow normal Presidents, and you’ve got to somehow inhabit the role. He did want to reëstablish the idea that the President of the Fifth Republic needs to have a certain weight and so on. He talked about verticality and about being Jupiterian. That’s all Gaullist. And what I said about ignoring intermediary institutions, very Gaullist. But of course what he didn’t have is what nobody could have really, which is that de Gaulle could do this with all the history that went with being de Gaulle in 1958, when he came to power. Macron arrived with a history of being a palace special adviser and a Rothschild banker. De Gaulle could do this because he had all the weight of legitimacy that came from being de Gaulle. I don’t say that Macron’s a lightweight, but he simply couldn’t do that. He couldn’t be that.

I’m quite lucky you haven’t asked, but usually people ask me the question, What would de Gaulle do now? And I always say to them, it’s such a stupid question because he was a man of his own time, and what de Gaulle would think about #MeToo or A.I. or the environment, who knows? But the great thing about de Gaulle was his extraordinary pragmatism. He was very adaptable despite his strangeness. But with Macron, I think he was preparing himself to reinvigorate the institutions that de Gaulle created, but failed. ♦

items.title: The Unlikely Friendship Behind the Knicks’ Title Run
items.description: Running an NBA team had never been part of his plan, but now, not long after news broke that he’d be doing exactly that, Leon Rose was on the phone with a friend, outlining how he intended to save one of the most embattled franchises in sports. It was February
items.author: Yaron Weitzman
paragraphs: Running an NBA team had never been part of his plan, but now, not long after news broke that he’d be doing exactly that, Leon Rose was on the phone with a friend, outlining how he intended to save one of the most embattled franchises in sports. It was February 2020, and after 25 years as an NBA agent, he knew the snake pit he was walking into.

These, after all, were the New York Knicks. In the previous 20 years, they had endured three times as many losing seasons (15) as winning ones (five), dumped one franchise icon (Patrick Ewing) and fought with another (Charles Oakley), and regularly filled the tabloids with the kinds of scandals typically reserved for reality TV. Even Phil Jackson, just three years after being welcomed as a savior, had been run out of town a few years before. The Knicks were the first NBA riddle the legend was unable to solve.

All of which was why Rose was now telling Mike Dunlap, a longtime coach and one of his earliest clients, that he’d start with the simple stuff. He’d be patient with his roster. Build a relationship with team owner James Dolan. Come in asking questions and being ready to learn. And there was one more thing, Rose told Dunlap. Something he could bring to the table that no one before him could.

“He thought Wes would be really important,” Dunlap said. Wes was William Wesley, a fellow South Jersey native known in sports as “World Wide Wes.” “Maybe the greatest connector I’ve met in my 50 years in the business,” said David Falk, Michael Jordan’s longtime agent. Whether you were a veteran general manager trying to defuse tension between a coach and a star, a rookie needing career advice, or a shoe executive wondering whether a kid was worth an investment, Wes was likely one of your first calls.

Rose understood this better than most. Over the previous four decades, he and Wes had built one of basketball’s most successful and unlikely partnerships. Neither had played college ball at a high level, let alone in the NBA, but together they’d climbed to the top of the sport.
“They’re like Batman and Robin, except they’re always swapping those roles,” said Lynn Merritt, a longtime Nike executive.

That June, with the NBA paused due to COVID, the two sat outside Rose’s Jersey Shore home and mapped out their plan. “Family is how we’re building this thing,” Wes told a friend soon after. At times, that approach seemed destined to fail. The members of their family didn’t all get along. Some had to be traded or fired for the good of the group. Others were given chances, or contracts, they might not have deserved. Over the years, rival executives and agents — and even some employees within the organization — would joke that the true genius of Rose and Wes was that in Dolan they had suckered a billionaire into handing over his checkbook so they could line their friends’ pockets. Many of these insiders, along with NBA reporters (including, it should be said, the one writing this story), believed they were in over their heads.

Yet six years after their chats at the Shore, there were Rose and Wes standing side by side, tears streaming down their cheeks, watching the team they’d built celebrate the snapping of a 53-year-drought.

Jalen Brunson may have been the catalyst, and OG Anunoby’s game-four tip might be the moment fans remember most. But the true story behind the Knicks’ magical title run is one of two outsiders — a Black kid from Camden and a Jewish kid from Cherry Hill — coming together and conquering the sport. And it’s a story that doesn’t begin in a glamourous gym but in a run-down shoe store on a nondescript stretch of South Jersey road.

It was the late ’70s, and Leon Rose wanted a pair of Julius “Dr. J” Erving’s signature shoes. So he did what most athletes in the area did at the time: He went to The Pro’s Shoe — though most in the area referred to it as Pro Shoes — in Cherry Hill. Known for its rare models and hard-to-find large sizes, the store drew ball players of all levels and ages. The owner rang up customers on an old crank register and strolled around with an unlit cigar dangling from his mouth. The heart of the store, though, was an enterprising teenager who, at around age 13, had started walking over every day after school. Most customers didn’t know his full name. To them, he was simply Fresh Wes, the kid who always outfitted them with the perfect pair of kicks.

Quick-witted and sharp, Wes had the people skills of a professional twice his age. He was a worker too — sometimes, to fund the high-school parties he and his friends liked to throw, he’d borrow a truck and go searching for old washers and dryers around town to bring to a scrapyard.

Pro Shoes became Wes’s second home. He’d talk up anyone who walked in, no matter their religion or race — an ability he’d picked up in middle school, after his family moved a few miles east to Merchantville, where “he was the only Black kid in our class,” said Jeff Selverian, one of his closest childhood friends.

By the late ’70s, the store had become a local hot spot with Wes making new friends every day. Some, like Milt Wagner and Billy Thompson, were high-school basketball stars from Camden. Others were just regular kids who needed shoes. On this day, it was a point guard from Cherry Hill High School East.
Wes made his way over to the customer.

Rose’s first dream was to become a coach. This concerned his father. “I said, ‘What you should do is go to law school first,’” Zev Rose, a commercial-real-estate lawyer, recounted. They compromised: Leon became an assistant at his old high school while enrolled at Temple’s law school. After graduating in 1986, he became a Camden County prosecutor and moonlighted as an assistant coach at Division III Rutgers–Camden.

Wes, meanwhile, was carving out a path of his own. South Jersey had become a wellspring of athletic talent with future pros seemingly on every corner. College coaches flocked there; one of the first was Wade Houston, a Louisville assistant. “On my first trip to the gym, everyone told me that if I wanted to really learn about these kids, then I had to go see this guy at the shoe store by the mall,” Houston said. Wes was in the stockroom when he heard someone asking for William Wesley. His first instinct was to hide. “At least until he realized I wasn’t someone looking to hurt him,” Houston said. Houston was impressed by Wes’s eye for talent, but what he liked most was how much Wes seemed to care about the recruits: “He was almost like their protector.”

Little by little, Wes’s roots spread. He organized parties, worked doors, and by the end of the ’80s was managing Sixers big man Rick Mahorn’s Cherry Hill nightclub. By then he’d also gotten close with David Falk, whom he’d first called after Billy Thompson hired Falk as his agent in 1986. “I never met him, I didn’t know who he was, and he told me he was Billy’s cousin,” Falk recalled. “I learned later on that Wes is everybody’s cousin.” Falk had introduced Wes to his biggest client, Michael Jordan, back when Jordan was just a few years into his NBA career. The two hit it off, giving Wes the ultimate endorsement.

Rose wasn’t yet hanging with basketball royalty like his friend, but his career was moving forward. By then, he had left the prosecutor’s office for a firm where his father was partner. He also made partner and worked on cases like a class-action suit over a toxic substance in Guam. With his law career secure, he started edging back into sports.

Rose and Wes (neither of whom the Knicks made available for an on-the-record interview) had stayed close over the years. First, there were sporadic meetings at Pro Shoes, then more frequent run-ins during pickup games at gyms around Cherry Hill, something they’d do multiple times a week. Then Wes started calling Rose whenever he or a family member needed legal advice, even for mundane issues like parking tickets. Wes viewed Rose as a mentor, someone he could lean on for all sorts of advice. Rose saved Wes on a few occasions, too, like the time an agent offered to pay $500 for every player he referred. Thinking he had hit the jackpot, Wes was ecstatic and shared the news with Rose over a meal at Houlihan’s in the Cherry Hill Mall. Then Rose laid out the math: Even if the agent signed only one of those players to an NBA contract, he pointed out, Wes would still be getting robbed.
Wes realized two things that day: that he still had a lot to learn and that the man sitting across the table would always have his back.

As Rose took on more sports work, he found his niche. In a world of Jerry Maguire aspirants, he was the agent who drove around in a Nissan Altima, favored baggy sweats, and started every other sentence with “Yo.” More than that, he was the agent players could turn to after being burned. He signed two Temple alums whose previous agency the players union had charged with improperly withdrawing client funds. And his first client was another kid from Temple whose agent had dumped him after he went undrafted. His name was Rick Brunson.

Rose gave everything he could to Brunson. He would rebound for him in the morning and work the phones during the day. When Brunson (who declined an interview request) was playing in Australia, Rose regularly made the 22-hour flight to see him. When Brunson had trouble getting and keeping NBA contracts, Rose stuck with him. Rose’s son, Sam, and Brunson’s son, Jalen, were of similar ages and often played together.

Word of Rose got around the Philadelphia area. That he had Wes’s seal of approval — and was often seen hanging with Wes before Sixers games — only boosted his credibility. In spring of 2002, Sixers superstar Allen Iverson signed with Rose, in part because “he told us he’d take care of Allen as if he was his own son,” said Iverson’s longtime manager, Gary Moore. Iverson wasn’t just a basketball star; he was a cultural icon revered by NBA players — and the kids trying to become them. Rose was now a made man.

Around the same time, Dajuan Wagner, the son of Milt Wagner, became a high-school phenomenon at Camden High. When it was time to enter the NBA, there was no question whom he’d pick as his agent. The Cleveland Cavaliers drafted Wagner sixth overall in 2002. This proved fortuitous. LeBron James, then entering his senior year of high school, was spending a lot of time around the Cavs, and he grew close with Wes, who had rented an apartment in the area to be near Wagner. “He’s been a great role model to me,” James told GQ when asked about Wes in 2007.

LeBron had hired a different agent before entering the draft but made the switch after his second season. In about a decade, Rose had gone from working on a class-action lawsuit in Guam to managing the careers of two of the biggest stars in the world.

Rose and Wes had become about as powerful as anyone in the sport. Their circle included many of the NBA’s top players, as well as elite coaches like John Calipari, whom Wes had first met in the early ’80s, when Calipari was a young Kansas assistant on a recruiting trip to Camden. Calipari had since become one of college basketball’s most successful recruiters and coaches, turning Memphis and then Kentucky into pipelines to the pros. Rose and Wes were also tight with “the Seals” at Nike — the term the company’s top NBA decision-makers used for themselves — and well liked in Reebok’s boardroom too.

By this point, Wes had become a subject of intrigue. Flip on a random game at night and there was a solid shot you’d see him, whether he was sitting next to an owner courtside or — as was the case during the infamous 2004 Malice at the Palace brawl in Detroit — jumping into the middle of the floor to keep one player from swinging at another. Put on a Drake or Jay-Z song and you might hear his name shouted out. All of this added to the mystique. In 2005, NBA reporter Henry Abbott began a series about Wes’s influence, first on his widely read blog, then for ESPN. Two years later, GQ asked in a headline, “Is This the Most Powerful Man in Sports?”
