With fame came the whispers. That Wes’s relationships were the result of him lavishing kids — or, as he referred to them, his “nephews” — with Nike gifts. That Rose’s client roster was merely a product of his relationship with Wes, whom, these cynics believed, Rose must have been paying so he’d have a Black face recruiting players. How else could Wes be funding his jet-setting lifestyle? (Whenever asked about how he made a living, Wes said he was a mortgage broker for a firm in South Jersey.)

I spent months reporting this story and asked everyone I spoke to about these allegations. “All I can say is if that were the case, I think I would have heard something from someone at some point,” said Chrysa Chin, who spent 34 seasons in the NBA world, at the league office, the players’ union and Nike, and was so close to players that she became known as the “NBA Mom.” “Because in those situations, when you inject money or anything, at some point, a relationship with a player falls apart or gets ugly, and I’ve literally never even heard a player complain about either one of them.” Moore, Iverson’s manager, stressed that he was the one who asked Wes for an introduction to Rose, not the other way around.

Maybe, NBA insiders say, there were times when Rose benefited from having a Black friend like Wes. “But once you get past that initial introduction with people, that stuff doesn’t usually matter,” said a longtime union executive. And despite their relationship now entering its fifth decade, no one has ever gone public with an on-the-record complaint about how the two have done business.

Around 2006, Creative Artists Agency decided it needed a basketball division under its newly formed sports umbrella. Rose’s client list made him an obvious fit. “And from the first time we met Leon, we didn’t have a conversation with him without talking about his friend Wes,” said Howie Nuchow, who has been co-head of CAA Sports with Mike Levine since its inception. It took a bit, but in 2010, Wes came out of the shadows and joined Rose.

Early in his tenure at CAA, Wes approached his new bosses with a plea. “He’d tell us, ‘You gotta get to know Jim Dolan,’” Nuchow said. At the time, no one at CAA Sports had much of a relationship with the Madison Square Garden owner. The firm’s leadership didn’t know much about him beyond his reputation, which was, and remains, less than stellar. “But Wes kept on us, saying, ‘You guys gotta spend some time with him. He’s a good guy,’” Nuchow said.

Wes and Dolan (who declined an interview through a Knicks spokesperson) had met years earlier thanks to one of Wes’s original connections. In 1996, Wade Houston’s son, Allan, a six-foot-six guard with a sweet shooting stroke, signed as a free agent with the Knicks, becoming a star in New York and a pillar of the beloved turn-of-the-century teams. He also, according to people with close ties to the organization at the time, became a favorite of Dolan’s, who would soon be named chairman of MSG. That relationship brought Wes into Dolan’s orbit. Frank Isola, the Daily News’ longtime Knicks beat writer, remembers flying to Louisville in May 2001 for a golf event Houston was hosting and finding Wes outside the clubhouse, regaling Dolan and others with stories.

Now at CAA, Wes believed there was more business to be done. He started bringing Dolan to the company’s All-Star Weekend parties and connected him and Rose. In February 2011, Rose helped orchestrate a megatrade that landed his client Carmelo Anthony with the Knicks, who were coming off nine consecutive losing seasons.

Around the 2020 New Year, with the Knicks mired in their seventh straight losing season, Dolan decided it was time to make a change at the top of the organization. “And it’s hard for Jim to trust people who he doesn’t have some sort of personal or historical relationship with,” a longtime Garden insider said. Dolan called Rose to gauge his interest. Rose huddled with Levine, the CAA Sports co-head, at the agency’s midtown offices; met with Dolan at the Garden; then huddled with Levine again that night. Within two weeks, he told Dolan he was in. Wes told him he’d join him, and a few months later received the official title of executive vice-president and senior basketball adviser.

The calls from friends came in fast. Some were hired. Others — like Eddy Curry, the former Knicks center who thought he could get a job because his “uncle” and former agent were taking over — were told it wasn’t a fit. “Wes was like, ‘Nah, we gotta figure this thing out first,’” Curry said. “It showed me how seriously they were taking the job.” Later that summer, an acquaintance asked Wes whether he and Rose were worried about working for a boss as tempestuous as Dolan. “Don’t worry about that,” Wes responded. “We’ve got five-year deals.”
The person on the other end of the line asked if that would be enough.
“It’s going to be,” Wes said.
Two years into their new jobs, the pair was at a crossroads.

The Knicks had ended their playoff drought in Rose and Wes’s first season at the helm — largely thanks to the defense-first culture instituted by new head coach Tom Thibodeau, who had previously been a client of Rose’s — but took a step back in year two. They’d yet to nab a star, something that, after Rose and Wes were hired, many assumed would be imminent given their vast networks. Some colleagues in the building and executives outside of it felt that, at times, the job was getting the best of Rose. A number of his moves had backfired. Thibodeau was complaining about the front office’s pragmatic approach. Wes, according to reports at the time, was blaming the team’s struggles on Thibodeau. The train looked to be headed off the rails. The roster needed an injection of talent. It also needed someone who could lead the group into the future.
The time had come for Rose and Wes to push in all their chips.

Rose spent the offseason clearing salary-cap space. The Knicks then hired Rick Brunson as an assistant coach and signed his son, an undersized former second-round pick who’d never made an All-Star team to a $104 million four-year deal.
Upon hearing the news, many pundits were aghast.

“Jalen Brunson isn’t the answer!” Stephen A. Smith shouted on ESPN. Brian Windhorst, the network’s longtime reporter, was more clinical in his analysis. “It is not going to be the type of player that elevates them into contender status,” he declared.

But Rose and Wes believed there was more to the younger Brunson than he’d shown during his four years with the Dallas Mavericks. It would prove to be one of the best bets in NBA history. The following season, the Knicks won a playoff series for the first time in a decade. Brunson, it turned out, wasn’t just a star but a generational leader. Years after Rose stuck by Rick Brunson, karma had found its way back through his son.

“It could have been a complete disaster, and that would have been the end of it,” the MSG insider said. “But the bet on Jalen was the right one, and it changed everything. It gave Jim the confidence that there was something being built.”

With an alpha in place, Rose and Wes were free to do what they did best. Rose had traded for Josh Hart, a jack-of-all-trades role player and, perhaps more importantly, Brunson’s best friend. Later, he’d add Karl-Anthony Towns, an All-Star big man who, not coincidentally, was a former client of Rose’s, a Kentucky alum and one of Wes’s “nephews.” Wes did Wes things, whether that meant serving as a sounding board for Rose, connecting with Dolan, spearheading the organization’s alumni program, or taking a disgruntled player to dinner on the road.
“They created a family atmosphere,” one former Knicks assistant coach said.

But loyalty, they learned, had its limits. In December 2023, Rose pulled the trigger on a deal for OG Anunoby, a big, athletic wing perfectly suited to play alongside Brunson. Doing so, however, meant parting ways with Immanuel Quickley, a “nephew” of Wes’s who had played for Calipari at Kentucky.
“This is a fucked-up day for me,” an emotional Wes told a friend after the deal.

Rose’s test came in the summer of 2025. Thibodeau had just led the Knicks to their first conference finals in 25 years. His intensity, however, was grating on players and colleagues, and after the loss to the Pacers, many in the organization, Dolan among them, believed the team needed a new voice. Rose could see it, too. That June, he fired his longtime friend. Family still mattered. But it needed to fuel winning, not come at the expense of it.
“That was really hard on Leon,” said a person close to Rose. “He knew it would change the relationship.”

Rose replaced Thibodeau with Mike Brown, whom he and Wes grew close with in the mid-2000s, when Brown was coaching LeBron’s Cavaliers. But there were times during the 2025–26 season when it looked like that bet might not pay off. Towns clashed with Brown over his role in the offense and, according to people around the team, Anunoby often felt the same way.
Wes stepped in. He built a relationship with Anunoby. “That was huge for us,” said a Knicks source. “Because OG was the person who needed the most massaging.” Wes also stayed close to Towns.
“Uncle Wes, man, he’s everybody’s uncle,” Towns said recently. When asked what Wes does around the organization, Towns replied, “Think about an uncle, man — he does everything.”

Midway through the first round of the playoffs, the Knicks found their stride, clicking in a way few teams ever have. The group, assembled by Rose and Wes piece by piece over six years, became dominant and unflappable, setting records for comebacks and scoring margins. This was not the star-studded product most expected when the pair first arrived, either. This was something different, a web of individuals — all with various historical connections to Rose, Wes, and one another — coming together to form a whole greater than the sum of its parts.

It all coalesced in game four of the Finals. With nine minutes and 40 seconds left in the third quarter, the Knicks trailed by 29 points. Little by little, though, they hacked away at the deficit. With less than two seconds on the clock, Anunoby soared through the air to tip in Brunson’s miss, giving the Knicks the lead. Towns then deflected an inbounds pass to save the game. The final buzzer sounded. The Garden erupted.
Watching from his suite in the stands, Rose screamed and fell into Wes’s arms.

A week later, after another come-from-behind win in Game 5, this one sealing the series, a sea of fans clad in orange and blue — about 2 million in total — flooded downtown Manhattan to toast the Knicks’ magical run. Mike Breen, the team’s legendary announcer, stood at a lectern outside City Hall. Boxes holding keys to the city sat on a table nearby. In the months ahead, fights over contracts and bruised feelings over who in the organization deserved a championship ring would dampen the mood. But those were problems for the future. This was a day for celebrating.

“Ladies and gentlemen,” Breen declared to a plaza stuffed with fans, some of New York’s most famous faces among them, “your 2026 NBA champion New York Knicks!” The starting lineup’s usual introduction song blared out of the giant speakers stationed around the stage. The crowd, eager to welcome its heroes, roared.

But first out of the tunnel wasn’t the team’s star. It wasn’t the owner either. It was a former shoe salesman from Camden followed by the kid from Cherry Hill who, nearly 50 years earlier, had come into his store. The two longtime friends took their seats on the stage side by side.

items.title: 7 Ways Trump Lost His 2024 Coalition
items.description: Though the results could yet surprise us, it’s very likely the key story of the 2026 midterm elections will be the Republican Party’s loss of support from non-MAGA elements of the electorate who temporarily backed Donald Trump in 2024. To that extent it’s not
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: Though the results could yet surprise us, it’s very likely the key story of the 2026 midterm elections will be the Republican Party’s loss of support from non-MAGA elements of the electorate who temporarily backed Donald Trump in 2024. To that extent it’s not just a matter of the White House party predictably losing ground in a midterm, which happens far more often than not. It’s a tale of trends reversing themselves that robbed Trump and his cohort of what many thought might be a political realignment making the GOP the majority party for years. So it’s worth a closer look: How, exactly, did Trump alienate these onetime supporters? Here are some tentative answers.
Trump’s 2024 coalition was never as big as he claimed

The president has incessantly exaggerated his winning share of the electorate in 2024. On Election Night, he claimed an “unprecedented and powerful mandate.” Shortly after taking office, he told supporters he had “achieved the most epic political victory our country has ever seen” and “the biggest mandate in 129 years,” and one of his spokespeople boasted he had “decisively won every battleground state and became the first Republican to win the popular vote in 20 years,” lines he would repeat often on Truth Social. In fact, he narrowly won the popular vote by 1.5 percent, far short of the usual 10 percent threshold for a “landslide,” which was smaller than the margins of victory for Joe Biden in 2020, Barack Obama in 2012 and 2008, and George W. Bush in 2004 (and smaller, for that matter, than Hillary Clinton’s popular-vote margin over Trump in 2016). Winning all seven battlegrounds is no big accomplishment, either; these were very close states, which is why they were called battlegrounds. Suffice it to say that Trump’s victory was legitimate but no great shakes by any historical standard.
Some of Trump’s gains were circumstantial, not a realignment

What had some Republicans buzzing about a “realignment” were the gains Trump posted among Hispanic, Black, and under-30 voters. The size of these gains varied by sources, but probably the most reliable, Pew’s “verified voters” analysis, showed Trump gaining 12 percent among Hispanics compared to 2020 (and 20 percent compared to 2016); 7 percent among Black voters (and 9 percent since 2016); and 4 percent among under-30 voters (and 11 percent since 2016). Considering how aggressively reactionary Trump had been in the intervening years, these were indeed impressive numbers in those demographic groups and cause for concern among Democrats, who had arguably taken them for granted. But Trump has now squandered these gains by every measurement we have.
The high price of breaking cost-of-living promises

Hispanic, Black, and under-30 voters are on average more economically vulnerable than other Americans, and there’s not much question a big part of their pro-Trump trend in 2024 involved unhappiness with Joe Biden’s record on inflation and Trump’s promises to lower the cost of groceries, fuel, and housing. He was not able at all to keep those promises, which were not realistic to begin with. While this isn’t the only reason he’s lost ground with these voters, it is clearly important, and it’s hard to overstate the depth of his failure. According to the latest high-quality New York Times–Siena survey of likely voters, Trump’s job-approval numbers on “the cost of living” are 20 percent approval and 79 disapproval (with 65 percent strongly disapproving) among Hispanics, 3 percent approval and 91 percent disapproval (with 88 percent strongly disapproving) among Black voters, and 13 percent approval and 86 percent disapproval (with 73 percent strongly disapproving) among under-30 voters. There is no way to sugarcoat these numbers on the most important issue of the midterms.
Latinos are unhappy with mass deportation

It was reasonably clear that the Latino/Hispanic voters who trended Republican in 2024 supported Trump’s border-control policies (most still do) and believed his claims that he would deport only violent criminals. But again, Trump broke his promises. A March 2026 Equus survey of Latinos found that by “a wide 65-30 margin, Latinos believe Trump’s actions on immigration ‘are going too far, and instead of deporting criminals, he is targeting the types of hardworking immigrants who strengthen our nation.’” The same survey showed 72 percent of Latinos weren’t happy with ICE, “whether that means they support reforming ICE to prevent violence and ensure accountability (37%) or abolishing ICE because it is out of control and no training or accountability could reform it (35%).” The Times-Siena poll showed 60 percent of Hispanics “strongly disapproving” of Trump’s immigration policies overall.
Trump has offended Black voters as much as possible

If you are a Republican who wants to increase your party’s fragile beachhead with Black voters, here are some things you should probably avoid doing: (1) devoting all the civil-rights organs of the federal government to a fight against alleged discrimination against white people; (2) virtually criminalizing diversity efforts in federal or federally supported hiring; (3) successfully encouraging the U.S. Supreme Court to atomize the Voting Rights Act of 1965; (4) successfully encouraging southern state legislatures to dismantle congressional and state legislative districts that elected Black people to office; and (5) making white Afrikaners from the former apartheid state of South Africa the one remaining recognized beneficiary of refugee status. That the Trump administration has done all these things helps explain why in the Times-Siena survey only 7 percent of Black voters gave the president a positive job-approval rating while 78 percent strongly disapprove.

Aside from being very sensitive to living costs, young voters are famously disinclined to support wars of choice (i.e., those that aren’t a matter of national self-defense), perhaps because they are often of the same generation as those who are dying or risking their lives in such wars. Trump’s war of choice against Iran is generally unpopular; according to the Times-Siena survey, 33 percent of likely voters support the war while 66 percent disapprove (57 percent disapprove strongly). Young voters really hate it, with only 9 percent supporting it (and just one percent supporting it strongly) and 86 percent disapproving of it (75 percent strongly). No wonder 79 percent of under-30 voters disapprove of Trump’s overall job performance (71 percent strongly).
Trump is now only focused on his base, because it’s all he has left

No wonder the president is traveling from red state to red state to rally his most loyal MAGA supporters to show up at the polls and mitigate his party’s losses. He has deliberately chosen to alienate everyone else, including voting groups that were open to changing sides. At this rate, Trump will leave the GOP in worse shape than he found it.

items.title: Kara Swisher Says Elon Musk’s Jail Threat Is ‘Toddler Behavior’
items.description: Elon Musk is having quite a month. In addition to being the subject of a “terrifying” new documentary, debuting a new flying car that may not actually be a flying car, and announcing that he is considering a megamerger of Tesla and SpaceX into a rocket-ship/ca
items.author: Intelligencer Staff
paragraphs: Elon Musk is having quite a month. In addition to being the subject of a “terrifying” new documentary, debuting a new flying car that may not actually be a flying car, and announcing that he is considering a megamerger of Tesla and SpaceX into a rocket-ship/car/robot/social-media/payments/satellite-internet/AI/data-center behemoth, he’s once again become a main character in multiple simultaneous scandals. Musk reportedly made the decision to abruptly throttle Ukraine’s access to SpaceX Starshield, severely limiting the country’s combat operations and ability to defend itself against Russia. That has become a full-blown international incident, prompting so much backlash that Musk and President Trump are each blaming the other for the move. In addition, the world’s richest man (Musk) has publicly attacked India’s richest man (Mukesh Ambani), alleging that the latter is blocking Starlink’s growth in the country. And Musk has now sunk more than $445 million into backing Republican candidates ahead of what may be a disastrous midterm election. Per usual, Musk is lashing out and tweeting through the turmoil. That includes attacking journalist and longtime Musk critic Kara Swisher, threatening her with jail time after she pointed out that he will likely face a reckoning when Democrats are back in power. Here’s her response in the latest episode of Pivot with co-host Scott Galloway.

Kara Swisher: Guess what? Elon Musk is pissed at me again. I said on the Bulwark podcast that Elon might need to be worried if the GOP loses the House and the Senate, and he tweeted, “Live by the sword, die by the sword. It sounds like Kara Swisher really wants to go to prison.” I really don’t.
Scott Galloway: Does this stuff bother you, or do you enjoy the attention?

Swisher: No, none of it. I think it’s toddler behavior. It’s kind of ridiculous. He threatened Congress, I think, too. And oddly enough, you were meaner to him this week on our clip. And of course he comes after me.

Galloway: Yeah, but I’m not important enough. It’s like when Trump goes after Jess Tarlov or Musk goes after you; I’m still waiting for my global important person to come after me. How come you and Jess get all the hate?

Swisher: I don’t know. Jessica’s the same way, and Kaitlan Collins. What happened was I gave an interview to Catherine Rampell at the Rampart and I talked to congresspeople and heard they were coming after Elon and it’s called reporting. And I said, in a Kamala Harris administration, all those investigations, there were several criminal things attached to them. So he could have gone to prison, but he got rid of them. I was making a point that he got rid of all the investigations either through his relationship with Trump or through DOGE. And now they’re going to come back. And I said, “And you’re going to see a lot of congressional people saying so.” And they did. The next day, all of them went on the record, not just Elizabeth Warren, but even a Republican was saying, “We need to investigate this Ukraine thing.”

And so I was just pointing out the dead fucking obvious of what’s going to happen if — she was asking me why he was throwing so much money at the midterms. I think it’s $400 million at this point. And I said it’s not because he believes in Trump; he believes in himself and he’s trying to save his own skin. Anyway, he for some reason lost his mind. And by the way, this is something Elon said to Tucker Carlson and his mother said “Don’t joke about it” recently. So it’s not something that he said the word “prison,” but then he just said this thing, “live by the sword, die by the sword.”

I don’t know who he’s talking about, and that I want to go to prison, which is like — I don’t mind being in a prison movie and acting in it. And if the ladies from Hunting Wives were in there, I probably wouldn’t mind prison, but I don’t know. Jess wrote me too. And I was on Kaitlan’s show last night and all of us just get relentless hate by all these really troubled men. And in the case of Jess and Kaitlan, it’s Trump. In the case of me, it’s Elon.

Galloway: Yeah. You get to say what you want. He gets to say what he wants. The difference is when you’re the president of the United States or the wealthiest man in the world and you have this cultlike following, I think you need to be a little bit more mindful of the potential knock-on effects of if you have a couple hundred million people that follow you religiously and have bought into yourself, proclaimed views of yourself as a Jesus-like figure, you have to recognize that there’s a nonzero probability that saying something like that about someone else might result in physical harm to them or their family.

And so you’d like to think that these individuals are a little bit more measured and realize that as you get more powerful, you are going to be subject to more attacks, some fair, some unfair. And I’m not saying your or Jess’s attacks against Musk or the president have been unfair. I don’t think they have been. This is the world we live in now where individuals say an autocrat thinks the following. If I go after these people and exert my power, I will silence my critics. And if you want to see a chorus, he’s about to find out what a real Kara Swisher criticism is on November 4 if the Democrats take the House and the Senate.

The fact that this individual is making geopolitical decisions around the fate of the West on a whim, and he’s blaming the president, the president’s blaming him, you don’t think every — right now, no [Republicans in Congress] want to raise their head above the parapet and piss him off because he might dump $200 million into their competitor’s campaign. On November 4, you are going to see the mother of all subpoenas and requests for him to come testify before Congress.

Swisher: They’ve already said it. They’ve already said save your communications about this Ukraine thing. I think it was a final straw for a lot of people, although it shouldn’t have been the final straw. I mean, DOGE should have been the final straw.

And he’s done this before. He said my heart was seething with hate or filled with hate. I got a few really strange phone calls. I wouldn’t call them death threats. They were not nice. They were not nice. And of course over on Twitter, all the VC stans of his are just losing their minds because they’re just suck-ups and acolytes in a way that’s really unattractive. And it’s just nuts. If you can’t stand the heat, Elon, get the fuck out of the kitchen. I don’t know what else to say.
This transcript has been edited for length and clarity.

items.title: Trump ‘Just Kidding’ About Renaming Oceans, Maybe Not About New Mexico
items.description: It’s been two months since Donald Trump changed the name of a landmark, institution, or geographic feature, and he’s clearly itching to rebrand something. Earlier this week, the president renewed his call for New Mexico to “immediately change its name to New A
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: It’s been two months since Donald Trump changed the name of a landmark, institution, or geographic feature, and he’s clearly itching to rebrand something. Earlier this week, the president renewed his call for New Mexico to “immediately change its name to New America” in a post on Truth Social:

As we learned when Trump first raised the idea in early September, this isn’t actually going to happen. The president has the power to direct federal agencies to use names like the “Gulf of America” and “Lake America.” And he successfully bullied tech executives into making those changes in their map apps, too. But he can’t simply inform a state that it now has an entirely different name. As the New York Times noted, he has no legal authority to do so, and in this case the state constitution says, “The name of this state is New Mexico,” before laying out its boundaries.

At a Wednesday-night rally in South Carolina, Trump suggested he’d moved on and was looking for other things to rename. He revealed he’d called up Sundar Pichai and floated the idea of renaming the Atlantic Ocean, but the Google CEO talked him out of it.
“I only like two oceans: the Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean,” the president said. “I’m not gonna put either ‘Trump’ or ‘America’ on any other ocean but these two.”

Trump continued, “So we seriously looked at the Atlantic Ocean. And I called Google Maps, who are really great with the lake. And I spoke to a brilliant guy, Sundar, he heads all of Google … You know they’re still rattled from the gulf. And I said, ‘Sundar, I’m thinking of the Atlantic Ocean. Could you handle it?’”
He said Pichai answered, “No, no, this time, I’m not doing it. Oceans are different, sir. They cover really a lot of countries. Please don’t ask us to do that.”
So, Trump concluded, he’d “probably pass” on renaming the Atlantic. But then he added, “Pacific Ocean, we’re gonna call it the American Ocean,” before weaving away to other topics.

Trump made a quip about renaming the Atlantic or Pacific back in August. It’s always hard to tell if he’s serious about his idiotic renaming proposals or just trolling. But it seemed like the latter after Trump told the Pichai anecdote again at a rally in Iowa on Thursday night.

“I called up Sundar. I got the lake, and I got the gulf. I said, ‘Sundar’ — I was only kidding — ‘I’ve have a new one,’” Trump recalled. “I actually sent him a picture of the Atlantic Ocean called the ‘American Ocean,’ and he actually called me and said, ‘Sir, this has to stop.’ I was just kidding. That would be a tough one. But you never know in life, do you, in favor of transgender mutilazation, that’s these people that you’re thinking about maybe voting for.”
Okay, so not the clearest presidential oratory ever. But Trump did say twice that he was just “kidding” about renaming oceans.

But then later in his remarks on Thursday, he casually used his new name for New Mexico. “If you were on the Texas border, if you were in Arizona or if you were in New America,” he said, pausing for applause.

So was this another joke, or is Trump just going to start referring to New Mexico by a new name to see if it sticks? Who knows. But while discussing the renaming of Lake Ontario earlier this week, Trump did confirm one reason why he’s so determined to continue his stupid renaming spree.
“I did it very lightly and the damn thing got changed! That’s power, right? When you sort of do it half-heartedly and it gets changed!” Trump said. “So that’s very, very nice.”

- Trump Helps Out by Dropping Antisemitic Slur at Kansas Rally

items.title: Iowa’s GOP Candidate for Governor Might Not Live in Iowa
items.description: The term carpetbagger was originally applied to Northerners who moved South after the Civil War to launch political careers under the protection of military Reconstruction; it referred to the hastily procured bags manufactured from carpet scraps the transplant
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: The term carpetbagger was originally applied to Northerners who moved South after the Civil War to launch political careers under the protection of military Reconstruction; it referred to the hastily procured bags manufactured from carpet scraps the transplants allegedly used. More recently, the term has been applied to politicians who conveniently relocate themselves into the vicinity of political opportunities. New York has often been a magnet for alleged carpetbaggers. In the 1960s alone, two former U.S. attorneys general, Robert F. Kennedy and Ramsey Clark, moved to the Empire State and ran for the Senate (the former successfully, the latter not so much), and a generation later, so did former Arkansas First Lady Hillary Clinton (like RFK, she won).

So in itself, the decision by conservative ex-lobbyist and businessman Zach Lahn to move from Kansas to Iowa in 2024 and then run for governor — winning the 2026 GOP primary in a big upset — isn’t so remarkable. Indeed, Lahn was born and grew up in Iowa, where his family had lived for generations, and owned property there.

What has made his case interesting — and for supporters of his Democratic opponent, Rob Sand, hilarious — is his difficulty making a clean break with it. He seems very involved in Kansas matters. He remains president of the board of an unaccredited Wichita private school he co-founded with his wife, albeit when they were both married to other people (in her case to a scion of the Kansas Koch family empire, with whom she financed the Wonder School, as they called it). And the children from the blended families he and his wife left in Kansas have given Lahn a reason to fly his private plane back to Wichita a lot — at least 37 times since he began running for governor, according to the Des Moines Register. But that isn’t the only evidence that Lahn has Kansas on his mind. Last month, the Daily Beast reported that a Strava fitness-app user with the name “Zach Lahn” recorded four long bike rides starting at Lahn’s Wichita estate over three months in early 2025, long after his supposed relocation to Iowa.

Perhaps more eyebrow-raising have been his public musings over the amount of time he’ll need to spend away from Iowa’s capital if he does become the governor of the Hawkeye State. “We’ve already had discussions about this and how that would work,” he told the Register in May. “But if I’m elected governor, it would be a different arrangement, and we’d work it out. Because, you know, we’d be in Iowa as much as humanly possible.”

That has to be comforting, but it certainly hasn’t quelled questions about Lahn’s state loyalties, considering his campaign’s Trump-modeled message is “Iowa First.” Or at least since October 17, 2024, which was when he transferred his voter registration to the state. You’re required to have Iowa residency for at least two years to run for governor there, so he got in just under the wire.
Unsurprisingly, Lahn’s shaky status as an Iowan has been bread and meat for Sand’s campaign, which has offered him Iowa travel tips:
And even more cleverly, Sand’s backers got Kansas’s Democratic governor Laura Kelly in on the action:

When Lahn first decided to run, his “outsider” status might have seemed like a positive credential. The current two-term Republican governor of Iowa, Kim Reynolds, is deeply unpopular (for many months, she’s reigned as “America’s most unpopular governor” according to polling from Morning Consult). So while he was campaigning in the primary against Iowa GOP Establishment candidate Randy Feenstra, Lahn made a logical choice by separating himself from the usual suspects in Des Moines and Washington. But Wichita is a little too “outside” Iowa for comfort. And in explaining the details of his family situation, Lahn has also drawn attention to his not entirely orthodox relationship with the insanely rich and controversial Koch family (for whom he worked as an Americans for Prosperity operative before marrying Chase Koch’s ex-wife). He’s not just any old dad with custody issues.

Other than the poor management of his residential status, Lahn was unlucky to have made his move back to Iowa for what is turning out to be a strong Democratic year in a state that turned deep red in 2014 and has remained so ever since. Democrats have even odds of winning the Senate seat being vacated by Joni Ernst and could flip three of Iowa’s four U.S. House seats as well. In Sand, the sole member of his party in statewide office, Democrats have a solidly established centrist candidate who is difficult for the GOP to label as a “radical” or “socialist” (though it has tried). Lahn has sought to adopt a populist stance by criticizing both major party establishments and has a MAHA strain in his ideology that has enabled him to attack polluters with whom Republicans often snuggle. The two candidates are more or less evenly matched financially.

In part because of a vast advantage in name ID, Sand has led Lahn in public polling from the get-go. In the Silver Bulletin polling averages, Sand leads by a robust 7.3 percent, though the most recent polls show the race tightening a bit. As in other midwestern states, Democrats are nervous about possible polling errors (Iowa is, after all, where the legendary pollster Ann Selzer infamously showed Kamala Harris leading Trump in 2024). The Trump administration, meanwhile, is working overtime to deliver tasty treats (e.g., fuel assistance to hard-pressed farmers and a new federally assisted steel mill) to Iowa voters.

If Sand nonetheless prevails, Republicans will naturally wonder if a more Iowa-centric candidate like Feenstra might have won. And Lahn may wonder whether he picked the wrong “home state” for his gubernatorial dreams.

items.title: Our ‘Design Directory’ 2026: The architects, studios and designers to know around the world
items.description: As the stories in our Design Directory have demonstrated, the global design industry is thriving. Here we have compiled an international directory of the firms, studios and individuals at the top of their game, drawing on the crafts and vernaculars of the coun
items.author: Kate Lucey
paragraphs: As the stories in our Design Directory have demonstrated, the global design industry is thriving. Here we have compiled an international directory of the firms, studios and individuals at the top of their game, drawing on the crafts and vernaculars of the countries where they work to produce objects and buildings that enhance our lives.

Europe’s architectural and design landscape has a rich history, from ancient castles and cathedrals to modernist masterpieces. Contemporary designers are using this as a foundation for cutting-edge adaptive reuse and the establishment of circular economies, setting global industry standards.
The country’s contemporary designers build on a foundation of secessionist art and early modernist rigour.

items.title: What would you bring to the afterlife? Sometimes the strangest things form the most moving picture
items.description: On Tuesday I walked over to Soho to see a preview screening of Spanish-language film La Bola Negra, directed by “Los Javis” (Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo). It’s a story set during the Spanish Civil War and the present day. It’s about love and desire. It’s
items.author: Andrew Tuck; Kate Lucey
paragraphs: On Tuesday I walked over to Soho to see a preview screening of Spanish-language film La Bola Negra, directed by “Los Javis” (Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo). It’s a story set during the Spanish Civil War and the present day. It’s about love and desire. It’s about secrets and telling the truth. It’s about being gay. The film could be an Oscar contender for Best Picture: a campaign that will be aided by the shimmering, mesmerising presence of Penélope Cruz and a poised performance from Glenn Close.

Now, press screenings are not the most intimate of settings. The room is usually packed with seen-it-all critics who make their living from finding fault, taking things apart, spending the duration of the film scribbling big thoughts in little notepads. But in this velvet-chaired cocoon, I found myself lost in this epic, weaving and sometimes fantastical tale. The directors deliberately take their time to stitch all the narratives together (at one point I wondered if I should ask my jotting-away neighbour if he knew what the hell was happening). But even this pacing keeps you transfixed.

Towards the end of the film – when all is finally clear – there’s a fleeting moment when a young man stoops to kiss the head of his boyfriend. It’s just an “I’m here for you” kiss but I felt a tear jog down my face, and then another. I brushed them away. Why was I crying? For them, for me, for us? I need to see the film again because there’s something buried there. A little bit of me? A little bit of you too?

There’s something that I forgot to tell you about my brother-in-law’s funeral. Phil had been partial to a Starbucks, so his granddaughter arrived at the funeral service carrying a venti latte. She placed this next to the coffin. I was desperate to see if, for once, a Starbucks employee had managed to spell a name correctly but I was too far away.

Anyway, this last order for Phil sat there throughout the entire service. It was even there as the curtains closed and the coffin was dispatched to the flames. I have mentioned this Starbucks detail to a few people and it seems that, just as the ancient Egyptians entombed their dear departed pharaohs with all sorts of crap for the afterlife – mummified cats, cooking utensils, electric barbecues – modern grievers are keeping the tradition alive. I have been told of a Sunday roast being brought to a church and numerous pints of beer (even, in one case, to the funeral of a gentleman who had died an alcoholic).

Just so you know, I think that I will be happy to go to the next world free of pizza or pies – even if, finally, the carbs don’t matter. Though if you order one final cheeky margarita, I might be up for that.

On Monday, London will discover that a 1km stretch of the famous retail strip Oxford Street has been pedestrianised overnight. I wrote about this news for the Monocle Minute yesterday. I am sure that the project will be a success but I grew up in a new, postwar town with a fully pedestrianised centre and it was rubbish. It would have been so much nicer with cars. To keep the retail streets pedestrian only, the town was ringed by ugly multi-storey car parks. And, at night, once the shops had closed, it was desolate. People preferred to drive to pubs and restaurants in nearby villages. Over the years the town centre became edgy at night; the walkways stank of wee. Meanwhile, neighbouring towns with traffic, movement and activity thrived.
The plans for Oxford Street seem full of potential. But just getting rid of cars is not enough. I will watch and wait a while before getting too giddy about this change.

items.title: The best new homewares, books and accessories for design lovers
items.description: Vite Espresso Coffee Maker
items.author: Nic Monisse; Kate Lucey
paragraphs: Vite Espresso Coffee Maker
Alessi is expanding its celebrated kitchen range with this screw-themed moka pot, which takes inspiration from machinery in the company’s factory.

London-based designer Philippe Malouin worked with Italian brand Alessi to create this take on the stovetop moka pot. The piece draws inspiration from the threads of screws, with its spiral ridges and grooves referencing the twisting motion used to assemble the pot – making aesthetics part of the pot’s intuitive use. Its lower chamber is made from die-cast aluminium and its upper section features a heat-resistant thermoplastic-resin handle. Its colours are taken from the surfaces of machinery inside the Alessi factory. Adding to its appeal is the fact that it features a magnetic steel base that works on induction, gas and electric stoves.
Rediscover the joy of traditional film photography with this revamped camera design.

Kodak has provided an upgrade to the traditional plastic disposable camera with its new 35mm film model, the Snapic A1. It features a sharp three-element glass lens for crisp images, a two-zone focus (which allows you to switch quickly between close-up portraits and wide landscape shots) and a built-in flash. It also has a wide focal length that keeps scenes sharp: perfect for everything from travel and street photography to casual indoor shoots. The main appeal, though, is in its simplicity.
Free from distractions such as digital screens or phone apps, the Snapic A1’s pared-back design keeps its user in the moment and on the task.
Fiio CP13 Portable Cassette Player
Chinese brand Fiio plugs into the trend for retro audio players with this superior throwback.

Though China has long been disparaged as the home of cheaply made electronics, its new domestic makers are proving that the country has the manufacturing chops for quality audio. Analogue tapes are enjoying a resurgence in popularity (fans point to the allure of being able to “own” music) and Guangzhou-based Fiio’s CP13 Portable Cassette Player has found its way into New York’s Museum of Modern Art shop. It features old-school physical buttons, while its modern touches include USB-C charging and a 13-hour battery life.
The CP13’s 13 hours of continuous playback marks a significant improvement on the classic Sony Walkman.
Hay Outdoor Market Fire Pit
Light up your garden party or campsite with this versatile portable fireplace and cooker.

Designed in collaboration with Jasper Morrison, this fire pit brings to life the London-based product designer’s “super normal” ethos – an approach that aims to make everyday objects feel essential. Made by Danish brand Hay, its stainless-steel construction is portable, making it equally at home on a terrace or a trail. More than just an outdoor fireplace, it doubles as a cooker, thanks to its removable grill and charcoal basket.
There’s something about a fire pit that lights up our brains. Humans have evolved to associate flames with warmth, nourishment, safety and connection.
Looking for guides to visionary contemporary architects and era-defining design movements? Here’s our pick of five books to add to your shelf.
Published by oro Editions, Chairman is a new monograph documenting chair designs by London-based Yinka Ilori.
Oríkì: Material Affirmations in Three Acts from Apartamento Publishing is the debut work of Nigerian designer Nifemi Marcus-Bello, telling the story of a three-part sculptural series.

The Albanian Files: Freedom and Architecture, published by Lars Müller, chronicles two decades of urban change in the Balkan country. Tadao Ando has released Towards Light, which outlines his philosophies on life and architecture.
Riverside Modern explores the homes of Melbourne’s Studley Park, with photography by Jack Lovel.

The challenge for any specialist design publisher is to blend the academic with the entertaining. A good architectural book should translate complex information into inspiring, visually engaging content that also pushes readers to build better.

items.description: Kinfolk’s Sixty First Issue examines play as a way to move through adulthood with greater joy, curiosity and wonder. “We don’t ever lose the desire to play; we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways,” Mia Sundstrom, who leads the National Institute
paragraphs: Kinfolk’s Sixty First Issue examines play as a way to move through adulthood with greater joy, curiosity and wonder. “We don’t ever lose the desire to play; we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways,” Mia Sundstrom, who leads the National Institute for Play, explains to us on page 154. Throughout the issue, we explore pathways to play, including expert advice on rediscovering your own play type as a busy adult and, failing that, five games devised and demonstrated by artist Carsten Höller for those who don’t know where to begin.

In a study of architects, psychologist Donald MacKinnon found that those considered most creative by their peers were often those who knew how to play; this is certainly true of John Outram, whose over-the-top masterpiece, Sphinx Hill, we visit on page 70. Painters play with color and line—a type of immersive flow state our fashion editorial explores on page 60. And musicians improvise and experiment, a process familiar to the band Balming Tiger (interviewed on page 78), whose alternative approach to K-pop subverts the genre’s perfectly synchronized image.

items.title: Balming Tiger - Kinfolk
items.description: An hour with the alternative K-pop group.
paragraphs: An hour with the alternative K-pop group.
- Hair & Makeup Mahito Ohtani

My Zoom interview with Balming Tiger is chaotic. Five of the eleven members are on the call, each in a different location in Seoul. Omega Sapien is at a salon, dyeing his hair green for a music video. Leesuho is munching on a snack with a soda. Unsinkable is strumming a guitar, on mute. bj wnjn is lying in bed in sweatpants. Mudd the Student sits calmly, his long wavy hair dyed like a lion’s mane. There are multiple conversations all happening at once as we wait for the other members, some of whom never show up.

When the interview starts, however, the group is focused and attentive. A self-described “alternative K-pop group” from South Korea, Balming Tiger is composed of two women and nine men. They’ve been described by critics and fans as pioneering, experimental, an artist collective beyond music and, last but not least, “a group of hairstyles that elderly Koreans would definitely hate,” a running joke among fans online. In their two studio albums and a debut mixtape, released in 2018, they sing about alienation, absurdist humor, friendship and love, pigeons and frogs.
“We want Balming Tiger to be its own genre,” says Omega Sapien, a rapper and singer-songwriter, holding up the phone as his hair, now fluorescent green, is being rinsed out in the sink.

Ironically, Balming Tiger’s alternative identity depends on its proximity to South Korea’s best-known cultural export. K-pop, literally Korean popular music, is itself less of a distinctive genre than a cultural phenomenon. Within South Korea, it can refer to a wide variety of styles including ballads, EDM and hip-hop. Abroad, K-pop most often means idols: entertainers whose music and image are strictly produced by massive entertainment conglomerates, such as mega-groups like BTS and Blackpink, or soloists such as Somi and G-Dragon. However you define it, K-pop is a glittering symbol of Korean soft power. The stratospheric success of different Korean musicians in the past decade—especially BTS on the US charts—has catapulted K-pop into a household name everywhere.
“Honestly, we don’t really think about what genre we are, other than during interviews,” says Leesuho, one of Balming Tiger’s producers and video directors.

True as that may be, the label they have chosen—alternative K-pop—is a strategic choice, devised by the group’s founder and creative director, San Yawn. With K-pop’s international popularity, Balming Tiger has smartly positioned themselves as adjacent to something familiar to the global audience—giving themselves a wide playground to try anything and everything.

“It’s always more fun when the possibilities are open,” San Yawn later explains over email. “Whatever we are now won’t be ‘the final version’ of us. We have no idea what we’ll be in the future, but we want to continue to express the little joys of the world in our own language.”

It’s true that the structure of Balming Tiger is wildly different from a conventional K-pop idol act. Idols are usually conceptually defined by an agency, with clear roles differentiating members, for example “lead vocalist” or “lead dancer.” Idol wannabes train, sometimes for years, to audition for a role. Once the group is formed, the performers are the faces of a much larger and more intricate corporate structure.

There were no trainees in Balming Tiger. And no auditions—think more “Wanna join?” conversations at waffle houses and barbecue joints. Nor are all of Balming Tiger’s members performers—their 11 members include producers, photographers, music video directors, A&R managers and DJs. Some faces are more familiar, like those who sing, rap and dance in the music videos (usually Omega Sapien, bj wnjn, Mudd the Student and Sogumm, with cameos by others), but behind the scenes, everything is more collaborative and collective.

Balming Tiger can be seen as less a band with a signature sound than a creative universe, a rainforest of different species colliding and coexisting with each other. From their critically acclaimed debut mixtape, Homie304, to their first studio album in 2023, January Never Dies, to the 2026 album, Gongbu, Balming Tiger’s music defies classification—as does their creative direction. Their videos embrace Hong Kong noir (“SOS”), a ’90s boy band parody (“Big Butt”), and the industrial-era alleyways of the Euljiro neighborhood in Seoul (“Sexy Nukim,” featuring BTS member RM). Their sounds traverse old Korean pop, EDM, psychedelic rock and—of course—hip-hop, many of the members’ first love and forays into music.
“We have our own thing: We’re Balming Tiger, young people living in South Korea, exploring our identities. Doing this is what’s Korean, what’s true to ourselves.”

The origins of Balming Tiger can be traced to Itaewon, one of the most culturally diverse neighborhoods in Seoul. It’s a place where the city’s only mosque towers over a hill, next to mom-and-pop stores and cockroach-filled villas, the US military base and ritzy alleyways that are home to the Samsung family and BTS members.

“Balming Tiger is basically a meeting of people that are full of holes,” San Yawn once said on the Korean talk show Moneygraphy. These “holes”—loneliness, for instance, and the desire to fill them through music and art—were what brought together this cacophonous collective through a random series of events starting in 2017, when San Yawn began looking for a crew.

They met at San Yawn’s home in Itaewon and spent much of their time together at Trans 201, on the second floor of a run-down villa in an area popularly known as Transgender Hill. The members started connecting in various ways: through friends of friends, an Instagram message, a chance listening to a future member’s SoundCloud account. “Trans 201 was Omega Sapien and bj wnjn’s house,” recalls Mudd the Student. “The space was very damp and full of dark energy.”

“After a heavy rain, the ceiling in my room was bulging with water, like a giant pimple,” Omega Sapien adds. “We had horrible mold problems. bj wnjn and I split the rent, which was like 600,000 won [approximately $400], and I didn’t even have that money, so my older sister helped pay half of my 300,000. It really was an awful time.”

“Not for me,” says bj wnjn, a vocalist, singer-songwriter and producer. “That space is one of the most memorable moments of my youth. Even with the cockroaches and all that noise from the clubs outside, there was a joy particular to that time.”

Memories like this are specific to Balming Tiger, to Seoul, and permeate their art in ways that can’t be manufactured. The evolving members remain consistently curious about their own experiences and the world around them. There have been some member changes over the years, including the exit of Byung Un, a beloved front man in the early years. But the joy—and the DNA—from that early, formative period is still alive, holding everyone together 10 years later. “There’s a childlike attitude that we never lost as a group,” Sogumm, a singer-songwriter and vocalist, says in an email. “A simplicity that feels honest.”

Often, Balming Tiger’s childlike experiments feel much deeper than mere fun and play, resonating like a sharp resistance against the norms imposed by others. Sometimes this critique feels particularly Korean—like in the 2023 music video of “Kamehameha,” where exhausted office workers are forced to drink with their superiors at a hoesik, an after-work company gathering notorious for heavy alcohol consumption. And at other times it feels fantastically delocalized, like in “UP!” where a cashier at a mega supermarket climbs up the mountain of objects he must clear, reaching for the sky.

“It’s different for me,” says Omega Sapien, who grew up in Korea, China, Japan and the US. “I’m not trying to be rebellious. But I do like provoking a sense of discomfort in others. I like creating differences of opinion through what we do.”

“I’m less interested in making others uncomfortable than in creating a sense of wonder,” says Mudd the Student, who is from Busan, down south. “I love art that makes me feel things for the first time. I suppose that can sometimes make people uncomfortable.”

Despite their almost tongue-in-cheek label as alternative K-pop, Balming Tiger is grateful to the K-pop industry for opening doors for other Korean musicians. The group has performed at major music festivals including SXSW in the US, Primavera Sound in Spain and Fuji Rock Festival in Japan. Their creative orbit is similarly wide-ranging: they’ve collaborated with artists including Japanese girl group ATARASHII GAKKO! and RM of BTS, while independently creating content celebrating figures they admire, such as Korean artist Lee Bul and Thai filmmaker Apichatpong Weerasethakul. Their music video with RM, “Sexy Nukim,” remains Balming Tiger’s most viewed, with 20 million views.

“People often think of idols as these puppets, who only do what they’re told,” says Omega Sapien. “But creative languages within the idol industry are changing too. I really love groups like CORTIS. I think their work is raw and fantastic.”

“I’m really interested in girl groups,” says Unsinkable, a producer and DJ. “These days we see groups that are more like crews, with more creative independence from their company. I sometimes wonder if new idol acts are inspired by what we do.”

In Gongbu, Balming Tiger explores themes of Korean and Asian identity. The single “Home” is absurdist and nostalgic, evoking Korean folk music while mixing synthesizers, rap and ritualistic chants. The music video is black and white, reminiscent of a Park Chan-wook film or a Lee Gap-chul photo. It’s inspired by the architecture of Kim Chung-up and the traditional marriage ritual hamjinabi.

“What does it mean to be Korean? To be Asian? When we were younger, we looked up to American hip-hop,” says Omega Sapien. “I wanted to be like J. Cole. But now I see that that’s his thing. We have our own thing: We’re Balming Tiger, young people living in South Korea, exploring our identities. Doing this is what’s Korean, what’s true to ourselves.”

items.title: Taking Play Seriously - Kinfolk
items.description: - Words Ellen Peirson-Hagger
paragraphs: - Words Ellen Peirson-Hagger
A conversation with the National Institute for Play.

In 1966, psychiatrist Dr. Stuart Brown was appointed by the governor of Texas to investigate a mass shooting at the state university—at the time the deadliest in American history. Brown realized there could be a connection between the gunman’s actions and his oppressive childhood, which had been dominated by his controlling father. He would go on to spend the following decades showing that the need for play is biologically hardwired into the brain stem—the part of the nervous system that governs our essential functions like breathing and heart rate.

“When we’re deprived of play, it can be similar to being deprived of sleep and nutrition and connection—the things that fundamentally make us human,” explains Mia Sundstrom, Dr. Brown’s granddaughter and the CEO of the National Institute for Play—a nonprofit organization Brown established in 1994 to champion play as a public health necessity. “I grew up through play,” she says, “and have firsthand seen the benefits of it.”
Appointed to her role earlier this year, her mission at the institute is to show “how people can incorporate play into their lives to promote cognitive, social, emotional and physical health.”
Ellen Peirson-Hagger: Why is play important?

Mia Sundstrom: Here’s the paradox—and it’s why it’s so difficult to convince people that play matters: One of the core definitions of play is that it’s purposeless, that it’s not done for any specific outcome. Yet there’s a ton of purpose in the outcomes we get. We have taught ourselves that play is the opposite of work, but actually play is productive, play is learning; it is not a waste of time.
EPH: What are the benefits of play?

MS: When we are in a state of play, it boosts the production of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, which is the neuroplasticity protein that helps to create new neural connections and strengthen existing pathways. Play also calms down our amygdala—our emotional processing center—meaning it takes us out of a stress response, which is great for emotional regulation. And in the case of social play, our mirror neurons—which light up when we observe the motor activity of someone else—allow us to develop the basic foundation of attunement, which is the first seedling of connection with another human being, and which in time leads to trust, to community, to belonging. So on a neurobiological level, play promotes our cognitive health, our emotional resilience and our social competence.

Physical play is obviously good for us: Exercise is healthy, whether we enjoy it or not. But we’re a lot more likely to sustain it when it’s something we enjoy, so we might as well try and find a form of physical exercise that feels like play.
EPH: If we don’t play, are those things lost?

MS: When we’re play-deprived, there can be really severe consequences. It can lead to cognitive rigidity, which is when you can’t think outside the box and solve problems creatively. We have seen that a lack of play can lead to susceptibility for anxiety and depression, and toward addictive behaviors, because we try to find those things that we need from play in other forms—alcohol, drugs, social media, sugar—all these things that offer short-term relief rather than long-term benefit.

And then there’s social incompetence: As my grandpa’s research showed, when we don’t play it’s hard to build tolerance and empathy for each other because we miss that fundamental level of attunement. This leads to diminished well-being.
EPH: How does our need for play change as we become adults?

MS: There’s a misconception that it has to change like crazy, that what you do as a kid is not what you should do as an adult. But we don’t ever lose the desire to play, we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways. For example, as you go through grade school, the playgrounds change—there is no longer the opportunity to go down a slide at recess—and then all of a sudden you forget that you love to do that, and you might never do it again.

I don’t think adults should stop swinging, or playing at parks, or jumping on a trampoline in the backyard. We often think that we outgrow these things, but we really shouldn’t. Lego is a breaker of this rule: Lego adult sets are selling so well right now because of their connection to nostalgia and childhood. And what’s great about moving from childhood to adulthood is that the possibilities to play open up significantly: Instead of exploring your backyard with a stick and turning your cardboard box into a rocket ship, you have access to a car and a plane.
EPH: Is play different to different people?

MS: Everyone is born with a deep natural predilection for play, but that looks different for each of us. There are people who love to make things—art, music, building, tinkering with objects. There are people who love to dream or get lost in a book or movie and create imaginary worlds in their mind. There are people who love to compete, who play through mastering. There are people who love to organize—collecting new things, arranging social gatherings, even cleaning out a junk drawer. These are all different play styles, and one of the greatest gifts you can give a child is to notice what those natural tendencies are and help nourish them.
EPH: Do you think we need to take a broader view of what play is or can be?

MS: Yes! Most of the time, when I ask people “What is play to you?” they say “a board game” or “my kid’s sport.” We have confined play to this really narrow scope, when actually play is any activity that brings us into the play state, which is an altered state of being, almost dreamlike, that takes us out of the usual experience of time and space and evokes positive emotions like joy and awe. It is intrinsically motivated, not coerced, so it’s done for its own sake, and it’s self-reinforcing, so the benefits of a play state last beyond the time we’re playing.

Any activity that meets that criteria can be play—that could mean coding for someone who loves to code, or cooking for someone who loves to cook. Heck, that could even be cleaning if you put on a great song and you turn your broom into a microphone.
EPH: Why is society so resistant to play?

MS: Well, the psychologist and play researcher Peter Gray would answer by taking us back to the 16th century, when the Protestant Reformation taught us to believe in the moral virtue of work and that play, by contrast, is the breeding ground of sin. And then you throw capitalism into the mix which calls for more production, more consumption: that’s what defines success in the capitalist dream, right? Then you add in the compounding effects of automation and AI. Of course play isn’t celebrated in a world that prioritizes those things.
EPH: Has digitization played a role?

MS: We can’t prove causation, but our screens do seem to be factor in why we’re not playing. Scrolling on your screen disguises itself as play because you lose track of time, and it feels fun in the moment. But it has long-term detriments in terms of our attention span and our loneliness. If we’re scrolling, we’re not connecting with each other on a human level.
EPH: What kind of society would we have if we all played more?

MS: Play dissolves our differences and reminds us of what we have in common. Our world is so polarized, but play brings us together and is one of the most powerful ways to create a better society. Play lowers our inhibitions—I want to shout that from the rooftops. If you disagree with someone and go play with them, you’ll see the humanity in one other. It can also help combat the trends that we’re talking so much about right now—loneliness, disengagement, burnout—because play brings us back to that deep intrinsic drive to do something for a sustained period of time that makes the time pass more quickly.
EPH: What should adults do to help recover their love of play?

MS: We help adults rediscover their natural spark—their thing that makes them most curious and fully alive—and then think about small ways to reintegrate that into their life. The first step is to think back to your earliest memory of play: What was that thing you loved to do before the world told you who to be? Second, based on that, what do you love to do now—is there something that you’ve forgotten about and haven’t done for ages? Third, nothing ever works when we try to create massive changes all at once. So we say that 30 seconds is enough. See if you can add a burst of play into your morning or evening routine, based on those two things you reflected on. What’s great about play is that it’s self-reinforcing, so as soon as you give yourself that permission, it will keep you coming back for more.
“We have taught ourselves that play is the opposite of work, but actually play is productive, play is learning; it is not a waste of time.”

items.title: Kyle Kuzma - Kinfolk
items.description: The NBA forward is playing the long game.
paragraphs: The NBA forward is playing the long game.

Kyle Kuzma is enjoying himself. He’s about to catch a flight for the south of France, where he’ll be attending the Cannes Film Festival, and is midway through the long, complex and, for him, extremely pleasurable process, of picking out what to wear. “If I’m going somewhere in three days, I may already be in my closet, just trying on clothes, seeing what I want to wear, thinking about what type of events I’m going to,” he says over a video call from his home in Miami. He’s planning ahead for the films, parties and red carpet events.

If a lot of this sounds like fun, Kuzma thinks so too. “Everything is play—unless, you know, it’s your profession,” he says. This is the challenge because Kuzma’s job is, after all, a form of play. He is in his 10th year in the NBA. A first-round draft pick in 2017, he’s currently a power forward for the Milwaukee Bucks; in 2020 he won the NBA national championship with the Los Angeles Lakers in only his third year in the league.
