items.title: A Magazine That’s Actually a Shop
items.description: Type in shop-magazine.com and you will enter the world of Magazine, an online “destination for divas everywhere” and love letter to wallet-draining excess. It’s a shop, but also a magazine, founded by shopaholic soulmates Coumba Samba and Sylvie Makower. Born
items.author: Marley Wendt
paragraphs: Type in shop-magazine.com and you will enter the world of Magazine, an online “destination for divas everywhere” and love letter to wallet-draining excess. It’s a shop, but also a magazine, founded by shopaholic soulmates Coumba Samba and Sylvie Makower. Born from a friendship stretched between New York and London, Magazine turns a shared fascination with fashionista-dom into a website. It’s a transatlantic affair for a medium that is, fittingly, both nowhere and everywhere: an online space that feels positively physical, practically begging you to swipe your credit card.

From a lime-green 1940s showgirl dress to a pink-and-white Betsey Johnson confection, the colors pop with an almost suspicious perfection. It’s clear that Samba and Makower have a knack for knowing what a girl wants, embracing the fun that comes with acquiring clothes.

But Magazine is not just a place to empty your wallet; it is somewhere to fill your brain, too. Every drop arrives with an online magazine, ranging from essays on a pair of Fall 2011 Lanvin heels, to the quest for the perfect black mannequin. It’s a pink-painted corner of the web where reading becomes wanting, and wanting is very much the point. If you like your money pixelated on a screen, you’ve found your destination, darling!
MARLEY WENDT: What are three colors that capture the spirit of this project?
SYLVIE MAKOWER: Bubblegum pink.

SM: I also love tangerine. Magazine has a very girly, diva-abundance vibe. Neither of us are minimalists by any measure, nor are we into the monochromatic stuff. So, exuberant bright colors, heavy on the pink.
How did Magazine come about?

SM: A year ago while we were having breakfast and drinking coffee Upstate, I was thinking “Oh, Coumba’s being awfully quiet.” She was just on her phone, and seemed to be working. Then I noticed the reflection in her big glasses: Vinted, scrolling by. It was such a beautiful image. It suddenly dawned on me that we are twin flames in being massive shopaholics.

CS: We kind of floated the idea, and I was like, yes, we need that. Especially here in New York, there’s lots of nice vintage places, but sometimes the curation doesn’t really fit with what I’m seeking, so I’ve resorted to online shopping.
The website has a slightly DIY early internet quality to it. Has your relationship to the internet shaped the way you think about Magazine?
CS: It does have this “blog vibe” to it. At least for me, I kind of grew up on Tumblr, so that has a part to play in it.

SM: We like the idea of having this slightly low-stakes, immediate form of online publication where nothing’s too overdone. The actual visual language of the website had a lot to do with our web designer, Alec Mapes-Frances, and also Coumba.

It was quite an organic process. We just kept adding elements. For instance, there’s a sticker of Coumba in a margarita glass in the corner of the website. This links to her many years of writing a personal margarita review. And we also have an agony aunt, Miss Chlo, who you can submit questions to. We wanted to bring many worlds and portals together on the site.
Coumba, what makes a great margarita?

CS: Honestly, I’m a simple girl at heart. I also don’t really like alcohol. The whole reason I started it was because I was looking for a classic cocktail, and wanted to keep tabs on it. I’m just looking for something straightforward, no riff-raff or weird orange juice in it.
On the website, for the listings of the items, there are GIFs of you guys that emulate self-tape videos. Tell me about that.

SM: We thought it would be funny to do a spoof on the walking video that your modelling agency requests, because it’s such a humiliating medium. I modeled for a long time as a teenager, and Coumba still does.
What makes a piece of clothing right for Magazine?

SM: A philosophy that I’ve begun to incorporate is “shop for yourself.” If I Iove something, I’ll buy it. We want to have a mixture of well-constructed, fancy designer pieces, and weird, accessible items. To me, there’s nothing worse than being dressed too well…
CS: You’re spot on. Everything is unique, special, and bright.
Describe your perfect day of shopping together.
CS: We once went to this vintage fair in London called Frock Me!, and just spent the whole day there. I put in my earbuds, walked around for five hours, and spent all of my money. It was beautiful.
SM: Coumba sent me these crazy messages a few hours in telling me I had to come. And when I came, I found her racing around as if she was possessed. I love those fairs so much.
Why did you want Magazine to be an actual magazine as well?

SM: We wanted to print out images of the clothes, like the books of images of counterfeit bags on Canal Street. We thought we could call the shop Magazine because it’s like a magazine. And then Coumba suggested that we make an actual magazine.
CS: It all just clicked. I was also doing zines while I was in uni, so it’s always been an interest of mine.

SM: We wanted somewhere to explore what’s going on in the shop and beyond in greater depth. The magazine is by no means just about the stock though. For our current feature, Fiona Alison Duncan has written a pseudo fictional essay about personal effects.
And if Magazine was an actual shop, what would it look like?

SM: There’s not a moment in my day when I’m not thinking about it! It’ll be very pink. My hypothetical dog, which I intend to own within the next calendar year, will be running around. It’ll be a watering hole for divas, where people can come to shop, but also to congregate and have tea.
What type of music is playing as you walk in?
CS: Probably some classic ’80s dance tracks.
What are your favourite shopping-diva words of wisdom?
SM: I would like to quote our agony aunt, Miss Chlo: “You don’t need to find yourself before getting dressed. Sometimes getting dressed is how you find yourself.”

items.title: Gisele Bundchen Interview: Motherhood, Happiness, Modeling Career
items.description: This story appears in i-D 377 “The Mother Issue” available now at select retailers and online.
items.author: Steff Yotka
paragraphs: This story appears in i-D 377 “The Mother Issue” available now at select retailers and online.
photography COLLIER SCHORR

When she was 15 years old, Gisele Bündchen left Horizontina, Brazil, and moved to Tokyo to become a model. It was 1995. She didn’t speak Japanese or English. To reach her parents, grandparents, and five sisters, she used an international calling card on a landline phone. She would speak to them every 15 days, exactly.

“It was, in a way, liberating because I felt like I was living life,” Gisele says, thinking back to getting lost on the subway, navigating teenage growing pains, and learning how to integrate into a foreign reality. “I was experiencing life.”

Thirty-one years later, there is little of life Gisele hasn’t experienced. She walked her first major runway show for Alexander McQueen in 1998, and for the next decade was a regular on the catwalk for Gucci, Dolce & Gabbana, Versace, Valentino, and Marc Jacobs. She signed an advertising contract with Dior, posing for Nick Knight amongst bubbles and saddle bags, then another with Dolce & Gabbana for its glittering perfume The One, and then another with Victoria’s Secret. She routinely wore the brand’s Red Hot Fantasy Bra—estimated to be worth $15 million in 2000.

Gisele was the Forbes highest-paid model for 12 years in a row, from 2005 to 2016. Her own website estimates she has appeared on an unprecedented 1,200 magazine covers (this issue will be her seventh for i-D). She walked the runway during the 2016 Olympic Opening Ceremony in Rio de Janeiro, released multiple singles, and has appeared in a handful of movies, from Taxi (2004) to The Devil Wears Prada (2006). Gisele has fundraised for Lotus House, Save the Children, The Red Cross, and more. In 2016, Taschen published a book commemorating her 20 years of modelling, retailing for $700 and selling out in one day. The cover shot is by Irving Penn of a nude Gisele. (“I still have the note from him saying that it was wonderful. ‘You did great.’”) Inside are now-legendary photographs by Steven Meisel, David LaChapelle, Inez and Vinoodh, and Juergen Teller. Gisele has published one autobiography and one cookbook, which is to say nothing of the digests she posts on Instagram to her 22 million followers. She is so famous and so known, from Brazil to Tokyo to New York to Mars, that it would be impossible for any one of us to calculate exactly where we know her from or how many times we’ve seen her face.

And yet, for Gisele, who turned 46 in July, those wandering Tokyo days are among her most special. “My whole thing is going back to that,” she tells me, tucked into an armchair in a white tank and jean shorts. “How can I create more of that reality in my life?”

You see, despite being the object of so many gazes, Gisele prefers to set hers on the sun, the sea, the sky. She was born on a farm in Brazil, surrounded by her grandparents, parents, sisters, and pets. Now, 6,900 kilometres away, she’s recreated that paradise in Northern Miami with her children Benjamin (16), Vivian (13), and a baby boy (16 months), her husband Joaquim, and a pair of dogs.

“Life is a gift,” she says. “I think I have so much joy in my life because I really see the ordinary as the extraordinary… The sun rises every day. You can walk around and be grateful for it, or you can just be disconnected from all these incredible things. You can be robbed of your life if you think life is this”—she mimics looking down at her phone—“and you forget life is so much more.”
She smiles, sipping from her room-temperature water. “Anyway, I’m sure you have more questions for me.”
Because we got into the meaning of life and Gisele’s very philosophy of being so quickly into our first meeting, here’s what happened in the lead-up—minutes one through seven:
1. I enter Gisele’s small ranch home a couple blocks from her larger, beachfront estate. I am promptly served her homemade granola and her proprietary tea (warming, like dark chocolate and honey).
2. Alfie, her gigantic German Shepherd, comes in first and gives me the once-over. “He’s my protector,” Gisele smiles, kicking off her sandals and wrapping me up in a hug.

3. “You smell amazing,” she says, and I just give her the bottle of perfume in my purse. She asks if it has parabens, and I say I don’t know, and she tells me never to use anything with parabens, especially on your wrists or neck. It’s been three months and I am still too embarrassed to research: Does Maison Louis Marie’s scent Aboukir have parabens?
4. She checks my astrological vibe to make sure this interview will go well: “What’s your sign?” she asks squarely.
“Cancer. I knew we’d talk about it. I read you’re a Cancer, Scorpio Moon. What’s your rising?”

“Oh, go girl! I don’t even know how I ended up doing this job. If you let me, I would just never leave my house, because I’m a crab. And with the Scorpio Moon, for me, if it’s not deep, I don’t want to talk about it.”

That’s the guiding premise of being Gisele: Always searching for depth, connection, and meaning. In some way, modelling was the perfect job for her—homey, crablike tendencies notwithstanding—because it allowed her to find connections the world over. The high-low of the industry, which led to anxiety attacks in her mid-20s, was the impetus for Gisele’s soul searching. “Shit happens to all of us, but I think I don’t stay there,” she says of the down days. “I learned how to meditate. It’s like you can take a step back: You can be having an experience and observing yourself having that experience at the same time.”

Meditation led her to yoga, which she practises routinely, and then to Pilates and then to jujitsu. Recently, she has added weight training. “I do weights three times a week. I do Pilates once or twice a week. I do yoga two or three times a week. I work out every day because, for me, working out—I don’t see it as something I have to do. I see it as something I get to do,” she says. “It doesn’t matter if I’m surfing, if I’m playing volleyball with my daughter, if I’m paddleboarding. Whatever it is, I feel like it’s a moment of being.” She bares a bicep. “Now for the first time in my life, I can do pull-ups.”

Early this summer morning, she took her baby to the park. Much like his older half-siblings, he has picked up on Gisele’s connectivity and generosity. “I have to show you this video.” For the first time, she whips out her phone and opens her camera roll. As she scrolls through—I promise I’m not trying to peek!—I realise almost every photo is of her kids. “He’s so funny,” she says of her son, captured waddling around the park with a paper towel. “I mean, he’s 16 months and he saw that I was cleaning the park—because Miami, it’s so damp all the time!—and he wanted to participate and he felt really good about it,” Gisele beams, watching her tiny son dry off the slide, the seesaw, the swing.

“Kids give us this opportunity to live again, to be more present and to experience life again. To do it maybe differently than we’ve done it before.” She pauses. “I don’t know. I find every little thing so amazing.” Gisele goes on to show me videos of Benny DJing in his bedroom, his baby brother dancing by his side. She has pictures of Vivi playing volleyball (“She’s amazing!”) and dancing with friends. She scrolls to a dancing video. “I mean, what is better than this? This is my daughter and she’s like, ‘Mum, let’s do a dance class.’ So this is us doing a dance class. I’m not so great,” Gisele laughs, “but look at her and her friend—and that’s her mum’s friend.”

She quickly scrolls through about 20 more videos before she chucks her phone away. “By the way, I don’t know if you noticed, my phone doesn’t ring. There’s no alarms. It never rings. It’s liberating.”

A silenced iPhone and spending all day with her family is a far cry from the past 30 years of Gisele’s life. To briefly summarise the lore: Her mother enrolled her, her twin sister Patí, and younger sister Gabriela in modelling classes in Brazil. Gisele was later scouted to participate in the Elite Model Look competition, and in 1995, she placed second. From 1996 to 2016, life didn’t stop—she spent the better part of her 20s and 30s at the white-hot centre of it all: Fashion, fame, celebrity, paparazzi, and money. She was signing bigger contracts than other models, getting bigger media attention, becoming an entity bigger than Gisele Bündchen from Horizontina, Brazil. She was, by 2004, a supermodel, capital S. Everything about her sparkled.

“I’ve experienced the rat race. I was on the hamster wheel in my early 20s,” she says. “I won Model of the Year at 19. I worked so hard from 14 to get to that place, I felt like I couldn’t say no [to major jobs].” And sure, Gisele encountered so much of the bullshit so many models of the ’90s and ’00s did. She tried not to let her industry’s lack of protection faze her. “Even though I wasn’t going to the parties, I was doing 360 days [of work a year]. I wanted to be the best that I could be every day. I wanted to bring my best.”

We start to look through some of her runway fits from her catwalk days and she sparks up with delight. “Girl, it was very tight inside. You couldn’t really move so much—but, I mean, look how he made you look!” she cheers of a supersized Fall 2004 Christian Dior look by John Galliano. “I’m forever grateful to McQueen, I’m forever grateful to John. I was always so excited to do the Dior shows because I never knew what I was going to look like.”

She singles out a Galliano show for Dior held at Versailles. “This was 60 years of Dior and I wasn’t even doing shows anymore. John was like, ‘Please, Gisele. This is all my muses and it’s going to be the 60 years, it’s to be in Versailles.’ I was like, ‘I must do it,’” she remembers. “Look at these shoes. It was like a platform without a heel. I was walking on cement, like bricks. It was crazy. I was like, ‘Am I going to fall and break my ankle?’”

But that’s the thing about Gisele: Even if she’s struggling to walk or struggling to feel beautiful—as she often recounts of that first-ever McQueen show, where she hit the runway topless with a trompe l’oeil white tank painted on by Val Garland, rain falling and her lashes dripping into her eyes—she is always going to do her best. “I didn’t say no or complain because people were giving me the opportunity,” she reflects. “I came in, I did my job, I went home… and I think what I really appreciate and really enjoyed about fashion is that it got me to access and experience different sides of me. I really wanted to be the best canvas for the creatives. I felt like it was my way of contributing.”

But working in the oil-slick glossy world of new millennium modelling meant that few people saw Gisele as a full person—because of her beauty, her chameleonic qualities, and her prowess, she was quickly regarded as an idol. Nice to look at, nothing to say. The first time she appeared in i-D, on the cover in December 1998, she wasn’t interviewed. Instead, the photographer who took the picture was, and here’s what he had to say about the smart and vibrant Gisele: “She’s certainly gorgeous. I’d marry her.”

Her “godfather” in the turbulent fashion industry was Steven Meisel. (Are you surprised that the greatest model of her generation would find kinship with the greatest photographer of his?) In one of the earliest pieces of press about Gisele, a New York Magazine article from 1999, Meisel already saw her as more than a body to stand in front of his lens. He felt her spirit. “Gisele is able to change because she wants to—it’s not in her looks; it’s in her mental process. She is malleable and is willing to be a silent screen star because she understands that modelling is acting,” he told the mag. He later wrote the foreword for her Taschen book, and she still speaks of him as her guardian angel. “I’m grateful for him. I don’t think I would have been the model that I was if it wasn’t for him, for real. We got to play together. I shot with him every week.”

And yet, after weekly Meisel shoots, over 130 Vogue covers, and decades on billboards and TV ad spots, Gisele wanted more. Well—maybe not more in the way you and I might think of it. She wanted to actually enjoy what she’d accomplished, and that meant leaving the fracas behind. After a decade in Boston, she relocated here, to Florida, to co-parent her older children and set up a new world of sea and sun and sand. Being mum, practising gratitude, taking care of herself and her community have become more valuable than any seven-figure ad job: “I say no to 99 percent of the jobs I’m offered because, when I put it on the scale, I’m like, ‘Am I going to miss my daughter’s volleyball game? Am I going to miss going to the park with my son? Am I going to miss my son DJing?’”

That’s why, with the exception of a few trips to her home in Costa Rica, to see family in Brazil, and recently, to Tahiti, Gisele rarely leaves Florida. “Having a baby at this moment of my life is such a gift, because I’m in a different place. I don’t have anything to prove. I don’t feel like I really, quite frankly, care.”
“I’m not defined by other people’s opinions,” she continues, firmly. “I feel like I get to choose how I want to live my life.”

Being alive today can feel like a quest for more: Make more money. Diversify your portfolio. Get PRP+ to be more beautiful and then Ozempic to be more svelte. Become a brand and use that brand to become more famous. Every day of your life can be used to sell something or say something or self-improve. I don’t think I have ever encountered a person more satisfied with exactly how her life is than Gisele. She has a lot, sure, but it’s long been enough. She’s done a lot, sure, but she’s not looking back. She’s been everywhere, yeah, but she isn’t driven by getting in your face.

She’s not a brand. She’s not an entrepreneur. She’s not a self-help guru—even though I tell her she should have a podcast. She’s not forcing Gisele-dom down our throats and, in some way, it seems like she doesn’t really want to be famous at all. That she’s financially well-off, she tells me, is just an opportunity to take care of her sisters and her family. She doesn’t want fancy clothes. She hasn’t been to New York in over two years and she’s not eager to come back.

“At the end of the day, this is your temple, this is your life, this is your journey. How do you want it to look? What do you want it to be? Who defines success?” she asks, as concerned in that moment with my well-being as with her own. “What is success? Some people say success is power, money, fame, more. Some people say success is being able to spend time with your kids, to have food on your table, to have a home to live in, to have great relationships and actually enjoy every day. I find that, quite frankly, much more successful than…” she trails off, not eager to point a finger. “It’s up to each person to define, because when I was in my 20s, success was different than what I feel today.”
“What do you want your legacy to be?” I ask as we’re wrapping up our conversation.

“In the end, I ended up having the best time. I ended up enjoying it all, staying in it, learning from it, and growing up in it. It’s been a blessing. However people see me, that’s okay with me. I want to look back and think, ‘I really enjoyed this journey. I really loved fully. I really experienced every emotion. I really had meaningful relationships. I tried to make the world a better place, and I made my surroundings more harmonious and loving and beautiful.’ I want my kids to feel like I was a great mum and that I helped them become the best version of themselves. I want to feel like I lived striving to be the best version of myself. Hopefully, I can look back and say I did it.”

Today, after I pack up my things and head for Miami International Airport, she’ll go to a birthday dinner. It’s a rare night out for Gisele, and after decades of no carbs and no dairy, she might have some of her friend’s homemade sourdough. “What’s better than bread and cheese? Oh my god, I don’t know!” she laughs. Tomorrow, she’ll wake up early to paddleboard. She’s worried about me not seeing the sea one last time before I get on a plane back to New York, but she’s calmed when I tell her I spent two hours on the beach this morning. As I wheel away my little suitcase and say goodbye, she pops her head out the front door with a final blessing. “Live the life you want to live! Everything else is going to shake out.”

items.title: 'Artificial', Andrew Garfield, Olivia Wilde, and Seth Rogen Join Vanity Fair’s Slate of Screening Room Programming
items.description: Vanity Fair is pleased to announce its second wave of programming for its Screening Room event series in Los Angeles and New York.
items.author: John Ross
paragraphs: Vanity Fair is pleased to announce its second wave of programming for its Screening Room event series in Los Angeles and New York.

The inaugural edition of Vanity Fair’s Screening Room will be held at LACMA’s Peter Zumthor–designed Steve Tisch Theater from November 13–15. On Saturday, November 14, the weekend’s marquee screening will be Luca Guadagnino’s highly anticipated new film, Artificial. Guadagnino’s story follows OpenAI and the two-decade artificial intelligence arms race; as AI becomes more powerful, a battle wages in Silicon Valley over who gets to control this important technology. Director Guadagnino, Andrew Garfield, Yura Borisov, and Monica Barbaro will participate in a Q&A after the film.
Scene Selection Live will return with The Invite costars Olivia Wilde and Seth Rogen revisiting some of their pivotal work in film and television.

John Malkovich, the latest winner of the Volpi Cup for best actor at the Venice Film Festival, will join the Q&A for Wild Horse Nine. Penélope Cruz and Miguel Bernardeau will join Friday night’s La Bola Negra Q&A.

Just a few weeks later, Vanity Fair’s Screening Room will come to New York, where screenings and events will take place at the Cherry Lane Theatre from December 4–6. Alex Gibney, the director of Musk, will participate in a conversation with esteemed tech journalist Kara Swisher about covering the richest man on the planet.
Naza, the winner of the Special Jury Prize at this year’s Venice Film Festival, will screen in New York City with a special introduction.

items.description: Halloween is a special kind of holiday, and it requires a very specific kind of film. It needs to scare you in the moment, give you a couple of laughs, satisfy (but not depress) you with its ending…and boomerang back to give you the creeps the next time you’re
items.author: Eve Batey
paragraphs: Halloween is a special kind of holiday, and it requires a very specific kind of film. It needs to scare you in the moment, give you a couple of laughs, satisfy (but not depress) you with its ending…and boomerang back to give you the creeps the next time you’re alone in the dark.

But when you’re dealing with a candy-based month like October, you don’t want to mess with anything that feels like homework (sorry, Robert Eggers’s Nosferatu) or leaves you feeling worse about the world than you did before you pressed play (like David Gordon Green’s second and third Halloween films). You can watch gore for the sake of gore, nubile teens being tortured, or small children and pets die the rest of the year. The best horror movies for Halloween need to offer something a little richer, that mix of shivers and catharsis that makes this time of year so darned fun.

Below you’ll find our guide to the best horror movies available on streaming right now, all of which tick those Halloween-specific boxes. So fire up the popcorn popper, turn down the lights, and nestle into your favorite spot on the couch.
Available on: Netflix and Fubo

Ridley Scott had no idea what he was kicking off when he pulled together this ragtag crew of blue-collar workers awoken from stasis sleep to investigate a derelict ship. It’s easy to forget what a stunning and fresh film this was when it was released just two years after Star Wars. (My parents, assuming it was a similar film, took me to see it in the theater when it dropped. That experience I had at eight years old is probably why I am writing this article for you now, so parents, be warned.) The franchise has taken a lot of directions, some of which were ambitious failures (Prometheus) and some of which remain potential-filled side stories (Alien: Earth). But the OG, with the revelation that is Sigourney Weaver’s Ellen Ripley and the artist H.R. Giger’s innovative creature design, still feels relevant, vital, and terrifying.

Is Kane Parsons’s big-screen debut prepared to stand the test of time? Maybe not, but like its classmate, Curry Barker’s Obsession (now on Peacock), this extremely strong debut of a young YouTube auteur seems just as historically significant as some of the other innovations here. Obsession picks comedy and gore over Backrooms’ claustrophobic dread, which is why the A24 hit made the list—I suspect that in the long run, its striking depiction of trauma and toxic masculinity will have more staying power than Obsession’s villainous (and yes, Michael Johnston, he’s villainous) Cat Person. You know what? We can answer the question of comparable impact in a couple weeks, by tallying how many Halloween partygoers are dressed as Pirate Clark against how many are wearing this sad sack hoodie. Let’s circle back then.
Available on: Starz and Philo

Before dorks were hashtagging everything with #SnyderCut—gosh, before there were even hashtags—Zack Snyder rebooted George Romero’s mall-centric zombie movie with a level of style, humor, and scares that he hasn’t exhibited since. (Netflix’s Army of the Dead is fun, but comparably toothless.) A preretirement Sarah Polley, a post–Pulp Fiction Ving Rhames, and Phil from Modern Family go up against Olympic-sprinter-level zombies, a concept launched just two years before with 28 Days Later (Apple TV+). 28 Days is good, but Dawn is supersized in an especially American way. It’s the movie I go back to most often when I think about what to do—and not to do—when the zombie apocalypse comes.
Available on: AMC+, Roku, and Kanopy

Director Neil Marshall followed his promising 2002 werewolf film, Dog Soldiers (Amazon Prime, Fubo, and Shudder), with this all-female cave exploration movie that ruined me—both for driving behind trucks loaded with pipes and doing anything underground ever again. It’s got the one-two punch of spooky monsters and human ones, and it doesn’t argue that the supernatural beasts are the worst ones in the yarn. Oh, one thing that’s important to note is that the film had one ending when released in the UK and another for its stateside drop; as a depressed citizen of the US, I prefer the happier North American version.
Available on: Hulu, Peacock, and Philo

Has there ever been a more lankily beautiful offscreen-onscreen couple than Jeff Goldblum and Geena Davis? The former famously read David Cronenberg’s script for this movie while lying in bed with the latter, who was so intrigued by his visceral reaction as he read that she pursued her own role in the film. It’s sexual jealousy that drives Goldblum’s scientist to take his ill-advised teleporter ride with an insect stowaway, and his growing realization that the experience didn’t make him miraculously healthier, but instead is killing the best parts of him, is body horror at its finest. You’ll never look at your medicine cabinet—or a box of doughnuts—in the same light ever again.
Available on: Fubo, Philo, and AMC+

Here, let me save you a lot of time: The only Halloween you really need is John Carpenter’s original, especially when it comes to legitimate scares. Sure, you can do what my husband and I did last Halloween and watch them all in order, including the Paul Rudd–starring Halloween: The Curse of Michael Myers (Cinemax and HBO Max) and Josh Hartnett’s film debut, Halloween H20 (same). But stop before you get to Rob Zombie’s 2007 iteration and let Michael Myers rest. He did such a great job of scaring us just by driving down the street (best not to ask how he learned to get behind the wheel) or standing amid some falling leaves in the first film. The rest are increasingly warped and inferior attempts—Pirate Clarks, if you will—to capture John Carpenter’s early brilliance.
Available on: Kanopy and Tubi

Three years before he directed the slightly too cuddly Gremlins (HBO Max), Joe Dante brought us this dark werewolf tale, which takes on 1970s encounter-group culture, marital infidelity, and the cannibalistic nature of broadcast journalism. Now, I know what you’re thinking: All werewolf movies are inherently cheesy. You are not wrong! Transformation scenes can be unintentionally laughable, and no one has fully figured out how to make a wolf-human hybrid look less like a fall-season impulse buy at Home Depot and more like a terrifically terrifying beast. (Maybe Eggers will crack the code with his upcoming Werwulf, which drops on Christmas Day?) Dante and practical-effects master Rob Bottin get pretty close, though—but the scariest moment, in my opinion, involves only the werewolf’s hand.
Available on: Amazon Prime

There’s nothing supernatural in this Paul Walker–starring road movie, but that doesn’t mean it’s not scary as hell. The late Fast & Furious lynchpin got back in a car for this thriller just a few months after the now ubiquitous franchise made its debut, but this time he—alongside Steve Zahn—is a hapless near-victim of a rage-filled truck driver pissed off after the pair catfish him via CB radio. It’s all made even more intense because you never see the driver pursuing them, you just hear his voice, provided by the great Ted “Buffalo Bill” Levine. Director John Dahl made his mark in the early 1990s with a series of desert-set noir films, detoured into whatever Rounders was (Oreo spon?), and you could feel him exhaling and having a blast with this very funny, very scary film. Ever made a cross-country road trip and been unsettled when you see the same driver again and again? This movie is the worst-case version of that.
Available on: Netflix, Peacock, and Kanopy

While some prefer the original Japanese version, Ringu (AMC+ and Kanopy), Gore Verbinski’s English-language adaptation streamlines the scares to a stiletto point. For many Americans, this movie was the first time they were exposed to the “creepy pale girl with long hair” trope, now common to the point of parody. But the story of a cursed video tape somehow manifested by an evil kid named Samara holds up, jam-packed with unsettling images backed with an actual plot (yes, friends, it’s possible). Even after 22 years of rip-offs, Samara’s final reveal is still best viewed through one’s fingers.
Available on: Hulu, Peacock, and Kanopy

Ethan Hawke’s author/shitty person, Ellison Oswalt, is my favorite horror movie scribe, and I’d wear all of his writerly cardigans in a heartbeat. (I’m not counting Jack Torrance of 1980’s The Shining—available on HBO Max—as a writer; that guy never managed to produce.) Oswalt somehow manages to move his family into an infamous murder house without them finding out, then assumes he’ll be forgiven once his book about the case makes its inevitable splash. Surprise, surprise, the crime had a supernatural basis—and is linked to a number of others, all brutally depicted in reels of film left in his attic. Over a decade before Weapons’s Aunt Gladys (Amazon Prime and HBO Max) was luring kids to the basement, Sinister’s monster was enticing them to do far worse.

Jordan Peele’s Get Out (Peacock, Fubo, and FX) confirmed he was the real horror deal, and two years later, Us suggested his ambitions were more aligned with Stanley Kubrick than John Carpenter. What is this movie—about a trip to the Santa Cruz, CA, seaside that ends in a pair of Lupita Nyong’os in a bizarre and violent dance set to an instrumental version of Luniz’s “I Got 5 On It”—actually about? Is it about the people who make all the stuff we privileged classes thoughtlessly consume? Or is it an examination of the nasty, brutish, and short lives of the animals we eat? You can debate questions like that if you’re feeling clever, but you can also just dig how terrifying it would be to look down the driveway and see yourself, but in a set of red coveralls and driving gloves.
Wes Craven’s New Nightmare (1994)
Available on: AMC+ and Philo

I don’t think you need me to tell you that the late Wes Craven’s 1984 classic Nightmare on Elm Street (HBO Max, Philo, and AMC+) is a pretty big deal—you are reading this article, after all. But is it scary in a way that haunts you after? Even at his launch, Freddy Krueger is pretty corny, and a little too quick with a locker-room-level pun. New Nightmare is for grown-ups, Craven said at the time, a work aged up for his original audience, then a decade older. Marketed at the time as the horror genre’s take on Robert Altman’s Hollywood meta-take The Player, New Nightmare featured the original’s actors and director as themselves, exhibiting varying levels of comfort with their cult fame. This challenge is complicated when Freddy somehow makes the trip from the silver screen to the real world. Eventually, things get kind of goofy, as they always do in dreams. But it’ll be a while before you get Craven’s speech on the power of fiction to infect our real lives out of your head.
Available on: Amazon Prime, Roku, and Kanopy

Godzilla guy Adam Wingard bummed out legions of horror fans with his reboot of The Blair Witch Project, 2016’s completely unnecessary Blair Witch (I don’t recommend you watch it on Cinemax or HBO Max, but it’s a free country). But three years before, he thrilled them with this film, an elegant evisceration of the cliché of the final girl that plays like a Treehouse of Horror–style episode of Succession. It’s got terrifying animal masks, the worst-ever (and still kind of funny?) decapitation, and the hookiest earworm of a throwback signature tune, the Dwight Twilley Band’s “Looking for the Magic.” No ghosts, ghouls, or demons here, just the evil things that greed makes people do, at least until the little guy starts fighting back.

items.title: ‘Swipe Right on the Devil’ Exposes a Real-Life Tinder Murder
items.description: It’s been almost a decade since 24-year-old Sydney Loofe disappeared after connecting with a woman named Bailey Boswell on Tinder. After a single in-person date, Loofe would later learn that she had actually been messaging with a man named Aubrey Trail, who re
items.author: Savannah Walsh
paragraphs: It’s been almost a decade since 24-year-old Sydney Loofe disappeared after connecting with a woman named Bailey Boswell on Tinder. After a single in-person date, Loofe would later learn that she had actually been messaging with a man named Aubrey Trail, who referred to himself as a “powerful warlock,” at the head of a “coven,” which was, in reality, a coercive sex cult and criminal enterprise with Boswell as one of his “witches.” Boswell and Trail were in a romantic relationship themselves, a Bonnie and Clyde of online dating in small-town Nebraska. Within days of their first Tinder messages, Loofe was killed as a “sacrifice” by the coven’s leaders, her body dismembered and dumped in trash bags around a plot of rural land in small-town Nebraska.

In Swipe Right on the Devil, a new Ron Howard–produced, three-part true-crime series now streaming on Hulu, filmmaker Brian Biegel recounts the story of “witchcraft and its sister, black magic” in Wilber, Nebraska, as it “meets the modern-day digital dating world,” he tells Vanity Fair.

As part of the police investigation into Loofe’s death, authorities discovered that she had been recruited as the 13th member of Trail and Boswell’s “coven,” in which various women they met on dating apps were used for local thefts and sex in return for “love” and some money. “The headline is witchcraft, cult. But at its core is this more universal story of looking for belonging,” says producer Christopher St. John. “Obviously there’s the cautionary tale about tech.”
“With AI, it’s only going to get worse,” says executive producer and fellow Imagine Entertainment exec Sara Bernstein. “You really don’t know who you can trust.”

The documentary features interviews from multiple women who were scammed by Trail and Boswell, one of whom speaks in the third person to distance herself from the PTSD of her memories. “As documentarians, you want there to be a greater social value or conversation that can come,” says Bernstein, “as opposed to just retelling, frankly, what can be really graphic and gory details and having people relive their pain and suffering.”

In the documentary, Sydney’s sister Mackenzie Loofe expresses regret that she and her family didn’t offer more support regarding her sister’s sexuality. “Dating as a queer woman in middle America, there’s not a whole lot to choose from. Their way of coming out was through a dating app,” says Biegel. “So that alone made them vulnerable, because they really wanted to find their person. They wanted to feel a sense of belonging, and Sydney did. But what they couldn’t know, what was on the other side of the screen, was basically a trap waiting for them.”

The Loofe family “appreciated the opportunity to set the record straight” about Sydney, given what they felt was misleading press coverage around the case at the time of her murder, says St. John. “Sydney was misrepresented in their eyes as someone who was either involved in a crazy sex ring or involved in some sort of witchcraft, which she wasn’t,” he says. “She didn’t know these people, hadn’t met these people. It was this web of lies.”

The director spoke to Trail “on a daily basis for over a year until he agreed to give us audio and then eventually some video,” says Biegel. “Look, I watched the interviews the FBI had done with him, and he’s a game player. I also know he loves praise. So in order for me to build a rapport, I knew he was an artist, so I’m like, ‘Oh man, would you send me a painting?’ And his eyes opened up. I won him over.”

Once they had secured Trail’s participation from behind bars, they had to ensure it was used responsibly. “It’s a constant questioning, frankly, of everything he says, anything he’s promising,” says St. John. “We didn’t want to be another group of people manipulated by this guy, even from death row.”

Trail was sentenced to the death penalty following his trial in the summer of 2019. Boswell was convicted of first-degree murder and improper disposal of human remains in the fall of 2020 and was sentenced to life in prison the following year. “Bailey, we can say safely and without any doubt, is an incredibly complicated character. She wouldn’t talk to police, she wouldn’t talk to reporters, she wouldn’t talk to us,” says St. John. “She is a phantom at the center of this case. Since the trial, it seems she’s found it better to keep her cards close to her vest.”

As for those who escaped Trail and Boswell, “after experiencing a very harrowing issue in their lives, the girls in Aubrey’s group and even the Loofe family—everyone involved in this case—have gone on and lived happy, successful lives,” says Biegel. “And there’s an important message in that. People are more resilient than you think—they overcame a lot, and continue to do so.”

items.title: ‘The Pet Cemetery Murders’: HBO’s Latest True-Crime Tale Is a Microcosm of American Trauma
items.description: Stephen King’s horror novel Pet Sematary (1983) was published roughly two years before the real-life death of Dorothy Thompson, who owned and operated the St. Bernard Parish pet cemetery until her 1985 murder. Strangled, suffocated, wrapped in chains, and thro
items.author: Savannah Walsh
paragraphs: Stephen King’s horror novel Pet Sematary (1983) was published roughly two years before the real-life death of Dorothy Thompson, who owned and operated the St. Bernard Parish pet cemetery until her 1985 murder. Strangled, suffocated, wrapped in chains, and thrown in the Mississippi River, mere miles from the popular pet burial spot she ran, it would take nearly three decades to catch and convict groundskeeper Brandon Nodier, who in July 2014 pleaded guilty to manslaughter as part of a plea agreement and was sentenced to 10 years in prison for Thompson’s death.

When introduced to Thompson’s story about three years ago by true-crime writer Mikita Brottman, then working on a book about the case, documentarian Philip Cairney was struck by the amount of “historic trauma” that could transpire on one piece of land. “It became a litany of tragedy,” says Cairney, “the more you looked, the more you found.” So begins HBO’s The Pet Cemetery Murders, airing through October 25, in which Cairney unearths decades of death and dysfunction on one plot of rural Southern property.

“The killing occurred after Nodier duped Thompson into transferring possession of the property to him, then feared he would lose it after she sued to have the transaction voided,” St. Bernard Sheriff's Office colonel John Doran said at the time, as reported by Reuters. Police reopened the case in 2009 after a witness came forward saying Nodier had told him he was the killer and that Thompson’s ghost was haunting the witness’s dreams, Doran said in the documentary. “People genuinely almost fall down a foxhole when they become involved with this bit of land,” Cairney says, “because it does seem to suck you in and not let you go.”

Decades before the documentary’s central crimes, the Louisiana land was tied to racial violence—first against the region’s Indigenous population by white colonizers, then the dozens of formerly enslaved Black people murdered by mobs of white men during what became known as the Reconstruction-era 1868 St. Bernard Parish Massacre. “These are America’s original sins—enslavement, Native American genocide, women’s role in society,” Cairney says. “It’s that rich, fertile soil—to use a terrible metaphor—that means any story, if it’s got those layers, is interesting.”

Twenty years after the investigation into Thompson’s death went cold, in 2005, Hurricane Katrina wiped out key evidence from the case and decimated much of the pet cemetery. Touring the resulting land, “you’re forced to look Katrina in the eye,” says Cairney, who says being from Scotland offered him the right amount of distance from and perspective on the American atrocities tangled up with the place. “As an outsider, I wasn’t coming with the same cultural, social, political baggage that Americans might,” he tells VF. “The trauma of America is in the land, and whether that’s a metaphor or a literal fact you can decide for yourself. But the people in these areas with histories of enslavement, colonization, opioids, they’re dealing with the trauma, and it’s getting passed on from generation to generation.”

Even production on The Pet Cemetery Murders faced some paranormal activity, “from cameras jamming during interviews, to ghost sightings,” the director says. “The director of photography, whenever he put his camera on the ground, it would flip between stills and video. When he would pick it up, it would be fine. So you’re forced to reconcile an empirical rationalist worldview with something far more inexplicable.”

There are plenty of spirits who could be lurking around. In addition to the residents of the cemetery (a snake named Sarita that performed on The Johnny Carson Show was among the more famous pets laid to rest), a string of other deaths occurred on the property while Thompson had run of the place with her mother, Grace. As recounted in the docuseries, two men who were married to Dorothy died on the same plot of land—the first was fatally shot by Dorothy in 1970 in what authorities determined was an act of self-defense, and the second death, in 1978 by two gunshots to the back, was ruled a suicide by police.

Cairney was intrigued by the idea of exploring Dorothy as an “imperfect victim” still deserving of justice. “That was really important to remember: You can have a woman who died a horrible death, but she also can be a complicated character, and they can both sit side by side,” he says.

That duality was best embodied by the presence of Dorothy’s estranged daughter Kristine Wood, who was raised by her paternal grandparents in the wake of her mother’s substance abuse issues and is interviewed in the documentary. “We’re conditioned to want, especially female victims, to be ‘pure.’ This is a woman who had a really, really difficult life, and a really difficult death,” says Cairney, “and you have a daughter who’s been forced to reckon with that intergenerational trauma and to stop the cycle of it. That kept me committed to telling this story.”

There are more mysteries to unfurl in future episodes of Pet Cemetery Murders, starting with the isolated Grey Gardens–esque dynamic between Dorothy and her own mother, Grace, who opened the pet cemetery in 1946. “When we meet Grace, she looks like this kindly old lady sitting on a rocking chair,” Cairney says. “Then you realize she managed to reconcile a devout Christianity, with a pet cemetery, with mafia connections...I mean, you couldn’t make it up.”

The Louisiana land where remnants of the pet cemetery still stand invites plenty of local intrigue. “It’s one of those places locals go with a metal detector trying to find a hidden treasure supposedly buried there,” says Cairney. “It does attract an audience, even without us making the series.” But now that the filmmaker has become part of the land’s story, “you feel embroidered into the fabric of it,” he adds. “I’m never going to escape the tentacular grip of this place and this land, because it kind of gets inside your head, the story, and you can’t really get it out. So even though the series is done, dusted, and delivered,” Cairney shrugs a little, “it feels like it’s not done with me yet.”

items.title: ‘Widow’s Bay’ Creator Katie Dippold Would Marry Freddy Krueger, F Jason, and Kill Hellraiser
items.description: “I think this is a great way to start a podcast,” says Widow’s Bay creator and showrunner Katie Dippold. “If you can bring up semen in any way. That’s the publicity rule: The quicker you can get to that, the sooner you hook them.”
items.author: John Ross
paragraphs: “I think this is a great way to start a podcast,” says Widow’s Bay creator and showrunner Katie Dippold. “If you can bring up semen in any way. That’s the publicity rule: The quicker you can get to that, the sooner you hook them.”

Dippold has been telling me about sneaking into a movie theater when she was a kid and watching 10 minutes of The Silence of the Lambs. It was the scene when Hannibal Lecter first meets Clarice Starling; lucky for Dippold, she missed its ending, when Lecter’s cellmate flings bodily fluids at Starling as she walks away. “I remember seeing that part a couple of years later,” Dippold says. “[I was still] too young to understand it.” Eventually, Dippold saw the whole movie; she now counts the film as one of the greatest ever made, alongside Halloween and Jaws.

On paper, Dippold is a comedy writer. She worked on Mad TV, then Parks and Recreation, then started writing major studio comedies including The Heat, Snatched, and the all-women Ghostbusters remake (more on that later). But her love of horror has been a theme throughout her career, including a viral tweet of her dressed as the Babadook at a Halloween party filled with people in normal clothes. She marries her two loves in Apple TV’s word-of-mouth hit Widow’s Bay, a horror-comedy for which Dippold initially drafted the pilot in 2008.

The television business has evolved since Dippold first took the show’s pilot script to buyers. Initially, she says, Widow’s Bay “was more like a show you would see on network TV. I don’t think in that kind of show you would do a flashback from centuries ago.”

On this week’s Little Gold Men, Dippold reflects on the success of Widow’s Bay—which is currently up for 19 Emmy awards, including best comedy—the defining features of a comedy, her career thus far, and the internet’s love of all things Patricia.
Vanity Fair: Do you find comedy in horror films? For example, Ari Aster thinks that Midsommar is a dark comedy.

Katie Dippold: I completely get that. I saw Midsommar and I laughed so hard. The parts of the movie where the boyfriend is gaslighting her were so perfectly on the money. So I agree with him. I thought it was hilarious and terrifying. And then there are horror movies that are done by people I can tell just have a really good sense of humor. Jordan Peele and Zach Cregger are making horror movies, but they’re very playful and fun in moments. They are also brilliant comedy writers, even if they’re not making a comedy.

You know what’s funny about Jordan? I worked with him at Mad TV, and I remember he had a poster of The Descent in his dressing room. I remember he was telling me later about Get Out, and I just immediately assumed, “It’s like a horror-comedy?” And he said, “No, it’s a horror movie.” There are so many ways he could have done that movie where it was more of a comedy, but he loves horror.

It would’ve been so easy for him to get a comedy made. I remember I tried for years. I had a horror movie that I was trying to direct, and I just went down such a rabbit hole of it where every time it went somewhere, the place got shut down.
You have been working on this show in some form or another for 20 years. Can you talk a little about how it’s evolved?

I would say, first and foremost, TV has changed so much since I wrote the pilot. I just really hadn’t fleshed out the world or thought seriously about what this would be like as a full series. It was a little bit spoofier. It was just jokier. And it would’ve felt more like a parody.

Over the years, I kept thinking about Widow’s Bay as a real place. What would this island really be like? And what are the kind of scary things that I would want to see on the screen? I remember then TV started changing. I was watching shows like Atlanta and then Barry, and I just loved the stuff they were doing. It opened up the world to me of imagining all the different kinds of episodes you could do.

Then I sent it to Hiro Murai, who was my dream director for it because I loved Atlanta. He came on board—to my shock, because I was such a huge fan of his. Then we brought it to Apple and then Matt Cherniss [Apple TV’s head of programming] bought it in the room, as they say. He said, “Okay, great. Let’s do it.” And that is not something I had experienced before, and don’t know if I’ll ever experience again.
You shot this show on location in Massachusetts. Do you have a connection to Stephen King’s New England?

I grew up loving Stephen King. Growing up in New Jersey, I always romanticized New England. I like writing things where you just want to be there. Some people will write painful experiences, but I tend to write situations that I wish I were in. So when we scouted in January, you could still just feel all these buildings were real. It adds this authenticity that I think is so crucial. Because that’s the thing about the show, as ridiculous as it is: You have to buy everything that’s happening, or any false moment really takes you out of it.
Let’s talk about Kate O’Flynn, who plays Patricia. She’s become a favorite on the internet. What did she do in the audition that made you think that she could be Patricia?

Her audition was not what I expected. If you read the scripts, you wouldn’t imagine this person, if I’m being honest. I almost had to shake off what I thought Patricia was going to be and embrace what Kate did because it was so special. Patricia was a little bit based on my mom. There are some things about my mom that are in there. This sort of passive aggressiveness. I think Kate O’Flynn just made that her own.

Patricia is the conduit for a lot of jokes about gender on the show, which I thought really worked. Do you think that’s part of why the internet has just fallen so in love with her? I feel like there’s this underdog aspect to her that people relate to.

There is. I feel like she wants to be seen and heard, and she tries to do the right thing, but she’s also not self-righteous. There’s something authentic and real about her. There’s something about her that’s very inviting.

This is a weird thing to say. It’s a theory I have that I have not said out loud: People bring up that Babadook tweet of me and then relate it to the show. I feel like the connection is that there’s something inviting about these characters. Patricia puts herself out there in the way that the Babadook photo does.

This is a weird story—but I remember when I was in fourth grade, I was allowed to have a Halloween party. My parents said you have to invite everyone in your class. But there was this one kid who was the outcast, and I was like, “I can’t invite him. Then no one will come.” Which is terrible. But my parents made me invite him. I went around to every student and gave them their invitation. I remember this moment; it’s burned in my brain for the rest of my life. When I gave him his invitation, he welled up and was in shock and said, “Really, I’m invited too?”

That just stuck with me forever. Part of me loves Halloween because it is something everyone can do. Anyways, it’s a long, weird, emotional way to say there’s something about Patricia that would invite you in, and would never want you to feel bad.
When you wrote the Ghostbusters remake, were you shocked by the sheer amount of discourse about having an all-female cast?

When Paul Feig [the director of Ghostbusters] said he wanted to do a reboot with all women, even as a Ghostbusters fan, I was looking forward to a sequel with the original cast passing down the baton. I had friends working on versions of that movie, and I knew it wasn’t going to happen. So when Paul brought it up, I had a mixed reaction. I knew people aren’t going to like the reboot part of it. To be honest, I knew we were asking for it.

The reaction was more hateful than I would’ve anticipated. But it’s also Twitter. Sometimes a hundred people on Twitter feels like the entire world. It became this thing where if you said you didn’t like the movie, you were sexist. And that’s not true. You can not like the movie. But then there were also people who were very sexist. So both things were true.
We’re going to play a fun game: Fuck, Marry, Kill, horror-movie edition. First, final girls: Sidney Prescott from the Scream series, Laurie Strode from Halloween, Maxine from the X series.

This is painful to me because I don’t want to kill anyone, and I love all these people. But you have to marry Laurie. She’s the icon. It’s Jamie Lee Curtis, Halloween. That’s everything. I guess I would spend time with Sidney. I was 16 when Scream came out, so that was a real touchstone for me. I don’t want to kill Maxine. I love the X movies. I love Ti West. But that wasn’t a formative year for me when I saw those movies. So if I had to get rid of one, I would sadly have to. Sorry, Ti West.
Freddy Krueger, Jason Voorhees, Hellraiser.

I don’t want to marry any of these guys. But if we’re talking about who meant the most to me, then I would marry Freddy Krueger. Just the poster alone terrorized my childhood before I ever saw the movie. He seems like he would be a lot to deal with, but I would marry him. I would have sex with Jason because it’s like a summer-fling kind of movie. And I would kill Hellraiser. Even though there’s something fundamentally about Hellraiser that scares me the most, I would have to kill him.
Finally, quirky witches: Minnie Castevet played by Ruth Gordon in Rosemary’s Baby, Anjelica Huston in The Witches, and Fairuza Balk in The Craft.

Oh, that’s very hard. I have to marry Ruth Gordon. Yeah. I love that performance so much. She’s so incredible. Gosh, the other two? I can’t. I’m having sex with them both. I’m cheating. I can’t. I can’t kill all of them. I refuse.

items.title: Jack Antonoff Knocks Ed Sheeran for Caving to Billionaire's Demand to Drop Macklemore
items.description: Jack Antonoff said Ed Sheeran should have just canceled “the whole fucking tour” instead of caving to pressure to boot Macklemore over the rapper’s comments on the Israel-Gaza war.
items.author: Jon Blistein
paragraphs: Jack Antonoff said Ed Sheeran should have just canceled “the whole fucking tour” instead of caving to pressure to boot Macklemore over the rapper’s comments on the Israel-Gaza war.

Sheeran “missed a massive, beautiful opportunity there,” Antonoff told The Guardian in a new interview. “Just cancel the whole fucking tour, then play for free outside each venue, raise a bunch of money, rather than let a fucking billionaire tell you what to do.”

In September, Macklemore was dropped from the North American leg of Sheeran’s Loop Tour after the owners of several stadiums said he would not be allowed to perform at their venues. At the first two shows of the tour at MetLife Stadium outside New York City, Macklemore called for a “Free Palestine,” expressed solidarity with people in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, showed images of the devastation from Israel’s war in Gaza, and performed his protest song, “Hind’s Hall.”

After being dropped, Macklemore released a statement saying Robert Kraft — the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots — had barred him from playing Gillette Stadium. Macklemore claimed Kraft also “rallied some of the other stadium owners” to push Sheeran to drop him, or face having the shows canceled. Kraft, for his part, confirmed he barred Macklemore from Gillette, but did not address the claim that he rallied the other owners.

Sheeran’s decision to drop Macklemore caused a massive backlash. The other openers for the North American leg of his Loop Tour dropped off the trek, as did Finneas, who was set to open the South American leg of the tour. The Irish folk band, Beoga, who had been performing a short set of songs with Sheeran each night also left the trek.

Antonoff, who is Jewish, has also faced criticism for expressing solidarity with Palestinians and saying “Free Palestine” onstage. But he said the Macklemore/Sheeran debacle has only made him feel “way more emboldened to say it now, because it’s not in any way a strange, uncomfortable, or controversial thing to say, it’s a deeply human thing to say. If you think it is [controversial] you’re lost in some other sauce that is so crazy.”

Of possible pushback from promoters or venue owners, Antonoff quipped, “They’re going to let some fucking promoter tell me what I can say? Don’t book me. I’ll play for free outside.” He then added, “The reason it’s not an anomaly or niche issue is because we all live in a world where billionaires are constantly telling us what to do. So stand the fuck up.”

items.title: Flaming Lips Announce First Album in Six Years and Concert Series in U.S. and U.K.
items.description: The Flaming Lips have announced their first album of new material in six years, The Teardrop Throbs, which will arrive Jan. 22 via Third Man Records. Today, the band has released the lead single “God Will Control the Werewolves.”
items.author: Jaeden Pinder
paragraphs: The Flaming Lips have announced their first album of new material in six years, The Teardrop Throbs, which will arrive Jan. 22 via Third Man Records. Today, the band has released the lead single “God Will Control the Werewolves.”

“God Will Control the Werewolves” was inspired by a story about Wayne Coyne’s sons, Bloom and Rex, who were playing hide and seek during a full moon. “Bloom asked me if, while him and Rex were hiding , [if] the werewolves would get them,” Coyne said. “I told him God would control the werewolves for a little bit while we played hide n seek. The way I heard the song sounding (in my head) was kind of Pink Floyd Dark Side Of The Moon BUT Syd Barrett is still in the band.”

To celebrate the album, the band will play a series of intimate concerts in New York, Los Angeles, Nashville, Chicago, and London in 2027. The Flaming Lips will play two shows in each city, with one set highlighting their new record and tracks from their early career, and the other featuring The Teardrop Throbs reimaginings and songs from the aughts onward.

Pre-sales for the shows will occur Wednesday, Oct. 28 and Thursday, Oct. 29 at 10:00 a.m. local time. General on-sale begins Friday, Oct. 30 at 10:00 a.m. local time via the Flaming Lips’ official website.

The Teardrop Throbs will be the Flaming Lips’ 17th album, following 2020’s American Head. It’ll also be their first record without Steven Drozd, who joined the band in 1991. At the end of 2025, the multi-instrumentalist said he was “officially done” with the Flaming Lips after a “personal crisis” caused him to take a step back from touring duties.

While Drozd said he wanted to be a non-touring member of the band, he alleged that Coyne disagreed on what his new role would be. “Wayne and I disagreed on what I should do moving forward, so we just kind of agreed that I would step back,” he said. “Then stepping back turned into not coming back.”

Coyne, for his part, pushed back on Drozd’s characterization of his departure, writing on Instagram, “the reason he left is sad , and infuriating…. it is HIS responsibility to tell everyone what happened… what he told everyone was a lie.”
This year, the Flaming Lips celebrated the 20th anniversary of At War With the Mystics with a special reissue containing a massive selection of rarities.
