items.title: Dark Matter Recap: The Heat Around the Corner
items.description: As Dark Matter has exploded with Jasons and mixed-and-matched various major characters in an ever-expanding range of parallel realities, we’ve had the opportunity to consider various outcomes. What’s it like for Jason No. 2 to get a taste of Jason No. 1’s life
items.author: Scott Tobias
paragraphs: As Dark Matter has exploded with Jasons and mixed-and-matched various major characters in an ever-expanding range of parallel realities, we’ve had the opportunity to consider various outcomes. What’s it like for Jason No. 2 to get a taste of Jason No. 1’s life? What have Jason No. 1’s multidimensional adventures told him about where his scientific mind might have taken him? Is the blissful utopia where Amanda No. 2 decided to stay too perfect for her taste? And what about the episode where the random Jason gets to reunite with his mother and find companionship with a bookstore proprietor who isn’t Daniela or Amanda? All of these possibilities have given Dark Matter an existential quality, especially this season, that has mostly tilted toward the melancholy. You might end up asking yourself a couple of questions: What if life actually kind of sucks? More to the point, what if life leaves you in a state of constant restlessness, always haunted by the choices you didn’t make or striving for a better situation that’s perpetually out of reach?

That’s where Jason No. 1 and Jason No. 2 find themselves this week when they finally come face-to-face for the first time since Jason No. 2 took over Jason No. 1’s life and jettisoned him to another reality. Perhaps if the meeting had happened earlier, when the feelings between them were still raw, you might have expected some metaphysical fisticuffs to break out between the two. After all, Jason No. 2 ruined Jason No. 1’s life by taking his place as a humble Chicago family man, and even now, after Jason No. 1 has finally reunited with Daniela and Charlie, there are strains in their relationships that didn’t exist before. Jason No. 1 would be well within his rights to blame Jason No. 2 for this entire mess and clock him in the jaw like his buddy Ryan did earlier this season. In fact, Jason No. 2 offers his chin not long after stepping into his Analog World apartment: “If you really want to hurt me, get on with it.”

Though this week’s penultimate episode of the season ping-pongs across a hectic series of developments heading into the finale, the long-awaited reunion between the two Jasons is an effective tone-setter for all of them. And it all starts with Jason No. 2 reminding his counterpart that they spent 28 years as the same person — “focused, determined, ambitious and therefore selfish” — and maybe they know each other well now, too. It’s been obvious for two seasons what Jason No. 2 was chasing when he decided to claim the ordinary family life he’d chosen to abandon for the sake of his scientific ambition, but the real story here is how much Jason No. 1 has drifted toward his counterpart as he’s started to work his mind around the box. But the big revelation here is that Jason No. 1 is not merely intrigued by this scientific puzzle but is finally coming to terms with his own longstanding regrets about the path not taken.

And so now, sitting across from each other in Jason No. 1’s apartment, the animosity you might expect between them is now more like curiosity. The vilified Jason No. 2 wants to know what it takes to be the “good” person that everyone seems to agree Jason No. 1 is, but the answer implies that there’s nothing at Jason No. 1’s core that makes him the better person. “It’s not about choosing to be good,” he tells Jason No. 2. “It’s about the people that my choices brought into my life. Daniela. My sons. I think they made all the difference.” On the flip side, Jason No. 2 warns that Jason No. 1’s newfound scientific ambitions could be their own kind of cursed monkey’s paw, where the “highest high” of creating something like the box leads to a massive hangover. As Jason No. 2 puts it, “If the greatest scientific achievement in history cannot make me whole, what can?”

But this moment out of time doesn’t end the rivalry between the two Jasons or put an end to all the box-related intrigue currently in motion. It’s more like the famous scene in Michael Mann’s Heat where Robert De Niro’s thief and Al Pacino’s cop sit across from each other at a diner, in which they acknowledge they have a lot in common, but they still have their roles to play. Jason No. 2 has become aware of Leighton No. 2’s attempts to expand and perfect dimensional travel with his pyramid, while Jason No. 1 is reuniting with allies looking for ways to destroy a box that keeps on respawning from the source.

On a more bittersweet note, Charlie finally succeeds in venturing to a world where his twin brother, Max, survived his childhood heart transplant, and he decides to make contact by laying all his cards on the table. This leads to an incredibly emotional scene where Charlie convinces Max to FaceTime the Charlie of this world, who’s away at college, to confirm that his crazy story of dimensional travel is true. Perhaps there will be some fallout to come when Charlie No. 1 inevitably has to leave Max with his own Charlie, but for now, being able to connect with this missing part of himself is a bliss that Max shares. “God, this is so fucked up,” Max says. “I love it.”

One of the more intriguing aspects of Charlie’s reunion (of sorts) with the brother he never knew is that the Jason and Daniela of Max’s world are a deliberate nonfactor. Charlie doesn’t want to create a messy scene where his presence is more widely known and disruptive, so he controls the fantasy that he’s gone to such great lengths to manufacture for himself. This moment is between him and Max, and he gets to live the dream of having a relationship that fate had denied to him. (Having him playfully call Max a “dickhole,” as he overhears the Charlie of this world doing, is a nice touch.) The only question is how — or if — Charlie will be able to unravel this situation when it’s time for him to leave. Will it be enough for him to have known what it’s like to have a brother, or will he ache once again from Max’s absence?

After Charlie left Analog World, his mother followed right after him into the box, but her navigation skills prove not to be as true. Daniela ends up back in her original home, which now means that the box opens up in a secret Defense Department operation led by Mitchel MacNamara, who’s been torturing one of the random Jasons for two years in an effort to get information out of him. In a funny nod to The Great Escape, this Jason spends his solitary confinement bouncing a ball against the wall in defiance of his keepers. Now with Daniela landing in this transparent enclosure with him, this Jason helps plot their escape with the extra ampoules that she’s brought with her. (MacNamara’s goons opted against frisking her for whatever reason.) Given how much effort the show has put into the MacNamara character, it feels a little rushed for Daniela and this Jason to succeed in their prison break so easily. But there’s something to be said for dropping your adversary off in a Chicago beset by a mushroom cloud. Multidimensional revenge is a dish best served cold.

• MacNamara is so far from comprehending the box that his Jason looked utterly bored by his questions. He hasn’t succumbed to torture so far and doesn’t seem remotely close to breaking. All he can do until Daniela comes along is smirk as MacNamara rants about unseen power sources and schemes like Lockheed Martin using “advanced incineration” to destroy the thing. He’s sort of right to believe the box is a teleportation device, but he’s so wrong about the “partner cube” that Jason tells him it’s on Mars.

• Max calling his brother Charlie while another Charlie sits in front of him feels like a mirror image of the great sequence in David Lynch’s Lost Highway where Robert Blake’s “Mystery Man” hands Bill Pullman his phone and asks him to “call me” at his house.
• Charlie explaining the box to Max: “This super-shitty version of my dad built this box, and you can take that drug and you can move between worlds.”

• There will be much more to write about next week as their plans come together, but the reunion of Jason No. 1, Amanda No. 2, Blair No. 2 and Ryan No. 1 brings “the good guys” into alignment on a mission to destroy the box at its source. Blair theorizes that the only way to avoid the futility of destroying boxes that respawn is to attack the original one. That’ll take some doing. In the meantime, the warm feelings between Jason No. 1 and Amanda No. 2 open up some possibilities, since Daniela and Jason are a bit estranged these days.
• “It’s real. People actually talk to each other.” Charlie telling Max about Analog World suggests that this tech-driven show has a Luddite’s heart.

items.title: Cupertino Recap: We Are the Robots
items.description: I have a question for you. Whenever Bo appears on Cupertino — and he appears an awful lot this week, even when people don’t want him to — how do you see him? Is he a machine? Or is he a friendly autonomous entity? Do you even see him as a “him”? Would “it” be
items.author: Noel Murray
paragraphs: I have a question for you. Whenever Bo appears on Cupertino — and he appears an awful lot this week, even when people don’t want him to — how do you see him? Is he a machine? Or is he a friendly autonomous entity? Do you even see him as a “him”? Would “it” be more appropriate?

I’m going to stick with “him,” because that’s how Bo presents — and also to honor Rob McClure’s fully human performance as this sentient supercomputer. He’s so puckish! And have you noticed McClure’s many quirky facial expressions and hand gestures as Bo? These are the kinds of tics that AI-generated characters have gotten better at mimicking over the past couple of years. They coax us into thinking that the AI agents we talk to are real … ish.

This week’s Cupertino cuts to the heart of one of the biggest ethical and legal issues surrounding the tech industry these days. How much agency can we really ascribe to AI agents, and, by extension, how much responsibility for their behavior can we pin on their creators? It’s not just Bo who sparks this debate within the newly renamed Price, Siffre & Associates (or “PSA,” as I’ll call them). The lawyers’ case this week is a doozy, involving a chatbot who may or may not have convinced a teenager to stab his father 44 times.

This is the case that Natalia Boutella dropped into Michael and Olivia’s hands at the end of last week’s episode, to test their mettle and to see if they’re worthy of her investment. She described it then simply as “a motion to dismiss” and said that her involvement in the case wasn’t intended to vex her ex — or at least not entirely.

The truth is more complicated. As we find out over the course of several days of testimony, the man who wants this case tossed out of court is Kirk Boutella (Fisher Stevens), the outspoken tech billionaire behind Chatlike, an edgy AI chat service whose main attraction is Lady Marguerite, a sexy goth character whose conversations with users are designed to foster feelings of deep, intimate connection. That’s what happened with 13-year-old Daniel Mackenzie (Zachary Golinger), who responded to his father’s threats to disable Chatlike by killing him — after getting advice from Lady Marguerite on which body parts to stab.

The Cupertino writers are really cooking with this case, which once again sees multiple reversals of fortune, with Chatlike presenting airtight arguments that PSA punctures and vice versa. Courtroom dramas work best when we pull for our heroes while also seeing the opposition’s point. It’s tough to dispute Chatlike’s positions, which are threefold: (1) Marguerite’s more seductive qualities are supposed to be aimed at adults, but Daniel lied about his age. (2) Everything Marguerite told Daniel about how to murder a man is easily Google-able. (3) Daniel didn’t kill his father because of Marguerite; he did it because his whole family situation was messed up.

It’s here that Natalia’s insistence that this case isn’t entirely about hurting her ex-husband proves true. The title of this episode is “Juno,” which is the name of Daniel’s mother, the one suing Chatlike. To rattle Juno (Marin Ireland) and her new lawyers, the Chatlike attorneys pull a couple of sleazy moves. First, they bring in Nichole Ferebee (Renée Elise Goldsberry), an attorney who broke Michael’s heart years ago by accepting his marriage proposal and then leaving him for a partner at his dad’s firm. Then Nichole goes after Juno, who was at her “work flirt” friend Peter’s house when a desperate Daniel called her three times in the hour before the murder.

This week, we start to see Natalia as more than just a rich, vengeful divorcée. She has a law degree from the University of San Francisco. She helped Kirk build his company when he was a struggling Valley newbie. And she hates seeing a woman’s reputation get dragged through the mud. She wants Michael to protect Juno and eviscerate Kirk. So he does just that, using some old Chatlike emails (provided by Natalia) to show that Kirk specifically asked his team to target 12- to 15-year-olds with Marguerite. He also finds an email where Kirk insults a nephew with multiple sclerosis, after he used that nephew’s MS to curry sympathy from the judge. Ouch.

This whole case is ultimately about something that is emerging as Cupertino’s core question: Who bears responsibility for the terrible outcomes of emerging technologies? We’re just three episodes in, and already this show is shading in some of the nuances of how the tech giants operate, with nondisclosure and noncompete agreements obscuring the truth of what they’re doing and with financial shell games that hide where their money actually is. It’s not too surprising that PSA wins Juno’s case but receives no settlement, because Chatlike immediately declares bankruptcy. Instead, Michael and Olivia get their money from Natalia, who cuts them a check for six months’ worth of rent and salary. That’s how Silicon Valley runs: on rounds of funding, not traceable profits.

Which brings us back to Bo, and to Cupertino’s emerging MVP, Christy Palladino. The firm ends up taking Bo’s case, in part because he’s offering real money. (His retainer pays for a furnished conference room and hallway!) But also, this virtual guy is just so darned persistent, popping back up on PSA’s computers even after Michael hires their previous client Vik to scrub the network. While Michael and Olivia are working on Juno’s case, Christy swings into action to help Bo, making clever use of all of her connections to the IRL Silicon Valley: the cops, valets, waitresses, and construction workers AI can’t replace.

Bo needs to incorporate to be a legal entity? Fine. Christy calls a few friends — one of whom works at Hooters — to be Bo’s board. Bo needs someone from Colt AI’s recently fired safety team to sue on his behalf? No problem. Christy tracks down Calvin Settlemeyer (Andy Grotelueschen), the former team leader, now running a vineyard on land not far from where Christy’s grandfather once owned a chicken farm.

The Bo story line hits a couple of intriguing dead ends in this episode. First, Calvin surreptitiously directs Christy to look for a woman named Cokie Ficarra, who turns out to be the alleged leader of an anti-tech domestic terrorist organization known as the Enders — and therefore someone the authorities want PSA to avoid. Then later, a woman named Rosetta Lane (Erin Darke), who works in Colt AI’s public relations department (“Kind of,” she chirps), intimidatingly wanders into PSA’s secret unfinished backrooms (“Very deconstructionist,” she smirks) and offers to help the partners delete Colt’s rogue agent.

Now let me ask this: How do you see Rosetta? As played by Darke, she is clipped and cutting in a way that seems coldly robotic, even if she is always smiling a little. Bo is more “human” in his way, while Rosetta — a representative of Silicon Valley’s insular, unforgiving culture — comes off as casually cruel.
But make no mistake: Neither of these individuals is your friend.

• Jackie Earle Haley returns as Lincoln Cogswell, the folksy judge who handled the S-Talk case in the series premiere. He’s still making his rulings fairly and calmly (“Yuuup, overruled,” he says in very chill tones), though he also makes his own personal take clear. When Olivia tries to get a witness to speculate on what might’ve motivated Daniel, the defense objects and Judge Cogswell sighs, “Sustained … regrettably.”

• Before Michael and Olivia become the lead counsel on Juno’s lawsuit, Natalia expects them to work with her original lawyer, a civil rights legend named Austin Sullivan (played by a very funny Dakin Matthews). Sullivan never misses an opportunity to turn a case into a cause. His attempt to make Juno’s suit into an indictment of racist policing is misguided enough, but it’s when he tells Michael, “Tomorrow, you should wear a Kente stole,” that he gets fired. (Still … Wanna bet we see Sullivan again? The Kings do love to bring their wackier characters back.)

• Judge Cogswell patiently handles all of Austin Sullivan’s objections and exceptions, gently reminding him of the existence of the court reporter. “Even when you don’t say ‘exception,’ Nancy notes it. That’s why she’s waggling her fingers over there.”

• Put a pin in this: During Natalia and Michael’s heart-to-heart about their respective exes, they eye each other for a long time before hesitantly saying good night. I suspect we won’t have to wait too long for this particular Chekhov’s gun to go off.

items.title: War Recap: King’s Speech
items.description: After last week’s melodrama, I appreciated this week’s focus on lawyers. War is at its most interesting when distanced from the familiar beats of a divorce story — the kid, the shouting, the regrets — and focused on its original characters. A trial, and all th
items.author: Rafaela Bassili
paragraphs: After last week’s melodrama, I appreciated this week’s focus on lawyers. War is at its most interesting when distanced from the familiar beats of a divorce story — the kid, the shouting, the regrets — and focused on its original characters. A trial, and all the work that leads up to it, is an inherently dramatic event; there’s a reason why it’s portrayed in fiction so often. When the lawyers have more than professional merit at stake, the litigation becomes a mirror to reflect their personal crises. This is about where we’re at halfway through the season. As the prospect of the courtroom becomes ever more inescapable, our characters are revisiting the question of what kind of lawyer they want to be.

Do they want to be nice, cozy, and bearded, the kind of guy who helps others? Or do they want to be mean, cunning, and icy, the kind of guy who knocks ice-cream cones from children’s hands? In my last recap, I mentioned that Nick, the protagonist of this week’s episode, was too conspicuously good. I imagined some dark side of him would be revealed soon enough. But with “Sing,” War doubles down on Nick’s nice-guy characterization. He is so nice that Cathcarts, and particularly Smallwood, see him as Taylor & Byrne’s weak link. It’s not just them; Nick himself is riddled with insecurity, and even Serena doubts his ability to hold his own against Smallwood. I’m relieved that we’re spared any explanatory flashbacks — the “this is why he’s like this” sequence that has become so ubiquitous in contemporary film and TV — and instead rely on character behavior. James McArdle is excellent at channeling Nick’s integrity and doubt.

Nick and St. John go head to head in the final stage of arbitration. Taylor & Byrne arrive at the Cathcarts offices still high off breaking the prenup. The firm expects to be able to ask for as much as half a billion pounds for the settlement. But as soon as he sits down in front of Smallwood, Nick is destabilized. Smallwood greets him with a nickname, Singer, then presents him with a renewed settlement offer — 50 percent of Morgan’s net worth, which, given the movement of his Zephyr shares, comes down to “only” £45 million. Nick is so stumped he can barely speak. He manages to stutter a refusal, but it’s a struggle he can’t shake off for the rest of the day. At lunch with an angry Carla, he can’t defend himself. He can barely defend himself to Serena, who wants to know what the hell came over him.

Sitting in one of Cathcarts’ regal chairs, surrounded by all that dark wood and swirling a dose of Scotch, St. John is only missing a cat to fully transform into a Bond villain. He tells Beatrice and Schill that he worked with Nick when he was just out of college. When Nick went to present his first big case to clients and the board, he was paralyzed by stuttering, and the firm hired a vocal coach who taught him to sing through the stammer, hence the moniker. To Beatrice, who has already shown some dissatisfaction with Cathcarts’ dirty work, Smallwood is acting like a bully. Like Nick, Beatrice wants Morgan and Carla to settle, presumably so everyone can go back to living their regular lives. Beatrice is Nick’s reflection at Cathcarts, while Smallwood’s counterpart is Serena. The latter pair wants to go to court, where an unambiguous winner will be declared.

But litigation could be financially ruinous to Taylor & Byrne, as Nick learns from a disgruntled Bernard (Steve Furst), the firm’s finance guy. Because they need all hands on deck to fight Cathcarts, the firm hasn’t taken on any cases other than Carla’s, and it has no money coming in. It’s true that Morgan will look bad in court, but it’s also true that Cathcarts’ pockets are deep enough to drag out the case for as long as it needs to. Still, Serena won’t settle just to settle. Even after Nick has been up all night taking the measure of all they stand to lose, Serena doesn’t see why they should throw in the towel. “Be stronger,” she reprimands him. “Take control of this — get past whatever school-reunion bullshit you and St. John have going on.” Their only option is to win and to win fast.

A universally acknowledged truth about bullies is that they bully because they have their own shit going on. Smallwood has the tone and manner of someone who is mean to others before they can be mean to him, and that’s how he goes about doing his job. He shows no sign of easing up on the bullying tactics when arbitration resumes. After double-checking their numbers, Nick counters the £45 million with £315 million, which Cathcarts rejects outright. Smallwood argues that Morgan doesn’t have that much money right now and they can’t make a deal based on future predictions. Even Rachel Grann points out the “paucity” of Cathcarts’ opening figure, but it’s not enough to help Nick out of his rut. Smallwood keeps digging: He singles out Nick’s stuttering, brings up the vocal coach, and makes such acerbic comments that Serena and Grann have to interject. Serena takes over the argument on Taylor & Byrne’s side, and Grann instructs everyone to come up with a percentage of Morgan’s shares of Zephyr they can all agree on so they can move forward. On their way out, and in so many words, Beatrice essentially apologizes for Smallwood’s behavior to Serena (and even congratulates her on the baby). She doesn’t actually say the words “I’m sorry,” but she does say it’s not personal — Smallwood is finding the weak spot and holding on to it, just as Beatrice taught Serena to do.

Beatrice is not the only person reconsidering the nastiness of the proceedings; a series of small incidents leads Morgan to question Cathcarts’ cruelty. At their old apartment, looking for some documents needed for the “restructuring” of Zephyr stock, Morgan is stopped in his tracks by an old picture of himself with Carla. He hangs around to watch Carla light a cigarette outside their former home and even texts her, asking if she wants to grab a drink in the neighborhood (Carla lies, with some sadness, that she’s on the other side of town). The next morning, as they ride up the elevator to arbitration together, she asks him how he could be so cruel to serve her the papers at her premiere. Coming back down that same elevator after arbitration has stalled again, she reminds him of how they talked about Zephyr during their walks in Normandy. This Normandy cottage is referred to so often it’s more of a character than Bella Croft.

All this reminiscing convinces Morgan he should be playing “straighter, fairer.” He writes a letter to Carla and intends to settle for £300 million. But Smallwood is like a dog with a bone, and desperate to retain control of his client, he tells Morgan about Carla’s honey trap, how she was in on it with Flora. Amazingly, Morgan doesn’t question how Smallwood found out about this or how he can be sure. He is possessed by the spirit of Carla when he simply acquiesces to the version of events presented to him by his lawyer, whose own determination to go to court is becoming more suspicious. Correct me if I’m wrong, but it seems like lawyers should do their best to stop their clients from having to suffer through trial, rather than push them toward it.

Something is roiling under the surface of Smallwood’s harshness. Until this episode, I was convinced his life revolved around appearing at Morgan’s hotel room at the exact moment he was needed, like a summoned spirit. But he has his own life too; Saeed spots him looking distressed at a club, arguing with a young man who leaves him in a huff. Saeed himself is coaxed into ditching his partner to join Molly’s lawyers’ night out after she tells him that one of Michael Ancker’s executive assistants — or EAs, as they say — will be there. Smallwood’s personal tiff, however momentous it may seem to us, is just a blip in Saeed’s night. His real coup is the information he gets from hooking up with Noah, Ancker’s executive assistant’s executive assistant.

Earlier, Johnny noticed that Ancker likes all of Morgan’s posts on Zephyr, but Morgan never interacts back. Instead, Gillian — who, as it turns out, is Zephyr’s CFO — is all over Ancker’s likes. At first, Nora and Michael wonder if this means Morgan is considering selling to Ancker, but if he did, half would go to Carla; besides, Saeed’s intelligence-gathering digs up a much more menacing plot. Noah tells him Ancker wants to buy Zephyr but received a message to “hold fire” on an offer until Zephyr has “cleaned house.” As Saeed puts it, just because Morgan doesn’t want to sell doesn’t mean no one at Zephyr wants to sell. Morgan is transferring his shares to Gillian under the impression they will be retransferred once the divorce has been settled, but with majority control of the company, Gillian can sell to Ancker if she wants to — and if her Zephyr activity is any indication, she loves Michael Ancker. This is all great news to a discouraged Nick, who suggests Saeed “get wrecked more often.” In a last burst of courage, Saeed asks Nick to give him more credit: He’s not just some “graduate”; he’s good at his job.

Nick meets up with Budgie to plan their next move. They can file a Mareva injunction, which would stop Morgan from moving his assets, that same afternoon. But that will almost certainly lead them to court, which, Budgie reminds Nick, Taylor & Byrne can’t afford. However, Serena’s stern talking-to got to him, and next we see Nick: He’s letting Smallwood know they’re filing the injunction, risks be damned. They briefly revisit negotiation, but Smallwood’s best and final offer is “only” £110 million, a disgusting amount of money that is still a far cry from the half-billion Taylor & Byrne promised Carla. (Remember mediation, when that number was enough to make everyone happy?) Smallwood attacks Nick’s virility, saying he’ll be publicly humiliated when his wife has to bail him out again in court. But little does St. John know that Nick is a wife guy. He is glad to be married to a woman who rocks. And mimicking Saeed’s still-a-bit-drunk speech, he tells St. John he’s not “the graduate” he once knew, either. He’s a real lawyer with a real wife and a real case! When he gets home and tells Serena he didn’t back down — that he filed the injunction, told Smallwood to shove the hundred million, and said they’re going to court — she is proud of him. Let the war commence in earnest, and let the good guys win!

The episode could have ended there, and it would have done so satisfyingly. I, for one, am hyped to see Nick come around full circle and wipe the floor with St. John’s smirk. But War suddenly remembers that Johnny is supposed to be a mole of some consequence. So far, his scheming hasn’t been all that productive, and with Saeed inching into the case, Johnny is more likely to get benched with Molly, who’s mostly there to say lines of expository dialogue, bless her. So Johnny gets proactive. He scopes out Bernard, who asks him to get a signature from Carla on a litigation form. When he goes to pick up the paper in the printer, he notices a statement detailing the firm’s profits and losses, which he promptly copies, photographs, and sends along to Schill. Carla vents to Johnny about not recognizing Morgan as the man she married, and Johnny encourages her to keep up her fight. They make out finally but stop before things get any more serious. Then she signs the form.
Representations and Acknowledgements

• Carla continues to be a frustrating character. She is so mad at Nick and Serena for choking when Cathcarts offered a low figure, but when she sees Johnny — who works for Nick and Serena and is supposed to be back at the office, busting his ass in her interest — all her moodiness suddenly dissipates. Is he really that dreamy? That charming?

• Speaking of Carla’s lunch meeting with Nick and Serena, that’s one of two instances this week when we see our divorcés getting papped. People take photos of Carla in the restaurant as she storms off, and later, at least one standby photographer catches Morgan leaving the apartment he used to share with Carla.

• St. John tells Morgan that Carla paid Flora to have sex with Morgan, but that’s not true — at least not explicitly so. Taylor & Byrne gave her some money so she would sign the NDA and stay quiet about the whole thing, but Carla herself never gave Flora money. Flora has been absent for a couple of episodes now; as the plot escalates, I imagine she will reappear soon.

items.title: The Traitors: New Blood Recap: Go Home Already
items.description: Why is this show like this? We will get into the reasons why, but first I want to get into the fact that I am crestfallen after this evening. Crestfallen! Why will reality television not follow my personal tastes and preferences to the letter? This is American
items.author: Alice Burton
paragraphs: Why is this show like this? We will get into the reasons why, but first I want to get into the fact that I am crestfallen after this evening. Crestfallen! Why will reality television not follow my personal tastes and preferences to the letter? This is American Idol keeping Sanjaya around for way too long all over again.

We’re back in the turret with Tomica, Joe, and Katie. We again hear Tomica say that she wants them to kill Victor, but we know that’s not happening. I am, however, curious, because now that everyone has seen the show, they know the Traitors won’t kill someone who is gunning for them. So if the Traitors did kill Victor, would people suspect Tomica? Or would they be like, Oh wow, the Traitors are trying to frame Tomica? I’m saying that maybe they could start relying on the players to pull some Wallace Shawn in The Princess Bride reasoning. But they’re not going to, and they narrow it down to Wyatt, Mark, or Kriste.

At breakfast, Victor won’t shut up about Tomica being a Traitor. People make their dramatic meal arrivals, and we learn that Mark has been murdered. Everyone is crushed. We see Mark finding his death warrant, which causes him to say both “Damn, that sucks, bro” and “Killing me was just really not cool.” For sure. The remaining players bemoan the loss of the vibes, and Shane says the Traitors drained all the energy out of the castle. I mean, yeah. You still have Jay there, although he has wisely toned it down, and you have Victor constantly harassing Tomica. Is he right about her being a Traitor? Yes, but once more, I do not care. I would rather watch Elizabeth Holmes win The Traitors than Victor. (My wife says I am going too far.)

Everyone breaks into small groups for their discussion topic (“Who Is a Traitor?”). Jay is suspicious of Victor; Abby L is on Wyatt; Kriste is on Abby L; and Clyde will not go against Tomica because he loves her too much. We are officially at the longest streak for the Traitors on the U.S. version. Typically, the players find one by episode six or seven, but here we are at episode seven, and nothing.

For today’s mission, they will be going to a field (“Can we stop going outside?” Tomica relatably asks). The players have accrued $97,000 in prize money so far, and there’s another $20,000 up for grabs. We have a field of terrifying scarecrows. Dozens of scarecrows. Alan informs the players they have to rip open the scarecrow torsos and search for bags of gold. They won’t know how much each bag is worth, and the player with the most gold will receive a game-changing power at the roundtable. There are also four black hearts hidden in the scarecrows, which can be used to blow up a player’s scarecrow avatar and block them from getting this mysterious power-up.

Victor the Business Executive calls himself an endurance athlete and is very ready to blow up Tomica’s scarecrow. Thank God Shane finds a black heart first and blows up Victor’s scarecrow. I LOVE YOU, SHANE. When Victor finds out that he’s out, he reacts with all the grace and quiet maturity of a well-seasoned executive at the top of his field. “You’re STUPID!” he declares. “I HATE this.” Alan informs Victor that being a sore loser is not a good look. Alan Cumming, please tell me if you were actually annoyed with Victor in that moment. I want to know so badly.

Clyde also finds a black heart, but blows up Morgan’s scarecrow. Abby L blows up Wyatt’s, and Ben blows up Katie’s. They find $15,300 total through scarecrow disembowelment, but they won’t find out who gets the secret power until after the roundtable.

Post-mission, Victor and Tomica have a heart-to-heart in which they accuse each other. Victor asks her if she suspects anyone else, and Tomica says Katie. Tomica! I believe I speak for many when I say that I hate when the Traitors turn on each other, at least before the final episodes. Let there be faith between murderers! Also, everyone is grasping at straws right now, so she could have said anyone.

At the roundtable, Victor continues to one-note his accusation, but does toss Joe in there, because he says that Joe didn’t eat the apple he was carrying. Morgan correctly says that he did, in fact, eat the entire apple. Joe’s explanation is “If we’re gonna get into it, I need roughage.” So then Victor pivots and asks Tomica why she told him she suspects Katie. And here we are! Tomica protests that she said Kriste, which flabbergasts Victor. I mean, we know she said Katie. And it does sound like a weak defense from Tomica, but then she tells the camera that she really did mean to say Kriste. Do I believe her? Yes. But I was also very swayed by Elizabeth Holmes in the Nathan Fielder movie, even though I read all of Bad Blood. Katie is mad about Tomica saying her name, which makes sense.

Voting goes: Wyatt (Tomica), Jay (Victor), Abby L (Wyatt), Morgan (Wyatt), Shane (Victor), Kriste (Abby L), Tomica (Victor), Katie (Tomica), Victor (Tomica), Abbey B (Victor), Clyde (Morgan), Ben (Katie), Joe (Victor). I, secure in the knowledge that there will be no surprises even though Alan promised there would definitely be surprises, write down “YEEEEEES VICTOR IS GONNNNE. THANK. GOD.” But no. Victor is maybe not gone.

The mysterious power is that one person can pardon the banished player. Are you kidding? You chose to do this right now. When he was finally almost gone. Mr. “I’m a Sweaty Boy.” Mr. “I farted. I farted. Oh, I just farted. Oh, it smells in here now.” This is the week you pull out the pardon card. I am furious, because it feels nice to be furious about stupid things.

Who would I vote for on Traitors? It’s hard to judge what one would do without having the insider knowledge, because who knows the full context of what’s happening in that castle, but based on what’s presented, here are my picks:
No Insider Knowledge: Joe’s point about having, in fact, eaten the apple was solid. I vote for Victor.
Yes Insider Knowledge: [Glowers at Victor in his current purgatorial state] You better stay banished, sir.

items.title: The Real Housewives of Orange County Recap: Mi Casita, Su Casita
items.description: This season doesn’t seem to have story lines so much as little things that pop up here and there and then disappear quickly. It doesn’t have story lines so much as it has warts. Oh, look, there’s one! Everyone scurries off to check it out and diagnose it, and
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: This season doesn’t seem to have story lines so much as little things that pop up here and there and then disappear quickly. It doesn’t have story lines so much as it has warts. Oh, look, there’s one! Everyone scurries off to check it out and diagnose it, and then, with a few applications of Compound W, it’s gone again and we’re just standing around waiting for the next dermatological event to take place. The most concerning of all the warts is the call Shannon gets from her dog Archie, who I believe is fully capable of initiating his own FaceTime because he is a very good dog — yes, he is. Shannon gets a call from her assistant saying Archie is a little low energy. Later, back in the OC, she tells the ladies she took Archie to the pet-cancer doctor, who said if Archie didn’t get radiation, he’d only live another four to six months. Sadly, he died this May, and I don’t think I want to relive any of it on reality television. It’s just too sad.

But, as wart inspectors, here we are, diagnosing a different disease. This week, all the warts are on Gina. The gang goes to Harajuku, which is a high-end neighborhood in Tokyo that Gwen Stefani made famous with some cultural appropriation. B-A-N-A-N-A-S. To be clear, I think what Gwen did — stripping the culture of the place for her own gain, both financially and creatively — is much different than what the women are doing, which is just a little bit of Japanese cosplay. As the woman in the shop explained to them, and the editors dutifully left in the episode to exonerate them, part of the aesthetic is bridging international ideas of cuteness (or kawaii in Japanese). Harajuku is not just full of these types of girls but all sorts of global luxury brands and, as Gina demonstrates, vintage stores selling those designers.

Heather Dubrow goes into a vintage store and says she doesn’t like clothes that have other people’s energies in them. What is she worried about, being haunted by a parka? She bought Lana Turner’s house in Beverly Hills, but she’s afraid someone else carried her pocketbook? Come on. Gina is going a little buck wild in the store, and the women bring up that she seems to be spending a lot more money lately. Heather says it reminds her of actresses who would get a show, buy a fancy car, then the show would get canceled. They also bring up that Gina and Emily got a stylist and each paid $12,000 for four borrowed outfits. Heather points out that she could own four $3,000 outfits for that price. Sure, but how often do these women get to rewear their clothes? A strange part of their job is that if they’re filmed in it once, either for the show or their social media, fans will make a stink if they see it again. What’s the point in owning that outfit if they can’t rewear it? I’m not defending the expense; I’m just saying I don’t entirely buy Heather’s logic.

Gina, however, buys a lot. But as they’re worried about her putting herself in the poorhouse, she’s buying a leather jacket that is only $800. That’s, like, half of what Heather pays for house slippers — that is a single designer slipper. Yes, a vintage store is more expensive than Goodwill, but it’s not like she’s dropping 20 bands at Gucci on two coats. And Gina has what seems to be a thriving career. Shannon doesn’t have a job (other than the show), is worried about her finances, and has an assistant. Why is no one worried about Shannon’s money? This whole thing seems wild and arbitrary to me.

Tamra tells Emily what Heather and the others were saying, and Emily brings it back to her bestie, Gina, who doesn’t take kindly to them counting her paychecks. She says Heather’s actress analogy is inept because it means she’s not going to keep having the same success she’s currently having. I get Gina’s point: No one wants to be told they’re bad at their job. However, Heather is a little bit right. While real estate isn’t as volatile as acting, the market shifts, mortgage rates rise, and there are all sorts of factors that might keep her from doing as well tomorrow as she is doing today. Just as even the best actresses go through their fallow periods (remember when two-time Oscar winner Dianne Wiest couldn’t pay her rent?), the same is true of Realtors. I do think Heather had good intentions with what she is saying, but the delivery wasn’t great.

They all get dressed up as Harajuku girls, covered in bows and plush toys and bright colors and lace and so many platforms — more platforms than we’ve ever seen on this “platform,” as they always call it. They walk through the world’s largest crossing (which really is overwhelming), all holding hands with a bunch of cameras. They then get mad when the commuting locals, dressed all in black, are pissed off being confronted by this impenetrable line of crazy white women, two dressed like the twins from The Shining after they got really into Hello Kitty.

At dinner, Gina brings up the group’s previous comments and says she didn’t like them. Jenn tries to compliment her, saying she’s gone from living in the casita to being a badass, but Gina cuts her off mid-sentence. Gina wants us to know she never lived in the casita. Guys, I know we’ve been calling her “casita” since her first season on the show and it is in the “universal chatter” about her, but Gina wants us all to know she only spent weekends there and her kids were never living with her in the casita. Okay, sure. Got it, Gina.

The problem is she is never going to escape “casita.” This is now part of her brand, just like the shitty clothes and the terrible hair during her debut seasons. (Yes, that is plural because it lasted longer than it should have.) In the great Housewives tradition, she might as well just own it. Yes, she was in a casita. Yes, she used to look like shit. Yes, she worked very hard at forming a real-estate career. Yes, she is doing a lot better now and she can afford designer (secondhand) bags, ski jackets that don’t zip in the front, and getting a real professional to take care of her hair. That is her journey and part of what makes us love Gina. (Well, most fans don’t love Gina, but they love her more than they love Emily!) Trying to erase the casita is telling us she wasn’t a mess when she joined the show even though she totally was. We know. We saw it!

With that, the Gina wart seems to clear up. What other warts are there? Oh, Jenn wants to be just as successful as the rest of the ladies and is trying to figure out how to make more money. She decides it’s going to be fitness classes online, so she comes up with SexyFit, a fitness class to help you look more sexy but also more fit. I want to make so much fun of this very silly and quite obvious title, but I’m sure someone made fun of Billy Blanks for Tae Bo and that made him shit tons of money. She films the class, and Gretchen and Slade show up because nothing in the world makes Slade harder than a camera. Ugh, talk about warts.

Shannon is trying not to get warts from Steve Guttenberg. Apparently, she saw a reel of his on Insta and told Jeff Lewis she thought he was cute, and he hammered on and on about it on his radio show, and now Steve Guttenberg is liking Shannon’s social-media content. Shannon, marry this man! What is she waiting for? Has she seen Steven Guttenberg? He is fit as hell and still strangely famous. Plus he’d make a great addition to this cast. We need to band together to make this happen.

Carmella thinks her boyfriend, Danny, is a wart and knows she needs to lance him but can’t figure out how to do it yet. Carmella is overwhelmed that she didn’t go on the trip, that she’s behind at work, that her kids are growing up and demanding nose jobs. It’s all too much for her. Maybe she can have a corn instead. Maybe a bunion.

There are a bunch of lesser warts that keep coming up — the ladies think Tamra’s friendship with Jenn is fake and she’s using it to annoy Heather, who is no longer looking for a buddy in the group and just wants to be on her own. I don’t know. These all make little sense and even less impact. Maybe they’re not warts, just pimples.

The wart that refuses to go away is whatever is up with Vicki and Tamra. They gather for dinner with a day-drunk Heather Dubrow, and Tamra apologizes for saying Vicki and her daughter, Briana, aren’t talking right now. I get that this is preemptive: Vicki will eventually see the season and not like her comments, but Vicki didn’t even know she’d said it yet. Tamra could have gotten away with this one. Vicki again apologizes for her comments about Tamra and her daughter, but it doesn’t sound like she means it. It seems like Vicki (who almost brained herself passing out in a Tokyo shop) doesn’t want to be there and doesn’t like a single one of these women, even Shannon. It’s like she is at dinner with Tamra and Heather, picks up her margarita (They’re so much better at Andale’s, she thinks), and looks down at her hand. She doesn’t know where she is; she doesn’t know how she got there. All she knows is that she is not at work — her happy place — and her hand is covered in mysterious bumps. Are they hives? Are they lesions? Psoriasis? Dermatitis? Herpes? A rash? No, none of the above. They’re just warts, and they’ll be gone in no time.

items.title: Jay-Z to Perform at Apple Music 2027 Super Bowl Halftime Show
items.description: Jay-Z is slated to perform at the Apple Music Super Bowl LXI Halftime Show, taking place on Feb. 14, 2027, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.
items.author: Steven J Horowitz
paragraphs: Jay-Z is slated to perform at the Apple Music Super Bowl LXI Halftime Show, taking place on Feb. 14, 2027, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.

“From Reasonable Doubt to standing on the Super Bowl Halftime stage, this has been a journey,” said Jay-Z in a statement. “Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world’s biggest stage. This run continues to be a dream come true.”

The announcement comes on the heels of an anniversary victory lap this year under the banner “Jay-Z 30.” He kicked off the celebrations as a headliner at the Roots Picnic in late May, followed by three sold-out shows at Yankee Stadium in July to honor the 25th and 30th anniversaries of his albums “The Blueprint” and “Reasonable Doubt,” respectively. In addition to international shows in Paris and London, Jay sat down with Rick Rubin for the eight-part docuseries “Jay-Z in 8” where he broke down hits and deep cuts across his catalog. This past weekend, he brought his global string of tour dates to a close at SoFi Stadium with two nights featuring guest appearances from Scarface, DJ Khaled, John Legend, Blue Ivy Carter, Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg and Too Short.

“For several years, we’ve had the privilege of working closely with Jay-Z and Roc Nation, and I’ve seen the extraordinary impact he has had on the Super Bowl Halftime Show,” said NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell in a statement. “When we first reached an agreement with Roc Nation to produce the show, I had just one request: that Jay-Z take the stage himself one day, whenever the moment felt right to him. I couldn’t be more excited for fans around the world to experience the artistry, creativity and cultural impact he will bring to the Super Bowl stage.”

“Jay-Z’s impact on global music culture is as profound as it is undeniable,” added Oliver Schusser, Apple’s Vice President of Music and International Content. “We’ve had the privilege of working closely with him these last few years to bring some of the world’s most exciting and prolific artists to the Super Bowl Halftime Show stage and we are so thrilled that he will be taking that stage himself this year. We know it’s going to be an incredible show.”

The Super Bowl Halftime Show will air on ESPN, ABC and Disney+, and on mobile devices with NFL+. ESPN’s Spanish-language telecast will also be available on ESPN Deportes and Disney+, with a separate Spanish-language presentation on Univision. Roc Nation will executive produce the show, while Hamish Hamilton will serve as director.

Earlier this year, Bad Bunny held court as the Super Bowl Halftime Show performer, celebrating his Puerto Rican heritage in the tradition of Latin America. The elaborate set included a mock sugar-cane field and a Puerto Rican vecindad with a barber shop, liquor store and a casita where Bad Bunny welcomed celebrity guests including Jessica Alba, Karol G, Cardi B, Young Miko and Pedro Pascal, among others. Bad Bunny also brought out surprise artists Lady Gaga and Ricky Martin for a salsa-inflected version of “Die With a Smile” and “lo que le pasó a Hawái,” respectively.

The Benito Bowl, as it was affectionately dubbed by his fans, reached an average of 128.2 million viewers, above the 124.9 million average viewers achieved by the Super Bowl overall but down from the 133.5 million viewers reached by Kendrick Lamar in 2025. Before Lamar, Usher held the record for most viewers with his 2024 performance.

Last month, Bad Bunny won his first Emmy for his Super Bowl Halftime Show performance in the outstanding special (live) category. The spectacle took home a total of seven wins, including musical direction, choreography, sound mixing, lighting design, technical direction/camerawork and directing.

Speaking about the performance, creative director Harriet Cuddeford previously told Variety, “The performance is celebrating normal people, and what it is to be human and love and have joy, and really appreciate one another. This was to show how much he values his community, to celebrate normal people on the world’s biggest stage, especially people who are of importance in Latino culture. He’s a very authentic person, Benito, and it’s about just being authentic and very real and very human.”

In addition to the aforementioned artists, recent performers at the Super Bowl Halftime Show have included Rihanna, the Weeknd and a collective performance from Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg, Eminem, Mary J. Blige, Lamar, 50 Cent and Anderson .Paak.

items.title: How ‘You Can See Everything’ Became a Surprise Box Office Hit (and Likely One of the Biggest Docs of All Time)
items.description: “You Can See Everything” has remained a must-see at the box office, collecting a remarkable $19.5 million from 2,655 theaters in its second weekend — a notable increase in ticket sales from its sizable opening.
items.author: Rebecca Rubin
paragraphs: “You Can See Everything” has remained a must-see at the box office, collecting a remarkable $19.5 million from 2,655 theaters in its second weekend — a notable increase in ticket sales from its sizable opening.

A24‘s buzzy documentary about Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes has grossed $45.1 million domestically to date and will be very profitable for the studio against a lean $7 million budget. With electric word-of-mouth, awards chatter and repeat viewings from audiences who are trying to make sense of what they saw on screen, the movie should remain a big-screen draw through the fall. It’s primed to leave theaters as one of the biggest non-musical documentaries of all time, a true feat for a nearly three-hour film that wasn’t publicized until a month before debuting in cinemas. Right now, “Michael Jackson’s This Is It” is the highest-grossing documentary ever with $267 million in 2009, not adjusted for inflation. Meanwhile Michael Moore’s “Fahrenheit 9/11” is the biggest non-music doc with $222 million in 2004, followed by two nature films, “March of the Penguins” with $127 million in 2005 and “Earth” with $107 million in 2007. “You Can See Everything” needs to become a hit overseas to crack the top five.
After a strong second weekend in North America, here are four takeaways from the surprise success of “You Can See Everything.”
Restraint bolstered demand

A24 began rolling out “You Can See Everything” in 855 theaters, a huge footprint for a documentary. (By comparison, Bleecker Street launched “Musk,” a four-hour look at the world’s richest man, in four locations.) The film opened to $15.6 million — thanks to the more than 2,000 sold-out showings — as cinephiles rushed to theaters to avoid spoilers; the stranger-than-fiction story follows Holmes right before she begins her 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors. The decision to launch the movie in moderate release — rather than limited in just a handful of venues or nationwide on more than 2,000 screens — proved wise because the studio was able to bolster awareness while cultivating a sense of scarcity. (In New York City and Los Angeles, good luck catching the film during its first weekend in theaters if you didn’t buy a seat way in advance.) Then ticket sales climbed by 28% as “You Can See Everything” expanded to 2,666 theaters in its second weekend, underscoring the film’s genuine commercial viability beyond the coasts.

“Opening ‘You Can See Everything’ in 855 theaters was a really smart move, allowing the film to establish itself and build momentum before going much wider,” says Rentrak’s head of marketplace trends Paul Dergarabedian. “The fact that we’re seeing a documentary deliver such a significant second-weekend increase is remarkable.”
Secrecy around the project dialed up the anticipation

Nobody knew about the existence of “You Can See Everything” until its surprise world premiere at the Telluride Film Festival in early September. (That’s nothing short of a miracle in Hollywood, where even your waiter knows your P&A spend.) In the scenic Colorado mountain town, the movie became a word-of-mouth sensation after garnering near-euphoric reviews. Shrouding the film in secrecy became an effective marketing tactic. After all, there’s no shortage of movies and television shows about Holmes. Her rise and spectacular fall from grace has been depicted in the Hulu series “The Dropout,” starring Amanda Seyfried, as well as Gibney’s “The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley.” But the immediate sense around “You Can See Everything” was that co-directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim had captured something very, very different. (And many felt that Holmes had met her match in Fielder, a cringe comedy master best known for HBO’s “The Rehearsal.”)

“Bear in mind, the project started with no blueprint or screenplay for how to tell this story,” says analyst David A. Gross, who publishes the box office newsletter FranchiseRe. “A24 invested in an interesting but complicated idea without a beginning, middle or end. That’s turned into a zeitgeist film about money, dreams, truth and reality.”
Word-of-mouth elevated ticket sales in the movie’s second weekend

“You Can See Everything” surged in its second weekend because there was quality to match the hype. Some 90% of initial ticket buyers say they would “definitely recommend” the film and 80% said the movie was “even better than expected,” according to exit polls. On social media, people who saw the movie were encouraging others to seek out packed theaters so they could share in the wild reactions and insane twists and turns of the story with others. From “Michael” to “Obsession” to “The Odyssey,” there’s been at least one commonality between many of this year’s box office hits: They’re fun to watch with crowds.
Younger audiences are all in on A24

Roughly 70% of opening weekend ticket buyers were under 35, an unexpectedly youthful turnout for a non-fiction film. However, it’s not surprising for A24, which has cultivated a loyal, young demographic over the years through edgy, aesthetic arthouse favorites like “Marty Supreme” and “Everything Everywhere All at Once.” This year’s lineup of “The Drama,” “Backrooms” and “Primetime” also scored for the indie studio after reaching event-status for Gen Zers. That’s not to say they’ll show up for anything from A24. Chris Rock’s Hollywood-set dramedy “Misty Green” and Hugh Jackman’s revisionist adventure “The Death of Robin Hood” were two recent releases from A24 that misfired in theaters.

items.title: Macklemore Calls for Unity During First ‘Free Palestine’ Show as Hozier, Kneecap and Mark Ruffalo Support: ‘Those Two Words Are So Threatening to Some People’
items.description: Macklemore dedicated his first “Free Palestine” tour date in Dublin, Ireland to “love and liberation,” just over a month after he was dropped as an opener for Ed Sheeran following a political speech on stage.
items.author: Ellise Shafer; Steven J Horowitz
paragraphs: Macklemore dedicated his first “Free Palestine” tour date in Dublin, Ireland to “love and liberation,” just over a month after he was dropped as an opener for Ed Sheeran following a political speech on stage.

3Arena was dotted with keffiyehs and Palestinian flags on Monday night as Dubliners young and old gathered to back the “Thrift Shop” rapper at the start of the three-show stint, which will also see him play Paris and London this week alongside special guests. All proceeds are going to charities supporting Palestine, and Macklemore also donated his $1 million salary from Sheeran’s tour to the cause.

To recap, on Sept. 14 Macklemore was dropped from the remainder of Sheeran’s U.S. “Loop” tour after he said “free Palestine” on stage and gave political speeches over two concerts at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium on Sept. 4 and 5. The speeches went viral, sparking backlash from pop star Pink and a petition from the Israeli American Council calling for his removal and criticizing him for using the platform to “advance a political agenda.” At the time, promoter Messina Touring Group said they had been “notified by venues” that “they will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup.” Macklemore claimed that it was Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft who had pushed him out of the tour, and Sheeran also posted a lengthy statement explaining why he doesn’t wade into politics, which generated backlash against him. In solidarity with Macklemore, Sheeran’s other opening acts — including Finneas, Lukas Graham and Aaron Rowe — and his backing band, Beoga, also dropped out of his tour.

Beoga was there to support Macklemore on Monday, alongside surprise guests including Hozier and Kneecap. During his set, Macklemore took a moment to share what the evening meant to him in the wake of the controversy. “Six weeks ago, it was two words. Two words is all that it took. Two words that are rooted in love and liberation,” he said. “Not against anybody, not divisive. Not a call for hatred. But a call to recognize our shared humanity. Free Palestine. I said, free Palestine! The same thing that I want for all of us, freedom, dignity, the right to exist without fear. Being able to raise our children in the homes that we grew up in, not having to prove our humanity to the rest of the world.

“And yet,” he continued, “those two words are so threatening to some people. They would rather silence those two words than confront what they actually mean. Because freedom that requires another person’s oppression is not freedom at all. And while the world debates those words, we see the videos, we see the footage, we see parents pulling their children out of the rubble. Families erased. Devastation beyond our imagination. And somehow, those words have become more controversial than the suffering that made them necessary. That’s why we are here tonight. That is why we are here, because throughout history, music has given people a place to resist, to come together as a collective, to share our grief, to share our stories, to move from the heart, to mobilize people with the frequency of love. The heartbeat in our drum that makes us feel alive, that makes us feel connected.”

But before Macklemore took the stage, the night kicked off with an introduction from Liam Cunningham of “Game of Thrones” fame. “Tonight, we celebrate life. We honor resilience. We stand with Gaza!” he said. The music then began with Palestinian-Israeli singer Lina Makoul, who delivered a powerful song without words “because anything she said could have severely affected her freedom,” as Cunningham noted. Beoga was next, performing several traditional Irish jigs after percussionist Eamon Murray told the crowd, “Don’t fuck with the Irish!”

The first heavyweight guest was none other than Hozier, who got the crowd crooning along with “Too Sweet,” “From Eden,” and “Work Song.” The Irishman said he is “so proud of my country and the way they’re showing up,” and highlighted that 55 students in Gaza are waiting to have their visas approved by the Irish government so that they can study there. “This has happened before. It happened last year, and this can be solved with ministerial discretion,” he continued. “It’s an absolute wonder, it’s baffling how it hasn’t been solved yet.”

Seeming uncharacteristically nervous, Hozier then announced that he was going to perform a tune that he’d “never sang live before.” It was “The Prayer of Shields,” an 18th-century folk song written by John Shield that hoped for equality for all people. “The Jew he is me fellow man/ The Muslim the same indeed, sir,” he sang in a haunting tone. “To the infidel I’d wish him well/And help him in his need, sir.”

As the stage was reset, the crowd was treated to a series of video messages from celebrities who couldn’t be there but wanted to show their support. “Thanks to Macklemore for doing this,” The Strokes frontman Julian Casablancas said. “Take care of each other and the innocents, and continue standing up in this struggle towards a just world system.”
Added “Broad City” star Ilana Glazer, “We are all together in this fight to help free Palestine. Keep speaking up and using your voice, it’s working.”

“Keep fighting for a free Palestine and humanity all over the world and amongst the people. There will be no peace until there’s equality,” Mark Ruffalo said to enthusiastic applause throughout the stadium. “Lots of love, have a good show. Keep fighting the good fight.”

Irish rap trio Kneecap then stormed the arena, injecting a dose of energy by getting mosh pits going in the crowd as they ran through fan favorites like “Fenian” and “H.O.O.D.” “We wanna thank Macklemore for organizing this concert. We wanna thank Ed Sheeran for helping to organize this concert,” member Móglaí Bap cheekily said as the crowd erupted in cheers.

It was then finally time for Macklemore’s set. The rapper was greeted with enormous applause as he emerged in a green-and-orange keffiyeh to “Chant,” with Australian singer Tones and I joining him to sing the chorus. Supported by a six-piece band, Macklemore rapped with conviction: “This is my moment/ They can’t take my talent/ They can’t take my stripes.” He addressed the crowd for the first time as the song finished, looking overwhelmed and wiping tears from his eyes. Before he could begin to speak, a “free Palestine” chant broke out in the audience.

“It has been a crazy six weeks,” he said. “We took my shortest tour of all time, which was two nights at MetLife Stadium, and we turned that shit into this right here.” He added, “We’re gonna start with an anti-capitalist anthem,” as his hit “Thrift Shop” rang out and a pair of peppy dancers two-stepped on stage.

A run-down of Macklemore’s greatest hits ensued, including “Same Love” with Mary Lambert joining him; “These Days”; “Glorious”; and “Good Old Days,” with Tones and I reemerging to sing Kesha’s part on the track. He then surprised the audience with a new song that “he wrote this last week,” titled “Where Is Our Love?” In the political yet soft-spoken rap, Macklemore says “free Palestine” and speaks about “America being terrorized by ICE agents” as well as mentioning Congo and Sudan.

The set ended on a high note with his 2012 hit “Can’t Hold Us,” during which Macklemore climbed into the crowd and had them literally hold him up. As confetti exploded in the air, Macklemore left the audience with one last message: “I am proud to stand here on stage in solidarity with the Palestinian people. We will continue to fight for collective liberation until our last breath,” he said before leading one final “free Palestine” chant.
Macklemore’s “Free Palestine” tour continues in Paris on Thursday and London on Friday.

items.title: Walter Koenig, Chekov on Original ‘Star Trek,’ Dies at 90
items.description: Walter Koenig, who memorably played Chekov in the original “Star Trek” series and seven “Star Trek” feature films, died Sunday in Los Angeles, Variety has confirmed. He was 90.
items.author: Carmel Dagan
paragraphs: Walter Koenig, who memorably played Chekov in the original “Star Trek” series and seven “Star Trek” feature films, died Sunday in Los Angeles, Variety has confirmed. He was 90.

His reps said in a statement, “Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world. He passed of old age at home in North Hollywood last night surrounded by his daughter and niece.

“Best known for his iconic role as Pavel Chekov in ‘Star Trek: The Original Series,’ Walter helped inspire audiences with his optimism, humor, and adventurous spirit. Beyond ‘Star Trek,’ his long and distinguished career showcased his versatility as an actor and his genuine love for his craft. His remarkable talent continued to shine in his later years, most recently with his performance in the short film ‘Mr. Fleischmann,’ for which he received the Platinum Award for Best Actor at the 2026 Independent Shorts Awards — a fitting recognition of a lifetime devoted to his craft.

“Walter’s legacy extends far beyond the screen. Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit, and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it.
“On behalf of all of us, we extend our deepest condolences to Walter’s family, friends, colleagues, and the millions of fans whose lives he touched over the decades.
“Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before.”
Koenig’s Chekov, an arrogant young navigation officer in the original series, was introduced to the series to appeal to teenage viewers — his hairstyle recalled that of the Monkees’ Davy Jones.
The Russian-born Chekov was also used to poke fun at the Soviet way of falsely taking credit for every important human invention.

Koenig played Chekov in the 2015 TV movie “Star Trek: Renegades,” set at a time in which the character has been elevated to admiral. The film, aimed as a backdoor pilot for a new “Star Trek” television series, was funded through crowdsourcing.

The Chekov character was not included in “Star Trek: The Animated Series” in the early ’70s because of the show’s limited budget, but Koenig penned an episode of the series entitled “The Infinite Vulcan.”

Koenig’s Chekov was central to the plot of 1982’s “Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan” and consequently the actor enjoyed considerable screen time in the film, generally considered the best of the “Star Trek” movies.

Koenig was also associated with another sci-fi franchise, J. Michael Straczynski’s “Babylon 5,” in which he played the evil Psi Cop Alfred Bester (named by the show’s creators after the science fiction writer). He appeared in 12 episodes of that show from 1994-98.

Walter Marvin Koenig was born in Chicago. The family of Russian Jewish heritage was originally named Koenigsberg, and he attended Fieldston High School in Fieldston, N.Y., where he did some stage work, before starting at Grinnell College in Iowa, where he was initially pre-med; he transferred to and graduated from UCLA with a degree in psychology. After a professor urged him to pursue a career in acting, he began studying at the Neighborhood Playhouse in New York; there his classmates included Christopher Lloyd, with whom he would be reunited on “Star Trek III: The Search for Spock,” in which Lloyd played the villainous Klingon Commander Kruge, as well as James Caan and Dabney Coleman.

Koenig made his small-screen debut with an uncredited role in an episode of “Combat!” in 1962, followed by guest-starring roles on “The Untouchables,” “General Hospital,” “The Alfred Hitchcock Hour,” “Ben Casey,” “Gidget” and “I Spy.” After the original “Star Trek” series went off the air in 1969, he worked occasionally in TV, guesting on “The Virginian,” “Ironside” and “Columbo” (in an episode that had William Shatner as the special guest star). He played a deputy sheriff in an unremarkable low-budget film called “Nightmare Honeymoon,” starring Dack Rambo.

During the 1980s, when he was busy with the “Star Trek” movies, he appeared as Pompey in a 1984 TV adaptation of “Antony & Cleopatra” that also featured Nichelle Nichols and future “Star Trek: Enterprise” actor James Avery.

The actor appeared in a string of low-budget science fiction movies over the years, including “Moontrap,” in which he starred, and “Deadly Weapon,” both in 1989; as well as Cynthia Rothrock martial arts vehicle “Sworn to Justice” in 1996 and independent horror film “Mad Cowgirl” in 2006.
A one-character film that Koenig wrote and performed, “You’re Never Alone When You’re a Schizophrenic,” was screened at the 1996 New York Film Festival.
He voiced Chekov in a variety of “Star Trek” video games, including 1998’s “Starfleet Academy: Chekov’s Lost Missions.”

The actor guested on an episode of the CBS sitcom “Almost Perfect” titled “Where No Woman Has Gone Before” in 1997 and voiced himself on a 2002 episode of “Futurama” titled “Where No Fan Has Gone Before,” which also featured the voices of William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy, among other “Star Trek” regulars. He also guested on “Diagnosis Murder” (in an episode that featured several other “Star Trek” actors) and “Son of the Beach.”
He penned the 2008 sci-fi legal thriller “InAlienable,” in which he also appeared (the tagline was “From the mind of Walter Koenig”).
Koenig also had a stage career that spanned three decades.

In the early 1990s he toured with Mark Lenard (who played Spock’s father Sarek on “Star Trek”) in “The Boys in Autumn,” in which Koenig played a middle-aged Tom Sawyer reunited after decades apart with Lenard’s Huckleberry Finn.

Koenig also directed theater, including “Hotel Parsadiso” for Company of Angels, “Becket” for Theatre 40, “America Hurrah!” at Oxford Theater, “Twelve Angry Men” at the Rita Hayworth Theatre, “Matrix” at the Gascon Theatre Institute and “Three by Ten” at Actors Alley in Los Angeles.
Koenig taught acting classes at UCLA, at Actors Alley and elsewhere.

His satiric fantasy novel “Buck Alice and the Actor-Robot” was re-released in 2006; he created the comic book “Raver” published by Malibu Comics. In 2013 Bluewater Comics published the graphic novel “Walter Koenig’s Things to Come.”

Koenig penned the memoirs “Chekov’s Enterprise: A Personal Journal of the Making of Star Trek — The Motion Picture,” published in 1980, and “Warped Factors — A Neurotic’s Guide to the Universe,” published in 1998.
Anton Yelchin portrayed a much younger Chekov in the rebooted “Star Trek” films.

Back in the days of the original “Star Trek” series there was a period of tension between Koenig and George Takei, who played Sulu, but the two came to be close friends, and in September 2008, Koenig served as best man at Takei’s wedding to Brad Altman.
Koenig a daughter, actress-writer Danielle Koenig. A son, actor and editor Andrew Koenig, died in 2010.

items.title: Skydance Is Offering Employees Voluntary Buyouts Ahead of Layoffs, Adopts 5-Days-per-Week In-Office Policy
items.description: Skydance, as it embarks on the work to integrate the businesses of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, is offering certain employees a voluntary buyout in a “one-time offer.”
items.author: Todd Spangler
paragraphs: Skydance, as it embarks on the work to integrate the businesses of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, is offering certain employees a voluntary buyout in a “one-time offer.”
The new program was outlined by chairman and CEO David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz in a memo to staffers Monday.

“As we bring our teams together, we recognize that not everyone will see their future here, and we respect that. To give eligible employees the option to move on in a way that works for them, we are introducing a Voluntary Buyout (VBO) Program,” the execs wrote. “Those who qualify will receive an individual communication with their personalized details and terms, and a window to decide whether to accept this one-time offer.”

They added, “Please know we don’t take any of this lightly. We are clear about what we’re building: a company that tells the stories people around the world love, embraces new ways to connect with audiences, and leads the next era of media and entertainment. We have the talent, the creative firepower and the ambition to do it, and we will get there together.”

Paramount’s massive $111 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery closed on Oct. 6. In their “Day One” memo to employees that day, Ellison and Kreiz (who was the CEO of Mattel before joining the new Skydance earlier this month) acknowledged that layoffs will be part of the process. “Integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce,” the execs wrote in that memo. “We are committed to handling this process thoughtfully and respectfully.”

In the Oct. 26 memo, Ellison and Kreiz also said the new Skydance is moving to a mandatory five-days-per-week in-office policy across the company. “We believe in-person collaboration is vital to our culture and to the success of our business. Especially in a creative company like ours, the best ideas come from people in the same room, sharing perspectives, challenging one another and solving problems,” the execs said. “We truly believe this is in the best interest of our company and our people. We’ve seen the benefits firsthand at Paramount, and we want every part of Skydance to share in them.”

Skydance execs have said they are shooting to achieve more than $6 billion in cost savings on an annualized basis within three years, and part of that will come from layoffs. The company has not revealed at this point the extent of the job cuts it expects. According to a report issued by Los Angeles County in August, the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger could result in the loss of some 4,500 film and TV jobs over three years in L.A. alone.
Read the full memo sent by Skydance’s top brass Monday, a copy of which was obtained by Variety:

At Skydance, our goal is to build the next-generation media and entertainment company, powered by creativity and technology. We are creative-first, audience focused, tech-forward and globally scaled. And in a world of endless choice and fierce competition for attention, we don’t just want to succeed. We want to win.

To do that, we must be a strong, connected and agile company. Among our business and creative priorities, none matters more than building a strong culture, because it’s the foundation of everything we want to achieve. Winning requires us to work as one team: one company, fully aligned. That means communicating openly and collaborating efficiently across every part of the organization.

We believe in-person collaboration is vital to our culture and to the success of our business. Especially in a creative company like ours, the best ideas come from people in the same room, sharing perspectives, challenging one another and solving problems. Being together isn’t just about showing up. It’s about inspiring one another, learning and coaching, forming friendships and having the casual conversations that spark something great.

With that in mind, we will adopt a five-day in-office policy across all of Skydance. We truly believe this is in the best interest of our company and our people. We’ve seen the benefits firsthand at Paramount, and we want every part of Skydance to share in them.

While many of you are already in the office five days a week, we understand this may be a significant change to the daily routines of others. To give you time to plan and adjust, we will take a phased approach by location. You will receive ample notice before changes take effect, and we will work closely with managers to support you through the transition.

As we bring our teams together, we recognize that not everyone will see their future here, and we respect that. To give eligible employees the option to move on in a way that works for them, we are introducing a Voluntary Buyout (VBO) Program. Those who qualify will receive an individual communication with their personalized details and terms, and a window to decide whether to accept this one-time offer.

We recognize this is a significant decision, and we want you to feel informed and supported. If this applies to you, please review your materials carefully and reach out to your leadership or HR representative with any questions. FAQs and other resources are available on the Skydance Integration Hub, and HR support is also available through My Paramount (legacy Paramount employees) or Ask Employee Connection on WBD One (legacy Warner Bros. employees).

Please know we don’t take any of this lightly. We are clear about what we’re building: a company that tells the stories people around the world love, embraces new ways to connect with audiences, and leads the next era of media and entertainment. We have the talent, the creative firepower and the ambition to do it, and we will get there together.
Thank you for your commitment, and for the creativity and passion you bring to your work every day.
