items.title: Jay-Z to Headline 2027 Super Bowl LXI Halftime Show
items.description: Jay-Z has been tapped to headline the 2027 Apple Music Super Bowl LXI Halftime Show.
items.author: Carly Thomas; Abid Rahman
paragraphs: Jay-Z has been tapped to headline the 2027 Apple Music Super Bowl LXI Halftime Show.
He follows in the footsteps of Grammy-winning artist Bad Bunny, who made his mark during Super Bowl LX earlier this year with his Emmy-winning performance.

The news was announced during halftime of the Cowboys vs. Eagles Monday Night Football game. “It will be Jay-Z in SoFi on [Valentine’s Day],” ABC commentator Scott Van Pelt said. “We’ll all be looking forward to seeing that.”
“He is the GOAT,” analyst Jason Kelce added. “He’s got more stadium-ready hits than most artists have songs, period. Should be a great show.”

“From Reasonable Doubt to standing on the Super Bowl Halftime stage, this has been a journey,” Jay-Z said in a statement. “Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world’s biggest stage. This run continues to be a dream come true.”

“For several years, we’ve had the privilege of working closely with Jay-Z and Roc Nation, and I’ve seen the extraordinary impact he has had on the Super Bowl Halftime Show,” added NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell. “When we first reached an agreement with Roc Nation to produce the show, I had just one request: that Jay-Z take the stage himself one day, whenever the moment felt right to him. I couldn’t be more excited for fans around the world to experience the artistry, creativity and cultural impact he will bring to the Super Bowl stage.”

“Jay-Z’s impact on global music culture is as profound as it is undeniable,” said Oliver Schusser, Apple’s vp of music and international content, in a statement. “We’ve had the privilege of working closely with him these last few years to bring some of the world’s most exciting and prolific artists to the Super Bowl Halftime Show stage and we are so thrilled that he will be taking that stage himself this year. We know it’s going to be an incredible show.”

Jimmy Pitaro, ESPN Chairman, added: “Jay-Z has been setting a standard of excellence for decades, as an artist, a cultural force and a winner of 25 Grammy Awards. The Super Bowl is already a defining moment in music, and his performance will be the latest milestone in a career synonymous with success. We look forward to showcasing the highly anticipated halftime set in the U.S. and around the world across our platforms, including on ESPN, ABC and Disney+.”

Jay-Z joins a coveted list of artists who have earned the opportunity to headline the NFL’s biggest night, including his wife Beyoncé, Bad Bunny, Kendrick Lamar, Michael Jackson, Rihanna, Madonna, Lady Gaga, Bruce Springsteen, Diana Ross, Katy Perry, The Weeknd, Usher, The Rolling Stones and Bruno Mars, among many others.

The billionaire rap icon already curates the Halftime Show through his company Roc Nation in a deal with the NFL that began in 2019 and was renewed in 2024. Given his close connections with NFL powerbrokers, it was inevitable that Jay-Z would pick himself at some point to headline the marquee event.
Super Bowl LXI will air on ABC and ESPN. The game will take place Sunday, Feb. 14, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California, home of the Los Angeles Rams and the Los Angeles Chargers.

Back in February, Bad Bunny brought his Latin love to the Super Bowl stage, turning Levi’s Stadium in Santa Clara, California, into a big dance party. During his 13-minute set, he performed a wide range of his biggest hits, including “Tití Me Preguntó,” “Eoo,” “BAILE INoLVIDABLE,” “El Apagón,” “CAFé CON RON,” “MONACO,” NUEVAYoL” and “DtMF,” among others.

The Puerto Rican rapper and singer also told a love story throughout the performance, which included several celebrity cameos, and ended with a message of unity and love displayed on the screens inside the stadium, which read, “The only thing more powerful than hate is love.”

Jay-Z and the NFL first linked up in 2019, in a deal that saw the league and Roc Nation work together on events and social activism. The NFL would consult Roc Nation on its entertainment offerings, including the Super Bowl Halftime Show, and also work with the company “strengthen community through music and the NFL’s Inspire Change initiative.”

The league working with Jay-Z came in the wake of the NFL’s controversial treatment of former San Francisco 49ers player Colin Kaepernick, who was effectively forced out of the NFL for staging protests against police brutality and systemic racism. The legendary rapper initially publicly supported Kaepernick in his fight against the NFL.

But after Jay-Z was brought on board to essentially revitalize the league’s brand that had taken a battering over the Kaepernick affair, the two fell out. “[Jay-Z] has built the alignment with the NFL, the NFL that has blackballed me, the same NFL that, in a players-owners meeting in 2017, said we need a Black face to help us get rid of the protests,” Kaepernick told NBC News in September 2026.
Puck was first to report the news of Jay-Z being named the headliner.
Ryan Gajewski contributed to this story.

items.title: Instagram Tests 90-Minute Horizontal Videos in Major Play for Podcasters and Creators
items.description: Instagram is testing features aimed at capturing a bigger part of the entertainment landscape, including the ability to play longform videos like podcasts and more on the platform.
items.author: Caitlin Huston
paragraphs: Instagram is testing features aimed at capturing a bigger part of the entertainment landscape, including the ability to play longform videos like podcasts and more on the platform.

Starting Monday, Instagram will be launching a test of horizontal videos of up to 90 minutes with select creators in the U.S. The product, called Features, is aimed at podcasters, comedians and other longform creators, with the ability to refer viewers to the full video from the shortform reels on the platform, which are typically around three minutes or less.

“What you’re now going to be able to do is, you see a clip of a podcast that you love, you can just click and continue watching or watch the full video, and you’ll be able to dive in and see the whole thing because creators are going to be able to link these Reels to their overall feature,” said Tessa Lyons, vp product at Instagram.

Instagram has already been testing the feature with creators in Brazil and has a plan to expand to tens of thousands of creators in the U.S. The videos will also be recommended to users on Instagram’s Explore page and in other areas. Early creators involved in the test include podcast host and Skims co-founder Emma Grede; beauty and fashion creator Monet McMichael; Preston Rakovsky, who interviews New Yorkers about love and relationships; and football content creator Donald De La Haye.

This comes as Netflix, Disney and more have been adding podcasts and videos from creators to their platforms, in an effort to capture more consumer viewing hours and compete with entertainment behemoth YouTube. One challenge for Instagram and others in the battle against YouTube has been competing against the platform’s lucrative revenue-sharing deals, with YouTube offering qualified creators offered 55 percent of ad revenue and helping generate brand deals.

Lyons said Instagram is currently working on “a few different deals” with the early creators for Features, but there’s currently no exclusivity around putting the videos on Instagram (unlike Netflix’s deals for podcasts). Additionally, existing ad deals will carry over into the videos, but Instagram will also work with creators without existing placements to find deals.

“For established creators who already have those relationships, they can bring that content with those placements and that branded content. And we also think that there’s a big opportunity for us to help creators who don’t yet have that infrastructure and that business behind them,” Lyons said.

Features will be available on mobile, but the goal is to carry the viewing experience over to Instagram for TV, which launched last year with Samsung, Fire TV, Google TV and is now expanding to Apple TV in the U.S. as part of Instagram’s move for more of the entertainment landscape.

“We think the best viewing experience for longform horizontal content is on a big, horizontal screen, and so I think that is where we will expect a lot of the deep consumption to happen over time,” Lyons said.

Additionally, given the rise of microdramas, as well as a desire among creators for episodic videos, Instagram has been experimenting with Series, which provides a home for episodic Reels on a creator’s profile. In June, the company began reaching out to microdrama studios in Southeast Asia to experiment with the feature and has since been reaching out to individual creators, who have been experimenting with their own episodic content.

In the coming months, Instagram plans to begin testing the feature in more countries and bring it to the U.S. by the end of this year or early next year. The company has also begun testing how it will appear on TV.

These join other new features Instagram has been testing out, including integrating live video into the Reels tab and showing live videos to audiences who don’t follow the users. This is launching in Indonesia and Brazil, with plans to expand it to the U.S. next year.

items.title: Aaron Sorkin After ‘The Social Reckoning’: “I’m Very Worried That the Parts of Directing That I’m Not Good at Are Those Parts That You Can’t Learn”
items.description: “I was my second-choice to direct it,” Aaron Sorkin candidly admitted as we sat down last week at the the Newport Beach Film Festival to record an episode of The Hollywood Reporter’s Awards Chatter podcast and began discussing the film for which he was receivi
items.author: Scott Feinberg
paragraphs: “I was my second-choice to direct it,” Aaron Sorkin candidly admitted as we sat down last week at the the Newport Beach Film Festival to record an episode of The Hollywood Reporter’s Awards Chatter podcast and began discussing the film for which he was receiving the fest’s Maverick Director Award: The Social Reckoning, which he also wrote.

This film about Facebook — specifically, about the social media company’s knowledge and cover-up of its harmful effects on society, and the whistleblower (Mikey Madison) who brought them to the attention of a journalist (Jeremy Allen White), creating problems for Mark Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong) — comes 16 years after another that Sorkin wrote, the massively acclaimed The Social Network, which David Fincher directed.

Of The Social Reckoning, Sorkin explained, “I would have rather David Fincher directed it — I would rather David Fincher direct everything — but David has an exclusive deal at Netflix, and this was owned by Sony.” And so it was that Sorkin himself ended up helming the $40 million film that Sony released nationwide on Oct. 9, which, to his disappointment, was greeted with considerably fewer enthusiastic reviews (it’s at 54 percent on Rotten Tomatoes) and ticket sales (it has grossed just $15 million worldwide) than the earlier film.

Sorkin has been writing movies for 35 years — among them 1992’s A Few Good Men, 1995’s The American President, 2007’s Charlie Wilson’s War, the aforementioned The Social Network (for which he won screenplay Oscar and Golden Globe awards), 2011’s Moneyball (screenplay Oscar nom), 2015’s Steve Jobs (for which he won a screenplay Golden Globe), 2017’s Molly’s Game (screenplay Oscar nom), 2020’s The Trial of the Chicago 7 (screenplay Oscar nom) and 2021’s Being the Ricardos — and is widely regarded as one of the greatest screenwriters of all time, in a league with his heroes Paddy Chayefsky and William Goldman. (He also wrote some of the most admired and provocative TV series of all times, most notably every episode of the first four seasons of NBC’s The West Wing.)

But over the past decade, as Sorkin stepped behind the camera to helm Molly’s Game, The Trial of the Chicago 7, Being the Ricardos and The Social Reckoning, he has taken more than a few knocks for his directing. And in Newport Beach, he was candid about how it has made him feel: “There’s a big part of me that feels like I just got into the movie business a few minutes ago, and that there’s so much I don’t know. From time to time, I get to speak with screenwriting students, and I’ll be asked, ‘Is screenwriting something that can be taught?’ And the answer is, ‘There are parts of screenwriting — important parts — that can be taught and can be learned, but there are parts that can’t be. And those parts that can’t be? That’s usually what we mean when we use the word ‘talent.’ I’m very worried that the parts of directing that I’m not good at are those parts that you can’t learn.”

Sorkin, whose pre-Molly’s Game films were directed by Rob Reiner, David Fincher, Bennett Miller, Mike Nichols and Danny Boyle, emphasizes, “I’m not done wanting to work with great directors, but when you work with the lineup of directors that you just read, you’d really have to not be paying attention to not learn anything.” Still, he admits, the learning curve has been greater than he anticipated — not in terms of working with actors, but in terms of knowing how to artfully use a camera. “I was surprised by how little of the science of filmmaking I’d managed to absorb.” He adds, “I have no visual sensibility, it turns out.”

The 65-year-old says that he relates to football coaches he has seen being interviewed after a losing game who insist that the elements for a win were all there, but just didn’t come together: “That’s how I feel about directing. There are things that I’ve been doing right along the way. Just give me one more chance, and one of these days I’ll be able to put it all together.”
Sorkin also weighed in on a number of other topics, as you can hear from yourself via the audio player above, or read select excerpts of below…
On potentially reviving The West Wing…

“I always want to rekindle the show. I love the show, I love those people and I miss it, especially nowadays. The problem is, you’ve got to have a story. They won’t let me just write dialogue. Also, the cast has gotten older; I didn’t know that was going to happen.”
On the demise of the mid-range-budget movie…
“This [The Social Reckoning] is my 11th movie, and except for A Few Good Men, I’m not sure if any of them would be feature films today; I think they would all have to be streaming.”
On the new Lincoln Center revival of A Few Good Men…

“This production is very different than the original Broadway production… I made my Broadway debut and became addicted to cocaine at roughly the same time… When I was 25, I was trying to write my first play, and I was having a hard time, and someone just kind of put a joint in my face, and I smoked a little of that, and then they laid out a couple of lines of coke, and I would end up losing a decade of my life to drugs, just gone. So I’m happy, this time around, to be working on it clean and sober. I’ve also been rewriting it, because I was very young when I wrote it — it was my first play — so in some ways, it’s a new play.”

items.title: Tailoring Nerds Love These Tie Brands
items.description: The best tie brands prove that the death of the necktie has been greatly exaggerated, and not for the first time. Yes, there's the continued relaxation of office dress codes, but all that means is that the necktie has now migrated from the boardroom to the str
items.author: Jeremy Freed; Louis Cheslaw
paragraphs: The best tie brands prove that the death of the necktie has been greatly exaggerated, and not for the first time. Yes, there's the continued relaxation of office dress codes, but all that means is that the necktie has now migrated from the boardroom to the streets, as confident young dressers and would-be prepsters embrace the tie as their latest style swerve—and leading designers like Dior's Jonathan Anderson and Celine's Michael Rider use it to set out their views of contemporary masculinity. So yes, you may not need to wear a tie to your office, a wedding, or a job interview, but that just makes the choice to wear one all the more significant—and plain smart.

Now, as ever, nothing makes a well-tailored worsted wool suit and a crisp white button-up look nattier than a well-dimpled four-in-hand. But it's also important to remember that neckties don’t just add sartorial gravitas to suits, blazers, and sport coats. Indeed, ties can be at their most impactful when worn with chore coats, safari jackets, bombers, and other essentials from the casual outerwear canon. So whether you’re pairing your tie with a navy blue power suit or a trucker jacket, you’ll be in good hands with any of the below brands, presented in alphabetical order, and which each offer a unique take on the medium.

It stands to reason that the land of soft-shouldered suits would also produce some certifiably killer neckwear. (And as you'll learn from this guide, it really does.) This particular Neapolitan brand’s wares don’t just live up to the high standards of the city’s tailors, they also contain many of the same characteristics that give southern Italian suiting its effortless style. With a typically soft, unstructured design, and a relatively narrow width, a Borrelli tie is one sure way to add a dash of sprezzatura to your wardrobe.

Regional differences are a pretty big deal in Italy, and—as you might expect—this legendary Roman tailoring house does things differently from its Neapolitan brethren. Roman tailors typically favor a more structured and conservative cut than their counterparts in Naples, and this has helped Brioni’s suits become the de facto uniform of a certain breed of high-powered business executives around the world. As such, Brioni’s ties are a lot like its bespoke suits: handmade from high-end materials and available in a range of solid, dark, serious hues.

Brooks Brothers didn’t invent the necktie, but as the brand that’s credited with introducing diagonal-striped repp ties to American men, it might as well have, at least on this side of the pond. Brooks Brothers’ fortunes have risen and fallen over the last 150 years, but it’s still a go-to for this Ivy-style staple, along with pretty much any other kind of classic necktie that you can think of. Note: The majority of BB’s Italian silk ties measure in at a traditional yet versatile 3.25-inches wide, which is exactly as it should be.

Back over to Europe now, where it doesn’t get much more bougie than Paris' Charvet, which has been outfitting discerning gentlemen since the 1830s (the word “charvet” is shorthand for a specific kind of silk fabric used in tie-making). Since the brand has yet to fully embrace the e-commerce era, a pilgrimage to its Place Vendome flagship is the best way to get a sense of its offerings, which might include half a dozen shades of gray knit ties. Until you make it to Paris, though, Mr. Porter is here.

If you’re looking to incorporate more tailoring into your wardrobe without becoming a full-on suit guy, Drake’s will show you how to do it right. In addition to vibing perfectly with its chore coats and Fair Isle cardigans, Drake’s famous ties are made in London from a range of unconventional fabrics like shantung (a more textured silk), grenadine (a high-twist silk prized for its rich colors), and wool.

You won’t go very far down the rabbit hole of respected southern Italian tie-makers without running into this Neapolitan stalwart and his hand-sewn, hand-rolled neckwear. Thanks to owner Patrizio Cappelli’s love of wool challis fabric (a lightweight wool or wool-silk blend made in England since the 19th century) his ties offer a unique provenance in addition to their selection of classic prints and brighter hues.

As you continue to explore the breadth of Neapolitan tie-making craft, you'll also need to consider this century-old brand that’s as famous for its heritage as for its client list of American presidents and world leaders. With a catalog spanning hundreds of prints—including an archival collection featuring reproductions of classic designs from the ‘40s and ‘50s, and the option of 3-fold, 5-fold, 7-fold, and 9-fold construction—if you can’t find something you want here, you’re not looking hard enough.

As revered for its ties as its signature loafers, this Florentine casa started out as a shoemaker to the stars in Hollywood more than a century ago, before expanding into scarves and ties in the ‘60s. Fortunately, things haven’t changed much since. Ferragamo’s ties are still made of high-end silk, cut and sewn in Italy, and available in a range of subtle animal prints, as well as the brand’s hallmark gancini lock motif. At 8 cm wide (about 3 inches), they’re the ideal finishing touch to an Italian power suit.

As legend has it, Hermès got into the tie business in the 1950s thanks to gamblers who arrived at its Monaco store in need of ties to meet the casino’s dress code. The brand responded with its usual blend of Parisian whimsy and uncompromising attention to detail, and subsequently became a go-to for anyone in search of a tie that says “I may work in [finance, law, government, insurance] but I also know how to have fun!”

As dress codes for C-suites (and casinos) have relaxed, the appeal of Hermès playful prints has spread far beyond the corporate elite. These days you can buy a Hermès tie in dozens of riffs on the maison’s unmistakable H logo, but why hedge? With a cast of characters including roaring lions, smiling koalas, and pencil-gnawing beavers to choose from, Hermès maintains its lock on tasteful novelty neckwear.

Rooted in the buttoned-down world of American Ivy style, J. Press has been outfitting the East Coast establishment since 1902, earning a reputation as the go-to tailor for generations of students, senators, and suited traditionalists. In some ways, its ties are a direct extension of that heritage (they’re made in the USA from robust repp silk, for example) but upon closer inspection, it also becomes clear that J. Press lets its sense of humor fly free when it comes to its neckwear. There's the one dedicated to "ambulance chasing" lawyers, another covered in pink pigs, and then below, one showcasing almost every famous type of sporting ball you could recite without help.

Unsurprisingly, one of the biggest names in high-end suiting is a major presence in the upper echelons of the tie world, too. Like Brioni, which offers a similarly widespread network of outposts in major global cities, Kiton’s ties are handmade in Italy from top-shelf silk. In contrast to their Roman counterpart (and in characteristic Neapolitan style,) Kiton’s ties tend to be more colorful and more jauntily patterned.

One of a select few brands in the world recognisable simply by its patterns, Missoni has spent decades turning zigzags, stripes, and kaleidoscopic colour into a kind of visual shorthand for Italian flair. Founded in the 1950s with a focus, initially, on knitwear, the Milanese house now applies the same textile know-how to its ties, which are all crafted in Italy from fine silk and wool blends. The designs are bold without being brash, and worn with a plain suit and crisp shirt, a Missoni tie really does all the talking (and that’s exactly their point.)

Despite his affinity for polo shirts, rugby jerseys, and other canonical pieces of Anglo-American sportswear, Ralph Lauren is a tie guy first and foremost. Lauren launched his namesake brand with a tie collection in the late 1960s, and they’ve remained a mainstay in the RL universe ever since. That means you can find an impressive range of neckwear on offer at Lauren’s various labels, from Ivy-inspired repp, knit, and bowties (Polo Ralph Lauren) to bolos that’ll complete your dressiest Canadian tuxedo (RRL).

As with all things Ralph, the most covetable options can usually be found in his top-shelf Purple Label line, which offers a sumptuous selection of Italian-made prints and solids in silk and cashmere.

If you’re the type of person who appreciates knowing the origins of the wool that went into your suit jackets and dictating the precise dimensions of your shirt collars—or just want a tie that no one else has—you’ll want to bookmark this custom neckwear specialist. Unlike the other brands on this list, each Sam Hober tie is made to order, meaning you can spec yours out in a truly staggering range of options, including custom lengths, widths, and monogramming.

After less than 15 years in business, this Neapolitan upstart has wasted no time in establishing itself as one of the city’s most in-demand tie-makers—which is pretty impressive in a city where tie-making is a sacred art on par with pizza and puttanesca. Its name, a Japanese word that translates to “understated elegance,” speaks to both the label’s aesthetics and sensibility. With a range of fabrics sourced from mills in Italy, the UK, and Japan, and a selection of classic geometric patterns and prints, each of Shibumi’s 3-fold hand-rolled ties tells a story about the many skilled hands that brought it to life.

A quieter but still very much bubbling upstart is London’s Speciale, who not only ship their ties globally, but also approach them with a refreshingly considered eye, fusing Italian craft codes with a confident British sensibility. Produced in small runs that tend to sell out incredibly quickly, all of their ties are woven or printed in Como, then made in Florence (what a life!), and the results are highly covetable—just look at the shimmer on that silk striped number. Until you can make it to their destination-status Notting Hill store, owning a Speciale tie is a great way to be early to their empire.

Say what you will about the British royal family, but if there’s one thing King Charles knows it’s where to get a decent necktie. The former Prince of Wales has been shopping at this 19th-century London haberdasher for the last 40-odd years, and anyone in search of something to pair with a waxed cotton jacket and a tweed blazer would be smart to follow his lead. With over 200 styles in its current catalog (all of which are made from fabric woven at a centuries-old English silk mill, and most of which are a generously proportioned 9.5 cm wide) it’s a sartorial flex on par with Northampton-made leather bottom shoes and Savile Row suits.

items.title: This New G-Shock Looks a Lot Like One of the Most Iconic Watches Ever Made
items.description: If we were playing matchmaker for some of our favorite watch brands, we wouldn’t have thought of pairing a Casio G-Shock with Patek Philippe’s iconic Nautilus. However, the Japanese watchmaker’s new GMC-2500 proves that opposites do attract.
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: If we were playing matchmaker for some of our favorite watch brands, we wouldn’t have thought of pairing a Casio G-Shock with Patek Philippe’s iconic Nautilus. However, the Japanese watchmaker’s new GMC-2500 proves that opposites do attract.

The 2500 Series is a new collection that “reimagines the design DNA of the watch that started it all,” according to Casio. The brand is nodding towards the original G-Shock ref. DW-5000C from 1983, a watch designed to be tough enough to keep ticking even when dropped. The team famously tested prototypes by hurling them out of the third-floor men’s bathroom of the Casio offices. The new 2500 series is a close descendant of the shock-absorbent watch's original design.

The first G-Shock featured an octagonal digital display, four buttons on the case flanks, and an integrated rubber strap. The 2500 Series incorporates most of those features—but this time, the display is analog rather than digital, and a pair of case “ears” makes the model look a lot like Patek Philippe’s famous flagship luxury sports watch.

Designed by Gérald Genta and released in 1976, the Nautilus is based on a porthole—hence the “ears,” which mirror the hinges/securing mechanism used to open and close a ship’s window against the elements. You may also recall that this isn't the first time that Casio has taken inspiration from a famous Genta watch: the GA-2100 Series (aka ‘CasiOak’), with its octagonal bezel design, bears a remarkable similarity to the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak.

The watch community has been waiting impatiently for the announcement of the 2500 series since Casio’s Japanese website accidentally listed these pieces back in September. In the months since, collectors have already given the watch the “CasioNaut” nickname. (What good is a watch without a clever nickname, after all?) The wait isn’t over just yet, though. The line will officially go on sale through Casio’s website on November 6th.

The 2500 Series is much more than a quartz-powered Nautilus copy. At the center of the design is the Multi-Mission Date function that operates through a three-cell display at 3 o’clock. Besides indicating the date, it can also display the watch’s current mode, elapsed stopwatch minutes, and setting information. Meanwhile, a small-seconds display at 9 o’clock shows passing seconds, but can also be paused and restarted as necessary. (Pausing the function can extend the battery life up to five years.)

The timepiece's tech uses G-SHOCK’s familiar four-button arrangement and comes packed with all the features we've come to expect from the Japanese brand. For starters, the watch automatically keeps rigorous time through 2099 after you input the year, month, and date. LED illumination ensures everything is legible even in low light, while a magnetic system steadies the watch’s hands even if dropped, bumped, or roughed up. Water-resistant to 200m, the 2500 Series is just as capable as you’d expect from a hard-wearing G-SHOCK. Available in simple resin cases with matching rubber bracelets for $145; with metal accents and rubber bracelets for $280-$300; and with full-metal bracelets for $350, the handful of launch references come in a variety of versatile colors and weigh between 47 grams (resin) and 160-180 grams (metal).

Though Casio releases oodles of fresh colorways in existing G-SHOCK families each year, it’s not every day that the world gets an entirely new model family. Fun, streamlined, and much more affordable than the watch it's nicknamed after, the 2500 Series is certainly on its way to becoming a hit.

items.title: Saquon Barkley Is a Luxury-Watch Designer Now
items.description: As a superstar running back for the Philadelphia Eagles, Saquon Barkley has had plenty of opportunities to flex his design muscle. He’s worked on his own shoes and branded apparel, but nothing comes close to his latest project: designing a custom watch with be
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: As a superstar running back for the Philadelphia Eagles, Saquon Barkley has had plenty of opportunities to flex his design muscle. He’s worked on his own shoes and branded apparel, but nothing comes close to his latest project: designing a custom watch with beloved Swiss watchmaker H. Moser & Cie that gave him an even deeper appreciation for timepieces.

“You don’t really get to be too detailed when it comes to designing apparel,” Barkley tells us. “But when it comes to a watch—the little stuff that’s within a watch—it’s just on a whole other level, and you just have a different appreciation of it.” The result of this hyperfocused approach is the new H. Moser Pioneer Cylindrical Tourbillon Skeleton Aventurine Saquon Barkley Edition, a $99,600 watch limited to just 97 pieces.

Barkley discovered Moser while preparing to attend the Met Gala in 2025. He needed a watch to wear and found his way to the independent Swiss house. It’s been a mad love affair ever since. Designing a watch is “something I’ve always kind of wanted to do,” Barkley says. “When you are living this life and setting goals, I want to do stuff that takes me out of the atmosphere of just being a football player. And there aren’t many NFL athletes that can say they have their own watch. And to do it with such a prestigious brand like H. Moser made it 10 times better.”

The Pioneer is Barkley’s first horological baby, and a classic Moser: It blurs the line between a sport and a dress watch and packs specs that are catnip for the biggest nerds. The most critical feature for Barkley was the skeletonized movement—“Being able to see inside was super important,” he says. The single element that prevents you from looking inside the watch is the subdial made of aventurine, a stone that resembles the night sky.

The watch is a tribute to Barkley in more ways than one. There are the obvious touches like the Super-LumiNova-filled numerals 2 and 6, which glow a different color from the rest of the indices in honor of his jersey number. But this wouldn’t be a terribly appropriate watch for someone like Barkley—renowned for his explosive speed and signature backward hurdles—if it couldn’t take some physical abuse. The Pioneer checks those boxes with 120 meters of water resistance and is hardy enough to be worn every day, in any situation.

Designing the new Barkley edition completely changed how the running back thinks about his timepieces. “Before, it was like, ‘How does the watch look? What’s the price on the watch?’ That was how you set the value of a great watch, and I thought about what I want to put on when going out for dinner or an event,” he explains. But designing a $99,600 luxury timepiece changed everything. He brought up hairsprings, tiny pieces of coiled metal that are essential to keeping time, more than once in our interview. “I understand the process behind making a really good watch,” Barkley says, “so my appreciation of it is different.”

items.title: Jacob Elordi's New Cartier Is Secretly Extra Fancy
items.description: Last month, Jacob Elordi did the impossible and made goatees not just socially acceptable but somehow sexy; the month before, the tall Aussie actor wore a suit to The Dog Stars film premiere alongside his canine co-star, and the internet started interrogating
items.author: Mike Christensen
paragraphs: Last month, Jacob Elordi did the impossible and made goatees not just socially acceptable but somehow sexy; the month before, the tall Aussie actor wore a suit to The Dog Stars film premiere alongside his canine co-star, and the internet started interrogating the length of his trousers.

People care a lot about Jacob Elordi and his appearance. That’s one reason he’s in the running to be the next James Bond; it’s also why I don’t think he will be 007. How could we possibly increase our thirst for the 29-year-old? It’s not possible really—unless we talk about his personal watch collection, where there’s quite a lot to talk about.

As a longtime friend of Cartier, Elordi likes to keep things pretty consistently Tank-coded. Over the past year, I’ve spotted him wearing different types of Tanks: a Française, à Guichet, a diamond-set one, green and black Tank Musts, you name it. He wears Cartier very well because, despite his imposing frame, he's comfortable wearing rather dainty pieces of horology.

The man has simple tastes and doesn’t seem to want his watches to do anything other than tell the time in a quaint, uncomplicated way. Second hands? Elordi doesn’t need them. Hour and minute hands will suffice.

Over the weekend, while on a date with girlfriend Kendall Jenner at the Academy Museum Gala in LA, Elordi wore his fanciest Tank yet. Although you really have to study the watch to see how special it is. Zoom in a little on the watch, which could be mistaken for a stainless-steel Cartier Tank, but is actually a new platinum version on a semi-matt burgundy alligator leather strap. The telltale sign is the shinier-than-usual case. Platinum is a heavier, prettier, and more expensive metal than stainless steel.

Unlike some of the vintage Cartiers he’s rocked recently—the majority of which have quartz movements inside—this one is packing a very handy automatic winding, calibre 1899 MC. So it's the real deal, and also makes the watch a tiny bit larger (38.1 x 27.75 mm) than his previous flexes.

No matter what Tank Jacob Elordi has worn, the dials always remain pretty much the same. The word timeless is bandied around far too often in the watch world, but the Tank can legitimately make such claims because the dial design has hardly changed in more than 100 years. Roman numerals, minimalist geometry, and a clear rectangular shape in the centre of the dial inside a very rectangular case make these watches unmistakably Cartier.
This story originally appeared on British GQ.

items.title: I Waited Years for Bvlgari to Make This Watch. It Was Worth It
items.description: It’s been so long that I can’t even remember when I first started asking for a smaller version of Bvlgari’s award-winning, record-breaking ultra-thin watch, the Octo Finissimo. I do remember that it became something of a tradition to badger Fabrizio Buonamassa
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: It’s been so long that I can’t even remember when I first started asking for a smaller version of Bvlgari’s award-winning, record-breaking ultra-thin watch, the Octo Finissimo. I do remember that it became something of a tradition to badger Fabrizio Buonamassa Stigliani, Bvlgari’s product creation executive director and design director. His reaction was always the same. He would flash his signature heavily bearded, friendly smile from behind a desk in the presidential suite of Geneva’s Hotel President and say, “Everybody asks me for this watch!”

This spring, Bvlgari finally made good on my long-standing wish. The brand unveiled a new 37-mm version of the Octo Finissimo, a much more wearable size for most wrists. The new diameter is especially important for this particular model’s shape. “The demand wasn’t driven only by the trend toward smaller watches,” Buonamassa Stigliani told me during an interview in April. “The Octo Finissimo is a square watch, so it wears larger than its dimensions suggest.”

The Octo Finissimo is an icon of modern watchmaking, which made the lack of a Goldilocks-size version even more glaring. Since Bvlgari debuted the OF in 2014, the collection has accumulated 10 world records for ultra-thin watchmaking, including two for the thinnest mechanical watch. The original Automatic, sized at 40 mm, followed a few years later and has since been made available in numerous iterations: sandblasted titanium, stainless steel, 18k gold, ceramic, and more.

Bvlgari rewarded my patience handsomely. The brand debuted three versions of the new OF37: in matte sandblasted titanium; brushed and polished titanium, and yellow gold. Excited beyond what should reasonably stir the emotions of a 36-year-old man, I requested to spend a week with the sandblasted titanium version—which, to my mind, struck a fine balance between graceful futurism and the utilitarian look of a classic tool watch.

Having the OF37 on my wrist really drove home that it looks and feels like nothing else on the market. For almost my entire adult life, I’ve worn a Rolex Submariner, which is in many ways the standard-bearer for modern watch design, and I was immediately struck by how much wearing the OF37 felt like a daring adventure. While I’ve come to love the weight and heft of the Sub, the legendary lightness of the OF was both lovely and slightly alarming. Looking down and seeing this thing—whose matte titanium body completely changes color from steel grey to black to light graphite depending upon the ambient light—is fascinating. On the other hand, I’m a fairly active guy: I’ve taken my Sub swimming and diving without thinking about it, I’ve owned it for 24 years and worn it for 15 without ever servicing it, I’ve donned it during patrols in the military, I’ve banged it into every conceivable surface and (almost) never worried about it. I’m not sure I’d be comfortable wearing the OF37 the same way.

The OF37 is the product of many years of refinement. “We’ve been collecting feedback for years—about the buckle, the case size, the movement finishing, and the needs of both clients and collectors,” says Buonamassa Stigliani. “This watch reflects all of that feedback. We explored several sizes—36, 37, 38, and 39 millimeters. Ultimately, 37 mm was the smallest size that allowed us to preserve the watch’s technical features.”

The change is what made a slightly imperfect watch perfect to me—looking at the older version was like seeing a painting hanging just slightly crooked. I’m of the mind that a well-designed watch should be framed by one’s wrist—not sit right up against the edge of it. This was precisely the quality that the condensed size offered: smaller, incredibly thin, and so comfortable I forgot it was there.

The OF’s similarities to other modern watches begin and end with the fact that it uses three hands to tell the time. You can certainly perceive some of the Gerald Genta-inflected heritage of Bvlgari’s watchmaking division, particularly in the obsession with eight-sided bezels. But compare it to even the luxury sports watch stalwarts out there—timepieces such as the Royal Oak and the Patek Philippe’s Nautilus—let alone to something like a Submariner, and you’re left scratching your head going, this is different.

What distinguishes the design is the clever octagon-within-a-circle-within-a-square architecture. The design starts with one of Buonamassa Stigliani’s famous hand sketches. The angular look is inspired by ancient Roman architecture (and its ample use of the octagon); Italian design; automotive motifs (Buonamassa Stigliani loves cars); and Bvlgari’s own jewelry. In fact, the OF37 wears much more like a piece of modernist sculpture on the wrist than a conventional wristwatch.

The OF37, regardless of material, boasts the brand-new Bvlgari BVF 100 movement. Measuring just 2.35 mm thick, it uses a platinum micro-rotor activated by the movement of your wrist to automatically wind the watch. The case itself at 6.45 mm is actually thicker than the 40mm version’s case at 5.15 mm, though you likely wouldn’t notice this given its smaller diameter and the fact that it’s only as thick as a few credit cards stacked together. The power reserve on the 40-mm version is 60 hours; impressively, that of the 37mm—a watch 20% smaller in volume—is 20% higher, at 72 hours.

The OF is almost a victim of its own success in differentiating itself from the rest of the market. I’m almost certain that the watch couldn’t be my personal daily driver. But could it be a part of my rotation? Hell yes. I can’t wait till the first celeb pairs one of these with black tie, frankly. Josh O’Connor, can you help me out there? The list price warrants discussion here: $16,600 for the sandblasted titanium version ($17,300 for the satin/polished titanium version and $48,300 for the gold version) is no joke. This probably won’t be someone’s first watch but rather the province of somebody for whom watch collecting is already a practiced sport.

Once or twice while wearing the OF37, I caught a glimpse of its sleek angles and strange profile in the window reflection of a parked car, or even the mirror in my bathroom. That it looks quite unlike anything that came before it means that it doesn’t have simple answers to simple questions: Is this an everyday watch? A dress watch? Something for serious collectors or splashy newcomers? What makes the OF37 special is that it refuses to be any one of those things.

items.title: Nathan Fielder on Reality TV, Elizabeth Holmes, and the Curiosity that Drives Him
items.description: In 2023, Nathan Fielder, who is known for his unique style of reality-based comedy, invited the documentary filmmaker Lance Oppenheim to the Magic Castle. Fielder is a member of that exclusive Los Angeles institution—a private club housed in a mansion, which o
items.author: Lynn Hirschberg
paragraphs: In 2023, Nathan Fielder, who is known for his unique style of reality-based comedy, invited the documentary filmmaker Lance Oppenheim to the Magic Castle. Fielder is a member of that exclusive Los Angeles institution—a private club housed in a mansion, which only magicians are allowed to join. In Vancouver, Canada, where Fielder grew up, he had worked as a magician at birthday parties and bar mitzvahs. “I was doing magic, and I worked at a magic shop from when I was 13 until I was 20,” Fielder told me. “I had to stop, because if you don’t stop, people will forever say to you, ‘Show me a trick.’”

Fielder had initially met Oppenheim because he is a fan of Some Kind of Heaven, Oppenheim’s documentary about the Villages, a retirement community in Florida. The two started talking, and Oppenheim mentioned that he’d heard that Elizabeth Holmes, the notorious indicted CEO and founder of Theranos—the company that fraudulently maintained it had invented a machine that could diagnose many diseases with a single drop of blood—had approached A24 about a documentary. Holmes and her life partner, Billy Evans, wanted someone to film their lives together, theoretically to reveal a more human side of Holmes than the one that had been depicted in the media.

“We were both intrigued by the Holmes story,” Oppenheim recalled. “But initially, we were just spending an evening at the Magic Castle. Nathan loaned me a belt and a tie because there’s a dress code, and we were in the close-up magic room and they asked for a celebrity name from the audience. Someone shouted ‘Elizabeth Holmes,’ and we took that as a sign.” Within days, Fielder had contacted A24, which had produced his show The Curse, and met with Holmes and Evans at their home in San Diego. That was the beginning of a three-year project: the documentary You Can See Everything, which premiered in September at the Telluride Film Festival with a super-secret screening.

The film, which takes place largely in the Holmes-Evans household in the days before Holmes is set to go to prison in Texas, is remarkably intimate and revealing, but also confounding. Fielder moved into the couple’s guesthouse, and Oppenheim and Fielder and their crew worked up to 17 hours a day. Holmes is inscrutable, despite the fact that Fielder and Oppenheim, using three different cameras, captured scenes of the couple in bed and in the kitchen making breakfast for their two young children, William and Invicta. There’s even a striking moment in which Billy is brushing his teeth in the shower.

The intensity of You Can See Everything is amplified by Fielder’s interviews with Holmes. “When I started the project, Elizabeth seemed black and white to me,” he explained. “In my mind, she was guilty. But I was very interested in her and her situation. Curiosity drove me. I’ve always tried to find out the truth in any situation, even if there’s a lot of artifice involved. But when I met Elizabeth, she was so different than I thought she would be. She was disarming in real life. I told her right away that I believed everything that I’d read about her, but that didn’t frighten her.”

Fielder and Oppenheim, who codirected the film, retained creative control over the project and also the right to pull the plug at any time. “Every day, I’d say, ‘If this is too much for you, we’ll bail,’ ” Fielder recalled. “But Billy and Elizabeth always said, ‘We want you to stay.’ We didn’t want the film to relitigate the past. This was about their present moment, but we still had to reconcile with who Elizabeth Holmes is, and was.”

In one stunning segment, Fielder asks Holmes about her veracity; Holmes maintains that she’s never lied in her entire life. Fielder gently probes: not even a white lie to get out of a dinner obligation? Holmes says no, never, I can’t recall ever lying for any reason. “That was one of the moments when I realized the documentary was about something meaningful,” Fielder said. “When she said she’s never lied, she widened the gap so much. I realized there’s more going on here than I thought.”

Fielder appears in the film as a classic journalist, though there is a non-journalistic twist in the second half of the film, which he asked me not to reveal. His other award-winning TV projects have also combined journalism with a sense of the uncanny. The four seasons of Nathan for You, which premiered in 2013, were definitely funny, but the premise of the series was that Fielder would offer professional advice to struggling businesses. His more recent show, The Rehearsal, helps people navigate difficult life situations by gaming out scenarios in elaborately designed sets. For example, in order to investigate communication failures in aviation, Fielder actually became a pilot and flew a large passenger plane.

He had a similar level of commitment to You Can See Everything. “I felt conflicted at times, which was new for me,” Fielder said. “There was always more going on than I thought, and, even now, there are certain aspects of the film where I don’t feel I have a clear conclusion. I want the audience to help me understand the experience.”
Three Questions With Nathan
Do you watch reality television?

I was into The Bachelor for a period of time. I prefer The Bachelor to The Bachelorette. The dynamic between women is more interesting than the dynamic between men. Chris Soules [as the bachelor] was a good season of the show. He’s a total blank thing—there’s nothing from him—but the women were really interesting. When it works, I think The Bachelor has the best reality show format.
What chronological age do you feel?

Twenty-two. I’m 43 now, and sometimes when I’m with people in their 30s, I feel like they are older than me. I don’t know things that other people know. I always feel that everyone knows more than I do. So it’s very easy for me to ask people questions.
Did you feel that way with Elizabeth Holmes?

Yes and no. It was immersive: I was living there, at their request. I didn’t go out of their gated community because there were paparazzi everywhere, and we wanted to keep our project a secret. I think linearly—I always believe there’s a way to untangle any mess. My curiosity with Elizabeth was to understand her. And, in my life, I’ve never been so confused by a person.

items.title: Pierpaolo Piccioli on His Vision for Balenciaga & the Power of Starting Over
items.description: It takes less than a minute for Pierpaolo Piccioli to steer a conversation about fashion into one about philosophy. More than a year into his tenure as creative director of Balenciaga, during an interview on the day after he showed his first couture collection
items.author: Eric Wilson
paragraphs: It takes less than a minute for Pierpaolo Piccioli to steer a conversation about fashion into one about philosophy. More than a year into his tenure as creative director of Balenciaga, during an interview on the day after he showed his first couture collection for the house in July, Piccioli explains how he has navigated a role that is both familiar and foreign to him by first quoting Friedrich Nietzsche and the concept of oblivion—oblio in Piccioli’s native Italian.

“Oblio is a moment when you are aware of your past, but you kind of forget everything for a moment and you see everything with new eyes,” says Piccioli, seated at a large conference table in his office suite on Avenue George V, in Paris. “And that’s what actually happened to me.”

For most of his career, over a quarter century, Piccioli was associated with one designer: Valentino Garavani, who made a lasting impression on his life and his eye. Starting in 1999, Piccioli, then in his early 30s, and his longtime collaborator, Maria Grazia Chiuri, rose through the ranks at Valentino, becoming co–creative directors in 2008, a year after Valentino announced his retirement. Then Piccioli led the Roman house solo from 2016 to 2024, while Chiuri served as creative director at Dior. He knew the seamstresses by their names, their skills, their peculiarities, and their very Italian way of working, and he adopted the rhythms and rituals, if not the formality, of Valentino himself. This would have been a lot to leave behind for a designer taking on the mantle of another legendary brand—let alone that of Cristóbal Balenciaga. That house’s own rich history includes two wildly successful modern interpretations, first under Nicolas Ghesquière, then under the now mononymous Demna. But in the words of Nietzsche, “Man will desire oblivion rather than not desire at all.” “I didn’t want to come here to find the same people with the same experiences,” Piccioli says. “I wanted to face something new.”

At his couture show the day before, under the blazing sun in a garden on the outskirts of Paris, Piccioli showed 52 looks that were captivating in their strange beauty. Some of them were outrageously glamorous in the bold style that Piccioli had once championed at Valentino: He opened with a cloud-shaped jacket trimmed with a flock of intense red feathers, worn over a white oversize silk duchesse satin T-shirt and voluminous beige trousers; another look consisted of a dark red shirt styled with big pink pants. But many others represented new territory for the designer, like a floor-length coat the color of a yellow highlighter, which he showed backward, slung over matching pants. There was a fluorescent pink silk “balloon bolero” dress trimmed with feathers made of tiny strips of curled organza. The designs seemed to demand close inspection to be fully understood.

“It felt like a real celebration of artistry,” said the actor Lily Collins, who has known Piccioli for more than a decade, since they first attended a Met Gala together. “Pierpaolo and Balenciaga are the perfect mix.” Naomi Watts headed backstage, where she raved about a tailored black dress adorned with a white ribbon scarf. “That’s the sort of dress I look forward to wearing in my 50s, 60s, 70s, and then some,” she said. Demi Moore, who wore a Piccioli-designed Balenciaga couture ensemble at Cannes in May, circled the boards showing photographs of the models in each of their looks, while Hudson Williams, who appeared in one of Piccioli’s first Balenciaga advertising campaigns, stood nearby, waiting to offer his congratulations.

“This collection is the result of a feeling,” Piccioli wrote in a printed program composed of 20 narrowly spaced pages, including detailed descriptions of all the looks, along with the names of the members of his atelier who helped realize them—Victor, Thomas, Léa, Margherite, etc. “We worked while getting to know each other, learning to understand one another,” Piccioli wrote. It was part of his broad effort to humanize the couture-making experience, which can feel cold and anonymous to anyone living outside that bubble.

The week before the show, Balenciaga wiped its social media history and then posted portraits of some 40 members of its atelier, all dressed in their white Balenciaga Couture work coats. Many of them appeared to be quite young, though a few were established hands and familiar faces, including Bruno Sialelli, formerly the creative director at Lanvin. Philip Treacy, the milliner, was also credited in the couture program for contributions that included a pink ostrich-feather headpiece that spiraled from the crown and around the torso, turning the model who wore it into a swan.

This meeting of minds, among Piccioli, his seasoned collaborators, and his younger team, has become as much a part of his vision for Balenciaga as the clothes seen on his runway. “When you don’t know the rules, you are more open to experiment,” he says. “And that is the key for me to interpret Balenciaga. I didn’t want to go back to any of the old shapes but to try to invent a new shape that could have been that of Cristóbal.”

The day after the show, the couture salon is packed with visitors examining the looks. Patti Wilson, the stylist, has been there for more than an hour. Amal Clooney is spotted among the mannequins. When he arrives, Piccioli, who is 59, is dressed in his usual uniform of a black T-shirt and trousers, with a necklace of coral amulets worn as protection from bad energy. He has a pack of cigarettes in hand and is still very much the picture of a Roman designer who cooks his own pasta most nights, now at his new home just across the Seine. “I’ve got my Roman ways in Paris,” he says. “It’s a sort of effortless approach that is maybe less formal than expected, more direct and more human.”

On his first day at Balenciaga last year, Piccioli traveled to Getaria, the tiny fishing village in the Basque region of Spain where Cristóbal Balenciaga was born in 1895, and where a museum dedicated to the master’s work today offers access to an enormous array of designs collected by his staff and clients. As Piccioli immersed himself in Balenciaga’s world, he began to understand that designs he had perceived through images as austere or strictly linear were, in fact, quite light. That would be his starting point for Balenciaga couture. “In every one of his silhouettes, the body was the protagonist,” he said.

To achieve similar results in new ways became an obsession for Piccioli, and this is where having a younger atelier was an advantage—the team was willing to experiment with techniques that break with the strict traditions of couture. Perhaps the biggest change was replacing standard Stockman mannequins with custom forms created from 3D scans of models’ bodies. Those ghostly plastic forms were used to shape fabrics through a complex process of layering cashmere upon leather that had been washed, stretched, and allowed to dry in place to hold its shape. Each mold took as long as a month to create, but eliminated the need for darts or seams. Piccioli also wanted to play with new fabrics and materials, using a lab-grown silk called AMSilk that purports to be fossil fuel–free and stronger than steel.

Despite these technical innovations, Piccioli believes in the classic model of couture as the pinnacle of fashion. “When you talk about couture, you talk about an approach in which there are no maps. A 3D conversation with the body can then apply to denim, T-shirts, and tailored jackets from prêt-à-porter. To me, a T-shirt has to be a T-shirt, as much as a pair of jeans has to be a pair of jeans. But if you meld couture and industrialization, you can make a more modern garment.”

Like most designers of his generation, Piccioli was raised to worship at the altar of the great Cristóbal Balenciaga, who worked in Paris from 1937 until his retirement, in 1968. The first image Piccioli posted on his personal Instagram account, in 2018, was of a 1967 Balenciaga wedding ensemble that had been included in the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Costume Institute exhibition “Heavenly Bodies” that year. “Simplicity is a solved complexity,” Piccioli wrote in his caption, paraphrasing the sculptor Constantin Brâncusi. It did not escape Piccioli’s attention that the wedding dress had been designed by Balenciaga the same year Piccioli was born. And although his reverence for Balenciaga is rooted in the maestro’s innovations, Piccioli made clear upon his arrival at the house that he respected the label’s more recent history as a modern luxury brand as well. Balenciaga is now a commercial behemoth that has been redefined by other famous designers. Ghesquière gave Balenciaga heat in the new millennium; Demna brought the house to the street over the past decade, and his flair for disruption ultimately drove Balenciaga well past $1 billion in sales. Both are difficult acts to follow.

With his initial ready-to-wear shows, Piccioli laid some of the groundwork. His spring 2026 collection was based on Balenciaga’s 1957 sack dress, which had a lightweight and unrestrictive shape that was revolutionary at the time; the following season was an ode to “finding lightness in the dark,” as illustrated by inky black skirts and coats, a few pieces rendered with imagery from Sam Levinson’s Euphoria. Piccioli also alluded to his personal love of sports with a techwear-meets-couture pre-fall collection, and with the introduction of a collaboration with the NBA in January that included four-figure varsity jackets, as well as hoodies and sweatpants that would not have looked out of place in the luxury streetwear oeuvre of his predecessor.

As Piccioli steers the future of Balenciaga while learning to embrace his own, he is facing change on a personal level. Valentino Garavani, to whom Piccioli remained close long after his retirement, died in January at the age of 93. Piccioli’s former design partner, Chiuri, has since left Dior and returned to Rome, where she made her couture debut for Fendi the same week Piccioli was presenting his for Balenciaga. His children, Benedetta, Pietro, and Stella, are all now adults and starting their own lives. Just as before, he returns to Italy to spend his holidays with his wife, Simona, and their family at their seaside home in the small beach town of Nettuno, near Rome, but their days there are more limited than they were before.

In Piccioli’s loose interpretation of Nietzsche, a designer might be able to forget his history out of necessity for a moment, but the past remains around him all the same. Acknowledging as much, Piccioli has kept the office he inherited mostly untouched. Its decor is aggressively gray, just as Demna left it last year when he was tasked with righting the ship at Gucci, which, like Balenciaga, is owned by the luxury goods conglomerate Kering. Piccioli layered some brightly colored rugs on the floor and retrieved from his own storage a three-person desk designed by Gio Ponti. Against the far wall is a billboard-size poster of a famous photograph of the same Balenciaga 1967 wedding ensemble Piccioli posted on Instagram, which shows the dress in such stark black and white contrast that its sharp silhouette forms an almost perfect triangle. Leaned against the photo is a bright pink surfboard designed by Piccioli for Zara’s 50th anniversary last year.

“I’ve added some elements and taken out others, but this is kind of metaphorical of what I’m doing here at Balenciaga,” Piccioli says of the office. “They are contradictory in the space, but in a way I feel that they have found their own harmony. I didn’t want to deny what has been done before me. I’d rather layer on top of that and create a bridge so that Balenciaga can go somewhere else.”
