items.title: The Past and Future of Giorgio Armani
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Chantal Fernandez
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

Pantaleo Dell’Orco is a shy 73-year-old with a scruffy mustache and round glasses that give him the look of a modish classics professor, one who is rarely out of black or navy clothes. In Milan, where he lives, he is known as Leo, the man who for five decades was Giorgio Armani’s shadow. The two of them shared a palazzo in the stylish Brera neighborhood and worked together at the vast fashion company Armani founded in 1975 and ruled independently as designer and chief executive until his death a year ago at the age of 91. Dell’Orco is now the creative director of menswear and the largest single shareholder in Giorgio Armani S.p.A., which is said to be worth between $6 billion and $8 billion. He is also the chairman of the board, the directors of which include Armani’s nephew Andrea Camerana and niece Silvana Armani, who is in charge of women’s ready-to-wear and haute couture.

In his will, Armani, a famously exacting boss who divvied up his fortune down to every last Andy Warhol and Man Ray, instructed his heirs to either pursue a public offering or sell the company to LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton, EssilorLuxottica, or L’Oréal. He gave them a deadline of March 2027 to start the process by selling an initial 15 percent stake.

The question of what happens next to one of fashion’s largest self-made brands has consumed an industry stuck in a multiyear sales slump and beset by change, especially in Italy, where Versace, Gucci, Valentino, and Bottega Veneta have all appointed new creative directors in the last few years with varying degrees of critical and commercial success.

Dell’Orco, who has shunned the limelight for most of his life, is unbothered by the speculation about the future. He has a friendly demeanor and carries himself like someone who knows he doesn’t have to speak too loudly to be heard. In fact, he seems amused by the gossip. “It’s good for the company, the chitchat,” he tells me in August. The following month, the company made its first big move since Armani’s death, hiring Dario Vitale, a 42-year-old Neapolitan who is the most exciting new name in fashion despite having lasted only one season at Versace. He will design the diffusion line Emporio Armani, as well as accessories for the Giorgio Armani label, reporting to Silvana and Dell’Orco. The appointment positions Vitale to one day take over all of Armani and shows that Dell’Orco, like his longtime partner, makes decisions on his own terms.

Dell’Orco and I first meet in May, less than a year after a public wake drew thousands of mourners over the course of two days to Armani’s austere Tadao Ando-designed Teatro. “The whole city was there,” says Carla Sozzani, the magazine editor and founder of the influential boutique 10 Corso Como. “It’s like the king of Milano passed away. He was one of those people that you think are immortal.” Dell’Orco didn’t have much time to grieve. It was weeks away from a 50th-anniversary spectacle, and there was work to be done. “I told myself, ‘I have to be strong,’” he says.

We are at the company headquarters, a 17th-century palazzo on Via Borgonuovo not far from his own. Dell’Orco is leading a design meeting ahead of the spring 2027 collection of the flagship label, which he and Armani designed together. Now he is in charge and his nephew Gianluca Dell’Orco is his deputy. Mood boards line the wall with reference images: loose linen looks from past shoots and runway presentations, Al Pacino in a billowing khaki jacket from the mid-1990s, a sweaty Richard Gere in a nearly sheer white top. At the bottom of one board, a pinned notecard reads DANDY LATINO and LA DOLCE ELEGANZA.

The collection does not appear to stray far from the signature soft-tailored look Dell’Orco helped define, though there are subtle differences: The pants are slimmer, the jackets longer. He is not inclined to stage some kind of flashy runway stunt or drop a surprise collaboration. “Doing something just so people talk, that’s not me,” he says. “I’m not interested in being Prada.”

A refusal to bend to trends served the company’s namesake well. Armani was fully in command of his empire — three stand-alone subbrands making at least six runway collections a year; lines of accessories, beauty, fragrances, furniture; clubs, restaurants, megayachts, and even residential buildings, such as a 12-story condo in Lenox Hill — and felt little obligation to cater to commercial whims besides his own. When he decided to crash the stuffy world of French haute couture with his own version, many were skeptical, but Privé just turned 20 and is said to be one of the most successful lines within the Armani Group.

Those who know Dell’Orco well say he is as single-minded as Armani, who appreciated his candor. “Italian fashion companies are like Renaissance courts,” says one former Armani executive. “They have their prince and the courtiers. Leo would say things to Giorgio other people wouldn’t dare say.”

For many years, Stefano Pilati, who worked with Dell’Orco in the ’90s before he went on to run Yves Saint Laurent and Zegna, was rumored to be the designer to one day take over Giorgio Armani. “I found it almost offensive because it was like a way of saying to Mr. Armani, ‘You should move on,’” he tells me. “Leo is the Armani man, period. Everybody’s waiting for Armani to change somehow, but Armani has never been like this. Modernizing the brand without losing its essence requires great skill. Who else could do it? The minute it’s not Armani, it’s not Armani.”

Sozzani, who met both men in the 1970s, sees Dell’Orco as the last thread connected to the label’s origin story, someone who can’t be easily replaced. “He grew up from a child, almost, with Armani. He was born of Armani. Who else has that knowledge, that experience, that taste?” she says. “Why look for somebody else? To do what, exactly? Stay there for three seasons and then go? The accent changes, the logo changes, the packaging changes.”

An employee since long before American Gigolo and Miami Vice made Armani a global sensation, Dell’Orco has watched the brand move from upstart to powerhouse to something taken for granted by snooty magazine editors and blatantly cribbed by younger designers. He is skilled at tuning out industry talk. “Sometimes I do listen to other people’s opinions. Ninety percent of the time, I decide to do exactly what I would have done anyway,” he tells me. Plus he is not a worrier.

“I am rarely stressed,” he says. Armani himself was the opposite. To the outside world, he was the imperial control freak called “King Giorgio” by the press. But Dell’Orco remembers the private Armani who would often have nightmares before runway shows, tortured by a nagging sense he had something to prove. “He was simple, he was instinctive, he would say exactly the words you wanted to hear. He was perfect at that,” he says.

It is after 3 p.m., and we are at Dell’Orco’s home, where he now lives alone with two cats and an Indian blackbird named Merlino who chirps “buongiorno” and “Giorgio.” He receives me in an immaculate living room with slick black floors and elegant 1930s-style furniture that he is keeping just as Armani intended. Armani’s presence is everywhere. From the corner of my eye, I see his blue eyes gazing out from a Warhol portrait. “The hardest part of all was when he was holding my hand and then suddenly, I could no longer feel his touch. It was absolutely devastating,” Dell’Orco says, his voice catching. He pauses. “Sometimes I still dream about him.” In his imagination, they’re getting ready for another runway show, as they did so many times: “There are clothes everywhere.”

Leo Dell’Orco and Giorgio Armani met in the summer of 1976. Dell’Orco was a tall, handsome, athletic 23-year-old hanging with two friends at a dog park off Via Gerolamo Tiraboschi. The group was debating whether to see a movie or hit a nightclub when a friendly dog, a boxer named Jago, wandered over. He belonged to a 41-year-old man with an intense stare and graying hair. “It was fate,” Armani wrote years later. “It was a particular meeting that could only have happened in that moment,” Dell’Orco says.

Dell’Orco had never heard of the designer, who had founded his business a year earlier with money from the sale of his Volkswagen Beetle. Dell’Orco was a technical draftsman from Puglia working at a large gas company, and soccer was his only interest outside the office.

Armani, meanwhile, had been a stilista since the 1960s, working for Nino Cerruti and designing lines for manufacturers such as Ungaro and Zegna. He ran his burgeoning namesake label with his partner, Sergio Galeotti, who focused on the business side of the operation and had encouraged Armani to strike out on his own shortly after they met at the beachside nightclub Capannina di Franceschi in Forte dei Marmi in the summer of 1966. The relationship was romantic for a time, but as Armani once put it, “the term love is too narrow. We were allies in the face of life and the rest of the world.”

At the dog park, Dell’Orco’s friend struck up a conversation with the designer, who invited them over to his house for an aperitivo. There, he asked if they might be interested in modeling in his upcoming runway show. “I said, ‘Hmmm, why not?’” Dell’Orco says. A few days later, he and a couple of friends showed up at a small studio on Corso Venezia, where a secretary handed them some clothes to try on. One friend was declared too short. Dell’Orco made the cut.

“The whole atmosphere of doing a runway show, the rehearsal, it was all very exciting,” he says. In a photograph in the trade newspaper Footwear News the following spring, Dell’Orco saunters down a runway with a jacket thrown over his broad shoulders, one hand in his pocket. He became a part-time fixture at Armani’s studio, doing odd jobs and helping to develop fabrics.

At the time, French fashion was more popular and prestigious than Italian labels. When Miuccia Prada handed out leaflets for the Italian Communist Party as a college student, she wore Yves Saint Laurent and Courrèges; the business her grandfather started in 1913 made only leather goods then. Armani was part of a competitive cohort of Italian designers, including Gianni Versace and Walter Albini, who challenged French superiority with wearable clothes for Italian yuppies, the paninari. “Milano became the capital of fashion in quite a short time,” says Sozzani, who until the late 1970s was almost always wearing Saint Laurent. “There was this square in Milan, Piazza San Babila, where everyone wore a down jacket, Armani jeans, Timberlands, and an El Charro belt,” Dell’Orco says. “It was a democratic fashion. That is to say, if you were good-looking, it showed.”

From his first collection, Armani’s sales pitch for men was a relaxed, unpretentious style, one he would obsessively refine again and again: unstructured suits made from soft, sensual fabrics such as silky gabardines traditionally used for women. “He invented the sexy suit,” says Gene Pressman, the former co-CEO of Barneys, which introduced the brand to the U.S. “Before that, men didn’t wear greens and browns. They were strictly navy and gray. Armani introduced a whole palette. He used all the wonderful colors of Tuscany. It was very revolutionary.”

At first, Armani’s suits were too avant-garde for most Americans looking for standard-issue office suits. Then, in February 1980, American Gigolo premiered, and Richard Gere turned Armani’s soft jackets and front-pleat trousers into the most seductive thing a successful man could wear. “Wall Street went nuts, and all of a sudden, these young kids were buying ten suits at a time,” says Pressman. “They’d lay out like 30 shirts, 20 ties, all kinds of accessories, and we couldn’t get them on the racks fast enough to go over to the alterations department.”

Months later, Armani staged an elaborate runway show underneath the Prometheus statue outside Rockefeller Center for 1,000 people, including Carrie Fisher and Lauren Hutton. Dell’Orco, on his first visit to Manhattan, modeled. “It was the most over-the-top place, a surreal place. You didn’t understand where you were,” he recalls. “It was exciting, doing the runway show next to Iman.” Emporio Armani launched in 1981, followed by jeans, fragrances, and a children’s line. Revenue tripled to 26 billion lire, the equivalent of $63 million today. “Armani, at that time, was really a god in Milan,” says Pilati. The next year, “Giorgio’s Gorgeous Style” landed on the cover of Time.

Around then, Armani and Galeotti hired some relatives to join a team that had grown to about 100 employees: Silvana, the daughter of Armani’s older brother, Sergio, and two of Galeotti’s nieces. “That marked the turning point. From that moment on, the company became more of a family affair,” says Dell’Orco, who had joined the men’s-design team full time. His relationship with Armani had also evolved. “There are some things that are hard to explain. It happened naturally,” he says. “A 20-year age difference was a lot, but I must be sincere: It’s something that came on its own.” Though it was not publicly discussed, everybody understood Dell’Orco to be especially close to the boss. “Leo was a humble assistant in a superior position because there was a relationship,” says another colleague from the early years of the business. “He learned everything from Armani. He was next to him all the time.”

In 1984, as sales soared, Galeotti was diagnosed with AIDS and sought treatment in New York. Armani visited every month. “A couple of times, I went along as well, and those were not easy visits,” says Dell’Orco. The disease was ravaging the fashion industry, and everyone knew someone affected. The designers Chester Weinberg, Willi Smith, and Roy Halston Frowick would die from AIDS-related illnesses by the end of the decade. Armani threw himself into the business. “During that dreadful year, I lived as if I was holding my breath, without thinking about the inevitable, working day in and day out,” he wrote in his memoir.

Galeotti died in August 1985 at his home outside Paris with members of his family by his side as well as Armani and Dell’Orco. He was 40. The New York Times attributed the cause to a heart attack brought on by leukemia. Armani was bereft. He described Dell’Orco as a great source of comfort: “I will never forget how much he helped me through the sad events surrounding Sergio’s illness, in that undisturbed countryside not far from Paris.”

Resilience was written into the Armani story from the beginning. In his memoir, he described growing up under Mussolini in Piacenza, which was a frequent target of Allied bombing during World War II. The oft-repeated story goes that he was 10, playing with friends on the street, when someone stepped on an undetonated packet of gunpowder, killing one boy and landing Armani in the hospital with severe burns. He never tired of telling people that doctors were convinced he wouldn’t see again. After Galeotti’s death, he felt underestimated once more. He was now the sole owner of a complex and growing company, and he didn’t have a partner to handle business affairs while he designed. A string of key deputies left, and the business seemed troubled. “Many believed I would collapse psychologically,” he wrote.

Instead, Armani took on Galeotti’s job as the head of the finances, assuming a dual business and creative role that he would hold for the rest of his life. The label flourished. “Giorgio never listened to anybody. He knew exactly what he wanted,” says Sozzani. “Until the end of the ’80s, early ’90s, there were five big players in Italy: Valentino, who was in Rome, and in Milano there was Gianfranco Ferré, Krizia, Versace, and Armani.” Today, none except Armani is independent — Versace, a once-formidable competitor, is owned by Prada, and a Qatari investment fund controls 70 percent of Valentino, the famous founder of which died earlier this year; Krizia and Ferré are glorified licenses owned by foreigners. Armani had the foresight to set up highly profitable licensing agreements for makeup and fragrances with L’Oréal and for sunglasses with the eyewear giant Luxottica. Throughout the 1990s, sales grew by double digits every year. And later, he brought manufacturing in-house so as to control a larger share of the profits. Through it all, Dell’Orco was by his side.

“The sense of calm I projected was something he appreciated,” Dell’Orco says. “I was happy there, and the years passed without me realizing it.” He doesn’t even remember when exactly he moved into the palazzo on Via Borgonuovo.

Though they had been together for decades, Dell’Orco remained in the margins of Armani’s public life. He was sometimes mentioned as a close friend in articles, but the news media, especially in Italy, afforded King Giorgio an unusual degree of privacy. Discretion suited Dell’Orco, too. Gay marriage isn’t legal in Italy, but when I ask if he and Armani ever talked about getting married, he shakes his head, as if I were breaking some unspoken rule. Did he feel married? “It is something I never thought, never said.” They were known to bicker over decisions small — hats in a collection, which Armani loved and Dell’Orco less so, or heels, which Dell’Orco preferred over Armani’s usual choice of flats — and big, like the 2004 launch of the activewear line EA7, which Armani initially fought but Dell’Orco knew would sell well.

“Leo is from another generation, so obviously he pushed for younger trends,” says Pilati. “Mr. Armani either took his ideas or said ‘Leo, piss off.’ But even if they were fighting, Leo never bitched about Mr. Armani. That was one of his best qualities. I’ve never seen someone so serene.” Federico Marchetti, the founder of the e-commerce giant Yoox, joined Armani’s board in 2020 and observed their dynamic. “Leo was the person Mr. Armani listened to the most,” he says. “In the middle of all these people saying ‘yes, yes, yes,’ he is someone who sometimes said ‘no.’ He’s that kind of a partner.”

Dell’Orco laughs when I ask about the quarrels with Armani. It took years for him to feel comfortable speaking his mind in the atelier. “Giorgio was, let’s say, more conservative. I wanted to inject a bit of youthfulness into things. Little by little, he came to trust me,” he says. “If we fought at 1 p.m., we would go have lunch after, and for me it had already passed. That’s the thing that made it work. If not, it would have been a whole drama.”

The duo finally took a bow together at the end of a men’s-fashion show in 2021. In matching navy T-shirts, slacks, and white sneakers, they raised clasped hands to a standing ovation from the crowd. Quietly, Armani, long resistant to public discussions about retirement or succession, had made moves to set up the company for the future. In the early aughts, when the luxury industry began to rapidly consolidate, he shared a much-scrutinized cup of tea with Bernard Arnault, the chairman of LVMH, and he came close to selling to what was then known as the Gucci Group, a precursor to Kering, before pulling out at the last minute. “He was very concerned about keeping absolute control over the company, which I respected,” says Domenico De Sole, who was CEO of the Gucci Group at the time.

The fear of losing control never left Armani, and in 2016, he created a foundation to oversee the management of the company, led only by himself, his financial adviser, and Dell’Orco. His will stipulated that the foundation would always retain at least a 30 percent stake in the company to ensure it is run with a series of founding principles, including a creative mandate to maintain “an essential, modern, elegant, and unostentatious style with attention to detail and wearability.” Dell’Orco, who now chairs the foundation, supported the approach, which would guarantee a continuation of what they had built: “He’d say things like, ‘Let’s sell everything!’ and I’d reply, ‘Sell it to whom?’ He never actually meant it.”

The two sometimes fantasized about retirement, but the idea was just as quickly shrugged off. “As long as he was working, he felt good,” Dell’Orco says. “Work was his life. He had no hobbies.” Once, a couple of years ago, Armani asked how much longer he intended to keep going. A decade, Dell’Orco told him. “Look, it’s tough,” Armani warned him. “You worked until you were 90. Why can’t I?” Dell’Orco responded.

Still, they never explicitly discussed Dell’Orco one day becoming chairman of the board and having voting power in the company’s most important decisions. “In a way, deep down, I understood that eventually I would be the one,” he says. “But it’s something I never voiced aloud, nor did I ever put myself forward for it. He figured it out on his own.”

At the end of the summer, Dell’Orco WhatsApps me while on vacation near Mykonos from the family’s 65-meter superyacht Maìn (the nickname of Armani’s mother). Armani preferred Pantelleria: He found Greece too windy, but Dell’Orco appreciates the water here, the local taverns. For once, he is out of his dark uniform, wearing a white T-shirt that highlights his gray hair. Armani would sometimes scold him for wearing other designers, but lately Dell’Orco has been adding to the mix — Rick Owens, Sacai, Comme des Garçons. By his sunburned face, I can tell he has been enjoying his time off. He even went out in Ibiza, though he was taken aback by the looks he saw. “Men are more dressed, and women are much less dressed,” he says. “I want a woman who’s more chic.”

The collection he had first shown me in May was well received during Milan Men’s Fashion Week, where it was presented alongside Silvana’s cruise lineup. Gone were the hats that were the subject of so many arguments with Armani. Shirts and pants looked lived-in, the bags almost beaten up. Fabrics leaned heavily on linen, washed silk, and ultrasoft denim. The styling was more casual, and the models seemed at ease, not like the stiff Italian Ken dolls of the past. It was the most relaxed Armani has looked in years, and still some critics complained that it lacked the cool of labels such as Prada, where punk skinny jeans and leather jackets portended a change in men’s silhouette, or Ralph Lauren’s surprisingly trendy prep maximalism.

From his floating mansion in the Aegean, Dell’Orco isn’t too broken up by the critics, nor is he overly impressed with the season. “I saw that quite a few designers tried to do things that were a bit out there,” he says diplomatically. “I like to stay the course. I don’t push just to push.” For now, that means embracing what the brand does best, like tailoring and suiting, a sound strategy given how popular vintage Armani is on the resale market. Last year, to capitalize on the hype, the label reissued several classic Armani styles, such as single-pleat trousers from 1990 and a double-breasted leather jacket from 1979, for a capsule collection called Archivio. “Giorgio always wanted to create something new so that people talked about him more,” Dell’Orco says. “For him, the suit was too banal. At this moment, I feel we need to get back to it.”

Perhaps more urgent than whether the pants are skinny enough is the looming question of Armani’s ownership. Since we last spoke, a report in La Repubblica suggests the initial 15 percent stake sale could be split among the three preferred suitors, a move that is widely seen as a way to leave open the possibility for a potential majority sale later on. The stake sale might also be delayed beyond Armani’s self-imposed 2027 deadline, sources told the newspaper, because of headwinds in the luxury market. Like many of its competitors, Armani is experiencing a dip — revenue, not counting licensing royalties, declined 5 percent in 2024, to $2.7 billion, and 2.8 percent in 2025, to $2.6 billion. It’s not a crisis, not yet, but it’s far from an ideal track record for going public or selling at a high valuation. A listing comes with its own complications, too. For one, the company has to demonstrate it can grow profitably at a vigorous pace and keep up quarter after quarter. “People are not buying the past in the stock market. They want to buy the future,” De Sole says.

Armani, though, is a unique asset: It is globally recognized and has substantial cash reserves and no debt. Its licensed lines with L’Oreal and EssilorLuxottica generated an estimated $2.3 billion in 2025. The brand is diversified while avoiding the kind of overexpansion that can turn blue-chip labels into discount slop. “The foundations are beyond rock-solid,” says Graziano de Boni, a former CEO of Armani’s North American subsidiary. “It is the only fashion brand that goes from fast fashion to couture and nobody complains.” The stability of the business, and its snoozy reputation, may actually work in its favor. “They didn’t have all these swings that many other fashion houses had in the past,” says Marchetti, who navigated the Yoox IPO almost 20 years ago. “That’s what the family and the board are trying to continue.”

Dell’Orco cannot make any major decisions about an outright sale or a public offering without the support of either Silvana Armani or Andrea Camerana. The family has so far avoided painful disagreements, the kind of succession drama that plunged Luxottica into a messy squabble after the founder, Leonardo Del Vecchio, who died in 2022, left the $46 billion fortune in the hands of eight heirs from three different marriages. That is not the Armani way. When Dell’Orco and Silvana meet with employees to discuss pending items, or sospesi, they still leave the head of the table, Armani’s seat, empty. “Managing to keep everyone together — the whole group — is the most important thing Giorgio did,” Dell’Orco says. “Before long, we’ll be bringing in some partners.”

Although he anticipates the initial stake sale will go forward as planned by next spring, Dell’Orco does not seem to feel much urgency. “We cannot simply remain as we are,” he says. “I want to grow gradually, to reach a revenue level that is a bit higher — let’s say $4 million or $5 million — compared with where we stand right now.” Instead of selling a majority stake, Dell’Orco tells me he hopes Armani will go public at some point: “Because I would feel more free.”

The first time we speak, his own future does not seem in doubt. Like Armani, he loves the work. Still, he allows that change is inevitable. “But change to what extent?” A month before Vitale is formally hired, he seems closer to answering his own question. An outsider, someone who is not beholden to the past, is good for the company, he says. “They need to be someone who has a clear vision. They need to be able to see things for themselves, to make a judgment and then step in.”

items.title: The Chrome Hearts Hustle
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Ezra Marcus
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

On a hot afternoon in August, I step off an elevator into a fluorescent-lit showroom on the second floor of an office building in the Financial District. Jack Jiang, the shop’s 19-year-old proprietor, is sitting behind a glass countertop, wearing gray sweatpants and a black hoodie that reads GO FUCK YOURSELF in lime-green cursive. There is no security guard, even though Jiang is surrounded by millions of dollars’ worth of luxury clothes and accessories: a Supreme x Ducati motorbike, a shelf full of Hermès Birkin bags, and racks and racks of Chrome Hearts. The brand’s signature crosses are everywhere: on jeans, biker jackets, and hoodies; on silver handcuffs, a stapler, a hacksaw, and a baseball hat. While giving me a tour of the space, Jiang pulls out a toilet plunger carved from ebony wood and capped with a silver cross, listed for $8,500. “It’s been used!” he tells me.

Jiang moves more than $20 million worth of product a year. Under the username Legos, he posts videos on TikTok of himself tracking down the items he later off-loads to his showroom. In one video, he shows up at a Beverly Hills high-school party. “We gonna finesse all these rich Beverly Hills kids’ Chrome!” he says to the camera. Inside, the attendees scream his name and clamor to sell him the clothes off their bodies. One says the diamond-studded necklace he’s wearing was a gift from his grandmother and he wants at least $2,500 for it; another strips off his Chrome Hearts pants while standing on a table. In another video, Jiang shows off a Chrome Hearts beanbag chair the rapper Bhad Bhabie sold him. He’d later resell it for nearly half a million dollars.

Jiang is not the only one buying and selling Chrome Hearts for exorbitant prices, nor is he the only one posting these interactions online. The brand has become extremely popular over the past few years among the young and wealthy and especially among crypto entrepreneurs fresh off absurd windfalls from meme coins and NFT projects. “A lot of young teenagers, they’re making $10 million, $50 million at the age of 19, 20 — it’s instant, so a lot of them don’t know how to spend it,” Raphael Badalov, a 22-year-old reseller who goes by the handle byraph, tells me recently, fingering his Chrome Hearts Star of David necklace. We are standing in the middle of a massive floor-through space overlooking West 25th Street, soon to be his new showroom. These same kids have spent the past half-decade “seeing their favorite rappers onstage in head-to-toe Chrome Hearts,” another reseller, Vincent Ferraro, says. “They wake up rich overnight. Like, why not live your dream? Get your dream car, get your dream jeans.”

Except they can’t. As with Hermès, according to the resellers and collectors I spoke to, it is impossible to purchase much of anything at a Chrome Hearts store unless you’ve cultivated a yearslong relationship with the brand. “You can go in these stores with a million dollars in cash and you’ll get nothing and then another guy will come in that has a relationship and they’ll offer him a bunch of cool stuff,” says longtime collector Mason Balbier. He would drop by the store and hang out with the salespeople, and eventually, “it just started happening,” he says. (The brand denies their pieces are dispersed based on “status.”) To get your hands on Chrome Hearts as a new buyer, then, your only option is to turn to resellers like Jiang, who charge whatever they feel like — five figures for jeans and leather jackets, higher for rarer pieces. The comment sections of Jiang’s reselling videos are full of people mocking the high prices. “Is it really worth that? I would say it’s not,” Jiang says. “I feel like it’s retarded.” Still, he added, “if there’s someone willing to pay that price, that means there’s logic behind it. There’s a saying in China: It makes sense if it happens.”

Chrome Hearts was founded in 1988 in Los Angeles by a carpenter, Richard Stark, and his two friends, the jeweler Leonard Kamhout and the leather craftsman John Bowman. They sold studded leather pants and custom motorcycle gear to other friends; in the beginning, they designed the costumes for a low-budget horror movie. After a few years, they managed to open a shop on the Upper East Side, which they filled with silver fleurs-de-lis, Gothic-style belt buckles, and handmade chaps. Cher and Lenny Kravitz were early fans, as were members of Guns N’ Roses and Aerosmith. By the mid-’90s, Stark and his wife, Laurie Lynn, had grown the brand into a multimillion-dollar company, opening stores in Tokyo and West Hollywood and collaborating with Rei Kawakubo and Rick Owens. Chrome Hearts continued to operate like a small family business, never releasing collections on a schedule, gifting to celebrities, putting on a runway show, or even expanding production outside its L.A. factory. In the aughts, as other companies began expanding their web presences, Stark and Lynn opted not to sell online.

The Starks’ three children, Jesse Jo, Frankie Belle, and Kristian, became involved in their parents’ company as they got older, roping in friends like Bella Hadid and Young Thug to model for the brand’s magazine and wear the clothes. Lil Uzi Vert’s 2020 album included the song “Chrome Heart Tags”; the YouTuber FaZe Banks got the brand’s cross tattooed on his kneecap. “The family’s ability to market without really marketing is flawless because they’re very, very good at seeding,” Badalov tells me. “They did everything in their power to make sure that wherever you go, you’ll never not see the brand, but you’ll never see the brand directly from the brand.” Eventually, Chrome Hearts became a sort of young-money uniform: Kim Kardashian wore it to the 2025 Met Gala; Timothée Chalamet, another friend of Kristian’s, wore it to a series of NBA games. Limited-edition collaborations only drove up the hype: triple-white Air Force 1’s, a limited-edition drop with Drake at the Aspen store.

The resellers have been swarming the internet since the early 2020s, cashing in on the fact that no one could get any of this stuff. Badalov remembers the moment he decided to go all in on reselling the brand. He was 17, working at a luxury vintage showroom. “One day, a client comes into the showroom I was working at and he brings in a bunch of Chrome Hearts rings,” Badalov says. He watched the man sell the collection for thousands of dollars. “I had an intuition. I’m like, This is going to be the biggest brand of our generation, guaranteed.” He started building his relationship at the Chrome Hearts store and snapping up pieces he knew he’d be able to resell.

The brand responded to the surge of resellers by bolstering efforts to shut them down — banning them from stores, introducing an appointment-only booking system, and training salespeople to look out for suspicious customers. Badalov had been selling for about a year when he was banned, but by that point, he’d established a customer base and a name for himself. Over the next few years, he managed to sell millions of dollars of Chrome Hearts, mostly jeans. On his Instagram, he posts his celebrity clients, including Playboi Carti, Central Cee, and Fabolous. He’s attuned to the absurdity of his life. “I’ve sold jeans for $300,000 before, and you and I are having a regular conversation about it. But let’s not forget that’s fucking insane,” he says. His prices come down to instinct. “There’s one-of-one jeans with Travis Scott’s name tag in them — those jeans you can get half a million for right now,” he says. “If you buy the Chrome Hearts Levi’s with green patches, those are probably worth $30,000 to $35,000. The same pair with crocodile patches is $100,000. It takes one person to buy it secondhand, and as soon as somebody does, word gets out and then boom — we have a market price.”

Jiang started his reselling career as a middle-schooler at a boarding school in Massachusetts. He followed sneaker resellers on TikTok and thought he could make some extra money. He started small, waiting on line at Foot Locker to buy shoes to flip, but quickly moved on to rarer kicks: sought-after editions of sneakers from Jordan, Off-White, and Yeezy. He made his first million at 16. During his sophomore year of high school, his friend offered to trade him a pair of Chrome Hearts jeans for two pairs of rare sneakers; he quickly off-loaded the pants to another reseller for a $4,000 profit. This never would have worked with sneakers, he realized, where the pros are sensitive to margins and obsessively track prices on resale sites like StockX. But with Chrome Hearts, there was a convenient information asymmetry. “You can’t find those details online. People who have Chrome Hearts, a lot of them don’t post it,” he says. “You might see a listing for $25,000, but I’m only selling for $15,000. So what’s the real price? You can’t really determine that.”

Also helpful was the fact that some of the items were produced in extremely low quantities, a core part of Chrome Hearts’ business model: only a handful of exclusive jeans made for a particular store or one-offs created for celebrities like Drake. This meant the resellers could set the market price wherever they wanted. All they had to do was find product. When they posted online that they were on the hunt, people with closets full of items they’d bought decades prior were more than happy to sell their jeans to a high-schooler offering ten times what they’d originally paid. As a teenager, “I would fly around the country,” Jiang says. “If today there’s a 40-year-old guy in Scottsdale, Arizona, who bought $400,000 worth of Chrome Hearts back in 2010 — all one-of-one pieces, gold — the advantage I provided was I would literally pull up to his house, wire ready.” He once spent $2.5 million buying out a single collection. Documenting the search turned him and his fellow Chrome Hearts traders into minor celebrities. In his videos, people scream after him and ask for selfies. Online, “Chrome Hearts reseller” has become yet another recognizable Gen-Z digital hustle, as familiar to the kids as “peptides booster” or “OnlyFans creator.”

Jiang breaks his clients into tiers. “If we’re talking about people spending more than $50,000 per item, then I have, like, 30 to 40,” he says, “mainly overseas buyers in Thailand, China, and Japan. Middle-aged, successful businessmen who love the brand. I’ll get a $100,000 item and it will sell within ten seconds because no one else has it.” Then, he says, he has the “$10,000-to-$50,000 range. Those are the 13-year-olds who can spend $20,000, the crypto kids, and the college athletes who are getting paid through NIL.”

He does whatever he needs to get the rarest items for his customers. In one recent TikTok clip, Jiang can be seen sitting on a couch in a palatial showroom, buying Chrome Hearts from a teenager recently embroiled in a crypto scam. “My boy used to buy Chrome when he was up!” Jiang jokes. The two haggle over the price of a pair of pants; Jiang ultimately buys them for $9,000. Then the boy pulls out a pair of women’s boots. “I found them in my mom’s closet,” he says. Ferraro employs proxies to shop on his behalf, going into stores, developing relationships, and eventually buying items secretly bound for the resale market.

“We all do it,” says Ferraro, chain-smoking out the window of his Soho showroom. He’s 36, a former club manager and relative elder statesman to the younger crop of resellers. “I was always on eBay, hustling like that,” he says. “It was always, like, my passion, whereas I was working nightlife just to pay the bills. Then COVID came and everyone’s getting their checks, so they’re buying more shit. So I was just pumping out more listings, buying stuff in Japan.” Ferraro shows me a parade of rarities: a custom kimono, a green crocodile-leather backpack studded with dagger zippers, a leopard-print beanbag chair, and a floor-length fur coat with a two-foot leather cross down the back listed for $225,000.

There is friendly competition among him and the other top resellers. If you are someone with a rare pair of jeans, “you’re not gonna just text me,” he says. “You’re gonna text Raph. You’re gonna text Legos.” It can be stressful. “People really made this their life. It’s my life. A lot of people live off this now. They quit their jobs, and they do this full time. So if jeans come up, people are fighting over them.”

This past winter, Ferraro got an alert from his security system at 4 a.m. When he opened his phone to check the footage, “I see fucking four guys in here with ski masks, and my heart dropped. And I’m like, ‘Fuck! Call the cops! We gotta get over there now.’” The group had planned the heist meticulously: Dressed as construction workers with vests and gloves, they pulled up to the showroom in a Ford SUV and carried a ladder to the scaffolding outside. “The ladder didn’t work, so they climbed the scaffolding,” Ferraro says. They broke a window and went in with bags ready to go, “just dumping it in. So the alarm is screaming. I think they really wanted to get more, but you can tell they were nervous.” They tossed bags of clothes off the fire escape to their getaway driver. On the way out, they split up and turned off their phones, he says, “because they got pinged by the cops and stuff. Super-thought-out.” They were long gone by the time Ferraro got to the showroom, where he found the floor covered with broken glass. “This was, like, a heartbreaking moment, bro,” he says. “They took over $1.2 million of stuff, which was, like, 60 pairs of jeans.”

Eventually, four people were arrested. One of them, a 21-year-old named Abdallah Diaby, turned out to be an agented model with over 90,000 Instagram followers. He showed up to court wearing thousands of dollars of John Varvatos necklaces and $1,500 Balmain biker jeans. (He has pleaded not guilty.) Ferraro was glad to see them prosecuted but frustrated that his clothing was never recovered, even though his store was insured. “None of the items have ever come up, which is insane because, bro — I’d say I’m the top, original, No. 1 reseller in the world, so everyone comes to me with specialty items. Lenny Kravitz jeans, Drake jeans, they put their name in them.” Even the noncelebrity custom jeans would have been findable given production variance between pairs. “My shit is so one-of-one. It was a bad place to rob. If they robbed a Louis Vuitton, they’re never gonna find it. There’s gonna be too many; that shit’s in rotation. So I don’t know what their plan is with it.” He claimed the cops offered the defendants time off their sentences if they revealed where they stashed or sold the clothes, to no avail. “They’re facing five to seven years, and they’re still saying they don’t know where it is. I’m like, Come on, bro.”

Theft is an increasing problem for the resellers. Recently, a pair of 17-year-olds came into Jiang’s shop trying to sell him goods that, he learned later, were stolen from a different reseller. They also, as it turned out, were casing the joint. A few days later, one of them broke in through a window at night and made off with over a million dollars’ worth of jewelry and pants. Jiang reached out to a resellers group chat and asked members to be on the lookout lest any of his pieces resurface. Sure enough, he soon got a ping from a reseller in Switzerland, where one of the alleged thieves had flown to try to move his items. “They are good,” Jiang says. “They know how to climb walls and stuff. Like, it’s crazy.” Still, he adds, they left fingerprints, and he believes they’ll be arrested. Jiang is planning on moving his showroom to a more secure location.

There’s another less tangible risk for the resellers: If the bubble pops, they will be left holding warehouses full of literal bags. After all, Chrome Hearts is now so overexposed, and the resale market so hot, that the brand is at risk of becoming a parody of itself. Recently, someone on r/MensFashion posted a picture of Chalamet and Kylie Jenner wearing Chrome Hearts jeans with orange crosses captioned “Chrome Hearts is the new Ed Hardy.” A better comparison, though, might be Supreme, whose once-frenzied resale market collapsed under its own weight after its late-2010s peak. “You kind of have to tell when your investment is over,” Gabriel Prensena, a young menswear influencer, tells me. He’s been posting his Chrome Hearts hauls for years and, like many young people, treats his designer-clothing trove as something akin to a basket of stocks to be bought and sold. Now, he’s wondering if the market is looking bearish. He’s begun trimming his Chrome Hearts collection “because I have a scary feeling the value is going to go down sooner than later.” The brand, to him, has started to feel gauche. “It’s one of those things that’s, like, you see the logo and then you automatically correlate it with some sort of money-slash-wealth.”

The resellers know their living depends on decisions being made by a company over which they have no control. “Longevity-wise, I think it all depends on a few factors,” Badalov says. “If they start making more shit, they’ll fuck up the market, obviously. And if there’s more inexperienced people or just money-hungry people selling bullshit, it’s not going to kill the market, but it’ll drive a lot of customers away.” And as with any bubble, even a brief dip in prices could spiral into a full-scale sell-off as spooked resellers try to unload their product ahead of a collapse. At the same time, the scarcity of the items means the market will never really be saturated. In one YouTube video, a Miami-based reseller who goes by the handle Chrome Plug shows off a one-of-one duffle bag he hopes to sell for $100,000. “This is what we’d call blue-chip Chrome. This is your Microsoft. This is your Tesla. This is your eBay and Amazon of Chrome. Your price will only go up,” he says. “It will never go down because there’s people that have spent a lot of money that were all kind of in conglomeration, holding the prices up together and making sure that we’re able to still get the price that we need for items like this.” In other words, at the very top, Chrome Hearts resellers buying from one another is enough to keep the prices elevated.

Badalov is trying to pivot to futureproof his empire. He recently started offering something like concierge services for people new to being rich. “You focus on the experience,” he says. “If you have a guy buying a $100,000 pair of jeans, he’s going to want to buy a $100,000 watch. He’s going to want to go to a cool restaurant. He’s going to want to book a private trip.” He’s had takers. But in the short term, he’s confident in his clothing stock: “People were saying Chrome was going to die two years ago. There’s nothing else to say about that.”

items.author: Allison P Davis
paragraphs: Three months ago, Dylan, a.k.a. Glute Max Guy, set out on a simple mission: “Glutemaxxing until my butt gets too big for my pants.” He’d been working out for a decade but tended to neglect his lower body. He wasn’t motivated solely by aesthetics, he said, but “I didn’t want to have the Hank Hill ass that most men seem to be content with. I wanted to look and feel athletic.” He thought posting every day would help him stay consistent.

Dylan is a fairly average guy: brown hair, brown eyes, a beard; he watches reality TV with his wife. He often works out in his condo or a basic gym, and he approaches his glutemaxxing methodically. Six days a week, he posts his workouts: three sets, 12 reps. He eats one gram of protein per pound of body weight (around 200 grams total); he takes ten to 15 grams of creatine a day.

There is nothing even close to thrilling about the pursuit of this ass. Yet the comments under his TikToks and Instagram Reels are full of men lobbing thirsty compliments and women asking for tips. The enthusiasm inspired Dylan to start the Glute Max Club community, sort of like a Patreon, where people chat about their own glute journey and follow along with his. Yes, his ass has gotten bigger, he reports. So has his follower count.

Dylan is but one man moved to action by the ass Zeitgeist. On television, even the most macho, hetero-coded shows, such as Paradise and Reacher, feature long shots of men’s bare cheeks — as did the horniest romance, Heated Rivalry, which turned a quiet appreciation for the male ass into a loud, panting yearning for juicy cakes.

Different eras have had different ideal butts: the square, flat bottom of the ’80s, like Patrick Swayze’s, was followed by the tight little tush of the ’90s. In the 2010s, the focus shifted to a woman’s pliant, movable butt, and the Brazilian butt lift surged in popularity as people tried to achieve it. Heated Rivalry can be said to have had a hand in repopularizing the male butt and informing its current ideal. Now when people say they want a butt, it’s a high, muscular bubble butt, or a “hard football booty,” says Azelion, a New York–based photographer who claims his own gets him a lot of attention on Sniffies and Grindr. It’s the ass of a cheeked-up hockey player, of soccer stars like Jude Bellingham, of tennis juggernauts Frances Tiafoe or Carlos Alcaraz. A cake so firm the cheeks look like they could crush a windpipe, it’s not an ass a Kardashian could call a plastic surgeon to replicate. The people want the bum of an athlete, one that sits atop strong thighs and requires tracking macros to build.

Now that athletes are embracing style — see the pregame fit check in most professional sports — some brand designers are taking notice of their sportier bodies.“People aren’t afraid to show it off,” says Ian Bradley, a stylist and fashion consultant. For Bradley, it’s become easier in the past six years to find pants that fit men with thick thighs and huge asses. “Generations of Black football players struggled to find pants,” he says with a sigh, but now he has a few go-to brands; he points to Thom Browne, who dresses LeBron James, and Zegna, a favorite for formalwear. “There are more options, even in high fashion. Not everyone is just doing a Hedi Slimane cut — no shade.”

Still, high fashion has been slower to evolve. Designers seem to understand that butts are the moment, but few are rushing to send more clappable cheeks down the runway. This past February, Gucci’s artistic director, Demna, dressed men in bum-snuggling pants that drooped so low they would have been pornographic if the models had any sort of ass. Prada’s spring 2027 show had men in pants as tight as Lululemon leggings, yet the cheeks were too microscopic to even fill those out. Emily Dawn Long, an upstart brand, seized on the moment with a butt-crack-centric collection, but the butts wearing it were barely there. Where were the fluffy cinnamon rolls I’ve been lusting after? Fashion is not quite reading the room, because the room is full of people making awooga noises over recent photos of Hudson Williams in Balenciaga pants: The trousers’ draping is best showcased on a firm apple ass. There is a disconnect, in other words, between the kind of butt we desire and the kind of butt designers are willing to dress.

For real men off the runway, it’s actually a hard time to find yourself in a butt deficit. At 39, Tom was pursuing, as he puts it, the typical Fire Island gay body with the help of a trainer. Through bodybuilding, he had sculpted a “pretty nice booty for a white guy,” he says, which became slightly less nice when he had to stop seeing his trainer during COVID. Then came the GLP-1, which he’s been on for years. Now, at 45, his butt is as “flat as a pancake.”

“I catch myself in the mirror sometimes, and I’m like, Oh my God, I have old-man butt,” Tom says. He’s trying to build it back through four-times-a-week workouts with two dedicated leg days. He eats protein. He takes creatine. He does a “million squats and dead lifts and hip thrusts and all these things that are supposed to activate your glutes.” But no matter how many he does, he just has “this sad, deflated whoopee cushion for a butt,” he says woefully. And still he tries.

Seeing your fat ass as an asset isn’t particularly new to women or gay men. What feels most revelatory in this era of ass fetishization is that more straight men have come to understand that a good backside can be as impressive as a well-developed torso.

At a party, I polled a group of straight, married men and their wives about their butts. A woman volunteered that her husband had started going to Pilates. One man lamented how only recently, as women he knew kept talking about the “butts on the hockey show,” did he realize how supremely flat his own ass is. It’s making him insecure.

Another one of the husbands has started developing his naturally big butt. Glute fitness, he notes, has been credited with improving longevity. Still, he’s not totally comfortable with the “nasty little move” he has to do at the end of a squat to ensure glute activation. He demonstrated, suddenly squatting down and popping up with a dramatic clench of his ass cheeks and an audible moan that made him, and everyone else, delighted but uneasy. I worried about him using the gym’s hip-thrust machine.

Azelion, the photographer, has noticed the current booty culture feels very straight. “You have a group of men who are realizing that women and gay men are responding positively to it, so it’s kind of like, ‘Wait, I have something to offer, too,’ ” he says. The proliferation of straight men on TikTok and Instagram pursuing perfect glutes, he says, has “changed the landscape of what it means to have a nice ass (for worse).”

I’ve noticed this too. Glutemaxxing has turned the basic desire for a good ass into an unnecessarily complicated quest to make one’s butt muscles as big, hard, and strong as possible. It can often feel like the erotic instinct for an ass worth lusting after has been sublimated into a whitewashed wellness obsession.

The math should be simple: three muscles (gluteus maximus, medius, and minimus), two firm cheeks, one perfect ass. And yet glutemaxxing requires an astonishing number of Romanian dead lifts, Bulgarian split squats, cable kickbacks, hip thrusts, glute bridges, elevated sumo squats. The number of ways one can fail to fully activate one’s glutes, the calculations of how much protein and fiber and creatine to consume, could lead to a certain kind of mania.

When I scroll Fitness Instagram or TikTok (sometimes for my own gains, other times because, well, butts are nice to look at), I am inundated with male trainers who seem to be the disciples of the original Glute Guy, Bret Contreras, who allegedly invented the hip thrust 20 years ago after watching MMA fighters fling their opponents off with their hips. I’ve screenshotted tips from @thelabootybuilder, a bro who helps women “grow their peach, inch by inch,” and become grotesquely obsessed with @iamnunzi, who has the exact snatched waist to round ass ratio I find to be my personal ideal. I am impressed and repulsed by how he wears the spandex workout shorts that lift and separate your ass cheeks and unsettled by how the conversation is one macro away from sounding like a pro–RFK Jr. fitness regimen.

Something vital gets lost when the goal is a perfect marble-statue butt. It’s beautiful to look at — and look we do — but the life force is gone when optimization enters the conversation. What is the point of a juicy booty if we’ve glutemaxxed the eroticism out of it? Is it still a desired object when its pursuit has been divorced from desire? I sometimes sense that though more straight men want bigger butts, the sexiness of an ass has become secondary to its functionality. You’re building your glutes so can pick up a heavy box at age 60? What about so you’ll have something for someone to grab on to? Straight men’s need to optimize their butts has arguably ruined butts.

Not according to Jacob, 29, who started working out his butt to alleviate hip problems. His glutes were weak, and he wanted to make them strong. He and his friend Yianni started getting into glute workouts. The workouts turned into a friendly competition, which has grown to include some 30 friends participating in something called the Great Cake Competition.

He laid out all the details for me: They took official measurements at the start. He made a Strava-like app that includes 3-D renderings and growth charts. A photographer took glamour shots for before and after pictures. He got custom thongs for all of his friends, and when they do the final measurements in November, the winners will get plaster casts of their own asses.

As a result of growing his ass, Jacob has spent a long time getting really heady about what growing an ass can do for humanity. He’s moved away from the realm of fitness and function and developed a philosophical outlook on the whole thing. He sees the butt as the epicenter of his spiritual power — the root chakra. Unlocking his glutes is an act of self-acceptance and a way to achieve freedom from shame. That shame, he adds, is at the core of a lot of men’s lack of interest in engaging with their glutes.

The longer we talk, the more reasons he lists for the revolutionary potential of building a butt: It’s counter to Ozempic culture (“Everyone should eat as much as they can and make their asses as big as they can!”); it’s a way to ground himself physically — to align himself with the earth. The glutes aren’t just the key to longevity but an antidote to the ills of the manosphere. “The ultimate power comes from restraint and groundedness, which are representative of the ideals of masculinity I think we should be venerating,” Jacob says. If more men did, he thinks, society would move away from fascist applications of power.
And here I thought the men’s butt moment was about sex.

items.title: My Botched Plastic Surgery ‘Down There’
items.description: It was roughly a month after my first labiaplasty and an hour into a threesome when I realized something was wrong. A finger went into my hole — or rather, a hole in my labia. The stitches holding one of my shiny new lips together had apparently failed. I rema
items.author: Jasmine Glass
paragraphs: It was roughly a month after my first labiaplasty and an hour into a threesome when I realized something was wrong. A finger went into my hole — or rather, a hole in my labia. The stitches holding one of my shiny new lips together had apparently failed. I remained clueless about this until the moment I felt a strange tugging sensation. I looked down and saw something no woman ever should. (What a way to discover that labia skin is stretchy like an earlobe!) I was with my crush and her long-term partner, and we’d all been drinking. It was a mess of limbs. Thankfully, neither woman seemed to notice the unspeakable horror that had just occurred. I jolted my hips back and guarded my loins for the remainder of our cursed three-way.

The next morning, I woke up with a Hall of Fame hangover. Then came a flashback to the previous day’s unnatural scene, flooding my body with panic. I had set out to improve my appearance down there, and now I found myself worse off than where I started. I shuddered, picturing myself with legs spread in front of a man with a needle and a knife, again. Still, I called my plastic surgeon’s office and made arrangements for a corrective procedure.

I can’t remember the address of the house I grew up in, but the phrase “beef curtains” remains burned into my brain today, more than two decades after I first heard it as a teenager. I couldn’t tell you which boy introduced it to our school or ICQ chat room, but I would bet this was a direct response to the depictions of women’s vaginas that these adolescent boys were discovering in the pages of adult magazines. Meanwhile, in the pages of Seventeen and Tiger Beat, I was learning the importance of femininity and How to Attract Your Dream Guy. (I took to padding my bra and folding thick squares of paper towel to pad the back pockets of my jeans.) Later, watching online pornography in the early aughts, these boys became accustomed to an even narrower representation of female anatomy. The message was loud and clear: Dainty, pink, and hairless was the aesthetic standard. If you commit the crime of existing differently, you will be cruelly mocked.

Beyond all the usual reasons a teenage girl sees herself as defective, my mother was also hard at work chipping away at my barely constructed identity. At home, I heard I was “worthless” and that I “won’t amount to anything” over and over (and over!) until the voice that started as hers became my own inner dialogue. My self-esteem bottomed out before I entered adulthood.

By my early 20s, imperfections that had once felt like an inconvenience now registered as deeply unsafe. A single, mildly derogatory comment from a friend about my toes was enough to make me give up wearing sandals. I kept my sweaty little piggies enclosed in the rubber toes of Converse All Stars even in summer. That discomfort was nothing compared to the sheer panic of being perceived and judged for my imperfections. I imagined everyone inspecting my flaws under a microscope, like I did, sure they would keep me from the validation I so desperately craved. One must be flawless to be worthy of love. This was my belief system.

It was around this time I noticed something while getting out of the bath one day. My labia were no longer tucked away politely out of sight. I grabbed a compact mirror and held it out in front of the offensive area. Oh, hell no! Even with my thighs pressed tightly together, I could still see them. I sat down on the toilet seat spread eagle, compact still in hand. Not only had they grown, they’d changed color! Like a goddamned mood ring. What the heck is that? Purple? Brown? I was so disgusted I couldn’t even bring myself to touch them. What I now recognize to be a perfectly natural result of puberty, I saw in that moment as a personal failing.

From that point on, I found ways to hide myself from those I was intimate with. Ambient lighting was my best friend. I spent a great deal of energy finding the exact right amount that obscured my body in flattering ways, without being so dim that it became obvious I was hiding. Still, I hooked up with fewer women than I otherwise would have. The thought of having someone’s face there was … unappealing. Men, however, have always been happy to get on with it. More than that, you get Cool Girl points for saying you don’t care about receiving oral. “I’m a giver,” I’d tell them. They fucking loved that.

Alas, my pathological self-abandonment and generous blowjobbing fell short of getting boys to be nice to me. By the time I turned 23, I had been mistreated so badly by so many, I closed myself off to them entirely. It wasn’t a conscious decision. I simply woke up one day and was no longer attracted to men. (It was the same week I discovered The L Word.) Now there was nowhere left for me to hide.

So I opened my six-pound brick of a Dell laptop, got on Google, and did some digging. Not having a clue of what the procedure was called, I’m sure I was searching for “pussy lips surgery” and the like.

At my consultation appointment, the only plastic surgeon I could afford — at $3,000 CAD — outlined the two ways to do labiaplasty. One technique involves cutting along the entire outer edge of the lip. The downside, if you have darker labia, is that you wind up with visible scarring. The other method is a wedge incision, which involves some stitches but leaves the outer edge intact. When he was done calmly explaining how he planned to mutilate my vagina, the doctor offered a smile. I did not find this comforting. I weighed my options for achieving a Barbie slit and decided to go with the wedge. I paid the deposit, and my surgery appointment was scheduled.

The big day arrived a few weeks later. Hopping up on the surgical table, I cursed myself for not scraping together the extra thousand bucks that would have allowed me to be unconscious for what was about to happen. My anxiety spiked as I put my heels into the stirrups and spread my knees. Annoyingly, the nurse rejected my request for ambient lighting in the operating room.

My eyes were fixed on the ceiling — or the backs of my eyelids — for the duration of the procedure. While I couldn’t see what was going on under my paper gown, and despite the numbing agent, I could still feel something, the sawing sensation of the scalpel slicing my lower lips. Sixteen years later, my stomach still turns just thinking about it. Luckily, it was over pretty fast. For untold reasons, the doctor showed me my surgically removed bits in a little glass jar before they were sent off to medical waste. (Good riddance!) I was told it would be a simple recovery process. The surgeon handed me two parting gifts: a prescription for pain pills and a thick medical pad to protect the site and collect blood crusties.

Back at home some days later, I found myself on the toilet. Turns out constipation was on the laundry list of side effects that came with my prescription. While trying to force the situation, I felt a pinch. But the meds were doing what they do, and the pain was muted enough that I didn’t think much of it. I gave up, plopped down on the couch instead, and carried on with my exciting day (probably binge-watching 30 Rock on DVD).

It wasn’t until after the threesome fiasco that I realized I had torn my stitches. Had my surgeon said anything at all about the risk of them coming loose and creating a hole that would require me to repeat this horror show, I surely would have taken that pinch more seriously. The damage caused by those failed stitches seemed to mean that corrective surgery could only do so much. I wish I’d spent those several thousand dollars on therapy instead, fixing my mind rather than my body.

Things are still a little uneven down there, but I’ve gotten used to it. Or maybe it’s that the rest of me has gotten less and less symmetrical over time, so it’s now part of a collection that includes two different breasts and a face that is definitely aging faster on one side.

Last spring, I took a writing course where the first homework assignment was to “write about your most humiliating secret.” I knew in an instant that mine was the story of my botched labiaplasty. But in the many years since it happened, I had never stopped to really think about why. When I finally did, I realized my deep well of shame was tied to a belief system I had already outgrown. That shame depended on me feeling that I owed the world sexual desirability. But I turned 40 last year and decided I was done playing the game. I choose the peace that comes with decentering my appearance in my life.

I came up with a mantra for whenever I catch myself obsessing over a new wiry white hair, hyperpigmentation spot, chin whisker, or whatever else. I say it out loud to myself: “Who cares?” … then I quickly shift my attention to somewhere more deserving. My two rescue pups, for example. If I’m feeling extra spicy: “Whooo fucking cares?!” Five stars. Very effective.
I reconnected with my crush a few years back. We had a little fling. One night, while she was going down on me, she looked up, smiled, and said, “It’s so beautiful.”

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: October 26, 2026
items.description: Tension between the sun and Pluto (in passionate Scorpio and rebellious Aquarius, respectively) could bring out the worst in everyone today … including you. People are likely to act irrationally, motivated by fear or jealousy, and defensiveness could have ever
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: Tension between the sun and Pluto (in passionate Scorpio and rebellious Aquarius, respectively) could bring out the worst in everyone today … including you. People are likely to act irrationally, motivated by fear or jealousy, and defensiveness could have everyone behaving in ways they won’t be proud of later. It’s normal to have intense, not necessarily “good” emotions — plus shaming yourself for what’s only human is a surefire way to make everything worse — just try to be thoughtful about how you act on those feelings. Find the daily horoscope for each zodiac sign, below.

Your social circle might seem more gossipy than usual today. Everyone has a wild, dramatic story to share, and nobody seems particularly concerned with whether the information they’re spreading around is actually true. You might hear stories involving you that you know are untrue — or at least incomplete — so try to take what you hear about others with a grain of salt too. If you plan to act on information that you learn soon, double-check that it’s accurate before doing anything.

Today, you might convince yourself that you need certain people around you and that if you lost their support or they stopped thinking highly of you, you’d be a failure. But while everyone needs community and human connection, you’re stronger and more independent than you’re giving yourself credit for right now. Don’t bend over backward trying to please other people, particularly if they don’t seem to appreciate or reciprocate the effort. Your relationships are important, but maintaining them shouldn’t require your sense of self to suffer.

You might struggle to maintain your usual sense of optimism. Your mind constantly jumps to the worst-case scenario, and you have a hard time convincing yourself that things will work out. So for now, rather than fighting it, give yourself permission to dwell (temporarily!) on your fears. Maybe everything does go wrong and maybe your fears do materialize — even if the worst comes to pass, that won’t be the end of the story. Remind yourself that you’ll keep going no matter what and you’ll find a way to deal with whatever happens.

In order to live the way you want, you may have to contend with a bit of judgment today. The people around you might be jealous of your creative spirit and your willingness to break the rules, especially if they feel that their own lives are limited or disappointing — they may try to tear you down to make themselves feel better. You might be tempted to back down in the face of any negative attention, but try to be brave. It can be scary to break the mold, but that doesn’t mean you shouldn’t do it.

Today, you might get the frustrating sense that you don’t have all the information you need. Maybe people seem upset with you, but they won’t tell you why; maybe there’s drama going on in your group chat, but nobody seems to be telling the full story. You’re trying hard to do the right thing, but you might not have the necessary context to determine what that is, so go easy on yourself if you make a mistake or two. Ask questions and do the best you can with the information you have.

Usually, you’re good at striking the right balance between talking and listening — but today, you might find that you’re rambling on and on. Perhaps you have a lot to say right now, or perhaps everyone else is just being uncharacteristically reserved and you feel like it’s up to you to keep the conversation flowing. Whatever the reason, it won’t be much fun for anyone. Try to notice when there’s an imbalance and make a point of including others in the discussion. Assume others do have things to say and they may need some extra encouragement to speak up.

Today, your expectations for yourself might be inordinately high. If the people around you seem to be accomplishing amazing things or hitting big milestones, you could feel that there’s something wrong with you if you aren’t keeping up. But try to be realistic: If you have less time, money, or support than others, it’ll naturally require more effort for you to achieve the same things. That doesn’t mean it’s impossible, but it may take longer, so cut yourself some slack. You’re doing great things with the resources you have.

Your challenge today is to tend to your own needs without unintentionally stepping on other people’s toes. It could be harder than usual right now: When you stand up for yourself, you could come across as rude; when you pursue your own dreams, you might need to compete with the people around you. Even when you’re actively trying to be considerate, some conflict may be inevitable. So do your best, but don’t be too hard on yourself either. And if you do hurt someone without meaning to, don’t be too proud to apologize.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

You try to come off as someone who’s bold and daring, someone impossible to intimidate. Sometimes you’re so convincing that even you start to believe it. But the truth is that you have fears and insecurities just like anyone else. Of course there are things that scare you — you wouldn’t be human otherwise! And today, the best thing you can do is be honest, even if only with yourself, about your fears. You don’t have to pretend that nothing scares you; you just have to face it anyway.

You understand that your friends’ behavior tends to reflect on you and so you try to be thoughtful about the company you keep. Sometimes, though, this attitude means you end up trying to control the people around you, pushing them to do the “right” thing. But now more than usual, any controlling behavior will only backfire. If you truly can’t tolerate a friend’s actions, then ask yourself whether they should actually be in your life. And if it’s only a small quirk or an inconsequential difference of opinion that’s bothering you, try to let it go.

You try to tell yourself that you’re unconcerned with what people think of you and that as long as you feel good about your actions, that’s all that matters. Today, though, you might be more concerned with your reputation than usual. Even if you don’t want to care, the fact is that you do. So for now, you might as well lean into it. Don’t go against your principles just for the sake of being liked, but if you’re choosing between equally good options, there’s no reason not to go for the one that’ll please the people around you too.

You might suddenly feel sick of your usual routines today — especially if they’re habits that just seemed to have fallen into place, rather than ones you actively chose. You’ll feel trapped in a life that’s too small for you, and it could make you quick to lash out at the people around you. The answer might be to make things more interesting for yourself so you don’t stir up unnecessary conflict. Give yourself something new to do, a productive challenge to take on. The less bored you are, the fewer problems you’ll create.
