items.title: Kristen Bell’s Happy Tears
items.description: Kristen Bell’s Happy Tears
items.author: Rachael Combe
paragraphs: Kristen Bell’s Happy Tears
As the third season of Nobody Wants This hits Netflix, the TV perennial, Frozen superstar, and modern-marriage poster girl reveals her secret sauce.

Kristen Bell appears on my computer screen eating a bowl of yogurt. She is backlit by a gauzy curtain in a corner of her California home, her blond hair in a top knot. She wears a black T-shirt and no visible makeup. She is 46, looks 16, and, almost immediately, is speaking with the wisdom of your coolest 76-year-old aunt.

“We all act like we’re not connected, but that’s the biggest joke. I see the world as a large family that f*cking fights a lot. I like that about myself, and I’m not planning on changing it no matter how much tribalism is presented to me,” she says. It’s a theme she returns to repeatedly in our conversation. “That’s what I love about Nobody Wants This. They’ve learned not just how to love, but how to fight and how to forgive and how to choose each other despite differences. I think that’s something the world could use more of.”

Bell speaks with her hands, fluttering and fanning her tapered pink nails, and expertly deploys eye contact — she’s not taking her eyes off of you, so you can’t take your eyes off of her. “I’m a feeler,” she says, her eyes welling up. “I wish I wasn’t sometimes. But I also know it leads me to a lot of my creative process. And I think creativity is one of the most important things in the world.” She sees her gifts — her ability to communicate emotion, her crystalline singing voice — as almost a moral imperative to improve the lives of those around her. “I do think thoroughly about how, hopefully, [a project] will land,” she says. “I could be in [viewers’] living room at night after they’ve had a hard day, and when they sit down, I could sweep them away into a world that is only imaginary, and for one hour, they forget that their hands and feet hurt.”

The third season of Nobody Wants This, Bell’s hit Netflix comedy, drops Oct. 22. The show, about agnostic, devil-may-care sex podcaster Joanne (Bell) falling in love with a careful, tradition-loving rabbi, Noah (Adam Brody), and the chaos it causes in each of their lives, is rom-com light. But it debuted in 2024 amid heightened antisemitism in the wake of the Oct. 7 attacks in Israel and the war in Gaza. Initially, the show was knocked by some for stereotypical portrayals of Jewish women — but it ended up being a huge win for Netflix, drawing 57 million viewers in its first three months on the platform. And as Joanne and Noah’s love story has developed, the series has blossomed into a surprisingly sweet treatise on tolerance, resilience, and the beauty of Jewish ritual and spirituality.
“Having people be disappointed in me is really hard for me. Like really hard. And with raising kids, that’s like a whole other level.”

Bell has made a career of making you root for other headlong women, rushing into danger (Veronica Mars), into the arms of oversexed rockers (Forgetting Sarah Marshall), into ice storms (Frozen), and into the afterlife (The Good Place). Though there are some Extremely Online People who don’t always manage to connect with Bell’s sense of humor on social media — the brouhaha about her tongue-in-cheek Instagram post to Dax Shepard on her last wedding anniversary comes to mind — she radiates likability even when she’s playing a next-level bitch (see her recurring guest roles in Party Down and Parks and Recreation). As Bell’s husband of 13 years, podcaster and comedian Shepard recently put it, “How on Earth could you hate this woman? She’s so lovely. If you hate this woman, clearly you’re bonkers.”

It’s true that in our stressed-out, maxed-out, polarized, atomized, rage-baited era, Bell is like a half-pint of lemonade: a sweet-tart all-American crowd-pleaser, able to take down the temperature and brighten the spirits of any room. Now that Dolly Parton and Betty White are no longer with us, Bell is probably in the running to take over their roles as America’s Most Beloved. But, as with Parton and White, what is sometimes missed thanks to Bell’s Labubu level of cuteness and killer comedic timing is the weapons-grade intelligence ticking away behind every performance. “People know she’s funny. But I don’t think anyone fully, fully grasps how wicked smart she is,” says Monica Padman, Bell’s longtime business and producing partner and co-host of the podcast Armchair Expert with Shepard. “She’s very quick and witty. Because she has all these other beautiful and shocking qualities … [that] does not really get mentioned.”

Bell has frequently claimed to have no big plan, no ambition for world domination, and yet, let’s face it: With her hit show, three upcoming movies (Violent Night 2, Sonic the Hedgehog 4, and Frozen 3), and a new role as a L'Oréal Paris spokeswoman, she’s dominating. “I’m a busybody. I like doing. I like creating. I like new experiences,” she says. “It’s hard for me to state my goals because my narrative tells me I don’t have them. Perhaps that’s because I would feel too arrogant. My goal is to be happy with the next decision. I go based on my gut. I have very strong gut feelings. Obviously, I wanted to create a life for myself and put food on the table, which is why I wasn’t doing plays in my backyard for free my whole life.”

Community theater in her native Detroit is where Bell caught the acting bug, playing a banana in a play about Raggedy Ann. “My mom had heard me singing all the time around the house,” she says, and took her for voice lessons and to an audition. Though Bell did ultimately get an agent and snag a few professional gigs before heading to New York University’s prestigious Tisch School of the Arts, she’s glad she grew up in the theater and not on set. (She has one pre-college major movie credit, as an extra in Claire Danes’ 1998 Polish Wedding.) “In theater, there is no craft service. There are no PAs. There is no driver. You show up on time or you’re fired, whether you’re the lead or in the chorus. You go sit in your moldy dressing room until your cue is ready, and you better be on stage. There’s more of a collective energy.”

Bell immediately connected with the tolerance in the theater community. “It was a group of people who were a bit weirder than the norm, just like I was. Everything was accepted. You could choose to wear something insane — a huge striped top hat — and you might feel nervous in the grocery store. Is anyone looking at me? You walk into a theater, and they’re like, ‘Oh, baby queen, gorgeous, I love it. Where did you get it? Can I try it?’ There’s such an effusive sense of celebrating everything.”
“I’m a little bit Veronica Mars, a little bit Sarah Marshall. I’m a tiny bit Joanne. But I’m the most like Anna [from Frozen].”

Bell dropped out of Tisch her senior year, in 2001, when she won the part of Becky in a Broadway production of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer. Soon she was scoring guest parts in TV series. Her big break came in 2004 with the titular role in Veronica Mars. She was the first person who auditioned with creator Rob Thomas, who says he saw 100 more actors before realizing Bell had nailed it in that first meeting. Bell went on to dazzle everyone involved with her flawless takes and ability to handle everything from screwball comedy to her character’s devastating rape. She earned the nickname “Money” because of her dependability in every take. Thomas told directors that if they ever had a difference of opinion about a creative choice with Bell, Bell was always right. “She had so much control. So much control,” Thomas says. “When you’re doing the CW shows that I was doing, you’re working with young actors. You see a lot of bad acting. But Kristen was like clockwork, just, like, done.”

Shepard, whom Bell met through mutual friends in 2007, wanders into the room as she is telling the story of their early romance. He was initially attracted to her passion for Bed Bath & Beyond coupons — as a fellow Michigander, he found her thriftiness familiar and hot. “I definitely stole those from my neighbor’s mailbox back in the day. And I’ll say that on the stand,” she says.

But he really fell for her during a game of “running charades” Bell organized at her house. Running charades, for the uninitiated, involves sprinting back and forth for clues before acting them out under a time pressure. Bell tells me she would gather 30 people, “theater folk. We played it full contact. You were allowed to move furniture as an obstacle. You were allowed to push an old dog into a hallway that someone could maybe trip [over]. You were allowed to hip check people.” The one thing Bell would not allow was folding up the clues — too much of a time waster to unfold. Bell had climbed onto her kitchen counter to give a “very harsh speech that if you fold your paper, you will no longer be invited back. I’m done with people folding their paper. This is a time game. If you do it, you’re out.”
She turns to Dax and says, “And then you said later on — right? — you thought that was very attractive.”

“I knew there was trouble ahead,” Shepard calls out from off camera. He describes it as the moment he realized she was “a boss, a force of nature to be reckoned with. I said, ‘Look at this little powerful [person].’”

Over the years, his instinct has been confirmed — “She’s not afraid of the gorilla she lives with,” Shepard jokes. The two got engaged in 2010 but postponed the wedding until after California legalized same-sex marriage. They finally tied the knot — after Bell re-proposed on Twitter and Shepard accepted — in 2013, after the birth of their eldest daughter, Lincoln (now 13). Their second daughter, Delta (now 11), followed in 2014.

Bell describes Lincoln and Delta as the primary factors in her decisions about which projects she accepts. “Is this going to pull me away from my kids too much? Will I still be able to be the mom that I want to be? That’s really the No. 1, to be honest. There’s nothing higher than that,” she says. “I would easily let my whole career and all its legacy and notoriety ‘disapparate’ tomorrow if it meant sacrificing something major in my kids’ lives, or not being there.”

This sounds like it could be a cliché celebrity homily to the sanctity of motherhood: Many mothers who don’t have to worry about their every word being picked apart online will admit that sometimes they wish their job and their kids would “disapparate” simultaneously, at least long enough to take a bath. But Padman says it’s true on an existential level for Bell. “She is a mom first. She is meant to be a mother. She moms outside of just her children, too,” Padman says. “She’s just such a maternal figure in so many people’s lives. People go to her for advice and nurturing. She oozes a maternal quality and she’s very willing to meet that across the board: with her kids, with adult friends, with other people’s children. She’s an open source of that.”
“I am not ashamed to admit I love my algorithm. You know what I did? I crafted it. I don’t pause on negative stories. I don’t pause on clickbait. I don’t pause on train wrecks.”

Which is not to say that Bell is some Pollyanna, twirling through her perfect life. Shepard and Bell have been admirably open about the challenges of marriage and family life. “It’s hard. Do not think because I am on your television that it is easy for me. It’s brutal. I cry weekly,” she says, citing Dr. Becky and Lisa Damour, Ph.D., as expert sources she regularly turns to for guidance. She says she wants to be honest about the strains of family life to make people feel seen. “Oftentimes when you’re in that cyclone of puberty, you could think, My kid is the only one doing this. And that is just simply not a fact.”

But Bell says that openness has become trickier to navigate as her girls have gotten older. “It’s always a debate between Kantianism and utilitarianism,” she says — yes, as in the 18th century German philosopher Immanuel Kant. “For the good of the people, we should share our dirty stories, we should share our shame, we should share our hardships. But for the good of the one? My main job in life is to protect those two. I guess a conclusion we came to at a time in our parenting journey is, like, we can share all the cute things when they’re little, but when they could possibly be exposed to [media] or possibly have a feeling in response to it … well, now, the equation has changed. There’s someone else in the mix, and you have to have enough self-awareness and consideration to consider that person. And that person is my daughter, so she’s No. 1.”
“Do not think because I am on your television that it is easy for me. It’s brutal. I cry weekly.”

The level of thoughtfulness Bell applies to, well, everything she does, does not come without a cost. Over the years, she has shared the work she does to stay on top of clinical depression and anxiety, starting from when she was in college. She wrote an op-ed for Time magazine, made a video for the Child Mind Institute, and was a mental health spokesperson for the telehealth company Hers. She’s advocated for therapy and destigmatizing medication and spoken about her success with eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) therapy.

Most recently, she has been touting her work with neuropsychologist Julia DiGangi, Ph.D. “She is a knife through the noise,” Bell says, confessing that she found her while scrolling online. “I am not ashamed to admit I love my algorithm. You know what I did? I crafted it. I took very seriously when [author] Yuval Harari told us to pay attention to what you consume, not just your food. I don’t pause on negative stories. I don’t pause on clickbait. I don’t pause on train wrecks. I keep informed, but when I’m participating in social media, it’s dogs doing funny stuff. It’s knitting. It’s crafts. It’s tiny tidbits that help you get through your day. She popped up.”

She did an online course with DiGangi “to soothe my anxiety” and started seeing “the biggest difference in my life than I have with almost anything I’ve applied.” Soon she was reaching out to DiGangi for individual coaching. “I still struggle with [anxiety] every day. It’s not anything that’s gone away. I think it takes a long time to change your neural pathways from habits you’ve created. Your brain is a pattern detector. That’s the main thing she talks about, and it’s so true. But if I can change my patterns, maybe I can change the amount of anxiety in my body.”

Lately, Bell has been examining her pattern of people-pleasing. On a podcast with psychologist Adam Grant, she blew this reporter’s mind when she said, “I’m accepting the fact that over-explaining is a form of begging.” Juggling the roles of mother, wife, friend, daughter, actor, celebrity, and involved citizen would seem to offer an almost impossible bind for Bell — one that is familiar to many women of her generation. You can’t say yes to everything; you want to show up for every part of your life; time and energy are finite; saying no means disappointing someone.

It is clear as Bell speaks that she compounds the problem by holding herself to exceptionally high standards. “I do things I love and care about... So oftentimes I will work myself to the bone or work till I’m exhausted because I genuinely care about how it lands in the world,” she tells me at one point. And, “Being considered arrogant makes me feel sick because I believe that no person is worth more than another.” She repeatedly checks in with me over the course of our call, hoping I’m getting what I need for this story and apologizes for getting “so philosophical so quick.” She says that “having people be disappointed in me is really hard for me. Like really hard. And you know with raising kids, that’s like a whole other level.”

When we commiserate about the unstoppable detritus and waste of raising growing kids, she admits that thinking so much about every plastic bag and candy bar wrapper that enters her home is exhausting. “My cognitive labor, much like yours, is an absolute burnout. It is always burnt out.” (Bell tip that turns out to be pretty helpful: She recommends the company Ridwell, which takes away otherwise hard-to-recycle items.)

“I’m a busybody. I like doing. I like creating. I like new experiences. It’s hard for me to state my goals because my narrative tells me I don’t have them. My goal is to be happy with the next decision.”

So the question (asking for a friend) is: If she’s no longer overfunctioning and people-pleasing — is she pissing people off? “It’s not causing difficulty. It’s causing a reckoning of my interiority,” she says. “It’s causing me to recognize when my people-pleasing is out of fear, which is about 50% of the time … and when it’s coming out of a genuine commitment to the health and happiness of my stewardship to the world around me. And just the enlightenment that it’s a choice reduces my fear by quite a bit.”

When you’re watching Bell play Joanne from Nobody Wants This, it can feel hard to square Bell’s meticulous caretaking with that more libertine character. Bell’s acting has a quality of being so natural as to seem like she’s always being herself on screen. “I almost never see performances that match her natural tone,” says Padman. “When you know her very well, you’re watching her play all these roles ... and you’re like, ‘Oh, she’s acting, because that’s not her at all.’”

Toward the end of our interview, Bell picks up her computer. “Sorry,” she says. “I’m going outside to get my little dose of sunshine today.” She arranges herself on a lounge chair and tips her head toward the sun as she considers what parts of herself she brings to each role. In sunshine, you can see a delicate earring glinting in her helix. There are a stack of life-size Halloween skeletons on the patio behind her chair, all face-down, like they’re trying to hide from the Zoom camera. “I’m a little bit Veronica Mars, a little bit Sarah Marshall. I’m a tiny bit Joanne,” she says. “But I’m the most like Anna [of Arendelle].”
“Oftentimes I will work myself to the bone or work till I’m exhausted because I genuinely care about how it lands in the world.”

Bell says the process of crafting the Frozen characters with Disney was the most collaborative project she’s ever been a part of. They worked through multiple iterations of the script, using improv and making character tweaks. “They were very open to each and every suggestion I had that rounded her out to be someone that I needed to see when I was a little girl. I needed to see a princess that did not have good posture,” Bell says. “I wanted that out there for the girls who felt a little quirkier, to see some representation.” Anna drooling while sleeping, her clumsiness — those are Bell’s input. She remembers telling writers, “I need her to talk too fast and wear her heart on her sleeve and just try because she wants to, because she cares.”

Some parts of the Frozen story were out of her control — “The Snow Monster will come when the Snow Monster will come,” she says — but as she’s explaining how she and her colleagues were able to influence how their characters reacted and “put words in [their] mouths,” Bell becomes visibly emotional. “It’s been one of the joys of my whole life that,” she says, pausing, her voice rising and growing thinner, “that project has been loved and accepted as it has been because I felt like I was very revealing in it.”

Her emotion is contagious. I tell her that Frozen came out shortly after I gave birth to my second daughter, and how, as a woman without a sister, I was so moved by the film’s ending that I could not stop crying, mostly with joy that my girls would know the sisterhood I had always longed for. “I love that. We are all connected. You may not have a sister,” she tells me, fixing me with her empathetic gaze, “but you can choose anyone to be your sister.” It’s an idea — along with a renewed commitment to recycle my candy wrappers and fix my Instagram algorithm — that stays with me.

items.title: Exclusive: Joe Amabile Shares His Thoughts On That 'Bachelor' Casting Rumor
items.description: Bachelor Nation’s Joe Amabile Is Sprinting To The Finish Line
items.author: Jake Viswanath
paragraphs: Bachelor Nation’s Joe Amabile Is Sprinting To The Finish Line
The reality TV star opens up about recovering from brain surgery, marrying Serena Pitt, and a Bachelor casting rumor.

Joe Amabile has had quite the eventful summer, to say the least. The Bachelor Nation alum (aka Grocery Store Joe) had to undergo brain surgery after doctors found a “blueberry-sized” tumor. However, through his recovery, the 40-year-old refused to lose sight of one of his goals: running the New York Marathon on Nov. 1.

“When I got my unexpected diagnosis of having a brain tumor and having to go through brain surgery, it was a goal that I set for myself to just keep me motivated and keep my mindset positive,” he tells Bustle. “Brain surgery is out of your control. I’m not going in my own head like the doctors are, so it was just nice to give myself that control.”

Naturally, Amabile’s medical crisis made him reflect on many aspects of his life, from friendships to his financial situation. He partnered with Northwestern Mutual to share why getting your finances in order is essential. “It’s so important to be flexible and able to switch things when something unexpected happens,” he says. “That’s what Northwestern Mutual does so well.”

Marrying his Bachelor in Paradise costar Serena Pitt gave him a new outlook on saving. “Before getting married, I don’t think I had any financial goals,” he says. “It’s just so important to save money and put it away for a family. You’re trying to build a life together, and regardless of what people wanna say, money is very important.”

After a gradual but successful recovery, Amabile looks forward to reconnecting with some of his fellow reality TV star runners. “I run it with Zac Clark every year, and Matt James is running it again,” he says. “I’m friends with Dylan Efron, and he’s running it.”
Below, Amabile opens up about his marathon journey, his wife’s support, and his thoughts on Bachelor Nation’s future.
After your recovery, what has become a bigger priority in your life, and what new goals have you set for yourself?

Being vulnerable is one. I wasn’t really vulnerable on social media at all, and once I decided to share, it’s honestly helped me so much. It’s comforting to hear other people’s stories about going through something similar and having good outcomes. Right now my goal is not to do too much, because I tend to overdo it.
Tell me how Serena’s been supporting you during this marathon journey.

[Laughs] Uh... I don’t know if she is so happy that I’m running the marathon. She is OK with it and will support me, but she’d rather I didn’t run it, if I’m gonna be completely honest. But she’s been wonderful. I’ve never been through [a major health scare], and neither has she, but she’s always been by my side. Her resilience and strength are a testament to who she is as a person.
You two are one of the few couples who are still standing from Bachelor Nation. What do you see for the future of the Bachelor franchise?

Oh, that’s an interesting question. It depends on who they choose as the Bachelor and the way they cast the women. There’s a lot of competition out there, but there’s still only one Bachelor and Bachelorette, so I think the show will be OK.
What do you think of the rumor that producers are eyeing Dr. Mike to be the next Bachelor?

That would be a great pick. He doesn’t need it financially, and his social following is already massive, so I’m sure that’ll help. If you’re looking for someone who is there for the right reasons, I think it’s him.
How has Bachelor Nation supported you during this health journey, whether it’s the fans or your fellow contestants?
So many people have just showered me with love and support. So many Bachelor alumni have reached out and sent me Uber Eats and DoorDash. Honestly, it’s almost been too gracious.
Your fellow Bachelor Nation star Joey Graziadei just returned from filming The Traitors. Would you ever consider doing that one day?
If they asked, I would be lying if I said no.
Do you want to be a Faithful or a Traitor?
I don’t have a preference. The way the show’s set up right now, it takes a lot of luck at the beginning, no matter if you’re a Traitor or a Faithful. It’s a little bit of a popularity contest.
How do you hope you’ll come out of the marathon, and what message do you hope to send?

I hope to finish. I don’t think I’ll beat my last two scores, but I want people to get that you can do anything. As long as you set that goal, something unexpected happening doesn’t necessarily have to change the outcome. It just changes the path.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: The 10 Best New Books Of October
items.description: Nothing says autumn quite like a good book. This October promises a slate of engrossing and cozy reads to get you through shorter days and chilly nights.
items.author: Sophie Fishman
paragraphs: Nothing says autumn quite like a good book. This October promises a slate of engrossing and cozy reads to get you through shorter days and chilly nights.

Literary giants have returned with force this month. Pulitzer Prize winner Barbara Kingsolver is back with Partita, a gorgeous novel set between rural Tennessee and a college campus in Indiana that reflects on paths not taken. Natalie Baszile, the voice behind Queen Sugar and We Are Each Other’s Harvest, has a new novel, Friends and Family, that examines friendship, loyalty, and privilege.

For those looking for Halloween frights: Charlotte B. Plumb’s debut gothic romantasy, Reap & Sow, takes readers on a journey through deals with demons. Meanwhile, Columbia University English professor Eleanor Johnson’s nonfiction work Monstrous Bitch examines the frightening ways women have been demonized by the patriarchy throughout history.
Whether you’re hunkering down inside or enjoying the crisp air, here are Bustle’s 10 best books of October.
Friends and Family by Natalie Baszile

Out October 6. Longtime best friends Babs and Nora share everything with each other. When Nora, a white woman, adopts a Black son named Nathan, Babs, who is Black, becomes a go-to source for advice. When their sons are alone at home, however, an encounter with the police leaves Nathan traumatized. Babs and Nora’s responses to the incident diverge, and the aftermath threatens the fabric of their families.
Partita by Barbara Kingsolver

Out October 6. Livia Cable has quietly resigned herself to life with her dairy farmer husband in rural Tennessee. Then she gets a call from a former lover that shakes her. Flipping between her married life and her past as a conservatory student studying piano at the University of Indiana, Livia reckons with the passions of her youth, paths not taken, and the price of artistic ambition.
Bad Words by Rioghnach Robinson

Out October 6. In this debut novel, writer Parker Navarro was on his way to literary stardom when critic Selina Chan dashed his hopes with a scathing review. Four years later, he has a shot at redemption with his newest novel. When Selina’s newest review threatens his success, their feud goes viral. As their squabble takes the internet by storm, boosting book sales and magazine subscriptions alike in the process, the two take up a softer conversation in private.
Every Story Is a Love Story by Imbolo Mbue

Out October 6. For three years, Wolo has grieved his wife and unborn twins who were killed in a tragic car accident. Then a letter arrives from Victoria, the woman behind the wheel that fateful day. Reeling, and against the guidance of his friends and family, Wolo resolves to meet Victoria face-to-face.
Carrying by Samantha Josephs

Out October 6. Martha seems to have the perfect life: She is a loving wife and stepmother to a doting stepdaughter, runs their home with finesse, and prides herself on her flawless body. Martha is also trans, a secret she hides from her family, staging miscarriages to keep her husband in the dark. When a chronic illness threatens her ability to keep up the lie, she explores experimental treatments that have strange side effects — including, puzzlingly, a real pregnancy.
Monstrous Bitch by Eleanor Johnson

Out October 6. For millennia, the patriarchy has tried to rationalize its fear of women. Eleanor Johnson argues that those beliefs manifest in a literary figure she calls the “monstrous bitch,” a haunting, promiscuous, outspoken woman. From Mesopotamia to Ancient Greece to contemporary cinema, Johnson traces the trope through history to highlight how misogyny still festers today.
Looks Perfect by Jessica Siskin

Out October 6. Fashion designer Stella has the life she’s always wanted: She’s built a successful businessand accrued one million adoring followers online, and she’s about to take her brand global. Behind the scenes, though, her relationship with boyfriend Alex is crumbling, threatening the perfect image she’s worked to build. Feeling lost, she signs up for Blindr, an anonymous dating app that promises real connections. When she meets an empathetic stranger on the app who calls himself Pineapple, his honesty takes Stella down an unexpected path.
Reap & Sow by Charlotte B. Plumb

Out October 6. In the fictional English town of Blackbridge, Eda Shaw and her brothers make a living brokering deals between the local poor and a nefarious demon, Mr. Night. When a bargain goes wrong and her brothers are arrested, Eda enlists the help of Kit’rath, the only demon Mr. Night fears. As the two work together to save her family, their allyship evolves into something more.
Back Where We Started by Becca Freeman

Out October 13. When Katie and Drew fell in love in high school, they dreamed of being a power couple: her in Hollywood, him in the White House. Although her acting career soared, their relationship crumbled. For years, she put her small Pennsylvania hometown — and its painful memories of her ex — behind her. But now, keeping a promise to her sister to come home for Christmas, she crosses paths with Drew again, and again, and again. Freeman’s sophomore novel is a second-chance romance for the ages, exploring themes of regret, fame, and ambition.
A Court of Splintered Harmony by Sarah J. Maas

Out October 27. For the sixth installment of the Court of Thorns and Roses series, old foe Koschei, the death god, threatens to return. As fear strikes the Fae territories, powerful actors begin to target the human lands. With tensions mounting, the Night Court must take action. But with past betrayals and new revelations coming to light, can they find a way forward to protect the innocent?

items.title: Why You Should Watch The WNBA Finals At A Women's Sports Bar
items.description: The WNBA Finals Are Better At The Women's Sports Bar
items.author: Frankie de la Cretaz
paragraphs: The WNBA Finals Are Better At The Women's Sports Bar
In 2022, there was just one bar dedicated to pro female athletes in the country. Today, there are more than 25, and you shouldn't miss out.

It’s a Saturday afternoon, and I’m standing shoulder to shoulder with strangers in a small Boston brewery. All eyes are locked on the televisions on the walls, which are playing Game 1 of the WNBA Finals between the Golden State Valkyries and the Atlanta Dream.

When Golden State forward and fan favorite Gabby Williams goes off, draining a huge 3-point shot, the bar erupts. When Dream center Angel Reese gets a tough finish at the rim plus the foul call, the bar is just as loud. Strangers high-five, friends hug, and co-workers cheer in between running pints to tables. For a moment, I look around at this diverse group of people who have come together to watch the WNBA and remember what it was like just a few years ago, when I couldn’t find a single bar willing to put on a game.

In 2022, there was only one bar dedicated to women’s sports in the United States. Today, there are more than 25, with more on the way. I’m watching the Finals at Drawdown Brewing, a queer-owned spot in the Jamaica Plain neighborhood of Boston. Until recently, the city lacked a dedicated women’s sports bar, so in 2023, Drawdown stepped in to fill the void.

It’s run by Liz Nicol, who spent a decade as a home brewer before winning VinePair’s “Brewer of the Year” award, and her wife, Jenn Batore. While they will sometimes put on men’s sports “as filler,” as Nicol puts it, their bread and butter is women’s sports. As the WNBA’s audience continues to grow, women’s sports bars across the country are meeting the demand by providing spaces where fans can gather during games.

“This is my Cheers,” says Noah Tobin, a regular who visits at least once per week. He says he likes it because even if he is alone, there is always someone there that he can connect with over a shared interest in women’s sports.

Ahead of a 3:30 p.m. tipoff, I get to Drawdown around 2 p.m. so that I will have time to chat with Nicol and hopefully snag a seat for later. Drawdown is a relatively small space — just 30 to 40 seats with a standing room capacity of nearly 100. When I get there, it’s empty aside from one couple visiting from out of town. On one TV, an NWSL game plays. On the other, men’s college football.

The beer list, written on a large chalk board above the taps, features brews with queer-specific names, like the IPA (“LGBTQIPA+”) and hard seltzer (“Gaydarade,” which also comes in a non-alcoholic version), and others that are named for local events or seasons, like the Scotch Ale (“No Scotland, No Party,” a World Cup reference) or pumpkin ale (“White Girl Wasted”). Below one of the TVs, there’s a shirt for sale emblazoned with “Beers, Gays, Sports.”

I’m curious to see who the crowd will be rooting for, as there isn’t a local team in the Finals (and, following the sale of the Connecticut Sun to Houston earlier this year, there is no longer a team in New England). It’s immediately clear that the patrons are just here to watch some good basketball, as by 3 p.m. I have seen a Dallas Wings hat, a Sun “KEESUSK” hat, a Kelsey Mitchell Indiana Fever jersey, and a WNBA Playa Society jersey that says “The WNBA is so important” on the back (a quote from WNBA journalist Ari Chambers).

The woman in the WNBA jersey — which, it turns out, she bought at the WNBA All-Star Game in Chicago this summer — is Andrea Lackey, who came to Drawdown to watch the game with her husband, Dan. The pair is in town from Orange County, California, to visit their son at Boston University. She tells me that they aren’t rooting for any particular team (“we’re more fans of individual players”) and that they travel all over the world to watch their favorites. They flew to Berlin for the International Basketball Federation (FIBA) tournament this summer, where they met Isobel Borlase, an Atlanta Dream rookie and Australia national team member. In the off-season, they’re going to watch her play Down Under.

Not everyone at Drawdown is a diehard fan. “I come here regularly, and there are some people who take it very, very seriously,” says Shelley Harrison, who is sitting next to me at the bar before the game. She’s wearing Valkyries gear but says she feels a little bad because she’s a huge Las Vegas Aces fan and her team lost to Golden State in the previous round. “But then you have people like my friends, who are just coming in for the playoffs because it’s fun.”

By the time tipoff arrives, the bar is packed. There are no empty seats, and some people are sitting on window ledges, while the rest stand. No one seems to mind; everyone’s focus is on the game. A decent amount of Valkyries merch is visible in the space, but when Angel Reese gets her first bucket, it becomes clear that there’s a huge Dream contingent at the back of the bar. Based on the cheering, the crowd seems pretty evenly split between rooting for Golden State and for Atlanta. Despite that, there is no sniping or bickering among opposing fandoms. Everyone is just there to have a good time.

I settle into a corner barstool with two people I only know from the Internet — subscribers to my newsletter who are also members of the associated Discord server who recognized me and came over to say hi. Another Internet friend, hockey writer Sara Civian, comes over and introduces herself; we’ve been trying to meet in person for years. Maybe this is becoming my Cheers, too.

The 2026 WNBA Finals is a historic series, and it’s reflected in the fans’ groans and yells throughout the entire two hours of basketball. The Golden State Valkyries have made the championship in just their second year, the fastest expansion team to ever achieve the milestone. Meanwhile, the Atlanta Dream haven’t been in the Finals since 2013 and had been swept all three times they’d made it there. Neither franchise has ever won a championship. Game 1 is a good one — a back-and-forth battle that remains a toss-up until the very last minute. Ultimately, the Valkyries are victorious, winning 68-64. About half the bar erupts into cheers, but the entire place claps its respect for the start of a competitive series.

It strikes me that a crowd of people gathered to watch two teams with virtually no local connection. (Valkyries point guard Veronica Burton is from nearby Newton, Massachusetts.) They sought out a place where they knew their game would be on the TVs, where no one would judge them for cheering on women hoopers. And they’ll keep coming back, because when you find a place like that, it’s worth keeping.

items.author: Jake Viswanath
paragraphs: Ashe’s life has reached a major turning point. The singer-songwriter is used to selling out theaters but not getting recognized in public, as she expects when we meet for lunch at Hillstone’s New York City outpost. But less than two minutes after we settle into our booth, a fan approaches and tells the 33-year-old California native, “I'm really proud of how your career has grown, and I’m really excited for your album.”
“I paid her to say that,” Ashe jokes afterward.

Years ago, that comment would’ve made Ashe — dressed like a posh mermaid in a sequined blue-and-green skirt and cropped sweater — feel more pressure about a new project. Now, it only adds to her excitement. “I feel like I’ve done so much therapy and healing that this is just fun. I am so lucky this is my job, and the fact that anyone cares at all is unbelievable.”

The album in question is Ashe’s fourth solo effort, The Girl of Your Dreams, which is poised to become her biggest yet. Her lead single “Stop The Wedding!” — a cinematic soul number that argues why it’s OK to leave your groom at the altar — is already a Top 3 hit in the U.K. and climbing charts stateside after going viral as part of a TikTok trend pointing out red flags in a relationship.

“I knew that ‘Stop The Wedding!’ was special,” she says, smiling as she digs into our focaccia, but even she’s surprised it’s reached Spotify’s global Top 10. “There are 12 tempo changes in that song,” she points out. “The fact that that's on radio is the craziest thing ever to me.” She does have a theory, though.

“I feel like it's latching on because people are putting their own stories onto it,” she says. “For some people, ‘Stop The Wedding!’ meant quitting their job and trying to chase a new dream. That's so cool.” For Ashe, the track is literal, born out of wishing she had canceled her first wedding in 2016. But before she could write about it, she had to reach a breaking point.

In 2020, Ashe got her first big break when Netflix featured her single “Moral of the Story” in the To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before sequel P.S. I Still Love You. “[Producer] Finneas watched a clip from the movie, and he called me that day like, ‘This is going to change your life,’” she recalls. “It was fun until it wasn’t. I didn't have any boundaries, so I didn't know what to say yes and no to.”

Following her divorce and the death of her brother in 2020, and her breakout success over the next two years, she experienced what she calls a “nervous breakdown,” leaving Los Angeles for Nashville and canceling her 2023 tour. Over the next year, she completed the final album in a trilogy titled after her birth name, Ashlyn Rae Willson, 2024’s Willson, but she still felt unfulfilled and wondered if she’d ever make music again.
After a lot of “therapy and gardening,” she asked Finneas for some advice. “I texted him like, ‘How can I make music again in a way that doesn’t make me want to gouge my eyes out?’” she says.

The answer was forming a band. In 2024, Ashe and Finneas made a collaborative album, The Dream, under a new stage name, The Favors, completely in secret. “We made the entire album before we shopped it to a label, because we didn’t want anyone to have an opinion about this,” she explains. “It gave us so much creative freedom.” The twosome dabble in sweeping, romantic Fleetwood Mac-esque ’70s rock, which made Ashe feel ready to go solo again with The Girl of Your Dreams. And this time, she’s ready to have some fun again.

“Lasso the Moon” is full-on ABBA whimsy, encouraging us to raise our standards (“I'm so sick of, ‘Well, he's a nice guy’ keeping people in mediocre relationships,” she says), while “Sweet Caroline” (not a Neil Diamond cover) is Ashe’s first time calling out a frenemy. “To pose as a girl’s girl but then be a backstabber really bugs the sh*t out of me,” she says, sipping her iced coffee. But don’t get out your detective hat. “She will know it's about her, but no one else will clock it.”

“Love Bomb” tackles the phenomenon over folksy instrumentation, inspired by Selling Sunset, of all things. “I was love-bombed by my ex, but no one was using the phrase. Then Chrishell [Stause] was telling [Emma Hernan], ‘You're being love-bombed and manipulated by this narcissist,’ and I was like, ‘Oh my God,’” she says. “I thought, ‘Wouldn't it be fun to flip it on its head and say you should be love-bombing yourself?’ You can take all of this insanity and kill yourself with kindness.”

The Girl of Your Dreams arguably continues Ashe’s pattern of self-titled albums, as she reaches the height of her powers sonically and emotionally. She credits her husband John Canada (yes, she also thinks his name is “c*nty”), with whom she just celebrated their one-year wedding anniversary, as a major part of her healing process.

“How many men have I been with?” she asks, counting with her fingers before laughing. “Enough to know that most are uncomfortable with me being bright, funny, smart, or big. When I walk in a room, I want to make people laugh and smile. That’s what I was doing as a 2-year-old at Christmas with my family, but I’ve always been with men who tried to dim that. He is the first guy who has never made me feel like I had to be... small.” However, she didn’t go as far as naming the album Canada, as Finneas suggested. “When they think I’m going to zig, I have to zag,” she says.

Ashe has never made a point of keeping her life private, and her level of fame up until this point has allowed her to do just that. Wikipedia doesn’t even list her birthday. “They don’t?” she asks, clearly surprised. “I don't care. I’m so proud of the life that I've made for myself, and it’s taken 33 years to get here. April 24, 1993. Print it, Wikipedia.” However, as “Stop The Wedding!” keeps rising, having a low profile may no longer be possible.

“That very sweet girl that just came up to me, what if I was just starting my period today and we were having an uncomfortable conversation?” she asks, concerned. “I have a hard time being like, ‘I'm so sorry, I don't want to take a photo right now’ without seeming like a b*tch.” As a result, her relationship with social media is now evolving. “I like that I don't take it all too seriously, and people see an authentic version of me, but I reserve the right to change my mind,” she warns.

Taking one last bite of her spicy tuna roll, Ashe reviews her week's schedule, which includes a few promo performances ahead of her tour announcement. “In such an AI world, I can't wait to put on a show with no digital screens,” she says. “I want to start on a vanity that rolls out, and take curlers out of my hair for the first song.” In becoming the girl of her dreams, Ashe is having more fun than ever.

items.title: Your Horoscope This Week: October 25 To 31
items.description: Cosmic beings, the final week of October is astrologically charged, with our first full week of Scorpio Season unfolding alongside our first full week of Venus retrograde in Libra. That combination of water and air asks us to honor the intensity of what we fee
items.author: Dossé-Via Trenou
paragraphs: Cosmic beings, the final week of October is astrologically charged, with our first full week of Scorpio Season unfolding alongside our first full week of Venus retrograde in Libra. That combination of water and air asks us to honor the intensity of what we feel while also recognizing what is no longer ours to keep carrying. Relationships, financial stress, beauty, self-esteem, and the way we measure our own worth can all come under review. Scorpio wants emotional truth, while Libra wants balance, so this week may reveal where holding on has become heavier than simply letting go.

On October 26th, the Taurus Full Moon brings some much-needed earth energy into the mix and turns our attention toward the practical ways our lives need to change. Taurus is fixed energy, so there may be something we already know we have outgrown but still feel reluctant to release because it is familiar, comfortable, or once made us feel secure. This Full Moon can make that evolution impossible to ignore. And because it is ruled by Venus retrograde in Libra, the release does not have to be dramatic. There is something powerful about peaceful detachment here: accepting that something had value in one chapter of your life without forcing it to remain valuable forever.

The second half of the week is about coming down from the Full Moon and simplifying. As the Taurus Moon begins to wane, spend less energy chasing answers and more time grounding yourself in what is already tangible: your body, your environment, the people who consistently show up, and the small pleasures that make life feel full. We end October being asked to define value beyond a number in a bank account or someone else’s approval. What feels stable? What feels nourishing? What is actually worth your energy now? Those answers can tell you a lot about what you are ready to carry into November.
Read your horoscopes for your Sun and Rising signs for the most in-depth forecast.

Aries, this first full week of Scorpio Season may feel like shedding a skin you didn’t  realize had become too tight. This is one of the more profound seasons of the year for you because it pulls your attention toward emotional, spiritual, and psychological transformation rather than outward momentum. You may feel more private, more intense, or more aware of the parts of yourself that are ready to evolve. Let the retrogrades slow the process down. You don’t need to force clarity or rush into the  “new you” before you have fully released the version of yourself you’re outgrowing. Some transformations work best when they are allowed to be messy, quiet, and deeply honest.

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th illuminates your money, security, and self worth sector. This could bring a financial windfall, an unexpected expense, or simply a sobering realization about the way you relate to money and stability. Whatever comes up, Taurus energy prefers a steady game plan over an impulsive reaction, especially with Venus retrograde right now. Review what’s working, release what’s draining you,  and get honest about what you actually need in order to feel secure both financially and emotionally. The end of October wants you grounded in what’s real, not rushing toward what is next.

Taurus, this first full week of Scorpio Season may make relationships feel a lot more  consuming than usual. You could find yourself excavating every layer of a connection,  reading more deeply into someone’s behavior, or feeling more possessive, protective, or even slightly obsessive about where you stand with people who matter to you. Scorpio energy can make intimacy feel all-or-nothing, and because it sits opposite your sign, it may pull you out of your usual comfort zone by asking you to confront the emotional undercurrents you would normally rather stabilize than dissect. Let yourself notice what is being revealed without turning every feeling into a final conclusion.

Then your annual Taurus Full Moon arrives on October 26th and brings the focus decisively back to you. A milestone from the past six months may become clear, or you may reach an emotional breaking point that ends up being the breakthrough you needed. This lunation asks you to come back to your body, your needs, your pace, and your own sense of self — the relationship that ultimately sets the tone for every other one. Let yourself feel whatever comes up without immediately trying to move past it, then use that clarity to create a steadier inner and outer foundation so you can end October feeling more rooted in who you are.

Gemini, this first full week of Scorpio Season asks you to go deeper than the surface level version of wellness. Green smoothies, strength training, and a perfectly organized routine can only take you so far if your mind is exhausted or your inner dialogue is constantly tearing you down. Scorpio energy pushes you to look more honestly at the psychological habits underneath your daily life: the way you speak to yourself, the stress you normalize, and the parts of you that are still performing “fine” when something clearly needs attention. This is a powerful week to shed habits and mindsets that no longer match the person you are becoming, and to replace self criticism with a much more compassionate form of discipline.

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th lands in your spirituality, solitude, and subconscious sector, which may pull you slightly out of your comfort zone. You’re usually happiest when there’s movement, conversation, and something new to think about, but this lunation asks you to slow down enough to face what has been lingering underneath the noise. Old memories, insecurities, or people from the past may resurface, and the release could be surprisingly physical or emotional. Turn your notifications off, spend more time alone, meditate, journal, sit under a tree, hug one if you feel like it… anything that helps you come back into your body and out of mental overdrive. If you give yourself that space, you could end October feeling dramatically lighter and much more ready to soar into November.

Cancer, this first full week of Scorpio Season can feel like your heart is turning the volume up on everything that makes you feel alive. Romance, creativity, pleasure, and inner-child healing all come into sharper focus, but Scorpio asks you to go beyond surface-level fun and notice where desire is tangled up with fear, control, or old emotional conditioning. You may feel more passionate, more magnetic, or more creatively obsessed, but also more aware of what still makes you hesitate to fully enjoy yourself. Let this week show you where joy has been carrying emotional baggage, and give yourself permission to want what you want without immediately interrogating it.

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th lights up your friendship, community, and future-goals sector, helping you see which people and plans actually feel stable enough to grow with you. A friendship, collaboration, or long-term goal may reach a milestone, or you may realize that a certain social dynamic has run its course. Taurus energy helps you come back to what’s consistent and trustworthy rather than what’s simply exciting in the moment. By the end of the month, you may feel much clearer about who belongs in your next chapter and which dreams are worth building slowly.

Leo, this first full week of Scorpio Season turns your attention toward home, family,  and the emotional foundation underneath everything else. You may feel more protective  of your space, more sensitive to old family dynamics, or more aware of where you have been carrying tension privately while still showing up confidently in public. Scorpio energy can excavate memories, loyalties, and emotional patterns that shaped you long before you had language for them. The goal this week isn’t to fix your entire past; it’s to understand what still has influence over you and decide what deserves to come with you into your next chapter.

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th lights up your career, reputation, and public-image sector, bringing a culmination around something you’ve been building over the past six months. Recognition, a professional milestone, a decision about your direction, or even a realization that a certain version of success no longer satisfies you could come to the surface. Taurus asks you to move from pressure into sustainability, so pay attention to what feels solid rather than what simply looks impressive. By month’s end, the balance between your private life and public ambitions may feel much clearer, and that clarity can help you build a version of success that actually feels good to live inside of.

Virgo, this first full week of Scorpio Season asks you to pay much closer attention to the stories running through your mind all day. Your communication, thinking, learning, and immediate environment are activated, but Scorpio wants more than surface-level  observations. You may become aware of a thought pattern you repeat when you feel insecure, a conversation you keep replaying, or a truth you have been editing because saying it plainly felt too vulnerable. This week is powerful for deeper mental cleanup:  questioning assumptions, naming what you actually feel, and shedding ways of thinking that keep you hyper-vigilant rather than genuinely prepared.

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th illuminates your expansion, travel, education, publishing, and belief sector, helping you zoom out after so much inner analysis. A goal you’ve been working toward over the past six months may reach a milestone, or you may feel ready to make a more grounded decision about where you want to go next. Taurus energy encourages you to trust the path that feels steady and sustainable rather than chasing movement for movement’s sake. By the end of the month, you may realize that your perspective has changed enough to make a whole  new future feel possible.

Libra, this first full week of Scorpio Season pulls you into a deeper conversation with money, self-worth, and the kind of security you actually trust. You may become more aware of where you spend to self-soothe, where you undervalue your time, or where your sense of worth still rises and falls depending on someone else’s approval. Scorpio energy wants you to get underneath the number in the bank account and look at the emotional story attached to it. This is a powerful week to shed scarcity habits,  comparison, or financial choices that no longer reflect who you are becoming, especially with Venus retrograde encouraging you to reassess what feels truly valuable.

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th illuminates your intimacy, shared resources, and transformation sector, bringing a deeper relationship or financial matter to a turning point. A debt, agreement, emotional bond, or trust issue may reach some kind of culmination, and the lesson is to stay grounded enough to see what is actually sustainable. Taurus wants clear terms, steadiness, and reciprocity, so this Full Moon may help you recognize where you are overextended or where support is finally becoming available. By the end of October, you may feel much clearer about what you are willing to share, what you need to protect, and what kind of merging actually feels safe.

Scorpio, this first full week of your birthday season can feel like your energy is finally returning to you. After weeks of retrograde reflection, emotional excavation, and questioning what you still want, the sun in your sign gives you permission to take up more space again. You may feel more magnetic, more certain of your instincts, and more willing to move toward the version of your life that feels deeply yours. This is a powerful reset point for identity, confidence, appearance, desire, and personal direction. Let yourself celebrate how much you have already shed. You are entering a  new solar chapter with more self-knowledge than you had a year ago, and that alone  changes the way you move through everything next.

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th illuminates your partnership sector and may reveal who’s actually equipped to soar with you into this next chapter. A relationship, friendship, collaboration, or commitment could reach an important milestone, while another may make it painfully obvious that loyalty has been keeping you attached past the expiration date. Scorpio can be loyal to a fault once someone has earned a place in your heart, but this Full Moon asks whether the connection is still reciprocal, grounded, and capable of growing with you. Let people reveal who they are. The right ones will not require you to shrink your evolution in order to keep them close.

Sag, this first full week of Scorpio Season may feel quieter than your usual rhythm, but there is a lot happening beneath the surface. Your solitude, subconscious, and healing zone is activated, so you may crave more privacy, more sleep, or simply more distance from people and situations that keep you mentally overstimulated. Scorpio Season can bring old emotions, fears, or unfinished chapters back into awareness, but the point is not to get lost in them. It is to understand what is draining your energy and what you are finally ready to release before your own season begins next month.

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th lights up your work, wellness, and daily routine sector, helping you turn that inner awareness into something practical. A habit, responsibility, health matter, or work situation may reach a culmination, or you may realize your body has been trying to tell you something for a while. Taurus energy wants consistency over extremes, so resist the urge to overhaul your entire life overnight. One steady change to your schedule, boundaries, or self-care could do more for you than another burst of motivation that disappears by next week.

Capricorn, this first full week of Scorpio Season puts your attention on the people,  communities, and future plans that actually have enough substance to grow with you. You may feel more selective socially, more protective of your long-term vision, or more aware of which friendships inspire you versus which ones leave you depleted. Scorpio Season can deepen your sense of loyalty, but it can also make you question whether certain alliances are rooted in genuine support or simply history. This is a strong week to get serious about the kind of network you want around the life you are building next.

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th lights up your romance, creativity, pleasure, and inner-child sector, bringing a much more personal kind of culmination. A love story, creative project, passion, or desire may reach an important milestone, and you may suddenly see how much joy you have been postponing in the name of responsibility. Taurus wants something you can actually feel and enjoy, so let this Full Moon reconnect you with what makes life worth all the effort. By the end of October, you may realize that pleasure deserves a permanent place in your plans, not just whatever time is left over.

Aquarius, this first full week of Scorpio Season puts real weight behind your ambitions and the way you want to be known. Your career, reputation, and public image are activated, but Scorpio energy makes this more than a simple productivity push. You may feel more strategic, more selective about what you attach your name to, and more aware of where you have been chasing visibility without enough emotional investment behind it. This is a strong week to deepen your commitment to the work that actually matters to you and to move with intention rather than trying to prove yourself everywhere at once.

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th pulls you back toward home, family, and your emotional foundation. A living situation, family matter, or private emotional need may reach a turning point, and you could suddenly realize that external success feels very different when your inner world is unsettled. Taurus energy asks you to stabilize from the inside out. Give yourself permission to slow down, protect your space, and define what security looks like beyond achievement. That grounding can help you end  October feeling much more centered about where you are going next.

Pisces, this first full week of Scorpio Season can make you hungry for meaning in a way that feels almost impossible to ignore. Your expansion, travel, education, publishing, spirituality, and belief sector is activated, so you may find yourself questioning whether the life you’re living is still big enough for the person you are becoming. Scorpio adds emotional depth to those questions, which can make a certain dream, destination, field of study, or spiritual path feel more urgent than usual. Follow what keeps pulling at you, but let the retrograde atmosphere keep you reflective enough to understand why it matters before you make any sweeping decisions.

Then the Taurus Full Moon on October 26th lights up your communication, learning, and immediate-environment sector, helping you bring all of that bigger-picture thinking  back down to earth. A conversation, writing project, sibling dynamic, decision, or piece of news may reach a turning point and give language to something you have been sensing for weeks. Taurus wants clarity that can actually be used, so simplify what feels overly complicated and say what you mean. By the end of October, you may feel  much more grounded in your own voice and clearer about which ideas are worth carrying forward.

items.title: The Full Hunter’s Moon In Taurus Will Make You Thirsty For Extra Attention
items.description: On October 26th, right after midnight on the eastern border, the Full Moon in Taurus appears. October's Hunter’s Moon (also known as the Travel or Falling Leaves Moon) brightly illuminates the sky, revealing all that is hidden. With Samhain and Halloween less
items.author: Lisa Stardust
paragraphs: On October 26th, right after midnight on the eastern border, the Full Moon in Taurus appears. October's Hunter’s Moon (also known as the Travel or Falling Leaves Moon) brightly illuminates the sky, revealing all that is hidden. With Samhain and Halloween less than a week after the lunation, this is an especially sensitive time; the veil between the physical and spiritual worlds is thin, offering moments of heightened intuition. The Hunter's Moon offers a chance to see in the dark as we shed our past and negative habits to work toward a better present and future.

Traditionally, the Hunter’s Moon is a time when people would forage for food and track their prey to ensure nourishment in the colder months of the year in the Northern Hemisphere. It is the middle of fall, urging us to work harder to provide for those we care about and wish to protect. This year, the Hunter’s Moon is in the sign of Taurus, exalting the lunar demand for security and indulgence. Not only do we want to build a strong foundation, but we also to have our cake and eat it, too. Nothing is too good for us, and we demand the best of the best. Why not? We deserve it!

The intensity of Pluto in Aquarius, forming a T-square with the sun in Scorpio and the moon in Taurus, isn't lost on us. The infamous Scorpio stingers may come out as a defense to safeguard our hearts. Hope for transformation and group growth exists if we are willing to access the higher vibration of these planets. However, most of us may not be able to be as levelheaded. When we feel as though others are attacking us right now, we may react fiercely and provocatively, striking back and asserting our feelings. The Scorpion's poisonous appendages may come out, causing us to use our words to hurt others. As much as we deflect our pain, it won't help, except for momentary vindication, which is why it's best to try to mend offenses and build a better dynamic instead.

Luckily, the moon in Taurus aims to give us a softer edge and a calmer approach, and to help us understand that the people in our lives are loyal; conversely, the caveat is that our stubbornness may cause us to dig our heels in the mud when we are pushed to the limit; we are going to scuffle and hustle. Still, the quarrel will be cathartic in the end; the Full Moon in Taurus doesn't want to end relationships, but enhance them. Keep that in mind before saying things we may regret. Do not take the drama to the extreme.

At this juncture, Venus (the planetary ruler of Taurus, the sign of the Full Moon) is retrograde in Libra (Venus backed up into the air sign on October 25th). Venus retrograde in Libra offers a combustible window of passion — our patience will be tested. The incessant need to partner with others puts pressure on both the other person and us. We might overlook their flaws to keep a commitment going, even though we criticize their behavior. Being kind and compassionate to our partners is essential if forging a relationship is on the horizon. We may also be thirsty for extra attention. There is nothing wrong with requiring affection.

Simultaneously, Mercury is moonwalking in Scorpio (the backslide officially began on October 24th). Revelations from the past will surface as the skeletons we buried deep in our consciousness come out. The reason is that Mercury retrograde in Scorpio is seeking to uncover the truth, and combined with the Full Moon, it offers an opportunity for us to tell those we are close to about our misfortune, insecurities, and emotional states, as we purge ourselves of what we felt was taboo in an effort to be understood.

Letting go of our old beliefs and invigorating our auras with newness isn’t something that comes easily. But we can shape and tend to who we are and what we value — and seek refuge in the tender arms of a friend, family member, or partner who supports us in these trying times.

items.title: 20 Last-Minute Halloween Costumes On Amazon For All Your Spooky Plans
items.description: 20 Last-Minute Amazon Halloween Costumes For All Your Spooky Plans
items.author: Victoria Montalti
paragraphs: 20 Last-Minute Amazon Halloween Costumes For All Your Spooky Plans
(And you can, of course, re-create Prime Video's Off Campus costumes too!)
13 Going On 30's Jenna Rink

Amazon sells a dupe of Jenna Rink's iconic party dress from everyone's favorite coming-of-age movie 13 Going on 30, and we couldn't be more grateful for the last-minute costume inspo. This Y2K costume is perfect for nostalgic gals, and especially those turning 30 this year! Accessorize with some butterfly clips, a sweet baguette bag, strappy heels, and you're all set to dance to "Thriller" in style.

We've been seeing tons of amazing vintage clown makeup tutorials on our feeds in the lead-up to Halloween, so we had to include a retro clown costume to match. This black-and-white set is spooky and sexy, and even comes with the pom pom hat and striped tights for a full head-to-toe look. Just add face paint and transform into your clown character.

We're expecting lots of Dolly Parton tributes this Halloween for the late, great singer. And while you can throw together any sparkly Western tops with flared pants, we think the most important part of the look is the hair. Luckily, this voluminous blonde wig is available on Amazon as the cherry on top of your diva-approved look.
The Nightmare Before Christmas's Sally

Is it a Halloween movie? Is it a Christmas movie? Also yes. However you classify it, The Nightmare Before Christmas is a classic and Sally is an icon, making this a tried-and-true costume. We especially love this set because of the light blue bodysuit with scar details that replicates Sally's skin (without having to put on body paint all over!).
Off Campus' Allie Hayes As JLo

Okay, we're getting a little meta here. You're not dressing up as JLo, but rather as Off Campus' Allie Hayes dressed as JLo for her own Halloween party. While many dupes of the iconic Versace dress won't arrive before Halloween, this luxe dress is ready to ship on Amazon, and can be re-worn on your next summer vacation.
Off Campus' Dean Di Laurentis as Top Gun's Maverick

Every JLo needs her Maverick... right?! The ultimate couples costume this year will be Allie and Dean dancing in the Prime Video Off Campus Halloween party scene. And this jumpsuit is pretty true to Dean's costume. Wear it with your partner or bestie for the best pop culture reference. Add some aviator sunglasses and combat boots for the full effect.

She was a fairy! Or an elf fairy! This Halloween costume is particularly perfect for romantasy book readers. Pick your favorite boho dress and add on these enchanting wings, flower crown, magic wand, hair tinsel, and elf ears for the most cost-effective and simplest yet impactful look.
Knicks Fan (or Jordyn Woods... or Taylor Swift)

Knicks in five! The Knicks finally took home the 2026 NBA Championship, but before that it was total basketball fan mania last season. Everyone repped their Knicks merch, but if you don't have any yet, here's your chance to cart some up. And to make it even more pop culture-y, add Jordyn Woods's lucky orange handbag or Taylor Swift's kitschy "Stevie Knicks" T-shirt to complete your costume.

If you can't wait to hear "The Dead Dance" this season, you should probably dress as Wednesday Addams for Halloween. This costume kit mimics the Netflix series' viral black tulle dress with a Jenna Ortega-esque wig, black accessories, and even the Thing hand for an extra spooky touch. Even better, it costs under $50!
Zara Larsson's Midnight Sun Era

2026 was Zara Larsson's year as her Midnight Sun era catapulted her career and made us all fans. While you can truly wear your favorite swimsuits and coverups, it may be a bit too chilly, so we recommend a matching skirt set in a sunset ombre. Further get the Midnight Sun look with vibrant and sparkly makeup, like this bold glitter gel.

Another classic costume that you can't go wrong with. Dress as Little Red Riding Hood in this stunning under-$50 dress. To get the full effect, add a woven basket. And to win your costume contest, fill it with Halloween candy and hand it out at your house parties and bar crawls.

One of the biggest films of the year was undoubtedly Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey. While there aren't exact costume replicas of Athena, Calypso, or Queen Penelope, we think any Grecian goddess costume will get the point across, especially if you're paired with your Odysseus.
Pirate (or Renaissance Maiden)

We haven't had a good old-fashioned pirate movie in a while, and we're craving it. So consider dressing as a badass pirate for Halloween with this costume kit. It's not too kitschy and feels more upscale. And if you remove the eye patch, you can re-wear the outfit for a Renaissance fair!
Dallas Cowboys Cheerleader
Even if you're not a football fan, you may be a Dallas Cowboys Cheerleader fan, especially after binge-watching Netflix's America's Sweethearts documentary series.
Pick up your pom poms, slip into white cowboy boots and channel the DCC girls' "Thunderstruck" energy.

Sure, you can be a Disney princess, but dressing as a villain or sidekick is typically more fun to channel. And whether you love the original book or the movie remakes, the Mad Hatter is a character primed for Halloween. This top-rated Amazon costume gives you a quirky head-to-toe look, including a top hat, bow tie, and over-the-knee socks.

Picture it: You're dressed as Anxiety from Inside Out 2 while Doechii's "Anxiety" plays in the background of your TikTok video. Instantly iconic. The character we love to hate makes for a quirky and cute costume for all the anxious gals out there. Just add brown flared pants for the complete look.

When all else fails and you can't put together a totally unique Halloween costume, channel your spiritual and spooky senses, and be a witch. You can quite literally throw on any black dress (we personally like this corseted midi dress) and a pair of fall boots for an effortlessly chic look. Then, add this witch hat, choker, and mesh gloves for a total transformation.

Summer 2026 was defined by the World Cup and sporty style. But one person went beyond the field, and took over our feeds: Erling Haaland. The Norwegian Viking, um, we mean soccer player, became famous for his terrifying height and speed, but mostly for his luscious hair and signature man bun. So if you have long blonde hair, you simply have to do this costume. Add your soccer jersey and you have an easy, funny 'fit.

Spoiler: Fiyero turning into the scarecrow in Wicked: For Good was one of the biggest plot twists for those of us who didn't see the Broadway show. And since we won't have a third November in a row of Wicked mania, we're soaking up our favorite characters this Halloween. To make this a couples costume, have your bestie dress up as Cynthia Erivo's Elphaba and re-create the "As Long As You're Mine" scene!
