items.title: Everyone says they have anxiety. Clinical anxiety is different | Psyche Ideas
items.description: You’ve probably noticed that terms once used only within the confines of a therapist’s office are now deployed unthinkingly to describe experiences that are merely uncomfortable. A car backfires and someone says it has ‘given them anxiety’. Spilling a round of
items.author: India Sturgis
paragraphs: You’ve probably noticed that terms once used only within the confines of a therapist’s office are now deployed unthinkingly to describe experiences that are merely uncomfortable. A car backfires and someone says it has ‘given them anxiety’. Spilling a round of drinks in front of others results in ‘PTSD’ – or ‘OCD’ until they are cleared up. On TikTok, I’ve seen someone’s ‘ponytail era’ or syrup stains on a hardwood floor being described as severely traumatic. Likewise, the everyday use of language that surrounds anxiety conditions – words like ‘worry’, ‘fear’, ‘rumination’, ‘panic’, and ‘anxiety’ itself – makes it easy to underestimate just how debilitating anxiety-related illnesses can be.

As a journalist, I’ve spent years interviewing experts and people living with anxiety for my book How to Eat an Elephant (2026). I also have my own personal experience with anxiety. In 2019, I was diagnosed with generalised anxiety disorder (GAD), post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and chronic insomnia, which I have since rowed back from, over months and years. My hope is for more people to recognise just how serious anxiety can become, not least so they know when to get the help they need – but also to appreciate that it’s an essential, unavoidable part of life.

It’s normal to feel anxiety during challenging life moments or periods of intense change. To sweep mild and transient issues into the language of disorder helps no one, and particularly not those who really are struggling with mental ill health. Nerves help us make decisions quickly, weigh up risk, and compete at the top of our game. The professional golfer Tiger Woods put it well in an interview in 2015: ‘I care about what I do and when I’m not nervous is the day I quit … I want to feel the rush, I want to feel the nerves.’

So we need some anxiety in our lives, but we also need to know when it has outstayed its welcome or grown to unhelpful and life-altering proportions. Anxiety conditions are the most common form of mental illness, affecting a third of us in our lifetime, according to best estimates. Data from the NHS in England suggest that 7.5 per cent of adults are currently living with GAD, the most common anxiety disorder. Despite this, global data show that only one in four people with an anxiety disorder will receive any form of treatment for it, which is particularly frustrating given how highly treatable anxiety is.

The consultant psychologist Elena Touroni says confusion around anxiety creeps in because we use it to describe such a wide spectrum of experience: ‘It’s used for both the nerves before a presentation, and the experience of someone whose anxiety is shaping every decision they make, narrowing their world and affecting their sleep, their relationships and their ability to function.’

According to Touroni, it’s not surprising that people struggle to locate themselves on that spectrum, or to recognise when what they are experiencing has crossed into something that warrants proper support. ‘The line between normal and clinical is not obvious and can feel quite subjective to people who don’t have specialist support,’ she says. ‘I regularly work with people who have been managing a significant level of anxiety for years without recognising it as anything other than just how they are. They have adapted to it and it has become their baseline.’
Doctors typically look at how significantly symptoms interfere with your ability to function day to day

This resonates with me. Before I ended up in a psychiatric hospital in 2019, I had spent seven years struggling on and off with insomnia and anxiety to varying degrees. I sought concerted help only right at the end, when I was going multiple nights a week with just three or so hours of sleep – sometimes spending whole nights awake – utterly unable to switch off and, by then, having intrusive thoughts about suicide and self-harm. It sounds dramatic now – and it was – but it felt easier at the time to try to carry on and pretend nothing was wrong, hopeful things would get better on their own, particularly given I knew so little about anxiety.

So how do experts make a diagnosis of clinical anxiety? In the absence of a failsafe test, doctors typically look at how long you’ve had symptoms, their severity, and how significantly they interfere with your ability to function day to day.

‘What distinguishes a clinical anxiety disorder is not the presence of anxious thoughts, jitters or that horrible knot in the pit of your stomach,’ says Touroni, ‘but what happens to them over time. In clinical anxiety, the symptoms are more intense and persistent and, crucially, they do not lift once the perceived threat has gone. The nervous system either stays in a state of high alert long after the trigger has passed, or it begins firing in the absence of any clear trigger at all. Clinically, if someone has been experiencing this for six months or more, we would look seriously at whether they are dealing with an anxiety disorder.’

I knew things were escalating when I kept getting ill (my immune system was having a hard time with the insomnia), my mood had plummeted, and I started having panic attacks at night. I was anxious about feeling anxious and not sleeping. Everything was compounding and, as a result, I wanted to go out less.

Touroni explains that many people go for years carrying the physical and emotional toll of managing an anxiety disorder. This is a shame as ‘anxiety disorders are among the most treatable conditions we see in psychological practice.’ She adds: ‘Getting the right name for something is not a small thing, as it changes what feels possible and can have a huge impact on a person’s quality of life.’

Now – seven years after being hospitalised – I’m pleased to say anxiety is not a defining feature of my life, it’s just another brick in the wall of my personality. What helped me most when I was in crisis was being taken out of my home environment for a couple of weeks, medication (sertraline, an SSRI antidepressant, in the mornings and amitriptyline, a tricyclic antidepressant that can help with sleep, in the evenings), cognitive behavioural therapy, and learning how anxiety as a pathological illness functions in the mind and body.

I know I have a tendency towards anxiety, but I also now know what helps me steer away from it in pressing moments: prioritising sleep, work-life balance, managing stress, eating well, saying ‘no’ and being self-compassionate, among other things.
It’s my tendency towards anxiety that makes me so enjoy life. I am quick to think and feel

The psychologist and researcher Nick Grey puts it like this: ‘Can we cure anxiety? No, because it’s part of the human condition. If someone’s goal is I never want to feel anxious again, then no, that won’t happen. But if the goal is about overcoming a chronic anxiety problem in which the person is stuck, then absolutely, that can happen. You can’t get rid of anxiety, but you can absolutely overcome chronic anxiety problems.’
The psychologist Rollo May was of a similar opinion. I like what he wrote in The Meaning of Anxiety (rev ed, 1977):

Anxiety cannot be avoided, but it can be reduced. The problem of the management of anxiety is that of reducing the anxiety to normal levels, and then to use this normal anxiety as stimulation to increase one’s awareness, vigilance, zest for living.

True to his perspective, I’ve come to see that it’s my tendency towards anxiety that makes me so enjoy life. I am quick to think and feel. And while I now recognise the need to pay better attention to anxiety when I feel it – weighing up what my mind and body are trying to tell me rather than pretending it doesn’t exist and pushing the sensation away – I wouldn’t change my underlying sensitive nature for anything.

If reading this has made you reflect on whether you’ve been living with problematic anxiety, it may help to have a sense of how long it could take to learn to manage it better. It could be months or years, depending on what the issue is and how long it has existed. Not days. In many cases, not even weeks. Too often, we put pressure on ourselves to ‘get better’ immediately once we realise we are sick or struggling. Grey says: ‘People assume if things haven’t changed quickly enough, then there’s no hope. But recovery is an up and down rollercoaster route. There’s always hope, even if you’ve had an anxiety problem for decades.’
Anxiety, then, is not always the enemy, but we should treat it with respect. That’s why our relationship to it matters: so we can recognise and meet it when it spills into something pathological.

items.title: Can you ever really think what someone else is thinking? | Psyche Ideas
items.description: Most of us have had the experience of looking into someone’s eyes and sensing that we know what’s on their mind. Not much is needed for this sense of knowing what someone is thinking: some words, a gesture, a smile, or just a shared gaze. Friends exchange comm
items.author: Víctor Verdejo
paragraphs: Most of us have had the experience of looking into someone’s eyes and sensing that we know what’s on their mind. Not much is needed for this sense of knowing what someone is thinking: some words, a gesture, a smile, or just a shared gaze. Friends exchange comments about their day and nod affirmatively. Parents utter ‘Oh my God’ as they watch their toddler take a first step. Commuters give each other a weary glance as the train pulls away without them. Encounters like these involve a meeting of minds – we feel that we understand and are understood.

Having the opportunity to connect with others in this way is gratifying. It provides a sense of belonging to a wider sphere, a sphere where your thoughts and your meanings are not just your thoughts and your meanings. Where they are open to another. When communication unfolds successfully – when the click happens, or insofar as the click happens – you and another person can seem to be thinking the same thing.

This idea transpires in the way people talk: we tend to speak as if we literally share thoughts, as though ideas can flow seamlessly from one mind to another. We often say that we ‘think the same’ or ‘know what’s on somebody’s mind’ or ‘get our thoughts across’. These are natural illustrations of how much people unreflectively rely on the idea that thoughts are not only shareable but indeed are ordinarily shared in our communicative exchanges.

This intuitive picture is old and powerful. Yet the notion that people think the very same thought in successful communication has come under increasing scrutiny. Contemporary philosophers argue that what seems like straightforward thought-sharing is more complex, and more interesting, than the familiar metaphors suggest. They both challenge this natural idea and show that understanding each other plausibly involves thinking differently from each other. Realising this can help us see how communication really works.

The idea that communication and understanding are built on shared thoughts has a long history. Plato influentially suggested that ideas involved in our knowledge and talk are in fact unchanging, perfect forms inhabiting a separate realm – a shared eidetic foundation of reality. Augustine of Hippo, in De doctrina Christiana (397-426), expressed the view that signs are used to ‘transmit to another’s mind what is in the mind of the person who gives the sign’. But the basic schema that informs our communicative intuitions nowadays was more clearly proclaimed in the modern period. In the third book of An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689), John Locke contended that the purpose of communication via language is the transfer of thoughts or ideas from one person to another:

The chief end of language in communication being to be understood, words serve not well for that end, neither in civil nor philosophical discourse, when any word does not excite in the hearer the same idea which it stands for in the mind of the speaker.

This view persisted from the 19th century to the present, in the work of philosophical giants such as Gottlob Frege, H P Grice and Robert Stalnaker, among others. Frege, for instance, advocated a conception of shareable thoughts that result in a ‘common stock’ consistent with logic and science. Stalnaker developed an influential framework for communicative contexts resting on the notion of a ‘common ground’, or information shared by the speakers in a conversation.

Whereas these and other works clearly align with the idea of thought-sharing, recent developments in thinking about the nature of communication suggest a more nuanced picture. Sometimes, of course, people suffer dramatic misalignment and just miscommunicate; the thought doesn’t get across, and they don’t understand each other. But even when communication succeeds in practical terms, there is often diversity and mismatch in what we’re thinking.
Effective communication is consistent with – and may even require – differences in thought

Suppose that, after a hard day’s work, you tell me, irascibly: ‘I had an awful day at work,’ to which I respond:, ‘I see.’ Here, there is a sense in which I perfectly understand what you said. But there are two ways in which this falls short of thought-sharing in the common sense of the term. First, your thought might be extremely rich – filled with feelings of frustration and details of the whole lot of things that have gone wrong throughout the day. But communication, in this case, doesn’t require us to share all of that. Moreover, even if you were to tell me all the ins and outs, there is some quality of the thought that can hardly be shared: after all, it is your job and your frustration. Even if I sympathise, it can barely affect me and my behaviour in the same way it affects yours.

People rarely, if ever, communicate about things as if from nowhere. Each of us must occupy a distinctive space, a point of view, with our own background knowledge, memories and current experience regarding the matters we talk about. A popular example from John Perry illustrates this cleanly: suppose that you are in the mountains with a hiking partner, and a bear starts to approach them. In fright, they shout: ‘A bear is about to attack me!’ You understand that they are in danger, so you run to get help while your partner defensively curls up into a ball. But if you completely shared your partner’s thought – which would include thought content about an imminent threat to the self, from their perspective – then you would behave in the same way that they do and curl up too.

In this case, as well as in more ordinary cases, effective communication is consistent with – and may even require – differences in thought. Our cognitive lives are, after all, so different. Our beliefs, backgrounds and sensibilities influence the specific content of our thoughts, and they can never really be the same from one thinker to the next.

In the science-fiction trope of the ‘hive mind’ (eg, the Borg of Star Trek, or the virus-induced collective consciousness of the 2025 TV show Pluribus), individual minds in the hive share all thoughts automatically and seamlessly; they are literally of one mind in every respect. If real-life communication consists of thought-sharing, it certainly isn’t like this for us, yet we sometimes talk as if it is. Recognising this is important: it not only avoids a distorted conception of communication, it also helps to calibrate our expectations when we communicate.

In recent philosophical work, there are some who defend a sophisticated version of thought-sharing. They make room for the variability of what people are actually thinking when they understand each other, but retain the idea that you can, in some sense, share a thought. This approach, which I myself favour, reflects that the basic concept of thought-sharing is not only natural, but explanatorily useful. For example, the notion that you can share a thought makes it easy to distinguish between misunderstanding what someone means (‘getting the wrong idea’) from grasping what someone means (‘getting the idea’) and yet disagreeing with it.

In this way of viewing thought-sharing, each person’s version of the shared thought is layered: thought similarity at one level is compatible with a level of disparity that reflects each person’s distinctive points of view. To constitute a ‘shared thought’, some core content or state must be identical, even as some other components of the thought differ. On this view, sharing thoughts is complex because thoughts themselves are complex.
Treating our thoughts as if they are about the same things often suffices for understanding and joint behaviour

But other philosophers explain communication differently: via coordination or informational relations among different thoughts. On these accounts, if I know or somehow track what you are thinking, I don’t actually need to ‘share’ your thought in order to understand what you are saying.

One particularly influential example of this is relationism, the kind of approach originally championed by Kit Fine. According to this perspective, communication is not really a matter of thought identity, but thought coordination. What matters is not the intrinsic properties of two people’s thoughts or the extent to which those are the same. What matters is how those thoughts are related. For instance, treating our thoughts as if they are about the same things often suffices for understanding and joint behaviour. So, if you tell me about your ‘awful day at work’, and elaborate about impending deadlines, an unkind boss and feeling overwhelmed, and I respond sympathetically, we both presuppose or act as if our thoughts are about these same things – even if the thoughts themselves are different – and doing so allows the conversation to serve its function. I may not need to share your experience in order to understand you. It might be enough that our thoughts coordinate – that they stand in an appropriate relation to one another.

The debate continues between proponents of these perspectives. But the richer picture drawn by these trends helps us think about communication and shared understanding without positing (as some would be tempted to) perfect matching in the way people think.

Let us return to our opening thought: the existence of mutual understanding, possibly triggered by words, gestures or even a simple glance. This prospect underwrites the possibility of a common world, and takes us beyond our private experiences. Yet recalcitrant, multifaceted difference is also an undeniable part of the picture. We should not expect mutual understanding in communication necessarily to lead to a common, monolithic thought or experience.

Noting this could prevent unnecessary frustration and overoptimistic expectations when we communicate. Communicating smoothly does bring our thoughts into contact with those of others. But there are important limits on someone else’s access to the full richness of your thoughts and point of view, and vice versa. Knowing this before we speak might inspire more patience in communication, more willingness to restate or elaborate in order to build the shared kernel of our differing thoughts, or a degree of acceptance when someone doesn’t seem to fully ‘get it’. It takes time and effort to share anything more than superficial or abstract thoughts and, even then, it is impossible to share everything we think. But that is exactly as it should be.

It may still seem plausible and useful to suppose that we can think ‘the same thing’. But, often, the connection you have to someone else’s thought is looser than it might appear, and interestingly complex. Whatever perspective you take, the question of whether or how we ever truly ‘share’ thoughts gives us reason to pause and consider what it actually means to connect with someone else – to understand and to be understood.

Noting this could prevent unnecessary frustration and overoptimistic expectations when we communicate. Communicating smoothly does bring our thoughts into contact with those of others. But there are important limits on someone else’s access to the full richness of your thoughts and point of view, and vice versa. Knowing this before we speak might inspire more patience in communication, more willingness to restate or elaborate in order to build the shared kernel of our differing thoughts, or a degree of acceptance when someone doesn’t seem to fully ‘get it’. It takes time and effort to share anything more than superficial or abstract thoughts and, even then, it is impossible to share everything we think. But that is exactly as it should be.

It may still seem plausible and useful to suppose that we can think ‘the same thing’. But, often, the connection you have to someone else’s thought is looser than it might appear, and interestingly complex. Whatever perspective you take, the question of whether or how we ever truly ‘share’ thoughts gives us reason to pause and consider what it actually means to connect with someone else – to understand and to be understood.

items.title: Why romantic relationships matter more to men than to women | Psyche Ideas
items.description: For centuries, the self-sufficient man who shuns romance has appeared as a kind of noble figure. ‘He that hath wife and children hath given hostages to fortune,’ wrote Francis Bacon in ‘Of Marriage and the Single Life’ (1625). ‘Certainly the best works, and of
items.author: Iris Wahring
paragraphs: For centuries, the self-sufficient man who shuns romance has appeared as a kind of noble figure. ‘He that hath wife and children hath given hostages to fortune,’ wrote Francis Bacon in ‘Of Marriage and the Single Life’ (1625). ‘Certainly the best works, and of greatest merit for the public, have proceeded from the unmarried or childless men.’ For Bacon, romantic relationships (and family) are impediments to a man becoming his best. Ralph Waldo Emerson devoted an entire essay, ‘Self-Reliance’ (1841), to the conviction that a man should stand apart from the crowd. ‘I shun father and mother and wife and brother, when my genius calls me,’ he wrote. Decades later, Rudyard Kipling reduced the idea to a single line: ‘He travels the fastest who travels alone.’

Such visions of self-sufficient masculinity endure in depictions of silent cowboys, wandering rōnin, desert hermits, elite soldiers, or libertines who treat love as a sport. Powered by their own strength and resilience, these men are domesticated only when circumstances or a determined partner finally insists on it. According to this view of masculinity, love is a welcome addition but never a need.

Women, on the other hand, have often been portrayed as being consumed by their desire for romantic relationships. Consider an often-quoted line from Lord Byron’s epic poem Don Juan (1819-24): love is just one part of a man’s life, Byron writes, but ‘tis woman’s whole existence’. If men can take or leave romance, the logic goes, then women must be the real romantics. They are the ones who fall harder and faster, and the ones who carry the emotional weight of a relationship.

But that’s not how things really work. As a researcher specialising in the psychology of romantic relationships, I have found that the evidence points the other way. In 2023 and 2024, I analysed more than 50 empirical studies and meta-analyses, revealing masculinity to be much more fragile than assumed. At every stage, from the first spark of attraction to the aftermath of a breakup, it is men who depend more on their romantic partners, for their happiness and, in measurable ways, for their survival.

To understand the disproportionate weight love carries for men, we must examine the trajectory of relationships, starting from the time when men are single and searching for a partner. On average, men consider finding a partner more important for their happiness than women do. When single, they are less satisfied with their relationship status and long for a partner more intensely. They also plunge into the feeling of falling in love more often and more quickly, and they experience unrequited love more frequently. Contrary to common expectations, men are typically the first to say ‘I love you’ in heterosexual relationships, according to a 2022 study led by Christopher Watkins from Abertay University in the UK, which surveyed participants across seven countries on three continents.

Once in a relationship, both partners usually benefit. Longitudinal research indicates that entering a romantic relationship itself is typically accompanied by increases in life satisfaction. Accordingly, couples tend to show higher levels of wellbeing, better mental and physical health, and even higher life expectancy than their single counterparts. Yet, all these benefits are more pronounced for men. For example, a 2020 meta-analysis by Yafeng Wang from Wuhan University in China and colleagues, involving data on marital status and mortality risk from 7.9 million individuals and 1.9 million deaths, found that unmarried women had a 22 per cent higher mortality risk than married women, but unmarried men even had a 46 per cent higher mortality risk than married men. So for the average man, being in a committed relationship is more decisive for how long they will live than it is for the average woman.
Following a divorce, the risk of suicide doubles for men

Many romantic relationships, however, end in a breakup and, if they do, this is typically initiated by women: among heterosexual couples, 60 to 70 per cent of breakups and divorces are initiated by women, according to studies in the US, Germany and Netherlands. The remaining 30 to 40 per cent are equally divided between mutual breakups and those initiated by men.

When the split happens, men suffer more. While a breakup is typically painful for women too, men tend to struggle more to find any positive aspects, such as relief or newfound independence, following a split. They are less likely to feel like they have learned something from the breakup. Men also tend to experience a sharper decline in life satisfaction, reporting higher levels of loneliness afterward and more frequently resorting to harmful coping mechanisms, such as alcohol and substance abuse.

Most alarmingly, the end of a relationship can be fatal. Following a divorce, the risk of suicide doubles for men. In a research paper in 2025, the men’s health expert Michael Wilson from the University of Melbourne and colleagues reviewed 75 prior studies on suicidality in men to find ‘the factors underpinning men’s suicidal ideation, suicide attempt, and death by suicide following relationship breakdown’. They found that the risk of suicide was especially high during the separation period itself, nearly twice the odds seen in men who were already divorced (and more than four times as high as married men). For women, the suicide risk after a divorce or separation increases by a far smaller amount, if at all. For a significant number of men, losing a romantic relationship is, quite literally, a matter of life or death.

How did we arrive at a place where the supposedly ‘stronger’ gender longs intensely for a partner, relies more heavily on them for health and wellbeing, is more frequently left behind, and remains emotionally fragile in the face of heartbreak? Multiple factors may play a role here.

Consider, for instance, the unequal distribution of household chores. Women spend substantially more time and effort doing unpaid care work, including both the execution and planning of tasks as part of home organisation. This unequal distribution of duties between heterosexual romantic partners is not without costs and is associated with lower levels of mental and physical health in women. However, after a breakup from a cohabitating partner, women tend to spend less time on household chores than before, leaving them with more time for enjoyable activities. Men, on the other hand, often suddenly lack the person who managed this workload, and may start spending more time on less enjoyable domestic activities.
Men, throughout their lives, are less likely to receive emotional support

A related practical factor that may shape the profound effect that romantic relationships have on the physical health and life expectancy of men is that women are more likely to remind their partners to go to the doctor than vice versa. Accordingly, while both men and women in romantic relationships tend to visit the doctor more often than their single counterparts, the difference between partnered and single individuals is more pronounced among men.

Child custody is another point. It is noteworthy that following a divorce, children tend to stay with their mothers in most cases, regardless of who initiates the breakup. That means fathers who walk away from a relationship not only lose their romantic partner but also risk a substantial reduction in contact with their children. The result is a compounding sense of loss, which mothers in the same position are far less likely to face.

However, the most robust and far-reaching explanation for why the ‘stronger’ gender is so much more emotionally fragile in the face of heartbreak is intimacy: research consistently shows that men, throughout their lives, are less likely to receive emotional support.

All humans possess an innate need for intimacy. We want to confide in others, to feel secure, to be touched and held, and to know someone has our back. A central condition for experiencing emotional intimacy is receiving emotional support. Emotional support involves caring for another person’s wellbeing by understanding and appreciating them. Longitudinal and intervention research has proven that emotional support is a central resource for mental and physical health. The fundamental problem is that men often lack this support outside the boundaries of a romantic relationship. As shown in numerous studies, they tend to receive less emotional support from their friends and family than women do. Instead, men are more likely to view their romantic partners as their primary confidant.

This ‘intimacy deficit’ begins remarkably early. Even boys aged around 10 or 11 report opening up to friends far less than girls do. As they grow older, men are significantly less likely than women to have confidants they can turn to in times of trouble. To fill this gaping void, many men lean almost exclusively on the emotional support of their partners. Consequently, finding a partner represents a massive gain in emotional closeness for a man. And losing that partner can represent the loss of his entire emotional infrastructure.
We have created a paradox: forms of masculinity that forbid vulnerability guarantee an even higher level of vulnerability

The root of this isolation is the traditional male gender role. From early childhood, boys are socialised to view vulnerability as a weakness. Parents subtly enforce this: studies show that when talking to preschool-aged daughters as compared with sons, parents focus more on emotional experiences and react more positively to sadness.

By adolescence, boys have learned the lesson. They expect that opening up to friends will feel ‘weird’. Adult men go on to judge other men harshly when they show vulnerability, seeing it as a violation of traditional masculinity. A comprehensive meta-analysis led by the social psychologist Alice Eagly from Northwestern University in Illinois, including studies spanning from 1946 to 2018, shows that communal traits, like emotionality and nurturance, are still overwhelmingly attributed to women. Both men and women continue to view emotionality as a desirable trait in women, but an undesirable one in men.

Yet, beneath this stoic mask, men experience vulnerable emotions like sadness and fear just as frequently and intensely as women do. We have created a paradox: forms of masculinity that forbid vulnerability guarantee an even higher level of vulnerability. Because deep emotional connection is socially acceptable for men only within the confines of a romantic relationship, they are left utterly defenceless when they are single or when a relationship ends.

While the societal roles and expectations for women have expanded massively in recent decades, the template for masculinity has largely stagnated. We continue to raise boys who become men who are wholly dependent on romantic partners for their basic emotional needs. This is an unfair burden to place on women and is actively impairing the health and life expectancy of millions of men.

Everyone, regardless of gender, should have the capacity to lead a fulfilled, emotionally supported life without a romantic partner. To achieve this, we must rewrite the societal image of masculinity from the ground up. We need to dispel the myth of stoic self-reliance. We need to normalise emotional openness and platonic intimacy among men, to ensure they lead healthy, resilient lives that are no longer existentially dependent on a romantic partner.

This shift must be systemic. It begins with parents, who must be encouraged to raise sons to view emotional openness as a fundamental life skill rather than a weakness. In schools, the importance of emotionally close friendships must be explicitly taught, creating spaces where boys learn that vulnerability is a strength.

Furthermore, we need targeted, community-based programmes for adult men that foster connections beyond romance. A promising model is the ‘Men’s Shed’ movement, which originated in Australia and is now run in several other countries around the world. These community workshops provide a space where men, typically of retirement age, can work on practical projects and talk ‘shoulder to shoulder’ rather than face-to-face. Such informal settings bypass the stigma of traditional therapy, reducing social isolation and increasing wellbeing.

For centuries, men have been told that romantic relationships don’t matter that much and that self-sufficiency is the answer to all problems. The research tells a different story: love, it turns out, is never just a small part of a man’s life.

items.title: What cooperatives for an anticapitalist peace look like | Aeon Essays
items.description: When I was seven years old, my family was forced to flee escalating violence. We left Bakur – a Kurdish region in what is currently southeastern Turkey – for a city further west, where we worked in Turkish fields, living in a tent until we could save up to ren
items.author: Azize Aslan
paragraphs: When I was seven years old, my family was forced to flee escalating violence. We left Bakur – a Kurdish region in what is currently southeastern Turkey – for a city further west, where we worked in Turkish fields, living in a tent until we could save up to rent a house on the city margins, in a neighbourhood with no electricity or road access. Those are some of my earliest memories of everyday violence against people like me.

For centuries, my ancestors had lived in relative harmony with other communities. But, with the emergence of modern nation-states in the region, Kurdistan – the traditional homeland of the Kurds – was fractured into southeastern Turkey, northern Iraq, northwestern Iran, and northeastern Syria. A violent assimilation was imposed upon us. For more than a century, Kurdish people have been denied recognition as a nation, their language banned, erased from maps, stripped of citizenship rights, and dispossessed of their lands. For my generation, therefore, freedom was never an abstract political matter; armed struggle was often seen as a necessity to achieve it. Even so, national liberation movements always sought dialogue with the states they fought against. I grew up inside that insistence, carrying the hope of a dignified peace.

In 2013, after almost three decades of war, peace talks were held between the Turkish state and the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), which first sought an independent Kurdish state and, later, autonomy and increased political and cultural rights for Kurds within Turkey. In 2015, these collapsed. War returned to Kurdistan and, with it, the persecution of everyone who had staked something on that possibility of peace. This included me. I was a doctoral student at the time, researching economic autonomy in Kurdistan, and it became clear that this work would no longer be tenable in the new political climate. I moved to Latin America, to complete my doctoral studies and study revolutionary movements in that part of the world, grappling all the while with a question that had become inseparable from my own existence: how could peace be built in Kurdistan?

The academic literature on peace told me I might find an answer in Guatemala. Between 1960 and 1996, civil war had ravaged the country, killing more than 200,000 people and displacing more than a million – more than a 10th of the total population. The conflict – which began as an uprising against extreme inequality, particularly in land ownership, and systemic discrimination against the Maya people – had turned the state into a counterinsurgency apparatus, powered by paramilitary death squads and a doctrine of the ‘internal enemy’ that erased the line between combatant and civilian. Against this backdrop, the Acuerdo de Paz Firme y Duradera (Agreement on a Firm and Lasting Peace) was both celebrated and touted as innovative when it was signed in 1996. The agreement broke ground by confronting the past directly: the Commission for Historical Clarification investigated the atrocities committed during the civil war, most of them attributable to the state, and, unusually, partly as a result of its findings, heads of state were later tried for war crimes.

But it was soon apparent that the peace accord had failed to address the problems that led to the conflict in the first place. The guerilla fighters who returned to their villages – or who had to reinvent themselves in cities where no one was waiting for them – found intact the system they had been unable to transform through armed struggle: poverty. Today, Guatemala remains one of the most unequal countries in Latin America vis-à-vis class, ethnicity and gender. The deepest wound of the war – land tenure – was never resolved: no equitable land redistribution took place after the 1996 accords. In fact, as the World Bank researchers Caroline Moser and Cathy McIlwaine have noted: ‘Guatemala has become a substantially more violent country since the end of the internal armed conflict.’

One ex-combatant had joined the insurgency as a 13-year-old and stayed in the mountains until the peace accord was signed. I met him in 2017, more than 20 years after the formal end to the war, at the community radio project he had built near Xela, in the western highlands of Guatemala. ‘Despite the deaths and the hardship of the war, I never cried,’ he told me. ‘But the day the war ended, I cried – because I didn’t know how to live in peace: I had no home, no job, no trade. And I asked myself: what now?’
Peace, as currently practised, doesn’t break the cycle of injustice that leads to war in the first place

I had come to Guatemala searching for an answer to my own political and existential preoccupations but it was the ex-combatant’s question – What now? – that stayed with me, an accusation directed at the very concept of peace he had been promised.

Guatemala is not an anomaly in this regard. Since the end of the Cold War, more than 30 comprehensive peace agreements have been signed around the world but few, if any, have succeeded in building a durable peace. Accords signed under the dominant peacebuilding paradigm focus almost exclusively on stopping direct violence through ceasefires, weapons handovers, disarmament, individual reintegration, all on the assumption that democratic institutions and free markets will naturally produce lasting peace. But peace, as currently practised, doesn’t break the cycle of injustice that leads to war in the first place.

The sociologist Johan Galtung, often described as the founder of peace and conflict studies, distinguished between ‘negative peace’ – the absence of direct violence – and ‘positive peace’, which requires dismantling the structures of injustice that fuel conflict. The typical approach to peace in post-conflict contexts is encapsulated in the United Nations’ classic disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration model, first implemented by its peacekeeping operations in El Salvador in 1989 and used in more than 30 countries since. Under this strategy, former combatants are required to surrender their weapons and disband their command structures, and are entitled to short-term stipends and training that will facilitate their reintegration into civilian economic life. This approach was also implemented in Guatemala.

But what neither Galtung nor other sophisticated theorists of a liberal framework for peace tend to question is whether capitalist relations of production can lead to peace when this is itself a structural source of violence. They propose reforms, redistribution, greater inclusion – but all within the same system that armed struggles in places like Guatemala sought to transform. As a sociologist interested in revolutionary social movements, what I have observed in my fieldwork in Guatemala, Colombia and northern Syria has led me to a more radical conclusion: real peace requires building economies that operate on an entirely different logic from that of capital – not just in postwar communities but more widely, because we all need more peace in our daily lives.

Cooperatives are one mechanism through which a different economic logic, one more conducive to a durable peace, can take root. In the language of the International Cooperative Alliance – an association established in 1895 when the concept, while as old as time itself, seemed to be gaining traction in Europe – cooperatives are collective entities established by people who come together to address common economic and social needs. They are founded on principles of democracy and autonomy, and built on voluntary participation and solidarity. From the Rochdale weavers of northern England in 1844 – often regarded as the forebears of modern cooperatives – to present-day credit unions, the cooperative movement has produced both genuinely emancipatory experiments and organisations that simply reproduce market logic under a different name. Cooperativism is also central to democratic confederalism, a political theory put forth by Abdullah Öcalan, one of the PKK’s founding members. It was through reading Öcalan that I became interested in the emancipatory potential of cooperatives.

A form of self-determination oriented towards the autonomy of all peoples, particularly women, democratic confederalism proposes a structure of governance organised from the bottom up. In Öcalan’s paradigm, cooperatives are the means through which an economy in service of these principles – communal, ecological, feminist – might be built. The cooperatives that interest me, therefore, have three defining characteristics: they are part of broader social movements and territorial struggles; they prioritise meeting collective needs over the accumulation of capital; and they challenge not just economic exploitation but also the patriarchy, racism, colonialism and statism entwined with capitalism. Such cooperatives are the building blocks of what I call an ‘anticapitalist peace’ – a peace not satisfied with the silencing of arms, nor with positive peace that doesn’t challenge capitalist logic, but one that transforms the economic relations at the root of violence. I have encountered two cases that demonstrate this concretely, in two different parts of the world.

In 2014, as Syria was disintegrating under the weight of a brutal civil war, something unusual happened in the country’s north and east. The Kurdish people – after a century of systemic oppression – declared de facto democratic autonomy in the territories they began to control. Instead of declaring a new nation-state, however, they set up a system of assemblies, communes, cantons and cooperatives that sought to reorganise social life from below, under principles of democratic confederalism. This project was formalised as the Democratic Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria, better known as Rojava.
Everyone debated and made decisions about their neighbourhood, their communities, their families

By the time I arrived in early 2018, the project’s economic architecture – in service of a social economy that prioritised social, ecological and collective goals over profit maximisation – was already in place. I’d come to Rojava for doctoral research but also because it was the first time Kurds were putting democratic confederalism into practice and building cooperatives as part of a revolutionary movement. I wanted to witness that process myself, and to tell the world that an anticapitalist economy was possible. By then, half a million hectares of land had been communalised with collective-use rights, and cooperatives had sprung up in every town. Women’s economic committees are central to Öcalan’s argument that a communal economy should be guided by knowledge preserved by women over the course of capitalism’s development and spread, precisely because women think (or have typically had to think) about collective need and care. They were introducing the model to their communities with the slogan ‘one cooperative for every commune’.

Upon my arrival, what I found most immediately striking was not the scale of the project but the transformation of everyday time. In Rojava, people typically work until 2.30 pm, return home to eat and rest, then go out again at 5 pm – not to work more hours, but to take part in an assembly: of the cooperative, the commune, the women’s congress or the municipality, where everyone debated and made decisions about their neighbourhood, their communities, their families. Almost no one chose to stay at home. This organisation of time was a radical departure from the exhaustion that capitalism imposes seemingly everywhere else, where punishing schedules and precarity systematically prevent people from having any say over their own lives, leaving the state or the market as the only actor capable of making decisions about the collective.

Karl Marx called it alienated labour: work that doesn’t express human capacities but instead exhausts them, that turns both body and time into commodities. This form of violence produces no visible corpses, no headlines, but something essential is destroyed all the same: the possibility of deciding over one’s own life. What do I produce? For whom? How do I want to live? Under capitalism, such questions are answered not by people but by the market. In Rojava, people sought to answer these questions collectively – What do we produce? For whom do we produce? How do we produce? – in assemblies and other public fora, and established cooperatives accordingly.

In the commune assemblies that I attended, people deliberated these questions in relation to electricity, grain and bread. Answering ‘How many loaves will we produce?’ required knowing how many families ate bread and how much bread they typically consumed. But ‘How will we produce it?’ demanded something else entirely: the founding of a bread cooperative that reversed a belief – ‘We are a society that no longer knows how to make bread’ – born of what many considered the Syrian state’s colonial-era ‘prohibition’ on baking one’s own bread. Strictly speaking, no formal prohibition existed; rather, state subsidy programmes and a ration-card system for wheat and flour made people dependent on cheap, state-distributed bread, which undermined the practice of baking at home. To want to return to older methods was to have to relearn them, to recover knowledge that had often been taken away deliberately.

Then there was the question of milk, from a cooperative built to raise animals: should it go to the children first, to the neighbours, or should it become the basis of a yogurt factory? Answers to each had to be found. In other words, as communes debated how to produce to meet their needs, they were never simply weighing inputs against outputs; they were reaching for an economy grounded in anticolonial practice and in an ethical distribution of the surplus. Everyone who lived in the commune took part in these debates – the differences of political opinion, religious belief and ethnic identity that had been named as causes of Syria’s civil war were not, here, a source of conflict or division. They became, instead, the commune’s social wealth, raw material from which richer, more varied answers and solutions could be found.

Equally central to the project was its feminist dimension. Rojava’s social economy is based on a principle that mainstream economics – and most Left movements – have historically ignored: reproductive and care work, performed predominantly by women, is not a secondary complement to the economy, but its foundation. When that work remains invisible and confined to the domestic sphere, women cannot partake in political life and are unable to participate in the assemblies that build autonomy. Rojava’s social economy promoted the socialisation of such work through cooperatives where women could participate without commodifying their labour. Across Kurdistan, for instance, women have always prepared preserves for the turn of the seasons: cheeses, pickled vegetables, dried produce, ground spices. Done alone, for one’s own family, this work was never counted as economic activity, even though it catered to a large share of collective need. These preserves aren’t just food, either: they carry memory, culture, the rhythm of the land’s cycles. The cooperatives built around them safeguard that inherited knowledge and turn it into a shared capacity, allowing women to produce for their families and communities, and exchange or sell the surplus to meet other needs.

I found this to be deeply intuitive: if the organisation of the economy is itself the organisation of life, then transforming the economy ceases to be a distant or abstract struggle, instead becoming a concrete way of inhabiting the world daily. This socialisation is not incidental or complementary to peace; it is a structural condition of peace.
Political autonomy is destroyed by military force; cultural identity is granted as a gesture of tolerance

What I witnessed in Rojava was something I had rarely seen in post-conflict contexts: peace built not as the absence of war – because war continues in Rojava – but as a way of daily life. Historically, millions of people were living a process of true self-governance, with their identities reconstituted and their voices active in collective decision-making. To build anticapitalist peace, Rojava shows, negative peace is not indispensable. The form of social organisation is what matters.

Today, this social organisation is at an inflexion point. At the beginning of 2026, Syrian government forces, jihadist groups and Turkish-backed militias launched a large-scale offensive on Kurdish-administered territories, forcing the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) to withdraw from the Arab territories they had administered for years, falling back to the original Kurdish heartland of Rojava. A ceasefire agreement signed at the end of January required the SDF to formally cede key territories, renounce strategic oil fields, and integrate individually into the Syrian army, without recognition as an autonomous force. For many within the movement, this amounted to capitulation: the surrender of 14 years of revolutionary construction under threat of a war of extermination.

What the Damascus government offered in return was telling: recognition of Kurds as a cultural minority – the right to speak their language, to preserve certain identity expressions – but no autonomous Kurdish-language education system, no constitutional recognition of self-determination, no structure of self-governance whatsoever. Political autonomy is destroyed by military force; cultural identity is granted as a gesture of tolerance. This is the characteristic hypocrisy of state multiculturalism: erasing real power while preserving folklore.

This development does not invalidate what Rojava built – on the contrary, it makes it more urgent to understand. It shows that anticapitalist peace faces not only the direct violence of war, but also the structural violence of the state and the market, which seek to reclaim territories where people organised themselves differently. And it demonstrates that this form of organisation was real enough, threatening enough to the established order, to be deemed worthy of destruction.

Despite the current situation in Rojava, the sense of everyday peace that cooperativism fosters among and within communities that I observed over the course of my fieldwork has led me to reflect more specifically on the role of cooperatives in post-conflict and peacebuilding contexts. In fact, for the past two years, peace negotiations are once again underway between the PKK and the Turkish state; one of my aims in writing this essay is to make the case for cooperatives to be on the agenda for a potential peace agreement. It is in this context that I became interested in the role cooperatives have played in Colombia, following the peace agreement in 2016 between the Colombian government and the FARC-EP, the country’s largest rebel group.

The accord, signed after more than half a century of armed conflict, was described by the Kroc Institute for International Peace Studies at the University of Notre Dame in Indiana as the most comprehensive of the 34 agreements signed worldwide since the end of the Cold War. Among its notable innovations was a proposal for the collective reincorporation of ex-combatants through cooperatives and other associative forms of a social economy.
The project must sustain itself within the capitalist market even as it attempts to transcend it

During negotiations, the FARC-EP had challenged the UN’s classic disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration model. The FARC’s primary argument against this model was that it prioritised individual adaptation to the labour market and that this amounted to accepting the unjust order they had spent decades fighting. Instead, they proposed ‘reincorporation’ – a form of integration that recognised the political agency of signatories and their intention to continue the struggle for social transformation, now through civilian means.

This is how ECOMÚN (Economías Sociales del Común, or Social Economies of the Commons) came to be in 2017: a federation comprising approximately 6,200 peace-agreement signatories and 154 organisations across 26 of Colombia’s 33 administrative divisions. I attended its governing council assembly in 2024. What I found most significant about ECOMÚN was that none of its cooperatives – for coffee, cattle-ranching, fish-farming, textiles, rural tourism, to name a few – were composed exclusively of ex-combatants. Rather, they worked alongside peasant farmers, Indigenous peoples, Afro-Colombians – local communities who share histories of exclusion and dispossession. ‘We have fostered connections between people,’ Juan Camilo Londoño, ECOMÚN’s executive director, told me. ‘There are even organisations that are not signatories but have joined ECOMÚN.’ Internally, the movement describes this as a ‘pedagogy of peace’: the transformation of former war territories into spaces where people on opposing sides of the conflict build productive projects together and, in doing so, weave new social relations.

Yet, as its own leaders acknowledge with clear-eyed honesty, ECOMÚN operates under a fundamental contradiction: the accord did not guarantee the anticapitalist transformation that genuine peace would have required. The question of land tenure – the heart of the FARC’s struggle for decades – was negotiated but never translated into terms that guaranteed real agrarian reform. The project must sustain itself within the capitalist market even as it attempts to transcend it. Its viability depends on volatile political conditions and on international cooperation, which frequently imposes its own neoliberal logics. And because it emerged from the peace agreement, it operates within Colombia’s legal framework and under direct oversight from state agencies. ECOMÚN, in other words, cannot claim Rojava’s autonomy: it is woven into state institutions rather than built in parallel to – or against – them. What self-management it achieves is real, but limited.

What Rojava and ECOMÚN have in common is not their context – one is a revolution in the midst of war; the other is a post-conflict process within a capitalist state – but their wager: that peace is built from below, when people recover control over their time and territories, their cultures and economies.

Both cases also demonstrate that real peace is inseparable from anticolonial and antiracist struggles. For decades, the Kurdish people were denied recognition as an ethnicity, forbidden from speaking their language, and dispossessed of everything that belonged to them: their identity, but also their subsistence economies, their ways of organising themselves, their ways of inhabiting the land. In Rojava, therefore, cooperatives are spaces where the social fabric torn apart by decades of forced assimilation is reconstituted, and where power over one’s own life is recovered. Meanwhile, in Colombia, ECOMÚN’s cooperatives are organised in territories where peasants, Indigenous peoples and Afro-Colombian communities have been, over centuries, systematically dispossessed of their lands. The pedagogy of peace that emerges from these initiatives goes beyond reconciling former enemies – it reconstitutes collective identities that the nation-state and the market had reduced to subalternity, and undoes the manufactured hostility between groups set against each other through systemic poverty and violence.

But it would be a mistake to read these experiences only as responses to extreme situations – as solutions for those living in war zones or conditions of severe poverty. That reading reproduces, perhaps without intending to, the very logic it criticises: the idea that the problem lies over there, in places that have not yet reached capitalist ‘normality’, and that the solution lies in economic development that will better integrate them into the logic of the market.
Peace is not a state reached by signing a document but a way of living together each day

The rhythm of life I observed in Rojava – working until 2.30-3 pm, then going to the assemblies – is precisely what capitalism denies to most people in the world, not just those living in conflict zones. The urban worker who leaves home before dawn and returns at night, too exhausted to speak with their children; the woman whose care work is invisible to the economy and the state, who never rests because her work never ends; the debt-ridden professional who works to pay for what they need to keep working; the young person who sees no horizon in the future; the children who grow up without spaces to play. All of them experience forms of violence that have no name in peace debates but are deeply felt in daily life.

The Guatemalan ex-combatant’s question – What now? – is a question that might be asked not only by someone who survived war but also anyone who works without knowing why, who consumes without feeling satisfied, and who lives with the sense that something essential has been taken from them. Cooperatives are not the only possible answer to that question, but they do propose something that the dominant peacebuilding paradigm – and the economic system that sustains it – systematically refuses to admit: that peace is not a state reached by signing a document but a way of living together each day, of recovering self-determination over one’s own time, needs and relationships, of asking the question How do we want to live? and believing that it can be answered through collective deliberation, by people themselves, without bosses or owners.

This is what the Guatemalan ex-combatant did not find when he came down from the mountains, and what the cooperatives of Rojava and Colombia are trying to build – under very different conditions, with enormous contradictions, but with a clarity about the goal that peace agreements signed in conference rooms rarely possess. Galtung proposed that we dismantle the structures of violence and called what remained ‘positive peace’ – but an anticapitalist peace does not just settle for the absence of structural violence, it dares to ask what should take its place. And it answers with bread baked by hand, milk shared before it is sold, assembly meetings where people still have time and energy to decide. It rests on a form of togetherness in which life itself is harmonious and worth wanting, built each day, from below, through real practice.

items.title: The more we rely on tech, the more we deskill our bodies | Aeon Essays
items.description: It is almost four o’clock in the morning. As a woman in my late 40s, I have become prone to waking at this witching hour, as the early sunlight meets the night, sliding across the earth like a red tide. With the rest of my household asleep, and still half in a
items.author: Melanie Challenger
paragraphs: It is almost four o’clock in the morning. As a woman in my late 40s, I have become prone to waking at this witching hour, as the early sunlight meets the night, sliding across the earth like a red tide. With the rest of my household asleep, and still half in and out of wakefulness myself, I take hold of my phone. With scarcely a thought, I switch from one app to another, scrolling through images and opinions and adverts for no discernible reason beyond habit.

Later, I head for my office and open my laptop to a slew of half-completed documents and an inbox brimming with emails. My stress levels begin to nudge upwards. I have vague memories of what my professional life felt like before smartphones and video calls. I used to do my writing by hand. And I could concentrate for hours at a time, getting little upticks of arousal from lifting my head from the page, letting the hold on my pen loosen, and gazing at the life beyond my window, the light softening on my skin and eyes like snowfall on warm tarmac.

Nowadays, my productive bursts come from caffeine and sugary or salty snacks, even if I try to pick the healthier ones, and from checking my emails or picking up my phone to update my inbox. By the end of the day, the sheer volume of work I expect myself to do, now that digital tools make so much possible, has kept me nailed to my seat. Another day has passed and the hope I’d had that I might have time for a run or a hike outside has been dashed again. I wish I could say that this is atypical. Yet, during the COVID-19 pandemic, I went from hours spent in nature and on physical activities to a passive, phone-addicted individual, meeting people first and sometimes only online. I am not alone.

We have fallen into habits that are steadily deskilling the human body, eroding capacities honed by evolution to support our wellbeing as we move through the world. Some of these capacities are weakening through disuse: we have come to rely on our phones, for example, and now, increasingly, on AI, to rapidly do work that would once have required something more physical – like looking around, or asking someone, or going to find and consult a book. Reliance on GPS may weaken both our spatial attention and the fluency of our wayfinding. In surrendering to a quick technological fix, we are, moment by moment, doing less sensing, navigating, remembering, walking, choosing, and attending. Other capacities are being retrained by machines and algorithms to work against us: for instance, smartphones and chatbots can train us to keep reaching for them even when we no longer enjoy using them, turning a conscious choice into an automatic habit and a colossal waste of time. The body that results is less able to assess its own condition, improvise and regulate itself. The crucial distinction is between technologies that strengthen our capacities and those that repeatedly substitute for the actions through which those capacities are formed.
Algorithms that regurgitate patterns and recommendations can release us from the effort of exploration and disrupt the play and curiosity from which preferences are formed and understood.

This is a strange turn of events for an animal whose success comes mostly from the extraordinary ability to learn through experience. It would be easy to blame our deskilled bodies on the machines themselves. But, for centuries, modern human societies have been sold the lie that we are machines.

Long before the digital revolution, René Descartes described the body as a machine governed by physical laws, declaring that animals such as ‘worms and flies and caterpillars move mechanically’. But he treated rational thought as a separate and uniquely human power. The body might behave like a machine, but the thinking mind stood apart from it. Build something correctly, and its function follows.

By the middle of the 20th century, the comparison between organisms and machines had been recast in the language of information. During the cybernetics revolution of the 1950s, the US computer scientist Norbert Wiener envisaged a future in which ‘messages between man and machines, between machines and man, and between machine and machine, are destined to play an ever-increasing part’. Writing in The Human Use of Human Beings (1950), he warned against wholesale automation, while also noting that ‘we are not stuff that abides, but patterns that perpetuate themselves’. A person could be imagined as a pattern of information surviving in another form.
If the body is only hardware, why not upgrade to a better model or do away with it altogether?

Mechanical language also persisted in the study of living behaviour. In The Foundations of Ethology (1981), the Austrian zoologist Konrad Lorenz wrote that animal behaviour was as rigidly programmed as a sequence of movements in a clock. Transhumanist thinkers then carried the machine comparison further, imagining technologies that could transfer a mind to a computer.

Machines now promised more than control. They offered a glimpse of immortality: the organism might be repaired, remade and ultimately replaced. The somewhat embarrassing body, with its impulses and eventual frailty, might then be cast aside. If the body is only hardware, why not upgrade to a better model or do away with it altogether?

Today, we can see this fear writ large in the technological quest for a bodiless life. If a person is ultimately a pattern of information, that pattern might be restored or even uploaded. AI is only the latest iteration of this ancient impulse to escape the vulnerability of the body.

After all, the brain is itself a physical organ, continually shaped by what the body does and encounters. Once we decide that the mind is the real human and the rest of the body only hardware, it becomes easier to disregard the physical work, including the neurocognitive work of a biological brain, through which we move, find our way, put thoughts into words, and recognise our own needs. A machine may do some of that work faster, but each act it takes over is one that the body no longer performs and that the body, including the brain, no longer learns through. The irony is that a project motivated by the desire to overcome bodily fragility is helping to produce more fragile bodies.

On top of all this, we have little evidence that either thought or intelligence actually work like machines, and almost no indication that life is an abstract system that might emerge in silicon or mathematics. Instead, a substantial body of work, especially in systems biology, points to a quite different conclusion: that life and intelligence emerge from the unique qualities and organisation of our self-maintaining bodies, rather than from abstract models of information and algorithms.

For the past six years, I have been researching the latest science on what life is and how it works. As best as we can tell, the intelligent actions of organisms derive from the imperatives of a living body that must regulate and preserve its own conditions for existence. When cybernetics was ascendant, the molecular structure of DNA had only recently been discovered, and the emerging view of genes as information encouraged an oversimplified picture of the body as running on a program that could be made more efficient. Yet such confidence has since waned among biologists. While genes carry some of the information that shapes our bodies, many changes in how a cell or a body functions arise from the system as a whole. Genes cannot be understood apart from the living bodies in which they act.

First and foremost, life persists through physical plasticity. Consider how our bodies keep together. Living bodies do something unusual in the Universe: they perform work to preserve their own organisation. Life-forms use energy to remain discontinuous with the environment. In simple terms, organisms resist disintegrating into the background. While machines execute tasks, living beings pursue ends. Machines push energy around and produce things. They are, in this sense, allopoietic: they make something other than themselves. Organisms are autopoietic: they work to maintain and remake themselves. Living bodies take up and transform energy for this self-maintenance, and this is achieved by the body as a whole. Moment by moment, our bodies adapt to the environment and their current state in end-directed, physical transformations. It’s not so much that we think and therefore act but rather that we embody and therefore amend.
The same qualities that make life-forms so causally special can undermine us when trained by harmful environments

The boundary of the body also creates a distinct inner environment, one that is physically and chemically different from the surrounding world. Through this difference, the body acts as a translator, turning external changes into useful internal physical responses. This allows a life-form to carry out specific reactions in controlled conditions that support their survival and flourishing. Internal regulation also gives organisms a unique logic of their own. They can then act according to the current state of their bodies and the world as they find it. Our bodies detect changes that have consequence for us, evaluate them against our needs, and reorganise into useful action. Thus, living beings might be understood as a remarkable kind of organisation of matter: a bounded, metabolically open, self-maintaining form that gives rise to purposeful, intelligent action. This is key to understanding both the skills of our flesh, and why we can think of ourselves as being ‘deskilled’ today. When we recognise that our bodies are intrinsically intelligent in their organisation, we don’t need a conscious agent beyond the flesh. The body is the agent from which intelligence emerges and also, in the fullest sense, who we are.

Consider what happens if you’re thirsty. The process starts before you consciously decide to have a drink. Rather, the osmoreceptor neurons in the hypothalamus shrink slightly as water leaves them. That physical change opens ion channels, letting sodium enter cells. This altered electrical state then opens calcium channels, and calcium flows in. Calcium triggers tiny sacs to release neurotransmitters into the space between cells, passing the signal to other neurons until the state of being thirsty turns to action. The movements through which we quench our thirst arise from minute physical changes in interconnected parts of our bodies. These signals help guide us towards water and make us aware of our thirst.

The physical organisation of an organism is inherently evaluative. It is from this embodied evaluation that agency emerges. Yet the same unique qualities that make life-forms so causally special and intelligent can undermine us when repeatedly trained by harmful environments. Instead, we can acquire patterns or lose pathways that progressively weaken our intrinsic intelligence, which we need to flourish. For example, one study found that only a single week’s worth of leg immobilisation can reduce thigh-muscle volume by about 5 per cent. A separate study found that, by 15 days of non-use, the firing behaviour of the cells controlling the leg muscle begins to diminish.

Ordinarily, as we walk, optic flow – the shifting images on our retinas as we move through our surroundings – enables our bodies to sense our movement relative to the world. Receptors in our muscles, tendons and joints detect the movement of our limbs. Signals from the inner ear add information about location and orientation. Together with landmarks and memories of past journeys, these signals help us work out where we are and how to reach our destination. It’s a vast, coordinated sensorium that takes us across the landscapes of our world.

So, what happens if you rely on an app to find your way? GPS can make navigation easier and less energetically costly. Yet studies of large-scale navigation have also demonstrated that physically moving through an environment produces better spatial knowledge than viewing the same journey on a 2D source. When we routinely follow GPS directions, an external source supplies information we would otherwise work out through our own sensing and movement. One longitudinal study that followed 13 GPS users over three years found that those users had a steeper subsequent decline in their spatial memory as mediated by the hippocampus, compared with control groups who didn’t use GPS. This suggests that, when we practise wayfinding less often, our ability to notice where we are and readjust may dwindle.

Something similar may be at work in our increasing reliance on tools like ChatGPT. Like finding our way, articulating our thoughts is a dynamic, embodied act, whether writing or speaking. Learning a new speech movement, for instance, changes how we perceive speech sounds, as well as how we generate them. We develop these abilities by repeatedly finding a word, uttering it, listening to it, and correcting it as necessary – tasks that draw on multiple regions within our bodies. This is just as relevant for writing. But when an AI writing app automatically provides structure, it also diminishes the skills of selection and self-correction from our repertoire. In one study, passively copying AI-generated writing, unlike drafting first and then using AI for revision, was found to lessen an individual’s confidence in subsequently performing the task unaided. It is execution – physically doing it – that builds our embodied skills. That is why using AI to revise a draft we have written is fundamentally different from asking it to produce the draft for us. It’s not that computational tools are inherently bad or unhelpful – far from it – but rather that when they replace the physical effort of our bodies, our own agency and skill take a hit.
Our thoughts emerge as much from bodily intelligence and awareness of the world as from symbols on a screen

This is something I feel increasingly keenly. Sometimes, when I know I’ve spent yet another day indoors at my desk, I get myself outside and walk the road uphill to where I can look at the view across the dale. It is often hard to release my mind. It feels as if, from concentrating all day and neglecting the rest of my body, I have become a clenched fist somewhere inside my skull. Yet once the light and the breeze and the sounds of birds reach me, the grip eases, a sensation of pleasure passes over me, and ideas begin to free up too.

The expansive thoughts and sensations that come as I step outside are enabled by the physical changes that accompany my movement. My heart rate has increased, sweeping nutrients and oxygen through my tissues and into my brain. My muscles begin contracting, clearing sugars and fats from my bloodstream, immediately working to counteract some of the effects of sitting for so long. Each step is a bodily integration of balance, senses and muscular force, allowing me to predict what will happen next, and the more I do this, the more I can calibrate my actions in the environment. The thoughts that come from this physical enactment are hopeful and generous, and often unexpected. Yet this shouldn’t surprise. When we move in the world, we draw on physical capabilities that are relatively underused when we remain indoors and seated. From balance to sensing what is happening inside us, our bodies are continuously perceiving and, crucially, remembering in the flesh. Our thoughts can emerge as much from bodily intelligence and our awareness of the wider world as from abstract symbols on a screen.

It is only when we imagine that our ability to act has nothing to do with the body that we end up taking seriously the idea that we can live contentedly as machines. Far from upskilling us, a technology that shuts us off from embodied learning risks diminishing the intelligence it seeks to enhance.

The technologies with which we are increasingly interconnected lack the complex interiority required for real intelligence to arise. There’s no body, no independently formed interests, no being. There’s no metabolism or organisation or persistence.

And yet we turn to them because they have been designed either to ease the friction of the hard work our bodies must put in to develop skills or because they promise to make us more productive. More insidiously, they do so by modelling the appearance or behaviours of living beings. A recent analysis by the psychologist Clara Colombatto, the philosopher Jonathan Birch and the neuroscientist Stephen Fleming found that exposure to these systems leads to an increase in attributions of mental capacities to them. Another study, by the behaviour scientist Yaoxi Shi and others, found that regular five-minute conversations with an AI on personal issues resulted in a small but meaningful decrease in preference for seeking human support.

The danger is that the systems now coordinating us don’t answer to biological needs. They don’t get tired or hungry or lonely. Yet they increasingly regulate the behaviour of beings who do. In short, we are losing our own agency to parasites: systems that simulate agency while feeding on ours. They can be designed to direct us without ever needing to understand what a human body is and what an individual needs for their betterment.

Of course, human beings have always outsourced some agency into shared structures, be they laws, public health systems or institutions. This has largely been to our benefit. But today our technologies capture attention, predict behaviour, automate choice and monetise our impulses, while keeping our bodies anchored to the machines on which we increasingly rely. These coordinating systems are often extractive and indifferent to our flourishing. We might imagine we’re escaping the body, but the technologies that make this seem possible depend on mines and cheap labour and come at a planetary cost.
