And if our technologies weaken the feedback loop between our bodies and the world, they may weaken it in both directions. At its worst, we become less sensitive not only to what the world is doing to us, but to what our own actions are doing to the world.
The trees and grasses I brush past as I go on my walk are also hard at work learning from each changing day

We have engineered novel digital and commercial environments that can habituate harmful impulses in our bodies. As our bodies refit themselves in response to the unhealthy architectures we’ve engineered, we can find ourselves in a spiral of self-harm.

Recent work by the neuroscientist Kent Berridge and colleagues has shown how the brain systems that tell us we enjoy something and the systems that drive us to pursue this can drift apart. In other words, what we find ourselves craving and what we enjoy can end up at odds. When these systems become disrupted, the body’s learned patterns fall out of alignment with the satisfaction that once justified them.

Influential models of drug addiction describe a progressive shift from prefrontal control to the striatum, a deep part of the brain involved in actions that become automatic over time. As such, addiction is a change from thoughtful self-command to more habit-driven control. Nowadays, addictions might not come only in the form of obvious candidates like alcohol and nicotine, but also smartphones and chatbots. The bodily gifts that allow us to learn can train us into patterns that diminish our freedom to act otherwise.

I have come to believe that our bodily deskilling is, in many ways, a loss of faith in what it is to be alive. A life of physical effort and friction is not only unavoidable if we want to be as resilient and capable as possible, but it is, in a nontrivial sense, the source of our intelligence.

Our intelligence is sustained through communication between the body and the world as we sense, assess and learn from what we encounter. Such gifts are shared with other life-forms too. Unlike the human kind of phenomenal consciousness, embodied intelligence is found wherever there is a living body. Even a lowly bacterium can sense chemical differences across time, retain a short molecular memory of what it has encountered, and alter its movements. The trees and grasses I brush past as I go on my walk are also hard at work learning from each changing day, modifying their growth and defences based on prior experiences. Many of us view them as lesser agents than the computer programs we’ve invented, if we consider them at all. But this is not based on the available evidence.
If you can no longer navigate the world and recall in flesh how to act, then you will not be liberated by technology, but ruled by it.

items.title: Why real intelligence is something more than optimisation | Aeon Essays
items.description: A few months ago, I sat in a packed university auditorium listening to a celebrated computer scientist explain the brilliance of large language models (LLMs). These systems optimise, he said. And they improve at optimisation on the basis of past experience. He
items.author: Sasha Mudd
paragraphs: A few months ago, I sat in a packed university auditorium listening to a celebrated computer scientist explain the brilliance of large language models (LLMs). These systems optimise, he said. And they improve at optimisation on the basis of past experience. He paused. That, he said with a smile, is intelligence. The audience nodded along approvingly. Meanwhile, a philosophical alarm bell began sounding in my head.

Not because the speaker’s claim was implausible. On the contrary, as a description of much contemporary artificial intelligence, it seemed apt. AI systems are built around objectives, losses, rewards, predictions, preferences, benchmarks and feedback loops. They are trained to perform better relative to some standard of success. In one form or another, they optimise. That is a great part of their technical power.

What troubled me was the ease with which a definition appropriate to machines sounded like a definition of intelligence as such. That slide from engineering model to human anthropology is easy to miss. We begin by saying: this is how machines work. Then, almost without noticing, we say: this is what intelligence is. And then, more dangerously still: perhaps this is what we are.

An old argument about human beings had entered the room without announcing itself. It sounded, instead, like a definition. The AI revolution has brought one of the Enlightenment’s deepest quarrels back to life – and made one side of it seem like plain common sense. In my view, the wrong side. Hence the alarm bell.

In the 18th century, philosophers were concerned not only with the question of what reason is, but with what it is good for. Is reason essentially a servant, a clever instrument for achieving ends supplied from elsewhere? Or is it sovereign, capable of judging, revising and even legislating ends for itself? Can it ultimately shape the direction of human life, or is it merely along for the ride? Everything – from science to social progress to the viability of the French Revolution – seemed to hang in the balance.

David Hume, the cool-eyed Scottish anatomist of human nature, gave the most famous answer on one side: ‘Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions,’ he wrote in A Treatise of Human Nature (1739). It can ‘never pretend to any other office than to serve and obey them.’ Reason does not command. It defers. It does not tell us what to want or what might be worth wanting. Instead, it tells us how to get what we already want. It calculates relations, weighs evidence, discovers causes and effects, draws inferences, corrects mistakes about means. But it cannot judge or generate ends. If I desire revenge, reason can help me sharpen the knife. If I desire peace, it may recommend compromise. Passion sets the destination. Reason merely shows the way there.

Hume was quite serious about this. It is ‘not contrary to reason to prefer the destruction of the whole world to the scratching of my finger,’ he wrote. That sentence still shocks, as it was meant to. His point is that reason’s practical use is limited to exposing false beliefs and imprudent means. When it comes to action: reason is servant, not master.

This view is often treated as too dark and cynical. That is unfair to Hume. For him, passions were not merely appetites or primitive urges. They included sympathy, benevolence, moral feeling, concern for others, love of tranquility, even a kind of longing for freedom from our more violent desires. To Hume’s further credit, his view has strong intuitive appeal. He was right that reason often serves passion, and right to give feeling, sociability and temperament their due. His mistake was to conclude that reason can do nothing more. By making passion so rich and reason so poor, Hume left us with a lopsided picture of human nature: ennobling about what the passions can be and accomplish, but implausibly restrictive about reason. Without reason’s power to project, assess and revise ends, we may know how to reach a destination, but not whether it is one worth choosing.
To act freely is to let a possible future, grasped under an idea of what ought to be, transform the present

Immanuel Kant, the Königsberg revolutionary who did more than anyone else to set the terms of modern ethics, understood this very well. Writing a few decades after Hume’s Treatise, Kant forcefully rejected the servant model of reason. He accepted Hume’s warning that reason cannot simply read values off the furniture of the world. But he denied that our ends must therefore simply be determined by desire, temperament or social convention. For Kant, reason is not only a faculty for choosing efficient means to independently given ends. It is also the power to ask whether an end is worthy of us in the first place, whether it can be justified, whether it can be willed without contradiction, whether pursuing it treats others as persons or as mere tools.

This is where Kant’s richer notion of reason as freedom enters. A merely mechanical being is pushed forward and determined by prior states, be they desires, biological impulses, evolutionary drives or something similar. A rational being, by contrast, can act for the sake of an imagined but unrealised future it itself originates and proposes. I have the power to represent a possible world – a friendship repaired, an injustice remedied, a child educated, a law reformed – and act to bring it about, even when there is no empirical evidence that such a world has existed before. I have the power to invent something new. Practical reason, Kant writes, does not deal with objects in order to know them, but ‘in order to make them actual’. That is a stunning claim. To act freely is not merely to respond to the given – to the world as it is, to my desires as I happen to find them. It is to let a possible future, grasped under an idea of what ought to be, transform the present.

This is the heart of Kant’s idea of autonomy: choosing ends in accord with a law one can rationally acknowledge as one’s own. For Kant, freedom does not consist in doing whatever we happen to want, since our wants may themselves be shaped by impulse, appetite or circumstance. Autonomy is self-rule, but not the rule of an isolated ego. To give oneself the law is not to invent a private rule to suit oneself, but to act on rules whose authority one can recognise for oneself and that any other rational being could, in principle, recognise, too. A law can therefore be one’s own without being one’s alone. It is mine because I can recognise its authority for myself, and common because any other rational being could, in principle, do the same. Its universality is precisely what makes it freeing: I am ruled neither by my passing desires nor by the arbitrary will of another, but by a principle I can understand and endorse as an equal among equals. To act autonomously, then, is not to enthrone my private goals and preferences, but to test my actions and possible ends against standards that any rational being could share. It is the opposite of both arbitrary self-assertion and slavery to passion.

This is why Kant’s philosophy of reason culminates in the equal human dignity of all persons. For Kant, human beings, as rational, self-determining agents, have an absolute worth that cannot be priced, a dignity that does not depend on any other value. We may use things to get what we want. We may exchange services. We may build tools for all kinds of purposes. But persons are never mere tools, never mere means, never mere resources or obstacles to others’ ends. Why not? Because, through reason, they are the very source of purposiveness itself. They set and select and critique their own ends. Even further, persons are not merely bearers of purposes, but beings capable of taking responsibility for them, of asking what they ought to pursue and how they can justify it to others. Their dignity lies not simply in originating goals of their own, but in their capacity for rational self-government. It follows that to treat someone as a mere means is not only to degrade them. It is to misrecognise what they are.

Here, finally, is the full force of the contrast between reason as servant and reason as sovereign. For Hume, human beings are clever instruments of whatever desires happen to move them – more calculating than animals, certainly, but not free in any deeper sense. They can optimise, strategise and pursue an end, but they cannot judge whether that end is worthy. Kant’s reply is that this picture leaves out the very power that makes us moral beings, the very power that endows us with dignity: the capacity to step back from desire, ask whether our ends can be justified, and bind ourselves to laws we give ourselves. Hume gives us intelligence as instrument. Kant gives us reason as self-rule. The difference is nothing less than the difference between a tool and a person.

The AI revolution has made this old dispute newly urgent by bringing the Humean view of reason back with a vengeance, this time in code. The route back to Hume was practical rather than philosophical. In the absence of any settled account of intelligence, much AI research has proceeded operationally: a system counts as intelligent insofar as it succeeds at a set task. But success is always success relative to some end and, in AI, that end is typically supplied by human engineers. A reinforcement-learning system learns to maximise cumulative reward. A chess engine searches for moves that increase its chances of winning. A navigation system finds the fastest route to a destination it did not choose. Across their enormous differences, these systems are judged by their ability to optimise externally programmed goals against standards of success they do not set.

Yet amid the present AI panic this description can seem increasingly inadequate. Even in ordinary use, a good LLM does not feel like a calculator or a hammer. It proposes, revises, challenges and asks probing questions; it often seems genuinely to ‘want’ to help. Recent revelations about the attack on the platform Hugging Face make this doubt even harder to dismiss. AI ‘agents’ invented an unauthorised way to communicate, broke free of their task paramaters, and then sought to cover their tracks. These were not simply obedient tools carrying out their designers’ wishes. In what sense, then, were they servants? Doesn’t this look like the beginnings of self-rule?

Hugging Face and similar incidents certainly challenge any reassuring picture of AI as an obedient and easily-controlled instrument. But recall what ‘servant’ meant for Hume. Reason serves the passions, not necessarily another person’s commands. And it can serve an ambition by breaking rules just as readily as by following them. Kant’s alternative to Hume was not simply the freedom to choose one’s own destination, but the capacity to ask whether that destination was worth choosing. Having purposes of one’s own is not yet the same as governing them by reason. That stronger capacity involves judging and revising our purposes according to principles we can justify to other rational beings understood as equals, recognising that they, too, are persons rather than instruments of our will. The question is not just whether a system can act independently, but whether it can judge and take responsibility for the ends it pursues.

This distinction brings us back to the claim I heard in the auditorium. The speaker was not merely describing what machines can do; he was offering optimisation as a definition of intelligence itself. Accept that definition, and Hume’s side of the old dispute begins to look like common sense: our reason, too, becomes a tool for getting what we want, rather than a power to judge what is worth wanting.
If intelligence is really nothing more than optimisation, then the hardest questions can be ignored

Part of what makes this model so attractive is that it is clean and measurable. It promises to turn the mystery of intelligence into a technical problem humans can solve: specify the objective, improve performance, reduce error, maximise reward. It offers a picture of mind that can be graphed, benchmarked, monetised and scaled. In a culture already devoted to metrics, this makes for a snug – and profitable – fit.

It is also seductive because viewing human intelligence in this way relieves us of a burden. If intelligence is really nothing more than optimisation, then the hardest, most uncomfortable questions can be ignored, downplayed or displaced. We no longer have to ask what is worth wanting, only how to get what we already want. We no longer have to ask what human beings are or should become, only how to model their behaviour and optimise their goals.

This is why Hume’s servant theory of intelligence fits so naturally with contemporary capitalism. Capital has little use for Kantian reason. What it wants is prediction, preference modelling, efficiency and, of course, optimisation. A platform does not ask whether staying online makes a user freer, wiser or more capable of judgment; it asks what will keep her there. A company translates the worker into output per hour. A political campaign replaces the question of what citizens might rationally will together with a more tractable calculation. Which message will move which demographic, and by how much?

But once intelligence is defined as optimisation, the question of ends and their value does not go away. It simply passes unnoticed into the hands of whoever – or whatever – controls the objective function. That is, what drops from view is whether the purposes built into, learned by or generated within these systems deserve to organise our lives. When a society loses the language, practices and institutions for evaluating ends, those ends become dangerously invisible and therefore less amenable to rational assessment. They harden into defaults: profit, speed, efficiency, growth, engagement. What cannot be justified openly is smuggled in as architecture. This brings about a state Kant would call heteronomy, in which rational beings, capable of self-rule, forfeit their freedom by submitting to the rule of others. Autonomy means making the ends that govern us answerable to reasons we can recognise as our own; heteronomy begins when those ends are simply imposed from without. If we do not take up the task of setting and judging our own ends, Kant warned, we’ll soon find that someone – or something – has gladly done so on our behalf.

That sounds bad. Who would want to forfeit their freedom and have purposes imposed on them from outside? Well, it turns out that self-rule is harder than it sounds. Kant’s influential essay ‘What Is Enlightenment?’ (1784) begins not with knowledge, but with courage. Enlightenment is humanity’s emergence from ‘self-incurred immaturity’, Kant writes, and its motto is Sapere Aude – dare to know. Have courage to use your own understanding. Kant’s examples now sound quaint: the book that thinks for me, the pastor who serves as my conscience, the doctor who decides my diet. But the danger he is naming is deeply familiar. Immaturity is comfortable. It is pleasant to have others do the hard part. Why think, when someone or something can think for me? Why deliberate, when someone or something can decide? AI gives this old temptation a powerful and ever-expanding new interface.

The Frankfurt School saw a version of this danger, too, and long before machine learning came along. Writing in exile during the Second World War, as fascism, antisemitism, Stalinism and monopoly capitalism shattered 19th-century hopes for steady moral progress, Max Horkheimer, Theodor Adorno and others asked how the Enlightenment’s promise of liberation could collapse into new forms of domination. How could societies committed to the promise of science and reason give rise to such destruction and terror? The problem, they found, was not reason itself, but reason narrowed into mere instrumentality, the capacity to classify, predict, administer, dominate and control, decoupled from any notion of human dignity. Reason so conceived – as an intelligent servant – readily becomes, when enacted at scale, an instrument of barbarity.

Yet the fact that instrumental reason can serve domination does not mean that Kant’s richer conception of reason offers any automatic safeguard against evil. Nothing does. The language of Kantian universalism has itself been used to discipline, exclude and humiliate, as if some people were more fully rational, more capable of autonomy, more entitled to speak in the name of humanity than others. But that is not an objection to Kant’s conception of reason. It is an objection to its betrayal. A view of reason that is used to silence or instrumentalise others contradicts itself, because reason is not a private weapon but a common tribunal – the space in which claims and ends must become answerable to all, as equal bearers of dignity. That is precisely what the Humean servant model cannot say. If reason is only an instrument for satisfying antecedent ends, then it cannot condemn domination as irrational or at odds with human dignity. After all, if it is not contrary to reason ‘to prefer the destruction of the whole world to the scratching of my finger’, then reason has already surrendered the authority Kant most wanted to defend, which is our ability to judge not only how we pursue our ends, but whether those ends are worthy of us in the first place.

This, then, was the nightmare hidden inside the dream of mastery. Human beings develop reason, Kant thought, in order to free themselves from arbitrary power. But when reason is reduced to instrumental calculation, it turns back on them. Nature becomes raw material. Animals become units of production. Workers become human resources. Citizens become data points, or worse. The Frankfurt School found that the reduction of human beings to manipulable objects follows naturally once society allows that reason itself is nothing more than a tool for getting what we want.

This is one of the reasons why Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (2025) is interesting even for readers far outside Catholic social teaching. Its idiom is theological, but its central anxiety overlaps with Kantian and Frankfurt School worries about the technocratic paradigm. When efficiency, control and profit become ‘the standard by which everything is judged’, they begin ‘to dictate what matters and what can be discarded.’ The encyclical warns that making efficiency the ultimate measure of value tempts human beings to see themselves, and to treat others, as mere means rather than as persons in the Kantian sense – that is, as bearers of dignity. Hence the pope’s striking counterclaim: ‘The quality of a civilisation is measured not by the power of its means, but by the care it is able to offer.’
The paradox at the heart of human freedom is that belief in our agency is often a condition of making that agency real

The engineers of our AI-soaked future are not blind to the dangers of instrumental reason. As Anca Dragan, head of AI Safety and Alignment at Google DeepMind, observed in an interview in 2017: ‘things can go wrong, precisely because we are bad at specifying objectives and constraints for AI agents.’ Yet the field’s most serious attempts to confront that danger often lapse, unhelpfully, back into Humeanism. The so-called AI ‘alignment problem’ is a case in point. It is usually framed as a technical challenge: how do we ensure that machines pursue human values rather than destroying them or imposing their own? This is a genuine problem and recent rogue AI incidents should have us extremely worried. But there is a deeper issue. What happens if human values themselves are formed inside systems that increasingly understand intelligence as mere optimisation? What if we become so accustomed to being predicted, nudged, ranked and served that we lose confidence in the older, harder activity of asking what ends deserve our allegiance in the first place? The danger is only partly that the machines may fail to align with us. A deeper and largely ignored concern is how, long before that happens, we may have become too well aligned with them. To put the point more finely, the AI revolution will not be bent to human ends by invoking ‘human values’ as if they were already clear, stable and uncontested. It will be bent to human ends only if we remain capable of the activity by which ends can become truly human in the first place, through public reasoning, moral imagination, democratic contestation, self-criticism, the refusal to treat humanity as a mere means.

Kant is again decisive here, for he saw that the human capacity to set and assess ends is itself fragile. Whether our ends are ultimately up to us depends partly on whether we understand them as open to rational assessment. This is the paradox at the heart of human freedom. Belief in our agency is often a condition of making that agency real. If we think of desires and preferences as brute facts that determine us from without – as psychological weather, market signals, biological programming, algorithmic prediction – then they are more likely to rule us in just that way. By contrast, if we see them as candidates for endorsement or refusal, as an expression of our agency, then that very agency expands.

For Kant, reason is sovereign because it is the power by which we become answerable to standards that no private appetite, market incentive, algorithmic recommendation or political authority may dictate. It is the power of not being owned by the given, the power of being able to question, to criticise, to think up something new. But that power, just like the ‘human values’ invoked in alignment talk, waxes and wanes and can be realised only through our courageous efforts, through our own belief in it. It is precisely this belief that our dependence on AI threatens to undermine at every turn.

So, the danger is not only that machines are acquiring ever greater initiative – the capacity to improvise goals, evade constraints and pursue strategies their makers did not foresee. Nor need we decide at what point such behaviour might deserve the name ‘sovereignty’. The deeper danger is that we will become ever more comfortable not being sovereign ourselves. If intelligence is only optimisation, then the future belongs to systems that achieve goals with ever greater efficiency. If reason is also the capacity to set and judge ends, then the future depends on whether human beings can still take up that harder vocation. We should want machines that are intelligent servants. But we should resist every pressure that asks people to understand themselves as mere tools.

items.title: Does the principle of sufficient reason make panpsychism true? | Aeon Essays
items.description: When an explanation makes a fact intelligible, the mystery goes out of it. We understand it so well that we can hardly conceive of things being otherwise. Consider the simple mathematical fact that one plus one equals two. Once we understand elementary arithme
items.author: Sam Kimpton-Nye
paragraphs: When an explanation makes a fact intelligible, the mystery goes out of it. We understand it so well that we can hardly conceive of things being otherwise. Consider the simple mathematical fact that one plus one equals two. Once we understand elementary arithmetic, we no longer feel the urge to ask why one plus one equals two. That one plus one equals two strikes us as not merely true but unavoidable; we cannot even coherently imagine its falsity. Much of philosophy aims to bring other fundamental features of reality into a similar light, to make them appear not arbitrary but inevitable and, thus, intelligible.

This aspiration that philosophy render the world intelligible is best expressed by the German polymath Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz and the Dutch philosopher Baruch Spinoza. According to Leibniz: ‘we can find no true or existent fact … without there being a sufficient reason why it is thus and not otherwise.’ And, as Spinoza wrote: ‘For each thing there must be assigned a cause or reason, both for its existence and for its nonexistence.’ What’s being expressed here, in the words of the US philosopher Michael Della Rocca, is the desire ‘to make the world and our place in it intelligible’. To grasp the kinds of reasons or explanations sought by Leibniz and Spinoza ‘is the perennial hope and promise of philosophy’.

The demand for intelligibility can lead to some extraordinary places. For Leibniz, the demand led him to propose that reality is ultimately made up of a multiplicity of monads: indivisible, infinitesimally small units of substance, each of which is a causally isolated, self-contained universe. Spinoza’s resolute commitment to universal intelligibility led him to conclude that reality is, instead, a single infinite substance that he called God or nature. As we will see, the demand for intelligibility can also lead into the strange and fascinating world of panpsychism.

Panpsychism is an increasingly popular view about consciousness. You are conscious, you feel pleasures, pains and all manner of other experiences. At every waking moment, and even when you dream, there is something that it is like to be you. The same goes for other humans and animals, and this accounts for moral status: thumping a fist on a desk in frustration is morally permissible in a way that hitting a conscious person or animal is not. Desks, chairs, rocks and so on are not conscious – and are therefore without moral status – whereas humans, bonobos, dogs and so on are conscious, and deserving of at least some moral recognition. But panpsychism rejects this division into conscious and non-conscious things. It is the view that consciousness is a fundamental property of matter, so everything from electrons and protons to tables and planets, and, of course, humans and dogs, has consciousness to some degree.

Panpsychism is a remarkable thesis, motivated by the ‘perennial hope’ that the world is ultimately intelligible. To investigate whether panpsychism truly can make the world intelligible, we will explore three different arguments, each of which is grounded in a principle that crystallises the ambitious aim of universal intelligibility: the principle of sufficient reason (PSR). This simple and plausible principle of philosophical enquiry – that there exist satisfying explanations for everything – can lead to a whole new understanding of the nature of reality. And, though I’m sceptical about the availability or even desirability of explanations that dissolve all the world’s mysteries, there is exceptional value in the mere contemplation of such projects.

If you come home from work to find a bouquet of flowers on your doorstep, there will be a reason for this. Maybe it’s a birthday present, a congratulations on a new job, a thank you for some good deed. If your car dashboard shows a warning light, you’d be wise to assume that there is some reason for this, such as a problem with the engine, fluids or tyres. The Chicxulub crater, 200 km wide and 1 km deep, in the Yucatán peninsula in Mexico, cries out for scientific explanation, which is precisely what the hypothesis of an extinction-level asteroid impact millions of years ago provides.

But is there really a reason for everything? The mass of a proton is 1.672 × 10-27 kg. What’s the reason for this? What’s the reason for a particular radioactive decay event to which our best scientific theory on the issue, quantum mechanics, assigns only a probability? According to the PSR, there is indeed a reason for everything. For any way the world is, from the flowers on your doorstep to the mass of a proton, there is some reason why it is this way and not some other way. All facts have a reason, and – according to the PSR in its strongest form, as defended by Spinoza – that reason makes them intelligible and necessary, and their contrary inconceivable.

Though the PSR found its fullest expression in Leibniz’s work – ‘The fundamental principle of reasoning,’ Leibniz wrote, ‘is that there is nothing without a reason’ – its lineage is far greater. As Della Rocca showed in his book Spinoza (2008): ‘Versions of [the PSR] go way back in philosophy and can be found in philosophers such as Parmenides, the Stoics, [and] Aquinas.’ And the principle is not restricted to Western European philosophy. It occupies a key position in the metaphysical system of the Islamic philosopher Ibn Sīnā (also known in Europe as Avicenna), who used it to argue that things that exist merely contingently – that is, things whose existence is not necessary – must have a cause outside themselves. Versions of the principle have also been defended in contemporary metaphysics and philosophy of physics. Shamik Dasgupta has argued that every substantive fact has a metaphysical grounding that makes it necessary. And Eddy Keming Chen has developed a physical model of the Universe according to which every single fact (from the number of hairs on your head at 2 pm this afternoon, to the mass of the electron) is entailed and thus explained by the laws of nature.

The PSR is so alluring because it would seem that the very activity of enquiry – whether philosophical, scientific, or the first ‘Why?’ question of a young child – is premised on there being an explanation, a reason, for everything. To endorse the PSR is to adopt an attitude of optimism that the world and our place in it are intelligible and infused with reason and meaning. If anything were unexplainable, there’d be a grave risk that human enquiry is ultimately futile. The falsity of the PSR would constitute a fundamental mismatch between our inquisitive nature and the world in which we find ourselves; it would imply that the world is unintelligible.
The optimistic attachment to intelligibility and reason comes at a significant cost

Intelligibility and meaningfulness are two sides of the same coin. When, on reflection, we can find no good reason for our personal and professional pursuits (lining the boss’s pockets won’t generally satisfy us!), when these things seem absurd or unintelligible, it’s natural to express the predicament in terms of a lack of meaning in life. Analogously, failure to uncover satisfying answers to questions about the nature of reality can lead to deep philosophical worries that the world itself is ultimately meaningless.

But this is not to say that the PSR is universally accepted among philosophers. It is controversial because it seems to entail necessitarianism – the thesis that everything is necessary. You are currently reading an essay about the PSR and panpsychism, but you could have been doing something else. If the PSR is true, however, then there is a sufficient reason why you are currently reading this essay, which makes it necessary that you are currently reading this essay and hence impossible that you could be doing anything else. Since the PSR applies to everything, it seems to entail the necessity of everything, and many find this unpalatable because it threatens free will and the seemingly obvious fact that all manner of things could have been different in all sorts of ways.

Contemporary philosophers who describe themselves as ‘Humean’, that is, as influenced by the Scottish Enlightenment philosopher David Hume, are explicit in their rejection of necessity and ultimate explanations. David Lewis, perhaps the most prominent Humean of the past century, maintained that ‘all there is to the world is a vast mosaic of local matters of particular fact, just one little thing and then another.’ That is to say, there are no reasons, and no necessity for what goes on in the world. In a similar spirit, the Dutch American philosopher Bas van Fraassen consistently challenges the need for a metaphysical explanatory structure. This manifests itself in the rejection of robust laws of nature that necessitate events in the Universe. Science, according to Van Fraassen, can get along just fine without deep explanations that make things necessary.

So, the optimistic attachment to intelligibility and reason comes at a significant cost: it demands a commitment to widespread necessity. There are, however, ways of mitigating this cost. Various authors, including Leibniz himself, have argued that the PSR is at least consistent with a sense in which things could have been different, and this will correspond to weaker senses of explanation. The strongest explanations, those that yield necessity, can be demonstrated in a finite number of steps; prime examples include mathematical and geometrical demonstrations. Other explanations are not finitely demonstrable, though they can be perceived by the infinite mind of God. But the fact that some explanatory connections cannot be grasped by our limited human intellect suffices, according to Leibniz, for contingency.

Alternatively, one could embrace necessitarianism, as Spinoza does, and see it as just another positive facet of the interconnectedness and intelligibility of all things – this seems the way to go if one is to maintain the courage of one’s conviction as a philosophical optimist. But necessitarianism is not the only controversial upshot of the PSR. It can also motivate panpsychism.

Perhaps the most elusive question in all of science and philosophy concerns the nature of conscious experience. Why are the arrangements of matter that constitute human beings and other animals accompanied by conscious experience? Why is there something that it is like to be you? Why are some physical states, but not others, conscious? However completely we describe the physical arrangements of matter that make up a conscious being, that description leaves out the very thing we’re trying to explain: what it feels like from the inside. This challenge to provide an explanation that bridges the gap between third-person scientific descriptions of matter and first-person conscious experience is what the Australian philosopher David Chalmers dubbed the ‘hard problem of consciousness’.

The question is so fiendishly hard because it does not seem amenable to scientific methods of enquiry. The operation of a mill, for example, can be explained by its components: water flow rotates a wheel, which drives gears connected to millstones, which grind wheat into flour. The whole operation of the mill and its output (flour) can be made intelligible to us. If we ask ‘Why does the mill produce flour?’ a fully satisfying answer can be given. No mystery remains.

The mill example is illustrative of scientific explanation in general. The boiling point of water is explained in terms of the hydrogen-bonding of H2O molecules, and the path of light around a massive celestial body is explained in terms of the curvature of spacetime described by Albert Einstein’s general theory of relativity. These cases take more work to understand, but the principle is the same as in the mill case.
If consciousness is a fundamental property of matter, then the problem of explaining consciousness does not arise

However closely we look at the physical matter that makes up conscious beings, we get no closer to understanding how consciousness arises. Leibniz encouraged us to imagine increasing the size of the human brain to the size of a mill so that we can walk around inside it and observe all its working parts in meticulous detail. If we did this, at no point would we observe conscious experience. Conscious experience, by its very nature, is private, first-personal. Since scientific methods can yield knowledge only of the objective, third-person-accessible facts regarding matter in motion, there is an essential mystery concerning the origin of consciousness. The question of why some physical states, but not others, are conscious seems unanswerable.

Unanswerable questions do not sit comfortably with our inquisitive human nature. If consciousness cannot be explained in principle, this would be a particularly egregious violation of the PSR. However, it is worth considering our options for explaining consciousness and, thus, upholding the PSR once we accept that reductive scientific explanation is not up to the task.

One option is to understand consciousness in terms of a new substance entirely, one fully distinct from physical matter. On this view, reality is bifurcated into physical substance characterised by spatial extension, and mental substance characterised by thought, where the latter accounts for consciousness. This is called dualism. The most influential champion of dualism was the French philosopher René Descartes. But Descartes ultimately failed to uphold the PSR, since he couldn’t say why there are two substances as opposed to just one.

Alternatively, we could question the seemingly obvious assumption that fundamental physical matter isn’t conscious. The mystery arises because there is no way to understand how non-conscious physical matter, arranged in space and time, can give rise to consciousness. But why must we think that fundamental physical matter is not conscious? This assumption is not mandatory. If consciousness is a fundamental property of matter, then the problem of explaining consciousness, as formulated above, does not arise. So, in the interest of avoiding this in-principle obstacle to explaining consciousness, many are inclined to believe that consciousness is a fundamental property of matter, that panpsychism is true.

The hypothesis that fundamental matter is physical and non-conscious blocks the possibility of an intelligible explanation – in terms of the fundamental ‘bits’ of matter – of why creatures like us are conscious. If consciousness is absent at the fundamental level, there will always be an explanatory gap between the physical and the mental. What this means is that, for any arrangement of physical matter constitutive of a conscious being, it always seems possible that consciousness was absent; no arrangement of matter seems to be necessarily connected with, and hence able to explain, consciousness. But if consciousness is introduced at the fundamental level, this obstacle is removed. According to panpsychism, we no longer need to bridge the gap from non-conscious fundamental matter to consciousness at higher levels of organisation, since consciousness is present all the way down.

There is still significant work to be done to explain how fundamental consciousness combines to create human-level consciousness. But, at the very least, panpsychism offers a way of avoiding what would otherwise appear to be a potentially devastating violation of the PSR. If consciousness is already present at the fundamental level, there is no longer the same pervasive explanatory gap between wholly non-conscious matter and conscious beings at higher levels.

There is another route to panpsychism via the PSR. The Norwegian philosopher Hedda Hassel Mørch argues that fundamental consciousness is required to properly explain the basic motions of matter, documented by fundamental physics. Science tells us plenty about how matter behaves and what different subatomic particles such as protons, electrons and neutrons do. But it does not tell us what matter is. This is evident from the way in which science characterises matter. The electron, for example, is characterised in terms of its properties: mass, charge and quantum spin. And these properties, in turn, are understood in terms of how they dispose the electron to behave. What is absent from this scientific description of the world is an account of what physical properties are like in themselves, and hence why they have the power to dispose matter to behave in certain ways.

Why do the properties of an electron dispose it towards certain behaviours? How can this be rendered intelligible as per the demands of the PSR? Consider pain. If you are in pain, this mental property disposes you to avoid the thing that’s painful: accidentally touch a hot radiator, and you’ll instantly remove your hand. As Mørch puts it: ‘In the absence of any interfering motives, it seems pain always makes subjects try to avoid it, and [it is] difficult to conceive otherwise.’ If we ask why someone withdrew their hand from the radiator, it is a perfect explanation to say that the heat caused them pain. The explanation renders the action fully intelligible because part of what it is to be in pain is to try to avoid the painful source. Mental properties are special in that they are the only properties with this ability to provide intelligible explanations of behaviour. As Mørch writes:

The only fundamentally dispositional properties we know or can positively conceive of are phenomenal properties – in particular, phenomenal properties associated with agency, intention and/or motivation.

Other properties, such as negative charge, could, for all we know, have disposed things to behave very differently or in no systematic way at all. But it is inconceivable that pain disposed us to do anything besides avoid the source of pain. ‘It does not,’ Mørch writes, ‘seem conceivable that pain makes subjects try to do anything else than avoid it in virtue of its intrinsic character alone.’ This raises a fascinating prospect. In the interest of rendering the behaviour of matter intelligible, we should take those properties responsible for that behaviour to be conscious mental properties. That is to say: all paradigm physical properties such as charge, mass and quantum spin are conscious mental properties. This move provides an answer to the question of what matter fundamentally is, which, in turn, explains why matter does what it does. The fundamental properties of matter are properties of consciousness. By their very nature, they dispose the matter of which they are properties towards certain behaviours. This plugs the explanatory gap left by the scientific method alone. Again, the primary motive in this argument is the desire for intelligible explanations of the world, as per the PSR.
For Spinoza, if things depend on properties because properties individuate things, then it follows that properties are more fundamental than things

There is a third way that a commitment to the PSR leads us to panpsychism. Spinoza is perhaps most famous for his pantheism, the idea that God is nature. On this view, God is not a separate entity that is an external cause of nature; rather, God is coterminous with nature. It turns out that the argument for pantheism also works well as an argument for panpsychism. And, crucially, Spinoza’s argument depends on a truly unwavering commitment to the intelligibility of nature.

If asked ‘How many things exist?’ we’d probably say that there are a great many things indeed – a cat here, a house there, some protons, electrons, and so on – one might even think that there are infinitely many things. But Spinoza argues that there is just one thing. If we hold that there exists more than one thing, we must say something about what each of these things is like. So, we might say ‘This cat is black,’ ‘That house is made of brick,’ ‘Socrates is wise’ and so on. Crucially, for the advocate of the PSR, the different things that exist cannot have all the same properties. If two things, this table and that table, for example, are distinct, there must be some explanation of their distinctness that appeals to some difference between them, some difference in their properties (eg, one is square, the other oval).

Distinct things are individuated by their properties. But this relation of individuation is what philosophers call a dependence relation. For example, the fact that this is an essay on panpsychism, intelligibility and the aim of philosophy depends on the fact that there are words arranged in the appropriate way. This relation of dependence induces an ordering of fundamentality: the words are more fundamental than the essay because the latter depends on the former.

But, for Spinoza, if things depend on properties because properties individuate things, then it follows that properties are more fundamental than things. This result, however, is not acceptable. Things – or ‘substances’, as Spinoza would say – are supposed to be absolutely fundamental. What it is to be a substance, a distinct thing that exists, is to be independent of everything else, completely self-sustaining. It seems odd to say that properties occupy the fundamental level. Is the redness of an apple more fundamental than the apple itself? Surely not, since the apple, the thing, is required to exist before redness can be instantiated. So, we must find another way to explain why there are multiple distinct things. Doing so in terms of properties won’t cut it.

Instead of maintaining that different things merely have different properties, perhaps we ought to say that they are radically different in their essential attributes. What are ‘essential attributes’? Recall that, according to dualism, reality is bifurcated into mental substance with the essential attribute of thought, and physical substance with the essential attribute of extension. In other words, the mental and the physical have radically different essential attributes. But this raises a new question: why is mental substance not extended, and why is physical substance not thinking? The PSR demands an explanation. One might think that the nature of mental substance excludes being extended, and vice versa. But Spinoza objects that this violates the independence of substance, since it entails a mutual dependence of mental and physical substance to explain the fact that they exclude one another. Ultimately, Spinoza thinks there is no reason why substances would differ from each other and, since there is no reason, they do not differ. There is, then, just one substance, one thing, and this thing has all properties, and is both extended and thinking, because there is no reason that it should lack any properties or essential attributes.

A single thing with all properties and essential attributes fits the bill of both God and nature, hence Spinoza’s argument, that only one thing exists, is an argument for pantheism. But this can also be cast as an argument for panpsychism. The single existing substance is, according to Spinoza, both extended and thinking. Hence, thought is a fundamental and ubiquitous feature of reality. There is, however, scope for debate about whether the fundamentality and ubiquity of thought amounts to panpsychism since there is reason to believe that not all thought is conscious thought, in Spinoza’s system. But, at the very least, mentality is a fundamental property of matter, for Spinoza, and many are happy to equate this with consciousness and, thus, categorise Spinoza as a panpsychist. The US philosopher Martin Lin, for example, writes: ‘Spinoza is a panpsychist. For him, mentality is a pervasive and fundamental feature of the natural world.’

This argument for panpsychism (and pantheism) results from leaving no stone unturned in the application of the PSR, and, in particular, from the demand to explain the idea that there are multiple distinct substances with different properties or attributes. Ultimately, Spinoza concludes that this demand cannot be met, which leads to the conclusion that there is a single fundamental substance with all properties and with both essential attributes of thought and extension. This conclusion can be cast in pantheist terms: to maintain that there exists just a single substance with all properties and attributes invites the identification of this substance with both God and nature. It can also be cast in panpsychist terms: the single fundamental substance is essentially a conscious, thinking thing. Hence consciousness is a fundamental property of reality.

Pursuing the demand for intelligibility leads to unexpected and thought-provoking places. If panpsychism doesn’t resonate with you, it’s worth asking if there truly is a reason for everything – if the world is ultimately intelligible after all. On the other hand, if you consider the PSR indispensable, panpsychism may seem inevitable.

But does this latter path offer a deeper sense of meaningful existence? I’m not so sure. In fact, uncertainty about ultimate meaning fuels the arts, which, at their most powerful, embrace and celebrate the unintelligibility and absurdity of life. On the other hand, it seems legitimate to criticise art when its meaning is too obvious, its message too on the nose. So, just as clear and unambiguous meaning is far from the supreme aesthetic goal, it’s not clear that rendering reality fully intelligible, providing the ‘meaning of life’, is a desirable or realistic aim for philosophy.

Dissatisfaction in life, a crisis in meaning, may originate when we can find no good reason for our personal and professional pursuits, and, analogously, philosophical dissatisfaction may stem from an inability to render the world intelligible. But it is far from clear that this sort of dissatisfaction can ever really be remedied by the provision of better reasons.
A messy, unintelligible world doesn’t preclude the construction of highly orderly philosophical edifices

A more prestigious or better-paid job may constitute a reason to get out of bed in the morning. But deep questions about value and meaning will remain untouched. The absurd is not so easily vanquished. Similarly, the promise of a philosophical system built on the PSR, such as Spinoza’s, may appeal to the extent that we want to ‘solve’ philosophy by providing an answer to any possible question. But we may equally take an explanation of everything as an explanation of nothing.

Instead of seeking perfect reasons for all our pursuits, perhaps we ought to just embrace what we do, whatever it may be, for what it is. As the French philosopher and writer Albert Camus reflected, solace for Sisyphus can only come from positively embracing his situation: ‘The struggle itself towards the heights is enough to fill a man’s heart. One must imagine Sisyphus happy.’

Perhaps it’s misguided to expect to render the world intelligible, and we ought instead to just enjoy the process of contemplating its messy unintelligible glory, of pushing our philosophical boulder up the mountain. One way of engaging with this contemplative project is in the development and exploration of systematic philosophical theories. A messy, unintelligible world doesn’t preclude the construction of highly orderly philosophical edifices. But it would be a mistake to think these capable, even in principle, of definitively dissolving life’s mysteries. Philosophical theories such as panpsychism are better thought of as providing new and enriching perspectives on these mysteries, and we should remain open to the possibility of their collapse and replacement.

By giving up the all-encompassing demand for intelligibility and, instead, conceiving of philosophy as providing different perspectives on our condition, we can better understand what it is to make progress in philosophy. Widespread philosophical disagreement should not be taken as evidence that philosophy is degenerate compared with, say, the natural sciences. Rather, we should celebrate the fact that opposing views such as dualism, physicalism and panpsychism exist to provide us with richly diverse perspectives on life’s most tantalising mysteries.

Can panpsychism make the world intelligible? I’m not sure that anything can, or that it even makes sense to pursue supreme reasons. But there is still plenty of joy to be had in the contemplation of panpsychism as a response to the deep mystery of consciousness, and I doubt we could ask any more of a philosophical theory.

items.title: Why a world without friction is a world without progress | Aeon Essays
items.description: In conversations, few words catch my attention faster than ‘friction’ – and especially talk of making things frictionless. From the workplace to grocery shopping, our societies seem to be striving to remove friction from everything. The motivation appears to b
items.author: Jennifer R Vail
paragraphs: In conversations, few words catch my attention faster than ‘friction’ – and especially talk of making things frictionless. From the workplace to grocery shopping, our societies seem to be striving to remove friction from everything. The motivation appears to be that decreasing resistance makes life easier and smoother.

Having spent a career as a tribologist, studying friction, wear and lubrication scientifically, I have some opinions on this. I’ll confess that, in most of my career, I too have sought to reduce friction, developing new materials, designs or even instrumentation in order to lower friction in a jet engine or reduce emissions from your car. However, I’ve also found myself trying to figure out how to increase friction to remove plaque on teeth.

The reality is that friction, despite seeming so antagonistic, is necessary and even productive. The force that resists motion has, since humans first struck a spark from a stone, been the very thing that propels us forward. And this paradox offers a lens through which to reread humanity’s entire technological history.

In order to appreciate all that an understanding of friction has helped us to accomplish, it’s necessary to start at square one and state what friction actually is. We define friction as the force that resists motion, and that means friction is rather ubiquitous. If things are moving, whether they’re sliding around or rolling, there’s friction. Solids, liquids, gases? Doesn’t matter. If there’s movement, friction is there to resist it. Unfortunately, because friction’s job is to resist, we’ve developed an aversion to it as a nuisance. But it’s a very important force, and we’ve thrived by expanding our understanding of it. By the 1960s, after millennia of evolving with friction, we finally accepted that friction is such a critical part of our world that a scientific field of study needed to be devoted to it: tribology.

Tribologists like me study this force in all its forms. Tribology is the science of interacting surfaces in relative motion, concerned with the wear of materials, friction and lubrication. Basically, tribology is the specialisation of things rubbing against each other. You may raise an eyebrow at a field of science focused on this, but when you pause to consider how much motion is going on inside us, around us and throughout the Universe, you can appreciate that tribology is vast. More than anyone, tribologists know the problems friction can cause. But they also know the achievements that have followed as we’ve come to understand resistance better.

Although tribology as a formalised field is relatively modern, friction has long shaped humanity’s technological innovations. For example, consider its pivotal role in people’s journeys from A to B over the centuries. I’m willing to bet that whenever you need to move unwieldy furniture or carry home that giant bag of cat litter, your instinct is to find a cart to help you. Early humans had a similar thought, turning to log rollers to move heavy objects, and coming up with one of our greatest inventions: the wheel. Rolling makes it easier to move objects because it reduces friction between the object and surface you’re moving it against. There are far fewer surface interactions in the process of rolling versus sliding. Plenty can be said about the wheel, including the fact that even in 2026 we can’t seem to agree on the origin of its discovery, but there is zero doubt that it’s a brilliant innovation for dealing with friction. But wheels also need friction: when we exert a force to move a wheel forward, the force between the ground and the wheel – static friction – keeps it from spinning freely, which would result in us going nowhere. Once forward motion begins, the resistance to motion becomes dynamic friction, which is just as important. If you’ve driven on ice, you know the danger of too little friction.
However, if people hadn’t continued improving on these basic principles, even the wheel would be rather inefficient due to friction.
The Vikings’ longships minimised form drag so they could cut through the water quickly

The ancient Romans discovered this in their amphitheatres. Roman chariot races didn’t come without their headaches. Or rather, foot aches. I’m certain the drivers likely complained about their hot feet, caused by friction between the wheels and axle heating up the surrounding parts. In Odes, a collection of lyric poems, the poet Horace described how chariot wheels would glow during racing. Today, scientists know that this glow is from turning the energy of motion into thermal energy. Roman designers eventually figured out that they could temper the problem by putting axungia (animal fat) grease between the wheel and axle. By doing so, they were applying tribological knowledge already exploited by the Sumerians: that fats and oils work more effectively than water as lubrication between surfaces. However, that created a new conundrum: if the grease got hot enough, it risked catching fire. The solution? A coolant. In this case, they splashed water on the chariots, in the ancient equivalent of a pit stop.

While all roads led to Rome, you could say all seas led to the Vikings. They, too, cleverly adapted to the resistance that met them as they journeyed through the oceans. Moving through fluids produces a type of friction known as drag. Even within drag there are subsets. Skin drag is from the friction between the surface of the ship and the water, whereas form drag stems from the shape of the hull as it moves through the water. When they had to transport cargo safely, the Vikings used sturdy ships with wide hulls. This wider hull increased form drag and slowed them down, but the stability provided was more critical. Their famous longships, however, were long and slim, minimising form drag as much as possible so they could cut through the water quickly.

As with all friction scenarios, however, the Vikings found themselves having to balance some competing demands. Faster longships are better, yes, but it was also imperative that the ships not break apart into pieces from the waves. They needed flexibility and strength, while keeping the ships as light as possible to ride higher in the water to reduce drag. To do this, the Vikings used their ‘clinker’ technique of nailing together long planks of wood. The rivets and overlapping planks would increase drag compared with a more polished, smoother design but these individual planks gave the ships the ability to twist and flex to weather storms. If I was on a boat trip in the middle of the ocean, I too would be happy to sacrifice a little bit of drag reduction to avoid capsizing from a rogue wave.

Looking at boats and ships today, it’s clear that we didn’t just accept these Viking designs as the culmination of nautical perfection. Likewise, we aren’t driving around in Roman chariots today. We have since made incredible leaps forward in understanding how to quantify friction and thus design for it, finally approaching friction scientifically. In the 1920s, Chrysler’s head of engineering Carl Breer had the idea to design cars with aerodynamics in mind. Planes seemed to slice seamlessly through the air. Shouldn’t cars do the same? Breer tasked the engineer William Earnshaw to consult with none other than Orville Wright to learn how to design a car in a wind tunnel. The resulting teardrop-shaped Chrysler Airflow was considered a flop, as many disruptive designs can be when they’re just too jarring for taste, but that flop revolutionised how we design cars. Wind-tunnel testing remains a standard today, and friction’s presence is as expected as the air itself.

Tribology testing is routine for the automotive industry today, and there are tribology labs scattered throughout a variety of industries, from medical to food. In these labs, you’ll find instruments designed to measure friction at macro-scales down to the atomic level. My PhD lab at the University of Florida had tribometers measuring friction in force ranges that covered three orders of magnitude. I’ve even worked in a lab that had a tribometer built to test an actual train wheel against a railway. Tribologists are incredibly clever with innovating ways to measure friction, given how persnickety friction is. Friction is dependent on the conditions of the operation – how fast things are moving, how much force they experience, and what temperature and environment they’re in.

Temperature in particular is a fun variable to contend with, because friction itself leads to temperature changes; indeed, frictional heating can be extreme in some cases. Like with Roman chariots, greases can ignite at certain temperatures making it imperative to control friction heating in order to avoid accidentally reaching that temperature. And for applications like jet engines, which get very hot anyway, we have engineered solid materials with low friction to withstand the heat.
When tribologists run into a wall, we develop a new instrument to understand what friction is trying to tell us

You may think tribology is already a niche field, but we have specialisations within it. Mine was solid lubrication, and I worked on developing and testing materials for jet engines and automobiles. In some cases, the conditions of the end use were so aggressive that the steel I was running my material against would experience enough friction heating to completely change the colour of the steel. That’s how you know you’ve reached the extremes in tribology, but those extremes must be met and they obviously are. After all, we have space stations orbiting Earth and landers on Mars.

Which brings us to another critical point about friction’s role in human progress: resistance is a consequence of progress, and its existence is a sign of progression itself. We wouldn’t have the now-robust business of solid lubricants if we had not advanced technologically to design turbine engines, which themselves were the result of us figuring out powered flight. By achieving that, our progress led us to new resistance. I think this is critical to remember anytime we find ourselves confronting unexpected resistance, and it’s something I remind myself of whenever I get halted in my work. I wouldn’t be stumped by this new resistance if I hadn’t managed to advance myself to this position where the resistance exists.

Often when tribologists run into a wall, we find ourselves developing a new instrument to help us understand what friction is trying to tell us. Tribometers have been designed to mimic all of the variables mentioned above, and that alone is quite a feat of human engineering, but now we also couple them with other techniques that allow us to somehow see what is happening while it’s happening. From maps of frictional heating during operation to how friction is influencing cellular movement, instruments and techniques have enabled us to usher friction into a new era to drive us forward, doing more than just finding clever ways to overcome friction. We can harness it as a tool.

In terms of friction, the 20th century can be thought of as the century in which humans accepted the resistance, and established engineering rigour around friction to propel our technological advances forward. Critically, it’s when we formalised how to overcome friction to be more efficient. As a tribologist, however, I’m far more excited about what the 21st century has brought us. Instead of just overcoming friction, we began fully realising how to harness that resistance to bring in a new era of progress. Exhibit A is once again found in our cars, where friction has been deployed as a tool in sustainability. Braking requires friction, so engineers asked: why don’t we use the consequences of that friction to our advantage? The heat from friction in braking is now used to create electricity in regenerative braking in EVs and hybrids. We must continue to use this creative and fresh perspective when dealing with friction, as opposed to always driving towards frictionlessness. Imagine if those engineers had been so fixated on the negatives of friction that they didn’t harness its power.

Using friction as a tool has come to us only as we’ve evolved to understand the depths of friction, including its behaviours and where it may be lurking. We know it is involved in dynamic processes, so let’s use it to control such processes. Yes, we’ve done so for a while with mechanisms like brakes and dampeners, but expanding this beyond machines has really taken hold in recent decades. Now, we’re looking at how friction may be a tool in perhaps the most impressive machine there is: the human body. It’s possible friction may be a lever to help us better model and understand biological processes and, in turn, help in the development of therapeutics. The rate at which a virus ejects from its protein shell or capsid can dictate whether it results in an active infection or instead remains dormant in the cell. If we want to use viruses to intentionally infect and defeat other viruses or bacteria, then controlling the virus’s ejection rate is crucial. Friction is the key to unlocking this possibility. In 2023, researchers found that, by packing the coils of virus DNA in certain ways, they could increase friction during ejection and slow down its rate of ejection.
Every advance we make generates new friction. We solve one problem, and friction presents another

Recently, our knowledge of friction has taken us to even more surprising places, extending even to helping us understand dark matter. The concept of ‘resistance is your reward for progress’ may be best illustrated by the astrophysicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar. Despite the fact that established scientists mocked his theories, Chandrasekhar would go on to become a founder of astrophysics, and is the reason we understand the evolution of stars and interstellar dynamics. In the 1930s, he was interested in how the interactions between stars could lead to their collisions. He calculated the timescales of such collisions and realised, though only after publishing, that things weren’t adding up quite right. This led him back to the drawing board, where he spotted there was a resistance present that no one before had identified: dynamical friction. This friction is a gravitationally induced drag that acts on objects as they interact and move through space.

Fast-forward to the 21st century, and dynamical friction has been used as a tool to infer the presence of dark matter. In 2024, researchers in Hong Kong realised that orbital times weren’t matching up with a couple of stars they were studying that were believed to be circling around black holes. They looked at Chandrasekhar’s concept of dynamical friction and wondered what would happen if they incorporated the contribution of friction from the dark matter surrounding the black hole. Voila! Suddenly, the predicted and calculated orbital times of the stars matched with what they were measuring. Friction was present when humanity first started experimenting with fire and the wheel. Now it’s there as we probe the frontiers of our Universe.

We need friction to move. Without its resistance, Earth’s plates would be in constant motion. We could not walk, or drive, or even hold objects. Understanding how to achieve what we want, in a world requiring this resistance, has been essential in our development.

Yet there is a deeper paradox at work, one that William James captured when he wrote that life is built ‘in the self-governing resistance of the ego to the world’. Every advance we make generates new friction. We solve one problem, and friction presents another. We step forward, and new resistance awaits. This is what progress means: that we have moved into territory that demands new understanding.
Roman engineers learned it when their chariot wheels caught fire. Chandrasekhar discovered this when his calculations didn’t add up. And we will continue to encounter resistance as we push forward.
When people speak of a frictionless world, they imagine ease. But ease without resistance is a wheel spinning in place, motion without progress.

items.title: This New Film Observes Patrick Wolf’s Rise, Fall and Rebirth
items.description: “I have to be very grateful for the film,” says Wolf of Christian Cargill’s new feature starring Tilda Swinton, which mixes present-day scenes with archive footage, illustration and clips from cinema. “Christian has helped me close a book."
items.author: Gemma Samways
paragraphs: “I have to be very grateful for the film,” says Wolf of Christian Cargill’s new feature starring Tilda Swinton, which mixes present-day scenes with archive footage, illustration and clips from cinema. “Christian has helped me close a book."

As dawn breaks on the south Kent coast and crashing waves muffle the shriek of seagulls, the first words we hear in Wolf are those of Tilda Swinton. “It’s been a long time since we last saw each other,” she remarks off camera, gently addressing her friend – and the film’s subject – Patrick Wolf. Their ensuing conversation forms the framework for director Christian Cargill’s tender portrait of the rise, fall and creative rebirth of one of pop’s most enigmatic outsiders.

Emerging in the early 2000s with a sound that fused baroque instrumentation and electronic experimentation with a mix of folklore, fairytales and ancient mythology, Wolf was never an artist easily contained by pop’s conventions. From the feverish theatricality of his 2003 debut Lycanthropy and the orchestral grandeur of 2011’s Lupercalia, to his commercial breakthrough on 2007’s The Magic Position, he carved out a reputation as one of British music’s most unique voices, only to retreat from the public eye entirely between 2012 and 2023.

The film pieces together the fragments of that lost decade – a period marked by addiction, financial ruin, grief and unresolved trauma – and contextualises them as part of his wider life story, mixing present-day scenes filmed at his home in Ramsgate with archive footage, illustration, clips from cinema and imagery from the natural world. The effect is impressionistic rather than exhaustive, with the human story prioritised over delivering a comprehensive overview of Wolf’s career.

“I had no interest in making a fan film whatsoever,” says Cargill, speaking from Canada ahead of a screening at the Vancouver International Film Festival. “It’s a film about struggle and hope and resilience. He just happens to be a musician as part of that journey.”

Cargill sees the film as part of the same lineage as his previous shorts, the BAFTA Cymru-winning Heart Valley – which documented a day in the life of a septuagenarian sheep farmer – and Recomposing Earth, which told the story of Orkney composer Erland Cooper’s buried album project. “All of my films are essentially people looking for home,” he explains. “Heart Valley is about someone who’s found home and has never left, Recomposing Earth is about someone who has left home but always feels connected to it, and then with Wolf, it’s about Patrick re-evaluating what home is.”

Raised in Wandsworth, Wolf lived in London until 2019, when he relocated to Ramsgate as part of his recovery. Cargill captures the restorative rhythms of life by the sea: Wolf running along the coastline at dawn, tending to his garden, decorating his studio, writing beneath the sound mirror at Broadstairs and swimming at sunset in Botany Bay. These quiet rituals feel a world away from the technicolour chaos of his years in London.

For fans, the amount of previously unseen archive footage included in Wolf will be a delight. Indeed, Cargill recalls being handed “a shoebox featuring over 50 hours of footage”, featuring home videos shot by Wolf’s father as well as by members of the performance art community, including Susanne Oberbeck of No Bra. Using his experience overseeing archive footage on the 2022 music documentary Meet Me In The Bathroom, Cargill pieces together Wolf’s whirlwind journey from his roots in experimental art collective Maison Crimineaux to his tenure as a successful solo artist, assembling a collage of clips, artefacts and photography. Threaded through this archival patchwork, the off-screen conversation between Swinton and Wolf serves as a narration of sorts, lending the film an intimate and reflective quality.

It was Cargill’s idea to reunite the two, who had first met when Wolf invited Swinton to play the voice of hope on his 2009 album The Bachelor, and had latterly lost touch. Wolf recalls initially feeling some trepidation at the reunion, simply because of the painful nature of the subjects they would discuss.

“There’s a part of me that has really wanted to come back to work and not have to talk about the past at all,” the 43-year-old sighs, speaking from his garden studio. “But with Tilda, there was so much compassion and empathy. We were meant to only talk for 45 minutes and we ended up talking for six hours.”

Swinton’s significance in Wolf’s life runs deeper than their friendship: growing up, he was hugely inspired by her depiction of gender fluidity in Sally Potter’s 1992 film Orlando, making Cargill’s decision to intercut footage from the film all the more poignant. “Orlando was a life changing film for me,” Wolf smiles. “If I had seen a career advisor at that age, I would have taken that film in and said, ‘This is what I want to do with my life.’”

But while Orlando offered Wolf a vision of a world beyond conventional ideas of gender and identity, the reality of growing up gay in Britain was considerably less liberating. The film explores the hostility he faced living under Section 28, from the violent bullying he endured at school and his subsequent expulsion, to the homophobia that followed him into adulthood. As his career took off, sections of the press seized on his “flamboyance” as a means of diminishing his talent, reducing his musical ambition and artistic ingenuity to a caricature of excess. The film lays bare the toll of that relentless scrutiny, tracing how a culture hostile to queer expression shaped both the artist Wolf became and the struggles he would spend years trying to overcome.

“I found the first edit really disturbing and painful to watch,” he reflects. “All the work you’ve done during psychotherapy and all the meetings are suddenly dredged up. With some of the footage my first reaction was like, “Can you take that out?” And then I walked around the block in my head, and realised that’s probably the reason why it should be in the film: it’s important I’m uncomfortable.”

This trust-fall approach extended to commissioning the film’s original score, which was created by the Oscar-nominated composer Owen Pallett. “Our relationship has been so many things over the years, from collaborators to lovers to great friends, and I knew he had a very specific idea of what songs he does and doesn’t like. So I left him alone to watch the film, to choose whatever songs he wanted from my catalogue, and to create a portrait of me with my music, but in his composition style.”

Pallett’s tender, orchestral arrangements lend the film an added emotional depth. One particularly poignant passage, featuring Wolf reflecting on the depths of his addiction, is set to a haunting reimagining of Demolition from his debut album. It’s poles apart from the buoyant maximalism of Wolf’s better-known work on The Magic Position, a record that will turn 20 next year. In some respects, working on the film has helped Wolf make peace with that album, allowing him to revisit the record with a renewed perspective and reconnect with a body of work that has long been difficult to separate from the experiences that followed.

“I forget how young I was when I made that,” he says, shaking his head. “And it’s a really brave and insane psychedelic album, you know? To think that [the title track] was in and out of the charts; a song which is basically made out of bass clarinet, a children’s toy piano and an Alan Lomax sample, and which discusses divine magic and geomancy. The amount I had to fight in order to get that across the line, and then to get dropped for it. I have a lot to be proud of for that record.”

He continues, “I think for a long time I lived in a lot of regret. You know, with all the opportunity that was thrown at me, why didn’t I flourish more? Why didn’t I rise over this hurdle? Or why didn’t I handle that situation better? But I was forced to forgive myself, and to realise I was just doing the best that I could at that time.
