So really, I have to be very grateful for the film, as Christian has helped me close a book.”
Wolf will premiere at Barbican on 22 October and at The Castle in Homerton on 8 November, which will be followed by a Q&A with the director

items.title: The Gentle Horror of Kate Zambreno’s Foam
items.description: Inspired by the soft sculptures of Eva Hesse, the author’s experimental new novel, published by Semiotext(e), explores the demands of caregiving and work on artistic life
items.author: P Eldridge
paragraphs: Inspired by the soft sculptures of Eva Hesse, the author’s experimental new novel, published by Semiotext(e), explores the demands of caregiving and work on artistic life

There’s a distinct, lingering atmosphere that settles over the pages of Kate Zambreno’s new novel, Foam – a weight that feels at once ephemeral and suffocating. An experimental novel punctuated with doubles – a multiplying sequence of figures named “Eva” – Foam exists as a space of domestic cataloguing, art criticism and bodily fragmentation; an assemblage of residues, grief and routine. And beneath its sensory observations nestles a sharper, far more terrifying confrontation – “a gentle horror”, as Zambreno puts it: an examination of how contemporary creative existence is drained by capitalist institutions, and how, with the precarity of rental housing and caregiving, we inadvertently reconstruct those same frameworks within the walls of our own homes.

The American novelist, essayist and professor has long been a master of capturing the precarious position of the artist operating at the margins of academia and the gig economy. In Foam, the narrator is an adjunct writing professor without the luxury of maternity leave across two births – the latter depicted in a strange horror-filled pandemic delivery stripped of compassion. The pressure of unrelenting deadlines and classes to cover summer rent fuses institutional logic directly to the domestic walls. The modern machine demands metricised efficiency and a total monetisation of interiority. Creativity dissolves into administrative labour: emails, grants, and constant Zoom presence. Exhausted yet persistent, the narrator navigates these oppressive demands while trying to care for two young children.

The opening of Foam traces the narrator’s transition into postpartum caregiving and the presence of “The Evas” – writing students hired as in-home helpers and assistants for the narrator – but this is no bourgeois nursery memoir. Care is navigated in a rundown, shabby apartment amid landlord hostilities and lead paint. “The Evas” who occupy the first part of the novel are not traditional nannies but former students whose own ambitions, jealousies, and anxieties mirror the narrator’s desire for creative autonomy. Foam’s narrator experiences a profound collision between the gendered expectations of selfless devotion and the pressures of becoming a disembodied parental role model when trying to cover rent and survive. “I’ve had to reason with writing about the exploitation and extraction of adjuncting; to look at these episodes in my life that have brought me the most guilt,” Zambreno tells me over Zoom from their home in New York. “I honestly think there’s no truly ethical way to pay someone else to take care of your child.”

Foam’s scope then broadens into durational performance, material decay, art criticism, institutional violence, and physical breakdown. The narrative shifts in unconventional ways, functioning like the philosopher Peter Sloterdijk’s description of foam, which is the novel’s epigraph: “Almost nothing, yet not nothing. A something, if only a delicate web of cavities and subtle walls. An actual thing, but a construct fearful of contact that yields and bursts at the slightest touch.” The novel’s form physically transforms, as you read, into its title; fissures and soft structures that reject rigid demands or expectations.

This shift is not without an anchored, deep engagement with feminist art practices and soft sculptures. Zambreno weaves art criticism directly into the fiction, thinking through artist Eva Hesse’s latex and fibreglass works – Repetition 19 and Expanded Expansion – which degrade and rot over time. Hesse’s ethos becomes the intellectual spine: “Life doesn’t last: art doesn’t last” … “I have lost my fear of the ugly.” This obsession with ephemerality and non-form extends to Senga Nengudi’s RSVP – sculptures stretched and weighted by sandbags to reflect the “sagging form after pregnancy” – and Gabriela Salazar’s study of apartment windows that shows “the melancholy of apartment living. The walls become shabby, and only after the tenants disappear, so there’s no trace, do the walls get painted over, as if no one ever existed before,” as Zambreno writes. The name “Eva” rattles and echoes through the text, not merely as the former writing students, but as an expansive motif: the artist Eva Hesse, the cardiologist named Eva, a childhood doll, a friend’s child, a couple’s vibrator, and the mother of a previous lover – multiplying until the self becomes a soft sculpture in flux.

Through this scaffolding, Foam and its language become preoccupied with the body under extreme stress and pressure: postpartum haemorrhaging, repetitive nursing, high blood pressure, the “100-day cough” and a sudden fainting where the narrator collapses on a busy Brooklyn street while clutching a baby. The medical apparatus is no refuge either, delivering cold gaslighting where a cardiologist dismisses heart pain and trauma with automated advice.

Institutional cruelty occurs throughout Foam, as much in the domestic sphere as in the university. Zambreno charts the horror of student suicides – where neoliberal universities respond with hollow wellness initiatives like handing out polyurethane foam stress balls – and the Kafkaesque bureaucracy of middle managers. The novel insists that under capitalism, institutions will never love you; a reminder that you can’t escape the conditions of your own life, nor the conditions of governing institutions and how they hold power, class privilege, and control over you; and you, whatever your creed, might be inadvertently reconstructing facets of a politic you’re against in the most political of all places: your home. We’ve all heard the adage, ‘the personal is political’. Foam is the first novel worthy of that simple yet guttural language, having built an extraordinary, durational monument out of a “wildly interior book” that is fragile and absurd, carved from the residues of physical exhaustion.

Ultimately, Foam stays with the textures of the everyday. It pays exquisite attention to the fragile, useless, and unquantifiable moments of union that resist capitalist capture: the softness of a child’s sweater, the erratic drift of thought, the accumulation of clutter, the tactile sensation of foam itself, and the ephemerality of durational performance and sculpture. “Foam is maybe not the most transformational or optimistic work, but it’s shot through with that gentle horror of pessimism […] Nothing too bad happens, but there’s a bad feeling, alongside the moments of joy which act as a relief from capitalism,” says Zambreno. By centering these fleeting, mutable and anti-capitalist textures, Zambreno acknowledges that while we may never fully untangle our domestic lives from the institutional logic that feeds us, we can still cultivate moments of pleasure within the ruins of a mouldy home.

Zambreno achieves something profoundly tender by turning the very things capitalism dismisses as waste into a sacred liturgy. The brilliance of the novel is that it doesn’t offer any grand political escape route. You and I and Zambreno are stuck in something truer: a clear-eyed account of precarity, domestic captivity, bodily endurance and a delicate insistence on making art out of the very residue of our own enervation.
Foam is out now, published by Semiotext(e)

items.title: Death and Entrances
items.description: This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:
items.author: Susannah Frankel
paragraphs: This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:
Among the earliest and most famous depictions of a female nude is the Venus of Willendorf.

There are many Venuses, a broad – and obviously retrospective – nomenclature for figurines originating from the Upper Palaeolithic period, dating back 10,000 to 40,000 years. The Venus of Willendorf is carved in oolitic limestone. Standing a mere 11.1 centimetres tall, she is reputedly 30,000 years old. She has swollen breasts and a protuberant belly, both suggestive of pregnancy. Many thousands of words have been written about her. Is she, in fact, pregnant? Is she an ancient fertility doll, designed to be held in the hand of prospective or birthing mothers? Is she not pregnant at all but a symbol of beauty as it was perceived at that time? Also conjecture: the perspective of this Venus and more than a few of her Venus sisters, the fact that she has no facial features, or indeed feet, has led some to surmise that her creator was female – she is a self-portrait. Of course, nothing is proven. The issues this little Venus’s provenance raises, though, seem pertinent now for Harley Weir, whose exploration of the female form – and just the female – including her own, has led to some of the most striking and evocative imagery of the past decade.

In the history of art, depictions of pregnant women are few and far between. They are predominantly seen through the eyes of male artists. Their bodies are either hidden – through the medieval and Renaissance periods it was the fashion for women to wear voluminous clothing – or idealised. The Madonna is the most prevalent of all pregnant females in art history – the mother of all art historical clichés? – and her baby’s conception was immaculate. In myriad portrayals, myriad Annunciations, that purity is signified by the presence of a white dove. Of that same era, for many years critics speculated that the female figure in Jan van Eyck’s The Arnolfini Portrait (1434) was pregnant. Emblems of fertility – a carving of Saint Margaret of Antioch on a chair by the bed, ripe oranges, a symbol of prosperity but also fecundity, on the windowsill – are present in the painting’s background. The fullness of her famous green dress has since been attributed to the extravagance of its fabrication, however. Three-dimensional laser scans of Leonardo da Vinci’s Mona Lisa (1503–17) captured some 20 years ago now are not so easily dismissed. A fine gauze veil – or guarnello – seen over her dress, until that point hidden by aged varnish on the painting’s surface, is typical of those worn by soon-to-be or new mothers of that time. Representation of pregnant nudes in classical painting, meanwhile, are likely negative. Titian’s masterpiece Diana and Callisto (1556–59), which hangs in the National Gallery in London, is the best known. Nymph Callisto’s shaming, the revelation of her naked, pregnant body and subsequent fall from chastity, is subject to the goddess Diana’s fierce disapproval. Raped by Jupiter, Callisto was later transformed into a bear by that god’s wife, Juno. Or so the story goes.

A few centuries on, and modern artists from Gustav Klimt to Pablo Picasso and Lucian Freud painted (and sculpted) pregnant women, but always – inevitably – from a distance. Klimt’s Hope paintings, dated 1903 and 1907–08, of his favourite model Herma were executed against her better judgment, and the earlier rendition, portraying her naked surrounded by mythical monsters, caused a scandal. Picasso’s 1950 sculpture La Femme Enceinte was inspired by his partner at the time, Françoise Gilot, who had recently given birth to their second child, Paloma; he used ceramic bowls and pitchers to create the figure’s rounded breasts and stomach. Freud’s portraits of pregnant women, some carrying his own children, were forensic in their attention to detail: the subject as specimen.

It wasn’t until the last century that female artists’ representations of pregnancy began to enter the gallery setting. Paula Modersohn-Becker’s nude self-portrait of an imaginary pregnancy in 1906, Alice Neel’s paintings of pregnant women, clothed and nude, in the Sixties and Seventies and Chantal Joffe’s pregnant self-portraits are impassioned in their bid for reclamation, showing not only pregnancy’s beauty and power but also its complexity. For the first time, there is a sense of women’s alienation from their own bodies antepartum, for their feelings of intense love alongside, and never unreasonably, fear.

Harley Weir is no stranger to the self-portrait. Her 2022 Beauty Papers monograph, dedicated to “all the dolls in the world”, is an unflinchingly visceral – at times grotesque – representation of the tropes of femininity and the preconceptions those raise. Four years on, and ten weeks pregnant, Weir began to regularly take pictures of herself naked or near-naked in the relative privacy of her bedroom. At 32 weeks a further, more studied series was taken, including portraits of Weir, now helped by John Kelleher, her husband and the father of the baby, and of a body double wearing a pregnancy belly and Harley Weir mask. With styling by her friend and longtime collaborator Georgia Pendlebury, these images serve as Weir’s visual response to her physical and emotional transition at a time that may be as challenging as it is joyful. And intimate, but: “The real private self isn’t this though,” she says. “It’s still a performance, especially in a self-portrait.”
SUSANNAH FRANKEL Do you know the Venus of Willendorf? She’s got no feet. People think a woman may have made her.

HARLEY WEIR Because she’s looking down at her body? I’ve been documenting my pregnancy from week ten and there are a lot of looking-down pictures and also looking up in the mirror. When you’re pregnant there are so many blind spots. My husband helped take many of the pictures for that reason. The series is called Death and Entrances because, from what I’ve read, it’s like an ego death. You’re giving birth but you’re also dying, you change. I felt, physically in this story, as if I was wearing a disguise.

That’s something I think connects back to the Venus of Willendorf, this idea of a woman looking down at a body that is powerful, but also unfamiliar. During pregnancy, your body becomes the most visible thing about you, but at the same time it can feel like it no longer belongs. Here, I don’t have my usual breasts, I don’t have my usual stomach. I felt almost free from the shame of being nude because the bump isn’t me or us.

SF The physical state of pregnancy is extreme. We are taught from an early age to control our bodies and our body image. When you’re pregnant, you surrender that control. Perhaps your body is preparing you for becoming a mother, because once that happens your life is not your own in the same way.

HW Yes, it feels like that. It feels good. I’ve always been self-conscious about my breasts because they were so small. Now they are engorged and full of stretchmarks, but I don’t care who sees them. They’ve become functional objects. And there’s a safety in that. I feel much more at ease. I love being this blob that will bring purpose to someone new and it in turn gives my body purpose, a reason for its irregular shapes that before felt like deformities.
SF Is there any fear involved?

HW There was a lot more at the beginning. But I’m still at the stage where you don’t really know what’s about to hit. I’m in the phase where I feel this is the baby, it’s this bump. But no, the baby is going to come out and rock my world.
SF Have you looked at the way pregnant women are represented in art?
HW I haven’t seen much pregnant art – especially from the past. There’s the Virgin Mary, but we rarely see her pregnant. She didn’t even have sex. The virgin and the mother.
SF There’s that – the Christian ideal – but also some quite violent portrayals.

HW I have to say I can’t think of one classical painting where you see a pregnant woman. Klimt maybe. My mother talks a lot about how, even when she was younger, you had to cover the bump up, you couldn’t show it freely. I feel now we’re having a renaissance for mothers. The mother is more celebrated. I didn’t feel secure enough to be having a kid until now. And I’m getting on. I’ll be 38 when it comes out.
SF People called me a geriatric mother. I was 37.
HW But they’ve changed it now.

HW I would have been, but they stopped using that term recently, which is great. I do think this is an amazing moment for mothers. On Instagram there are so many inspirational women sharing their motherhood stories. Once you get pregnant your algorithm knows and they’re everywhere. So many cool mothers online, which I feel is something you wouldn’t have seen in the early Noughties. Mothers were dismissed or hidden. There was the fear of overpopulation and that having children was bad for the environment,

I used to hear that a lot. Now in the west fewer people are having babies, pregnancy is a positive thing again. It goes in cycles, I suppose. I’ve just finished reading Born [The Untold History of Humanity by Lucy Inglis]. It’s fascinating how attitudes shift. During the Roman Empire, people would kill unwanted babies, by “exposure” – especially girls.
SF In China and Japan they are now rolling out financial incentives to persuade people to have babies.
HW Exactly. First China wasn’t allowing more than one baby. Now there aren’t enough. For now, it feels like we’re in a baby-positive cycle.
SF The death part of the equation is the old you saying goodbye to your old life.

HW And saying hello to the mystery of what is about to begin. I have already said goodbye to my old body. It’s all very physical now. The changes being made are visual, my insides are yet to be rebirthed.

SF You’ve photographed yourself before. How much of that process is about showing yourself to the world and how much is it about introspection, working out what, in this case, your pregnancy means for you?
“I have already said goodbye to my old body. It’s all very physical now. The changes being made are visual, my insides are yet to be rebirthed” – Harley Weir

HW My life is already very bump-forward. Wherever I go, it’s the focal point of conversation. It’s hard not to be obsessed by the pregnancy. At one point people argued that because the baby takes so much nutrition, the mother’s brain shrinks by 20 per cent. Now they are calling it rewiring. I’m rewiring. And my way of coping with things is photography – it’s like therapy. It’s a way for me to work out those ideas and also to detach from them. I was thinking how I’m kissing goodbye to this flat-chested girl and becoming a woman. The pregnancy at this stage is visual, the changes are reflected in the mirror. Every Wednesday I read my update that tells me how big the baby is.
SF How big is your baby now?
HW Honeydew melon. You know, it’s so silly. Apparently, there’s a dog one too.

SF How interested are you in the relationship between us as voyeurs and you as the subject? I looked at Beauty Papers. That’s overtly sexual, about fetishising women. This is almost more like you fetishising your own pregnant body.

HW I do think there’s something in the fact that I’m still a sexual being. In old tropes you become a mother and your sexiness was stripped from you. Almost as some kind gesture of respect that we never asked for. That’s what is interesting about fashion. It’s been a way to explore the female – that’s what I do. There are also many personal secrets tucked away inside the images, where they often look overly sexual – rarely my first thought, if thought about at all. There’s an undercurrent of personal meaning. Some images in the story are overlaid with pictures from my dad’s favourite beach. That’s seaweed. Mother earthing. My dad has Benson’s disease, so he’s not able to communicate any more. But I still want to include him in my life in ways that I can. It’s sad when I think of how good he would have been as a grandfather.
SF This story is so intensely autobiographical. Do you think all of your work is?

HW It is. I graduated from art school in 2010. I loved emotive art and started as a painter, which seemed to be the most primitive and uninteresting trade at the time. There was a bit of a backlash against people like Tracey Emin – who wore their heart on their sleeve. People whose work was too autobiographical, too self-involved. I loved her diary works and felt a kinship to them but my era was having a conceptual moment that I didn’t fit in with. I will always be an artist first but fashion allowed me to continue to use emotive language more freely and the impulse has never left me. There’s a picture of me with a pushchair on fire. I wanted to express the fear of being a bad mother. That’s my neighbour’s shed. It’s like a doll’s house. The dream gone wrong.
SF Very few artists have represented fear in pregnancy. Probably because they are mostly men, so maybe it’s not their place to look at that.
HW Yes, that was nice. They left it for us.
SF But being pregnant can be really frightening at times.

HW Part of the story I wanted to show was my thoughts of, oh God, am I going to be a bad mother? Am I going to drop the baby? Am I not going to love the baby? Am I going to have postpartum depression? What’s amazing is that there is so much information about those things now and people talk about it all the time.
SF That anxiety goes on for ever, I think. Did working with a body double in a mask feel strange to you?

HW So strange. Every time I look in the mirror now, I see the mask. It’s terrifying. When you ordinarily look in the mirror you see what you want to see. You think you look good or you think you look terrible. It doesn’t matter what you actually look like. I asked Chaïm, who made the mask, to get all the bits and bobs in there. Go hard on the skin blemishes. I knew they were there but when you actually see them looking back at you, it’s quite grotesque. My face like a piece of meat, you really see it that way. When I show the photos to people, they can’t understand that it’s not me in those pictures.
SF Did you do it for purely practical reasons?

HW Not only. There is something very laborious about taking a self-portrait, the tripod, the focusing etc, but I also wanted to divide myself – the divided self. She was supposed to be the idealised version of me, unstretched and glossy. It’s a shame we didn’t have more time with Anna, who wore the suffocating mask along with the fake bump and wig. There was so much more fun to be had.
SF The image with the snake is referencing Avedon’s Nastassja Kinski and the Serpent [1981]?
HW Yes. I thought that was funny. It’s my “pregnancy picture”.
SF You know the thematic of this issue of the magazine is cliché?

HW So much of what I do is about cliché. The tropes of being a woman are so clichéd. If you want to put a signal out, it’s as simple as a little make-up and people treat you totally differently – it’s a totally different day, a different mask.
That’s a real snake crushing me in the picture. I put make-up on in that one too, to cover the pigmentation on my face, to be the idealised pregnant woman for her pregnancy shoot.
SF And there’s an apple in another image. Eve’s apple.

HW Yes. Purity lost. And for taking the apple we must suffer in childbirth. But I actually feel purer than ever. There’s something in the body becoming so functional, it’s before shame. The instinctiveness and the nakedness of breastfeeding, for example, feels like that moment before the apple when there was no shame attached to the naked body. There’s one really disturbing breastfeeding image, the masked me breastfeeding me, the idea of a mother still needing a mother. There’s also me breastfeeding from John. Which takes the breast even further away from the sexual, because he doesn’t have one. It’s about becoming dependent on each other in a new way as a family and recognising that we all need to be nurtured.

SF You are photographing something that is transient, and by photographing it you’re fixing it in time. I suppose that is what photography is more generally, but it feels somehow more pronounced in this context.

HW The permanence is scary sometimes. I only thought about showing my child these images today. I thought maybe the baby never sees these. It’s very different because it’s still inside me. Baby out, different.
SF Do you think about that often, with explicit imagery?
HW I think about it all the time, but I try to be free. I don’t always get it right and people correct me. I like that conversation though.
SF Do people ever talk about your nudes, or look at your nudes, in a way that makes you feel uncomfortable?

HW It’s hard to put yourself out there and be judged. The real private self isn’t this though. It’s still a performance, especially in a self-portrait. Looking back, I realised I was trying to seem approachable, not too attractive or too sexy. But I’m obviously aware of the camera and that annoys me. I wanted to catch myself in a real state, but because I’m the one taking the photograph, that’s almost impossible. Some pictures are ugly because I felt I should include them, so I wouldn’t seem vain, which is probably the vainest thing you can do. In one I’m standing nicely, in another I’m slumped and badly postured. Sometimes I feel I can be quite vulgar. That’s part of me, letting people see a little too much. Not necessarily deliberately.

“So much of what I do is about cliché. The tropes of being a woman are so clichéd. If you want to put a signal out, it’s as simple as a little make-up and people treat you totally differently – it’s a totally different day, a different mask” – Harley Weir
SF And you don’t lie awake at night thinking about that.

HW Sometimes. You don’t want to read the comments too much. I don’t put much on Instagram for that reason. I would say that I have some boundaries, but the idea of vulgarity is something I subconsciously play with a lot. Or at least it seems my tolerance is higher than most. There is me covered in milk with my legs up. It reeked, because it came from France in a heatwave with Leana the make-up artist. I was trying to photograph what the baby would see coming to get the milk. Unfortunately, I didn’t get a linea nigra, the dark line that can appear when pregnant, apparently as an arrow to direct a new born to the breast.
SF There’s also the cliché of the earth mother, and that huge power, but equal to that is vulnerability.

HW Since I’ve become obviously pregnant, when I’m not with John, I don’t like walking around at nighttime. I want to be with my husband. I know most people are not thinking bad thoughts, but I feel vulnerable. There’s something of the mother earth in the photo of me feeding the fawn. This instinct to nurture, but also suggestive of how exposed motherhood can make you feel. I read that, in England, they used to use puppies to keep the milk supply going if your baby was away from you, fawns or pigs in other countries. And if your milk wasn’t working, they would bring round a donkey or a goat for the baby to suckle from.
SF Some of your self-portrait imagery displays a complete lack of vanity.

HW Art and fashion both rank quite high in the thoughts of the self. Oddly with fashion, being the voyeur that I am, possibly the less self-absorbing of the two. It’s so much about the other. It’s rare to see the photographer. We’re like ghosts haunting the image but we are never really there. I often photograph some of the most attractive people in the world and then sit with retouching comments to make them look even more attractive. So it’s hard to think, damn I look hot here, because in my mind, by comparison, I look like a gremlin. Me looking vain as hell to the public is probably me thinking I look real and unfiltered. It’s hard to be objective when it’s me in front of the lens but I like to think I show both sides. Perfection isn’t interesting.

Styling: Georgia Pendlebury. Hair: Alex Brownsell at Streeters using KEUNE and BLEACH LONDON. Make-up: Leana Ardeleanu at Artlist using MAKE UP FOR EVER. Mask: Chaïm Vischel. Manicure: Lauren Michelle Pires using Le Vernis in Garconne and La Crème Main by CHANEL BEAUTY. Set design: Phoebe Shakespeare. Casting: Gabrielle Lawrence for People-File at MiniTitle. Model: Anna Ramfel. Talent: John Kelleher. Studio manager: Melissa Arras. Lighting director: Jordan Lee. Photographic assistants: Chiara Croserio and JJay Johnson. Styling assistants: Ethan Barbara, Michiel Heemskerk and Stoyan Chuchuranov. Hair assistant: Tommy Stayton. Make-up assistant: Gwen Ryan. Set-design assistants: Freya Purkhardt and Keelin Coyle. Production: Partner Films. Executive producer: Kimberly Arms. Producers: Star Santos Hannan and Valeria Rocca. Production assistant: Thea Levine. Special thanks to Ruben Riley Garrett

Charting fashion from the 19th century to the Nineties to now, the stylist Panos Yiapanis combines garments from his own personal archive with pieces from Pieter Mulier’s five-year tenure at Alaïa. The approach connects Yiapanis, Mulier and Azzedine Alaïa himself – all collectors of historical and contemporary fashion – via a shared passion for clothes of the past, present and future.

items.author: Craig McLean
paragraphs: In mid-April 2003, I stood in Fifty Acre Wood, five miles west of Bristol, watching Thom Yorke stomp, slowly, repeatedly through the undergrowth. Under the watchful eye of filmmaker Chris Hopewell, he was shooting scenes for the Jan Švankmajer-inspired, stop-motion video for ‘There, There’, the first single from Radiohead’s upcoming sixth album.

Hail to the Thief was the follow-up to the game-changing, sound-shifting, back-to-back Kid A and Amnesiac, the lengthy, intense, making of which had nearly ripped the band apart. The new record, in contrast, had been recorded with energy, directness, speed. So much so that here was the frontman making – of all things – a pop video.

‘I’m trying to persuade the record company to shell out on lots of singles and all that stuff,’ Yorke told me when we talked in Oxford that month. Hail to the Thief, he insisted, ‘is a pop record. It’s really direct. It has this energy to it. I’d love to know that it was on the radio. Just ’cause that’s where my head's at. I don’t want to be on the top shelves at the back. ’Cause I’m into it too much. I like it. It is,’ he repeated, just for clarity, ‘pop music.’

In mid-October 2026, I stood in the rehearsal space of the National Youth Theatre in north London, watching Yorke tell a bunch of musicians – not Radiohead – that he wanted to hear again the bass being played in a new version of Hail to the Thief track ‘Where I End and You Begin’. Around him and the band, who were arranged in and under scaffolding-type boxes, a troupe of actors were working out moves under the watchful eye of choreographer Steven Hoggett and stage director Christine Jones.

This was the end of the third week of off-site rehearsals, one more to go, on Hamlet Hail to the Thief. This kinetic, musical, theatrical marriage – you might say mash-up – of Radiohead’s 2003 album and Shakespeare’s play premiered in 2025, with brief runs in Manchester’s Aviva Studios and at the Royal Shakespeare Company in Stratford-upon-Avon. Now, it was preparing to open at the Barbican in London for a three-month run.

I watched the company, led by returning actor Samuel Blenkin (Alien: Earth) as Hamlet, work on scene 12. Titled State of Play, the script notes describe it as a ‘physical sequence replac[ing] dialogue. The actors and the scenes it replaces [include] Hamlet witnessing Gertrude and Claudius sexually entangled, creating an emotional arc going from “the play’s the thing” and “to be or not to be.”’

The scene is scored by Yorke’s reworking of ‘Where I End and You Begin’, the sixth track on Hail to the Thief, with a male and female vocalist in the corner repeating the climactic lyrics: ‘There’ll be no more lies, I will eat you alive…’
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.
Even in rehearsals, cast and crew and band in mufti, the effect is utterly thrilling.

This is one of the 27 scenes that the play has been edited down to for a running time of between 90 and 100 minutes, the action soundtracked by Yorke’s jigsawed versions of the album’s 14 songs. As the musician, ever the iconoclast, describes Hamlet Hail to the Thief: ‘It moves at a fast pace. It's not four hours. It doesn't have long soliloquies where you can go to sleep, wake up again, you’ve still not missed anything...’ He caught himself and smiled. ‘Um...Did I say that?’
He did indeed, and a lot more besides, when, over lunchbreak, I sat down with Yorke, Jones and Hoggett to discuss the third and biggest outing for their innovative show.
Wallpaper*: Thom, how did constructing this show last year, and now again this year, compare to making an album?

Thom Yorke: When you put a record together, you hope that one piece may move one way. But when it moves in another direction for another track, they're complementing each other. So there's an accumulated emotional effect that happens. Which is the bit that, when we set about this, I hadn't thought about.

There are all these people involved, and everything's happening all around the stage. And some nights the first thing that Hamlet does is get a laugh. And you're like: ‘What, already?’ That kind of thing. That affects how you see the music, too.
But there's also a very selfish element to it. The arc of whatever this is has to satisfy something in my musical head, too.
W*: Christine, what are the origins of this idea?

Christine Jones: I saw the Hail to the Thief tour in 2003 at Madison Square Garden. It was the first time I'd seen Radiohead live, and I was blown away. It changed my DNA structure. Not long after, I was working on a production of Hamlet as a designer. I often write the text out, and I listen to music. I was fresh off this concert, so I was listening to the record, and I literally started writing lyrics along with words from the text. That planted a seed.

Over time, that seed kept growing, and I kept thinking about it. And it was a number of years later when I had the opportunity to ask Thom if it was something that he'd consider collaborating on. And that took a bit of time.
TY: You got a predictable answer!
W*: …which, of course, was ‘no’. But you did say yes, Thom…

TY: Eventually, yeah. It took about five years to get over the presumption of putting those two things together. This is not my world. So I didn't realise, as much as anything, that there's no sense of having to pay homage. This version of Hamlet is not a definitive version of Hamlet.

Then the more you read about these things, the more you realise that nothing is a definitive version of anything. There's no definitive version of a Pinter play. So I had to jump over a few humps in my head before eventually we started properly talking about it.

CJ: In this case, the synergy and uncanny resonances between the play and the music are a particularly fertile collision. But it's us all coming together, and bringing the work that Steven and I have done together for years, bringing experiences of being at Radiohead concerts, of being at other concerts, and seeing how everything impacts each other.

Steven Hoggett: There was something about seeing [Yorke and bandmate Jonny Greenwood’s side-project] The Smile the year before last in New York. The gig was really cheeky. And we were talking for a second about [doing this show] in the round [like The Smile shows] after seeing that gig. But it was the tonality of this cheeky band, that was still as complex and as sophisticated, but were taking our ears on a journey.

It was a big shift watching that gig. We've got 27 scenes. So it's like a greatest hits as a feel and a listening event. And I guess it is akin to – sorry to make the analogy like this, Thom – a Radiohead gig to The Smile. Somebody called The Smile the cheeky younger cousin of Radiohead, and this feels like the cheeky younger cousin of the Hamlet play. It's got an errant nature to it, but it's fleet-footed and it keeps turning itself over.
W*: When you were editing the text, Christine, to get to this ‘greatest hits’ idea of Hamlet, were you trying to shape the remaining text to individual songs? Or was it more freeform than that?

CJ: The first thing I did was, I edited the script. I took a pass at what I call creating a spine-line and pulling out all the pieces that felt the most resonant. Then once I had that, as an exercise, I did say: ‘OK, what if I start at the beginning of the album and I go to the end?’

And that first time through, there was a sense of how different characters connected to different songs thematically. The court being established was [album opening track] ‘2 + 2 = 5’. The ghost being established was ‘The Gloaming’. Ophelia being connected to ‘Sail to the Moon’. Rosencrantz and Guildenstern were ‘Where I End and You Begin’.

We ended up changing a lot of that… Although, as we realised the other day, we do start at the beginning of the album and end at the end of the album. We've made a lot of adjustments and flipped scenes around, flipped songs around, but there is that container.
W*: How has it been for your dancers, Steven –
SH: Oh, I love that you call them dancers. They will love you for that!
W*: – getting their heads around the tricksy rhythms of these songs?

SH: There was that big question, and I do enjoy when somebody does this – a friend of mine, when we said we were doing this, went: ‘Who needs that? Dancing to Radiohead...?’ I was like: ‘Yeah, I understand that. I don't think I want to see that either.’

SH: We don't dance to Radiohead. They actually do a courtly restoration piece of choreography at one point. It's mocked, it's heightened. But the rest of it, we make a real distinction in the room, which is why I made the comment about you calling them dancers. Because they don't dance, they move. The minute you say to somebody ‘dance’, people do weird shit. Whereas if they're moving and it's intrinsic and has a qualitative nature [to] what they're thinking or saying, you can make tonnes of material. So the d-word is not one we drop in the room. Because it inhibits.
W*: When we met in 2003, Thom, with the paint still wet on Hail to the Thief, you insisted it was a pop record. Do you stand by that assessment?
TY: [winces and squirms] I don't f*cking know, do I? Clearly, I've been thinking I've been making pop since we started! So I should probably give up. You laugh, but I'm serious.

W*: The other thing you said was that you'd taken ‘a long six months off’. And then someone close to you said: ‘Why don't you just do a record where you let it happen? Just go in and do it, no agenda, nothing.’ And for you, ‘that made things click’. That energy and that drive – are you seeing a parallel energy and drive here?

TY: We were all [in the band] in agreement with that [idea]. Because we'd been through this [experience]. Kid A was a very long, tortuous process. It was really fun, but we did go a bit f*cking mad. I mean, you build your own studio, and you give yourself no deadline at all... And then after about eight or nine months, [producer] Nigel [Godrich] called it and said: ‘We have to stop. We have to finish whatever the f*ck this is.’

So, yeah, [with Hail to the Thief] we were going the other way. And because we were going the other way, there was no time to go over things. Which, as soon as it came out, I was like: ‘Oh, I kind of wish we had...’ But it's one of those weird things, you lurch from one extreme to the other.
W*: But does that directness now help with this production? Because there's a propulsion to this music, these songs.

TY: I mean, yessss... In the sense that: a lot of the songs lend themselves to be reinterpreted quite easily. And put on different instruments, and slowed down, sped up. I was actually really surprised.

My first test of the whole thing was, they did a read through in New York and they sent me it. I tentatively stumbled through it with acoustic guitar or piano or very basic [instrumentation] underneath to try see what it feels like. To have that music under the words. And I realised quickly: oh, OK, there's a lot of licence here. I can take Jonny's riff on ‘2 + 2’, I can turn it into [something] and it can go anywhere it wants. As soon as it's on the synthesiser, it's almost unrecognisable.
W*: Can you tell us, Christine, about the visuals you've designed for this show?

CJ: I worked with Brett Banakis and Sadra Tehrani as part of a collective. When we first started thinking about this, we were thinking about operating theatres. And recording studios and sound stages. I love recording studio porn. I could just look at recording studios all day long.

Even in the beginning, we weren't sure if the band and the actors were in the same space. [But] we wanted them all to feel like they were definitely in the present together, making this happen. Then over time we started looking at isolation chambers, solitary confinement chambers.

Then we found this piece of research from Nasa, on a resonant acoustic chamber. It's this space where they test the effect of sound waves on objects. They'll put a rocket ship in this room and blast it with sound. That felt like the perfect metaphor for what this world does to Hamlet. He's put into this space, and it is a kind of cruel experiment where the play and the music keep betraying him. And disorienting him. And lying to him. This experiment in how much can one soul take before it completely breaks. So the space is informed by sound.

SH: We liked the idea how speakers can sometimes look really scary. They're big, with those cones. Of course they're sexy and they're black and we see them in gigs and we love them. But actually, there’s the propensity of them to become something to weaponise.
W*: What did you learn from Manchester and Stratford in terms of what worked and what didn’t?
CJ: One of the things that was interesting is that in Manchester, it was a warehouse space. The seating was all made out of bleachers, and it felt like a gig.

TY: Metallic bleachers. When people came into the show, they'd have had three pints thinking it was going to be a gig. Then realised it wasn't. Then they ran for the toilet during the soliloquy. [Which meant the seats going] bang, bang, bang, bang, bang, bang, bang...

CJ: We've been in this balance between it's a gig and it's a play. When we went to the Royal Shakespeare Company, we were in a thrust theatre space. There it felt like a play. Now at the Barbican, we get to land in a sweet spot – the brutalist architecture, the shape of that [room]… We're finding that it can exist in some space in between. Hopefully the Barbican lets us be both a play and a gig instead of one or the other.
TY: It's crazy intimate in there. F*cking bonkers.
W*: Finally, Thom: did your reconstruction or reimagining of these songs inform the performance of any of the Hail to the Thief songs on the Radiohead tour last year?
TY: [splutters] Doing this? Oh, no! What, I come to the Radiohead gig and say, ‘hey, the other band, they kind of nailed this one...’? No, no. That was not happening!
Hamlet Hail to the Thief runs from 31 October 2026 to 23 January 2027 at Barbican Theatre, Silk Street, London, EC27 8DS. Ticket information here

items.title: Zaha Hadid built just two private houses; one’s now for sale
items.description: It's exactly ten years since Dame Zaha Hadid passed away unexpectedly at the age of 65, leaving an unassailable legacy in her Issey Miyake-clad wake. In a strange piece of synchronicity, there’s now an incredibly rare chance to own one of her buildings in the
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: It's exactly ten years since Dame Zaha Hadid passed away unexpectedly at the age of 65, leaving an unassailable legacy in her Issey Miyake-clad wake. In a strange piece of synchronicity, there’s now an incredibly rare chance to own one of her buildings in the heart of London.

Constructed from 2014 onwards, this house in Belgravia’s Grosvenor Crescent Mews has the distinction of being one of only two private residential projects completed by the studio (the other being the Capital Hill Residence outside Moscow).

A unicorn in the London property market, 6 Grosvenor Crescent Mews isn’t just a rare example of Hadid’s work but it’s also a 3,980 sq ft house with integral garage just a stone’s throw from Hyde Park Corner, located in what is Belgravia's only private gated mews.

Gaining permission for such an avant-garde structure in the midst of a thicket of Conservation Areas and listed buildings was no mean feat, even for an architecture of the calibre of Zaha Hadid. The site had boundaries with no fewer than nine different neighbours, placed in such a way that the only public-facing façade was just six metres in width.
That element, a rippling curtain of back-lit brickwork lattices and patterned glass, belies the scale of the house behind it, which extends over four generous 1,000 sq ft floorplans.
Basement kitchen, dining and living area
Basement kitchen, dining and living area

The garage was a planning condition, but it was fitted out to a residential specification so that it can be used as a study area if needed. It adjoins the main reception room, a space bounded by the curved interventions of the polished balustrade rail and the custom-designed staircase, formed from polished concrete and shaped to wind sinuously between the floors.
Atrium views from the lower ground floor
Atrium views from the lower ground floor
Atrium views from the lower ground floor

Like many London mews and conversion projects, the house goes down as well as up, with a kitchen and sitting room located in the basement, beneath a double height space which in itself is topped by a glazed terrace at first floor level. With windows, parapets, courtyards and walls arranged so as to avoid overlooking from surrounding properties, the entire house is cleverly folded into its site, making the most from the available space.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

Utility, plant and stores are tucked away in the basement behind the kitchen, another area that is defined by a trademark Hadidian swoop, this time in the form of a polished kitchen counter that projects out from the wall like a geological form.

From here, the two-storey atrium rises up to the gauzy light that filters through the glass roof, with the polished balustrade playing off the curved concrete stair risers contained behind a glazed wall.

The first floor houses the principal bedroom suite, complete with curved glass and sole access to the terrace. A living wall flanks the perimeter of the property (it’s joined by a brown roof system designed to improve the house’s insulation), while the glazed stair tower rises up beneath the fluted forms of another skylight. On the second floor there are two further ensuite bedrooms, each winding around a central dressing room space.
The artistry and style of 6 Grosvenor Crescent Mews is sadly unrepeatable, making this project a rare opportunity to acquire a functional work of art in the heart of London.

In the decade since her death, the firm Hadid established in Studio 9 of a former school on Bowling Green Lane in Clerkenwell has gone all out into making her wildly exuberant approach into a clearly defined architectural style, Parametricism, translating Hadid’s wild, analogue forms into a heady, AI-infused cocktail of data-shaped aesthetic adventures.
Design details, 6 Grosvenor Crescent Mews
Design details, 6 Grosvenor Crescent Mews
Design details, 6 Grosvenor Crescent Mews
Design details, 6 Grosvenor Crescent Mews
Design details, 6 Grosvenor Crescent Mews
If you can ignore the Succession-like shenanigans that have swirled around ZHA in the years that followed, the Zaha Hadid Foundation holds a fascinating archive of her work.
6 Grosvenor Crescent Mews, London SW1X is for sale at £11.95m through Forbes Gilbert-Green, ForbesGilbertGreen.com

items.title: OKA’s Mori is a new digital companion to brighten up solo living
items.description: Many of us already live with some kind of domestic digital companion, even if it is in the acceptable form of a smart speaker like an Amazon Echo or Google Nest Hub. But what if these inanimate objects were imbued with a little more character? Would interactio
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: Many of us already live with some kind of domestic digital companion, even if it is in the acceptable form of a smart speaker like an Amazon Echo or Google Nest Hub. But what if these inanimate objects were imbued with a little more character? Would interactions become less fraught, frustrating and functional (‘Google, what’s the weather like in London today’)? Might we all just slow down a little, snagged by the lure of a ghost in the machine?

OKA was founded by Wesley Chen and Hua Wang, a self-described ‘nomadic entrepreneur’ with a very specific reason for his approach to robotics. ‘I spent ten years designing mechanisms to make people come back to their phones,’ Wang says candidly, explaining how his new robotics venture OKA (One Kind Artifact) set out to be something different. ‘I watched Fritz Lang’s 1927 film Metropolis and it made me question why robots are still not a part of our lives, nearly 100 years later,’ he says over video from New York.

For Wang, the answer boiled down to two things; the expectations that a robot should be able to do everything a human could do, and the corresponding need for them to be human-scaled, large and mechanical. ‘I couldn’t imagine having such intrusive machinery in my house,’ he admits.

The answer is Mori, a ‘robot that belongs in a home’. At 30cm tall, roughly the same size as a desk lamp, Mori (Japanese for ‘forest’) is explicitly not an appliance, nor a Terminator-style humanoid that needs a whole afternoon to fold your laundry.

The most obvious visual metaphor is a mushroom, with an illuminated hat/cap above a bulbous fabric-covered stem. In between the two sits Mori’s ‘face’, two illuminated eyes and a button (camera) nose. Servos activate a discrete range of fluid movements, eyes dart left and right, eyelids flutter and the little robot offers a convincing portrayal of an introvert tucking itself away beneath its hat and hiding from the world. It’s a distinctly non-threatening piece character design, a static yet personable object that feels part Pixar, part Studio Ghibli, part Flos.

Switch Mori on and tap the stem to wake the device and an elaborate start-up theatre ensues, with the device appearing to run through phases of shyness and curiosity as it wakes. The illuminations cycle through a range of colours, responding to touch and voice, while the fabric body (25 per cent real wool and available in four colours) also incorporates sensors. Mori’s onboard AI will, in time, learn to recognise different people and environments, as well as run through actions in response to commands or taps. New 'personality' quirks and responses will continue to evolve and emerge.

So what’s it all for? Wang describes the device as ‘something to relax and calm you down’, with inbuilt relaxation programs triggered by resting a hand on Mori’s 'head'. In this mode, ambient sounds and lights are generated as part of a guided breathing session. These immersive sessions – forests, seashores, etc – are all accompanied by a swirling light show to help transport you into a different state of mind. Of course, Mori also functions as a regular light.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

Ultimately, OKA wants Mori to be a piece of mindful technology, an object that becomes more and more in sync with the humans around it, thanks in part to the company’s ‘Attentive Intelligence Engine’. Think of it as an alarm clock with character, one that welcomes you home after work, with eyelids that flicker and droop as the evening turns into the small hours, perhaps encouraging you to finish up and go to bed.

This dependence on contextually powered AI also shapes Mori’s response to other stimuli, which it usually translates into movement and light, rather than speech and sound. In this respect, it’s more adjacent to a giant Tamagotchi than it is to an Alexa, but still a step down from a cat.

Mori is the first in what OKA hopes to be a suite of five such mindful ‘Artifacts’, each of which uses robotics and AI technology to offer a new spin on emotional response. Mori’s role is to ‘explore the relationship between humans and their immediate physical environment’, rather than chase diary dates or offer reminders for chores. No two Mori devices will ever be alike – put two or three together and watch them communicate in different ways.

Whether you treat it as animated nightlight, spirited sound therapist, or just a digital pet, Mori shows the potential of immobile yet highly engaged AI-powered objects. With OKA poised to reveal its portfolio of more animated Artifacts in the months to come, we’ll keep you posted.
Mori Founder Edition (limited to 500 units), $649, OKA, OneKindArtefact.com

items.title: Gee’s Bend quilts dress an intriguing furniture debut
items.description: Marfa Stance was built on the belief that surplus materials are not something to conceal, but rather something to celebrate. Those familiar with the British label will instantly recognise its modular, fully reversible outerwear, which combines sophisticated pa
items.author: Ali Morris
paragraphs: Marfa Stance was built on the belief that surplus materials are not something to conceal, but rather something to celebrate. Those familiar with the British label will instantly recognise its modular, fully reversible outerwear, which combines sophisticated patchwork construction with an approach informed by artist Donald Judd's functional design philosophy. Judd lived and worked in Marfa, Texas, from which the brand takes its name.
Crafted in Italy by female-led factories using surplus Japanese and Italian nylon, wool, and cashmere deadstock, the pieces are both utilitarian and luxurious.

This month, seven years after its founding, the brand unveils its first furniture collection, designed in collaboration with Stephen Kenn Studio. ‘We've never believed design should live within one category,’ says Marfa Stance’s founder, British designer Georgia Dant, who describes the move as the ‘logical next step'.

The choice of Los Angeles furniture designer Stephen Kenn as a collaborator was a natural one, she recalls: his studio had supplied the furniture for the brand’s first New York flagship a few years earlier. Like Marfa Stance, Kenn embraces reclaimed materials, celebrating their history, irregularities and inherent character rather than seeking uniformity.

‘The way we think about a piece of outerwear, how it's made, what happens to the materials, how long it can live, how it can change with its owner, is actually very close to how Stephen approaches furniture,’ says Dant, who founded the brand in 2019 after leading men’s and women’s design teams at Burberry and Rag & Bone. ‘We share a belief in utility, longevity, and making something beautiful from what's already around us. This collaboration lets us take that philosophy somewhere completely new.’

For Marfa Stance, Kenn has created a series of three steel-framed chairs and a bench, each with a chunky seat upholstered in quilts made by Alabama’s Gee’s Bend quilters – a community of African American women living along a bend in the Alabama River in Wilcox County, where quilting traditions have been passed down through generations. Marfa Stance has collaborated with the community since 2022, transforming deadstock fabrics sourced from Italy into colourful quilted jackets and blankets.

‘When I first saw a Marfa Stance jacket I was transported back to some of my earliest days studying vintage military clothing,’ says Kenn. ‘The careful consideration and thoughtful details evoked an admiration and immediate kinship. I couldn’t help but wonder, if this jacket were a reversible slip cover, what would it look like?’
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

The chairs are the answer to Kenn’s question. Each is upholstered in a Gee’s Bend quilt and installed at a different Marfa Stance store – Montecito, Chicago, Madison Avenue in NYC, and Chelsea in London – inviting customers to experience the collaboration first-hand.

The chairs are based on two of Kenn's existing designs – the Inheritance Collection – with its blackened steel frame and cotton webbing and leather belts holding loose chunky cushions – and the Ease Collection, with its curved upholstered form made from a combination of different foam densities providing both structure and softness.
Following their in-store debut, the chairs will be available to buy online, with prices on enquiry.

Due to the unique nature of the quilts, each chair is one of a kind and made to order in Los Angeles by Kenn’s small team and local vendors, many of them family-run businesses in East and South LA. They are designed to be repaired and adapted, acquiring character through continued use. Marfa Stance hints that more home pieces could follow. For now, the chairs demonstrate a clever and considered brand expansion that carries Marfa Stance's emphasis on adaptability, craftsmanship and longevity from wardrobe to home.

Ali Morris is a UK-based editor, writer and creative consultant specialising in design, interiors and architecture. In her 16 years as a design writer, Ali has travelled the world, crafting articles about creative projects, products, places and people for titles such as Dezeen, Wallpaper* and Kinfolk.

items.title: How do you create a design to last for a 1,000 years?
items.description: Madhav Kidao and Brando Posocco, the founders of London-based architecture and design studio Nebbia are used to thinking monumentally. Among their works stands out a cathedral-like installation made of stacking blocks for Coachella in 2024, or an aluminium pav
items.author: Rosa Bertoli
paragraphs: Madhav Kidao and Brando Posocco, the founders of London-based architecture and design studio Nebbia are used to thinking monumentally. Among their works stands out a cathedral-like installation made of stacking blocks for Coachella in 2024, or an aluminium pavilion floating over the fountain at the V&A’s John Madejski Garden for London Design Festival.

Their latest commission, as part of Paererewā, a New Zealand national initiative that aims at creating 1,000 works that will last 1,000 years, has led them to rethink their practice’s propensity for monumentality, through time and material.
What is Paererewā? Creating 1,000 works for 1,000 years

The initiative is the brainchild of Still, a company led by Japanese entrepreneur Hideaki Fukutake who gathered a group of like-minded companies that together work towards a long-term plan to enhance local communities through culture and art. Each piece (incorporating sculpture and seating) is commissioned to be a threshold between the mundanity of everyday life and an opportunity for deeper reflection.

The second to be completed, Nebbia’s Interlude is installed on a cliff at Jardine Park, in the south of Aotearoa, with views across Lake Whakatipu and The Remarkables mountain range. When tasked with the commission, Kidao and Posocco had to dig deeper into the idea of longevity through design and architecture.

‘Our first thought was to comprehend what 1,000 years means, both anthropologically and ecologically,’ they recall. ‘New Zealand was uninhabited by humans 1,000 years ago, with the first people arriving only around 800 years ago. Would it still be inhabited in the next 1,000 years? If not, who or what are we designing for?’ The questions led them to design a portal-like sculpture, that can be climbed and sat on: ‘a place for two strangers to serendipitously meet and share knowledge, wisdom or simply an emotional connection.’

The sculpture is made of locally-sourced basalt bluestone, from nearby Timaru. The practical part of the project formed yet another conundrum, as both the millennium element of the project and the seismic conditions of the region (‘forces beyond our control’) led them to imagine a piece evolving over time.

‘We were never tied to the idea that it needed to exist in the same state for 1,000 years,’ they observed. ‘It could grow, degrade or fragment. This led us to research growing something, but we discovered that no native plant species lives for 1,000 years. Stone taps into a conception of time beyond the human-centred viewpoint. Many of our projects explore the idea of impermanence: everything came from somewhere and will become something else, and our interaction with it is fleeting, be it one day or 1,000 years.’
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

Rosa Bertoli was born in Udine, Italy, and now lives in London. Since 2014, she has been the Design Editor of Wallpaper*, where she oversees design content for the print and online editions, as well as special editorial projects. Through her role at Wallpaper*, she has written extensively about all areas of design. Rosa has been speaker and moderator for various design talks and conferences including London Craft Week, Maison & Objet, The Italian Cultural Institute (London), Clippings, Zaha Hadid Design, Kartell and Frieze Art Fair. Rosa has been on judging panels for the Chart Architecture Award, the Dutch Design Awards and the DesignGuild Marks. She has written for numerous English and Italian language publications, and worked as a content and communication consultant for fashion and design brands.

Known for its unfiltered, human approach, each issue brings long-form conversations with artists, writers, designers, and thinkers across disciplines, accompanied by photography that unsettles conventional categories.

The values of the magazine extend beyond print. Through events, collaborations, exhibitions, design objects, and a growing body of short and documentary films, Apartamento builds community in real spaces around the world.

Since 2015, Apartamento has published books across a range of formats: monographs, cookbooks, photobooks, architecture series, artist books, and even a graphic novel. The publishing programme extends the editorial curiosity of the magazine into longer, more sustained forms, spanning art, design, architecture, food, and visual culture.

items.title: A conversation with Eileen Myles for Apartamento magazine issue #37
items.description: Marfa: ‘For a time I / stole trays / from hotels / & now I steal / cups’ writes Eileen Myles in ‘Göteborg’, a poem which becomes a love letter to desire itself. I wonder if any of the stolen objects exist in Eileen’s real world: ‘Yeah, and it was a beautiful w
items.author: Valeria Tusquets
paragraphs: Marfa: ‘For a time I / stole trays / from hotels / & now I steal / cups’ writes Eileen Myles in ‘Göteborg’, a poem which becomes a love letter to desire itself. I wonder if any of the stolen objects exist in Eileen’s real world: ‘Yeah, and it was a beautiful wooden tray. That lives here’. Despite famously moving to New York City to become a poet in 1974, a metropolis which serves as the backdrop for much of their work, in this instance, ‘here’ is Marfa, Texas. Situated in North America’s largest desert with a population currently under 2,000, Marfa became a magnet for creatives after the artist Donald Judd moved there from New York in the ‘70s, and there has been an uneasy truce between outsiders and locals since then. Jokingly referred to as their ‘fortress of solitude’, Eileen’s Marfa home looks like many on their street, with a pickup truck parked outside a chain-link fence and little city blocks of prickly pear cactus dotted around their lot.

Eileen’s work has been translated into dozens of languages, and they have published more than 20 books across poetry, fiction, and nonfiction, earning them a Guggenheim Fellowship and an Andy Warhol Foundation Arts Writers Grant. One of Eileen’s many superpowers as a writer is their ability to marry first-person narrative with more ephemeral truths, or, as they say, ‘trusting the mechanism of desire…[the] desire for certain language to sit over some curve of a moment’. This realness, coupled with writing about a character named ‘Eileen Myles’, has also led to being flattened by labels—another Charles Bukowski or Patti Smith—as they slid between poetry and prose. ‘I have a specific system that downplays grammar in a lot of ways’, they say, but their system of delaying any easy resolution is also grammatical; there’s a really tight thought, but they don’t let it resolve immediately. We are taken away, shown something new. The action is deferred until the text realises its necessary climax.

Inside their home, cut-outs between rooms create a flow where kitchen peeks into office peeks into bedroom peeks into living room. A big picture window in their office, paid for when the show Transparent bought some of Eileen’s poems and based a poet character on them, looks out into the yard towards their ‘writing shack’ which sports a clawfoot bathtub, a bench press and weights, and a desk facing double sliding doors out onto the porch where we sit and sip Topo Chico. While access to DC Comics’ original Fortress of Solitude is controlled by a key carved from super-dense dwarf star material weighing half a million tonnes—imagine lifting 100 elephants or the weight of a small cloud—Eileen’s own abode is guarded by three desert-coloured pups who sound an imposing alarm when we pull up.

items.title: PRE-ORDER: Making a Show, Sabine Marcelis
items.description: Making a Show is a photobook with Dutch artist and designer Sabine Marcelis, published on the occasion of her first museum exhibition at Museum für Gestaltung Zürich, Sabine Marcelis—Light and Color, on view from October 30, 2026 to April 4, 2027. Photographed
paragraphs: Making a Show is a photobook with Dutch artist and designer Sabine Marcelis, published on the occasion of her first museum exhibition at Museum für Gestaltung Zürich, Sabine Marcelis—Light and Color, on view from October 30, 2026 to April 4, 2027. Photographed by Mattia Balsamini inside Sabine’s Rotterdam studio in the months before the opening, the book documents an exhibition in transit: light, colour, and material stretched, poured, altered, and refined until they reach the simplicity that is Sabine’s fingerprint. Smashed mirrors, pink resin slabs, perfect droplets—all part of a symbiotic world, where the work produced inside the studio is in constant conversation with the hands that supply it from outside. Alongside, curator Damian Fopp grounds the book with a written introspection on living inside her universe as the show took shape, declaring by the end that ‘what appears effortless is anything but’. Punctuated by WhatsApp messages and email snapshots between Sabine’s team and the museum’s, Making a Show distils the incantatory movement of an exhibition in the making and the infrastructure of people behind it.

Sabine Marcelis is a Dutch artist and designer based in Rotterdam. Working across installations, objects, and spatial projects, she explores light, colour, and material, collaborating closely with a network of local manufacturers to push each to its limits. For the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival 2026, Sabine designed one of the headlining large-scale art installations, an immersive temporary installation titled Maze. She has also received multiple Designer of the Year honours (2020–2024) and her works are part of permanent museum collections worldwide, including MoMA, the Stedelijk Museum, and the Vitra Design Museum. Sabine Marcelis was previously featured in Apartamento magazine issue #21. Find her story from our digital archive here.

Mattia Balsamini is an Italian photographer based between London and Milan. After joining David LaChapelle’s studio in 2010 as a studio assistant and archivist, Mattia went on to develop personal and editorial projects through collaborations with institutions including MIT and NASA. His work has been exhibited at the Triennale di Milano, MAXXI, the Sandretto Re Rebaudengo Foundation, and the Italian Cultural Institute in San Francisco.

items.title: The Complete Works of Le Chateaubriand (2006–2026)
items.description: This is the story of Le Chateaubriand, the Paris bistro that broke every rule fine dining had. In 2006, Inaki Aizpitarte and Frédéric Peneau took over a humble, century-old bistro in Paris’ 11th arrondissement. Untucked shirts, stubble, blaring music, a photoc
paragraphs: This is the story of Le Chateaubriand, the Paris bistro that broke every rule fine dining had. In 2006, Inaki Aizpitarte and Frédéric Peneau took over a humble, century-old bistro in Paris’ 11th arrondissement. Untucked shirts, stubble, blaring music, a photocopied piece of paper as a menu: punk star chef Inaki and his disciples triggered a tsunami of gastronomic insurrection, launching ‘bistronomy’ and its devious subculture. Le Chateaubriand, originally published in French in 2024 and now translated into English by Florence Beretta and Christine Muhlke, is a memorialisation of their labyrinthine quest for adventure, experimentation, and a really good time.

Inside, a chorus of your favourite chefs’ favourite chefs, critics, regulars, and fundamental players document the uncanny dishes, drunk escapades, Michelin stars, and one-star reviews of a restaurant so notorious the conformists loosened their buttons for it.

As Inaki bows out, two decades later, he leaves behind a mythical record of an indisputable marathon to achieve something unheard of in the 2000s kitchen: freedom. At Le Chateaubriand, the customer is not always right.

Chef Inaki Aizpitarte, the son of Basque immigrants, grew up in Besançon and Bordeaux in the south of France. In 1999, at the age of 27, he travelled to Tel Aviv where he began washing dishes in a restaurant kitchen and discovered his passion for cooking. He moved to Paris in the early 2000s, where he worked at various establishments across the city, including Le Petit Marguery, La Fourchette des Anges, Ishtar Café, Le Café des Délices, La Famille in Montmartre, and Le Baratin. He then helped launch the restaurant at the MAC VAL contemporary art museum in Vitry-sur-Seine.

In 2006, he opened Le Chateaubriand at 129 Avenue Parmentier. His second venture, Le Dauphin, opened in 2010, two doors down from Le Chateaubriand. More recently, he opened Petit Grill Basque, this time in Saint-Jean-de-Luz, in the French Basque Country. Over the years, Aizpitarte has become widely regarded as the ‘godfather of bistronomy’, helping to redefine the Parisian dining scene through his distinctive, informal approach to fine dining.

items.title: ADRIEN BRODY - FANTASTIC MAN
items.description: Special rendezvous with the precise American movie star
paragraphs: Special rendezvous with the precise American movie star

Twenty-two years after he became the youngest ever winner of a best actor Oscar, for ‘The Pianist’, Adrien Brody has gone and done it again, this time taking home an Academy Award for his deeply moving performance as Hungarian architect László Toth in ‘The Brutalist’. What makes it all the more remarkable is that only a few years ago Adrien had all but given up acting. The awards are much deserved, of course. Adrien, 52, is an intense and uniquely gifted actor, which also makes him entertaining company. He doesn’t do things in half measures. He’s all in, all the time, and not afraid to speak his mind. In the following story Adrien engages in some energetic verbal ping-pong and gets dressed up in fashion by his friend Thom Browne. It captures some of the essence of what makes him such an incredible performer.
From Fantastic Man n° 40 – 2025
Photography by ILYA LIPKIN

The instant Adrien Brody sweeps into the room, he begins to express what I will soon come to think of as his resting affect: a kind of intense but fuzzy gratitude. “I just got back from London yesterday night,” he tells me. “Feeling very blessed with all the love that’s been coming my way. It’s a really special moment. It really is.” Maybe it’s just for now, in these hectic weeks promoting ‘The Brutalist’ ahead of the Academy Awards, but it’s with words like these that Brody seems at his most comfortable, and throughout our conversation he will periodically return to similar sentiments, restating and expanding upon them with evident sincerity.

With other kinds of words, though, it will often come to feel as though there are fault lines everywhere. Seconds after this initial declaration, I ask Brody – my question intended as little more than small talk to fill the empty space between us as we greet each other and take our seats – whether it feels like he’s being carried away in a whirlwind. He responds – not just in his words but in his body language too – as though he’s being somehow misunderstood or as though something wonderful is at risk of being spoiled.

“No, it’s not that at all,” he says, correcting me firmly. “No, my feet are on the ground. I’m ultra-present. I’m ultra-present and able to reciprocate the love. It’s different. Being older gives you a degree of perspective. It’s been a very long time since I’ve had an opportunity to do the work that I’m yearning to do. And the work is completed. So this is just something magical.”

Brody will prove to be engaging, fascinating company, and a man with plenty to say. In our conversation there will also be moments where he exudes a sense – verbally, but also through a repertoire of expressions that seem to hover between saddened and harried – that the world doesn’t quite get him.

What I then find myself wondering is whether such a sensibility might be a consequence of setbacks and reversals he has faced along his idiosyncratic chosen path, or whether it’s such a sensibility which sends you down that path in the first place. Conversely, I also find myself wondering whether it’s exactly this kind of off-kilter mindset which, when everything comes together in just the right way, somehow fuels Brody’s singular ability to inhabit and transmit a role like ‘The Brutalist’s’ László Toth with such compelling, all-consuming mastery.

It was back in 2019 when Adrien Brody was first given the script of ‘The Brutalist’, the expansive tale of a visionary Hungarian architect who escapes the Holocaust and makes his way to America, where he finds a new life – one of opportunity, but also one with horrors all of its own. Brody read it in the apartment he and his partner, fashion designer Georgina Chapman, then had in Manhattan. “I found myself very moved by the writing and the breadth of the storytelling, the complexity, the flaws of the character,” he remembers. “The opportunity for me to play someone that is experiencing so much and contending so much in life [was] wonderful. And I did consider parallels of László’s lived experience with my mother’s and my grandparents’ journey.” Brody’s mother, whose maternal grandparents were rounded up and taken to Auschwitz, survived the war in Budapest. She escaped in 1956, at the age of 13, buried under corn in a horse-drawn cart as she and her parents crossed the Austrian border. In New York, Brody grew up around his Hungarian grandparents. “So that, too, definitely is evident to me in reading it – saying: ‘Wow, I’m quite right to play this character.’”

After reading, Brody met with the director, Brady Corbet, who had written the script with his professional and personal partner, the filmmaker and actor Mona Fastvold, for brunch downtown. “A very long meeting – conversed a lot about lots of things,” Brody recalls. Nonetheless, he learned in due course that another actor had been chosen. “The message comes from your agent,” he says. “It’s either you get the message or they hope you’ve forgotten.” That’s the pattern. “I mourned the loss of this one,” he says. “I did not have expectations that it would be what it is today – I still mourned the creative loss of what I wanted to pour into it.”

Brody makes clear that over his career he has learned that this will happen, and maybe even why. “As an actor, you may be right for certain roles and you’re not necessarily eligible for them,” he says. “Even if you are quite a well-known actor and quite a successful actor. Because there are all these factors that are out of your control. You know, there are lists, and lists are based on a number of things that one might deem as an indication of success. Right? You know, consistent box office earnings are the primary reason you would be on the top of a list. But if you do make experimental choices and interesting choices in an artistic pursuit in a business, it’s not met with the same appreciation as, you know, your mother might have for your varied tastes.”

Brody points out that he’s balanced experimentation with “big blockbuster movies,” and that he enjoys those too. “But I like the range,” he says, and his suggestion seems to be that too much range has consequences. “I’m aware of how it has made certain things, such as this even, challenging,” he says. “Where I’m probably the most right performer for the role, but I wasn’t deemed valuable enough.”

This time, thankfully, everything eventually worked out. The film’s shoot was delayed several times, in part because of Covid, and by the time the project fell back in place the actor previously scheduled to play László Toth, Joel Edgerton, was no longer available. Brody heard from his agent that the role was back in play. Even then, it wasn’t as though Brody simply got a call saying the part was his. “No, not at all,” he says. “Not at all.” In the end, though, it was. Finally given the chance, he threw himself into it. “I knew we were making something special,” he says. “I wish I knew why things come when they do. This moment is because we’re very fortunate – all of us who have been involved in this project – that every collaborative creative element lifted up the other.”

It’s around now, a few minutes into our meeting, when another question seems to throw Brody, though this time the person asking is not me. It is the waiter, asking what Brody might like to eat or drink. From Brody’s reaction, you could easily think that he finds such an inquiry – at a pre-booked table by the window in a high-end New York hotel bar – somewhat perplexing. He talks aloud through this latest dilemma. “I’m not sure what I’m needing,” he says, then considers one kind of option. “I’m happy to have a drink,” he weighs, “but I’m also not needing it just yet.” He expands this thought. “I don’t really need anything.”
After vacillating further, he orders an oak milk decaf latte.
“Not too much milk,” he adds. “Just nice and strong.”

That ‘The Brutalist’ would allow Brody such a remarkable professional and creative renaissance is all the more marked given the place he has described finding himself in in recent years: sufficiently dejected by the opportunities coming his way that he had, unannounced, more or less turned his back on movies. As he recently put it, “I didn’t announce I was retiring, but I stepped back.” For a time, he concentrated on other artistic pursuits that he found more fulfilling, principally painting.
