items.title: The 500 Greatest Songs of All Time
items.description: Editor’s note, February 2024: In the two and a half years since Rolling Stone rolled out the all-new, fully revamped version of our 500 Greatest Songs list in September 2021, artists like Beyonce, Lana Del Rey, and Taylor Swift have all released classic tracks
items.author: Rolling Stone
paragraphs: Editor’s note, February 2024: In the two and a half years since Rolling Stone rolled out the all-new, fully revamped version of our 500 Greatest Songs list in September 2021, artists like Beyonce, Lana Del Rey, and Taylor Swift have all released classic tracks. So we’ve updated the list. We kept the update light; the 2021 list covered many decades of popular music, and was the result of a vote among more than 300 artists, writers, producers and industry figures; this update covers three years, from 2021 to early 2024.

In 2004, Rolling Stone published its list of the 500 Greatest Songs of All Time. It’s one of the most widely read stories in our history, viewed hundreds of millions of times on this site. But a lot has changed since 2004; back then the iPod was relatively new, and Billie Eilish was three years old. So we’ve decided to give the list a total reboot. To create the new version of the RS 500 we convened a poll of more than 250 artists, musicians, and producers — from Angelique Kidjo to Zedd, Sam Smith to Megan Thee Stallion, M. Ward to Bill Ward — as well as figures from the music industry and leading critics and journalists. They each sent in a ranked list of their top 50 songs, and we tabulated the results.

Nearly 4,000 songs received votes. Where the 2004 version of the list was dominated by early rock and soul, the new edition contains more hip-hop, modern country, indie rock, Latin pop, reggae, and R&B. More than half the songs here weren’t present on the old list, including a third of the Top 100. The result is a more expansive, inclusive vision of pop, music that keeps rewriting its history with every beat.

- Harry Styles, ‘As It Was’ The lead single from Harry Styles’ third album balances its agitated inner monologue, where the shape-shifting pop star picks at the details of a relationship in crisis, with spun-sugar synths that give cover to his torment. From its playful opening — Styles’ goddaughter Ruby giggling “Go on, Harry, we want to say goodnight to you!” — to its singsong bridge, during which Styles’ thoughts are ping-ponging around his head at “high-speed internet” velocities, “As It Was” paints an unusually vivid picture. Everything might seem fine on first glance, but it all becomes more troubling (“What kind of pills are you on?”) with each repeated glimpse.

- Townes Van Zandt, ‘Pancho and Lefty’ An epic story-song about a bandit and the friend who betrays him, “Pancho and Lefty” became a country hit thanks to Willie Nelson and Merle Haggard’s 1983 duet. But it’s the songwriter’s own forlorn reading, on 1972’s The Late Great Townes Van Zandt, that best conveys the doomed fates of the main characters. It begins with what might be one of the most descriptive opening verses in the country-folk canon: “Living on the road my friend/was gonna keep you free and clean/now you wear your skin like iron/your breath as hard as kerosene.” “It’s hard to take credit for the writing,” Van Zandt said in 1984, “because it came from out of the blue.”

- Lizzo, ‘Truth Hurts’ “That song is my life and its words are my truth,” Lizzo wrote at the time. She had to tack on a writing credit to British singer Mina Lioness, who had tweeted its iconic line “I just took a DNA test, turns out I’m 100 percent that bitch,” but the power of this gale-force breakup banger was pure Lizzo, uproariously swaggering and endearingly soulful. “Truth Hurts” was originally released in 2017, but the song got a big boost two years later, when Gina Rodriguez day-drunkenly sang it in the Netflix show Someone Great, and it became Lizzo’s signature hit.

- Harry Nilsson, ‘Without You’ “We did it because my career was on the wane and we wanted something to make a hit,” Harry Nilsson bluntly told an interviewer when asked why he covered Badfinger’s near-despondent ballad: “I heard it and searched through every Beatles album for two and a half weeks, trying to find out which one of their tunes it was.” Producer Richard Perry agreed, piling on the strings to showcase Nilsson’s desperate lunge of a vocal. Both were right — the song went to Number One and earned a Grammy nomination for Record of the Year.

- Carly Simon, ‘You’re So Vain’ The holy mother of all diss tracks, “You’re So Vain” contains one of the most enduring musical mysteries of all time. Just who is so vain that he probably thinks the song is about him? Simon previously revealed that actor Warren Beatty inspired the second verse of the song (“Oh, you had me several years ago/When I was still naive”), but speculation abounds regarding the other man (or men) behind the ire. Either way, the track — boasting omnipresent Seventies arranger Paul Buckmaster’s orchestration and Mick Jagger’s background vocals — is pure soft-rock fire.

- Cyndi Lauper, ‘Time After Time’ Cyndi Lauper was nervous about “Time After Time” — the aching ballad she wrote in the studio with keyboardist Rob Hyman to finish off her blockbuster solo debut, She’s So Unusual. “I asked them to please not put ‘Time After Time’ out as the first single,” Lauper said. “People would never have accepted me. If you do a ballad first, and then a rocker, that doesn’t work.” Her instincts were right: Following the jaunty “Girls Just Want to Have Fun,” “Time” became her first Number One.

- The Pixies, ‘Where Is My Mind?’ No song typifies the freakish pop instincts that made the Pixies stand out in a sea of gloomy Reagan-era bands better than “Where Is My Mind?” Joey Santiago’s lead guitar is catchier than most Top 40 hooks, and by the time Fight Club made this song iconic a decade after its release, it had already formed part of the DNA of countless alternative-radio hits in the years between, from Nirvana to Korn. When an interviewer in 1988 asked about his unique ability to crank out great songs, Black Francis’ answer was typically cryptic: “It’s nice to have space. How much can one brain deal with?”

- Kanye West, ‘Stronger’ Explaining the tighter, broader-reaching songs on his third album, Graduation, Kanye West said, “I applied a lot of the things I learned on tour [in 2006] with U2 and the Rolling Stones, about songs that rock stadiums. And they worked!” West found the inspiration for his most grandiose statement to date from Daft Punk’s “Harder, Better, Faster, Stronger,” which he sampled and reshaped. West is a big fan of the French duo: “These guys really stick with the whole not-showing-their-faces thing. Just amazing discipline — that’s straight martial-arts status.”

- Miles Davis, ‘So What’ It’s likely that no song on this list has soundtracked more dinner parties than Kind of Blue’s warm, welcoming first track. But at the time it was a jarring departure, trading bebop chord changes for a more open-ended modal style. According to pianist Bill Evans, the trumpeter worked up his material just hours before recording dates, but the all-star band here sounds like it’s been living with “So What” for years: Saxophonists John Coltrane and Cannonball Adderley turn in solos that have since become as iconic as any in jazz history, and the rhythm section of Evans, bassist Paul Chambers, and drummer Jimmy Cobb swings like it’s dancing on air.

- Bad Bunny, ‘Titi Me Pregunto’ “Tití Me Preguntó” is a showcase for Puerto Rican superstar Bad Bunny’s unbridled creativity and eccentric pop genius, mixing frantic dembow beats, a classy sample by bachata master Anthony Santos, and a coda with a dash of Latin psychedelia to the global mainstream. He does it all with panache and a healthy sense of humor. Using the archetype of the concerned Latin American aunt asking about her nephew’s potential girlfriends as a starting point, he launches into a hilarious tirade of salacious puns to a bouncy party vibe that — in typical Bad Bunny fashion — unexpectedly morphs into moody self-reflection.

- Lil Nas X, ‘Old Town Road’ Montero Hill was an Atlanta college dropout sleeping on his sister’s couch and looking to break into music when he came across a track he liked by a Dutch 19-year-old called YoungKio that was based around a banjo sample from a Nine Inch Nails track. “I was picturing, like, a loner cowboy runaway,” he told Rolling Stone. Within a year “Old Town Road” was the longest-running Number One song of all time, seeming to sum up eons of American cross-cultural love and theft in just one minute and 53 seconds.

- The Breeders, ‘Cannonball’ Notified by fax that her services in the Pixies were no longer required, Kim Deal called up her twin sister, Kelley, to be her new guitarist (never mind that she didn’t know how to play guitar) and had the last laugh when this absurdist gem became an MTV phenomenon in 1993. “When people were talking about the Breeders being a one-off,” Kelley told Rolling Stone, “I was like ‘No, actually … the Pixies are a side project.'” A little over a year later, the Breeders were on an extended break of their own, but the effortlessly fun trampoline bounce of “Cannonball” is one for all time.

- The Weeknd, ‘House of Balloons’ Far from the international superstar he’d become, Toronto singer-songwriter Abel Tesfaye didn’t even send out photos or do any interviews when he released the first Weeknd album. “The whole ‘enigmatic artist’ thing, I just ran with it,” he said. “No one could find pictures of me. It reminded me of some villain shit.” But the title track of House of Balloons nevertheless set the course for his career, both thematically — drugs and sex, meet depression — and musically, with its sample of Siouxsie and the Banshees’ “Happy House” announcing a new direction for R&B.

- Solange, ‘Cranes in the Sky’ In an interview with her sister Beyoncé, R&B innovator Solange Knowles described how this song was inspired, in part, by overzealous real estate development she noticed around Miami: “This idea of building up, up, up that was going on in our country at the time, all of this excessive building, and not really dealing with what was in front of us.” She turned the metaphor inward to examine her own feelings about change, self-doubt, and aspiration, finishing the song years after it was originally conceived with producer Raphael Saadiq to create a lavish moment of neo-soul introspection.

- Lil Wayne, ‘A Milli’ Producer Bangladesh looped the opening chords from Gladys Knight and the Pips’ “Don’t Burn Down the Bridge,” then segued to a drill-like volley of trap drums. He gave the beat to his friend Shanell — a onetime R&B singer on Wayne’s Young Money Entertainment — to pass along. Wayne initially had grand plans for “A Milli”: He wanted to use the instrumental as skits for rappers like Tyga, Hurricane Chris, Corey Gunz, and Lil Mama. In the end, though, “A Milli” is just Weezy solo, blacking out in the booth and dazzling everyone who hears him.

- Azealia Banks, ‘212’ In 2011, Azealia Banks was a teenage rapper-singer whose clear talent yielded a development deal with XL Recordings but little else. “She had been working on a collection of tracks and there was one Dutch house-sounding one that was just absolutely insane,” producer Jacques Greene recalled. Banks freestyled ferociously about her New York hometown and, uh, cunnilingus over the jittery beats of Belgian house duo’s Lazy Jay’s “Float My Boat.” Initially released in 2011 as a viral track, “212” was a hip-house banger that earned Banks a deal with Interscope and served notice that this uninhibited provocateur would not be constrained.

- Weezer, ‘Buddy Holly’ Never has geek been so chic as in Weezer’s 1994 breakout single, “Buddy Holly.” Written for frontman Rivers Cuomo’s girlfriend, the poppy ode to nerdy romance was almost left off the band’s self-titled debut, also known as the Blue Album, due to Cuomo and now-ex-member Matt Sharp’s reticence. “We had the sense that it could be taken as a novelty song, and people aren’t going to take the album seriously,” Sharp told Rolling Stone. After producer Ric Ocasek heard the receptionist at the recording studio humming it, he insisted they keep it in.

- The Four Tops, ‘I Can’t Help Myself (Sugar Pie, Honey Bunch)’ One of Motown’s most rousing anthems, “I Can’t Help Myself” was inspired by songwriter Lamont Dozier’s grandfather, who’d call the women his hairdresser wife fixed up “sugar pie” and “honey bunch.” During the recording, engineer Harold Taylor recalled, “People were banging on the door of the studio; they were so ecstatic about what they heard.” Nevertheless, Levi Stubbs asked Brian Holland if he could do another take. Holland promised him they’d do it soon — and Stubbs’ first pass hit Number One.

- Lady Gaga, ‘Bad Romance’ Shortly after Gaga had established herself as a star, she catapulted to a next level of weirdness with this Nadir “RedOne” Khayat production, which drew upon the electronic music Gaga had been inundated with while touring Europe. “I want the deepest, darkest, sickest parts of you that you are afraid to share with anyone because I love you that much” is how she summed up the idea behind the song. Fittingly, she debuted the hit-to-be at Alexander McQueen’s show at Paris Fashion Week.

- Robert Johnson, ‘Cross Road Blues’ The primal terror in the Mississippi bluesman’s voice, and his mystifying slide guitar playing, transfixed the Sixties generation of British rockers: “I could take the music only in very small measures because it was so intense,” said Eric Clapton. Recorded during a session at a San Antonio hotel room in 1936, two years before Johnson was murdered at 27, “Cross Road Blues” is a mythmaking statement of spiritual desolation and scorched-earth betrayal — even if the legend that it’s about Johnson selling his soul to the devil in exchange for his monster guitar chops is, as far as we know, apocryphal.

- Biz Markie, ‘Just a Friend’ Nobody beats the Biz (1964-2021), an impossibly good-natured DJ, rapper, producer, human beatboxer, and hip-hop personality who broke big with this ode to the friend zone off his second album. Built on a fat beat, plinking piano, and his charmingly off-key singing, “Just a Friend” interpolates Freddie Scott’s 1968 song “(You) Got What I Need” as Biz warbles about a love that will never come to pass. It was based on real life. As he told Rolling Stone in 2000, “I was talking to this girl from L.A., and every time I called her, this dude was at her house, and she’d say, ‘Oh, he’s just a friend.’ I hated that.”

- Santana, ‘Oye Como Va’ Growing up in San Francisco, Carlos Santana was shaped by the city’s psychedelic explosion. “You cannot take LSD and not find your voice,” he once claimed, “because there is nowhere to hide.” And while his early heroes were bluesmen, he changed history with this foundational Latin-rock reworking of a 1962 salsa number by Cuban percussionist Tito Puente. Santana kept the original’s cha-cha pulse but replaced its horns with Greg Rolie’s organ and Carlos’ lysergic guitar flares. Said Puente years later, “He put our music, Latin rock, around the world, man.”

- Juvenile feat. Lil Wayne and Mannie Fresh, ‘Back That Azz Up’ In the late Nineties, Mannie Fresh’s diamond-sharp productions for Cash Money Records helped put New Orleans in the center of the hip-hop map. The title of this hit was so reminiscent of local artist DJ Jubilee’s single “Back That Thang Up” that Jubilee sued (unsuccessfully) for infringement, and the beat rode the “Triggerman” rhythm that is foundational to New Orleans bounce. Juvenile freestyled his best shit-talking bounce rhymes, and Lil Wayne shut it down with a “drop it like it’s hot” hook. As Mannie said, “[He] immediately was just like, ‘Shit, I’m getting a piece of this.’”

- The Go-Gos, ‘Our Lips Are Sealed’ The radiant first hit of the Go-Go’s was influenced, according to writer Jane Wiedlin, by “the Buzzcocks and Sixties girl-group stuff.” It was also inspired by a clandestine relationship she was having with Terry Hall, of U.K. ska group the Specials, who got a co-writing credit because Wiedlin based the lyrics on some poetry he’d written her in a letter. “It was pretty personal,” Wiedlin recalled. “I mean he had a fiancee at the time — nowadays I wouldn’t touch that with a 10-foot pole, but I was 19, and I was like ‘fiancee shmiancee.’”

- Kris Kristofferson, ‘Sunday Mornin’ Comin’ Down’ The desolation of spirit in Kris Kristofferson’s “Sunday Mornin’ Comin’ Down” is so heavy, so apparent, that it’s almost hard to listen to. But that despair is exactly what drew Johnny Cash to sing it on his TV variety show in 1970. Kristofferson cut his own stunning studio version that same year for his debut album, Kristofferson. Cash’s interpretation, more shuffling and accessible, is the one most listeners turn to, but listen to them back-to-back if you can, and marvel at how Kristofferson’s lyrics about being hung over, alone, and desperate shake your soul.

- Janet Jackson, ‘Rhythm Nation’ Jackson’s socially conscious Number Two hit came together late in the sessions for her blockbuster LP Rhythm Nation 1814. Co-producer Jimmy Jam recalled being in the studio and “switching between MTV and CNN. Watching music videos on one side and watching atrocities on the other. Somehow they all merged together. The idea for ‘Rhythm Nation’ was you can dance, but we can also do something more intelligent.” When Jam heard Sly and the Family Stone’s “Thank You (Falettinme Be Mice Elf Agin)” at a restaurant, he raced to the studio to sample it.

- Curtis Mayfield, ‘Move On Up’ Mayfield’s irresistible “Move On Up” was politically empowering, morally demanding, and effortlessly propulsive, powered by swinging horns and tangy congas — the nine-minute LP version, with its powerful drum break, laid a foundation for disco and hip-hop alike. Mayfield’s message was just as steadfast: that pride and dignity were paramount for Black America to rise. “I’m not trying to say anything to make you think, ‘Well, this is the way, this is the only way,'” Mayfield said. “I’m trying to cover the whole subject.”

- Tammy Wynette, ‘Stand by Your Man’ From the start, this pledge of wifely devotion, the first song Wynette ever co-wrote, was a cultural lightning rod. Feminists recoiled from its pledge of unquestioning fidelity in the Seventies, and Hillary Clinton defined herself a modern woman by slamming the song during Bill Clinton’s first presidential run. But the recording itself steamrolls over ideological objections, as the catch in Wynette’s voice on the verses gives way to a vocal swell that rises to meet the epic sweep of Billy Sherrill’s production.

- Peter Gabriel, ‘Solsbury Hill’ Shortly after Gabriel quit Genesis in 1975, he climbed to the top of Little Solsbury Hill in Somerset, England, to reflect on his life-changing decision. It inspired his debut solo song, in which he explained to fans why he felt the need to go out on his own. Musically, it was a departure too, a pastoral tune with a 12-string acoustic guitar lead that was pointedly different from Genesis’ prog-rock. The song has since become ubiquitous in movies and film trailers. “Maybe I’ve let it go too much,” he admitted to Rolling Stone in 2011.

- The Animals, ‘The House of the Rising Sun’ “We were looking for a song that would grab people’s attention,” said Animals singer Eric Burdon. They found it with the old American folk ballad “The House of the Rising Sun.” In 1962, Bob Dylan had sung this grim tale of a Southern girl trapped in a New Orleans whorehouse. The Animals, from the English coal town of Newcastle, changed the gender in the lyrics, and keyboardist Alan Price created the new arrangement (and grabbed a composer’s credit). Price also added an organ solo inspired by Jimmy Smith’s hit “Walk on the Wild Side.”

- Gladys Knight and the Pips, ‘Midnight Train to Georgia’ Songwriter Jim Weatherly originally composed this as “Midnight Plane to Houston,” only to change it for Cissy Houston (Whitney’s mom) to something “more R&B … in order to get it onto Black radio.” Weatherly had already penned “Neither One of Us,” Knight and the Pips’ Number Two hit, and when they heard “Midnight Train,” they took it to the top. “I never really imagined writing R&B songs,” Weatherly admitted. “I really thought I was writing country songs.” It reflected the times; the 1970s were the first decade since after World War I in which more African Americans were moving to the South than leaving it.

- Dixie Chicks, ‘Goodbye Earl’ A murder ballad with a modern, feminist twist, this jaunty song about poisoning an abusive husband spawned disparate reactions. Some stations banned it, apparently concerned that it would spawn a rash of hubby offings; others shared the number for domestic-abuse hotlines. When the label reps listened to the Chicks’ Fly album, though, they were more concerned with another song: “Sin Wagon,” with its reference to “mattress dancing.” “You can’t say [that],” Natalie Maines recalls their manager’s relayed message from the execs, “but they love the song about premeditated first-degree murder.”

- Mazzy Star, ‘Fade Into You’ Singer Hope Sandoval and guitarist Dave Roback, the prime movers behind Mazzy Star, were active in the 1980s neo-psychedelic Paisley Underground scene in Los Angeles. After Sandoval replaced singer Kendra Smith in the band Opal, David Roback and Sandoval reconstituted the band under the name Mazzy Star. Their second album yielded this spaced-out hit, perhaps dream pop’s ultimate statement of blurry desire. “We’re not so concerned about the outside world,” said Roback. “[Each song] is its own world unto itself.”

- Nirvana, ‘Come as You Are’ “It’s just about people and what they’re expected to act like,” Kurt Cobain said. “The lines in the song are really contradictory. They’re kind of a rebuttal to each other.” The song is driven by a simple riff that Butch Vig goosed with a flanged, subaquatic guitar effect. Cobain apparently lifted it from a 1984 song by U.K. art-metal band Killing Joke, who Dave Grohl paid back 12 years later by drumming on their 2003 album. In the wake of Cobain’s suicide, though, the most haunting lyric would become, “And I swear that I don’t have a gun.”

- Luther Vandross, ‘Never Too Much’ The Eighties’ major male R&B balladeer’s solo debut was financed in part from money he made singing jingles for KFC and 7UP. Vandross had been pushed to do his own thing by Roberta Flack, for whom he’d sung background. Said Vandross: “She said, ‘Luther, you’re too comfortable sitting on that stool singing “ooh and aaah.”‘ Roberta was single-handedly responsible for me starting my own career.” What pushed her was hearing the demo of “Never Too Much” — one of the most buoyant love songs of the Eighties, with Vandross’ high notes as delicate as soap bubbles.

- Daft Punk feat. Pharrell Williams, ‘Get Lucky’ When Pharrell Williams volunteered to appear on Daft Punk’s fourth album, he told them he’d been thinking about Chic legend Nile Rodgers musically; fortuitously, the French dance producers could play him a track they had on hand that they’d made with Rodgers himself. The result was “Get Lucky,” which, as the lead single from their disco-flavored album Random Access Memories, rose like a phoenix to become the song that defined its year. “I think the robots are leading,” Williams told Rolling Stone. “Daft Punk, they’re definitely leading.”

- Joni Mitchell, ‘Help Me’ Mitchell’s 1974 album, Court and Spark, her biggest-selling ever, was also the one that she held the tightest amount of musical control over to date. “I guided everything into place on Court and Spark — even though I didn’t play it, I sang it, and then they played it from that, and it was pretty much as writ,” she said. (Her next album, The Hissing of Summer Lawns, was looser and more jazz-oriented.) “Help Me,” recorded with the jazz group Tom Scott’s L.A. Express, features one of Mitchell’s sultriest vocals and most brocaded arrangements, inspiring Prince, 13 years later, to pay the song lyrical tribute in his “Ballad of Dorothy Parker.”

- John Lee Hooker, ‘Boom Boom’ Hooker, whose canny blues boogie became a root integer for early rock & roll, said this swinging, swaggering bit of primal thump was inspired by his inability to get to a regular gig on time. “There was a young lady named Luilla,” Hooker said. “She was a bartender [at the Apex Bar in Detroit]. I’d always be late, and whenever I’d come in she’d point at me and say, ‘Boom Boom, you’re late again.’ One night she said, ‘Boom boom, I’m gonna shoot you down.’ She gave me a song, but she didn’t know it.” Keith Richards said of Hooker, “Even Muddy Waters was sophisticated next to him.” That was a compliment.

- Van Morrison, ‘Into the Mystic’ Delectably arranged, transportingly sung, this may be the definitive Morrison song — an evocation of “the days of old” that feels like a lover’s whisper. The highlight of 1970’s classic Moondance, “Into the Mystic” benefited from a new, more organic way of recording for him: “It was more like working with an actual band rather than a bunch of session guys,” Morrison said. As for the lyrics, he’d admit, “So many of my songs from that Seventies period, I haven’t a clue what they’re about. A lot of the time, I was just picking up on a vibe.”

- Roy Orbison, ‘Crying’ Orbison said he wrote this lush, dreamy ballad after an encounter with an old flame: “Whether I was physically crying or just crying inside is the same thing.” His near-operatic performance culminated in a high, wailing note, which Orbison never lost the capacity to hit before his death, in 1988. “He sounded like he was singing from an Olympian mountaintop and he meant business,” Bob Dylan wrote in Chronicles. “He was now singing his compositions in three or four octaves that made you want to drive your car over a cliff. He sang like a professional criminal.”

- Steel Pulse, ‘Ku Klux Klan’ The first great British reggae band — and some of the style’s finest songwriters — made their Island Records debut with this incendiary look at the rising tide of racist violence in late-Seventies Britain: “The Ku Klux Klan/Here to stamp out Black man.” They underlined the lyric by actually performing the song live — including a memorable BBC appearance — wearing white Klan headgear. “The hoods seemed extreme at the time, but that’s what we are in a way,” vocalist Michael Riley said. “When we wore them, people started questioning what the song was about instead of just dancing to it.”

- Sade, ‘No Ordinary Love’ Helen Adu’s small but fully inhabited range has been her secret weapon from the beginning. “I decided that if I was gonna sing, I would sing how I speak, because it’s important to be yourself,” she said. Her voice cracks before she reaches the first chorus of this 1992 hit, playing up the romantic drama of the lyric. Even better, so does Stuart Matthewman’s guitar; in the middle of this otherwise mellow groove, he overdubs a seriously moody and low-key noisy part that gives the whole thing a welcome edge. Sade — it’s not just the singer’s name, it’s also a band.

- Beck, ‘Loser’ In 1992, 22-year-old Beck Hansen was scraping by as a video-store clerk while performing bizarro folk songs at L.A. coffeehouses. After friends offered to record some songs, Beck cut “Loser” in his producer’s kitchen. It became the centerpiece of the album Mellow Gold. At first people took “Loser” to be a mere novelty hit, but Beck knew better. “You’d have to be a total idiot to say, ‘I’m the slacker-generation guy. This is my generation.… we’re not gonna fuckin’ show up,'” he said. “I’d be laughed out of the room in an instant.”

- Bon Jovi, ‘Livin’ on a Prayer’ Like his New Jersey model Bruce Springsteen, Bon Jovi concentrates on working-class heroes and heroines. “Livin’ on a Prayer,” co-written with guitarist Richie Sambora, pumped the everyday struggles of Tommy and Gina full of grandeur — guitar-pick slides, dramatic pauses, the inevitable key change — and continues to resonate today. “It’s great that we wrote songs so long ago that people can still relate to,” Bon Jovi said in 2005. “When I hear ‘Livin’ on a Prayer,’ I think to myself, ‘We wrote that. That song has really made its mark. I guess that works.'”

- Lana Del Rey, ‘A&W’ “A&W” is maximum Lana Del Rey: a sweeping, seven-minute epic that follows the sunburned, SoCal folk rock she’s perfected on recent albums back to the hip-hop-inspired pop productions of her early discography. That musical scope is paired with a narrative that’s no less ambitious — vulnerable and lurid, nostalgic and hopeless, funny and utterly bleak. And the bow tying it all together? The name of classic root beer brand, “A&W” used as shorthand for “American Whore,” because no one bends American iconography to their will like Lana Del Rey.

- Jefferson Airplane, ‘White Rabbit’ The song that brought acid rock to Middle America was a heady rock bolero written by vocalist Slick, reportedly after taking LSD and listening to Miles Davis’ Sketches of Spain. She first recorded it with her earlier band, the Great Society, before rebooting it with the Airplane. “Our parents read us stories like Peter Pan, Alice in Wonderland, and The Wizard of Oz,” Slick said. “They all have a place where children get drugs, and are able to fly or see an Emerald City or experience extraordinary animals and people.… And our parents are suddenly saying, ‘Why are you taking drugs?’ Well, hello!”

- Sister Nancy, ‘Bam Bam’ Nancy (a.k.a. Ophlin Russell) was the DJ (mic controller) for Kingston’s Stereophonic sound system when she met reggae producer Winston Riley in the late Seventies. “I really admired how he took recording serious,” Nancy said. “You couldn’t go into his studio and do any foolishness.” Their peak, “Bam Bam,” is one of the great early dancehall anthems, booming but bright, tough but playful — and it’s been sampled extensively by everyone from Lauryn Hill to Kanye West.
- Missy Elliot, ‘The Rain (Supa Dupa Fly)’ As producers, Elliott and Timbaland had already made their rhythmic impact on hip-hop and R&B before Missy’s first single. And some high-profile features

items.title: Bill Burr: 'I Didn't Want to Be the Angry Guy'
items.description: B ill Burr would like to make one thing crystal clear: He never wanted to be “the angry guy.”
items.author: David Fear
paragraphs: B ill Burr would like to make one thing crystal clear: He never wanted to be “the angry guy.”

Oh, the legendary stand-up knows that he has a reputation as someone who can rage with the best of them. His unparalleled ability to vent his spleen onstage and on his twice-weekly Monday Morning Podcast, which Burr started way back in 2007, has long fueled his popularity. “Believe me, dude,” the 58-year-old comedian says, “I can blow my top like anybody. I can still lose my shit. I’ve got 50-something years of practice of that.”

But Burr has been working on himself a lot over the past few years. And while there is no shortage of things that still make him mad — social media, tech billionaires, your everyday displays of blatant hypocrisy, the whole left-versus-right thing — he has finally mastered the art of anger management, as well as letting go of a lot of the pain behind it. Part of this change was spurred by a mind-blowing mushroom trip Burr took in the early 2020s, which he memorialized in his seventh comedy special, Live at Red Rocks. Part of it was the result of therapy, which Burr has credited with saving his life. Part of it involves his loved ones and realizing that he had accidentally become the very person he vowed to never be.

And part of it, as Burr will confess during our hour-plus conversation, was an unexpected moment of clarity that happened when he was preparing for his role in The Social Reckoning, writer-director Aaron Sorkin’s return to the world of Facebook, some 16 years after he helped give the world The Social Network. Burr’s character, a composite of several longtime investors, is worried that Mark Zuckerberg (played with characteristic intensity by Jeremy Strong) isn’t taking a whistleblower and a series of Wall Street Journal exposés seriously enough. Coming on the heels of his turn in the all-star Broadway revival of Glengarry Glen Ross last year, it’s a great example of both Burr’s facility as an ensemble player and his ability to parlay his comic persona into a legitimate acting career. But there was an added benefit: A spontaneous crying jag while rehearsing lines prompted Burr to finally address decades’ worth of issues and become a much happier version of himself.

Yes, Burr still blows gaskets — but on a scale of one to 10, he’s no longer “coming in at an eight because someone got my dinner order wrong.” Yes, Burr is still hilarious — probably more than he’s ever been, both in his own estimation and gauging by the dozens of record-breaking, sold-out shows he’s played everywhere from Boston to London to Greece. No, he hasn’t lost his edge, even if he knows he’s lost some fans who expect him to be a misanthrope 24/7. But as he’s been touring his latest stand-up hour around the U.S., he’s now dedicated to countering the divisiveness he believes is tearing this country apart. Enough with the angry guy. “I want to be the meet-in-the-middle guy,” Burr says.
Watch the video interview below
The Social Reckoning is not a follow-up to The Social Network, exactly. But it’s Aaron Sorkin, it’s about Facebook …

Yeah, it’s about a whistleblower that was working at Facebook. When it started to go sideways, she reached out to somebody at The Wall Street Journal, which caused all of this internal strife with the company. It put some information out there that people needed to know. Social media platforms are [still] new. We’re just seeing the fallout of them now. It started off as fun and silly, and then it got monetized, and then it just got evil.
One minute you’re using it to talk to an old high school buddy. The next, somebody’s being dragged before Congress to talk about why Instagram is evil for teenage girls.

That is kind of what happened. The internet’s this crazy place. I don’t understand why you can’t say curse words on TV, but you can post whatever you want on the internet, and there’s no rules of libel or slander and all of this stuff. And now with AI, everybody is just like, “Well, you know, it’s here … so you just have to deal with it.” It’s weird.
Who asked for this AI wave?

Nobody. Nobody wants it. That’s the thing. Maybe CEOs want AI because they don’t want to pay anybody. They’ve never wanted to pay anybody. But we’re too busy yelling at each other about red ties and blue ties, so we don’t realize we’re on the same team.
So if you’re in an ensemble with an actor who’s maybe got a certain process, a certain way that they need to kind of get into a scene …
How do you work with somebody who needs to approach things in their own specific way?

Everybody’s got a process. And if their process starts spilling over to your cup, you gotta let them know that doesn’t go in this cup. You go drink your shit over there. Whatever the fuck you need to do.
“You learn the most through the failure of bombing.”
Why are you laughing? It’s like you think I’m referring to someone in particular.
You know what? I’m going Henry Hill. “I’m just listening.” I’m just listening [laughs].

The Social Reckoning is getting into this stuff that you’ve been talking about in your act for the past few years — the lack of accountability, how the media works, the way tech is taking control of our lives. Did this seem like a natural extension of what you’ve been doing onstage?

It’s way deeper. You know, I’m a stand-up. I’m joking around. But we live in a world where if somebody tells their version of the truth of what’s going on, it’s like they’re trying to escape Russia in the Eighties. It’s insane. [Facebook] is an American company that seems to function like the CIA, which is really sort of indicative of you’re doing something wrong.

I mean, if you look at the response to the Luigi [Mangione] thing. It wasn’t “Maybe we need to look at what we’re doing if it makes some crazy person do this.” [Healthcare executives’] response was to take their faces off of the internet and get security. It’s like, “You don’t think you need to examine this? You’re just the CEO of a business. Why do you need this level of security?”

Even just touring as a comic, I’ve seen it change. It used to be we hated the Russians. Now it’s like, Texas hates California, California hates Texas. These people hate Florida. Everybody hates New York. It’s like, “Guys, same teams. We’re on the same teams here.”

I was talking about that ICE stuff onstage, talking about my people, white people. We’re not nearly as upset as we need to be, because we don’t see ourselves going into the van. I go, “Who do you think’s going in the van next?” And this guy in the crowd yells, “Liberals!” And I go, “Did you just say liberals?” Like, dude, you’re literally talking about half of your team. They’re gonna work their way back to you eventually. People think they’re in the in-group. They think they’re gonna get under the mountain or get on the spaceship. You’re not. They’re using you, and they’re making you not like me, and they’re trying to make me not like you.
Part of the impetus to start working on yourself came from an acting gig, right?
Yeah, this acting gig. The Social Reckoning role.
As my therapist would say, let’s hear more about this.

I was in my hotel room, getting ready to do this big scene the next day. I got about a page and a half in, and one of the lines was my character was disappointed, probably in the Mark Zuckerberg character. I said the line, and it made me choke up, like I was gonna cry. But it didn’t serve the scene. The scene was not at that emotional level. I was thinking, “What is this?” So I stopped myself, because that’s what you do as a guy. You’re not allowed to cry.

So then I went back to the top. I went through it again — and the same thing happened. And then I started freaking out, being like, “I’m gonna, like, emotionally lose it, I’m gonna look stupid, and they’re gonna fire me.” Some actors think if you’re crying that’s good. Well, not if it doesn’t call for it. It would have been bizarre. I literally just went, like, “OK, what is this?”

It’s almost like when you’re on mushrooms and you get an answer. For some reason, I got an answer, and I realized the way that I was raised, like 99.9 percent of my emotions were sort of shamed away. “That’s not what a man does.” I had basically three emotions. I navigated my life with laughing, being angry, or not giving a fuck. Everything else I just had in a vault.

But when I act, these characters feel emotions that are in the vault. So I’ve got to go in and get them, and then what happens is, like, a cry from 50 years ago sees the light and tries to run out. I had to sit there in this hotel room and cry for five minutes, and I didn’t even know why. Then the next day I went down and I did the scene, and it was totally fine. I realized, “OK, in my life I have the door closed. I need to open the door.”
How did you start opening the door? It’s exactly what you’re talking about in your most recent special, 2025’s Drop Dead Years, where sad men are only allowed to have, like, two emotions.
Yeah, that was the beginning of me starting to acknowledge other feelings. I will tell you what’s fucked up about my last special.

I thought that bit saying, “Why is the Ku Klux Klan still legal? Why is it that in those groups, the Proud Boys and all of them, there’s the white privilege where you can join a terrorist fucking organization?” I was thinking I’d get a lot of shit for that from racist people. Nothing. It was more people going, [mocking voice] “Do you think there’s a lot of sad men, Bill?” No one wanted to talk about the dangerous topic.

All of these years we watched [people] not do the right thing with a lot of other [countries], and now it’s happening here, and that’s why so much of the world’s like, “Well, yeah … you fucking deserve it.” But I think that we’re going to get on the other side of it.
“You’re gonna get punched. and it’s gonna hurt. But you take the hit and you get back up.”

Yeah, because the one thing I think people agree with on all sides is that people don’t want to live in an oppressive, not-free society, which is what we’re going towards. Just the amount of surveillance that they have on you and I — like, we’re not John Gotti in a social club. They have this level of surveillance on us, not because of what we’re doing but because of what they’re doing. Like, why the fuck do you need to know that I just went to 7-Eleven and got a Big Gulp? I got to walk around like Joe Pesci and [Robert] De Niro in Casino now, talking to my wife in my fucking driveway? Like, what are we doing here?
So what do you think it’s going to take for a change to happen?
I don’t know. It would have to be a fucking bloodbath. It would be like Braveheart, except everyone was wearing Lululemon shit.
Behind every massacre is a man in a suit, they say.
Let’s go back to that anger thing. So, how soon did this happen after you had taken that first big mushroom trip, which you said helped kind of open things up?

Yeah, the mushrooms helped me realize how fucked up I was. If you’re not feeling 99 percent of your feelings, how do you know that you’re sad or you’re depressed or whatever? So, the first time I took mushrooms, as they were coming on, it was the normal giggly sort of thing. And then, all of a sudden, this profound sense of sadness washed over me. So I left the room, and I was in this dark room, just, you know, having a bad trip. I started thinking about the people in my life. I’m like, “Is it my wife? No, I love her to death. Best thing that ever happened to me. I know it’s not my kids.” I just kind of went around, and then I finally ran out of stuff. And then the answer came: This is how you felt growing up. I was like, “Oh. Yep.”

Right? That bothered me. After that … I wasn’t really drinking at that point. But for like six weeks, I didn’t smoke a cigar. I didn’t do anything. I just wanted to work on myself, which is why I think that mushrooms are the best. It’s the only drug I’ve ever done that didn’t make me want to do more of it. It made me want to fix myself.

It’s funny, it’s such an East Coast thing: [Tough-guy voice] “Hey, man, don’t go out to West Coast and lose your edge.” What, don’t start enjoying my life? Don’t be a chill person to be around? In comedy, there’s this big thing of “Don’t get happy, you’re not going to be funny!” And it’s the exact opposite.

You can have access to all these emotions that you can add into your act, and you can revisit topics that you were looking at through the lens of anger and rage. This whole journey of being a comedian is when I stopped doing this and started doing a little more of that. Like, “Hey, Bill, maybe chicks aren’t psychos. Maybe you’re bringing something to the party, you know?” [Laughs.] My whole view on women is changed now. I look back on all of the dumb shit that I said, it had nothing to do with how I felt. I wanted to be married. I wanted to have kids. I just didn’t know how to do it. So what did I do? I blamed what I wanted. It’s stupid. I missed out on a lot of good times, being that brooding guy with this three-quarter Donnie Brasco leather jacket, hiding in the corner.
Only Nixon could go to China, and only Bill Burr can get guys to go to therapy and deal with their shit.

I know a lot of angry people that like my comedy. I want to tell them, “Look, if I can get on the other side of it, anybody can, because I was a first-ballot lunatic.” I didn’t want to be the angry guy.

My whole career, it’s “Oh, you’re the angry comic.” It was always embarrassing to me. Anger was embarrassing because it reminded me of my dad, who had no control, and I used to always be like, “I’m not going to be like him.” And what happens? You’re doing exactly what he was doing. So I always felt shame. Then that would make me hate myself, which made me go darker, which made me get angrier. I didn’t know how to get out of it. It was just this spinning-down thing.
When you started to lose the anger, were you afraid you had gotten rid of your creative fuel?

No, I felt liberated. Before, it was like, “You’re going to write a song on this piano — but you can only use these notes.” As opposed to, you can use the whole piano now. The best thing that happened to me, in terms of learning, was becoming a comedian. Because you learn the most through the failure of bombing. You can learn other things faster by just going into the same mindset.

Oh, recently. I was in Vegas, and I opened with that Luigi shit. Oh, my God! That ate a big dick. And then — this is what’s good about getting on the other side of my emotions. So it didn’t work, and rather than judge them and blame them, I went, “All right, I get it. You came to Vegas, you’re blowing off steam. I get it. I was wrong. I came out too hard. So … how’s everybody doing?” [Laughs.] And then, like, they were all laughing because I did, I came out guns a-blazing.

Yeah, bombing never goes away. If you’re continuing to try new jokes and push yourself, it’s a part of it. It’s like boxing. You’re gonna get punched, and it’s gonna fucking hurt. Even if you win. But you take the hit and you get back up.
You’re raising a son now, right?
Yeah. I’ve got a daughter and a son.
So how are you helping him avoid some of that “men can’t cry” shit?

I just let him be who he is. I let my daughter be who she is. And then I just go, “Hey, a little too much of this or that, guys! Ease up.” I expose them to all different kinds of music and sports and stuff, and I see what they gravitate towards. My wife is amazing with that. I learn a lot by watching her. And it helps that I remember what it was like to be a kid. To be scared, to not be listened to, and all of that awful stuff. I learned how to be a really good father by not doing what I saw. I remember the first time I felt it was working was when my daughter, who was probably two at the time, there was something that was upsetting to her. I was sitting on the stairs, and I said, “Well, come over here and talk to me about it.” And she walked over, and both of us just held each other’s hands. It was like … [Starts crying.] Sorry.
That’s all right. I don’t know what your growing-up situation was necessarily …
It was the exact opposite of that.
“This is not a battle of left and right. This is the working man vs. robber barons.”
It must have made you feel good to have an organic connection like that with your kid. That’s huge.

Yeah! Yeah, it is. I mean, it’s funny, because my kids are not afraid of me at all, which I love. But then sometimes when I’m going, “Dude, I’ve told you three times, go to bed,” they’re still just doing a dance, thinking I’m joking around.

They’re hilarious. They roast me. Like my daughter one time, I was like, “How are you still up? Go to bed. Come on. I’ve asked you like 10 times.” I said, “This isn’t fair.” And she just goes “Life isn’t fair.” I was like, “Shouldn’t I be telling you that?” And she comes back with: “Yeah, well, you didn’t.” I was like, “Well, I lost that one” [laughs]. They’re good kids. They’re emotionally intelligent, and you know, kind of everything I’m not.
Is there an itch that acting scratches that stand-up doesn’t?

Yeah. The collaborative thing. I really like working with other people and seeing what they’re gonna do. I like hearing other actors say a line and thinking, “Wow, I never would have thought to do it that way.” I’ve gotten better just watching the choices, and to see somebody fearless as an actor. The way I gravitated towards a fearless comedian, to then be like, “OK, what is being fearless as an actor?” And then seeing that, and it’s the same thing. Like, “Oh, that’s like some Dave Attell stuff, but in the acting world.”
How did doing Glengarry Glen Ross on Broadway for a four-month run make you think differently about acting?

It combined stand-up and acting. In stand-up, I say the thing, you guys react positively or negatively. I get immediate feedback, and silence is bad. On a set, silence is a good thing. If somebody doesn’t come up to you after a take, that means you did a good job. With theater, there’s feedback. And when you’re with the other actors, you’re seeing how everyone else does it and how it changes every night. It made me love theater. I was a typical sports guy. I thought theater was Cats. It’s like, I don’t want to watch a bunch of people dressed like fucking felines.

I never read plays growing up. That was for the kids that got beat up. I was trying not to get beat up in high school. So I went back and I read a bunch when we were doing Glengarry. Sam Shepard plays and The Motherfucker With the Hat. Just great stuff that made me want to do more of it.
I hear there’s a revival of Cats. You might want to look into that.
You started your podcast before Joe Rogan and Marc Maron started theirs, right?

Before they eclipsed me, you mean? “Bill, didn’t you do a podcast before those other guys became vastly more rich and famous than you?” [Laughs.] Yeah, I was there early. I still just do it into my phone. It’s just random thoughts. I don’t have guests a lot. I got into this to have fun, and I felt when you took it to the next level with a studio, employees, guests, it became a job. Not saying I would have done what Rogan and Maron did. I just kept it my way out of laziness.
When did you feel like you first found your voice as a comic?

I feel like I’m finding it now. Before, that was Traumatized Me. Fight-or-flight mode, alopecia, losing clumps of hair and shit. I was a fucking mess. That tropey sad-clown thing. How many years was I going to go up there and take out my childhood on the crowd?

When you were doing press for Drop Dead Years, you talked about how the country is divided and you wanted people to feel like they could find common ground at your show. How’s that working with the hour you’re touring now?

Oh, it’s been really fun. I just did a casino gig, and it was a really MAGA crowd, and my opener was a joke making fun of Trump, and half the room laughed, and then the other half really enthusiastically booed. So I was able to go up there, and just by what I was talking about, make it what I think it’s about.

This is not a battle of left and right. This is the working man versus this new era of robber barons. So I just was saying we got to stop these nerds with apps. They keep fucking over the working man. But then I was able to make fun of Trump, and they’re still laughing. And then I go, to the left, “Well, you know, you can’t laugh at them. You elected Joe Biden. I mean, both of these guys should be in a fucking home.” Like, we both kind of fucked up here.
How are you judging success now?

A lot of liberals don’t like me and a lot of conservatives don’t like me, which makes me feel like I’m doing something right. The extremes on both sides are pretty vocal, but I feel like the people in the middle aren’t like these butt-hurt idiots. I travel everywhere. Eighty-five percent of people are cool. They can listen to somebody. “Oh, that’s how you see it. OK, cool. You want to get a sandwich?”
Let’s end on something less fraught. How did you get into flying helicopters as a hobby?

I got into reading about the Federal Reserve, and I’m like, “The dollar could collapse at any moment. I live in L.A. I can barely get out of this city in two hours when it works. What happens when the shit hits the fan?” Up and out was the easiest way.
So this is your version of a mobile panic room?

The thing about a panic room is once you go in it, you can’t get the fuck out of there. The thing I like about a helicopter … I can put one gallon of fuel in there, maybe take off and fly the pattern. But I still have to come back. I have nowhere to go. There is nowhere to go. You should stay and fight. All these fucking people moving to other countries. It’s just, like, that’s not what you do. You stay and fight.
Entertainment editor DAVID FEAR has interviewed Francis Ford Coppola, Daniel Day-Lewis, Leonardo DiCaprio, and more for Rolling Stone.

items.title: The Lowdown Recap: Take the Cup
items.description: Broadly speaking, The Lowdown isn’t a subtle series. Its protagonist is boorish and loud — and not just when he talks. Lee is forever grunting and scratching and clearing his throat. Tripping into things, then cursing under his breath. His whole human body is
items.author: Amanda Whiting
paragraphs: Broadly speaking, The Lowdown isn’t a subtle series. Its protagonist is boorish and loud — and not just when he talks. Lee is forever grunting and scratching and clearing his throat. Tripping into things, then cursing under his breath. His whole human body is loud, and he lives in a world where cacophony is the norm: gunshots and bar fights, blasting car stereos and screaming matches.

And yet what makes “Truth’s Easy” such a treat to watch is the episode’s restraint. Lee, emerging from the dark woods beyond McMann’s cabin, gets picked up by a guy who nicknames himself the Boontill Oracle, a do-gooder who waits outside highway bars to give safe rides to local drunks. Played by Steve Earle, Dale offers Lee a sandwich, but Lee is more intrigued by a novelty mug in the cab of his truck. “Truth’s Easy,” the mug proclaims, but that has not been Lee’s personal experience. Pursuing the truth is how you end up divorced with alternating weekend custody. It’s how you wind up marooned on the side of the road at 5 a.m. When Dale drops off Lee at the van he abandoned at the strip club the day before, he tells Lee to keep the mug.

It’s a callback to the unsolicited advice Lee received from Vickey as she read his tarot cards back in “The Rupidoop.” On a lesser show, Lee would have thrown Dale a meaningful look, baffled that the material world was aligning with the woo-woo. But The Lowdown has more nuance. It’s not until the episode’s third act, as Lee updates his murder wall, sipping whiskey from the mug, that he mutters to himself, “Take the cup.” (Lee can never be silent.) Just like that, the mug is transformed into a visual motif — an echo of the idea that Lee can’t see what’s in front of him, even as he literally plots the points of this season’s mystery on a pinboard.

It’s not that Lee doesn’t want to see the cup. He’s curious about the world. He remembers. When he and Ginger visit Mekko’s uncle at a low-rent cultural center–slash–tourist trap, Lee warns Ginger not to inflect. If you want to ask a Native American person a question, you have to say it as a statement, he tells her, which is the advice Deidra gave Lee at the Indian Center back in season one.

The problem is that if you live as loudly as Lee does, it’s harder to hear, definitionally. He wants to carve his way to the truth but ends up stumbling onto it. His brashness is his principal liability as an investigative journalist and his best asset, though of course that’s not how Lee would put it. As chaos builds around him, he resists the idea that he’s chaotic. Even as he whispers the words “Take the cup,” Lee has no idea what they mean. Lee never quiets long enough to notice the outstretched cup.

As an episode, “Truth’s Easy” takes the shape of Lee’s hectic life. After hopping back in his own van, he heads for Ginger, who has been blowing up his phone with increasingly panicked text messages since Lee stopped responding. Before he can make it to her house, though, he urgently diverts to Sweet Emily’s to dramatically stop Francis and Frog from sharing the coffee they’ve already shared — a shortsighted parenting strategy that’s only going to make Francis more determined to spend time with her grandfather. Is Frog a good influence? Probably not. But how much harm can he do in a single morning?

After alienating his daughter, Lee finally makes it to Ginger’s house to deliver the hard news: Mekko isn’t missing; he escaped and he didn’t come see his girlfriend. We learn that Mekko was in Boontill for armed robbery, though, like many a beguiled prison groupie, Ginger isn’t convinced he pulled the trigger. But other than being aware of his rap sheet, she knows suspiciously little about his life outside. She has no clue where he would go next. She remembers a shifty uncle from Mekko’s appellate trial — maybe he can help.

Ginger’s living at Lee’s breakneck pace now. They hop into his bullet-holed van and drive out to Rakko Eco Big Deer Village, where Uncle Otis throws axes or something — Ginger isn’t sure. Otis confesses that he saw Mekko last week and gave his nephew some clothes and 200 bucks before they said their final good-byes. Mekko is in the wind now, a lifelong fugitive. To my ears, it sounds like the end of the investigation for our mismatched gumshoes, but clearly, my internal lie detector is malfunctioning. “He’s full of shit,” Lee and Ginger say in unison before trailing Otis out of Rakko Eco.

Otis inadvertently leads them to the nearby hospital, where Lee runs into Mekko Jr. waiting for his mom, Angie, to clock out. Otis had gone there to warn Angie that people were asking after Mekko the Elder. Eventually, Angie tells Lee and Ginger that Mekko visited her house two nights ago to see his son. She tells them Mekko was pissed, ranting about being forced to sit with a dead kid’s body for hours. She doesn’t think he’s about to disappear; she thinks he’s about to rain down vengeance for which she and her son will eventually have to suffer. The Mekko whom Angie knows is capable of pulling the trigger.

Ginger didn’t know her client had a son. Earlier in the episode, she explains to Lee that she and Mekko bonded over Steinbeck. “A guy needs somebody — to be near him. A guy goes nuts if he ain’t got nobody,” Mekko had quoted to her. She thought he was talking about their shared loneliness, but here she finds out he had a kid this whole time — a family. In Mekko, Ginger believed she had found someone with whom to be still. Now she has to go home and ruminate over the fact that she’s a public defender who got duped by her jailhouse-phone lover.

Later, Lee and Frog continue the confrontation that started at Sweet Emily’s. Lee forbids his father from contacting Francis ever again. Or else what, Frog would like to know. Will Lee call the cops on his elderly father? Will he have him committed to a psychiatric facility … again? The history between these men is more noxious than your garden-variety case of paternal neglect — there’s been emotional and physical abuse. Lee tells Frog to leave the bookshop by morning, but it’s clear he won’t go far. He told the cop who drove him into Tulsa that he’s back to settle scores. “Tell Francis her grandfather says ‘hello,’” he taunts his son.

Frog’s response to Lee — callous and rotten — didn’t surprise me, based on what little we know of the man. But Francis’s petulance threw me. Until now, we’ve known her to be thoughtful and compassionate; if anything, she’s been too eager to take Lee’s side. In “Truth’s Easy,” though, she’s so preoccupied by her parents having lied about her grandfather’s death that she’s completely unsympathetic to why they did it. Even when Lee divulges more than perhaps he should — about Frog sleeping with his teachers, shooting him with a BB gun, telling him he was unloved — Francis suggests that Lee should forgive a man who’s never once said “sorry.” In season one, it was cute that Fran seemed to have inherited her father’s sense of justice. But over a blended family dinner with Sam and Johnny, she comes off as selfish and unfeeling.

It’s hard to imagine that supper at their house is usually this loud or drunken. Samantha, though technically on Lee’s side in the argument with their daughter, is swigging wine at a rate that makes her an unreliable ally. Eventually, a haggard Lee excuses himself to cool off. When was the last time this guy slept in his own bed two nights in a row? When he sees a motion-sensor light flick on in Sam and Johnny’s backyard, how can he be sure it’s not a hallucination?

It’s not. Since the beginning of the episode, Lee’s been tailed by McMann’s skinny accomplice — the guy Ginger shot in the neck at the end of the season premiere. He’s alive, he’s armed, and like everyone else, he wants to find Mekko. By his ex-wife’s recycling bins, Lee tries to fend off the guy with a fire poker, but eventually, Johnny comes to Lee’s rescue, putting the trespasser in a sleeper hold until he passes out — not bad for a dentist. Johnny’s really a decent guy. When Sam comes out on the deck to inquire about the racket that always seems to follow Lee, he makes up a quick excuse.

Johnny politely endures Lee’s snide put-downs. He welcomes Francis’s loud and lawless father into his home, which Lee insults for being too nice. But we may have finally found Johnny’s limit. Lee told Johnny the guy passed out by his hot tub was a gangbanger, but the wallet they pull from his pocket says he’s Lonnie Reed, the deputy sheriff. The episode ends with Lee smiling a bloody smile, the tooth Lonnie just broke on full display for the dentist who lives with his family. No, The Lowdown is not a subtle show, but it is a rewardingly intricate one. Ideas and mysteries are layered to unfold in unison. Truth’s easy? Lee’s still answering for the last lie he told as the next one comes tumbling from his mouth.

items.title: Eric Bauza’s ‘Looney Tunes’ Legacy: ‘Coyote vs. Acme’ Producer Says Voice Actor Behind Bugs Bunny and More Had a ‘Deep Love of the Craft’
items.description: Chris DeFaria, the former president of animation and innovative technology at Warner Bros. and producer of “Coyote vs. Acme,” shared his thoughts on the sudden death of Eric Bauza, the voice of many “Looney Tunes” characters.
items.author: Chris DeFaria
paragraphs: Chris DeFaria, the former president of animation and innovative technology at Warner Bros. and producer of “Coyote vs. Acme,” shared his thoughts on the sudden death of Eric Bauza, the voice of many “Looney Tunes” characters.
I’m heartbroken to share that my friend and colleague Eric Bauza passed away last night. The world lost a great voice.

Eric carried the legacy of Looney Tunes with a devotion few bring to their work. He voiced Daffy Duck, Bugs Bunny, Porky Pig, Marvin the Martian, and so many more. And he never treated them as a job. To him, they were icons who deserved to be honored, protected, and kept alive for new generations. He championed these characters tirelessly in every room he walked into.

Eric never forgot whose shoulders he stood on either. He had enormous reverence for Mel Blanc, the master who gave these characters their original voices, and he used to say he was only borrowing Mel’s Cadillac, and that he promised to return the keys when he was done. That was Eric.

A man handed one of the great legacies in animation, who treated it as a trust rather than a trophy. He drove it with love and cared with a little bit of mischief, and he left it in better shape than when he found it.
After Mel’s passing in 1989, the voices he carried by himself were divided among many talented performers.
He started by trying a few of the voices, and in what felt like no time at all, he was doing nearly all of them. It’s a feat that few, if any, had pulled off since Mel himself.
But what Eric achieved went far beyond impressions. Learning the sound of a character is hard enough. Eric did something deeper.
He learned to be them, to think like Bugs, to scheme like Daffy, to stutter and squirm like Porky. That’s why they never sounded like imitations when he performed them. They sounded alive.

What made it more remarkable was that his talent was largely his own. He was self-taught, and he built that astonishing range through curiosity, relentless practice, and a deep love of the craft. You could hear that love in every line. I was lucky enough to share time with Eric at Warner Brothers, and luckier still to have worked alongside him most recently on “Coyote vs Acme.”
Eric had a devilish wit, and was never more alive than when he stepped into those characters with a mischievous spark that made them feel new while honoring everyone who came before them.

And yes, Eric was always late. I like to think that somewhere right now, Bugs, in fact, is tapping his foot and checking his watch, and Eric is strolling in with a grin, a perfect excuse in a line so funny that all is forgiven within seconds.
He was worth the wait every single time.
Thank you, Eric, for the laughter, the artistry, the joy you gave us all. I know you promised to return Mel’s keys when you’re done. Take your time. You always did.

items.title: Chris Brown Gets Suspended Eight-Month Sentence for ‘Vicious and Unprovoked’ Attack at U.K. Nightclub
items.description: Grammy award winning singer Chris Brown has received a suspended eight-month sentence – therefore avoiding jail time – in relation to a “vicious and unprovoked” attack at a London nightclub in 2023.
items.author: Leo Barraclough
paragraphs: Grammy award winning singer Chris Brown has received a suspended eight-month sentence – therefore avoiding jail time – in relation to a “vicious and unprovoked” attack at a London nightclub in 2023.

Before sentencing, Judge Tony Baumgartner had warned Brown, “I take account of your employment and long-established career in music. Your fame, commercial success and professional standing do not entitle you to special treatment. The law applies equally to everyone.”
In July, Brown pleaded guilty to a count of affray at London’s Southwark Crown Court for attacking a music producer with a tequila bottle on the head.

His co-defendant, Omololu Akinlolu, had also pleaded guilty. The U.K.’s Crown Prosecution Service (similar in function to the District Attorney) described Akinlolu, a Florida rapper also known as HoodyBaby, as Brown’s vocal coach. He received a sentence of four months, suspended for 12 months.

In July, Southwark Crown Court heard that the duo attacked the victim, Abraham Diaw, at the Tape London nightclub in February 2023. Brown was accused of twice hitting the victim with a tequila bottle to his head while Akinlolu punched him.
“They continued their assault whilst the victim attempted to flee through the club,” the CPS said in a statement. “The victim was kicked while he was seated defenseless on the floor.”

After the victim went to hospital with injuries to his head and knees a warrant was issued for Brown and Akinlolu’s arrest, although they had left the U.K. by that time. Brown was arrested in May 2025 when he returned to the U.K. as part of his world tour to perform in Manchester.

“This was a vicious and unprovoked attack by Brown and Akinlolu in a crowded nightclub where Brown used a glass bottle as a weapon to strike the victim’s head twice,” Claire Campbell, a senior prosecutor at CPS London South, had said after securing the conviction.
The two men denied charges for assault and grievous bodily harm as well as Brown having an offensive weapon, and these were subsequently dropped.

items.title: Hulu’s Rumored Clavicular Doc Is Actually a True-Crime Series (Exclusive)
items.description: Look(smaxx) here: We finally have actual information on that rumored Clavicular Hulu documentary.
items.author: Tony Maglio
paragraphs: Look(smaxx) here: We finally have actual information on that rumored Clavicular Hulu documentary.

The Hollywood Reporter can first reveal that all that beef between the 20-year-old looksmaxxer, whose real name is Braden Peters, and Disney has resulted in a three-part true-crime documentary series titled Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death. The Hulu doc is not and was never a documentary about Peters; rather, it was about the dangerous and competitive worlds of looksmaxxing and social media. Peters just happens to be the most famous individual on that scene, and his likeness is only used briefly. Specifically, the docuseries is about a mysterious death in Thailand (that has nothing whatsoever to do with Clavicular).

But since it’s been a while, the backstory: Peters served Disney/Hulu a cease and desist letter after he says he caught documentarians Jennings Brown and James Kristofik filming him backstage at the Elena Velez fashion show in February in New York City without permission. Peters did not like that, but the encounter would be far from his biggest legal case this year.

Just last week, Peters pleaded not guilty to raping an underage girl after she was given alcohol while appearing on his livestream in 2025. In September, Peters was charged with two felony counts, one for rape and another for drugging a person for sexual intercourse. He also faces a misdemeanor count for providing alcohol to someone younger than 21.

Peters has denied the allegations, saying that the encounter was consensual. He has posted a video to his social media accounts showing screenshots of a text conversation and a photo of a handwritten letter, which were intercut over footage of Peters, shirtless and fixing his hair at an urban inner harbor. Beneath the posts, he’s written, “Theres better ways to make money then suing someone because they don’t want you,” and “Yeah still texting me to this day … totally not just trying to be greedy and get a check.”

Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death presents what producers call “an unflinching portrait of masculinity in the influencer age, where extreme biohacking, online performance and a series of suspicious deaths converge.” The series debuts Nov. 10 on Hulu (and Hulu on Disney+ for bundle subscribers) in the U.S. It will stream on Disney+ internationally.

“Deep in the manosphere, an underground movement promises to unlock human potential — bulging muscles, bigger penises, eternal youth. At its center is Dr. Tony Huge, a guru pushing homemade biohacks on a devoted following willing to risk everything for the cause,” the logline reads. “When Leo & Longevity, a penis-enlargement expert and one of Tony’s closest allies, is found dead in Thailand, alpha-male influencers become online sleuths, running wild with theories and questioning Tony Huge and his right-hand man, Connor Murphy. Soon, a darker pattern emerges: Leo isn’t the first of the inner circle to die under mysterious circumstances. Will he be the last?”

Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death is directed by Stacey Lee and produced by Boardwalk Pictures (Welcome to Wrexham, aka Charlie Sheen) and Hyperobject Industries (Don’t Look Up, Stormbound). Executive producers include Adam McKay and Todd Schulman for Hyperobject Industries; Andrew Fried, Lana Barkin, Jordan Wynn and Dane Lillegard for Boardwalk Pictures; William Crouse and Stacey Lee for Lovely Days; Jennings Brown for Nocturne Media; and Brett Neichin.

items.title: Следы древней собаки нашли среди руин поселения бронзового века в Турции
items.description: В Турции нашли отпечатки собачьих лап возрастом около 4000 лет
items.author: Виолетта Ефимова
paragraphs: В Турции нашли отпечатки собачьих лап возрастом около 4000 лет

Археологи обнаружили в западной Турции кирпич с отпечатками собачьих лап, оставленными около 4000 лет назад. Находку сделали во время раскопок поселения Тавшанлы-Хююк в провинции Кютахья. Отпечатки сохранились на сырцовом кирпиче, который использовали при строительстве дома в бронзовом веке.
О находке сообщил министр культуры и туризма Турции Мехмет Нури Эрсой. Раскопки возглавляет профессор Университета Биледжик Шейх Эдебали Эркан Фидан.

Вероятно, собака прошла по ещё влажному кирпичу до того, как тот высох и затвердел. Позже строители встроили его в стену дома. Здание пережило пожар, после которого обрушившиеся конструкции погребли кирпич под слоем обломков. Благодаря этому следы сохранились до наших дней.

Тавшанлы-Хююк — одно из крупнейших доисторических поселений западной Анатолии. Его площадь составляет не менее 45 гектаров, а история заселения насчитывает около восьми тысяч лет. С 2021 года исследователи изучают здесь слои бронзового века. Ранее археологи обнаружили обгоревшие человеческие останки, керамику, следы обработки металла и цилиндрическую печать возрастом около 3750 лет, свидетельствующую о торговых контактах с другими регионами Анатолии.

Отпечатки лап не позволяют определить, кому принадлежала собака и жила ли она в доме или свободно перемещалась по поселению. Однако такая случайная находка сохраняет редкую деталь повседневной жизни, которую обычно невозможно восстановить по предметам и руинам.

Павел Осовцов и Рената Харькова
