items.title: Trump’s Repudiation Is at Hand, Right?
items.description: Is this, finally, the repudiation of Donald Trump? In decades of covering American politics, I cannot think of a midterm election which has more directly posed that question about a President—never mind one where all indicators point, ever more starkly, to a s
items.author: Susan B Glasser
paragraphs: Is this, finally, the repudiation of Donald Trump? In decades of covering American politics, I cannot think of a midterm election which has more directly posed that question about a President—never mind one where all indicators point, ever more starkly, to a straightforward answer: Yes.

As Trump has barnstormed around the country this fall, he has reverted to the playbook he tried in his first midterm campaign. “Pretend, please,” he says wherever he goes, “that I’m on the ballot.” As always, he wants this to be the Trump, Trump, Trump election. The problem for the President is that that’s precisely what it is shaping up to be—and, with only days left before his November 3rd reckoning, Americans overwhelmingly do not like him, his policies, or his party.

By just about any metric except the obscene, record-setting amounts of cash that Trump and a small circle of billionaires are spending to save the Republicans’ Senate majority, this fall’s contest looks like the wipeout that so many have predicted (and so often been embarrassingly wrong about) since Trump first entered politics 4,146 days ago: historically low approval ratings, an unpopular war with Iran that has led to high prices and surging inflation, corruption so flagrant that two-thirds of Americans now believe he is profiting off the Presidency. Most notably, Trump’s sagging popularity is not just with Democrats and independents but with many Republicans in red states whose unwavering backing has, time and again, saved him during this insane past decade in American politics.

In the final Times poll of the election cycle, Democrats had an eleven-point advantage in the generic ballot, which is four points higher than in 2018, when the Party picked up forty-one seats and regained the House. As for the issues driving voters, the Democratic pollster John Anzalone summed up the current state of the race. “Democrats lead on everything,” he wrote on X after the Times poll was released. “Like Literally Everything!”

The result has been an entirely unexpected series of tossups in the American heartland, where control of the Senate—once seen as unattainable by Democrats given this year’s map—may be decided in states such as Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, and Texas, none of which have elected a Democrat to that chamber in decades. (Ninety-four years, in the case of Kansas.) Democrats also have a strong chance to win a majority of state governorships for the first time since 2010. In the race for the House, where Democrats need to pick up only three seats, the Party is seen as a virtual lock to win.

This is not just a matter of Democratic hopium. Republicans began panicking weeks ago, spending hundreds of millions of dollars on ads in states they once reckoned on winning comfortably and all but withdrawing from previously competitive Senate seats in places, such as North Carolina and Georgia, where Trump won decisively just two years ago. On Monday, Trump will campaign in Mississippi—staunchly Republican Mississippi—where the Senate seat is now officially “in play.” As for the House, “exceedingly grim” G.O.P. insiders have been telling reporters for weeks that they are braced for a midterm blowout.

“The economic center of the American electorate is collapsing on Republicans,” Greg Strimple, a Republican pollster, declared on Tuesday. His new joint survey with a Democratic colleague for the Cook Political Report found Democratic Senate candidates narrowly leading in Iowa, Ohio, and Texas—all states which voted three times for Trump. According to Strimple, “Voters are so upset with the lack of leadership on reducing their cost of living, they appear willing to propel Democrats to upset victories in reliably Republican states despite the fact that Democrats are less popular than either President Trump or Republicans. The level of voter discontent is truly unprecedented.”

So why, then, are so many Democrats no more than what Rahm Emanuel called, in an interview for The New Yorker’s Political Scene podcast the other day, “small ‘c,’ small ‘o,’ cautiously optimistic” about their prospects for dealing Trump a decisive blow by winning the Senate?

History suggests one obvious reason. Trump may never have been President at all if not for the Party’s fatal overconfidence about him, in 2016. In the final two weeks before that election, with some national polls giving Hillary Clinton a seemingly insurmountable double-digit lead, her doomed campaign did not even bother to send the Democratic nominee to the decisive battleground state of Wisconsin, instead looking to expand the map to traditionally red states such as Arizona and Utah. Even in 2018, when Democrats did come back from Clinton’s defeat with a strong performance, the split decision—with Republicans keeping the Senate even as Democrats won the House—meant that Trump was unlikely to face real accountability or meaningful constraints from Congress. It was seen as a rebuke, not a Presidency-ending repudiation.

The point here is that winning in American elections is about expectations as much as who claims more seats. At the start of 2026, Democrats taking back the House and running competitively for the Senate across a daunting map might have been seen as a rousing recovery from the Party’s poor state two years ago. Now, even though polls show that control of the Senate remains up for grabs, with key races all within the margin of error, the baseline has shifted. As a Democratic friend said to me the other day, “I’ll be disappointed if we don’t win the Senate that I did not expect to win a month ago.”

There is also the question of what lesson the parties take from the election. In 2022, Democrats bought their own spin about how successfully they’d held off a red wave, convincing themselves that losing the House by only five seats and holding on to a bare fifty-one-seat majority in the Senate was a great victory. The better-than-expected performance helped spur Joe Biden to announce that he planned to run for another term, and we all know how that worked out. After Trump’s 2024 win, Republicans believed a political realignment of such importance had taken place that they undertook an unprecedented mid-decade redistricting designed to blunt the Democrats’ advantage going into this year’s midterms. At the start of this year, that redistricting looked like it could help them gain as many as a dozen seats; now, with many 2024 Trump voters turning against the President in places such as South Texas and Florida, the net effect might be as little as one seat.

But, as the election that might spell the beginning of the end of Trump’s long, strange hold on the American electorate finally looms, it’s not the hubris of the victors or the inevitable flood of bad punditry that has me most concerned. It is, as always, the President himself.

Ever since he returned to office, Trump has been hedging against the possibility of a midterm embarrassment by preëmptively attacking the results, questioning the legality of mail-in voting, pretending there is an epidemic of illegal noncitizen voting, and threatening to mobilize the considerable federal resources at his disposal on Election Day and beyond. The Times found that he has publicly cast doubt on the elections on more than seventy per cent of the days since his second Inauguration took place, with recent comments focussing on “rigged polls,” which he said, “have ALWAYS underestimated MAGA.” In the post-2020 world, is there anyone among us who thinks we should not take these threats seriously?

In private, many Democrats (and I’m sure plenty of Republicans, too) self-soothe with talk of a blue wave that will be too big to rig. No less a stolid figure than the former Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin is so alarmed about this complacency that he warned the public this week of the “meaningful risk” that Trump might seek to interfere with or outright “usurp” the election results. I have no doubt that, if the President who was willing to unleash a mob on America’s Capitol rather than concede defeat sees a way to try, he will.

Most of all, I am sure of this: Trump remains who he has always been. He has never publicly accepted blame for anything, and he will not start now. There will be no course correction, no pivot to the center. He will not, as George W. Bush and Barack Obama both did after their midterm shellackings, acknowledge the voters’ anger and vow to do better by working across party lines. The worse Trump and his Republicans fare on Election Night, the more we should worry about his response. Repudiated Trump may turn out to be the most dangerous Trump of all. ♦

items.title: New York’s EMS Crisis Could Kill You
items.description: Sooner or later, the slow-motion collapse of New York’s response system for medical emergencies will force city leaders to get off their asses and address problems that should have been fixed long ago. Innocent people are already paying the price of City Hall
items.author: Errol Louis
paragraphs: Sooner or later, the slow-motion collapse of New York’s response system for medical emergencies will force city leaders to get off their asses and address problems that should have been fixed long ago. Innocent people are already paying the price of City Hall perennially starving ambulance first responders of the salaries, benefits, and work conditions they deserve.

Over the last decade, response time on life-threatening medical emergencies has jumped by nearly four minutes, an increase of more than 41 percent, according to a recent report by City Comptroller Mark Levine. Non-life-threatening response time has more than doubled, by almost 15 minutes. That extra time can be the difference between life and death.

“Most critical, which would be cardiac arrest, was somewhere around 14 minutes. That’s serious,” Vincent Variale, president of the Uniformed EMS Officers Union, told me. “We know brain death begins at four to six minutes. So if I’m arriving at 14 minutes, I still need time to get into your house or your building and find you, that’s probably another three to four minutes. So it’s almost 20 minutes before we actually get down and work on the patient. Brain death has already started. The survivability of that patient has plummeted.”

Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration is aware of the problem. “We know this is unacceptable, and we are working tirelessly to reverse this trend,” said FDNY’s chief of department, John Esposito. (Emergency Medical Services is a division of the Fire Department).

The root of the problem, as union leaders warned in March, is the absurdly low pay that New York’s frontline “street doctors” get. First-year emergency medical technicians (EMTs) make only $43,932, far lower than the entry-level salaries of firefighters ($54,122) and cops ($55,942), and less than what we pay first-year sanitation workers ($47,752). And while other uniformed personnel hit $100,000 within five and a half years, EMTs have smaller increases and top out at $68,700, with paramedics capped at $86,348.
“You have EMTs starting out at minimum wage, a little over $18 an hour,” says Variale. “To live in New York City at that kind of salary, it’s very hard to do it. And that’s why people are leaving.”

The low wages have led workers to look for part-time work; take the exam to snag a better-paying job as a firefighter; sleep in their cars a few nights a week; or simply quit. Some even end up in homeless shelters, according to union leaders, and 14 have committed suicide since 2020.

“More and more EMTs and paramedics are leaving the job. We estimate by the time this is over, 1,500 will be gone,” says Variale, noting that 500 EMS workers have left so far this year. “It’s terrible. The main cause of response times going up is people leaving the job.”

A shrinking workforce prevents the city from having a sufficient number of ambulances ready for action. The average number of ambulances in service over the last five years was only 332, a number that recently rose to 416, but remains far below the department’s official target number of 488, according to Levine, even as volume has hit a record high of more than 1.1 million calls per year.

Reports of long waits for help during medical emergencies are starting to multiply. Last year, 14-year-old Kevin Daly had a stroke while at school; after an hour of waiting that included three calls from the school nurse, Daly’s mother came to the school and drove him to the hospital herself. In another case, the closest responder to a call on Staten Island was an ambulance in Manhattan that took 64 minutes to arrive, says Variale, who estimates that the slowing response times means 4,000 excess deaths a year.

Fixing the problem won’t be cheap. Prior to getting elected, Mayor Eric Adams promised EMS workers parity with other uniformed workers, winning the union’s endorsement, but he reneged after his inauguration; the workers have been without a contract since 2022. Levine estimates that bringing EMS workers into full parity with firefighters would cost about $1.23 billion if applied to the current contract period (2022 to 2027) and then cost an additional $289 million a year. A less expensive alternative, pegging EMS salaries to what private ambulance companies pay, would cost $352 million for the current contract and then an additional $98 million a year.

The missing ingredient here is leadership. A recent City Council hearing raised important workplace issues like the fact ambulances tend to be stationed at key intersections to speed response time, leaving EMS workers unable to take meal and bathroom breaks. The hearing also touched on the idea of increasing the number of FDNY personnel trained as paramedics ready to handle complex medical emergencies, a “fire-medic” model used in the other cities. But operational changes don’t address the core problem of low pay.

I recently asked Mayor Mamdani why New York doesn’t follow the lead of cities like Philadelphia, Portland, and Denver, which have established a minimum wage for municipal workers. “We’ve been having productive conversations with our partners in organized labor, especially when it comes to EMS workers. And we’re talking about people who it’s truly not hyperbolic to describe their work as having the consequences of life or death for New Yorkers,” Mamdani told me. “And yet, we’ve seen that they haven’t been recognized as such. I’m hopeful that those conversations not only continue but they continue to be productive.”

But hope, as they say, is not a strategy. City Hall should not wait for a tragedy to occur to make EMS first responders a job that pays a living wage and enables these public servants to build fulfilling careers saving lives.

“This mayor and this administration did not cause this problem. This problem started before they got here. And I’m happy to hear when they talk about affordability and pay equity and stuff like that. This should be right in the mayor’s wheelhouse,” says Variale. “I just think it needs to be moving a little quicker to get there. Because every day that goes by, more people are dying. Literally.”

items.title: Why Liberals Keep Getting Education Wrong
items.description: The second season of Sold a Story, a podcast about education, opens in 1966 in an Illinois classroom. The teacher is a former Chicago marketing executive named Siegfried Engelmann. Before him sit seven Black children. He calls out arithmetic questions and they
items.author: Alexander Nazaryan
paragraphs: The second season of Sold a Story, a podcast about education, opens in 1966 in an Illinois classroom. The teacher is a former Chicago marketing executive named Siegfried Engelmann. Before him sit seven Black children. He calls out arithmetic questions and they answer together, as is the norm in direct instruction, the teaching method Engelmann pioneered. The lesson moves on to algebra. The children keep pace. Then the creator and host of the podcast, Emily Hanford, cuts in. The children, she notes, are in preschool.

Sixty years later, we have UC Berkeley math teaching professor Zvezdelina Stankova complaining, in a San Francisco Standard op-ed that went viral this summer, that students at the University of California’s flagship campus were struggling with “fractions and basic algebra you would expect students to learn in middle school.” What happened?

The first season of Sold a Story was a sensation in 2022, focusing on how American education had lost the plot when it came to the basics of reading. Hanford took aim at a ubiquitous form of instruction known as balanced literacy, a fuzzy idea that encouraged teachers to surround children with books but often provided those children with little actual instruction. Soon enough, Hanford had listeners indignantly wondering why educators had largely scrapped the tried-and-true approach of methodically sounding out letters, known as phonics, in favor of cueing, which involves having students guess at a word through contextual or visual clues. In response to the podcast, state legislatures across the country passed laws overhauling reading curricula to make sure they are grounded in scientifically proven methods.

Hanford’s latest project ventures into math instruction as well as broader questions of pedagogy that Engelmann’s controversial approach raised. The question that hangs over this podcast like a storm cloud is why educators, and particularly liberal educators, keep getting the fundamentals of teaching wrong.

A year after Engelmann showed off his method in a recorded half-hour lesson, President Lyndon B. Johnson instructed education officials in his administration to evaluate the best way to teach poor children. The study would take close to a decade, tracking 22 different models. They landed on direct instruction, which involves a teacher leading students through scripted, sequential lessons. Hanford lets Engelmann, in an archival clip, summarize the results: “We beat ’em in everything.” But it was never implemented nationwide. The reason was Engelmann’s “militaristic” approach to education, as the education writer Alfie Kohn explained in his criticism of direct instruction, which he said is today favored by “right-wing activists” who “wanted to make sure that learning itself is conceived as a fundamentally passive process.” Engelmann’s supporters’ politics were off, which meant his ideas were bad. And since Kohn gave this assessment in 2022, it seems that little has changed.

Or maybe the change is just building. Sold a Story is for liberals who know that something is wrong with American public education but don’t know what to do about it. “We’ve underappreciated the power of teaching,” Hanford, who lives outside Washington, D.C., told me. She said that after the first season, many teachers thanked her for voicing their private frustrations. “They want to hear this,” she said. What’s less clear is if they are willing to overcome their allergy to common-sense reforms, if those reforms, like direct instruction, don’t radiate liberal vibes.

Educators have hopefully taken note that the conversation about public education has become brutally downbeat. “These schools — it’s not good in this country,” the comedian Sam Morril observed in his new Netflix special. “It’s never ‘The Test Scores Are Up.’ You never see a headline like ‘The Kids Are Doing Better In School.’ It’s always like a murder or a teacher who fucked a kid.” I don’t know about that last part, but the joke neatly captures our collective disenchantment.

It’s been a slow-building crisis. Education used to be a top-tier issue in American politics, leading to major Bush- and Obama-era reforms (No Child Left Behind, followed by Race to the Top). But under Trump, conservative education proposals have swung between installing the Ten Commandments in classrooms, PragerU edu-slop, and book bans. On the left, education discourse has largely disappeared at the official level, supplanted by a concern (shared by Bill de Blasio and Zohran Mamdani) for affordable child care. Mamdani’s lack of a muscular educational agenda became apparent in the wake of Nikole Hannah-Jones’s recent essay for The New York Times Magazine describing a deepening dismay with her daughter Najya’s education in New York’s public schools.

Hanford believes reform starts with overcoming reflexive polarization. “I wasn’t necessarily rejecting the curriculum as much as I was rejecting Bush,” one teacher concedes in the first season of Sold a Story (it has been lost to time that Bush was in Florida on 9/11 to promote a return to phonics). In 2002, the Washington Post reported that educators at a Department of Education phonics training complained upon discovering that “many presenters were authors of Direct Instruction materials” (phonics is perfectly suited to Engelmann’s iterative, teacher-guided approach). A study published earlier this year, and conducted by the conservative Thomas B. Fordham Institute and the RAND Corporation, found that 41 percent of K-3 teachers in high-poverty schools remained wary of phonics instruction despite the fact that the approach is legally mandated by about 40 states.

Education is one of the few segments of society where the energy for serious reform comes from the right. That explains why Hanford’s podcast has been embraced by some conservatives. “I was surprised at how impactful it was,” the conservative education reformer Frederick Hess said of the podcast. “Most insiders vastly overestimate how much parents and voters know about something like reading. It was positioned to land as credible with the sort of highly educated, left-leaning parents and influencers who are prone to be skeptical of phonics and who have an outsize impact on schooling.”

Hanford’s detractors say her work will inevitably be weaponized by enemies of public education: radical free marketers, Christian nationalists. One writer on Substack suggested that her podcast was a Trojan Horse for “Project 2025,” former Trump officials’ and the Heritage Foundation’s plan for the second Trump administration.

Others say her story is too neat. “This idea that there was a secret to learning how to read that researchers or policymakers or teachers were holding out on students is completely fallacious,” said Alina Lewis, an adjunct assistant professor at the City University of New York and a former New York high-school teacher and administrator (we both helped start Brooklyn Latin, a selective high school in East Williamsburg). About a year after Sold a Story premiered, New York City began rolling out a phonics-forward curriculum. Lewis was stunned by the readings her children, who were at a gifted-and-talented program in Bensonhurst, brought home. The supposedly rigorous new materials, the New York Post would report, offered “kids a chance to coast by with simplistic passages about ‘superhero squirrels’ and ‘an African mouse,’ instead of actual books.” This was the new new thing?

The curriculum Lewis fought against was created by Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, the textbook publishing giant, which in 2022 was bought by Veritas Capital, a private-equity firm. Changing a curriculum in a single school — to say nothing of a district or an entire state — is like a restaurant deciding it will transition from smashburgers to omakase. Most teachers need new materials, which are outsourced to corporations that are not necessarily equipped to make them. “Then they produce stuff that they say is evidence based, but it’s actually just the company commissions a study,” Lewis said.

The teachers also need someone to teach them how those materials work and how they interact with new standards. Teachers can be resistant to such retraining, and understandably so: “You’ve been doing it wrong” is a message nobody wants to hear. Lewis is concerned about the return of Sold a Story. “I’m terrified of what this woman’s going to do to the conversation on ed reform,” she told me.

But what, exactly, is the alternative? Progressives have been quick to point out flaws with charter schools and standardized testing, but they’ve rarely suggested sensible solutions other than going back to the way things used to be. And what could be more conservative than that?

Hanford is trying to give liberals a new way to think about public education, a middle road between culture-war minefields. She feels that an enormous amount of time is wasted in schools. That may be fine for kids whose parents can afford math tutoring and music camp, but it’s devastating for destitute children whose parents rightly expect something transformative. As Hanford put it when we spoke, “kids from more advantaged backgrounds have a fallback plan.” Other students don’t.

Whereas the first season of Sold a Story lacked a protagonist, Engelmann is very much the hero of the second. “There was a sense of urgency about this,” Hanford says of direct instruction. She does not elide the fact that Engelmann could be impatient and demanding if he thought teachers weren’t living up to his standards. But ineffective educators don’t deserve the benefit of the doubt any more than he does. His dictum should resonate with everyone who wondered where to apportion the blame for the mess Hannah-Jones described in her essay: “If the student hasn’t learned, the teacher hasn’t taught.”

Teachers’ unions have limited the ability of administrators to fire underperforming teachers. When I pressed Hanford on her stance on unions, she had nothing to say. “I’m trying to get into some of the deepest, most controversial, most important issues, but I’m trying to do it in a careful way,” she explained. “I’m not trying to pound people over the head. I’m trying to show people things the way you’re supposed to do in journalism.”

Listening to Sold a Story reminded me of what I loved about teaching, the youthful energy that coursed through a classroom even on sluggish June days, the infinitely original ways a kid from Inwood or Canarsie might gloss Whitman or Chaucer.

But the podcast also evoked what I found so frustrating about public education, especially in a progressive city like New York. Above all, there was an unstated aversion to excellence, as if urging children to rise to the occasion were asking too much of them. And there was a related fear of failure, both ours and theirs, that worked like quicksand over the years, so that there you were, doing the same lesson on the subordinate clause that you’d always done, because why change something that works, or at least works well enough?

Even if you’re resistant to Hanford and her message, I ask that you please listen to the first three minutes of Sold a Story’s second season. Literally just three minutes. Do it while on line for coffee or waiting for the L train. It’s thrilling to hear what Engelmann could do in a preschool classroom 60 years ago. It also shouldn’t be a relic, plangent evidence of what we could have done but didn’t.

items.title: Macho Man Hegseth Had His Staff Manhandle Ike’s Globe
items.description: Pete Hegseth’s tenure as secretary of Defense has largely been defined by the words “cringeworthy” and “embarrassment” — not only because of the accidental texts to journalists and accusations of war crimes but because he seems to care far more about superfici
items.author: Bess Levin
paragraphs: Pete Hegseth’s tenure as secretary of Defense has largely been defined by the words “cringeworthy” and “embarrassment” — not only because of the accidental texts to journalists and accusations of war crimes but because he seems to care far more about superficial details than actually protecting Americans and engages in what could charitably be described as dumb shit on the daily. For example: spending millions to rename the DoD the Department of War and damaging a priceless artifact in service of playing out some kind of World War II fantasy.

Yes, the Washington Post reports that earlier this year, Hegseth’s staff tried to move a floor globe used by General Dwight D. Eisenhower during World War II into the secretary’s office and “lost control of the artifact and dropped it, sending the globe crashing onto its base and impaling the fragile shell near Antarctica … The resulting gash appears to be several inches wide.” Why did the staff try to relocate the globe? Because its “historical significance was attractive to Hegseth.” Were Hegseth’s people supposed to just wing it? No, they were meant to “consult with experts at the U.S. Army Center of Military History on how to ensure its safe transport and properly document its relocation to Hegseth’s office.” Why weren’t those people brought in? Because they were furloughed during a partial shutdown and couldn’t be reached. Why didn’t Team Hegseth wait until the move could be overseen by professionally trained curators? Because of an “apparent lack of patience,” according to one person familiar with the matter.

Is there precedent for how to do this properly? Yes, a different globe linked to Eisenhower was moved from a storage facility to an Army installation in recent years with the moving company writing in 2022 that, as the item was “considered priceless,” careful measures were taken to ensure a “safe delivery.”

The Army acknowledged to the Post that the damage to the globe Hegseth wanted occurred during an “attempted move” on February 3, adding that it was ultimately not relocated. A DoD official later added, in an unattributed statement, that “Accidents happen” and “we are grateful no one was harmed, and the globe is being repaired.”

The incident reportedly “became instant fodder for gossip and jokes inside the Pentagon, with some decrying the apparent brashness and affinity for World War II nostalgia that they characterized as common themes throughout Hegseth’s tenure as Defense secretary.” Ty Seidule, a former brigadier general and history teacher at West Point, told the Post: “Hegseth wants an Eisenhower totem to be like Ike, brilliant in war and peace. Hegseth is no Ike. The globe won’t give him Ike’s attributes of humility, intellect and judgment.”

In addition to Globegate, Hegseth’s time at the DoD has been marked by a war on “wokeness,” mandatory testosterone testing, keeping service members who don’t meet his physical standards out of view, and trying to make the word “lethality” happen. Maybe next year, as a treat, he’ll have George Washington’s dentures sent up from Mount Vernon.

items.title: Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes Doc Met With Shock and Awe at Secret Screening
items.description: The audience that walked into the Werner Herzog Theatre at the Telluride Film Festival on Sunday night didn’t know exactly what they’d be watching because the screening had been kept top secret all week. Many wondered if it could live up to all the hype. And h
items.author: Rebecca Ford
paragraphs: The audience that walked into the Werner Herzog Theatre at the Telluride Film Festival on Sunday night didn’t know exactly what they’d be watching because the screening had been kept top secret all week. Many wondered if it could live up to all the hype. And honestly, even after it was revealed by festival director Julie Huntsinger that it was You Can See Everything—a top secret documentary about famed Theranos founder and felon Elizabeth Holmes, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim—some in the audience still weren’t sure if that was a big enough deal. Holmes’s downfall has, after all, been chronicled in multiple storytelling forms, including the podcast The Dropout and the popular Hulu series of the same name starring Amanda Seyfried.

But the 174-minute documentary was indeed worth the wait. It’s full of unexpected twists and turns and shocking reveals, with Fielder and Oppenheim having incredible access to Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, in the weeks leading up to her prison sentence for her conviction of defrauding investors. The enigmatic and controversial Holmes and her partner say they want to give Fielder and Oppenheim unrestricted access to their lives so that they can refute the narrative that they claim has been created about Holmes in the media, including that in Hulu’s dramatic adaptation.

Fielder, who appears on camera as a part of the documentary, speaks at length to both Holmes and Evans, who were raising their two children in San Diego before Holmes turned herself in to begin her 11-year sentence in 2023. In the days leading up to her having to leave her family, Fielder actually lived at their home with them. The documentary reveals that the couple are planning on pursuing a new version of the Theranos health technology, despite the fact that Holmes is days away from going to prison for fraud.

After Holmes begins her sentence, the documentary continues, but takes an extremely unexpected twist that involves the appearance of a notable Hollywood actress. The audience was asked by Fielder and Oppenheim to not reveal the person who appears in the doc because of the overwhelming shock of that twist. Fielder uses a technique similar to that in The Rehearsal, in which there are reenactments of scenes he was unable to film.

From there, the documentary offers many surprising revelations, especially pertaining to Holmes’s partner. Fielder discovers that Evans seems to be very involved in—or perhaps even controlling over—many aspects of Holmes’s image, including her Twitter.

During a Q&A after the screening (moderated by Emma Stone), Fielder and Oppenheim revealed that they felt they had a story to tell after they began filming Holmes and her family, and realized that everyone on the crew felt differently about what they’d just witnessed. “Lance and I would talk with the rest of the crew about what we thought happened or what we thought these moments meant, and no one could reach a consensus,” said Fielder. “And that’s when we really realized, Oh, this is really interesting to follow this. We’re all smart and we’re really working at the top of our intelligence. Why can’t we make sense of what’s happening in this house?”

During their three-year journey in making the film, Fielder says they didn’t get all the answers about Holmes, and the documentary attempts to dig into if she’s a master manipulator, or being manipulated. “I really am struggling to this day to understand exactly what I experienced,” Fielder said. “And one of the things I’m genuinely excited about is for this movie to come out and for people to help me understand what I experienced. Truly, to this day, I don’t quite know what I went through.”

Fielder and Oppenheim also revealed that they had reached out to numerous people who knew or had worked with Holmes, but really struggled to get anyone to participate. “Liz is toxic to people,” said Fielder. “People did not want to appear in this, or people from the past were just sort of done with her.”

A24, which released the first trailer just after the screening, will release You Can See Everything in October. Fielder and Oppenheim said that Holmes and Evans have not yet seen the finished film, but are aware of its existence. “Near the end of the process, Billy was trying to exert, we felt, a lot of control over the process,” said Fielder, “and what he sort of had desired, and it sort of caused our communication to break down a little bit.”

items.title: Making the Elizabeth Holmes Doc Fried Nathan Fielder’s and Lance Oppenheim’s Brains
items.description: Half an hour before the New York Film Festival’s one and only screening of You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, the standby line to get into the theater was dozens of people deep—stretching across the
items.author: Hillary Busis
paragraphs: Half an hour before the New York Film Festival’s one and only screening of You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, the standby line to get into the theater was dozens of people deep—stretching across the front of Alice Tully Hall and around the corner, all the way to the Juilliard Store on West 66th Street. The first person in line, looking relatively comfy in a camping chair, told me he’d gotten there nearly 12 hours ago, at 8 a.m. The next had been standing in line since 10:45.

“We’re probably not going to get in,” the queue warrior said. But he and the others kept standing there anyway, clinging to a delusional hope that they could change their fate just by wanting something hard enough.

Their plight reminded me a bit of Holmes herself, the disgraced Theranos founder who in 2022 was found guilty of defrauding investors and sentenced to serve 11 years in federal prison. Throughout her ordeal, Holmes has insisted on her own innocence. She’s so convinced of it—and utterly certain that everyone else will believe her too, if only she has an opportunity to speak her truth—that in 2023, just weeks before surrendering herself to Federal Prison Camp Bryan in Bryan, Texas, she invited Fielder and Oppenheim into her home.

Holmes allowed the filmmakers to document her final days with her children and her fiancé, Billy Evans, in their San Diego rental—swimming in the Pacific Ocean, eating pink pineapple, plotting their next biotech endeavor. It’s unbelievable that Holmes and Evans are trying to launch a new company; it’s even more unbelievable that this company is, in fact, another medical testing enterprise. And these remarkable facts are just the tip of the iceberg—of the single-finger-prick needle?—when it comes to what’s contained in this remarkable movie.

Nobody understands the situation’s baseline insanity better than Oppenheim and Fielder. During a post-screening Q&A, Oppenheim said that the movie was actually Holmes’s idea: “She was looking for someone to document her life, and she had reached out to A24. Which I thought was strange for a few reasons.”

At first, added Fielder, he wasn’t sure there was much more to say about Elizabeth Holmes. “She wanted to speak, but I didn’t really see a documentary project in it because it felt like the story was very told. But I was really curious to meet her, just as a personal thing.”

Oppenheim has helmed a variety of documentaries as well as the To Catch a Predator–inspired Primetime, starring Robert Pattinson. Fielder, though, is known for more experimental and less categorizable work, like the cringey faux-reality show Nathan for You and The Rehearsal, an HBO series that once inspired Vanity Fair to write these sentences: “Why is Nathan Fielder doing this to himself? What is the end goal, beyond Fielder having entertained himself with how hard he can mindfuck people into doing his strange bidding?”

You might not think that someone who’s interested in image rehabilitation would enlist Fielder, of all people, to make a film about her. Yet Holmes did just that. Why? Fielder still isn’t sure. It seems clear Holmes didn’t know much about him or his work; he speculated in the Q&A that she didn’t want to ask an actual friend of hers or Evans’s to make a movie, because “no one would take that seriously. Or something? So I don’t know. It’s so hard to speculate as to what…”

Here, Oppenheim cut in. “It felt like we were in the Zone, from Stalker, every day when we were there,” he said, referencing the no-man’s-land in Andrei Tarkovsky’s 1979 postapocalyptic drama. “Just literally, the laws of reality and everything we thought was going on outside just evaporated. I feel like our brains were scrambled, and we were also unsure for so long if we even had anything worthwhile.” They did.

It’s hard to say much about You Can See Everything without discussing the incredible pivot the film makes in its second half, after Holmes is incarcerated. Without getting too far into spoiler territory, though, it’s fair to say that, like Oppenheim and Fielder, you, too, may leave the movie not knowing whether Elizabeth Holmes is an unrepentant con artist, a quixotic zealot, an alien from outer space, or some even more outrageous fourth possibility.

It’s somewhat easier to pin down Evans, who gradually emerges as the movie’s true villain: a smarmy, self-satisfied Svengali figure who sniffs conspicuously and blithely brags about his own prowess in a variety of arenas. “I’m pretty strategic and well-resourced,” he tells Fielder at one point. “I know people who can do just about anything.”

Perhaps it comes as no surprise to hear that in the time since they finished shooting, the filmmakers and Evans have become estranged. “Near the end of filming, Billy was trying to exert a level of control over the project that made us uncomfortable, and communication with him sort of broke down because of that,” said Fielder. As of the Telluride Film Festival, Evans hadn’t seen the movie; as of NYFF, that was still true. Maybe that will change October 16, when it’s released in theaters.

By the time the Q&A was over, it was past 11:30 p.m.—about 90 minutes later than Fielder’s usual bedtime, he joked from the stage. A bleary but charged-up audience spilled into the street. Some headed straight to the post-premiere party at the Waverly Inn. (Though a friend of mine thought she spotted Fielder with his rumored girlfriend, novelist Emma Cline, at the event, a source with knowledge says Cline was not there.) Other would-be attendees were stopped in their tracks by a truck parked right in front of Lincoln Center, which bore an LED screen displaying a portrait of You Can See Everything’s subject and a three-word message: “Free Elizabeth Holmes.”

A crew of energetic canvassers flanked the truck, handing out free T-shirts and fliers promoting a website called justblood.com, which apparently aims to exonerate Holmes via the use of illegible AI slop. It is run not, as you might suspect, by Evans, but by a completely unrelated weirdo. As Oppenheim and Fielder might say, you really can’t make this shit up.
This story has been updated.

items.title: Inside Elizabeth Holmes’s Final Months at Theranos
items.description: Elizabeth Holmes appeared to know exactly what she needed to do. It was September 2017, and the situation was dire. Theranos, the blood-testing company that she had dreamed up more than a decade ago, during her freshman year at Stanford, was imploding before h
items.author: Nick Bilton
paragraphs: Elizabeth Holmes appeared to know exactly what she needed to do. It was September 2017, and the situation was dire. Theranos, the blood-testing company that she had dreamed up more than a decade ago, during her freshman year at Stanford, was imploding before her very eyes. John Carreyrou, an investigative reporter at The Wall Street Journal, had spent nearly two years detailing the start-up’s various misdeeds—questioning the veracity of its lab results and the legitimacy of its core product, the Edison, a small, consumer blood-testing device that supposedly used a drop of blood to perform hundreds of medical tests. Carreyrou had even revealed that Theranos relied on third-party devices to administer its own tests. Theranos, which had raised nearly $1 billion in funding for a valuation estimated at around $9 billion, now appeared less a medical-sciences company than a house of cards.

Owing largely to Carreyrou’s reporting, the fallout had been colossal, unprecedented. Theranos was under investigation by the Securities and Exchange Commission, the Department of Justice, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. It had been sued by investors. Walgreens, its largest partner, terminated the relationship and shut down 40 testing sites. Forbes, which once estimated Holmes’s wealth at $4.5 billion, wrote it down to zero. The young founder, who was once compared to Steve Jobs, had recently been dubbed a “millennial Madoff” by the New York Post. According to two former executives at the company, Theranos had as many as nine different law firms on retainer, including the formidable Boies Schiller Flexner, to handle the mess—what appeared to be the end of a long, labored, highly visible, and heinous corporate death march.
iTunes user? Just tap here to listen to Inside the Hive at your convenience. And don’t forget to subscribe.

But Holmes had other ideas. Despite the chaos, she believed that Theranos could still be saved, and she had an unconventional plan for redemption. That September, according to the two former executives, Holmes asked her security detail and one of her drivers to escort her to the airport in her designated black Cadillac Escalade. She flew first class across the country and was subsequently chauffeured to a dog breeder who supplied her with a 9-week-old Siberian husky. The puppy had long white paws, and a grey and black body. Holmes had already picked out a name: Balto.

For Holmes, the dog represented the journey that lay ahead for Theranos. As she explained to colleagues at the company’s headquarters, in Palo Alto, he was named after the world-famous sled dog who, in 1925, led a team of huskies on a dangerous, 600-mile trek from Nenana, Alaska, to remote Nome, Alaska, bearing an antitoxin that was used to fight a diphtheria outbreak. There is even a statue of Balto in New York’s Central Park, Holmes told one former employee. The metaphorical connection was obvious. In Holmes’s telling, Balto’s perseverance mirrored her own. His voyage with the life-changing drug was not so different from her ambition.

In Silicon Valley, founders and C.E.O.s often embrace a signature idiosyncrasy as a personal branding device. Steve Jobs wore the same black turtleneck every day and tended to only park in handicap spots. Mark Zuckerberg went through a phase during which he would only eat the meat of animals he had personally killed. Shigeru Miyamoto, the Nintendo video-game legend, is so obsessed with estimating the size of things that he carries around a tape measure. It can get even weirder. Peter Thiel has expressed an interest in the restorative properties of blood transfusions from young people. Jack Dorsey drinks a strange lemon-water concoction every morning, and goes on 10-day silent retreats while wearing designer clothing and an Apple Watch. Holmes, too, had seemingly cherry-picked from her elders. She wore a black turtleneck, drank strange green juices, traveled with armed guards, and spoke in a near baritone. In an industry full of oddballs, Holmes—a blonde WASP from the D.C. area—seemed hell-bent on cultivating a reputation as an iconoclastic weirdo. Having Balto seemed to help fortify the image.

Immediately after returning to California, Holmes decided that Balto would hardly leave her side on the quest to save Theranos. Each day, Holmes would wake up with Balto at the nearly empty Los Altos mansion that she was renting about six miles from her company’s headquarters. (Theranos covered the house’s rent.) Soon after, one of her two drivers, sometimes her two security personnel, and even sometimes one of her two assistants, would pick them up, and set off for work. And for the rest of the day, Balto would stroll through the labs with his owner. Holmes brushed it off when the scientists protested that the dog hair could contaminate samples. But there was another problem with Balto, too. He wasn’t potty-trained. Accustomed to the undomesticated life, Balto frequently urinated and defecated at will throughout Theranos headquarters. While Holmes held board meetings, Balto could be found in the corner of the room relieving himself while a frenzied assistant was left to clean up the mess.

Around this same time, Holmes says that she discovered that Balto—like most huskies—had a tiny trace of wolf origin. Henceforth, she decided that Balto wasn’t really a dog, but rather a wolf. In meetings, at cafés, whenever anyone stopped to pet the pup and ask his breed, Holmes soberly replied, “He’s a wolf.”

Silicon Valley can often feel like a lawless place, and for good reason. Many of the people who run the largest technology companies on earth don’t often suffer the consequences of their actions. Despite their unequivocal role in upending our democracy, Zuckerberg and Sheryl Sandberg still run Facebook. Dorsey is still the C.E.O. of Twitter, even though he has not been forthright about the number of bots on the service, and has done almost nothing to stop the spread of hate speech on his platform. The C.E.O. of Tesla, Elon Musk, has been charged with securities fraud, and yet he’s still running the company. (Musk later agreed with the S.E.C. that he would step down as chairman and pay a $20 million fine.)

Holmes is that rare exception in which consequences occur. And the public, perhaps fed up with the behavior of other tech giants (and Wall Street bankers before them), has been captivated by her downfall. Three years after Carreyrou began his investigation, Holmes has again become a figure of extraordinary pop-culture fascination—a distinct rarity for a businessperson. Her story is the subject of the HBO documentary, The Inventor, and ABC News’s podcast series, The Dropout. Bad Blood, Carreyrou’s book, has sold half a million copies and is being developed for Hollywood by Adam McKay. Jennifer Lawrence is set to play Holmes. (Disclosure: I was a consulting producer on the HBO project, which was partly based on an article I wrote about Theranos nearly three years ago.)

The fascination with Holmes often fixates on her extraordinary rise—her ability to convince Stanford scientists to believe her idea despite a lack of formal training; her aptitude for getting wisemen (Henry Kissinger, James Mattis, George Schultz) to sit on her board; and her skill for obtaining early funding from eminences such as Rupert Murdoch, the Walton family, and others. But the final days of Theranos were equally chilling. After all, Holmes wasn’t just an inexperienced scientist; she was also a wild-spending fiduciary.

Holmes had always enjoyed a certain lifestyle. From the early days of the company, she had insisted on flying in a private jet. As the company’s legal problems mounted, its costs skyrocketed, but Holmes had a hard time weaning herself off certain luxuries. She still had her own personal security detail, drivers, personal assistants, and a personal publicist who was on retainer for $25,000 a month, according to one of the former executives. Theranos had an indemnity agreement with Holmes and Sunny Balwani, the company’s C.O.O., with whom she had been romantically involved. (They are no longer dating.) Theranos paid all their legal bills, which totaled millions of dollars a month, according to both executives.

By late 2017, however, Holmes had begun to slightly rein in the spending. She agreed to give up her private-jet travel (not a good look) and instead downgraded to first class on commercial airlines. But given that she was flying all over the world trying to obtain more funding for Theranos, she was spending tens of thousands of dollars a month on travel. Theranos was also still paying for her mansion in Los Altos, and her team of personal assistants and drivers, who would become regular dog walkers for Balto.

But there were few places she had wasted so much money as the design and monthly cost of the company’s main headquarters, which employees simply referred to as “1701,” for its street address along Page Mill Road in Palo Alto. 1701, according to two former executives, cost $1 million a month to rent. Holmes had also spent $100,000 on a single conference table. Elsewhere in the building, Holmes had asked for another circular conference room that the former employees said “looked like the war room from Dr. Strangelove,” replete with curved glass windows, and screens that would come out of the ceiling so everyone in the room could see a presentation without having to turn their heads.

But by the end of 2017, it became clear that it was financially untenable to stay in 1701, largely owing to Theranos’s legal expenditures. The remaining employees were told they would be moving to the Theranos laboratory facility, across the bay in Newark, California. Employees who were still at Theranos at the time describe Newark as “crummy” and a “shithole.” The building was formerly home to a solar-panel maker, and it had a huge floor space. Employees were set up on the second floor, where people would sit four to a table in the open-floor plan. Holmes took the corner office with Balto.

The move may have been a last-gasp attempt to save the company, but morale at Theranos was already at an all-time low. The S.E.C. and other government agencies had started to subpoena current and former workers. Remaining employees started to resign or were let go, almost on a daily basis, it seemed. As two former employees told me, you could go to Antonio’s Nut House, the famous Palo Alto bar, any night of the week and there would reliably be a goodbye gathering for at least one Theranos employee.

Yet through all of this, former employees of the company have told me, Holmes had a bizarre way of acting like nothing was wrong. Even more peculiarly, she appeared happy. “The company is falling apart, there are countless indictments piling up, employees are leaving in droves, and Elizabeth is just weirdly chipper,” a former senior executive told me. One former board member also noted that Holmes would come to board meetings “chirpy” and acting as if everything was “great.” She would walk up to people in the office who could have just testified in front of the S.E.C., or been questioned by lawyers at the F.D.A., and she would give them a hug and ask how they were doing. She was so confident that the company would be fine, executives who worked with her said, that she enrolled Balto in a search-and-rescue program. Holmes spent weekends training him to find people in an emergency. Unfortunately, huskies are not bred for rescue; they are long-distance runners, and Balto failed out.

For years, Holmes had relished in the ritual of giving speeches to the employees. When Balwani worked at Theranos, the speeches ended with chants. Some were positive, and some were more famously negative, such as when employees in lab coats would chant “fuck you” to a competitor or journalist. But such rhetoric was usually followed by excited cheers and roars. One day in late December 2017, Holmes showed up at the Newark building and held an all-hands meeting. She appeared excited beyond restraint. Brimming with enthusiasm, she told her employees that Fortress Investment Group, one of the world’s largest private investment companies, had agreed to offer a $100 million loan that would allow the company to survive.

But Holmes didn’t appear to receive the response that she craved from her colleagues. One executive who was there told me the room was silent. After an uncomfortable beat, Holmes said, “Does anyone have any questions?” Again, nothing. Just a bristling silence. By this point, “The morale had been completely drained out of the company,” the employee explained. Months later, Holmes was charged with 11 criminal felony counts, including wire fraud and conspiracy. Theranos was essentially gutted by the spring of 2018. It shuttered in September 2018, one year after Holmes adopted Balto. Fortress got ownership of all of Theranos’s patents. The $900 million she had raised was up in smoke.

Since Theranos’s collapse, observers have wondered how Holmes kept the company going for so long—how she was able to convince those scientists, investors, and colleagues that her quixotic idea for a portable, revolutionary blood-testing technology could somehow come to fruition. Recently, I posed a similar question to a former Theranos board member: how did the board of directors, composed of such accomplished people, not stop her. This person admitted that board members asked tough questions but were fed contrived answers. (Notably, the board was stacked with dignitaries, not scientists.) After the Journal broke the news that the company was being investigated, the board suggested that Holmes take the Theranos blood test and compare it with results from two other competing labs and one university lab, this person said. If all the results were the same, Theranos could prove to regulators and the media, so went the logic, that their blood-testing products worked perfectly. If the tests showed that Theranos’s results were off, the board suggested that Holmes could direct the company’s considerable raised capital toward fixing the problem.

Holmes agreed to the trial but then withheld the results, the former board member told me. When the board asked about the findings, Holmes seemed to offer a series of obfuscations. Sometimes she would say she was waiting on results; at other times, she said there had been problems with the tests. Eventually, this got heated. At one meeting, according to the former board member, a Theranos employee presented financials that indicated that a Theranos lab in Arizona had not generated the revenues that Holmes had communicated to her directors. This was one of the few times where board members criticized their C.E.O., this person said. One board member was visibly irate; it appeared that Holmes had been deceptive. Soon after, Holmes shook up the board.

Holmes will almost certainly face consequences, but it may take a while. Justice Department officials, according to a filing from January 2019, are combing through between 16 and 17 million pages of documents. And there could be more charges filed against Holmes and Balwani, and even other people close to them. Assistant U.S. Attorney John C. Bostic said in court recently that the “story is bigger than what’s captured in the [original] indictment.” And that it “doesn’t capture all the criminal conduct” that the investigation has uncovered so far. Holmes faces up to 20 years in prison.

Holmes and Balwani have stated that the charges are baseless. Theranos represented a business failure, according to one line of exculpatory logic, but it was not created to rip off investors or mislead consumers—it wasn’t actual fraud. Also, according to another argument, neither of them actually made any money from Theranos. But their lifestyles were partly funded by the company. Holmes’s travel, security details, and publicists were all paid for by Theranos. Meals, clothing, and other social activities were almost always expensed. As one of the former employees said to me, “Someone had to be paying for all those Birkin bags.” This employee said that Holmes’s expenses were somewhat of a joke at the company. “The company paid for everything,” they said. “She would submit her miles if she drove the six miles to her house in Los Altos.” The employee said that the only time Holmes evidenced defeat during Theranos’s collapse was when the company cut her off financially, after the criminal charges were filed. “She lost her cool. She had a fit,” they said. “She had to give up the house in Los Altos.”

When I asked the former executive close to Holmes if she has come to regret what happened, the response surprised me. “Elizabeth sees herself as the victim,” this person said. “She blames John Carreyrou, she blames David Boies, and she blames Heather King.” Boies, the star lawyer, had sat on Theranos’s board, and represented the company during the Carreyrou crisis. King, Theranos’s general counsel for 15 months, overlapped with this period. (King now works at Boies’s firm.) Holmes, according to the former employees, blames the lawyers for giving her bad advice, and their inability to contain the bad press stemming from Carreyrou’s reporting. According to this person, Holmes thinks that she could have somehow convinced a Pulitzer Prize–winning reporter into believing that Theranos was going to change the world despite the fact that its core technology didn’t work. “She often confuses the message for the messenger,” the former employee told me.

When I asked Carreyrou what he thought about this theory, he told me: “I just reported the facts. If there had been nothing to my reporting, federal prosecutors wouldn’t have brought criminal fraud charges and those charges wouldn’t be supported by 17 million pages of evidence.” (Boies and King declined to comment, citing bar obligations. Neither Holmes nor her counsel responded to requests for comment.)

In his book, Carreyrou muses about an oft-raised question regarding Holmes. Was she just a young person who got in over her head? Or, more dramatically, is something more serious afoot. Is she a sociopath? “I’ll leave it to the psychologists to decide whether Holmes fits the clinical profile,” he writes, “but there’s no question that her moral compass was badly askew.” Former employees raise this question with frequency. One pointed to a formative experience: Holmes’s father, Christian, was an executive at Enron, and the family’s finances were affected by its collapse. Did Holmes, scarred by this experience, vow to revive the family’s fortunes at all cost? Was she a hustler or a con artist, or merely a staggering Mr. Ripley? “One of Elizabeth’s superpowers is she never looks back,” this person said.

Holmes is currently living in San Francisco in a luxury apartment. She’s engaged to a younger hospitality heir, who also works in tech. She wears his M.I.T. signet ring on a necklace and the couple regularly post stories on Instagram professing their love for each other. She reliably looks “chirpy” and “chipper.” She’s also abandoned the black-turtleneck look and now dresses in athleisure, the regrettable attire of our age. Notably, she is far from a hermit. She tells former colleagues, according to the two executives, that she is greeted by well-wishers on the street who are rooting for her resurrection. It’s a stark contrast to many of her old colleagues. Former Theranos employees I have spoken to have relayed horror stories about their inability to find work after leaving the company, now with a permanent stain on their résumé.

Holmes, for her part, still doesn’t seem to think the work of Theranos is finished. Like her dog’s famed namesake, she still wants people to know that Theranos was going to save the world. But in order to do so, she needs to share her side of the story. She has recently held more meetings with filmmakers to try to collaborate on a documentary about her “real” story. And Holmes desperately wants to write a book. In Holmes’s eyes, according to former employees, this is only the beginning of yet another redemption story—possibly one that is too good to be true. As for Balto, Holmes still tells people he’s a wolf.

items.title: Elizabeth Holmes Speaks About the “Hell and Torture” of Prison, New Inventions, and Pregnancy “Optics”
items.description: Elizabeth Holmes, the Theranos founder who is serving an 11-year sentence for fraud, has described her life behind bars as “hell and torture,” in her first interview from prison, published in People on Wednesday.
items.author: Kase Wickman
paragraphs: Elizabeth Holmes, the Theranos founder who is serving an 11-year sentence for fraud, has described her life behind bars as “hell and torture,” in her first interview from prison, published in People on Wednesday.

Before reporting to Federal Prison Camp in Bryan, Texas in May 2023, Holmes welcomed two children with partner Billy Evans, significantly drawing out the timeline of her trial process. The timing of the pregnancies, she told People, “wasn’t planned and I can’t worry about what others think.”
“I know how the optics look, but I always wanted to be a mother,” Holmes said.

There’s 3-year-old son William, whose July 2021 birth further pushed back her thrice-postponed trial, and 2-year-old daughter Invicta (meaning “invincible”), who was conceived after Holmes’ January 2022 conviction and born about three months before Holmes she began serving time. Holmes’ team cited the two young children when they asked for a lighter sentence.
“I truly did not think I would ever be convicted or found guilty,” she insisted. “I kept talking to my lawyers and they also assured me we would never get this far.”

She maintains her innocence, and pled not guilty in her trial, where she was ultimately found guilty of three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, of an initial 11 charges, and said in the interview that “there are things I would have done differently.”
Still: “I received a considerable amount of time I wasn’t expecting,” she said. “I always wanted a big family, Billy wanted even more kids.”
She is currently scheduled for release on April 3, 2032, having already gotten two years of her sentence reduced for good conduct. Her children will be 10 and 9 years old on her planned release date.

A May 2023 New York Times profile of Holmes caused an uproar when reporter Amy Chozick admitted in the piece that her editor at the paper said Chozick had been “rolled” by Holmes—please, call her “Liz,” she insisted—when Chozick found her to be “a devoted mother” and “authentic and sympathetic person.” Times employees protested the vaseline-lensed portrait of Holmes and questioned the integrity of the piece.

This latest interview highlights that after bringing two breast pumps to prison with her “because it was a way to love her [daughter] in here,” Holmes successfully lobbied for the addition of lactation rooms for breastfeeding mothers to have privacy in the prison housing. She teaches French to fellow prisoners, and has a job in prison helping women work on their cases for compassionate release and editing resumes for their re-entry into society. She also mentioned that she hand-wrote a seven-page document to change criminal procedure, including advocating for incarcerated parents. This Holmes is a doting mother torn away from the children she calls “angels,” determined to help others in her position find justice.
“This will be my life’s work,” she said.

Holmes acknowledged that the public seems to be suspicious of her, to say the least. “It’s surreal,” she told People. “People who have never met me believe so strongly about me. They don’t understand who I am. It forces you to spend a lot of time questioning belief and hoping the truth will prevail. I am walking by faith and, ultimately, the truth. But it’s been hell and torture to be here.”

And then there’s her other life’s work, one with a strong connection to her high-profile past: Holmes still dreams of innovating in the healthcare space, despite the very public scandal of her sham blood-testing technology company, Theranos.
“There is not a day I have not continued to work on my research and inventions,” she said. “I remain completely committed to my dream of making affordable healthcare solutions available to everyone.”

items.title: Exclusive: How Elizabeth Holmes’s House of Cards Came Tumbling Down
