items.author: Nick Bilton
paragraphs: It was late morning on Friday, October 16, when Elizabeth Holmes realized that she had no other choice. She finally had to address her employees at Theranos, the blood-testing start-up that she had founded as a 19-year-old Stanford dropout, which was now valued at some $9 billion. Two days earlier, a damning report published in The Wall Street Journal had alleged that the company was, in effect, a sham—that its vaunted core technology was actually faulty and that Theranos administered almost all of its blood tests using competitors’ equipment.

The article created tremors throughout Silicon Valley, where Holmes, the world’s youngest self-made female billionaire, had become a near universally praised figure. Curiosity about the veracity of the Journal story was also bubbling throughout the company’s mustard-and-green Palo Alto headquarters, which was nearing the end of a $6.7 million renovation. Everyone at Theranos, from its scientists to its marketers, wondered what to make of it all.

For two days, according to insiders, Holmes, who is now 32, had refused to address these concerns. Instead, she remained largely holed up in a conference room, surrounded by her inner circle. Half-empty food containers and cups of stale coffee and green juice were strewn on the table as she strategized with a phalanx of trusted advisers, including Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, then Theranos’s president and C.O.O.; Heather King, the company’s general counsel; lawyers from Boies, Schiller & Flexner, the intrepid law firm; and crisis-management consultants. Most of the people in the war room had been there for two days and nights straight, according to an insider, leaving mainly to shower or make a feeble attempt at a couple of hours of shut-eye. There was also an uncomfortable chill in the room. At Theranos, Holmes preferred that the temperature be maintained in the mid-60s, which facilitated her preferred daily uniform of a black turtleneck with a puffy black vest—a homogeneity that she had borrowed from her idol, the late Steve Jobs.

Holmes had learned a lot from Jobs. Like Apple, Theranos was secretive, even internally. Just as Jobs had famously insisted at 1 Infinite Loop, 10 minutes away, that departments were generally siloed, Holmes largely forbade her employees from communicating with one another about what they were working on—a culture that resulted in a rare form of executive omniscience. At Theranos, Holmes was founder, C.E.O., and chairwoman. There wasn’t a decision—from the number of American flags framed in the company’s hallway (they are ubiquitous) to the compensation of each new hire—that didn’t cross her desk.

And like Jobs, crucially, Holmes also paid indefatigable attention to her company’s story, its “narrative.” Theranos was not simply endeavoring to make a product that sold off the shelves and lined investors’ pockets; rather, it was attempting something far more poignant. In interviews, Holmes reiterated that Theranos’s proprietary technology could take a pinprick’s worth of blood, extracted from the tip of a finger, instead of intravenously, and test for hundreds of diseases—a remarkable innovation that was going to save millions of lives and, in a phrase she often repeated, “change the world.” In a technology sector populated by innumerable food-delivery apps, her quixotic ambition was applauded. Holmes adorned the covers of Fortune, Forbes, and Inc., among other publications. She was profiled in The New Yorker and featured on a segment of Charlie Rose. In the process, she amassed a net worth of around $4 billion.

One of the only journalists who seemed unimpressed by this narrative was John Carreyrou, a recalcitrant health-care reporter from The Wall Street Journal. Carreyrou came away from The New Yorker story surprised by Theranos’s secrecy—such behavior was to be expected at a tech company but not a medical operation. Moreover, he was also struck by Holmes’s limited ability to explain how it all worked. When The New Yorker reporter asked about Theranos’s technology, she responded, somewhat cryptically, “a chemistry is performed so that a chemical reaction occurs and generates a signal from the chemical interaction with the sample, which is translated into a result, which is then reviewed by certified laboratory personnel.”

Shortly after reading the article, Carreyrou started investigating Theranos’s medical practices. As it turned out, there was an underside to Theranos’s story that had not been told—one that involved questionable lab procedures and results, among other things. Soon after Carreyrou began his reporting, David Boies, the superstar lawyer—and Theranos board member—who had taken on Bill Gates in the 1990s and represented Al Gore during the 2000 Florida recount case, visited the Journal newsroom for a five-hour meeting. Boies subsequently returned to the Journal to meet with the paper’s editor in chief, Gerard Baker. Eventually, on October 16, 2015, the Journal published the article: HOT STARTUP THERANOS HAS STRUGGLED WITH ITS BLOOD-TEST TECHNOLOGY.

During the two days in the war room, according to numerous insiders, Holmes heard various response strategies. The most cogent suggestion advocated enlisting members of the scientific community to publicly defend Theranos—its name an amalgam of “therapy” and “diagnosis.” But no scientist could credibly vouch for Theranos. Under Holmes’s direction, the secretive company had barred other scientists from writing peer-review papers on its technology.

Absent a plan, Holmes embarked on a familiar course—she doubled down on her narrative. She left the war room for her car—she is often surrounded by her security detail, which sometimes numbers as many as four men, who (for safety reasons) refer to the young C.E.O. as “Eagle 1”—and headed to the airport. (She has been known to fly alone on a $6.5 million Gulfstream G150.) Holmes subsequently took off for Boston to attend a luncheon for a previously scheduled appearance at the Harvard Medical School Board of Fellows, where she would be honored as an inductee. During the trip, Holmes fielded calls from her advisers in the war room. She and her team decided on an interview with Jim Cramer, the host of CNBC’s Mad Money, with whom she had a friendship that dated from a previous interview. It was quickly arranged.

Cramer generously began the interview by asking Holmes what had happened. Holmes, who talks slowly and deliberately, and blinks with alarming irregularity, replied with a variation of a line from Jobs. “This is what happens when you work to change things,” she said, her long blond hair tousled, her smile amplified by red lipstick. “First they think you’re crazy, then they fight you, and then, all of a sudden, you change the world.” When Cramer asked Holmes for a terse true-or-false answer about an accusation in the article, she replied with a meandering 198-word retort.

By the time she returned to Palo Alto, the consensus was that it was time, at last, for Holmes to address her hundreds of employees. A company-wide e-mail instructed technicians in lab coats, programmers in T-shirts and jeans, and a slew of support staff to meet in the cafeteria. There, Holmes, with Balwani at her side, began an eloquent speech in her typical baritone, explaining to her loyal colleagues that they were changing the world. As she continued, Holmes grew more impassioned. The Journal, she said, had gotten the story wrong. Carreyrou, she insisted, with a tinge of fury, was simply picking a fight. She handed the stage to Balwani, who echoed her sentiments.

After he wrapped up, the leaders of Theranos stood before their employees and surveyed the room. Then a chant erupted. “Fuck you . . .,” employees began yelling in unison, “Carreyrou.” It began to grow louder still. “Fuck you, Carreyrou!” Soon men and women in lab coats, and programmers in T-shirts and jeans, joined in. They were chanting with fervor: “Fuck you, Carreyrou!,” they cried out. “Fuck you, Carreyrou! Fuck. You. Carrey-rou!”

In Silicon Valley, every company has an origin story—a fable, often slightly embellished, that humanizes its mission for the purpose of winning over investors, the press, and, if it ever gets to that point, customers, too. These origin stories can provide a unique, and uniquely powerful, lubricant in the Valley. After all, while Silicon Valley is responsible for some truly astounding companies, its business dealings can also replicate one big confidence game in which entrepreneurs, venture capitalists, and the tech media pretend to vet one another while, in reality, functioning as cogs in a machine that is designed to not question anything—and buoy one another all along the way.

It generally works like this: the venture capitalists (who are mostly white men) don’t really know what they’re doing with any certainty—it’s impossible, after all, to truly predict the next big thing—so they bet a little bit on every company that they can with the hope that one of them hits it big. The entrepreneurs (also mostly white men) often work on a lot of meaningless stuff, like using code to deliver frozen yogurt more expeditiously or apps that let you say “Yo!” (and only “Yo!”) to your friends. The entrepreneurs generally glorify their efforts by saying that their innovation could change the world, which tends to appease the venture capitalists, because they can also pretend they’re not there only to make money. And this also helps seduce the tech press (also largely comprised of white men), which is often ready to play a game of access in exchange for a few more page views of their story about the company that is trying to change the world by getting frozen yogurt to customers more expeditiously. The financial rewards speak for themselves. Silicon Valley, which is 50 square miles, has created more wealth than any place in human history. In the end, it isn’t in anyone’s interest to call bullshit.

When Elizabeth Holmes emerged on the tech scene, around 2003, she had a preternaturally good story. She was a woman. She was building a company that really aimed to change the world. And, as a then dark-haired 19-year-old first-year at Stanford University’s School of Chemical Engineering, she already comported herself in a distinctly Jobsian fashion. She adopted black turtlenecks, would boast of never taking a vacation, and would come to practice veganism. She quoted Jane Austen by heart and referred to a letter that she had written to her father when she was nine years old insisting, “What I really want out of life is to discover something new, something that mankind didn’t know was possible to do.” And it was this instinct, she said, coupled with a childhood fear of needles, that led her to come up with her revolutionary company.

Holmes had indeed mastered the Silicon Valley game. Revered venture capitalists, such as Tim Draper and Steve Jurvetson, invested in her; Marc Andreessen called her the next Steve Jobs. She was plastered on the covers of magazines, featured on TV shows, and offered keynote-speaker slots at tech conferences. (Holmes spoke at *Vanity Fair’*s 2015 New Establishment Summit less than two weeks before Carreyrou’s first story appeared in the Journal.) In some ways, the near-universal adoration of Holmes reflected her extraordinary comportment. In others, however, it reflected the Valley’s own narcissism. Finally, it seemed, there was a female innovator who was indeed able to personify the Valley’s vision of itself—someone who was endeavoring to make the world a better place.

Holmes’s real story, however, was a little more complicated. When she first came up with the precursor to the idea of Theranos, which eventually aimed to reap vast amounts of data from a few droplets of blood derived from the tip of a finger, she approached several of her professors at Stanford, according to someone who knew Holmes back then. But most explained to the chemical-engineering major that it was virtually impossible to do so with any real efficacy. “I told her, I don’t think your idea is going to work,” Phyllis Gardner, a professor of medicine at Stanford, said to me, about Holmes’s seminal pitch for Theranos. As Gardner explained, it is impossible to get a precise result from the tip of a finger for most of the tests that Theranos would claim to conduct accurately. When a finger is pricked, the probe breaks up cells, allowing debris, among other things, to escape into the interstitial fluid. While it is feasible to test for pathogens this way, a pinprick is too unreliable for obtaining more nuanced readings. Furthermore, there isn’t that much reliable data that you can reap from such a small amount of blood. But Holmes was nothing if not determined. Rather than drop her idea, she tried to persuade Channing Robertson, her adviser at Stanford, to back her in her quest. He did. (“It would not be unusual for finger-stick testing to be met with skepticism,” says a spokesman for Theranos. “Patents from that period explain Elizabeth’s ideas and were foundational for the company’s current technologies.”)

Holmes subsequently raised $6 million in funding, the first of almost $700 million that would follow. Money often comes with strings attached in Silicon Valley, but even by its byzantine terms, Holmes’s were unusual. She took the money on the condition that she would not divulge to investors how her technology actually worked, and that she had final say and control over every aspect of her company. This surreptitiousness scared off some investors. When Google Ventures, which focuses more than 40 percent of its investments on medical technology, tried to perform due diligence on Theranos to weigh an investment, Theranos never responded. Eventually, Google Ventures sent a venture capitalist to a Theranos Walgreens Wellness Center to take the revolutionary pinprick blood test. As the V.C. sat in a chair and had several large vials of blood drawn from his arm, far more than a pinprick, it became apparent that something was amiss with Theranos’s promise.

Google Ventures wasn’t the only group with knowledge of blood testing which felt that way. One of Holmes’s first major hires, thanks to an introduction by Channing Robertson, was Ian Gibbons, an accomplished British scientist who had a slew of degrees from Cambridge University and had spent 30 years working on diagnostic and therapeutic products. Gibbons was tall and handsome, with straight reddish-brown hair and blue eyes. He had never owned a pair of jeans and spoke with a British accent that was a combination of colloquial and posh. In 2005, Holmes named him chief scientist.

Gibbons, who was diagnosed with cancer shortly after joining the company, encountered a host of issues with the science at Theranos, but the most glaring was simple: the results were off. This conclusion soon led Gibbons to realize that Holmes’s invention was more of an idea than a reality. Still, bound by the scientific method, Gibbons wanted to try every possible direction and exhaust every option. So, for years, while Holmes put her fund-raising talents to use—hiring hundreds of marketers, salespeople, communications specialists, and even the Oscar-winning filmmaker Errol Morris, who was commissioned to make short industrial documentaries—Gibbons would wake early, walk his dogs along a trail near his home, and then set off for the office before seven A.M. In his downtime, he would read I, Claudius, a novel about a man who plays dumb to unwittingly become the most powerful person on earth.

While Gibbons grew ever more desperate to come up with a solution to the inaccuracies of the blood-testing technology, Holmes presented her company to more investors, and even potential partners, as if it had a working, fully realized product. Holmes adorned her headquarters and Web site with slogans claiming, “One tiny drop changes everything,” and “All the same tests. One tiny sample,” and went into media overdrive. She also proved an effective crisis manager. In 2012, for instance, Holmes began talking to the Department of Defense about using Theranos’s technology on the battlefield in Afghanistan. But specialists at the D.O.D. soon uncovered that the technology wasn’t entirely accurate, and that it had not been vetted by the Food and Drug Administration. When the department notified the F.D.A. that something was amiss, according to The Washington Post, Holmes contacted Marine general James Mattis, who had initiated the pilot program. He immediately e-mailed his colleagues about moving the project forward. Mattis was later added to the company board when he retired from the service. (Mattis says he never tried to interfere with the F.D.A. but rather was “interested in rapidly having the company’s technologies tested legally and ethically.”)

At around the same time, Theranos also decided to sue Richard Fuisz, an old friend and neighbor of Holmes’s family, alleging that he had stolen secrets that belonged to Theranos. As the suit progressed—it was eventually settled—Fuisz’s lawyers issued subpoenas to Theranos executives involved with the “proprietary” aspects of the technology. This included Ian Gibbons. But Gibbons didn’t want to testify. If he told the court that the technology did not work, he would harm the people he worked with; if he wasn’t honest about the technology’s problems, however, consumers could potentially harm their health, maybe even fatally.

Holmes, meanwhile, did not seem willing to tolerate his resistance, according to his wife, Rochelle Gibbons. Even though Gibbons had warned that the technology wasn’t ready for the public, Holmes was preparing to open “Theranos Wellness Centers” in dozens of Walgreens across Arizona. “Ian felt like he would lose his job if he told the truth,” Rochelle told me as she wept one summer morning in Palo Alto. “Ian was a real obstacle for Elizabeth. He started to be very vocal. They kept him around to keep him quiet.” Channing Robertson, who had brought Gibbons to Theranos, recalls a different conversation, noting, “He suggested to me on numerous occasions that what we had accomplished at that time was sufficient to commercialize.”

A few months later, on May 16, 2013, Gibbons was sitting in the family room with Rochelle, the afternoon light draping the couple, when the telephone rang. He answered. It was one of Holmes’s assistants. When Gibbons hung up, he was beside himself. “Elizabeth wants to meet with me tomorrow in her office,” he told his wife in a quivering voice. “Do you think she’s going to fire me?” Rochelle Gibbons, who had spent a lot of time with Holmes, knew that she wanted control. “Yes,” she said to her husband, reluctantly. She told him she thought he was going to be fired. Later that evening, gripped and overwhelmed with worry, Ian Gibbons tried to commit suicide. He was rushed to the hospital. A week later, with his wife by his side, Ian Gibbons died.

When Rochelle called Holmes’s office to explain what had happened, the secretary was devastated and offered her sincere condolences. She told Rochelle Gibbons that she would let Holmes know immediately. But a few hours later, rather than a condolence message from Holmes, Rochelle instead received a phone call from someone at Theranos demanding that she immediately return any and all confidential Theranos property.

In hundreds of interviews with the media and on panels, Holmes honed her story to near perfection. She talked about how she didn’t play with Barbies as a child, and how her father, Christian Holmes IV, who worked in environmental technology for Enron before going on to work in a number of senior government jobs in Washington, was one of her idols. But her reverence for Steve Jobs was perhaps most glaring. Besides the turtlenecks, Holmes’s proprietary blood-analysis device, which she named “Edison” after Thomas Edison, resembled Jobs’s NeXT computer. She designed her Theranos office with Le Corbusier black leather chairs, a Jobs favorite. She also adhered to a strange diet of only green juices (cucumber, parsley, kale, spinach, romaine lettuce, and celery), to be drunk only at specific times of the day. Like Jobs, too, her company was her life. She rarely ever left the office, only going home to sleep. To celebrate her birthday, Holmes held a party at Theranos headquarters with her employees. (Her brother, Christian, also works at Theranos.)

But the most staggering characteristic that she borrowed from the late C.E.O. was his obsession with secrecy. And while Jobs had a fearsome security force who ensured that confidential information rarely, if ever, left Apple’s headquarters, Holmes had a single enforcer: Sunny Balwani, the company’s president and chief operating officer, until he stepped down in May. Balwani, who had previously worked at Lotus and Microsoft, had no experience in medicine. He was hired in 2009 to focus on e-commerce. Nevertheless, he was soon put in charge of the company’s most secret medical technology.

According to a number of people with knowledge of the situation, the two had met years before he began at the company, when Holmes took a trip to China after she graduated from high school. The two eventually started dating, numerous people told me, and remained very loyal even after their relationship ended. Among Holmes’s security detail, Balwani was known as “Eagle 2.”

When employees questioned the accuracy of the company’s blood-testing technology, it was Balwani who would chastise them in e-mails (or in person), sternly telling staffers, “This must stop,” as The Wall Street Journal reported. He ensured that scientists and engineers at Theranos did not talk to one another about their work. Applicants who came for job interviews were told that they wouldn’t know what the actual job was unless they were hired. Employees who spoke publicly about the company were met with legal threats. On LinkedIn, one former employee noted next to his job description, “I worked here, but every time I say what I did I get a letter from a lawyer. I probably will get a letter from a lawyer for writing this.” If people visited any of Theranos’s offices and refused to sign the company’s lengthy non-disclosure agreement, they were not allowed inside.

Balwani’s lack of medical experience might have seemed unusual at such a company. But few at Theranos were in a position to point fingers. As Holmes started to assemble her board of directors, she chose a dozen older white men, almost none of whom had a background in anything related to health care. This included former secretary of state Henry Kissinger, former secretary of state George Shultz, former Georgia senator and chairman of the Armed Services Committee Sam Nunn, and William J. Perry, the former defense secretary. (Bill Frist, the former Senate majority leader, and former cardiovascular doctor, was an exception.) “This was a board that was better suited to decide if America should invade Iraq than vet a blood-testing company,” one person said to me. Gibbons told his wife that Holmes commanded their attention masterfully.

Theranos’s board may not have been equipped to ask what exactly the company was building, or how, but others were. While Holmes was bounding around the world on a private plane, speaking on panels with Bill Clinton, and giving passionate TED talks, two government organizations started quietly inspecting the company. On August 25, 2015, months before the Journal story broke, three investigators from the F.D.A. arrived, unannounced, at Theranos’s headquarters, on Page Mill Road, with two more investigators sent to the company’s blood-testing lab in Newark, California, demanding to inspect the facilities.

According to someone close to the company, Holmes was sent into a panic, calling advisers to try to resolve the issue. At around the same time, regulators from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which regulates laboratories, visited the labs and found major inaccuracies in the testing being done on patients. (The Newark lab was run by an employee who was criticized for insufficient laboratory experience.) C.M.S. also soon discovered that some of the tests Theranos was performing were so inaccurate that they could leave patients at risk of internal bleeding, or of stroke among those prone to blood clots. The agency found that Theranos appeared to ignore erratic results from its own quality-control checks during a six-month period last year and supplied 81 patients with questionable test results.

While the government was scouring through Theranos’s inaccurate files and data, Carreyrou was approaching the story not as a fawning tech blogger, but rather as a diligent investigative reporter. Carreyrou, who had worked at the Journal since 1999, had covered topics ranging from terrorism to European politics and financial misdeeds before returning to the New York newsroom and taking over the health-and-sciences bureau. As a reporter of obscure and often faceless subjects, he was not enticed by access, nor was he afraid of lawyers. In fact, he had won two Pulitzer Prizes for taking on nemeses as significant as Vivendi and the U.S. government. After a team of seasoned lawyers arrived at the Journal newsroom, Carreyrou was simply emboldened. “It’s O.K. if you’ve got a smartphone app or a social network, and you go live with it before it’s ready; people aren’t going to die,” he told me. “But with medicine, it’s different.”

Meanwhile, Theranos had its lawyers send a letter to Rochelle Gibbons’s attorney, threatening legal action for talking to a reporter. “It has been the Company’s desire not to pursue legal action against Mrs. Gibbons,” a lawyer for Boies, Schiller & Flexner wrote. “Unless she immediately ceases these actions, she will leave the Company no other option but to pursue litigation to definitively put an end [to] these actions once and for all.” Others who spoke to the Journal were met with similar threats.

Back in March 2009, Holmes returned to the Stanford campus, where her story had begun, to talk to a group of students at the Stanford Technology Ventures Program. Her hair wasn’t yet bleached blond, but she had started to wear her uniform of a black turtleneck, and she was just beginning to morph into the idol she would soon become in Silicon Valley. For 57 minutes, Holmes paced in front of a chalkboard and answered questions about her vision. “It became clear to me,” she said with conviction, “that if I needed to, I’d re-start this company as much as possible to make this thing happen.”

This is exactly what Holmes seems to be doing now. Executives from Theranos, including Holmes and Balwani, declined to sit for interviews. But on a recent July afternoon, I traveled to the company’s headquarters anyway. From the outside, Theranos seems to be in a sad state. The parking lot was devoid of cars, with more than half the spaces empty (or half full, depending on your outlook). The giant American flag that hangs in front of the building was flaccid at half-staff. On the edge of the parking lot, a couple of employees were smoking cigarettes as a single security guard stood nearby, taking a selfie.

On the Friday morning that they gathered in the war room, Holmes and her team of advisers had believed that there would be one negative story from the Journal, and that Holmes would be able to squash the controversy. Then it would be back to business as usual, telling her flawlessly curated story to investors, to the media, and now to patients who used her technology.

Holmes and her advisers couldn’t have been more wrong. Carreyrou subsequently wrote more than two dozen articles about the problems at Theranos. Walgreens severed its relationship with Holmes, shuttering all of its Wellness Centers. The F.D.A. banned the company from using its Edison device. In July, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services banned Holmes from owning or running a medical laboratory for two years. (This decision is currently under appeal.) Then came the civil and criminal investigations by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of California and two class-action fraud lawsuits. Theranos’s board has subsequently been cleaved in two, with Kissinger, Shultz, and Frist now merely “Counselors.” Holmes, meanwhile, isn’t going anywhere. As the C.E.O. and chairwoman of Theranos, only she can elect to replace herself.

Forbes, clearly embarrassed by its cover story, removed Holmes from its list of “America’s Richest Self-Made Women.” A year earlier, it had estimated her wealth at $4.5 billion. “Today, Forbes is lowering our estimate of her net worth to nothing,” the editors wrote. Fortune had its mea culpa, with the author stating boldly that “Theranos misled me.” Director Adam McKay, fresh off his Oscar for The Big Short, has even signed on to make a movie based on Holmes, tentatively titled Bad Blood. (On the bright side for Holmes, Jennifer Lawrence is attached as the lead.)

Silicon Valley, once so taken by Holmes, has turned its back, too. Countless investors have been quick to point out that they did not invest in the company—that much of its money came from the relatively somnolent worlds of mutual funds, which often accrue the savings of pensioners and retirees; private equity; and smaller venture-capital operations on the East Coast. In the end, one of the only Valley V.C. shops that actually invested in Theranos was Draper Fisher Jurvetson. Many may have liked what Holmes represented about their industry, but they didn’t seem to trust her with their money.

Meanwhile, Holmes has somehow compartmentalized it all. In August, she flew to Philadelphia to speak at the American Association for Clinical Chemistry’s annual conference. Before she stepped out onstage, the conference organizers played the song “Sympathy for the Devil” for the ballroom, packed with more than 2,500 doctors and scientists. Hol

items.title: Introducing Rolling Stone's National Affairs Newsletter
items.description: “It never got weird enough for me,” Rolling Stone’s original National Affairs correspondent, Hunter Thompson, once complained. Well, Hunter — the journalist who helped define the Watergate era with Fear and Loathing on the Campaign Trail — never got to experie
items.author: Sean Woods
paragraphs: “It never got weird enough for me,” Rolling Stone’s original National Affairs correspondent, Hunter Thompson, once complained. Well, Hunter — the journalist who helped define the Watergate era with Fear and Loathing on the Campaign Trail — never got to experience the madness of Donald Trump. We are living in a time that historians and journalists will be studying for many years to come, in part because the firehose of political stories that the president generates has been so dizzying to follow, and shows zero signs of slowing down.

All of us, myself included, need help sorting which political stories are important and which are just distractions. To that end, I’m thrilled to announce Rolling Stone’s National Affairs Newsletter, delivered every Friday exclusively to subscribers’ inboxes. We aim to help readers keep up with the chaos, highlighting the news you may have missed, diving deeper into the stories defining the moment, and breaking down this last chapter of the frenetic Trump era — and the start of whatever comes next.

Our National Affairs team — senior politics editor Ryan Bort, senior writers Tessa Stuart and Jack Crosbie, and reporter Nikki McCann Ramirez — will be delivering reporting and analysis from the 2028 campaign trail, as well as covering Congress, global conflicts, and the movers and shakers of the political scene. Columnist Matt Bai will provide critical insights and in-depth interviews. Veteran reporter Katherine Eban will continue her rigorous investigations into the shocking changes Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has been enacting — sweeping away decades of policies on vaccines, food safety, and healthcare — which affect every person in the country.

The 2026 midterms are shaping up to be consequential — possibly as big as any since the Newt Gingrich Republican revolution of the 1990s. Are the polls correct, and will we see a Democratic blue wave? If that happens, will the president even accept the results? Or are we heading for yet another political crisis in the Trump era? These are open questions, and Rolling Stone’s political team will be working tirelessly to bring answers to our subscribers. If you don’t already subscribe to Rolling Stone, there is no better time than now — Sign up here to get National Affairs in your inbox every Friday. The next presidential election kicks into gear as soon as the midterms are settled in early November.
Like it or not, the race for 2028 is about to begin. Join us on the historic journey. As Hunter Thompson wrote: “Buy the ticket, take the ride.”

items.title: Wade Bowen Is Texas Music

items.author: Josh Crutchmer
paragraphs: When Wade Bowen walked into Sean McConnell’s studio in 2020, he was struggling. The previous year had tested him personally and professionally in ways he had never experienced in his 20-year career. Chronic vocal cord issues, and a subsequent surgery, forced him to cancel a long stretch of shows, including a European tour. He was grieving the 2018 death by suicide of his nephew and member of his touring crew, Chase Cavender. In the wake, the album he made with McConnell turned out raw, unpolished, and heavy. The pandemic compounded matters. “The timing just wasn’t right for it,” Bowen recalls now. As soon as he and McConnell finished the record, they shelved the whole thing.

Since then, Bowen released two studio albums — most recently, Flyin’ in 2024 — plus his second collaboration LP with Randy Rogers, Hold My Beer, Vol. 2. The New Braunfels, Texas, resident kept a frenetic touring schedule, headlining major Texas venues and mid-sized dance halls around the country, with occasional arena or amphitheater stops opening for Koe Wetzel thrown in. Then, in 2025, five years after he recorded that album with McConnell, Bowen gave it a fresh listen.
“When I revisited it, I went, ‘Dang, this record’s better than I remember,’” Bowen tells Rolling Stone.

McConnell gave the LP a fresh mix and — six years after it was recorded — Bowen dropped The Version of Me You Get in September. In the moment, it was an open diary as Bowen navigated his foggy headspace, but in hindsight, the 10-track album is a portrait of a songwriter pushing his lyrical and musical boundaries.
“I love this record so much, because it’s as vulnerable and raw and intimate as I have ever been,” Bowen says. “I didn’t really mean for it to be that way.”

Since getting his start in 1998, Bowen ascended to the pinnacle of the Texas country scene with a mix of love songs like “Who I Am” and two-step numbers like “Saturday Night,” but his catalog has always been country, and often honky-tonk country. The Version of Me You Get, however, puts an undeniable rock edge on Bowen’s gravelly Texas drawl. The opening line of “Rain,” the first track — “That was one hell of a storm. Almost didn’t make it, wish to God that I was warned” — lays bare the angst that gave rise to the record.

The title track showcases piano while Bowen laments the friends and family who stood by him throughout his career. On “Turpentine,” he asks for a drink stronger than most bars can pour. And the haunting “Weight on the Levee” is a collaboration with Dan Tyminski, whose version of “Man of Constant Sorrow” was used in the movie O Brother, Where Art Thou?. Tyminski and McConnell had written “Weight on the Levee,” and it was McConnell who suggested bringing the bluegrass artist on board.
“It seemed to me like a no-brainer,” Bowen says. “How can you go wrong with the man of constant sorrow singing with you on a song that he wrote?”

In November, Bowen will find himself on a double-album cycle. His 2006 album Lost Hotel — which established Bowen as one of the biggest acts in Texas at the time — will hit its 20-year anniversary, and Bowen will celebrate it with a deluxe version featuring unreleased studio tracks, live cuts, and demos.

“I don’t know if it’s my favorite, because that’s hard to say, but it’s the one that I’m most proud of,” Bowen says of Lost Hotel. “I was trying really hard at that time to prove myself as a songwriter to my peers, trying to open shows and trying to prove to people that I could do this. It was a stick-my-head-above-the-crowd kind of record, and those are always important in artists’ careers.”

The career Bowen ultimately carved out for himself is one that most artists never attain. He had McConnell and the late Keith Gattis produce some of his biggest records. Wetzel cites him as an influence. He and Rogers still tour together frequently, and he was part of the 2025 Cross Canadian Ragweed reunion tour, opening a sold-out show at McLane Stadium in Waco, Texas, that August. In November, he’ll headline the intimate Hill Country Reserve festival in Fredricksburg, Texas. He also produced the comeback EP that Bleu Edmondson dropped last year. Now 47, Bowen says that legacy is what drives him. He knows he’ll likely never have a chart-topping hit or headline arenas, but what he has found instead is art he is happy to pursue and content to keep making.
“I’ve established a good career and that I can do this as long as I want,” he says. “That’s success in its own right. I lean on that.”
Josh Crutchmer is a journalist and author whose upcoming book, Sonoran Sounds, is set for release in March 2027 via Back Lounge Publishing.

items.title: The 100 Best Grateful Dead Songs
items.description: The Grateful Dead are one of the great American adventures — an outlaw band from the psychedelic frontier of the Haight-Ashbury streets, doing everything their own way. The magic they made onstage every night, improvised without a net or a set list, was a free
items.author: Rolling Stone
paragraphs: The Grateful Dead are one of the great American adventures — an outlaw band from the psychedelic frontier of the Haight-Ashbury streets, doing everything their own way. The magic they made onstage every night, improvised without a net or a set list, was a freewheeling 30-year collaboration with their audience. That’s why the Dead’s music remains so fiercely alive, now more than ever. As Jerry Garcia told Rolling Stone in 1971, “We’re trying to guide ourselves into a place where we can become more music.”

The Dead have always shared a special bond with Rolling Stone, and our histories are intertwined. The band and the magazine both rose out of the heady days in San Francisco in the 1960s, flipping off the establishment way of doing things. It was in our pages that so much of the world followed the Dead’s prankster journey from afar, before the internet or the tape-trading network, from Garcia’s epic interviews to our iconic photos. And both managed to keep evolving through the decades, living up to that not-fade-away spirit.

The Dead gave the world a beautifully chaotic body of music, never slowing down long enough to let anyone pin them down. So let’s celebrate that with our tribute to the 100 best Grateful Dead songs. It’s all here: their rock hollers, their ballads, their brain-melting electric jams, their country-folk hoedowns, their jazzy excursions, their covers. Hell, a few of these songs were even hits, though never on purpose.

Some of these 100 tunes are classics from the Garcia/Robert Hunter or Weir/John Perry Barlow songbook; some are traditionals older than anyone in the band. But what all have in common is that the Dead took these songs somewhere different every night. We’re releasing our list during the Days Between, a sacred time for Deadheads that honors the period between the day Garcia was born (Aug. 1) and the day he died (Aug. 9). We made the list by taking a poll of longtime Dead fans like Jim James, Chloë Sevigny, and Al Franken. You can see who voted here.

The Grateful Dead took the longest, strangest trip in rock, and invited the world to follow along, show by show, song by song. Jerry Garcia, Bobby Weir, Phil Lesh, Bill Kreutzmann, Mickey Hart, Ron “Pigpen” McKernan, Donna Jean and Keith Godchaux, and so many of their kindred spirits — they kept telling their story as they went along, never dreaming that the story would just keep getting bigger and crazier over the decades. But thanks to the music they made, their story will never end. And just like that weeping willow beside the river, it will grow, grow, grow.

- ‘Drums/Space’ (1978) The launchpad for countless interstellar inner-eyelid psychedelic journeys and untold dashes to arena restrooms and beer stalls, the second-set, double-drummer, free-form instrumental jam to be forever known as “Drums>Space” was a welcome touchstone of Dead concerts, and it deserves status as a song unto itself. Indeed, it “became some of the most far-out moments of the Grateful Dead music,” as Kreutzmann wrote in his memoir. Sure, there were drum solos and spacey improvs dating back to ’68. But it was early ’78, with Hart back in the fold, that “Drums>Space” became a fixture, a multiarmed beast of beats sculpted with percussion devices from around the world and, increasingly, electronics. Some ‘Heads maintain latter-day “Drums>Space,” even recent Dead & Company excursions, bested the 20th-century ones — only proving that the best Dead songs, then or now, are the ones that blew your mind and heart wide open. —Will Hermes
- ‘I Need a Miracle’ (1978)

The title of Shakedown Street’s Side Two opener became a popular phrase in the Deadhead lexicon. A “miracle” meant a free or extra ticket for a Dead show. The ticketless would put an index finger in the air, maybe make a sign, and hope for the best. The miracle concept is explored at the end with a gospel refrain that repeats the title, adding, “Everyday.” But the lyrics that precede that (penned by Barlow) are head-scratchers about a man seeking a woman “’bout twice my age,” “’bout twice my height,” and finally “’bout twice my weight/A ton of fun who packs a gun with all her freight.” Garcia takes a nimble midsection solo, and Matthew Kelly adds harmonica wails worthy of the late Pigpen. —Steve Bloom

- ‘Don’t Ease Me In’ (1966) Another folk cover the band reanimated, this swingin’ ragtime number was first recorded in 1928 by Henry Thomas, a.k.a. Ragtime Texas, for the Vocalion label. It was in the repertoire of the proto-Dead Mother McCree’s Uptown Jug Champions, and the Dead released it in 1966 as their first single (backed with another ‘20s jug-band tune, “Stealin’”), on the short-lived Scorpio Records. It didn’t do much. But they revived and rerecorded a more polished version for 1980’s Go to Heaven and released it once again as a single. It still didn’t do much, never denting the charts. But it reentered the Dead’s live sets, and it never failed to rock the house — one reason why Dead & Company designated it a go-to over the years. —W.H.

- ‘Dark Hollow’ (1970) This lonesome folk song was first recorded in 1958 by Bill Browning with his bluegrass group the Echo Valley Boys, but the Dead might’ve actually learned it from the British group Pentangle, who did a variant titled “Cold Mountain” when they opened some fabled Fillmore West shows for the Dead in 1969. They began playing their “Dark Hollow” in 1970, and it was both an acoustic and electric favorite, landing on the History of the Grateful Dead, Volume One (Bear’s Choice) album and the acoustic Reckoning. (It also turned up in live sets by Garcia’s ’70s bluegrass side hustle Old and in the Way.) The song was deep enough in the Dead’s DNA that Hunter echoed the line “where the sun don’t ever shine” in what turned out to be one of the final Dead songs, the wistfully self-referential “So Many Roads.” —W.H.

- ‘Alligator’ (1968) With its snarling guitar tone, sideways chord progression, and kazoo intro, this Anthem of the Sun smoker is among the most delightfully weird early Dead jams. It’s also the first of their songs to feature Hunter’s lyrics. (“Alligator,” by the way, was New Orleans slang, sometimes pejorative, for a white jazz musician.) Among Pigpen’s greatest non-covers, and surely his wildest, it was an early live staple he owned so fully, the band never played it after his death, though it resurfaced in latter-day Dead revival projects. The Allman Brothers Band always cited Anthem of the Sun-era Dead as a formative influence, and you can hear the shared DNA clearly in “Alligator” — i.e., the allusion near the jam’s peak to Donovan’s “There Is a Mountain,” which became the root of the Allmans signature “Mountain Jam.” —W.H.

- ‘Greatest Story Ever Told’ (1972) “Greatest Story Ever Told” is a crazed Biblical fable where Weir begins with the line, “Moses come riding up on a quasar.” (Hunter originally wrote “on a guitar,” but Weir tweaked it.) Moses ends up sharing wine and wisdom with Gideon, Abraham, and Isaac. It’s one of the classics the Dead debuted at their famous Feb. 18, 1971, show at the Capitol Theater in Port Chester, New York — the same night they introduced “Bertha,” “Playing in the Band,” “Loser,” and “Wharf Rat.” (It was also Hart’s last show for three years.) “Greatest Story” became a standout on Weir’s solo gem Ace, as well as Hart’s Rolling Thunder as “The Pump Song.” But the Dead loved it — they chose this tune to kick off the first show of their Europe ’72 tour. —Rob Sheffield

- ‘Believe It or Not’ (1999) During summer tour in 1988, the Dead began workshopping the initial batch of songs that they would record for their final studio album, Built to Last. Unlike “Foolish Heart,” “Blow Away,” or even Weir’s long-gestating “Victim or the Crime,” all of which garnered steady rotation, this late career Garcia-Hunter ballad never quite found its footing and received only seven total plays. The band did briefly slot it in its rightful place as the heartrending Garcia tune after “Drums/Space,” but he reportedly didn’t feel altogether comfortable with the song’s raw sentiment. This is unfortunate, as the tune (eventually released on the 1999 box So Many Roads) has the appeal of a country classic, with lyrics that Hunter has described as “reminiscent of the kind of stuff I remember hearing coming from tavern jukeboxes in 1948, when my father would stop in to have a few while I waited out in the car.”—Dean Budnick

- ‘We Bid You Goodnight’ (1969) In 1968, the Dead started closing shows with a version of the traditional Bahamian funeral song “I Bid You Goodnight,” which they’d heard performed by Joseph Spence and the Pindar Family on a collection of music from the Caribbean island that was popular in folk circles. On Live/Dead, it’s just under 40 seconds, but it evolved into a kind of psychedelic a cappella jam over the next few years, a ritual of their sets that stretched out to three and a half rapturous minutes with their joyous crowds clapping along. They didn’t do “We Bid You Goodnight” very often for about 20 years but revived it in the late Eighties, sending home enrapt stadiums of Deadheads who’d grown up with Live/Dead and greeted it like any other beloved Dean anthem.—Jon Dolan

A live staple of the Dead in the early Seventies — before Pigpen died in 1973 — this tune never appeared on a studio album but was famous for its inclusion in the Europe ’72 tour and LP. The band played it at every one of those Europe shows, but the term “Mr. Charlie” is an American construction, used by slaves to describe the boss or plantation owner. In the case of Hunter’s lyrics, the protagonist appears to be working for the man. “Gonna scare you up and shoot you,” Pigpen growls. “’Cause Mr. Charlie told me so.” Played as a shuffle, Garcia pitches in a bluesy solo, and Pigpen finishes by repeating for emphasis, “Mr. Charlie told me, Mr. Charlie told me so.” —S.B.
- ‘Alabama Getaway’ (1980)

By the time they got into the studio to cut it for 1980’s Go to Heaven, “Alabama Getaway” had already been road-tested. Indeed, it had become one of the group’s tearaway numbers: Its late-’79 live versions featured the Dead tossing solos back and forth on it with aplomb. The album it was on was the Dead’s return to the studio after two years, and AOR’s strictures had tightened considerably compared to the band’s early-Seventies freedom. “Alabama Getaway” reflected that shift. The song was startlingly radio-ready and propulsive, with hooky organ swells thick in the mix. It plateaued at Number 68 on the Hot 100, but it remained in their repertoire till the end. —M.M.

- ‘Viola Lee Blues’ (1967) Before “Dark Star” and “China Cat > Rider,” this was the Dead’s signature jam vehicle — you can see them rocking it out in the ’68 film Petulia, while the light show bubbles and the hippies frug. Retooled with their hearty train-wreck harmonies, it’s a cover of a late-1920s acoustic nugget by Cannon’s Jug Stompers, a touchstone for the early Dead, who also tapped their “Big Railroad Blues” and “Minglewood Blues” (remade as the twice-removed “New, New Minglewood Blues”). “Viola Lee” was always a party starter. At the seminal 1967 Monterey International Pop Festival, the band opened with a 14-minute version, after Weir told the crowd: “You know what the foldin’ chairs are for, don’t you? They’re for foldin’ up and dancin’ on!” And Phishheads may recall a pistoning version from Sept. 17, 1999, with the dueling basses of Lesh and Mike Gordon. —W.H.

- ‘Till the Morning Comes’ (1970) Another song that shares its title with a Neil Young joint (see “Comes a Time”), the Dead played this deep cut live just five or six times. A shame, since its full-tilt boogie tempo and juicy CSNY harmonies brighten Side Two of American Beauty like a fireworks bloom, and it could surely have set hippie skirts a-spinnin’. The song finally got its due in the 21st century, reborn in sets by Furthur and other latter-day Dead projects, albeit without the benefit of Garcia’s sweet high tenor voice in the mix. Hunter’s shaggy lyrics (“‘til we all fall down …”) riff on the nursery rhyme “Ring Around the Rosie,” a move later repeated memorably by Weir and Barlow in their apocalyptic “Throwing Stones.”—W.H.
- ‘It Hurts Me Too’ (1972)

Written and recorded first by bluesman Tampa Red in 1940 and defined by Elmore James, who recorded it multiple times and had a hit with it in 1963, “It Hurts Me Too” is one of the best-loved and most widely covered blues songs. It became a Dead staple, a languorous blues sung by Pigpen, who blew harp on it as well, beginning in 1966. The high-lonesome version, with Keith Godchaux’s piano fills urging him from the back, that the band included on Europe ’72 was one of Pigpen’s, and the band’s, last. When he died in 1973, they retired this number. —Michaelangelo Matos

- ‘Death Don’t Have No Mercy’ (1969) There was no way Garcia was going to achieve the kind of bone-rattling shout that Reverend Gary Davis declaimed on this song in his original version from 1960. But Davis’ plainspoken lyric gives a singer many options, and Garcia’s pained empathy, from a whisper to a cry, communicated them with deep commitment. So did his stinging guitar — the Live/Dead version, recorded in early 1969, contains some of Garcia’s most deeply felt blues playing as well as singing. —M.M.

- ‘Saint of Circumstance’ (1980) Weir indicated that the rousing final verse to “Saint of Circumstance” came to him while experiencing a rogue lightning storm atop a Wyoming mountain. Weir’s sense of exhilaration entwined with the inscrutable design of nature informed the song he was writing with Barlow. “Saint of Circumstance” began its existence as the younger twin of “Lost Sailor,” which was completed earlier in the same session and premiered live a few weeks ahead of “Saint” in August 1979. The two selections both reference the “dog star” Sirius and collectively relate a journey that begins amid roiling weather conditions and eventually finds rapturous purpose. The songs were juxtaposed on Go to Heaven and then in concert to such a degree that “SailorSaint” became common Deadhead parlance until Weir dry-docked the former tune in March 1986. “Saint” soon embarked on swelling solo excursions, typically building momentum early in the second set. —D.B.

- ‘Cream Puff War’ (1967) Released as the B side of their first single after signing to Warner Bros. Records, “Cream Puff War” is explosive garage rock that’s faster and more raw-sounding than pretty much anything else the Dead recorded. Driven by Garcia’s bracing guitar leads and Pigpen’s swirling organ, the song could have easily fit in next to the Electric Prunes and the Seeds on the classic garage band compilation Nuggets. The Dead began playing it in 1966 (a version from the Fillmore West appears on the 1999 box set So Many Roads), and they cut it for their self-titled 1967 debut. “This is the only song that I claim totally,” Garcia said in a 1967 interview. “This is mine from beginning to end.”—J.D.

- ‘West L.A. Fadeaway’ (1987) Hearing how this song evolved exerts a fascination of its own. An alternate studio version from 1984 approaches, but stops short of, the high-gloss rock sound of other California rockers of the era (compare it to, say, Don Henley’s “Dirty Laundry”). The official version from In the Dark, the Dead’s full commercial arrival, rides a far slipperier groove, with buoyant percussion touches and the synthesizers more fully integrated into the Dead’s sound. As for the lyric, it’s one of Hunter’s most overtly cynical — as much an artifact of the Eighties as “Dark Star” was of the Sixties. —M.M.

- ‘Weather Report Suite’ (1973) The bridge between the multipart, tripping-balls pileup of Anthem’s “That’s It for the Other One” and the sublime architecture of the “Terrapin Station Medley,” “Weather Report Suite” is the Grateful Dead melding songs compositionally like they did onstage through improvising. Written by Weir and Barlow, with a lyrical assist from veteran folk singer-songwriter Eric Andersen, it’s the finale of Wake of the Flood. And with its Renaissance-flavored guitar overture, Spanish melodies, and mariachi-tinged horn arrangements, it was the most sophisticated Dead presentation anyone had heard at the time — so much so it barely scanned as Dead music. At least until the back end, a.k.a. “Part 2 (Let It Grow),” when Weir and Donna Godchaux emerge from the wintry darkness of “Part 1” into summer sunshine. Recorded in 1973, “Weather Report Suite” was only played in full that year and the next. The “Let It Grow” section, however, surfaced regularly as a first-set closer, always offering Garcia a beautiful flight path for extended solos. —W.H.

- ‘Black Muddy River’ (1987) The penultimate song the Grateful Dead performed at their final show in 1995, this mournful ballad would have been the last of the night had bassist Lesh not called an audible, insisting that the band play “Box of Rain” rather than end their final date on such a melancholic note. The song’s protagonist seeks solitude, a luxury Garcia privately longed for. Thirty years of being the ringmaster of the high-flying circus that was the Grateful Dead had left Garcia feeling alienated and isolated, even when he was onstage in front of tens of thousands of adoring fans. His vocals on the dozens of live versions performed between its 1986 debut and the band’s final performance are fragile, vulnerable, and desperate: “I will walk alone by the black muddy river/And sing me a song of my own.” They would be the last words Garcia would ever sing live.—Benjy Eisen

Long before he made a full album of cowboy songs with 2016’s Blue Mountain, Weir had been a cowhand. In his teens, he worked on the Wyoming cattle ranch run by the parents of his future collaborator, John Perry Barlow; the two would later write songs on the same land. Weir’s attraction to cowboy songs led him, naturally, to Marty Robbins’ classic “El Paso” — a pop and country Number One in 1960 — which the Dead started playing in 1970 and would continue to, on and off, until 1995, making it “official” with the live Steal Your Face (recorded in 1974, released in 1976). There and elsewhere (Cornell May 8, 1977), Weir’s droll delivery and the double drummers at their friskiest stamped it as a classic Dead change of pace. —M.M.

- ‘So Many Roads’ (1999) Befitting the Grateful Dead story, “So Many Roads” could have been one of the band’s biggest and greatest hits, but almost every live version is flawed, and no finished studio recording exists. It transcends its imperfections as a wabi-sabi artifact of the Dead’s final days. Like so many of their beloved late-era ballads, it is impossible to hear “So Many Roads” without imagining Garcia co-opting the lyrics for something that veers more toward the tragic than the romantic: “So many roads I know/All I want is one to lead me home.” Rarely had Garcia sung so earnestly or vulnerably. The band knew it created something striking, and from the song’s debut in 1993 to the group’s final bow in 1995, the Grateful Dead performed “So Many Roads” at nearly 20 percent of their shows — almost as often, rotation-wise, as their biggest commercial hit, “Touch of Grey.”—B.E.

- ‘Me and My Uncle’ (1971) This might be Weir’s greatest cowboy song, alongside the Marty Robbins cover “El Paso” and his self-penned (with Barlow) “Mexicali Blues.” Though it sounds like a standard, “Me and My Uncle” was in fact written by John Phillips of the Mamas and the Papas during a tequila drinking session and popularized by Judy Collins, who released it on The Judy Collins Concert in 1964. (Joni Mitchell covered it in her early days, too.) The Dead, who probably learned it from the Collins LP, sped it up, played it in 1966, and never took it out of rotation. It’s widely considered the most-performed cover tune in the band’s repertoire (600-plus shows, by some accounts). And while it never got a studio recording, a definitive version was minted on Skull & Roses. More recently, it has turned up in live sets by Billy Strings. And The Lone Bellow covered it on the excellent Bryce and Aaron Dessner-curated Dead tribute Day of the Dead. —W.H.

- ‘Loose Lucy’ (1973) “Loose Lucy” debuted during the Dead’s remarkable Feb. 9, 1973, concert at Stanford’s Maples Pavilion, alongside future classics including “Eyes of the World,” “Row Jimmy,” and “China Doll.” Released the following year on From the Mars Hotel, the track pairs Garcia’s warm, fluid guitar work with Hunter’s characteristically vivid storytelling. Set to an infectious, New Orleans-inflected groove, “Loose Lucy” is both a tale of romance and infidelity and, some say, a sly nod to the seductive allure of LSD. Either way, its narrative slipperiness has only served to deepen its enduring appeal. With playful good humor and a sense of easy mischief woven into the track’s loping, cool-guy strut, this is the Dead embodying their Trickster archetype to the hilt. After disappearing from the band’s repertoire for 16 years before finally returning in 1990, “Loose Lucy” remains a fan favorite, celebrated as much for its unflappable swagger as its wit.—Jessica Hundley

“Crazy Fingers” is an elusive entry into the Dead canon that earns its spot more on feel and suggestion than on jams or meaning. The lyrics have often been mislabeled by Deadheads as “haikus,” due to haiku-like qualities (nature imagery, juxtaposition, ambiguity), and the music has been mischaracterized as reggae and grouped in with other Caribbean influenced mid-1970s Dead songs like “Estimated Prophet” and “Fire on the Mountain.” The song is a confluence of classic Grateful Dead elements from that time period, where seemingly disparate sections are delicately woven together under a storyline absent a narrative. The ambiguity has led many a Deadhead to feel like the song is relatable, even if they couldn’t articulate what it’s about, exactly. Garcia and Hunter seemed to place value on just such a predicament, hence the lyrics, “Gone are the days we stopped to decide where we should go, we just ride.”—B.E.
- ‘Black-Throated Wind’ (1972)

Weir sings the U.S. blues of a long-haired American kid on the road, feeling like a stranger in his own country. “Black-Throated Wind” is one of the loneliest tunes he ever wrote — he stands out on the interstate, trying to hitch a ride. But his only company is the headlights of the buses and truckers who pass by without picking him up. It’s a standout of his solo Ace, but the Dead played it constantly in 1972, with a groove inspired by New Orleans R&B king Allen Toussaint. Barlow based the lyrics on a bleak cross-country motorcycle trip. It’s a long, cold night on the highway, with no direction home, but Weir sends out a Jack Kerouac-style prayer to “Mother American Night.” It never sounded colder or windier than the definitive Aug. 27, 1972, version in Veneta, Oregon, in the 100-degree sunshine.—R.S.

One of Merle Haggard’s greatest hits, “Mama Tried” was a country Number One in August 1968 and entered the Dead songbook almost a year later, in June 1969. Weir always kept his ear to country radio, telling a reporter, “There wasn’t a huge difference — still isn’t, for that matter — between the country presentation and the rock & roll presentation.” The song helped augur a new direction for the Dead, into the acoustic opening sets that became prominent in the early Seventies, with “Mama Tried” sealed in the repertoire thanks to its appearance on 1971’s live double-LP Skull & Roses. —M.M.

- ‘Comes a Time’ (1971) No, not the Neil Young song. This Garcia/Hunter tearjerker debuted in fall 1971 at pianist Keith Godchaux’s first show with the Dead — where he was basically replacing Pigpen, sidelined from liver disease tied to his alcohol consumption. A handsome but heavy song about a benumbed man in a dark place, with echoes of Oedipus and poems by Dylan Thomas (“Was There a Time”) and Yeats (“The Empty Cup”), Garcia rarely performed it. But it took on new meaning in the wake of his addiction struggles, which included a band intervention and a subsequent arrest in January 1985 for possession of heroin and cocaine. After being retired from the repertoire for a half decade, its return for the band’s 20th anniversary run at the Greek Theater in Berkeley, California, that June — just as Garcia was getting clean — was profound, especially when he keened lines like “Never in my mind/To cause so much pain” and “the day may come when you can’t feel at all.” —W.H.

On this highlight from Side One of Workingman’s Dead, Pigpen and Hunter set the down-and-dirty tone with the opening lines, “I been ballin’ a shiny black steel jack-hammer/ Been chippin’ up rocks for the great highway.” Like “Casey Jones,” also on the album, it’s about riding a locomotive — ”ballin’ that jack and drinkin’ my wine.” Pigpen (on harmonica) and Garcia team up on a swampy middle section that features one of the guitarist’s greatest recorded solos. A concert rarity, the Dead only played it 43 times. —S.B.

One of the oldest and most remarkable covers in the Dead oeuvre, best as we can tell, it first turned up in a live set in 1966. That same year, the Young Rascals had a Number One pop hit with their own version (itself a cover of the 1965 release by the Olympics, an excellent Black doo-wop group who had worked with Billy Preston). Notwithstanding lapses, “Good Lovin’” never fell from rotation, yet somehow didn’t surface on a proper album until 1978’s Shakedown Street. If that recording lacked the fire of the Sixties versions, it was probably worth the wait — released as a 7-inch single with another oldie (“Stagger Lee”) on the B side, it was certified gold in the U.S., and the band got to play it on its Saturday Night Live debut that year, along with “I Need a Miracle” and — fittingly, given the then-cast members’ drug habits — “Casey Jones.”—W.H.
- ‘Throwing Stones’ (1987)

The second single off the Dead’s double-platinum In the Dark, this Weir/Barlow collaboration dates back to its 1982 live debut. Inspired by the nursery rhyme “Ring Around the Roses,” the chorus repeats, “Singing ashes, ashes all fall down.” That’s preceded by, “And the politicians throwing stones.” Railing against “petty wars” and “rudies looking for a fight,” the song builds to a crescendo with Garcia nailing several solos. As one of the Dead’s most political songs, “Throwing Stones” continued to resonate through the years; in 2022, after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, Dead & Company played the song with the phrase SAVE OUR RIGHTS projected on a screen behind them. —S.B.

- ‘It Must Have Been the Roses’ (1976) This Hunter stunner first appeared on Garcia’s 1976 solo album, Reflections, but those roses kept blooming with the Dead, who delivered the country-folk ballad onstage from 1974 to the very end. Its finest moment arrived in 1980, when the band performed it all four nights at Radio City Music Hall that fall, with one of those versions landing on their live acoustic masterpiece Reckoning. It’s severely underrated, though musicians like Norah Jones, Sierra Ferrell and Lukas Nelson, and Gillian Welch & David Rawlings (on their recent, fantastic Reckoning Tour) have helped keep it alive. Come for the lines that possibly nod to The Odyssey (“Ten years the waves rolled the/Ships home from the sea”), stay for Annie and those ribbons in her long brown hair. —Angie Martoccio

- ‘Days Between’ (1999) “Days Between” was the final song that Garcia and Hunter wrote together and, in Hunter’s view, it felt like the two had unlocked a new level that should have been the first of a new batch instead of the last of all of them. As far as swan songs go, “Days Between” has a haunting prescience to it, binding the passage of time to life’s major milestones. “And there were days I know/When all we ever wanted/Was to learn and love and grow/Once we grew into our shoes/We told them where to go,” Garcia sang with the appropriate weight. After its release in 1999 on the So Many Roads box, “Days Between” took on added significance and complexity: Weir’s many post-GD renditions served as a requiem for Garcia that felt personal, and fans have adopted the title for the calendar days between Garcia’s birthday on Aug. 1 and his death on Aug. 9.—B.E.

- ‘The Eleven’ (1969) An exercise as much as a song — a skipping romp through 11/4 time, the double drummers keeping everyone on their toes — “The Eleven” was part of the core late-Sixties Dead repertoire, but effectively retired by mid-1970. Still, its placement on side two of the February 1969-recorded Live/Dead has put it high on the fans’ live list, and just for the hell of it, the double LP’s lyric sheet included some differing Hunter-written lines than the band sung. “I wrote this stuff out to be printed on this and I just did it out of my memory,” Hunter said. He continued to perform the song himself: “I throw in all those extra verses that are on that Live/Dead thing.”—M.M.

- ‘Feel Like a Stranger’ (1980) Over the 15 years following its live debut on March 31, 1980, “Feel Like a Stranger” opened more Grateful Dead performances than all but two songs. (“Jack Straw” is in first place, followed by “Hell in a Bucket.”) In part this can be attributed to the nature of Barlow’s lyrics, as Weir intones, “So let’s get on with the show …” Beyond this, the song, which appears on 1980’s Go to Heaven, Brent Mydland’s first album with the group, manifests the potency and potential of the Mydland era, as his contributions on organ and background vocals elevate the tune. “Feel Like a Stranger” is funk-infused Dead, in which Mydland and Weir would sometimes get frisky and pledge, “It’s going to be a long, long, crazy, crazy, tour” (instead of night) as they did at Hampton Coliseum in October 1989 during the version tha

paragraphs: Welcome to our weekly rundown of the best new music — featuring big singles, key tracks from our favorite albums, and more. This week, Rachel Chinouriri struts to the club on a sparkling synth stunner, Fontaines D.C. grapple with feelings of inadequacy on a glowing Dopamine Chamber highlight, and Olivia Rodrigo recruits Chappell Roan for a fiery remix of “Expectations.” Plus, new tunes from @, Tate McRae, Zach Bryan, A$AP Rocky, and the Avalanches.

items.title: Fights With Bob Dylan, Magic With U2: Daniel Lanois on His Life in Music
items.description: It’s easy to associate Daniel Lanois with a distinct sonic approach shared by many of the classic albums he helped birth, from Emmylou Harris‘ Wrecking Ball to Bob Dylan‘s Time Out of Mind. The Canadian producer/musician creates songs that feel like they’re ha
items.author: Brian Hiatt
paragraphs: It’s easy to associate Daniel Lanois with a distinct sonic approach shared by many of the classic albums he helped birth, from Emmylou Harris‘ Wrecking Ball to Bob Dylan‘s Time Out of Mind. The Canadian producer/musician creates songs that feel like they’re haunted by their own ghosts, laced with intertwining echoes, tiny sonic fractures, and a palpable sense of place. But in the new episode of Rolling Stone Music Now, Lanois says his job is much bigger than that. “People talk about the sound, but what about the soul?” he says. “The sound of a record, well, that’s a given… But how about the soul of a record? Sound is my thing. But that’s not the main thing that I bring to the table.”

Lanois’ new solo album, Belladonna Nocturne, is a trippy collection of instrumentals that lean hard on his gift for atmosphere, from the Spanish-guitar-propelled “Inside the Walls of Puebla” to the wild, chopped-up feedback excursions of “Warp Sustain.” In our interview, he talked about creating that album and looked back on his work with U2, Peter Gabriel, Bob Dylan, D’Angelo, the Neville Brothers, and Neil Young. To hear the podcast version, check out Apple Podcasts or Spotify, or just press play above.
What are you up to right now?

I just came off of this tour in Texas with Micah Nelson, Willie’s son. We’ve made an [upcoming] album called The Ocean Floor, under the name Particle / Lanois. And we were invited to be on the bill with the Outlaw Tour people, which included Willie’s Fourth of July picnic. We had a nice time. And now, after the whirlwind of that, I’m getting ready to go to Canada to do some touring up there, which bumps into Scandinavia.
Let’s start with Belladonna Nocturne. It has a real sense of place that changes from track to track. Explain how this all came together.

I see every song as a scene. I have one, “At the Foot of the Skyway Bridge,” which is a bridge where I grew up in Hamilton, [Ontario,] which is not too far from Buffalo. It’s a steel town. And the Skyway Bridge is a place that I would ride to with my motorcycle-riding buddies, and it all had a little bit of rock & roll in it, old-timey, as if a throwback to the Fifties, let’s say. It’s a place that I like to go to, to cleanse the palate and remind myself of who I am and where I grew up. And it will likely build another picture for somebody else. We like to transport the listener to a location.
“Steel Mill” is definitely a vibe.

“Steel Mill” paints a picture of more of an urban landscape and has Jermaine Holmes on the drums, and he comes from the hip-hop world. I met him through D’Angelo. His backbeat is what we call a cross-stick. It’s not a lot of sound. It’s just a very clear striking point, and it means that it leaves more room, more air in the picture for other sounds to come through. It’s basically just three instruments. It’s bass, drums, and steel guitar. I just kept adding what I call my dubs to it, and any orchestral tones that one hears in there, l built through my electronic process of dubbing.
Your process is that you sample from the song itself and then build additional material into the song using those samples.

Yeah, that’s the process that got used on this track. I just sample from the steel guitar in this case and then expand upon it. You could call them unknown sounds, because you hear them and you wouldn’t say, “Oh yeah, that’s a flute,” and something else is a euphonium. No, they’re more mysterious than that. The reason that it works for me is I’m just drawing from already existing source material. I’m not adding a new sound. So there’s a reassurance that it’s cut from the same cloth.
You recorded “Unshaken” with D’Angelo for the soundtrack to Red Dead Redemption 2. What were the extent of your collaborations with him?

I met D’Angelo quite early on in the Red Dead Redemption music making. I met him at the Rockstar Games office in Manhattan. We hit it off nicely, and I played him a track that I had at the time. It’s a 6/8 rock song that he loved, and he said he would be happy to work on that with me. And that track did not pan out. He worked on it for a couple of days. He said, “Dan, I’m not really getting anywhere with this.” And I said, “Well, D, we’re here to have a good time and get to a special place. Give me a chance. Give me a day, and I’ll come up with another track.” And I built a new track for him. We already had one line that was used on the soundtrack. And that line, “May I stand unshaken amidst the crash of worlds,” which is something we had recorded in New Orleans — it was written by Rocco DeLuca, that line. And I took that line to D’Angelo, but I wrote then the 30 other lines to the song.
Did you guys stay in touch?

We did keep in touch. Only so much. We talked about doing some more work together and, you know, he came up as a church man, and I came up through church and worked quite a bit with church folks, including Brian Blade and his family in Shreveport, Louisiana. D was very touched by my having worked with the Neville Brothers. He was a fan of the Neville Brothers, and they always were a point of reference for him, for magnificent work done in the South by the Meters and so on. And so I think there was an underlying respect there that we were both in this for the right reasons.

I was just listening to “Ballad of Hollis Brown” that you did with the Neville Brothers. It was one of the two songs that you played to Bob Dylan right before you did Oh Mercy with him. I think it’s one of the best Dylan covers ever recorded.

Oh, yeah. Well, thank you for bringing that up. That was a little bit of a test track that we did with the Nevilles. I didn’t have a studio set up very well in New Orleans yet. I had a little apartment, and they showed up at the apartment, and we knocked out that version of “Ballad of Hollis Brown.” I just had a 12-track Akai at the time and I mixed it on a little Sony cassette machine, my little shoulder-strap Sony machine. And I never bettered the mix. I didn’t tell anybody, but we just took the cassette and mastered from that because it had the vibe on it. You never know how are you gonna get ’em, in regards to technology. Would anybody ever recommend a 12-track Akai mixed to cassette? But I never had any complaints.
To go back to Belladonna Nocturne — was this recorded in a bunch of different places? What was the process there?

It pretty much a grab-bag of beginnings, let’s call them. I have a studio in Los Angeles with a very nice piano, a nice Steinway piano, and then I have the same thing in Toronto. So wherever I happen to be, if the inspiration comes to me, then I go to the piano. It was not a sit down and let’s make an album in three weeks [situation]. It was a collection of inspirations from along the way.
Tell me about “Canadian National.”

That was recorded in Toronto on my little Steinway O. I laminated every hammer with additional felt, so the piano has a little softer touch, you might say, closer to a Fender Rhodes. Which allows me to crank up my mic pre[amp], and then I get to hear more aftereffect. We call that the harmonics. And I’m only so much of a piano player, but I’m very good with a razor blade. Having decided on a mode, let’s say, I would improvise within that mode. And if I was lucky enough to get an eight-bar section that I fall in love with, then I look to connect that eight bars to another eight bars further on down the line. Glenn Gould used to work that way, one phrase at a time, and then chop it together with a razor blade. So thanks, Glenn.
Your friend Brian Eno once showed me that he keeps all these starts to songs, little four-second sonic landscapes that sometimes become something and sometimes don’t. Do you do something similar?

We all collect our seeds, let’s call them. I have a lot of them that I love. They’re not finished works by any means, but it might be something to a melody that I wanna get back to at some point. So we keep a stockpile of our seeds. I used to call it the melody orphanage. Songs-to-be, but haven’t found a home yet. I think it’s interesting to revisit old seeds. They obviously got put in the orphanage for a reason. There’s something special about them, and they might just be looking for a family.

When I was writing the Rolling Stone cover story on U2’s No Line on the Horizon, you played me a very roiling instrumental that you said summed up your feelings about the process. How do you look back on it now?

So we went to Morocco to make that record. And we already had a great record before we went to Morocco. And I, at a lunch table in the south of France, I suggested to the band that we finish up the 10 [songs] that I recommended. Of course, we went to Morocco and didn’t work on any of that, and came up with a whole batch of new material, which makes for more fun because we keep hoping that the great track has yet to come. But in Morocco, everybody got sick. And so it became this very, very long process of record-making. I think we ended up back in Dublin. I was pretty worn out. That’s probably when you spoke with Eno. In the end, we got what we got. But there was a great record before we went to Morocco, and the adventure kept rolling along.
Eno told me a lot of the more quiet stuff had to go because they were looking for stuff that could be performed onstage.

I’ve had this conversation with many artists I’ve worked with. “Are we being responsible to the stage?” Because obviously, in a concert situation, if you’re a big band, then you’re not gonna be playing a bunch of soft material, ’cause people are looking to jump out of their skins. So there’s always that responsibility of, what will we bring to the stadium? But I’m a record-maker, you know. I don’t think so much about the stage. I think about how will we transport our listeners, and what might there be in this that will really touch somebody and cause them to think a bit differently or jump out of their skins in their own house. It doesn’t have to be in the stadium.
You performed with U2 at the Sphere a couple years ago. Any moments that stand out?

Playing at the Sphere was really special to me because it was the last show that they did. I suggested to Edge that if he needed a guitar-playing buddy, then I would join him on “One.” And he said, “Well, Danny, let me look into it,” ’cause they were filming at the time, and he said, “We’re gonna need some kinda consistency from night to night.” But as it turns out, Edge invited me to join him. There’s a mantra line that runs on through that song. It was played on guitar and with Eno on synth. So that line is the line that I decided to play with Edge. It felt the same as it did in the studio for me. I was close to my mates. And Bono said, “Just pay attention to me, and we can sing ‘One’ together,” and we did that. So what can I say? A great moment of celebration for a great song and some great friends.
Have you been involved with the new project that they’re working on at all?
