I’ve had a little bit of an involvement with their new work. But I’ve not heard the album. I just saw that they released a video with the lead track. But I did do some work on some other things, so let’s see if I made the finish line. Both Eno and I did a little something in there somewhere.
Yeah, a couple or three songs. Jacknife Lee produced the album, who’s a great music man. Eno and I might be guest appearances in there somewhere.
Certainly one of the genres that I’d put your new album into is themes for an imaginary movie. It’s definitely soundtrack-ready.

I think in visual terms and sometimes I’m a little bit surprised that filmmakers don’t call me more often. Am I the only one who thinks that this music is cinematic? Maybe I need to call my filmmaker friends and network a little bit, which is not my inclination.
It certainly worked out for Sling Blade, so you would think it would happen more often.

Yeah, Sling Blade. What was special about Sling Blade was the one-on-one relationship I had with Billy [Bob Thornton]. I don’t remember there being a lot of opinions going around or music supervisors and all that kind of stuff. We were just — I’d come up with something, and Billy’d stop into the studio. I’d play him what I had, and he’d comment, “Oh, maybe that would be good here,” to repeat a theme. I really appreciated the simplicity of our communication and relationship. I just saw Billy last week in Texas, and we sat on a little porch together, and it might as well have been a Diane Arbus photograph. Couple of lost misfits on a back porch philosophizing about this and that and the other thing. It was pretty great. Time stands still with Billy. That’s what I like about him. And there’s nothing wrong with a bench on a porch, picket fence, and overgrown grass, watching the world go by. Not bad.
Shortly after No Line on the Horizon, you did Le Noise with Neil Young.

Yeah, we made Le Noise in the room that I’m speaking in right now. This is where I worked with Neil, and the invitation was to record 10 acoustic songs and film him, ’cause I was making films with my friend Adam Vollick at the time. The idea was to film with one camera, and as seen through the eyes of an individual rather than the eyes of an editing room. I think viewers really feel the vérité in that. And if we had a pretty good take from Neil, I would listen back to the take, make a mix as we listen, hand that to Adam Vollick. He’d go upstairs and lock that to his one-camera shoot, and in a matter of minutes, we were looking at a film with a great sound. I’ve explained this to my fellow filmmakers, and they say, “That’s a bit cowboy, isn’t it?” Because normally you gotta go in the editing room and fiddle around for a couple of weeks before anybody sees anything. And that tone suggested a pace, and that pace dovetailed into a more electric angle, and he pulled out his Les Paul and we went up that street. And so what can I say? Two Canadians having a pretty good time. We come from the same neck of the woods, so there was a lot — the humor was intact and a lot got left unsaid, because we were able to communicate just by looking each other in the eyes pretty good.
Did you butt heads with Neil less than you ended up doing with Dylan?
I don’t remember butting heads with Neil. It was a fabulous exchange. We had an excess of material and I was helpful to him with choosing the best ones so that we had the most concentrated record.

With Dylan ,that’s a different situation because, you know, I made two albums with him, and we go back to New Orleans on the Oh Mercy album, which was a very private record, as I like to call it. Almost as if the lens went into the secret place of Dylan. And I recognized that quite early on. I thought that we had really hit on something in the tangibility of it. I sat next to Bob. We played guitars together and had a nice microphone on him, and we cut most of the record to a Roland 808, which is just a little beatbox. And so that record had a very nighttime feeling, speaking of nocturne. And Bob recognized that pretty early on, and he said to me, “Dan, let’s only work at night on this record ’cause it seems to be where it’s going.” And I agreed with Bob on that, and we chose not to have a lot of people around. And we had Willie Green living around the corner. I kept a drum kit set up, and he would come by on my request and overdub the drums. I played the bass on the record mostly. If there was any kind of a conflict, it would’ve been that Bob was missing the presence of a band, and I didn’t want the presence of a band. I wanted all of the intention to go on the songs and his voice. And I got a very beautiful sound on his voice on that record. So I stood my ground, and we did have other musicians come by, but largely, once we sorted out our differences that way, then we embraced the more private part of the record, let’s call it.
What’s an example of that on the record?

I like to reference the song “Most of the Time.” I played four Les Paul tracks through my Vox amp up on 10, and it’s those four Les Paul tracks that sound like a string quartet in the distance. You don’t quite know what you’re hearing, but it’s almost as if a quartet is being blown in by the wind from the next town. And the depth that it creates is very much part of the mood that that song has in it. I played the bass on it. I came up with a very nice bass hook. And because I’m a guitar player and not a bass player, I was afforded the flexibility of going to a melodic place. There’s something special about that little bass line, as it’s almost like the bottom punctuation to Bob’s “Most of the Time.” And I stand by that track. The only regret I have on that album is we excluded one of my favorite tracks, which was “Series of Dreams,” which came out later on a bootleg, I believe. And if I had to go back, I would try make an effort to include that one. “Series of Dreams.”
I never understood from either of you why that particular song, which is so fantastic, didn’t make the record.

I have to take some responsibility with that. You know, I think I did say to Bob that it was reminiscent of things I had done for other people on other records. And the part of me that likes works to be completely original cast a shadow of doubt on it, and he might have listened to that, and so I should have gaffered my face, and I didn’t.
A lot of the money that supported the work you do has vanished, hasn’t it, thanks to streaming?

I think what has gone away is career building. For sure. And let’s throw back to back in the day, an artist would be signed to a label, and they would look to build a career and keep expanding. And if you’re lucky enough to get hits, then we keep rolling. But they’re fascinating times, ’cause record companies aren’t paying for records anymore. Maybe they are for some artists, but most artists are just making their records at home, and they deliver a finished record to a label or a distributor. The idea that there would be budgets coming from labels and career building and all that, I think that’s naturally just disappeared.
And it’s affected the art — artists start to think it doesn’t make business sense to put in the kind of time that so many of the great albums you worked on had.

Yeah. How are people making records? The folks I’ve been speaking with lately are thinking of getting back to putting players in a room and knocking it out in a collaborative manner. Let’s say it might be nice to get away from e-mail rock. E-mail rock is a term that we’ve been throwing around here because, maybe driven by the pandemic, you’d send a track to a faraway place, and somebody would do an overdub on it. Somebody might come up with a riff, they send it to somebody else, send it to somebody else, and then you have now 10 composers on a hip-hop track. But I had a very nice recent experience in this very house here. With my good friend Micah Nelson, Particle Kid, we assembled a little band and brought some filmmakers in, and we replayed three of the songs from the record that will come out in the new year. And there was a very nice feeling in the room, and we captured a special vibe. That might be a way of making a record in the future. Just get some people together and knock it out. A futuristic technique, even.
With Bob, one of your guiding principles on Time Out of Mind was that you were less interested in songs that were blues structures. You were trying to push him into other forms.
Well, it was definitely a blues-based record. And I knew that from the beginning. Even “Love Sick” is blues-based.
Bluesy without being a 12-bar blues, I guess.

Yeah, without being a 12-bar blues. But you know, I knew what was coming, and that’s why I made the decision to bring in Brian Blade and Jim Keltner on the drums, because if it’s gonna be the blues, I wanted Brian to be involved ’cause he’s from the South and a church drummer, and so he would have a good understanding of blues. You don’t wanna sound like a bar band, and so how will you approach the blues in an original manner in modern times when you might say that the blues had disappeared a long time ago? And so I built some beat tracks with my friend Tony Mangurian in Manhattan. Tony’s a good drummer, and I’m pretty good on percussion. So we played over top of some old blues records that Bob had recommended we listen to. I knew those records already, but it was nice to hear them again. And so with Tony, we overdubbed a bunch of drumming and percussion on top of these old-timey records that were amazing. I did not use the old-timey records in the end. I just went to listen to what we had played on top and built these — if I had a magic eight bars of a groove, then I looped that and created about a dozen different loops as an insurance policy. So the band that Bob and I had put together, if I felt that we were going to too common a place, then I would feed these beginnings, these magic loop beginnings to the drummers. I knew that if we ran into trouble, then I could reference these beginnings and direct the music into a certain direction that would make it more original.
One song that I heard entirely differently after reading your book was “Can’t Wait.” The first take was best, and you kept trying to get Bob back to it.

Well, simply put, we had a pretty good demo of “Can’t Wait” with Tony Mangurian playing the drums, and he’s more of a hip-hop drummer. So I got very excited about this ’cause I thought the song might then have a chance to hit the airwaves with more of an urban rhythm.
In the end, “Love Sick” I guess was the hit. But there is unrealized potential in “Can’t Wait.” You were right.

Yeah. But, you know, you only get so much time on a record with Bob, and so that was just a dream of mine, and I was looking to pick up from where we left off with the group of the demos. But we got something else that’s pretty nice, so everything worked out pretty good in the end.
Dylan had that box set put out where they almost undid half the production on Time Out of Mind. What was your reaction?

Oh, you mean the remix of the album? Yeah. I got a call from Wim Wenders when that came out ’cause I hadn’t listened to it yet. And he said, “Daniel, I’ve gone back to listening to the original of that record because I couldn’t even listen to these remixes ’cause the feeling was not there.” I said, “All right, Wim. Well, thanks for the call, and I’ll let you know how I feel when I get around to listening to it.” So why remix records? I can only assume that this happened after Bob sold his catalog and whatnot, and those folks were probably looking to make a few bucks back and decided let’s do a remix. Let’s say Wim Wenders was right. But in my experience, people are never willing to say, “Well, we gave it a good try, but it didn’t quite work out.” Nobody ever says that. And so they released what they wanted to release, and that’s that. And what do you think, man? Did you hear it?
I heard it. I didn’t see the point of it. I thought that part of the point of Time Out of Mind was the sound. It felt a bit like a dismantling of what had been done.
Do you think he had anything to do with it?
He has had interviews where he’s suggested the album wasn’t quite what he wanted, which is pretty funny given all its success. So who knows?

Yeah, man. Have to ask him… The people who remixed that record, they might’ve done well to take a look in the mirror and say, “Well, I don’t think I bettered it.” And that might’ve been the most courageous thing to do, just to say, “Lanois got it right,” and leave well enough alone, and it’s a masterpiece, and let’s throw confetti and bust out the rum.
Bob is doing the hoodie thing onstage now, which he also did in the studio with you sometimes. What’s the hood about?
Maybe he doesn’t like his hair right now.
That was one of my guesses, to be totally honest.
You know, I’m doing the beanie, he’s doing the hoodie.
People don’t think of you as much when it comes to the huge stuff you did with Peter Gabriel on So. Nothing sounds like that album.

It was a very devoted time for me. I had already made an album with Peter before the So album. It was a soundtrack for a movie called Birdy. He invited me to work on this soundtrack with him, and we did some lovely things, very imaginative things. He said, “Well, why don’t you stay on and work on my singing record, my song record next?” I said, “OK.” And we worked together for a year almost to the day, which was apparently a fast pace for Peter. And I loved him like a brother, and it was very much a one-on-one. David Rhodes lived around the corner — Peter’s guitar player. So it was largely Peter and myself, and then we were the Three Stooges. We wore hard hats to work, and it was a very nice vibe. This place was right out in the middle of the country, and we were in a cow barn. It’s not a glamorous studio by any means, and I was OK with that. We put the glamour in the music rather than the curtains.
Something like “Red Rain” — it’s so distinct. I can’t think of another song that sounds like that.

I hit on a sound with “Red Rain.” Peter was playing a Yamaha CP70, which is an electric grand piano you could call it. And I got a really nice sound out of it, and I was very extreme in my processings and my sound manipulations at that time, and I managed to turn that piano into rainfall. These avalanches of harmonics, and I just kept at it. It’s a technique that I worked on with Brian Eno prior to working with Peter. Simply put, we print our effects, and then allowing the effects to go back through the effects, and then another print, and another generation. So to keep adding multiple generations to processing, it gets into far-out stuff where your voltage control oscillators take on a life of their own. And before you know it, it sounds like monks in the distance, and cherubs flying by, and solarizations by Man Ray personally done by hand, and so on. And that’s where I got to with “Red Rain.”
And then of course, “Sledgehammer” was very different from everything else on the record.

Yeah, we cut that to a beatbox. It was a nothing beat. It was just some little drum machine that Peter had in the house at the time. I wanted to speak on a high frequency. I wanted to have that sensation that there was somebody really delivering a great hi-hat part. Testimony. So I wanted an expressive hi-hat performance, and not done by a machine, and we were lucky enough to be introduced to Manu Katché from Paris, great drummer, and he came in and he knocked that out in one take. I said, “Please give me a hi-hat fill. I can’t find anybody to do it.” He laughed and did it. Thank you, Manu.
To go to U2’s The Joshua Tree, you talked about “Where the Streets Have No Name” in your book, conducting the band with chords written on a blackboard. Why was that needed?

Because, you know, people get in the heat of a performance and they might be learning the song still, so it’s not bad to be a science teacher with a pointer. Just point at the blackboard, then point at the next chord that’s coming up so they just look up, and they don’t have to think about following a chord chart. Thank you, Danny.
And that song started with something the Edge had recorded by himself, I believe.

Yeah, that’s correct. Edge delivered a very nice, symphonic beginning to that song. Same BPM, but a different time signature. I think it might have been in 5/4. And see, we used his home recording and transferred that to the multi-track, and essentially the band overdubbed what Edge had prepared at home. W just made sure that we built a transitional, rhythmic component for Larry [Mullen Jr.] to follow. And so by a little bit of technology, we were able to build a multi-track for the band to overdub onto. And at a certain point it went from 5/4 to 4/4.
When you get something like “Where the Streets Have No Name” or “I Still Haven’t Found What I’m Looking For,” you realize you have to make an entire album that lives up to this stuff.

Standards get set, and that’s what’s great about record-making. But the thing that is most significant is that as you’re going along, something will become the sound of the record. And that’s why albums have a certain vibe to them. Oh Mercy has that vibe to it because it was done in a private way. It was not a big orchestra or band, and so you feel that feeling — let’s get a little more snapshot from Bob’s point of view. When we got into The Joshua Tree, quite early on we found something. We found a sound to that record and it became the governor. And so this is not anything you can control ahead of time by spreadsheet or by song list or anything. It’s when you get into the thick of it, you find out what you’re dealing with.

Four years later, you did Achtung Baby. A lot of times when people do an album that completely changes the sound they were known for, they go to new people. But this was the same people deconstructing the thing that they had done.

Back to The Joshua Tree for a minute, having finished Unforgettable Fire with the lads, I said to Edge I thought we had something left to say together. I didn’t go on too much about it. I wasn’t campaigning for work. I said that because I love them, and I wanted their music to be the best for them. And I meant what I said. And after The Joshua Tree, obviously that was a very successful record, but we had such a team and we decided let’s just keep going with it. It was Bono’s idea that we would make a European rock record, and why not go to Hansa in Berlin for that? The wall had just come down. Eno had worked there with Bowie and Iggy Pop back in the day, and so there was a notion about that being far enough away from home but still Europe. So that’s what took us there.

We kept the team together. Flood kindly took on all the engineering duties, which freed me up to be in the band room with Eno. Now in regards to creativity, here we go. You got Eno, me, Flood, and all we e

items.title: Tokyo Film Festival Opens With ‘Sukiyaki’ and a Plea for Peace as Japan’s Government Restates Global Content Ambitions
items.description: The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival opened Monday with a rain-soaked red carpet and a ceremony at Hulic Hall, where Japan’s government used the occasion to restate its goal of selling JPY20 trillion ($133 billion) worth of Japanese content overseas by 2
items.author: Mark Schilling; Lin Ying-Hsuan; Naman Ramachandran
paragraphs: The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival opened Monday with a rain-soaked red carpet and a ceremony at Hulic Hall, where Japan’s government used the occasion to restate its goal of selling JPY20 trillion ($133 billion) worth of Japanese content overseas by 2033.

The festival received 1,892 film submissions from 112 countries and regions this year. It opened with “Sukiyaki,” which tells how the title tune was written and went on to top the U.S. Billboard chart in 1963. Director Zeze Takahisa took the stage with Okada Junichi, who plays composer Nakamura Hachidai, Matsuzaka Tori, who plays lyricist Ei Rokusuke, and Seino Nana, who plays Nakamura Junko.

Zeze said the film is set in the years after the war, as Japan entered its period of rapid economic growth, and that its founding idea is the war itself and how the characters come to think about what peace means. “Through this film, I hope this festival, too, can become a festival of peace,” he said.

Matsuzaka said the shoot began in April last year and that the film had taken a little over a year to reach audiences. “It isn’t just about enjoying the music. It’s a film where you can feel the live energy, as if you were actually in the venue,” he said.
Seino said she had watched her co-stars’ stage performances from the audience seats during filming. “Seeing everyone’s souls colliding, going beyond their roles, really moved me,” she said.

In a video message played during the ceremony, Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae said her cabinet has designated content, including film, as a strategic priority under its Japan growth strategy, with public-private domestic investment set to accelerate. To reach the 2033 target, the government plans production support for Japanese films and efforts to attract foreign location shoots.
“Film has the power to connect people’s hearts across countries and regions, and to deepen understanding of diverse cultures and values,” Takaichi said.

Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry Akazawa Ryosei said overseas sales of Japanese content have already grown to around JPY6.1 trillion ($40.7 billion), and that the government has sought roughly JPY250 billion ($1.67 billion) across ministries in its fiscal 2027 budget request to support growth investment in the content industry.

Akazawa pointed to the fifth “Kingdom” film, which made the franchise the first series in film history to see five consecutive installments pass JPY5 billion ($33 million) at the box office, with a cumulative gross above JPY30 billion ($200 million). He also noted that the festival’s Centerpiece film, “Godzilla Minus Zero,” the follow-up to Oscar visual effects winner “Godzilla Minus One,” will open worldwide next month, including in Japan, Asia and North America.

Festival director Hisamatsu Takeo, who said he is approaching 50 years in the film business, thanked guests for turning out in bad weather before declaring the festival open. “There are so many kinds of film in the world, each with its own appeal and its own way of being enjoyed,” Hisamatsu said. “Nothing would make me happier than sharing the appeal of such diverse and varied cinema with all of you and enjoying it together.”

Filmmaker Rolf de Heer, president of the competition jury, which also includes actor Watanabe Makiko, DI colorist Yov Moor and producers Oh Jungwan and Alex Lo, recalled seeing an Ozu film more than 50 years ago. “I still remember one shot, so perfect. And Oshima, and of course Kurosawa. ‘Dersu Uzala’ is in my brain,” de Heer said. “So we as the jury are very privileged to be able to work in the country of those masters.”

Actor and singer Nakajima Kento, serving as TIFF Navigator, said walking the carpet carried a special sense of occasion. “It was raining today, but I felt it was a blessing of rain that would help the future of film flourish even more,” he said.

Among those on the carpet were director Milcho Manchevski and the cast of “Sister Brother Manhole Cover,” including Sara Klimoska, on her third visit to Tokyo. Director Qiu Jiongjiong led the cast of “Fuxi: Four Tales of Feasting,” and Indonesian auteur Garin Nugroho the “Red Before Dawn” team.

Judy Ongg represented “Sunshine Women’s Choir,” a gala selection title billed by TIFF as Taiwan’s No. 1 hit. Ongg won best actress at the seventh Taiwan Film Critics Society Awards, was nominated for best supporting actress at the 28th Taipei Film Awards and is nominated in the same category at the upcoming 63rd Golden Horse Awards.

The carpet also welcomed Academy CEO Bill Kramer, Academy president Lynette Howell Taylor and chief membership, impact and industry officer Meredith Shea, who are in Tokyo for TIFF’s Academy in Tokyo program.

“This is the first time the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences has participated in an international film festival. To be part of such a major platform as the Tokyo International Film Festival makes this especially meaningful, and we feel honored to be here,” Kramer said.

items.title: Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Scores $19.5 Million in Huge Second Weekend, ‘Clayface’ Leads With $24 Million Debut
items.description: Just when you thought you’d seen everything… A three-hour documentary (in its second weekend of release) has earned almost as much as a new comic-book adaptation at the domestic box office.
items.author: Rebecca Rubin
paragraphs: Just when you thought you’d seen everything… A three-hour documentary (in its second weekend of release) has earned almost as much as a new comic-book adaptation at the domestic box office.

Although Warner Bros. and DC’s R-rated “Clayface” was comfortably at No. 1 with $24 million from 3,458 North American theaters in its debut, A24’s buzzy Elizabeth Holmes doc “You Can See Everything” was surprisingly close behind after defying box office expectations again. The stranger-than-fiction film collected a spectacular $19.5 million while expanding to 2,655 venues in its sophomore outing.

Ticket sales for “You Can See Everything” are 28% above its launch of $15.6 million from 855 theaters, which marked the best start for a nonmusical documentary in 20 years. So far, the Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim-directed movie has earned a huge $45.1 million domestically to date. It was produced for $7 million. After capturing the zeitgeist and selling out screenings across the coasts, awards sages are predicting “You Can See Everything” could become the first documentary to ever score a best picture nomination at the Oscars.

“Opening ‘You Can See Everything’ in 855 theaters was a really smart move, allowing the film to establish itself and build momentum before going much wider,” says Rentrak’s head of marketplace trends Paul Dergarabedian. “The fact that we’re seeing a documentary deliver such a significant second-weekend increase is remarkable.”

“Clayface” arrived on the lower end of the studio’s expectations of $25 million to $35 million. The comic book movie brought in another $19 million overseas from 76 markets for a global tally of $43 million. Along with a positive reception, the film seems well-positioned theatrically because it cost just $44 million to produce. That’s a way smaller budget compared to DC’s other recent tentpoles, including this July’s “Supergirl” and 2025’s “Superman.” Although “Superman” was a decent hit with $618 million against a $225 million budget, “Supergirl” was a setback for the newly relaunched comic book studio after bombing with $126 million against a $170 million budget. Meanwhile, DC has found success on streaming with its “Peacemaker” and “Lanterns” shows for HBO Max. DC wanted to keep costs low on “Clayface” because it’s a body-horror thriller that’s much darker than those family-friendly adventures. Directed by James Watkins, “Clayface” follows the titular Batman villain, a rising movie star who volunteers for a highly experimental medical procedure after his face is severely disfigured. Audiences enjoyed the film, which holds an “A-” grade on CinemaScore exit polls.

“Over the years, there have been a dozen spinoffs of superhero villains and antiheroes, from ‘Joker’ to ‘Venom’ to ‘Kraven the Hunter,'” says David A. Gross, who publishes the box office newsletter FranchiseRe. “This picture was wisely conceived as something different, costing a fraction of what those films cost, and it should be profitable when it finishes all ancillary business.”

“Clayface” opened alongside a smattering of new releases, including Laika’s stop-motion animated “Wildwood,” Black Bear’s offbeat romantic comedy “Wicker” and Sony’s literary adaptation “Klara and the Sun,” starring Jenna Ortega.

“Wildwood” debuted at No. 3 with $11.2 million from 2,718 venues, launching above projections of $6 million to $8 million. It’s a promising start for original animation, which has been challenged in the years following the pandemic. And “Wildwood” has the benefit of sterling reviews (a rare 100% on Rotten Tomatoes) and audience scores (an “A” grade on CinemaScore exit polls), which should help the film stick around beyond its opening weekend. However, this movie carries a hefty $100 million price tag (stop-motion animation is labor-intensive and takes years to produce) and likely won’t turn a theatrical profit.

“This is a very good opening for a new animated film from outside of the studio development and distribution system,” says Gross. “Audiences love this movie, but it needs a very long run to recoup its costs.”

So far, “Wildwood” has collected just $3 million internationally from 11 markets. The movie hails from Laika Studios, best known for making the 2009 stop-motion fantasy “Coraline.” This is the company’s first release since 2019’s “Missing Link,” which opened to $6 million from 3,413 theaters and ended its run with $26 million globally. “Wildwood” was directed by Laika’s CEO Travis Knight and revolves around a teenage girl who travels with a classmate into an enchanted forest after her brother is abducted.

“Wicker” captured fifth place with $5.75 million from 1,471 locations, a strong start for the low-budget film. Black Bear acquired the well-reviewed movie after Sundance for $2.5 million. Olivia Colman stars as an ostracized woman who commissions a local basketmaker to weave her a husband. Her unexpected romance with the creation (Alexander Skarsgård) sparks jealousy in the village.

“It is fantastic to see that the film is truly resonating with the audiences,” says Black Bear’s head of domestic theatrical distribution David Spitz. “This is a true testament to the filmmakers, cast, our innovative marketing, and our partnership with exhibition whose support proves that these types of films are what audiences want in their mix of movie-going experiences.”

“Klara and the Sun” collapsed at No. 15 with $720,000 from 880 locations. Sony scaled back the theatrical footprint after reviews panned the movie as “calamitous” and “confoundingly awful.” Luckily, the Taika Waititi-directed adaptation had a modest $20 million budget, so the studio’s inevitable box office losses won’t be too painful. Based on Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel, “Klara and the Sun” takes place in the dystopian future as an obsolete companion android (Ortega) tries to bond with her new owner, a young sick girl named Josie.

Meanwhile Amazon MGM didn’t report grosses for Sacha Baron Cohen’s mockumentary “Ali G: Who Iz I?” after dialing down the release to just 125 theaters for two days. It’ll premiere soon on Prime Video.

Paramount’s video game reboot “Street Fighter” landed in fourth place with $8.6 million from 3,575 theaters in its second weekend, a painful 72% drop from its debut. The movie has generated $46.9 million in North America and $79.6 million worldwide to date. Legendary and video game developer Capcom co-financed “Street Fighter” for $82 million, with Paramount only on the hook for distribution.

Disney and 20th Century’s “Whalefall,” too, took a tumble in its sophomore outing with $3.2 million from 3,065 theaters. The survival thriller, starring Austin Abrams as a scuba diver swallowed by a sperm whale, dropped to 10th place on weekend charts and has earned $14.1 million domestically and $31.1 million globally to date. “Whalefall” cost $60 million and requires substantial staying power, since theater owners keep about half of ticket sales.

Elsewhere, Netflix’s generation-spanning drama “La Bola Negra” earned $245,000 from nine locations — a decline of 12% despite expanding its theater count. So far, the streamer’s awards hopeful has collected $650,000 from two weekends in limited release. Netflix plans to keep “La Bola Negra” in theaters for 45 days, a traditional window in post-pandemic times, before the film’s Netflix release on Dec. 2.

items.title: From ‘Hoop Dreams’ to ‘Flee’: The 20 Documentaries That Deserved a Best Picture Oscar Nomination
items.description: In nearly a century of Oscars, not a single documentary has been nominated for best picture. But that shouldn’t be the case.
items.author: Clayton Davis
paragraphs: In nearly a century of Oscars, not a single documentary has been nominated for best picture. But that shouldn’t be the case.

While a documentary can win its own Oscar, reshape the cultural conversation and become one of the defining films of its era, these nonfiction feature films have been excluded from the top category meant to honor the year’s best filmmaking. When the Academy expanded the Best Picture lineup from five to 10 after the snub of “The Dark Knight” (2008), the press release led with the possibility of a documentary getting recognized. That has yet to happen … perhaps until now?

That assumption is finally being tested this season with “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s nonfiction sensation about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. Acclaim and box office success are raising the possibility that a documentary could finally break one of the Academy’s longest-standing barriers. If it earns a nomination, the achievement would be historic. But it would also raise an uncomfortable question: Why did it take this long?
To celebrate this potential historic nomination, Variety is ranking the 20 films that should have received a best picture nomination in the past 40 years.

The films mentioned here span genres, styles and subjects, from the pursuit of an NBA dream to a high-wire walk between the World Trade Center towers, from a confrontation with Indonesia’s history of mass killing to a real-time account of Edward Snowden’s revelations.
You can blame the Academy at large for some of these omissions; others tie directly to the Documentary Branch itself, which snubbed many of them in its own category.

If “You Can See Everything” finally breaks through, it will undoubtedly have earned its place in history. But it should not have been the first. Many others from this very year could also be deemed worthy, such as “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” and “Naza.”
Honorable mentions: “An Inconvenient Truth” (2006); “Senna” (2010); “The Act of Killing” (2012); “Apollo 11″ (2019)

- Daughters (2024) Angela Patton and Natalie Rae’s “Daughters” follows four girls preparing for a father-daughter dance inside a Washington, D.C., prison as part of a fatherhood program Patton helped build. The filmmakers’ choice to focus on the girls’ anticipation, anger and longing is its strongest element. It carries the film toward a dance sequence of almost unbearable tenderness. It won both the Audience Award and the Festival Favorite prize at Sundance, then made the documentary shortlist only to miss the nomination at the 2025 ceremony. Few films that year said more about love under impossible conditions.

- Man on Wire (2008) James Marsh’s “Man on Wire” reconstructs Philippe Petit’s 1974 high-wire walk between the World Trade Center towers. Through interviews, archival footage and recreations, Marsh builds a structure as a model for any good movie heist. “Man on Wire” won the documentary Oscar at the 2009 ceremony, and its success lives on, demonstrating how effectively a nonfiction film could deliver the pleasures of a caper.

- O.J.: Made in America (2016) There are strong feelings about whether or not Ezra Edelman’s Oscar winner is, in fact, a documentary feature, but it’s included nonetheless. Edelman’s nearly eight-hour “O.J.: Made in America” is an expansive examination of race, celebrity, policing and the American justice system, using the life of O.J. Simpson as a lens through which to understand the country’s social and cultural divisions. What begins as a portrait of an athlete becomes a sweeping account of Los Angeles and the forces that shaped one of the most consequential public dramas of the modern era. The documentary feature Oscar winner’s format also exposed the boundaries of the category. Its recognition prompted renewed scrutiny of how the Academy treats multipart nonfiction projects, contributing to subsequent eligibility changes concerning episodic work. Whatever the debate over its classification, the filmmaking is extraordinary. Its scope exceeds that of most narrative features.

- Won’t You Be My Neighbor? (2018) Morgan Neville’s portrait of television icon Fred Rogers became the highest-grossing biographical documentary of its time and became a sensation for all of us who grew up with the prolific figure. Rather than canonize its subject, Oscar winner Neville (“20 Feet From Stardom”) examines the radical patience behind “Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood” and the quiet conviction that children deserved to be taken seriously. The film made the documentary shortlist but, shockingly, missed a nomination at the 2019 ceremony, a snub that still stings. Few films that year moved audiences so completely, in any category.

- Flee (2021) Jonas Poher Rasmussen’s “Flee” uses animation to tell the story of Amin, an Afghan refugee who reveals the full extent of his childhood and his journey to safety. The decision to use the animation medium for the testimony allows Amin to revisit traumatic memories while preserving his anonymity, creating a visual language for experiences that would be difficult to reconstruct. “Flee” made Oscar history by becoming the first film nominated for documentary feature, international feature and animated feature in the same year. It lost in all three categories, and best picture remained out of reach. Rasmussen’s film is a reminder that nonfiction is not confined to one visual language or storytelling tradition.

- The Look of Silence (2014) Many will argue I chose the wrong Joshua Oppenheimer film, and that “The Act of Killing” is more worthy of a spot than its companion piece. That a filmmaker’s work can spark such a debate is itself a mark of genius. “The Look of Silence” approaches Indonesia’s 1965-66 mass killings through an optometrist whose brother was murdered during the violence. Oppenheimer resists the conventions of a historical exposé, allowing pauses and glances to communicate what his subjects refuse to say. The film landed a documentary feature nomination but lost to “Amy.”

- Cameraperson (2016) Kirsten Johnson spent decades as a documentary cinematographer, filming subjects in war zones, hospitals and interview rooms. With “Cameraperson,” she assembled fragments from that career into a moving essay about the ethics of looking and the emotional toll of bearing witness. The doc branch failed to nominate “Cameraperson,” a shocking omission for a work so widely admired for its originality. Johnson’s 2020 follow-up, “Dick Johnson Is Dead,” a playful and heartbreaking reckoning with her father’s decline, that could just as easily have claimed this spot.

- 13th (2016) Ava DuVernay’s “13th” examines the connection between the 13th Amendment, which abolished slavery, and the rise of mass incarceration in the United States. Through interviews with scholars, activists and politicians, alongside archival footage, DuVernay builds an argument about the enduring relationship between race and the criminal justice system. Rather than treating the amendment as a historical endpoint, she traces how its language became a blueprint for systems of control, and presenting a complex history with clarity and urgency. “13th” opened the 2016 New York Film Festival and landed a documentary feature nom, losing to “O.J.: Made in America.” A decade later, DuVernay returned to NYFF with the equally urgent “14th,” the festival’s 2026 closing night film, which Netflix will also release.

- Dear Zachary: A Letter to a Son About His Father (2008) No documentary has made me cry more than the one about a baby named Zachary. Kurt Kuenne began “Dear Zachary” as a film for the infant son of his murdered best friend, Andrew Bagby. And what starts as a tribute built from home videos, photographs and memories becomes a devastating account of grief, family and a legal system that fails those seeking justice. Kuenne is not a detached observer. As events unfold, the film’s purpose changes, and its structure takes on a force no viewer can anticipate. Kuenne’s mid-film narration is something your heart can never properly prepare for. Nonetheless, the documentary branch passed on “Dear Zachary.” It remains one of the clearest examples of why documentaries deserve to be considered among the year’s best films, not merely the year’s best documentaries.

- Exit Through the Gift Shop (2010) Banksy’s “Exit Through the Gift Shop” makes uncertainty part of the moviewatching experience. Is the film documenting an absurd art-world spectacle, manufacturing one or doing both at once? Banksy never provides a definitive answer, and the film’s refusal to settle the question gives it life. “Exit Through the Gift Shop” earned a documentary feature nom, losing to “Inside Job.” Moreover, it challenged the assumption that documentaries must present a distinction between observer and participant.

- I Am Not Your Negro (2016) Raoul Peck’s Oscar-nominated “I Am Not Your Negro” takes James Baldwin’s unfinished manuscript about Medgar Evers, Malcolm X and Martin Luther King Jr. and transforms it into a searing cinematic essay on race and America. Samuel L. Jackson narrates Baldwin’s words, with the film’s force coming from the collision between the writer’s observations and a country that still refuses to reckon with its past. It’s sheer brilliance, and always timely.

- Three Identical Strangers (2018) Tim Wardle’s film opens as a feel-good reunion of triplets separated at birth and curdles into an account of a secret psychological study that treated infants as test subjects. Wardle controls the revelations with the discipline of a thriller, letting each turn leave the viewer shocked before the next is revealed. Like “Won’t You Be My Neighbor?,” it was shortlisted and then passed over entirely by the documentary branch. Its story of nature, nurture and institutional betrayal deserved a much wider stage.

- Citizenfour (2014) Laura Poitras’ “Citizenfour” puts viewers inside a Hong Kong hotel room while Edward Snowden meets journalists and begins revealing classified information about government surveillance. Poitras allows conversations to develop in real time, building suspense through the simple act of watching history unfold. “Citizenfour” won the documentary Oscar at the 2015 ceremony, but no best picture heat would ensue.

- Searching for Sugar Man (2012) Malik Bendjelloul’s “Searching for Sugar Man” chases the ghost of Rodriguez, a Detroit musician whose albums vanished in America but became anthems in apartheid-era South Africa, where fans knew nothing about the man behind the music. By my estimation, it’s the single standout nonfiction film of its decade. Bendjelloul builds the mystery like a detective story, with an emotional payoff that feels almost too extraordinary to be true. Rodriguez’s incredible songs carry a story about fame, obscurity and the strange ways art outlives the circumstances of its making. Oscar voters handed it the documentary prize in 2013. Nobody mounted a best picture push for a film that had already proven it could hold a broad audience in its palm. Bendjelloul died in 2014 at 36, but the joyous discovery he left behind is well intact.

- Grizzly Man (2005) Werner Herzog’s “Grizzly Man” begins with footage shot by Timothy Treadwell, a self-appointed protector of Alaskan grizzlies who was killed by one of the animals he sought to defend. Herzog’s narration becomes a film unto itself, challenging Treadwell’s romantic vision of the wilderness. The footage is funny, unnerving and devastating, sometimes within the same frame. Few filmmakers have turned a real-life tragedy into a philosophical inquiry so effectively without losing sight of the person at its center. Unfortunately, this was yet another victim of the doc branch’s allergy to mainstream and successful films, even though it’s widely considered among Herzog’s most celebrated works.

- Stories We Tell (2012) Sarah Polley’s “Stories We Tell” is an investigation into her own family history and becomes a remarkably intricate exploration of memory, and the fragile relationship between personal truth and the stories people preserve. Polley interviews relatives and friends, reconstructing family moments with its most effective moments being best experienced without advance knowledge of the revelations it shows. “Stories We Tell” was snubbed for the documentary Oscar, let alone best picture. That omission is particularly striking given Polley’s command of structure and her willingness to question the very conventions on which documentary filmmaking depends.

- Bowling for Columbine (2002) Michael Moore turned the Columbine High School massacre into a mirror for America to see. “Bowling for Columbine” interrogates America’s relationship with guns, violence and fear, mixing interviews, archival footage and Moore’s confrontational on-camera presence into an argument that dared audiences to fight back. Few releases of 2002 commanded that attention. The Writers Guild made it the first documentary to win its original screenplay prize, and the Academy followed with the documentary Oscar, where Moore’s “shame on you, Mr. Bush” speech became the most talked-about moment of the night (and history).

- Hoop Dreams (1994) No documentary snub remains quite as painful as the Academy’s failure to recognize Steve James’ “Hoop Dreams.” Over five years, James followed Chicago teenagers William Gates and Arthur Agee as they pursued basketball dreams that promised an escape from poverty. The result is a nearly three-hour American epic about race, class, family and the machinery that turns young athletes into commodities. Critics embraced the film as one of the year’s finest, regardless of genre. The Academy’s documentary branch, however, failed to nominate it, prompting widespread criticism and contributing to voting changes in the documentary nomination process. Interestingly, “Hoop Dreams” managed to receive an Oscar nomination for film editing, but best picture was likely an even more distant possibility.

- The Thin Blue Line (1988) Errol Morris’ investigation into the 1976 killing of a Dallas police officer did something few doc films hope to do: It helped free an innocent man. Randall Dale Adams was released from prison within a year of the film’s debut, after Morris’ interviews exposed the holes in the case against him. Its stylized reenactments, Philip Glass score and noir structure reinvented the nonfiction form in many ways. Once again, the doc branch had other plans, with a snub measured just as scandalous in its moment as “Hoop Dreams” would be six years later. Leaving out the film that changed how documentaries are made is indefensible.

- Paris is Burning (1990) Jennie Livingston’s “Paris Is Burning” documents Harlem’s ballroom scene in the late 1980s, where Black and Latino queer performers built houses, families and an entire vocabulary of survival in the face of poverty, racism and the AIDS crisis. Its subjects, including Pepper LaBeija, Dorian Corey and Venus Xtravaganza, are among the most vivid figures nonfiction cinema has captured. The film won the Grand Jury Prize at Sundance yet was snubbed by the Academy’s documentary branch at the 1992 ceremony. Decades later, its influence has been felt in artistic achievements such as television’s “Pose,” “RuPaul’s Drag Race” and the mainstream itself.

items.title: Eric Bauza, Emmy Award-Winning Looney Tunes Voice Actor, Dies at 46
items.description: Eric Bauza, the Emmy Award-winning voice actor behind Looney Tunes characters like Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, died Sunday at his home as a result of hypertensive cardiovascular disease, according to Los Angeles County Medical Examiner records. He was 46.
items.author: Payton Turkeltaub
paragraphs: Eric Bauza, the Emmy Award-winning voice actor behind Looney Tunes characters like Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, died Sunday at his home as a result of hypertensive cardiovascular disease, according to Los Angeles County Medical Examiner records. He was 46.
Bauza’s death was announced by his family, who shared a statement to the actor’s Instagram account on Sunday.

“Eric Bauza, Emmy Award-winning voice actor and the modern voice of iconic Looney Tunes characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, along with dozens of other beloved cartoon characters, has passed away suddenly,” they wrote. “More details to come.”

Over the course of his career, Bauza was one of the industry’s most in-demand voiceover actors, lending his voice to characters like the aforementioned Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, but also Tweety, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, Porky Pig, Road Runner, Charlie the Dog and others in this year’s Looney Tunes film “Coyote vs. Acme.” He also voiced characters in “Space Jam: A New Legacy,” “Looney Tunes Cartoons” and more.

Bauza had more than 400 acting credits to his name, with his first, “The Ripping Friends” in 2001. He went on to voice characters in “Avatar: The Last Airbender,” “Chowder,” “Alvin and the Chipmunks: The Squeakquel,” “Scooby-Doo! Mystery Incorporated,” “Fanboy & Chum Chum,” “Ben 10 Omniverse” and many more. In 2026 alone, Bauza had already lent his voice to projects including “Chibiverse,” “Minions & Monsters,” “Forgotten Island,” “Rick and Morty,” “Superkitties” and “Avatar: Seven Havens,” among others.

In Variety’s Peter Debruge’s review of the 2024 film “The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie,” he called Bauza, who voiced both Porky and Daffy, a “vocal MVP” who “brings a manic energy to the pair.”

Bauza was nominated for five Daytime Emmy Awards for his work on “Looney Tunes Cartoons,” “Mupped Babies” and “The Adventures of Puss in Boots.” He won three Children’s & Family Emmy Awards for “Teen Titans Go!,” “Bugs Bunny Builders” and “Looney Tunes Cartoons,” and earned a nomination for “Daffy in Wackyland.”
At the time of his death, Bauza was in pre-production on two projects, “Bye Bye Bunny: A Looney Tunes Musical” as Daffy Duck and “The Dragon Masters” as The Shogun King.

Chris DeFaria, who produced “Coyote vs. Acme,” told Variety that he will remember Bauza as someone with an “absolutely tireless dedication” to the animation art form, and reflected on his “pure expression of dedication, talent, enthusiasm, love and fun.”

“He embodied everything we wanted from this film, including the major theme of the movie that a little guy can make a difference in this world,” said DeFaria. “He’s a voiceover artist for animated characters that have historic precedents and roles, and somehow out of that, he carved out a place in this business. And this past year, he had such an incredible impact, both on our movie, of course, but also on bringing attention to this amazing art form.”

“Eric Bauza was a unique voice talent who brought joy and laughter to millions around the world. During his 15 years at Warner Bros. Animation, he was the voice of Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck among countless other characters,” said Warner Bros. Television Group and US Networks Chairman Channing Dungey in a statement. “He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc. Eric said that carrying on the legendary legacy of the Looney Tunes was among the greatest honors of his life. In addition to his incredible talent, Eric was a treasured part of our animation family. Our hearts go out to his loved ones.”

Bauza was born on Dec. 7, 1979, in Scarborough, Toronto. According to his SBV talent bio, he began his animation career as a character designer at a production studio in Hollywood. He worked in the animation department on films including “Good Vibe,” “Nimbrod and Stinky’s Antarctic Adventure,” “The Drawn Together Movie!,” “Slacker Cats,” “El Tigre: The Adventures of Manny Rivera” and more.

items.title: Jay-Z Brings His ‘Jay-Z 30’ Concert Series to a Close in Los Angeles With Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg and Too Short
items.description: How does one measure their own legacy: In a series of shows, in the decades since a debut album, in an exhaustive eight-part docuseries breaking down the intricacies of rhymes laid down years ago? That seemed to be the existential question looming over “Jay-Z
items.author: Steven J Horowitz
paragraphs: How does one measure their own legacy: In a series of shows, in the decades since a debut album, in an exhaustive eight-part docuseries breaking down the intricacies of rhymes laid down years ago? That seemed to be the existential question looming over “Jay-Z 30,” a yearlong celebration that began with a spectacular one-off headlining performance at the Roots Picnic in late May and concluded on Saturday night with the second of two shows at Inglewood, California’s SoFi Stadium.

For Jay, legacy has clearly been weighing on his mind. A new generation of hip-hop artists has emerged, and the decade-long gap since he released an album has opened a space for that generation to question his legacy. So it made sense that he’d revisit his catalog brick by brick, show by show, celebrating a career-long work in progress that crescendoed to a global tour after nearly a decade of artistic dormancy. At SoFi, much like his previous concerts, his performance was a reminder — no, a reinforcement — that nothing at that scale is by accident. And he said as much as the curtain fell on an hour-and-a-half finale of his “Jay-Z 30” series, encouraging those in attendance to believe in what they’ve actually witnessed.

“You gotta be really real with what’s going on in the world,” he said during closer “Encore.” It was a direct rebuttal to the rash of tweets and social media posts claiming that SoFi wasn’t entirely sold out, or that many of the tickets had been given away. “People will tell you that nobody was in here tonight, but you got eyes. You can see. People will tell you that the music wasn’t great, but you got ears. You gotta understand, you gotta question everything. This world with AI and everything, it’s been going on forever. They called it propaganda before. But now, the technology has caught up and people are tricked. A lot of tricknology for us… Make sure you question everything you feel.”

Jay makes that music that you can feel. That’s been the thrill of his shows over the past five months. For those who experienced his rise in real time (and, frankly, many at SoFi probably had, based on their millennial look), Jay has been a pop impresario, a cultural touchstone who helped graft hip-hop culture onto the mainstream. He’s done it through a breathless string of number one albums and hits, and in boardrooms and closed-door meetings. “Jay-Z 30” was an invitation to revisit the path that he took to get there, a way to show that legacy isn’t about the hit that’s next, but rather the ones you landed to get there.

To witness it was where the details mattered most. Much like his other performances, the setlist at Jay’s final night at SoFi was somewhat static — “Girls, Girls, Girls,” for instance, once again bled into “’03 Bonnie & Clyde,” while “N—s in Paris” delightfully mashed into “Big Pimpin’.” But the finer details are what make a Jay show such an experience. At each of his shows, he’s found a way to pay homage to the city that’s welcomed him. In Philadelphia, that included guest appearances from Jazmine Sullivan, Bilal and his Roc-A-Fella crew, including Freeway, Beanie Sigel and Peedi Crakk. In New York City, throughout his three-night run at Yankee Stadium, he brought out Alicia Keys for “Empire State of Mind,” as well as Fat Joe and Jadakiss. Naturally, a narrative emerged: Can he really perform a solid headlining set without a supporting cast to sweeten the deal?

Perhaps that’s why the guest count at his SoFi shows was so thin compared to others. On Saturday night, he tapped Too Short to perform “Blow the Whistle,” shouting out the Bay Area. Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg came out to do a medley of their own massive hits, including “Nuthin’ But a ‘G’ Thang” and “Still D.R.E.” But it was mainly Jay, every day, in all his resplendence. He traipsed from era to era, hit to hit, his breath control and spark as refined as ever. This was performance at its peak, a marvel to behold of an artist who helped build hip-hop as an institution while adding to the story still being written.

As for what’s next? Rumors have swirled about a new album from collaborators who quickly backpedaled on their statements. The looming question mark of a Super Bowl Halftime Show performance hung in the air at SoFi on Saturday night. But for a string of concerts and a few activations here and there, it felt only right that Jay-Z justify the experience while rapping “Heart of the City (Ain’t No Love)” near the end of the show: “Jigga held you down 30 summers, damn, where’s the love?”
Check out the full setlist below:
Blow the Whistle (Too $hort)
N—a What, N—a Who (Originator 99)
Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem)
Murder Was the Case (Snoop Dogg)
The Next Episode (Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg)
California Love (Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg)
Nothin’ but a “G” Thang (Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg)
Still D.R.E. (Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg)
La-La-La (Excuse Me Miss Again)
I Just Wanna Love U (Give It 2 Me)
Heart of the City (Ain’t No Love)
N—s in Paris / Big Pimpin’
Public Service Announcement (Interlude)

items.title: Donald Trump Attacks Bill Maher in Scathing, 1,318-Word Social Media Post: “Complete and Total Loser”
items.description: President Donald Trump is once again criticizing Bill Maher, host of HBO‘s Real Time With Bill Maher — only days after the two had what he previously referred to as a “great dinner” at the White House.
items.author: Kimberly Nordyke
paragraphs: President Donald Trump is once again criticizing Bill Maher, host of HBO‘s Real Time With Bill Maher — only days after the two had what he previously referred to as a “great dinner” at the White House.
On Sunday, Trump posted a scathing 1,318-word diatribe on Truth Social blasting Maher as a “complete and total loser” (in all caps).

“Let’s talk about this COMPLETE AND TOTAL LOSER, Bill Maher,” he began. “He’s got a Low Rated Show on equally Low Rated HBO, which was once, long ago, a Network of Quality and Excitement — But that’s all gone. It’s not ‘HOT’ anymore!” (Capitals and uppercasing are all Trump’s.)

Trump then turned his ire to producer Chuck LaBella, who’s worked with Maher for years across multiple productions, nothing that LaBella was a “gofer” on Trump’s reality competition show The Apprentice, and also a friend of Trump’s at the time.

“[B]ecause of the success of that show, Number One and Top Rated on many weeks, with the Finale’ [sic] being among the Top Shows of the Year, he was automatically and quickly brought up through the Ranks of NBC, along with everyone else associated with that Historic ‘Happening,'” Trump wrote. “The Success of the Apprentice was so great that everyone partook — It built many careers, and that is a wonderful thing. Some people say it even built my career, because I became President (I would have won without it!). In any event, over the last few years, LaBella would call me nonstop to say, ‘Hello,’ be very nice, and tell me how much Bill Maher ‘loves’ and respects me, and would constantly ask of me, even before I was President, for any form of meeting with Maher and, would I do his show? When I became President, I agreed to meet, after the first one, and the last one, but never agreed to do his show, which he wants me to do, DESPARATELY [sic] — It won’t happen! When I have watched the show, which isn’t often, it always ends with dishonesty, about me at least, but, who cares?”

Trump apparently was upset with Maher over some jokes made on Friday’s installment of Real Time. In his monologue, Maher mocked the president’s approval ratings and recent comments about men’s physiques, while referring to his own recent visit to the White House.

“It’s just a little odd that Trump keeps gushing about men’s bodies, and how handsome they are, and their jawlines, and their asses, their physiques,” Maher said. “I’m a little hurt. I was there for dinner for four hours last week, and not a peep. Nothing.”
He added: “Trump has the lowest approval rating of any midterm candidate ever. Only 1 percent of the Republicans are mentioning him in their ads.”
In his post, Trump cited several polls claiming Trump is the most popular Republican of all time, beating out both Ronald Reagan and Abraham Lincoln.

Also on the show, Maher made a joke about Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who ran an ad featuring Democrat gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, calling her daughter “a liar.” Actor and Arthur reportedly have not been in touch since 1978, when Arthur’s second husband, Cledith Arthur, was indicted and charged with raping Actor, who was 12 at the time. The Ramaswamy campaign has said it will spend $4 million to promote the ad Ohio, with Trump and Vice President JD Vance both backing the decision to run the spot.
“Trump said this is fair game,” Maher said on his show. “A 12-year-old rape victim is fair game? I know that looks bad. It sounds better on a birthday card to Jeffrey Epstein.”

Trump and Maher had dinner at the White House earlier this month with Stephen A. Smith and Kid Rock. Afterward, Trump told reporters: “It was a great dinner. It was a very informative dinner, Smart people. Stephen A. is great. Bill Maher — I will tell you what. He likes me a lot more than people understand, and I actually like him. It was a good dinner.”

However, on Sunday, in his Trump Social post, Trump called Maher or LaBella a “pothead” and said he “looked like hell this time” (it’s really unclear which person he was referring to). He also said that Maher “was drunk and had alcohol in his hand as he walked through the White House.”
The president also wrote that Maher “lies about everything” and accused him of using a “Laughter Machine [sic]” because his jokes “aren’t funny or even any good.”
Trump then recalled their first dinner together, in March 2025, and how that came about.

“Chuck LaBella, and my friend, Kid Rock, called me incessantly about meeting with Bill Maher,” Trump wrote “My first response was, ‘Fellas, this guy’s a Goofball.’ They said, ‘He wants to go down to the White House, be with you, and talk. He said you’re very smart, but you’re not into the Liberal Platform. Will you start thinking about it?’ He invited himself to the White House! We had our first meeting, Bill was very nervous. He asked for a drink. He was very insecure, and he had a seriously bruised eye and nose area, as though somebody had just beaten him up — But it wasn’t me!”

After that dinner, Trump was at first complimentary but then later criticized Maher. On Sunday, Trump claimed LaBella pushed hard for a second dinner. He also disputed Maher’s statement that the second dinner lasted four hours.

“Overall, I thought it was a good meeting,” he wrote. “It didn’t last four hours, it lasted two hours, maybe less, and everybody was happy. We have the timestamps. I learned nothing, and felt it was a waste of time. After the first dinner, Bill Maher was friendly, I guess, everyone walked away pleased. He gave me a good first show, with lots of Laughing Machine laughter, which is a real term, but it is what it is, and then reverted back to his former self, and his old ways. I understand that. He’s doing his thing. I never took it very personally. I would always mock his Low Ratings, whenever I heard. He’s not a nice guy, and what he spouts isn’t what he believes. He has to cater to his base, which is mostly composed of Losers, and people who don’t like working.”

Trump ended his post by addressing Maher directly: “You’re also a coward who is afraid to tell the truth about how well our Country is running because of your few ‘fans,’ and how badly the Dumocrats have done, almost destroying the U.S.A. If I hadn’t won the Election, it would be DEAD! Also, turn your Laugh Machine off, it’s a joke when they laugh uncontrollably, even when you say nothing funny, and I’m going to have the Republicans not cover you anymore, because they try to talk about you as a guy who is transformative. You’re not transformative, you’re a Loser! I never watched your show much, but I will never watch it again, because it is nothing more than FAKE NEWS that America, and the World, is unfortunately subjected to. Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP”
The Hollywood Reporter has reached out to Maher’s reps for comment.

items.title: Eric Bauza, the Modern Voice of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Other Iconic Characters, Dies at 46
items.description: Eric Bauza, an Emmy-winning voice actor who was the modern voice of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and other Looney Tunes characters, has died. He was 46.
items.author: Kimberly Nordyke
paragraphs: Eric Bauza, an Emmy-winning voice actor who was the modern voice of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and other Looney Tunes characters, has died. He was 46.

The news was announced Sunday by his family via a post on his Instagram feed. “Eric Bauza, Emmy Award-winning voice actor and the modern voice of iconic Looney Tunes characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, along with dozens of other beloved cartoon characters, has passed away suddenly. More details to come,” the post reads.

It’s unclear when he died, but he was scheduled to attend the premiere of Warner Bros. Pictures Animation’s The Cat in the Hat on Sunday afternoon to support Daffy Season, a short that plays before the film, according to press documents.
Channing Dungey, chairman of Warner Bros. Television Group and U.S. Networks, paid tribute to Bauza in a statement.

“Eric Bauza was a unique voice talent who brought joy and laughter to millions around the world. During his 15 years at Warner Bros. Animation,” she said. “He was the voice of Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck among countless other characters. He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc. Eric said that carrying on the legendary legacy of the Looney Tunes was among the greatest honors of his life. In addition to his incredible talent, Eric was a treasured part of our animation family. Our hearts go out to his loved ones.”

Bauza recently landed on The Hollywood Reporter’s inaugural Animation Power list and attended the corresponding event honoring those on the list. “Bauza has quietly become the voice of an entire cartoon universe,” THR’s Scott Roxborough wrote of the voice actor. “One of the successors to the legendary Mel Blanc as the voice of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Marvin the Martian and a dozen more iconic characters, the Canadian actor outdid himself with Coyote vs. Acme, voicing everything from Bugs Bunny to Foghorn Leghorn and Tweety Bird.”
“A lot of talented folks worked really hard to make this film, and to be able to see it celebrated by so many people across the globe has really made the wait worth it,” Bauza said of the movie.

In the Looney Tunes film Coyote vs. Acme, which was released earlier this year, Bauza voiced several roles, including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Tweety, Daffy Duck, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, Porky Pig, Road Runner, Charlie the Dog, and more. Most of those roles, of course, originated with the late, legendary Mel Blanc. Bauza also brought several Looney Tunes characters to life in such productions as Space Jam: A New Legacy (voicing Daffy Duck, Porky Pig, Foghorn Leghorn, Elmer Fudd and Marvin the Martian) and Looney Tunes Cartoons (Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck), among others.
Born December 7, 1979, Bauza was from Toronto but more recently was living in Los Angeles.
He started his career in animation as a character designer working with a few production studios in Hollywood, according to his bio on SBV Talent, which represented him.

He received Daytime Emmy, Children’s & Family Emmy and Annie Award nominations for his work as the title character in The Adventures of Puss in Boots, Fozzie in Muppet Babies and Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck in Looney Tunes Cartoons.
Recently, he voiced roles in DreamWorks Animation’s animated film Forgotten Island.

His other TV credits include Unikitty, Archibald’s Next Big Thing, The Rocketeer, Ballmastrz: 9009, Rise of the Teenage Mutant Turtles, Star vs. The Forces of Evil, Breadwinners, Uncle Grandpa, Atomic Puppet, The Powerpuff Girls, The Fairly OddParents, Ultimate Spider-Man, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, Guardians of the Galaxy, Transformers: Robots in Disguise, Sanjay and Craig and Mighty Magiswords.
Bauza has voiced characters in The Book of Life and The SpongeBob Movie: Sponge Out of Water. Bauza also was Woody Woodpecker in Universal’s animated film Woody Woodpecker.

According to his bio, Bauza has also voiced characters in commercials, including Lucky the Leprechaun for Lucky Charms cereal, Trix Rabbit for Trix cereal and Marvin the Martian for Nike and in the Walmart commercial “Famous Visitors.”

items.title: Ted Sarandos Swoops Into Seoul as Netflix Celebrates 10 Years in Korea
items.description: After a tumultuous week of corporate shake-ups at Netflix, Ted Sarandos traveled to Seoul over the weekend to celebrate one of the streamer’s clearest success stories of the past decade: its big bet on Korean entertainment.
items.author: Patrick Brzeski
paragraphs: After a tumultuous week of corporate shake-ups at Netflix, Ted Sarandos traveled to Seoul over the weekend to celebrate one of the streamer’s clearest success stories of the past decade: its big bet on Korean entertainment.

The Netflix co-CEO joined a massive two-day fan event the company organized at Sangam Oil Tank Culture Park, a former petroleum storage depot converted into a cultural complex in western Seoul. The visit came days after Netflix replaced chief content officer Bela Bajaria with Peter Rice and announced layoffs affecting roughly 1,000 employees — but the mood in Korea was purely celebratory.

Dubbed “Netflix Janchi,” the festivities attracted more than 10,000 local fans with themed activity booths, interactive games, company merchandise, live music and appearances from the stars of Netflix’s best-known Korean titles. The event’s online broadcasts drew an additional 3.58 million cumulative views.

Sarandos took the stage Saturday to share his appreciation for the Korean creative community and personally preview Netflix’s forthcoming slate, including local filmmaking legend Lee Chang-dong’s Oscar contender Possible Love, the upcoming K-drama Tantara and highly anticipated series including Grand Galaxy Hotel, She, Wolf, All of Us Are Dead Season 2 and the live-action adaptation of anime phenomenon Solo Leveling.

“Ten years ago, we dreamed big, but none of us could have imagined that Korean stories would move hearts around the world, and land right at the center of global culture,” Sarandos said. “For Netflix, Korea is more than a market. It is where we discovered new possibilities, and where we learned how far a story can travel. And it is one of our most treasured partners for the future we are building together.”

To further mark the occasion, Netflix released a slew of data from its service showing just how bankable Korean content has become. According to the streamer, Korean programming is now its most-watched non-English-language content category, with more than 80 percent of Netflix members worldwide having watched at least one Korean title. Since the company began tracking its global Top 10 rankings in June 2021, more than 200 Korean titles have appeared on the charts.

The three seasons of Squid Game occupy the top three spots on Netflix’s all-time most-watched non-English television list, while this year’s Korean hit Teach You a Lesson recently joined the ranking at No. 10. Korean productions generated more than 12 billion viewing hours on Netflix between April 2025 and March 2026 — second only to U.S. content by country of origin.

Korean stars came out in force to support Netflix’s first-decade milestone. Squid Game favorites Lee Jung-jae, Lee Byung-hun and Park Hae-soo took the stage to reminisce about the show’s unprecedented global success, while KPop Demon Hunters voice star Ahn Hyo-seop took a moment in the spotlight, as did D.P. stars Koo Kyo-hwan and Jung Hae-in. The event also featured cast members from Netflix hits including Hellbound, Mask Girl, Culinary Class Wars and The Trauma Code: Heroes on Call, among others.

The company’s preview of its upcoming Korean slate brought another wave of shiny K-content favorites. Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung and Cho Yeo-jeong appeared in support of Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love, which won the Silver Lion Grand Jury Prize at Venice and is set to debut globally on Netflix on Nov. 6. And Song Hye-kyo, Gong Yoo and Kim Seol-hyun introduced Tantara, a period drama set against the Korean entertainment industry of the 1960s through the 1980s, which premieres Dec. 11.

Other upcoming projects highlighted by Sarandos included supernatural fantasy Grand Galaxy Hotel, starring Lee Do-hyun and Shin Si-a; She, Wolf, with Kim Min-ju, Lomon and Moon Sang-min; and the second season of Netflix’s zombie blockbuster All of Us Are Dead, whose cast members Park Ji-hu, Yoon Chan-young, Cho Yi-hyun and Lomon were present. Rising Korean leading man Byeon Woo-seok also appeared to introduce the much-anticipated live-action Solo Leveling, in which he plays protagonist Sung Jin-woo (release dates for those four titles have yet to be announced).

While a creative rethink is underway at the world’s largest streamer, the Seoul anniversary celebration demonstrated that at least one tenet of Netflix’s global content strategy is unlikely to change: the centrality of Korean entertainment.

items.title: ‘Clayface’ Rolls to $24M Box Office Opening as ‘You Can See Everything’ Shines in Second Weekend
items.description: Clayface made its mark in its opening weekend at the box office as the Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything continued to build on its momentum with an impressive sophomore frame.
items.author: Ryan Gajewski
paragraphs: Clayface made its mark in its opening weekend at the box office as the Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything continued to build on its momentum with an impressive sophomore frame.

Warner Bros. released director James Watkins’ body-horror feature Clayface in more than 3,400 North American theaters, and it grossed around $24 million domestically for the weekend. While just under the studio’s initial projection of $25 million to $30 million, this represents a solid result for the genre offering from DC Studios that carries a modest $44 million budget. It added $19 million from 76 international markets.

Thanks to the lean budget, this is a more promising result for DC Studios than its previous release, as Supergirl struggled in opening to $37.1 million domestically over the summer on a $170 million budget. Clayface centers on a Batman villain that has not previously been a household name for general audiences and, though not matching the level of opening for a typical superhero feature, is well-positioned to ultimately hit a profit through ancillary markets, according to FranchiseRe. It was made more affordably than some of the villain and antihero spinoff films in recent years, including Venom: The Last Dance ($51 million launch on a reported $120 million production budget) and Kraven the Hunter ($11 million opening weekend on a $110 million budget), both Sony releases from 2024.

Audiences and critics alike found Clayface worthy of smiles, as it earned an A- CinemaScore while holding a 75 score from reviewers on Rotten Tomatoes and a 94 from audiences. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter, critic Frank Scheck called Clayface “a big swing that definitely pays off.” Tom Rhys Harries and Naomi Ackie star in the story of Matt Hagen (Harries), an actor who turns to a scientist (Ackie) for assistance when his face becomes disfigured.

You Can See Everything went wide Friday in its second weekend and built on its hot opening, collecting $19.5 million from 2,600 North American locations to bring its domestic sum to $45.1 million. The A24 film, which has been the focus of awards buzz, becomes the rare title to gross more in its second weekend than its first — with a 25 percent increase over its initial frame — and gives the studio the second-biggest weekend for a documentary since Fahrenheit 9/11′s $23.9 million in the summer of 2004.

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim‘s three-hour movie about disgraced Theranos founder Holmes expanded after opening with $15 million from 855 theaters domestically, which gave it the highest-grossing launch for a release under 1,000 theaters since 2006’s Borat. After being made in secret over three years, You Can See Everything continues to reap success from its marketing that plays up the mystery surrounding the project that audiences adore, as it holds a 98 percent critics score on Rotten Tomatoes and a 96 percent score from audiences.

Overall, the weekend saw a collected sum of $94,912,775 for the domestic marketplace, which is down 11.2 percent from last weekend but up 21.8 percent over the equivalent frame in 2025, according to Rentrak. This puts the 2026 domestic box office at an estimated $8.36 billion through Sunday, which is up 20.2 percent over the same point last year.

Taking third place is Laika’s stop-motion animated movie Wildwood, expected to clear around $11.6 million for the weekend. This would represent a notable start for the independent original animated film that sees Fathom Entertainment handling distribution, and it nearly doubles the opening of Laika’s previous release when Missing Link debuted with $5.9 million in 2019. However, Wildwood, which has earned Oscar buzz, carries a hefty reported production budget of $100 million, giving the film a high bar for profitability that may be tough to cross.

Carey Mulligan, Peyton Elizabeth Lee and Jacob Tremblay lead the voice cast for Travis Knight’s feature about a teen girl venturing to an enchanted forest to save her baby brother. Earning an A CinemaScore, Wildwood holds a dazzling 100 percent approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes and a 97 from audiences, with Scheck heralding it as “stupendous in every aspect.”

After winning the box office battle last weekend, Paramount and Legendary’s Street Fighter landed $8.6 million with a roughly 72 percent decline to move its domestic cume to $46.9 million. Noah Centineo, Andrew Koji and Callina Liang lead director Kitao Sakurai’s adaptation of the Capcom video game centering on a combat tournament.

Rounding out the top five is Black Bear’s romantic fantasy Wicker, which is expected to open with $5.5 million from 1,471 North American theaters. Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgard star in directors Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer’s movie about a woman in a quiet village who gets a wicker husband.
In his review for THR, critic Richard Lawson praised Wicker’s “winning mix of irreverence and compassion.” It holds a 94 score on Rotten Tomatoes from both critics and audiences.

BTS fans came out with force to support BTS World Tour ‘Arirang’ in Buenos Aires: Live Viewing on Saturday. The three hour-plus live broadcast of the music group’s first performance in the capital of Argentina earned around $4.5 million from 1,020 North American theaters, giving it a likely sixth-place finish for Trafalgar Releasing.
