Having trouble rising to the occasion was Sony Pictures’ Klara and the Sun, with director Taika Waititi‘s film opening outside the top 10 with a gross around $725,000 for the weekend. The studio had dialed back the release with only 880 North American locations for the title that stars Jenna Ortega and Amy Adams. It adapts Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel about a robot companion connecting with a sick girl, with THR chief film critic David Rooney deeming the feature a “wretched mess.”
Additionally, Amazon MGM Studios released Sacha Baron Cohen’s Ali G: Who Iz I? in just 125 theaters on only Friday and Saturday ahead of its Prime Video debut and did not report grosses.

Netflix’s Oscar hopeful La Bola Negra screened in nine North American locations in its second weekend, notching $245,000 for an average of $27,222 per screen. This brings the domestic total to $650,104 for directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvowith’s movie that explores queer identity over three timelines and stars Guitarricadelafuente and Miguel Bernardeau.

This weekend was a pleasing one across the board, but the positive vibes won’t last forever, as the studios avoid new releases next weekend with Halloween falling on a Saturday. After that, such options as The Cat in the Hat, Godzilla Minus Zero and Wild Horse Nine are waiting in the wings for a Nov. 6 release.
This story was first published on Oct. 24 at 8:56 a.m.

items.title: The Real-Life Diet of Bijan Robinson, Who Runs on an Underwater Treadmill
items.description: In the third quarter of a recent Sunday Night Football game, Falcons running back Bijan Robinson took a handoff from quarterback Michael Penix Jr. and added another magnificent entry to his already considerable highlight reel. While running a stretch play to h
items.author: Jake Kring-Schreifels
paragraphs: In the third quarter of a recent Sunday Night Football game, Falcons running back Bijan Robinson took a handoff from quarterback Michael Penix Jr. and added another magnificent entry to his already considerable highlight reel. While running a stretch play to his left, Robinson cut inside toward Ravens cornerback Marlon Humphrey, who sized up an easy tackle for a modest gain. That is, until a split-second later, when the running back planted his right foot back into the turf, juked hard outside, and left Humphrey on skates, flailing for his jersey. Across the field, all wide receiver Drake London could do was shake his head and cackle at his teammate’s unfair agility.

The play was a small window into the freak athleticism the 24-year old Robinson is capable of unleashing every time he touches the ball. And so far this season, he has lived up to the expectations of his exponentially-growing gifts, allowing fantasy owners to revel in his inevitable production and laugh at their weekly opponents like London. As the engine of an otherwise inconsistent Atlanta offense, Robinson is averaging over 100 rush yards per game and on pace to amass career highs in total yards and touchdowns—enough to enter him into the early MVP discussion.

Indeed, there is plenty to smile about for Robinson, especially now that he’s using Invisalign to straighten his teeth. It’s just one of several decisions he’s recently made about his health as he contends with the punishing reality of being an elite NFL running back. It was only six years ago that he avoided disaster after a terrifying mid-air collision while at Texas that jeopardized his neck and spine. That’s partially why since entering the NFL, Robinson has worked with the Falcons training staff to build a meticulous gameplan for his strength and conditioning to set himself up for success. “They’re very intentional throughout the week on how I need to be used leading up to the game,” Robinson says. “They’re very specific on what's needed and how I can grow my body and how I get stronger, faster—everything.”

Below, Robinson details more of that work, including the recovery tips he learned from running back Christian McCaffrey, the supplements he takes before bed, and his go-to Taco Bell order when he’s fixing for a quick meal.

Bijan Robinson: Yeah, I feel great right now. Everything that I’ve been doing for my recovery up to this point and from previous seasons has been pretty cool. I’ve been taking care of my body every single week. It’s cool to have the guys at the facility recommend people to me. I’ve been using this guy, Dr. T. He’s a chiropractor, and he does cupping and all types of stuff. But to see how much it's enhanced compared to last year and the year before—and all the resources that I have now to sustain the optimal level of performance on the field—has been cool. I think now it’s about me getting the rookies into tip-top shape, because I know they've been having a long year, and they're trying to find their body routines. I’m just trying to help them out.

Yeah, it’s all the soreness, that lactic acid that gets built up in my system. I’m making sure that there's something that can release it and that I can just eliminate that soreness. Or if there's something going on in my shoulders that's super tight—that's something that just releases everything. And it's something that doesn't hurt, but you can feel the impact of your soreness. You can feel what's going on in whatever body part you have. So, cupping, needling, acupuncture—that will spark the jump in my muscle and release that soreness as fast as possible.

No, I've been doing it since my rookie year. I kind of stayed away from it in college. I just did more massage-based things at a facility in college. Even Hyperice, the Theragun, all that kind of stuff. But I think since entering the NFL, I've been really much bigger into the needling and cupping.

I would say my hips. My hips are always my source [of soreness], because I cut a lot. I do a lot of cutting, a lot of change direction, and that requires a lot of things in my hips. I think people think changing direction is more about your knees or your hamstrings and your lower back, but your hips are what controls everything up and everything on the lower half of your body. I have tighter hip sides. That's just how it works for me in my game. And then sometimes my shoulders are a little sore. But yeah, when I get out of bed, I’ve got to stretch my hips. It has always been the thing for me.

Yeah, so that'll be the off day. I'll do the cold tub and hot tub, and then I'll go in with the trainers, and they'll use the needles and cupping wherever I feel the most sore that week. It might change from week to week. And then, on a Tuesday, that's when Dr. T. will come and he'll do more of the chiropractic work. And then if something is bothering me or I want to loosen something out a little bit more, then he'll use one of his tools to remove it. That’s been something I've been doing this whole season, and it's been great for me.

Yeah, it's different, but not a big difference. The offseason is the more grueling, hard training. Everyday you’re doing things that just are abnormal—running hills, doing all types of change in direction. That's when the higher weights come in for lifting, squatting, and benching, because you're really preparing for a long season. That's why you want to train harder in the offseason. And then the season is more staying at that pace, where you're not going super heavy, you're not going super light, but you're more in the middle, maintaining strength in-season and not losing it.

You have to. I do a lot of core exercises during the week. And that's another thing. Your hips are your biggest thing, but then my core comes right after that. And your core operates everywhere in the upper body. It operates how you change your action, operates how you break tackles, and make people miss. You focus on one thing each day. Your upper body workouts—it's little movements in your shoulders, in your lower back, your core. And then on that Wednesday is when we focus all on the lower body and making sure that you're not just adding weight, adding strength, but stretching your Achilles, your feet, to operate at the highest level.

Sometimes you can do everything at once, but I don't think that's the best way to go about it. I think you should focus one day on the upper body. That's on Mondays. Give your body a rest on Tuesday. And then on Wednesdays, that's when you attack the lower body.

That's every day. I go into the training room and we'll do ankle exercises—just mobility, making sure that my ankles aren't stiff. A lot of people have stiff ankles because they don't stretch them out much. We do bands, a lot of heel lifts, and then balancing on one ankle, on both ankles, on the BOSU ball and the little balance circuit that we have. It only takes five minutes to do it. But those little things add up.
I started this in high school. But it got more elevated in Texas because they had so much more equipment. And then in the NFL, we’ve just kept on that same process. It’s been good.

Yeah, the pool is the biggest thing. He and I did water recovery with the cold tub, hot tub, the HydroWorx with the treadmill in the pool. All those things really enhanced my recovery plan. We did that every single day. After a hard workout, we would go in the pool, and we would do these pool recovery workouts that help your blood flow. Ever since, I've been doing it with him, I've been at the facility and we have the HydroWorx now. Doing that HydroWorx has been key after games because of all that soreness that's been built up. You want to release it as fast as possible the next day.

It just depends. After a workout, you typically want to do hot tub first to release it a little bit, and then go to the cold tub, then you go to the hot tub again, and then you'll go to the cold tub to finish it off.

So you're doing karaokes, high knees, a slight jog, but people really don't want to do that after a game. I've had to teach my mind, like, “This is what's gonna help when the game's over.” It'll take about 15 minutes, but you're really running in the pool. During the process, you're like, “Man, why am I doing this? I just played a game, I don't wanna do this.” But then when it's over, you feel great. It’s been a great thing for me.

So, I have a hyperbaric chamber at my house. But the hypobaric chamber, the Stratosphere that me and McCaffrey were doing in LA, that thing is unbelievable. I haven't done it since we trained together, but it's pretty special.
Oh no, I definitely want one. But you need somebody to control it for you. When I can figure that out, and if they can come out here and help me do it, I'm gonna do it. Those things are great.

So, you're going 18,000 feet in the air—and you get there in, like, five, six seconds. It's pretty unbelievable. But that form of recovery is great. And then you can [ride] the [stationary] bike in there. You can exercise in there. And then that just enhances it even more.

Yeah. In your blood flow, and definitely in your brain oxygen. You feel it quickly. I think, a week into it, on the field, my breathing was unbelievable. Like, I was breathing, and feeling like, “I can run for days.” That's the biggest thing with that Stratosphere. I hope they get it into all teams, everywhere, because everybody needs it.

I don't have a specific diet, but I do stay away from fast foods. My girlfriend cooks everything. And she just does it for fun. I don't tell her to cook, but she just wants to do it. And then, I eat at the facility in the mornings and for lunch. I just make sure that all those foods are hand prepared, really cooked. I know fast food is great sometimes. I might cheat and just, like, go to Taco Bell or somewhere, but—

It's not really a cheat day. It's just more of a day where I want to grab something real quick. I do that very minimally. It's been a long time since I’ve actually had McDonald’s or something. But that's the biggest thing in the diet: home-cooked meals.
I'm gonna get five soft tacos, and then like, two cinnamon twists, and a Baja Blast Freeze.

I’m not a caffeine guy. The biggest thing that I've learned is drinking water out of glass. Like, I've really been drinking all my water out of glass. I haven't been drinking water out of plastic at all. Because, one: drinking water out of glass is the most healthy thing for your body. And then two: you make sure all the toxins in those plastic bottles that get built up in the water are out of your body.

We don't because we're sponsored by Smartwater, but I just bring one. We have filtered water in the facility. I'll have the glass bottle with me, and then I'll just pour it in the bottle. It's been great.

Yeah, so especially on those prime-time games, we get back home at 3 or 4 a.m. I’m making sure I'm sleeping on the plane if I can. That’s the biggest thing. The team does a really good job of giving us a sleep routine for when we should sleep and how many hours of sleep we should have, especially on short weeks. I have this bed where it'll heat your body or cool your body, and if it detects that you're sweating in your sleep, it'll make the bed cool. Our dietitian is a sleep master, too, so he'll give us all the right timings of when to sleep and how to sleep and the vitamins to take before sleep. Magnesium has been a huge thing for me before I go to bed. I take three or four tablets of magnesium and it really just helps my body out a lot.

Oh yeah, especially, on some of the prime-time games. You just think about it so much. And then you have all day to think about it. But yeah, some games you just struggle a little bit. That's why I try to get ready for bed at, like, 9:30, 10 p.m. I know if my body is thinking about it, then I’ll at least be asleep by 11 or so.

Yeah, I smile a lot, so it’s just about having that confidence, and when I talk to people, when I do interviews or commercial stuff, making sure that my teeth are at a very optimal level. Not having wires and brackets has really been the biggest thing for me. I started using the clear liners, and it's been great for me. It's been a month and you can already see a shift happening. That's what makes the partnership perfect for me. It just creates discipline in myself, making sure I'm wearing those 22 hours throughout the day.

[I just want to] make sure I'm executing at a high level at all facets—understanding the plan that we have for the week and making sure that our brand of football is being played at the highest level. It's important using the gifts that God gives me at a high level, but taking it one week at a time, taking the one game at a time, and knowing that I’ve gotta be at my best self for this opponent that's coming in. Or if we're going there, understanding what's at hand. That's how you become your best self. Not looking ahead, but just being where my feet are.

My girlfriend and I will go watch movies in theaters at the iPic. We try to go maybe once a week, once every other week. And it's a private theater, so it's really, really cool. We just saw Tony. I think that was a really good movie. And then I'll play video games with my teammates. We'll be on 2K, we'll be on FC, the soccer game. I'm starting to read a lot. I like audiobooks. My girlfriend and I were reading this neurological faith book about life, which has been super cool. And then I just got a cat. I got a Munchkin cat.

Her name is Moochies. So that's another thing I've been super involved with. And she's super small, super tiny. I do a lot of different things when I'm not so focused on football. I just continue to expand myself.

In Real-Life Diet, athletes, celebrities, and other high performers talk about their diet, exercise routines, and pursuit of wellness. Keep in mind that what works for them might not necessarily be healthy for you.

items.title: Meta’s Ad Sales Are Suffering Now That Europeans Can Pick Less Personalization
items.description: Meta’s advertising growth in Europe is slowing now that residents have the option for less of their personal data to influence what advertisements they see.
items.author: Isabella Ward
paragraphs: Meta’s advertising growth in Europe is slowing now that residents have the option for less of their personal data to influence what advertisements they see.

Advertising revenue in Europe continued to decelerate in the three months through September, the company said on Wednesday, underperforming its global figures. In the region, advertising revenue grew 18 percent year-on-year, slowing from the previous two quarters and lagging the 33 percent growth seen in the US and Canada.

Though Meta did not explicitly blame the introduction of the Less-Personalized Ads model on Wednesday, chief financial officer Susan Li had previously warned “we’re seeing the impact of less personalized ads offering in Europe now that it’s fully rolled out, and that may be an additional headwind,” in July’s second quarter results follow-up call. The preceding two quarters had seen advertising growth fall from around 40 percent to 24 percent; in the US and Canada, it had accelerated from 30 percent to 31 percent.

“We believe the EU’s free, personalized advertising option is contributing to the European slowdown,” Dominic Ball, equity research director at market analysis firm Rothschild & Co Redburn, told WIRED.

Meta began to offer Instagram and Facebook users the LPA option at the beginning of this year, after EU regulators ruled that it was breaching its Digital Markets Act obligation to give consumers the choice of an equivalent service that uses less of their personal data and hit the firm with a €200 million fine. Sales growth has slowed in the region since the start of the year, when Meta rolled out the option. The European Commission said that charging EU users who did not want their personal data used for personalized advertising for an ad-free service—a measure Meta introduced in the EU in November 2023—did not satisfy this. Meta does not disclose how many people have chosen each option.

LPA uses 90 percent less data than personalized ads, Meta says, with ads shown based on what a person sees in a particular session on the site, plus some data points like their age, location, and gender. It leads to poorer returns for EU advertisers, it warned in a response to the EU’s ruling. Less-personalized ads are less efficient, leading to fewer transactions, and more ads being closed due to being irrelevant or repetitive, it said. Indeed, the price advertisers were willing to pay per ad in Europe is not growing as fast as in the US and Canada, Wednesday’s results showed.

Li told investors on Wednesday the company has “a lot of runway” to increase ad conversions and efficiency, as it is “continuing to find ways to either enhance the actual performance of the recommendation engine.” Rothschild & Co Redburn’s Ball believes the company will be able to use AI to improve its ad targeting in Europe despite working with fewer personal data signals.

Investors were keen to understand how this fits into Meta’s personal AI agent, Muse, launched last month, questions about which dominated the call. Li said the company is seeing high commercial intent from people using Muse—asking for product recommendations, researching alternatives, and comparing options—which will allow them to eventually tap into the advertising market with that product.

items.title: Mark Zuckerberg Agrees to Stay in California Despite Billionaires’ Tax Ballot Measure
items.description: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has agreed to keep living in Silicon Valley for eight years, potentially exposing himself to billions of dollars in one-time taxes if California voters approve a contentious ballot measure next month, according to a company regulatory
items.author: Paresh Dave
paragraphs: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has agreed to keep living in Silicon Valley for eight years, potentially exposing himself to billions of dollars in one-time taxes if California voters approve a contentious ballot measure next month, according to a company regulatory filing released Wednesday.

During a dinner with Meta board members on September 9, Zuckerberg informed them that he was considering leaving California because of the measure, known as Proposition 40, and that he planned to list his Palo Alto, California, home for sale four days later, the 109-page filing stated. The ballot proposal, which could be subject to lawsuits even if voters approve it, calls for a one-time 5 percent tax on stock and other assets held by billionaires in the state as of January 2026.

Many wealthy individuals, including Zuckerberg, currently avoid significant tax payments by borrowing against their shares and taking low salaries—$1 annually in the Meta CEO’s case. Zuckerberg purchased a home in Florida this past February, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time.

His potential cross-country move concerned a special committee of the board, whose members included attorney Robert Kimmitt, venture capitalist Charlie Songhurst, and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu. “The special committee was mindful about the difficulties the company faced during the COVID-19 pandemic when Zuckerberg could not be physically present with the company’s management team and did not want the company to face similar challenges going forward,” according to Wednesday’s filing.

Within days of the Meta board dinner, the special committee and Zuckerberg reached an agreement that links his ability to sell special company shares to his continued residence in California. It was finalized a week ago, and on Wednesday, Meta announced the details. It plans to create a new class of shares that hold no voting power. Selling these shares could potentially help raise funds for Meta’s expensive investments in AI data centers, without diluting Zuckerberg’s existing voting control.

All existing shareholders will receive the new nonvoting shares automatically in proportion to their existing holdings. Under what Meta called a “Founder Alignment Agreement” with Zuckerberg, he can sell 20 percent of those new shares to help pay any taxes he may owe. The remaining 80 percent would be available for sale in chunks over the next eight years as long as he remains in California. Any attempt to sell them early would require offloading some of his voting shares “unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere.”

Notably, the agreement specifies that Zuckerberg merely has to remain wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, so it’s possible that both he and the company could move together to another state. A number of California companies have left for Texas, Nevada, and other states in recent years. Google cofounders Sergey Brin and Larry Page are among the handful of billionaires widely believed to have exited California over the potential tax.

But with much of the most pioneering AI development happening in Silicon Valley, leaving the city of Menlo Park could be a difficult proposition for the Meta board to stomach. “The goal is to keep Zuckerberg continuing to lead the company from California and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs,” the filing stated, referring to the company unit behind its recent Muse AI models.
In the end, the exercise may have been for naught. Recent polling in California suggests that with about $129 million spent campaigning against Prop 40, it will fail to muster enough votes.

items.title: Apple CarPlay and Android Auto Make Your Phone Hot. Here’s How to Keep It Cool
items.description: Android Auto and CarPlay have transformed the way people drive.
items.author: David Nield
paragraphs: Android Auto and CarPlay have transformed the way people drive.

Rather than putting up with whatever infotainment systems car manufacturers have put together, we're now able to interact with our phones from our car dashboards—with our contacts, our music, our podcasts, and our mapping apps all available. And the list of supported vehicles just keeps growing.

Both the Google and Apple solutions for this are really simple to use too. Most of the time they'll connect up automatically once you've done the initial setup. What you might not realize, though, are the demands that Android Auto and CarPlay put on your phone. Your handset is essentially doing all the regular phone stuff and then powering a large tablet-like display at the same time. That typically includes constantly updating a map in real time.

With that in mind, your Android phone or iPhone can quickly start to lose battery life and heat up when it's connected to your vehicle, which you've perhaps already noticed. To keep your handset cool and your battery in good shape, here's what you need to do.
Go Wired if You Can (but Watch the Charging)

Wireless Android Auto and CarPlay are convenient, just like wireless charging is convenient, but it puts more stress on your phone. If you've got the option of a wired connection, that's preferable—but that introduces a new potential heat problem, which is that your phone will always be charging up.
To counter that, you can set charge limits (Battery and charging from Android Settings, Battery > Charging from iOS Settings), or simply make sure your phone is kept in a cool, dark spot of the car.

This wired option has the added bonus of letting you switch to airplane mode on your phone, which will go a long way to limiting heat. Again there's a trade-off though: No one will be able to reach you, and you'll need to have your maps, music, podcasts, and whatever else you need downloaded to your device in advance.

If you do stick with wireless Android Auto or CarPlay, try to avoid charging your phone at the same time, especially on the wireless pad built into the car’s dash (which generates more heat). You don't want to end up with a dead phone half way through the journey, so you may have to compromise at certain times.
Think About Where Your Phone Is Placed

As mentioned above, where your phone is in the car makes a real difference to how hot it's going to be. If you have your phone's interface up on your car dashboard, then you don't necessarily need to have it fixed to the dashboard, too, possibly under direct sunlight. The glove compartment will do just fine.

If you have a mount for your phone, think about attaching it in front of one of your car's air vents. Blasts of air conditioned air will significantly reduce how hot your handset gets, working like a DIY cooling system.

You might also want to think about taking the case off of your phone for the length of the trip, if your phone is fitted with one. Your handset is less likely to be dropped or knocked while you're driving anyway, and a case can trap the heat in.

The rules aren't too different to keeping your phone cool generally, though with the added wrinkle of needing to keep it connected to your car somehow. Make sure the cabin in general is at a comfortable temperature, though you're probably already doing that for your own sake. The bigger thing to remember is to avoid leaving your phone behind in a vehicle that's going to heat up in the sun if you're stopping off somewhere.
Limit the Work Your Phone Has to Do

If your phone is hooked up to Android Auto or CarPlay, then it's probably got some work to do—whether it's getting you to a destination or streaming music. However, you can still reduce heat by keeping phone tasks down to a minimum. If your calls and (voice-activated) messages can wait, leave them until the end of the journey.

We mentioned offline syncing above, but it doesn't have to go along with airplane mode. If you sync your tunes, podcasts, and maps to your phone ahead of time, your handset has less work to do while you’re driving since it doesn’t need to pull data from the cloud while also constantly searching for a wireless signal as you travel. Less stress on the modem means less heat overall.

Both Apple Maps and Google Maps let you download maps ahead of a trip. In Apple Maps, tap your profile picture, then Offline Maps, then Add Offline Map and find your location. With Google Maps, tap your profile picture, then choose Offline maps > Select your own map to choose the coverage.

There may be times when your phone has to be charging, wirelessly connected, making calls, in direct sunlight, and streaming music over a cellular connection, but try to keep these times to a minimum. Check regularly on how hot your phone is getting while connected to Android Auto or CarPlay, so you can take action if needed.

items.title: We Linked 150 of Ikea’s $10 Speakers to Make a Wall of Sound
items.description: When Ikea launched its super-cheap $10 Bluetooth Kallsup speakers in April, aside from the rock-bottom price and bright, white/green/pink colors, the claim that really caught WIRED’s ear was that the Swedish furniture brand said it was possible to chain 100 of
items.author: Jeremy White; Chris Haslam
paragraphs: When Ikea launched its super-cheap $10 Bluetooth Kallsup speakers in April, aside from the rock-bottom price and bright, white/green/pink colors, the claim that really caught WIRED’s ear was that the Swedish furniture brand said it was possible to chain 100 of these 2.75-inch sonic cubes together, should you so wish.

Now, because it’s highly unlikely any one household will ever own more than a handful of mini Bluetooth speakers, this is one of those consumer-tech statements that rarely gets tested. So we asked the good folks at Älmhult in Ikea headquarters if they’d let us do just this. To our surprise, Ikea not only agreed, but it also upped the ante, saying it might be possible to link up to 150 without breaking the connection, so that’s exactly how many it sent us. “No one has ever tried this, though,” an Ikea spokesperson said. “We haven’t.”

That is how we ended up building a literal wall of sound at our London office, stacking 150 Kallsups carefully on top of one another to test how many would chain-play from a smartphone. Sadly, one casualty during shipping from Sweden—a single Kallsup—despite lighting up correctly and looking ready to chain, made an ominous rattling sound as if its innards weren’t entirely secure. Sure enough, it refused to play ball (or anything else), so we ended up with 149 speakers.

The chain process itself is simple. Once you have paired a single Kallsup with your music device—in our case, an iPhone 16 Pro—and it’s up and running, simply power on another cube while playing and hold down the Play button until a chime tells you it’s in “multi-speaker” mode. It should then immediately start playing whatever the Bluetooth-connected Kallsup is playing.

Thanks to this near-effortless chaining process, linking up all these Kallsups took much less time than we'd expected, about 30 minutes. We stopped at 100 to test how loud the “system” sounded at that stage before resuming the build and moving on to the maximum amount. As the music continued while we chained the speakers, it would be obvious when the collective refused to add more cubes. But this didn’t happen, and the plucky Kallsups joined forces without grumbling right up to the full 149.

It’s tempting to preface the next few paragraphs with the phrase “for a $10 speaker,” because, despite Ikea’s vast buying power, experienced research and development team, and global presence, the ability to produce a tiny speaker that doesn’t sound absolutely horrible for less than a pint of half-decent craft beer is pretty incredible.
Each Kallsup has a single 1.8-inch, full-range driver powered by a 3-watt amplifier, with Bluetooth 5.3 support. No separate tweeter or woofer, just the one tiny driver.

On its own, the Kallsup speaker sounds fine. Yes, it lacks anything resembling the deep rumbling bass people talk about in audio reviews, but did we mention it’s a $10 speaker? It is a bit tinny, and you won’t want to push the volume very hard, but as a little desktop speaker, one by the side of the bed, or to throw in a suitcase, the Kallsup does the job. It doesn’t match the performance of one of our best Bluetooth speaker recommendations, but keep the cost in mind, and it’s hard to be disappointed.

Even at low background volumes, the Kallsups worked surprisingly well together, especially playing acoustic tracks. As we paired more speakers, the sound gradually grew nicely in scale. Nothing was overpowering or dominating, just the cumulative effect of all those tiny drivers moving small amounts of air.

With 149 individual 1.8-inch drivers, the combined surface area is roughly equivalent to one enormous 22-inch driver. Each Kallsup also has its own 3-watt amplifier, giving our wall a combined rated output of 447 watts. That doesn’t mean it behaves like a giant subwoofer or a conventional 447-watt speaker, but it explains why things got so loud.

But before we turned these up, if you will, to 149, we listened at 100, and when we pushed the volume, the collective Kallsups were seriously loud. But for the record, loud like a fire alarm, not a hi-fi system. With the wall complete, we worried the collective vibrations might send the whole thing crashing down. Disappointingly for the socials, it stayed resolute. Instead, we played Trans Lunar by Twin Dimensions (WIRED director of consumer tech and culture Mike Calore’s excellent band) and slowly increased the volume to maximum.

We almost wish we hadn’t. The noise was brain-numbingly loud as we blasted, somewhat appropriately, Richard Strauss’ Also Sprach Zarathustra. We couldn’t hear each other speak, and we could feel our internal organs vibrating. Any sense of fidelity disappeared, but—all power to the Kallsups—it worked. We’d successfully linked 149 Bluetooth speakers, though sadly we’re well short of the world record of 1,500 speakers set by Majority Audio in March 2026.

At more modest, realistic volumes, everything sounded considerably more composed, even if the music lacked levels of depth and detail. The overall lack of clarity could also be due to minor timing differences between the individual drivers.

At $1,490, a wall of Kallsups is quite an investment, and not one we’re recommending, but it is extremely impressive that we managed to sync and play music wirelessly through so many small, cheap speakers.

We also tested the wall alongside WIRED’s choice for best overall party speaker, the $500 LG Xboom Stage 501. Cranked up, both reached similarly ear-splitting, frankly uncomfortable volumes. But with two 5.25-inch woofers, two 2.5-inch full-range drivers, and clever digital signal processing, the LG delivered understandably fuller, deeper bass and a considerably more musical experience, as expected.

What’s remarkable about this experiment is that so little went wrong. Only one of the 150 speakers shipped didn’t work, clearly broken in transit. We managed to get all 149 sound cubes chained easily and quickly. And when we weren’t blasting the wall of sound at max volume, instead keeping levels moderate, the speakers sounded surprisingly competent as a collective.

However, there were hints of the Kallsup chaining capacity reaching its limit, as Ikea suspected. As we got beyond 100 units linked together, the incidence of failing to chain on the first try increased. Still, no speaker refused more than twice as we got toward the end of the build.

We also would have preferred indentations on the tops of the speakers, which would have given us a bit more confidence that the whole stack wasn’t going to collapse in a heap as volume ramped up (which it didn’t). Such a simple design feature would help whether you’re dealing with just a couple placed on top of each other, let alone 149—but this is splitting hairs.

Lastly, although this setup was impressively loud, no one in their right mind would do this in their own home. Ikea has been a good sport letting us try this out, but the ultimate, unsurprising lesson is: If you want high-quality audio, spend your money on a better speaker. As for the Kallsup? Simple to use, easy to chain, with approachable sound and clean design. You really can’t ask much more for $10.

items.title: In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
items.description: Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.
items.author: Jessica Hamzelou
paragraphs: Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.

I went in not really knowing what to expect. I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!). I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given how familiar many of us are with the Theranos story thanks to years of media coverage, the best-selling book Bad Blood, and the Hulu series The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried.

Like many others who have seen the film, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the somewhat disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything.

In case you’re rusty on the details, Elizabeth Holmes dropped out of Stanford University in 2003 to run Theranos, a diagnostics company she founded, when she was just 19. She went on to claim that her company had invented a way to run over 100 diagnostic tests on just a few drops of blood.

Holmes raised hundreds of millions of dollars for Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion in 2014. Forbes named her the youngest self-made female billionaire—she was worth $4.5 billion when she was just 30 years old.

Things started to unravel in 2015, when an investigation by the Wall Street Journal raised concerns by former Theranos employees that the tests didn’t work. Some also said that the company’s device had not been tested properly, and that blood samples had been analyzed on machines from other companies instead. MIT Technology Review named it one of the biggest technology failures of 2015.

Forbes had revised Holmes’s worth to $0 by 2016. That year, a damning government report said that the company’s lab was struggling with basic procedures and gave patients results even when they knew they could be wrong.

In 2018, Theranos, Holmes, and former company president Ramesh Balwani were charged with “massive fraud.” In 2022, she was sentenced to a little over 11 years in prison for defrauding investors. She began serving her sentence in May 2023.

It was around a month before this that filmmakers Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, and their colleagues began documenting Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, at home with their two young children. I’m not giving anything away when I say it’s an extremely intimate portrayal—at least of how the two adults interact with Fielder, who is also a central character in the film.

As you might know if you’ve seen the trailer, there are plenty of super close-ups. I felt as if I spent most of the film staring straight into the faces of those people. And almost the whole way through, they all seemed to be trying to figure each other out. Holmes is known for her dishonesty, but she invited cameras into her home in an apparent bid to reframe the narrative and position herself as an honest person with an unusual mind. Will anyone believe her?

I couldn’t help feeling some empathy for Holmes, a mother we see preparing to leave her two kids for a lengthy prison sentence. And even though I have long known the facts, Holmes is clearly an effective manipulator. You can see her plant the seeds of doubt in Fielder’s mind. At times, I felt she was convincing me, sitting in my cinema seat. Maybe she really didn’t mean to lie?

But then I remembered how other journalists felt after being taken in by her claims. “I blew it,” Fortune’s Roger Parloff reflected in 2015, a year after profiling Holmes and her company. “I’m pretty sure she lied to me,” STAT’s Matthew Herper wrote recently, having interviewed Holmes in 2015. Even the former employee turned whistleblower Tyler Shultz, who knew the product didn’t work, said that he could “have a five-minute conversation with her and walk away feeling like my work was changing the world,” he said in 2022.
I didn’t cover Theranos in the 2010s. If I’d interviewed Holmes, would I have fallen for it all?

One of the early red flags in the Theranos case was the lack of published, peer-reviewed data. Much of the company’s work was classified as a “trade secret.” Scientists tend to publish their work in journals—a slow process that involves having the work evaluated by often anonymous experts in the field, who provide feedback, highlight questionable conclusions, and often ask for clarification. Peer review is meant to add rigor to the publication process. You should be able to trust published scientific papers.
Except that sometimes you can’t.

Scientists aren’t perfect. Some will exaggerate their results or inflate their importance. Some manipulate data to serve a hypothesis. Sometimes these infractions are caught during peer review, but not always. There are plenty of examples of scientific findings that could never be replicated by other labs and ended up collapsing under the weight of real evidence. Many papers ultimately end up with corrections. Some are withdrawn—10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023.

At any rate, there’s been a shift to sharing research in other ways. Today, many scientists opt to publish their work at preprint servers like arXiv, medRxiv, and bioRxiv before they submit them to established journals. Those outlets bypass peer review. So do company press releases, social media posts, and many conference presentations. And I get a lot of my stories from conversations and interviews.
I’ll admit I’ve looked at a scientific finding and thought: A scientist has just said they’ve done that. How can I be sure they really have?

I like to think that I hold myself to high journalistic standards here, as does everyone at MIT Technology Review. I would never publish a story about some new scientific development without doing my own form of peer review, and asking scientists—ideally people I know and trust—what they think of a new claim.

But the film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative. While most scientists are, I hope, pretty honest, and Holmes is certainly an outlier, we should all continue to interrogate the claims being fed to us. If you’ve seen the film, let me know what you think!
This article first appeared in The Checkup, MIT Technology Review’s weekly biotech newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Thursday, and read articles like this first, sign up here.

items.title: Drake Is Ready for Christian-Girl Autumn
items.description: Happy 40th-birthday weekend to Drake, who rang in the big four-oh early with a dinner in New York Thursday night. In doing so, the Scorpio debuted a new alter ego: autumnal auntie on a GNO.
items.author: Emma Childs
paragraphs: Happy 40th-birthday weekend to Drake, who rang in the big four-oh early with a dinner in New York Thursday night. In doing so, the Scorpio debuted a new alter ego: autumnal auntie on a GNO.

Drake faced the crisp October nighttime air in black leather pants, a black crewneck sweatshirt, and a Frappuccino-colored suede shawl trimmed with fringe. It’s the type of outerwear you’d find in a Christian-Girl Autumn starter pack — a coat whose owner would throw punches for Rae Dunn at HomeGoods and has pumpkin-spice season marked on the calendar. A video posted on X shows the Toronto rapper walking into the Soho restaurant Mamo holding the buttery fabric tight around his shoulders, “When will my husband return from war?” style.

Naturally, Drake’s choice of outerwear on his birthday outing has made it a fruitful morning on the internet. “I know that’s right pashmina papi,” one Instagram commenter wrote. “Ok Auntie splurged at @kohls with this one!” and “Housewives of Texas I see you,” chimed in others. Here at The Cut, we thought about that Selena Gomez meme and started manifesting for Drake to star in a Nancy Meyers movie. “I see him as the new neighbor who just moved from a big city to a toney enclave and is clueless about homeownership and through that forges a beautiful bond with a group of 60-plus-year-old women on the block,” head of social Lucia Tonelli spitballed.

You know what? I enjoy Drake’s fringed birthday shawl. X sleuths later discovered it’s a vintage Hermès shawl, sourced by stylist Juliet Charlotte. (Because, duh; Champagne Papi is a bougie diva). The man’s a known fashion risk-taker, too — who could forget his denim Chanel lederhosen from Oktoberfest last year? — and I always support one’s journey of self-expression by way of style experimentation. Plus it seems Drake’s just a blanket-coat type of guy: Back in 2014, he layered an off-runway Chanel poncho over a “Hotline Bling”–themed groutfit. It’s his birthday; he’ll shawl if he wants to.

items.title: The Woman Giving Lap Dances All Night
items.description: This week, a woman’s crush talks to another dancer while she decides how to school him: 35, single, NYC
items.author: Alyssa Shelasky
paragraphs: This week, a woman’s crush talks to another dancer while she decides how to school him: 35, single, NYC

9:10 a.m. I keep my phone on Do Not Disturb for two hours as I drink coffee, burn palo santo, and finish Play It As It Lays. I’ve been separated for over a year. The divorce has taken a while due to my ex dragging his feet on paperwork. We were married for 12 years until I discovered he’d had a string of girlfriends throughout our relationship.

Noon Phone interview for a health-care job, which would be an industry change — I’m a stripper. A day job sounds draining, but I don’t want to run through my savings. The interview goes well. The manager’s passing me through to the next round.

2 p.m. Lie in bed watching The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City. I love these women. Then I pack my work bag: eight-inch Pleasers, blackberry Uncrustable, three outfits separated in baggies, water bottle, deodorant, phone charger, garters, purse for the floor. That purse contains rubber bands, gum, lip liner, lipstick, travel size of my perfume, and a tampon.
5:40 p.m. Check in with the club’s manager for my stage set time. Hurry to get ready because I’m going up on the hour, my favorite.

5:58 p.m. David texts asking when I’m free before he leaves for Asia for a month. We’ve hooked up weekly for five months. “Hooking up” doesn’t do our marathon sex justice. He’s sexy, exactly my size, and consistent. When we met on Hinge, we agreed to keep it casual. Surprisingly enough, it worked. If I ever get a boyfriend, I hope I’m allowed to keep David. I text back options.
7:32 p.m. Lucky catches me up on her romantic life. We started in the same month, then bonded over club dynamics and dating while working as strippers.

11:27 p.m. The club’s slow. Usually when there are no customers, I stretch and read, but I’m kicking myself — I didn’t bring a book. Scroll Reddit and think about who to text to come in and see me. Mentally willing the night to turn around.
2:12 a.m. Can’t bear it any longer. Ask my manager if I can leave early. He’s surprised I didn’t ask earlier. Cash out and throw on sweats. Leftover mac ’n’ cheese calls my name.

3 p.m. Drag myself out of bed. When I work back-to-back nights, I’m only capable of sleep, dance, repeat. Notice an Amazon package: rhinestones, boric-acid suppositories, and floss picks. Last week, I went to three stores for rhinestones before realizing it’s too close to Halloween. I despise Bezos, but I love glitter outfits.
5:40 p.m. Stop into Dunkin’ for an iced tiramisu latte and a sprinkle-frosted strawberry donut. I need the energy.

7:43 p.m. Spot John down the bar. Saunter over. Saunter sounds cheesy, but that’s what I do, smiling and slowly adjusting the waistband of my panties. Men go crazy for that. I win them over before I get there. John never buys dances but will stuff your outfit with singles if he likes you. He likes me because I’m quick-witted and can talk shit. I rotate in front of him like a rotisserie. He shoves bills in my panties, then each triangle of my bikini top. It’s worth being felt up if he takes multiple trips to the ATM. He likes when I walk him over to the cash machine, but he’s touchy about money. You can’t directly ask. He tells me to clear out my outfit so he can stuff it again. We do this for about an hour. I’ve always found making money sexy, so this job is exhausting but fun.

11:52 p.m. I send Mark, an infatuated customer, my schedule every week. He texts that he’ll visit Thursday. Recently, he asked to see me outside the club. I’m trying to decide what that means in terms of payment, work, and my patience.
11:59 p.m. Lap dance, giggle, flirt. Nothing memorable happens, which is good.

2:59 a.m. Ben texts asking if I’m working. He’s a pro skater I met at a bar. We see each other every few months for a little date and hookup. Last week, he came to the club and it was kind of a disaster. On top of not buying me a drink or spending any money on me, he groped my ass and told me I needed to find a real job. I haven’t decided whether I’ll ghost him or write out a long message about how rude he was (not to mention he’s never gone down on me). I firmly believe men don’t read long texts. It only embarrasses the writer. I don’t respond.
3:30 a.m. Home. I’ll sleep well knowing I made enough money to make up for yesterday. I’m trying to save, but a Marc Jacobs bag is calling me, as is a flight to San Francisco for a girls’ weekend.

Noon This is my first week without therapy after my insurance ran out. I call my other therapist, my mom. I haven’t told her I’m dancing, so it’s difficult to describe what I do during the week. I’m pretty sure she thinks I’m depressed.

12:30 p.m. Trek to Williamsburg to buy Uniqlo culottes, then Castelvetrano olives and 365 brand pretzels from Whole Foods. I’m wearing new boots that give me massive blisters; I’m dressed too warmly. Buy a T-shirt to change into. My mood improves, but RIP to my ankles.

6:20 p.m. Meeting friends at a bar. I’m nervous — I kissed the bartender earlier this year, then we stopped talking. (I have a thing for bartenders.) Nothing ended badly, but I’m uninterested in the awkward “Hiiii, how are you?” Duck in, see he isn’t working, order an old-fashioned, read by candlelight until my friends arrive. The bar’s cash only, so I cover our three rounds.
11:20 a.m. Buying Band-Aids for mutilated ankles.
7:56 p.m. Mark texts: He’s coming in. Yes! I love when customers stop by just for me. It means great money.

9:15 p.m. Getting my phone out to send Mark an ass photo when he walks in. He buys me a tequila soda and gets three lap dances. He massages my thighs while I grind on him. I make sure to tell him it feels like heaven so he keeps doing it. By the end of the night, my thighs could give out. A customer once asked if they’re rock hard because of muscle or knots. Thankfully muscle.

9:40 p.m. Between dances, Mark and I talk about Emma Cline’s The Guest. I read it quickly last week after he mentioned it; I invest in repeat customers. We exchange theories about what happened to the protagonist after the book’s end.

10:10 p.m. Get offstage after a set and start walking over to Mark. Star intercepts him; they talk. I’m pissed and sulking that he’s not acting like he’s there for me. I sit looking at my phone, stewing. Time is money. Try to decide if I should talk to someone else or wait it out.

10:41 p.m. Still waiting on Mark. Check my emails. One from my lawyer: My divorce is final. Text my friends those Nicole Kidman photos feeling minorly relieved, like when you cross an errand off your to-do list. When I’ve been severely wronged, I sever ties easily. I like that about myself.

11:12 p.m. Finish another stage set. Mark looks like a little boy who knows he misbehaved. I ask if he wants to hang out with me or other dancers. We get into a discussion about how he has a crush on me, is embarrassed other dancers know him, and only wants to spend time with me. He buys three more dances.

11:45 p.m. Mark wants to define our relationship, but I’m still annoyed. Unspoken club etiquette: Him conversing with another dancer shows he’s open to spending on other girls. I flirt along, hold his hand, and talk about movies we want to see.
12:55 a.m. Tell Mark to head home. During my next set, I need to make money off customers who still have full wallets. This sounds predatory, but I’m at work.

3:45 a.m. Shower and shove an Uncrustable into my mouth. One of the best things about dancing is the heavy calories you can pack in for energy: pizza rolls, Pop-Tarts, grilled cheese. A downside: I am nocturnal and can’t settle into sleep right away. I watch Law & Order to bore myself into drifting off.
4:30 a.m. Send my friend a voice note recapping my night. I call these “Tales From the Strip.”

10:30 a.m. Call Dad and sing “Happy Birthday” obnoxious opera style. He lets me finish before telling me he’s at Home Depot and I’m on speaker. I think he’s lying, but he sounds amused. I tell him about the divorce being finalized and he congratulates me. My dad likes to hear news before my mom. It makes him feel special. (I immediately call my mom after.)
3:42 p.m. David texts confirming tomorrow night. He’s not drinking so will come right over. Efficient!

5 p.m. Two-hour dance workshop in the city. My body’s exhausted, but I commit to dancing for myself at least once a week. The instructor lends me a ball to roll out a major knot in my calf from wearing heels so much.

8 p.m. Walk to a bar with friends. I met the bartender a few weeks ago at the club. It was his birthday; we hit it off. He told me I should swing by sometime, so this is me swinging. This is the first time I’ve been open to meeting a guy out of the club. Call it a dancer’s intuition, but it’s easy to discern who has a strip-club addiction and who goes for a special occasion. I’d never date a strip-club regular.

8:15 p.m. We see Bartender Eric, who says hi. My friends and I quietly toast my divorce so Eric doesn’t overhear. He comps two rounds and shots. We chat and realize we live very close to each other. He asks me to dinner. I give him my number and real name.

9:30 p.m. My friends leave. Eric sits on the barstool next to mine and holds my hand, asking what music I like and where I grew up. I’m at risk of kissing him at his workplace, so it’s time to go. Outside, we hug in front of his smoking co-workers.

10 p.m. Home posting my workshop videos to Stories. I dislike social media, but it’s important to stay connected to my dance community. I don’t let men follow me until we sleep together. I’ve had lurkers who never text me but instantly watch Stories of me dancing — ew.

10:30 p.m. Eric texts proposing a restaurant and time. He’ll walk to pick me up, then we’ll take a car to dinner. Maybe this will go somewhere. I haven’t had a second date in months, which is damaging my self-confidence. I can’t blame my looks … The issue must boil down to my personality.
10:10 a.m. Mark sends a photo of the book he’s reading. Decide to make him wait. Texting back inconsistently makes him respond faster.

2:45 p.m. Walk to the local diner with just-okay food. Order a veggie burger with cheese, fries, coffee, and a Bloody Mary. I could drink tomato juice all day. Read Lisa Taddeo’s Animal while I wait for my food, which is actually excellent today.

8:22 p.m. David arrives. He asks for a seltzer. I ask him to get in bed to warm me up. I keep my apartment cold but kept the windows open for too long today. Under my covers, he tells me about his week. Then a constant stream of kissing and touching. I’m on top, sliding his dick hot-dog-bunned between my ass cheeks. It’s sexy. I don’t question it. I love sex with David because there’s no judgment. Things get weird; we discover what feels good, then do it until our legs get too tired and we have to switch.

11:27 p.m. David and I have an unspoken mutual agreement that he doesn’t spend the night. I enjoy his company, but sleeping over’s too intimate. Before he leaves, I tell him I’ll miss him while he’s traveling, which is true.

11:30 p.m. I inhale everything in my fridge: a handful of shredded cheese, lemon-dill hummus, pretzels. Take magnesium and tuck myself in. It’s a new moon, and my astrology app told me to manifest what I want in relationships, so I try and figure that out before falling asleep.

10:24 a.m. I continue with Animal. It’s not lost on me that I’ve been reading a lot about sex workers. My next book is Larry McMurtry’s Lonesome Dove, recommended by several people, so I have high hopes. It’s nice to have something to look forward to.

1:55 p.m. Text my friends a draft of a message to Mark about him talking to other dancers. The tone is serious and sets boundaries (not my strength), but I think it’s too long and finger-wagging. They agree it’s not going to be effective. We brainstorm via voice notes. We conclude I should come across as flirty, not mention money, and keep trying to get him to come in to see me. I’m selling “fantasy girl who never gets annoyed” even though I’m consistently irked by men.

2:26 p.m. Instead of the workshopped text, I write Mark, “Since you showed me yours, I’ll show you mine,” with a photo of Animal. He replies right away saying he can’t wait to hear about it. Ugh. I’ll send the other text later.
3 p.m. Get ready listening to Dame Atlas.

4:30 p.m. Meet a friend for martinis and fries before we see Silence of the Lambs. We discuss the merits of dating an ugly man if he has money and is nice, then get into the different tiers of attractiveness. We settle on highest to lowest: gorgeous, sexy, hot, attractive, not ugly, ugly. We agree you never go for gorgeous but ideally land someone in the sexy-to-attractive range.

8:04 p.m. Walk to another bar after the movie. We smoke Chinese cigarettes and text our friend working a pop-up queer strip club about how it’s going. Conversation turns to how Pride & Prejudice (Keira Knightley version) and Silence of the Lambs are perfect movies. We laugh like maniacs over getting chills during P&P scenes we love. We both have obnoxious laughs — and we’re cheap laughs at that, so it becomes a cackle session.

9:13 p.m. Text Mark, “I want you to come in this week, but selfishly, I don’t want to share you with other dancers.” Sexy, flirty, making him feel wanted, and conveying my point. I don’t tell him when my shifts are. This way, he has to reply.
