items.title: Alex Winter Explains How He Brought Humanity to a Predator in 'Primetime'
items.description: On Nov. 5, 2006, as a camera crew from NBC’s hit tabloid news show To Catch a Predator descended upon his house alongside a seven-man SWAT team, Texas District Attorney Bill Conradt committed suicide with a Browning .380 pistol. He’d been communicating online
items.author: Andy Greene
paragraphs: On Nov. 5, 2006, as a camera crew from NBC’s hit tabloid news show To Catch a Predator descended upon his house alongside a seven-man SWAT team, Texas District Attorney Bill Conradt committed suicide with a Browning .380 pistol. He’d been communicating online and via telephone with someone he thought was a 13-year-old boy but was actually an adult working for the vigilante group Perverted Justice. The incident sparked a major lawsuit, and led directly to NBC’s decision to forever pull the plug on To Catch a Predator.

It also serves as the climax of the Lance Oppenheim movie Primetime, where Robert Pattinson embodies the role of To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen in such eerie fashion that a Best Actor Oscar nomination is almost a guarantee.

Joining Pattinson in the movie is an unlikely team of actors, including onetime NBC head Jeff Zucker, former child star Jonathan Lipnicki, The Office‘s Creed Bratton, and indie-rock star Phoebe Bridgers, in her first acting role.

For the role of Bill Conradt, Oppenheim selected Alex Winter, who is best known for his portrayal of Bill S. Preston, Esq. in the Bill & Ted trilogy. Over the past 15 years, Winter has directed a series of acclaimed documentaries, including Downloaded, Deep Web: The Untold Story of Bitcoin, Trust Machine: The Story of Blockchain, and The YouTube Effect. Many explore the devastating impact of social media and the internet as a whole on society, and Primetime takes place in a world just on the brink of many of these changes.

We caught up with Winter to talk about his sympathetic portrayal of Conradt, working with Oppenheim, his recent Broadway turn in Waiting for Godot alongside Keanu Reeves, and the moment he realized that Oppenheim had secretly been collaborating with Nathan Fielder on You Can See Everything over the past three years.
How did you first hear about Primetime?

My agent got a call from Francine Maisler, the casting director, saying that Lance was interested in talking to me about that role. And I knew of Lance through his documentary work quite well. Obviously he knew my acting stuff, but we knew each other from the doc space, which is tiny. There’s like six people in that space.

So I was a huge fan of the script, and really interested in the character of Bill Conradt right from the jump. I was surprised at the depth of the part. It’s a small part, but there’s a lot there. And I was very fascinated by Bill Conradt.
What about him did you find so fascinating?

I wasn’t familiar with [To Catch a Predator]. It just wasn’t my world. It was on at a time when I wasn’t checked into that kind of TV. So I had missed the whole phenomenon. But the script was such a shrewd examination of media right at that nexus point before the internet happened, which, I’ve made a lot of movies about this exact thing. So topically, the way our culture deals with sexual abuse and predators is of interest to me, and something I’ve tackled with the Showbiz Kids doc and have my own personal history in that space.

And then Lance, whose work I loved, his documentaries have a kind of narrative style to them. He’s got a very particular style. So that’s why Bill Conradt was of interest to me, was because of what the movie and Lance was doing with [his story].

I felt like there was an opportunity to represent this cultural taboo creature in a more human way. And not to exonerate him, but just to present him as an actual human being, which is what is not often the case. And so I just did a lot of research into Bill and his work environment and his life. I talked to DAs and ADAs and other people in the region where he practiced. I’m a character actor by trade and by training, so I love to research and dig into backgrounds, and having a real person to investigate was helpful and interesting.
As you learned more, did you begin to sympathize with him?

I mean, I come into these things with a sympathy for all sides. Because these are all people, and they’re people who need help, whether they’re survivors or predators, they both need help. Most of the time, neither of them are getting help. So I’d say I come into it with empathy and some degree of sympathy from the get-go — certainly empathy from the start, sympathy depending on the case. I’d say I have less sympathy for someone like Harvey Weinstein.

But with Conradt, I did sympathize. It seemed like a very tragic case that involved coercion and a kind of grotesque throwing to the lions for the sake of ratings, a desperation for greater ratings, and very little nuance and examination of human beings involved.

So it was, I felt, an interesting opportunity to portray someone who certainly had very bad flaws, and was operating in a way that was potentially very harmful, but was at the bottom of it all, a human being. And it’s something that I’ve gotten into with my docs quite a bit. So I dealt with it in the Silk Road case and I’ve dealt with it with other documentaries where they’re dealing with characters that are, like most human beings, not black or white.

In the scene where Conradt is on the phone with someone he believes to be a child, it really seems like he’s in agony over his own desires, and he knows he’s doing something awful. He’s a tortured person.

Yeah. Lance’s documentaries, he calls them “docufantasias.” So there’s a dreamlike, fantasy quality to the world he’s representing, and the portrayal of Chris Hansen. Certainly, the way I came at Conradt, I wasn’t trying to be Bill Conradt; it wasn’t a biography of Bill. So there’s other stuff going on in the character I’m playing that isn’t related to him and specifically trying to litigate his story.

But I do feel the character was tormented. This guy had deep loneliness and inner torment. But as you said, obviously a compulsion, which I was interested in interrogating a little bit. And again, it’s not a piece of activism, it’s acting. So I didn’t do it to plant a flag in the sand or to have a message, but it was gratifying to be able to investigate this person in that way.

I think Lance had a twofold interest in me — specifically, one, related to how the public perceives me. When you cut through the computer and you find me on the other end, it could be a real jump scare, which we both knew we were leaning into. “Oh, shit, it’s that guy? What the fuck?” You could hear in the screening that we saw, there was an audible gasp in the theater when I appeared. And that’s exactly what Lance wanted.

But he also knew my own history with abuse, and he knows I do a lot of stuff outside of my work with group therapy and helping kids in the abuse space. So he knew that I had a pretty deep understanding of the predator-survivor relationship and what that is.
Lance made so many interesting casting choices in this movie with you, Phoebe Bridgers, Creed Bratton, Jeff Zucker, Jonathan Lipnicki. Few people would have predicted them.

That’s right. And what I love about Lance is that he’s not being meta for meta’s sake. He’s going after people to get really deep performances out of them. I mean, Creed is amazing in the film, I think. He’s so good, and it’s such a powerful scene. It is really like a scene out of Lance’s docs, though. It’s like a scene out of Ren Faire.

And so it was helpful to me going into this, because Lance was using the same crew that he’s used on all his docs. He has a very specific creative team. So it was a fairly big movie, but it was shot in a nimble way. And because I knew Lance’s docs, I knew how to plug Bill Conradt into that world in terms of the creating.
As the authorities and To Catch a Predator production team are approaching Bill’s house, it starts to feel like a horror movie. You know something awful is about to happen.

Yeah. I could tell while we were shooting that sequence what the vibe of it was going to be. And obviously we shot a lot more than is in the movie. But I think they used the perfect amount. So the stuff that’s gone of mine, I was actually happy to see gone. But yeah, his approach was very specific, and the thing about him is he knows what he wants, so it was fun to work on in that way.

But to your point, it flips the monster, because in a way that whole sequence is set up like, “Oh, it’s a horror movie and they’re going to get Hannibal Lecter,” like a scene out of Silence of the Lambs with all the cops descending on that house. But of course, the monster ends up being Chris Hansen.
It’s amazing that the film kind of makes the audience feel bad for a wannabe child molester.

Yeah. Honestly, that was important to me, and it’s something I discussed with Lance. I wanted people to sympathize with Bill. Again, it doesn’t mean that you exonerate him, but I felt like if I could have some small part in creating a little bit of a tweak within the cultural understanding of these people, especially in the sort of post-Epstein world we’re in now, where it’s become so caricatured and politicized. At the end of the day, really, they are just people and they really do need help. And so I really did want people to sympathize with Bill. I mean, I won’t lie there.
Bill needed professional help before he hurt a child. He didn’t need an NBC camera team swooping into his house.

Yeah, exactly. He needed some help and he probably would’ve survived had he had it, and everyone would’ve been better off and it wouldn’t have been like we were unleashing a monster on the world. But we have a long way to go culturally before we’re there, I think. And some people said to me, some of my friends, “Is it odd for you as a survivor playing a predator?” It’s not, because I’m an actor and I’m playing a character. I’m not doing therapy through my acting work. I do therapy with a therapist.

But from my perspective, it will help survivors if we humanize predators. That’s the biggest problem I have with shows like To Catch a Predator, which I caught up on once I was doing research for this film. I was like, “Oh, well, this isn’t really helping either.” It’s not really helping the survivors and it’s certainly not helping the predators. It’s not really providing any kind of service other than pure, low-hanging fruit, vigilante justice for TV ratings. That’s all it is.
I’m sure you see this movie as a piece with Deep Web, Downloaded, The YouTube Effect, and a lot of your other work. They all fit together.

And Showbiz Kids. That’s kind of a biographical story told through other people, all of whom had experienced severe trauma within their work as child actors. So it’s an interesting nexus point for me. The internet, the exploitation of people via media, how society responds to media, and also the birth of the discourse that gave rise to online communities and the discourse online, all of that is in this movie, which is so rich.
Yeah. You’ve often explored the early days of new technologies like Napster and YouTube, and how they grew and changed in terrible ways nobody would have expected.

I think that the early days of the open net and even the early days of the web were pretty great. There was a freewheeling, democratized nature to them before they were really co-opted by big corporate interests and oligarchs, and also weaponized so that you had this hyper-angry discourse. I mean, that’s what The YouTube Effect is about. It’s where the internet ended up and how it was weaponized.

There was so much great promise in the early days of the web. We were told it would democratize information, and give people all over the world a top-class education in history, language, culture, philosophy. Everyone would have the greatest works of art at their fingertips. It didn’t play out like that at all.

I mean, it did break a lot of barriers down. It did create ways for people all over the world who didn’t have access to information and knowledge to get access to information and knowledge. Of course, what we’re seeing now with the land rush into AI is — and we saw it happen with music, we’ve seen it happen with movies — the theft of people’s works. Now you have all of the authors, all of the journalists, all of the text in the world is just being fed into these LLMs and then sold off by other people without helping the people who actually created this stuff. So I think we’ve landed at the worst of the worst of the worst of where this all could have ended up.
During the making of Primetime, did you have any idea that Lance was working on You Can See Everything with Nathan Fielder, or was that totally secret?

It was very secret. In fact, I was with Lance and the [Primetime] gang at the Venice Film Festival. We came out of the premiere, which was really, really great, and a great entry for Lance into the world as a narrative filmmaker. It was so great to be there with him for that.

But we were all hanging out at the party that night quite late, and he said, “I’ve literally got to stay up all night and get on a plane and go to Telluride in three hours.” And then they told me what they had done. They were like, “You got to keep it quiet, because it’s a secret.”

I saw the movie early. I saw it at the premiere in L.A. And I was blown away by it. The combination of Lance and Nathan Fielder’s sensibilities is really dynamite. And there’s a lot of Lance in that. I mean, obviously, Nathan is at the center of it, and he’s an amazing talent, but there’s a lot of Lance, [cinematographer] David [Bolen], and that sort of aesthetic in that project.
There’s already talk of a Best Picture nomination, which would be incredible for a documentary.

It’d be incredible, and it would be gratifying to see, because people, and Lance would say this, there’s been a growing evolution of the doc form for years, going back to Kiarostami’s [1990 film] Close-Up, the work that Robert Greene does in the doc space, we call it docufiction, a kind of cumbersome term, but it’s not the first docufiction film by any stretch. It’s already gratifying to see it reaching these kinds of popular heights where people all over the world are seeing it.

I also am really happy about it because I feel like it’s a really good way to tell the story of the negative effects of tech oligarchy. It’s a very effective delivery system for that story. And I think it’s interesting to watch [Alex] Gibney’s Musk come out at the same time. They’re both great movies, right? Gibney’s amazing. He’s the best at what he does in the world. But I think it’s easier for the public to grasp this thing through the Lance and Nathan project. It’s entertaining, it’s very human, but it really tells you the story of the negative impacts of tech oligarchy in a very effective way.
To switch gears, you did Waiting for Godot on Broadway with Keanu Reeves about a year ago. How do you look back on that now?

It was amazing. I mean, forgetting the play for a second, to work with Keanu in a non-Bill and Ted project as grownups where we are in our lives, and [director] Jamie Lloyd, who I’m a huge fan of… We went to Jamie with the project because we’re fans. And then to go back to Broadway, not having been on Broadway since 1981. I spent my whole youth on Broadway and Off-Broadway.

And speaking candidly, in respect to Primetime, [Broadway is] where the abuse happened, and it was a very loaded time for me. It was a mixed bag of the greatest time in my life and a very horrific time in my life, but it was years and years and years. I spent a lot of my youth and all of high school in two Broadway shows, eight shows a week, summers, winters, the whole time. So it was a real trip to go back to being in a dressing room.

It was honestly one of the greatest experiences of my life doing it. I would go back. I’m doing another piece of theater. We’re doing an Arthur Miller play, Incident at Vichy, in New York in May that I’m going to act in and I’m co-producing. [Godot] did kind of reawaken that in me, and really I’m happy to be doing more theater again.
Do you think it bonded you and Keanu even closer as friends?

We’re pretty damn good friends already. We’re kind of like brothers. So the depth of trust that we have enabled us to do the show. I think we were both really happy to see that it didn’t strain our relationship because it could have. Because it was fucking hard, and it’s scary. We were really well prepared, and we really had confidence in the concept that Jamie had, and the other actors with Brandon [Dirden] and Michael [Patrick Thornton], and we had confidence in the way we decided to play these two characters. But it’s a lot of pressure and it’s Broadway.

Opening night, we sat behind the screen that comes up before, and we looked at each other and we were like, “I think I’m appropriately terrified. How about you?” He goes, “Oh, yeah, I’m shitting myself.” I’m like, “OK, good. Because there’d be something wrong with us if we weren’t.” So the stakes were very high and there was a lot of pressure. And I would say the bond that we had carried us through the show. I mean, I’ve known the guy for so long. We were already so trauma-bonded already just from making the Bill and Ted movies, which are so hard and always such a trial by fire.
It’s pretty amazing you guys are so close. What usually happens when two people are strongly associated with each other, real resentments creep in and it pulls them apart.

Yeah, except… I’m not unaware that it’s what I’m most known for, but it’s not what I think of as myself at all. Put it all together, it’s like nine months of my life out of being on this planet for 61 years.

So I do so many other things, and Keanu does so many other things, that it’s not like we’re Abbott and Costello, like that’s all we do. I think if it’s all we did, yes, we’d probably never talk to each other at all off camera. But because we do them so rarely, we hang out. I think that’s where Keanu and I got the idea of doing something that wasn’t Bill and Ted was like, we hang out, and yet we’ve never done anything as who we actually are. We’ve always just done Bill and Ted. So let’s try to do that.
What are you working on now?

I’m actually working on another feature. And I made this movie, Adulthood, that’s out now. It’s about to hit streaming, but it’s on pay-per-view now with Josh Gad and Kaya Scodelario. It was a lot of fun. I’m working on the Incident at Vichy play, which is quite a bit of work. And I’m about to put another movie together that I’m going to shoot next year.
Cool. I’m really looking forward to the Oscars next year. It’s easy to imagine Lance up at that podium for Best Picture. It would be such a moment of triumph.

It would be a moment of triumph for him, for the doc space, for the fight against tech oligarchy. But also, I’ve got to say in complete honesty, he is such a good person, and he and his creative team are so wide-eyed and passionate and uncynical and humble. I sound like the old schmuck, but it really couldn’t happen to a nicer person. So I really do hope it happens for him in that way. But honestly, he’s had already an overload of abundance so far. I think that whole crew are deer in the headlights right now. So they kind of can’t lose at this point.

items.title: ‘Obsession’ And ‘Backrooms’ Win Big at Fangoria Chainsaw Awards
items.description: “Obsession” led this year’s Fangoria Chainsaw Awards with the most amount of wins, taking home five awards including Best Director for Curry Barker and Best Lead Performance for Inde Navarrette.
items.author: Tanya Fedak
paragraphs: “Obsession” led this year’s Fangoria Chainsaw Awards with the most amount of wins, taking home five awards including Best Director for Curry Barker and Best Lead Performance for Inde Navarrette.

Celebrating achievements in horror film, television and gaming, the fan-voted awards premiered Sunday on Shudder and were hosted by Devon Sawa (“Final Destination,” “Chucky”). Among the night’s most stand-out moments were “Insidious” star Lin Shaye presenting the final award of the evening for “Obsession” and “Cujo” star Dee Wallace presenting the Goodest Boy award to the leading canine in “Good Boy,” Nova Scotia retriever Indy.

“Like the genre it honors, the true fun of the Chainsaw Awards is that we have the audience’s permission to push the envelope. Horror fans not only want to celebrate the films and individuals who kept them watching, but they want to do it in a manner befitting the thing they love,” said Michael Varrati, who wrote and directed the ceremony. “That’s why we can present a special award to a dog who became a fan favorite or send our scream king host into a corn maze to contend with things lurking behind the rows.”

“Backrooms” earned the second highest amount of Chainsaw Awards, receiving three wins for Best First Feature, Best Cinematography and Best Score. “Widow’s Bay” took home Best Series, while “Resident Evil: Requiem” won Best Video Game.

Special honorees of the night include Joe Bird, (“Talk to Me,” “Leviticus”) who received the Editor’s Eyeball Award to recognize his rising career in horror. A second Editor’s Eyeball Award was presented to co-presenter James A. Janisse, honoring him and Chelsea Rebecca or creating the horror YouTube channel, “Dead Meat.”
The ceremony was executive produced by Armen Aghaeian, Tara Ansley and Abhi Goel, with Amanda Grace Collins serving as lead producer and Phil Nobile Jr. and Varrati as producers.

items.title: The Surprise Guest in ‘You Can See Everything’ Could Win an Oscar. Should They?
items.description: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for “You Can See Everything,” now playing in theaters.
items.author: Daniel D'Addario
paragraphs: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for “You Can See Everything,” now playing in theaters.

The question that’s consumed the awards-pundit class since “You Can See Everything” exploded into theaters last week is whether Amanda Seyfried, the unlikely linchpin of this hybrid documentary, can be nominated for or win an acting Oscar. A24 is planning to campaign her for one. Much of her time onscreen is as herself, reacting in real time — but she does, eventually, re-enact co-director Nathan Fielder’s remembered interactions with disgraced tech founder Elizabeth Holmes.

In this, she’s reprising a role that, with the 2022 Hulu series “The Dropout,” already won her an Emmy and a Golden Globe. It’s the role, now that “You Can See Everything” is on track to become one of the most financially successful documentaries in history, that’s become Seyfried’s signature. To this viewer, the question is at once an amusing thought experiment (sure, why not?), and a testament to Seyfried’s compelling screen presence — and more than a little beside the point. For once, an Oscar seems minimizing. What Seyfried’s doing in her most compelling screen work ever is something other, or more, than simply acting.

To be clear, the parts of “You Can See Everything” when she is literally acting are riveting on their own terms. Seyfried simply wears the role of Holmes easily. She’s doubly disadvantaged — in that we’ve just spent 90 minutes with the real Holmes, against whom we can compare Seyfried, and in that we’ve also spent time absorbing just how little Seyfried understands the enigma of Holmes’ motivations. And yet Seyfried somehow creates a coherent and compelling version of a woman we don’t understand, and we know she doesn’t, really, either.

To pigeonhole Seyfried’s appearance in “You Can See Everything” as, solely, an acting performance misses the rawness of Seyfried’s presence here. She allows herself to be seen thinking through a conundrum, as herself, and falling short of finding answers — in other words, after Holmes and husband Billy Evans, she’s the documentary’s other subject. Seyfried delivers a painful and unresolved excavation of the mind of an actor, seeming to land in a place of uncertainty as to how her own past work as Holmes has changed the story even as she willingly takes on the part once more.

Consider, for instance, the scene in which Seyfried visits Evans at home, after Holmes’ incarceration. This is impressively game and daring. And Seyfried is, I suppose, “acting,” both in the theorist’s sense that all of us are acting our way through life and in the particular that Seyfried has set out to lure information out of Evans to better understand the seemingly bizarre arrangement Fielder and co-director Lance Oppenheim had been excavating before Holmes went to prison. But is she acting, in the traditional sense, when she meets and interacts with Holmes and Evans’ two children, or when she defends her social media post criticizing the late Charlie Kirk against Evans’ mockery? Alternately tender and outraged, Seyfried allows us into her world, just as Holmes tried to. But Holmes, talking past real questioning, couldn’t get there, no matter how all-access her invitation to Fielder had been. Seyfried, by contrast, seems deeply in touch with emotions lying just under the surface. And her increasing befuddlement both matches our own and raises the question of just how deeply an actor can ever understand their subject.

Seyfried, just as Holmes and Evans do in their askew manner, knows her angles. It wasn’t lost on me that within the frame as Fielder speaks to her at her home is a miniature playhouse, of the sort her company Make It Cute sells. That the computer on which she and Fielder watch video of Holmes watching “The Dropout” is propped on coffee table books about Seyfried’s great passion, dogs, and that she and Fielder discuss Holmes while feeding her photogenic horses on her photogenic farm only burnish her brand further. And yet she cannot help but exposing more than she may mean to.

A conversation about the ethics of “The Dropout” — a drama based on real events that, as with any dramatization, used creative license, and that many viewers took as fact — places Seyfried in a surprisingly exposed position. Holmes did not, literally, say and do all the things that Seyfried says and does in the role, Seyfried admits, but she may well have, and the performance overall conjures the sense of a person who is unconcerned with scientific accuracy or with the truth. Shouldn’t that be enough? “I didn’t do that to her,” Seyfried concludes, after attempting to walk herself through a justification of “The Dropout” as plainly not depicting objective reality, no matter what viewers think. “She did that to herself.” She seems to be convincing herself not to feel guilty, up until her final line, delivered with a “It’s Chinatown”-style futility. “It’s very complicated,” she says, having indulged the complications long enough.

Coming into “You Can See Everything,” this viewer saw Elizabeth Holmes’ Theranos as transparently fraudulent and “The Dropout” as an excellent TV show that was in no need of moral justification. Leaving the theater, nothing about those beliefs had changed, but engaging the question of what Seyfried might have owed to Holmes allowed both women to be seen in intriguing new lights. Seyfried, painfully aware of the existence of the two young children she’d met, twists around the question of whether her past work might have been unfair, or have been presented as possessed of a truth its creators didn’t actually know. And in this moment, she seems less to be acting than to be, in a moment of painful frankness I admire her for allowing herself to experience on-camera, acted upon.

Say this much: “You Can See Everything” is undeniably a career high for an actor who has seemed at times in her career like an underdog. (A sliding-doors scenario for the ages: The role of Elizabeth Holmes originally went to sketch comedian Kate McKinnon, and Seyfried got the role only after McKinnon dropped out and Seyfried got a career-boosting Oscar nomination for 2020’s “Mank.”) Amiably loopy in interviews — including in red-carpet appearances at this year’s Academy Museum Gala, where Seyfried sidestepped discussing the film in favor of free-associative Dada — and impressively shifting between genres to avoid being pigeonholed, Seyfried is easy to root for, but can seem hard to know.

Which makes the Oscar talk make perfect sense. Seyfried has gone to a very raw place in “You Can See Everything” — and, not for nothing, has delivered some of the most memorable humor in its second half. (Her growing scandalization at Evans’ control over Holmes’ image and her life allows the viewer a compelling way to stay engaged with the story once Holmes herself leaves it.) But whether or not she can break through in what would, despite vaguely similar precedent — Maria Bakalova in the 2020 “Borat” sequel was nominated for reacting against real life — be close to an unprecedented case, Seyfried has done something more impressive than earning any award. She’s opened up her work as an actor — both her preparation and the moral question of what it means to play a living person — to careful scrutiny, and was vulnerable enough to attempt to talk it through, and to be shown to be uncertain. This appearance, or performance, or whatever, will be discussed far beyond Oscar season. It situates Seyfried as what we ought to have known she was all along: Among the most daring stars of her generation.

items.title: Sacha Baron Cohen Gets Real About Backlash, Death Threats and Resurrecting Ali G
items.description: Sacha Baron Cohen insists his new film, Ali G: Who Iz I?, is the last guerrilla comedy of its kind that he’ll make. He’s adamant. No more Borat. No more Bruno. No more Ali G. They’re too hard, he says, too risky. He’s tired of hoodwinking people to expose thei
items.author: Lacey Rose
paragraphs: Sacha Baron Cohen insists his new film, Ali G: Who Iz I?, is the last guerrilla comedy of its kind that he’ll make. He’s adamant. No more Borat. No more Bruno. No more Ali G. They’re too hard, he says, too risky. He’s tired of hoodwinking people to expose their prejudices, and he’s even more tired of the death threats that periodically follow. There are easier ways to make money in this business, and eventually his luck will run out.

The trouble with his declaration, however impassioned, is that he has been making it for years. He’d routinely say he was done before he made the 2020 Borat sequel, which, incidentally, earned two Oscar nominations, and he was even more insistent afterward. And each time he says it, he believes it to be true. He wants it to be true, he tells me. So, why are we here, I ask, discussing an Ali G revival?

“Because I’m terrified of where our society is headed, and the way I can comment on that is through my comedy,” he says. “I wanted to show the extremism on both sides of the political spectrum and the danger of virtuous violence.” There’s a level of seriousness that belies the 90-minute comedy film he’s made, which features an imbecilic white rapper who speaks in Caribbean-British slang and a contraption that shoots bullets out of one’s rear end. Recognizing this, he adds: “And obviously we wanted to make the funniest film that’s ever been made.”

His longtime collaborators have other theories about his return. Anthony “Ant” Hines, who’s been working with Baron Cohen since The 11 O’Clock Show, where the Ali G character originated, believes his pal had missed the adrenaline rush, just as he had. “It’s a visceral buzz you get from making a movie this way,” Hines says, “and nothing comes close to it.”

Dan Mazer, whose friendship with Baron Cohen dates back to secondary school in the U.K., wasn’t particularly surprised to get the call about dusting off Ali G, in part because they’ve never stopped talking about the character. In fact, whenever they got together, they’d often slip into Ali G’s voice, he says, and imagine what patently absurd things he would be saying or doing in different situations.

“I also think it’s a knowledge that Sacha is the Michael Jordan of this sort of filmmaking,” says Mazer. “And yeah, Michael Jordan went off and tried to play baseball, and you go, ‘OK, you’re a pretty good baseball player,’ but he’s not the Michael Jordan of baseball. And Sacha is the Michael Jordan of this, and to an extent, we all are. We invented this genre, and nobody else has matched what we’ve done.”

Whatever the reasoning may be, Ali G is back, rolling into theaters Oct. 23 before landing on Amazon Prime Video soon after. And like plenty else that Baron Cohen has done, it’s already prompted a full-blown meta-outrage cycle, complete with a campaign to boycott the film. With each new trailer or PR stunt posted to social media come fresh accusations of an outdated caricature and of cultural appropriation — the latter a central plot point in the film, in which Ali G’s progressive nemesis (also played by Baron Cohen) attempts to cancel him on those very grounds. Some in his camp have speculated that it’s more of a coordinated attack by pro-Palestinians who are critical of Baron Cohen’s past support of Israel. (Though he’s been quiet about Israeli politics and the conflict in Gaza in recent years, Baron Cohen is a prominent Jew who has sounded the alarm about the surge of antisemitism on social media, reportedly telling TikTok executives in 2023 that what was happening on their platform was “creating the biggest antisemitic movement since the Nazis.”)

Colton Dunn, an Emmy-winning Ali G superfan and one of three Black writers hired on the film, is aware of the cultural appropriation claims. “But we knew where we were coming from, and we dealt with it all in the movie,” he says, “and at the heart of it, Sacha and the movie want to defeat evil and hate. That’s the intention behind it.” Still, the internet has suggested the backlash has Amazon spooked. Courtenay Valenti, Amazon MGM Studios’ head of film, streaming and theatrical, offers this: “We want to be in business with exceptional storytellers who have distinctive creative visions, and Sacha is exactly that. He has always been fearless in his comedy, with a unique ability to tap into the cultural conversation in ways that are both provocative and entertaining.”
Over cappuccinos in the garden of the Chateau Marmont, Baron Cohen lets loose on the mounting backlash, his battles with studios and the $3 million day that nearly derailed his film.
In 2021, you allegedly performed as Ali G at The Comedy Store in Australia. How soon after did you explore the idea of another film, and what did those early conversations entail?

During the pandemic, our family moves to Australia, and when they lock down in Australia, you cannot leave where you are. My ex [Isla Fisher] is from Perth, so we applied to go there. She’s rejected. I find out that you have to show that there’s a financial benefit to Western Australia to be allowed in. You have to apply to the police. So I say, “Listen, I’m doing a stand-up tour. It’s going to create 300 jobs. It’s going to bring tens of millions of dollars into Western Australia.” Obviously I had no intention of doing it. But then the police accept me. We spent 14 days in lockdown, and at the end, a police car turns up, an inspector comes out, and she says, “I am in charge of your stand-up tour.”
So, you had to do a stand-up tour.

I did, and I had the police watching me. I ended up doing a 90-minute show, and what was interesting was that people really loved seeing Borat and Bruno, but when Ali G came out, there was a different response. It was as if people believed he was real. There’s going to be a lot of amateur psychology in this interview, but my observation was that because Ali G existed before I existed as a public figure — for five or six years, I didn’t give an interview [as myself] — people thought Ali was real and therefore there was this different response to him. So, I felt, “Hold on, is there a movie in this character?”

I came back to America at the end of 2021 and started talking with the team about it. We all felt Ali by himself wouldn’t be a satirical movie because he was from a bygone era — this relic from another period who’s unaware that he is deeply problematic. But what if we brought in another character, an ultraprogressive extremist [also played by Baron Cohen] who’s his rival and make it a thriller like The Fugitive? We had in our mind this line that goes, “We have a cultural appropriator on the loose,” from that famous speech in The Fugitive. That felt funny to me.

In the revisionist history of the film, you had ended Da Ali G Show because you couldn’t come to financial terms with HBO. It left me wondering if there were any conversations or interest, from either side, about doing more?

Oh, yes. HBO wanted to carry on. I said no because at that time, in Britain, I think a lot of comedians were snobs about doing multiple seasons. So, there was no expectation or desire to do 15 seasons — to do the American way. I’m very friendly with Larry David, and I’m jealous of him that he can do Curb again and again. I probably would’ve had a much easier life if I just carried on doing Da Ali G Show.

A decade ago, you said of this type of filmmaking: “It’s a young man’s game. You have to be prepared for a small amount of risk, and my philosophy was always: ‘Well, if something bad happens, I’m single and everyone’s going to be all right if I end up in hospital for two weeks.’ Now that I’m married with kids, it’s more difficult to justify.” So, did you find a way to do it differently, or did you just say, “Fuck it”?

I’m never cavalier. These movies are dangerous to make, but we try to limit the risks and keep everybody safe. But even physically, they’re incredibly demanding. So, the final scene of this film is an eight-hour continuous scene that takes place over 12 locations. It’s a continual shot. There’s gunfire in it. There’s a medical procedure. There are drones, there are explosions, and it’s taking place in the desert. On the way to shooting it, I bumped into one of the great stuntmen and he said, “You will go to hospital if you make this movie,” because I explained I’m wearing a prosthetic head in a fat suit. He said, “You’ll be so dehydrated you’ll be in hospital for two weeks.”
You hear that and think what?

That I have to fix the problem. So, I had an endurance specialist who does the Tour de France be by my side during the scene and they’re measuring my weight. I think I had 11 liters of Pedialyte. And listen, a number of people went to the hospital for dehydration, including the bodyguard. There were dangers in the scene as well. One of the people grabbed a gun and almost did something very dangerous. These really are the hardest movies to make, but I suppose I made it because I’m scared of this world of conspiracies and lies that are spread by social media and now by AI. If we don’t have these shared facts, then democracies crumble and we can’t have a tolerant society. And to make people laugh is therapy.
As I read your own quote back to you just now, you were laughing. Why?

Because I’m always surprised at my own idiocy. I’m very bad at looking into the future and imagining how I will feel. So, for example, the naked fight in Borat 1, we get to set and Ken Davitian, who’s not conventionally attractive, is naked, and he’s going to sit on my face. And I say, “I’m not going to do this!” At that point, Larry Charles, the director, said, “So why did you write it?!” I continually make these decisions that are very bad for my own health and sanity.
You are making this film in a very different moment, culturally and comedically. Do you derive some masochistic pleasure from that kind of challenge?

I’ll tell you, in the script, there was a moment where Ali G is canceled, and the way we wanted to do that was that I, Sacha, should be canceled in the real world and the idea was to use the footage of me being canceled and stick it into the movie. And we did actually get some of the second bit, but we didn’t have the money to open up the movie and put the footage in. That was the intention, though.
I’m told you get a fair number of death threats, which now come from both the left and the right. When have you decided something wasn’t worth it?

I was about to do a scene [in Borat 1] and we had a cop who had his gun on his thigh and I said, “Why is your gun on your thigh?” He goes, “Well, I need to be really fast to draw in this area.” I said, “Well, how close are you to me?” And he said, “I’ll be with you within three minutes.” I realized that was not a good thing to do, so I pulled that scene. I will never do a scene if I think I’m actually going to die.
You’ve filmed in a bulletproof vest, so you’ve clearly anticipated the possibility of being shot?
Yes, on Borat 2, there was a scene at a gun rights rally that I knew there was a risk of getting shot. But I felt it was an important film to be made.
Is there anyone who says to you, “Hey, Sacha, I know this seems noble to you, but maybe it’s not necessary”?

I don’t talk about my children. But my brothers tell me that. And my mom and some of my team as well, because there are much easier options. I made a movie called Ladies First. I shot it in three months. It came out. A lot of people saw it [on Netflix]. And it’s as financially beneficial as making something that takes years, and there’s absolutely zero risk. There must be some masochistic nature to me, but I don’t think it’s just that. I want to give the fans who’ve been loyal for the last 28 years something that they’ve never seen before. I want to give them the most ambitious movie I’ve ever made, which is a three-character movie. [Baron Cohen also plays a former Mossad agent.] It is my version of the Avengers.
I’ve always assumed that you were like Tom Cruise, after the same adrenaline rush that he is as he jumps out of planes.
I don’t think that’s the reason I do it.
You don’t? Your collaborators seem to …

No. The first [for-hire] movie I did, Talladega Nights, I walked into my trailer and there was a bed there. I realized I’d never been in a trailer before, and I go, “Hold on, this is a paid job where I can go to sleep?!” I couldn’t comprehend how relatively easy it was, and it was great fun. But as you’ll probably deduce from this interview, I’m not very self-aware.
I don’t know that I buy that.

OK. Do I enjoy it when something works? Yes. Am I upset when something doesn’t work? Yes. So, for example, this final scene is an eight-hour continuous shot over multiple locations and no one had ever done that before. Normally we shoot a scene or two scenes a day. Here, we put probably 40 scenes together and shot them continuously. I had a variety of line producers and assistant directors refuse to schedule it. And there are 400 or so beats that must all go perfectly, because you’re dealing with real people and if anything doesn’t feel quite right, they will stop and say, “Hold on, this isn’t real.”

So gunfire, the squibs have to go off perfectly. A medical procedure happens. That body that we use has to be believable. Then a fire breaks out during the first part of the scene. As we’re driving to the second location to kidnap somebody with these real people, I find out that location four is surrounded by fire, and it’s being evacuated, and we have to pull the scene. And each time we run it, it’s $4 million and we’re insured for $1 million, and I personally have to pay $3 million. So, we shut down production and we have a discussion, which is that it’s completely idiotic that we’re trying this.
And everyone is telling you it’s not possible?
Yes, and I’ve lost $3 million that day. Obviously it was my money, which is a very stupid idea.
But you ultimately got it?

We got it. We had some of the team that worked on the Oscars because I was like, “What is a movie or a TV show where nothing can go wrong? It’s the Oscars.” And even there, sometimes something’s going wrong! I said to them, “OK, this is the Oscars, it’s just taking place over 50 miles in 12 locations. And it has gunfire and blood.” But at the end of all of it, if you look at the behind-the-scenes footage, I’m not jumping up and down. I’m content.
With 2020’s Borat 2, you’ve said that several of the places you pitched were concerned by the political content and the idea of running it before the election. How did this pitch compare?

Well, the desire was always to have this come out a few days before either a presidential election or the midterms. A lot of my movies have come out around those times. Borat 1 came out almost 20 years to the day, on November 3, 2006, just before the midterms. It’s a time for people to think about the choices that they’re about to make. But this movie is more about the dangers of extremism on both sides.
I get that, but you’re also operating in an extremely risk-averse climate. I can’t imagine there weren’t any concerns …
Well, Hollywood is a superficial place.

I know. (Laughter.) But I pitched this after Borat 2 had won two Golden Globes and had Oscar nominations and was the most watched movie ever on Amazon. That’s enough to convince studio heads to buy it. And everyone tried.
It was somewhere else first, no?

Yes. Amazon and Universal were the final contenders. We ended up going with Universal but, in the end, the movie took so long that we went back to Amazon. And it was actually great because we’d had an incredible experience there with the last one. We really did. And that movie [Borat 2] also was at Universal and ended up at Amazon.
So, this one moved because —

It was taking too long. You have to understand the basis of this kind of movie is that we have to find people who don’t know who I am, which becomes harder and harder. I think our research department interviewed 5,000 doctors to get one [for a single scene]. Then we had a number of other things that kept on shutting it down. The fire. The writers strike. I ended up doing another movie in the middle.
Amazon came aboard a third of the way through. What did their notes look like?
For better or worse, maybe for worse, I’m a final-cut producer and director.
So, you’re saying it didn’t much matter what their notes were?
Well, executives can have really fantastic notes. And they can have terrible notes. But I always listen to the audience and I’m really guided by that.

You were once asked about comparisons between you and Andy Kaufman, to which you said, “In a way, he’s more of an artist than I am in that I don’t think he cared what the audience thought — and deep down, I really want to make the audience laugh. And that’s why I fight to get jokes to be funny … I’ll go to war with whatever studio has been stupid enough to pay me money to make a movie.” Again, you’re laughing …
I can’t believe how honest I was.
What did those fights look like on a film like this?

If something is funny, then I will go to war for it. And the studios know that because I make it clear when we do these movies, which makes me not very studio-friendly in some ways because my allegiance is to the audience. And I go to every single screening and I record the laughter and I grade the jokes and I have a few people that I’ve trained to grade them too, and then I cut the jokes within a frame. It’s obsessive and very intricate, but it’s designed to deliver really funny movies. Some people find me incredibly arrogant because they’ll come up and say, “You know that movie, Borat 2, wasn’t funny.” And I’ll say, “You’re entitled to your opinion, but you’re wrong. I have 5,000 people laughing at these jokes and I can show you they are empirically funny.”
You said that you’re not studio-friendly, but, as you noted, this is a superficial business and if your model can put butts in seats …

Yes, it’s about money. But I’m also a great supporter of the Oscars and other awards ceremonies because, however absurd they are, it creates another incentive for studio heads to make quality projects. Because studio heads do want to win Oscars and they want to get nominated. And we’ve been very lucky in that the Academy and the Globes and some other organizations have recognized our work.

In fact, I was sitting at that table [pointing to another table in the Chateau garden] in 2006 having done Borat, and Sean Penn came and sat at the table and he said, “Why don’t you do an Oscar campaign for your performance in Borat?” I said, “That’s absurd. They’ll never give me an Oscar nomination.” And he said, “They will.” So, we went to Fox at the time and they said, “Listen, we’ll pay for one Oscar campaign, but it’s either writing or acting.” At the time, I was actually winning some of the acting awards, to my great surprise, but I spoke to the team and we decided to push the writing. [The 2006 film was nominated for best adapted screenplay.] So, we gave up the acting campaign. Also, I was about to make Bruno and I didn’t want to go on a baby-kissing tour, which would destroy my next movie. Me doing this kind of stuff [an interview as himself] destroys the ability to make another one.
I know, I know. I’m sorry.
There we go. Look what you’ve done. You’ve ruined me.

As you anticipated, it didn’t take long for people to start lodging complaints. One criticism, which mirrors a plotline in the film, is that Ali G uses the character as a cover for enforcing racial stereotypes. What do you say to that?

Well, I’ll repeat what I’ve said for many years, which is that Ali G is a white cultural appropriator who steals from the musical artists that he admires. The reason Ali G says “West Side” is not because the Afro-Caribbean community in London was saying “West Side.” Nobody there was. It’s because Tupac Shakur, who he admires, is saying “West Side.” And so he is funny because he is delusional. He lives this boring, white middle-class life in a suburban town, and he deludes himself that he’s living in Compton, and that is the absurdity of Ali G. The core joke is that a white moron, possibly the stupidest man in the world, is interviewing a white expert or high-status politician, and that white expert or high-status politician believes that this imbecile played by me is real and that leads to comedy. And in my belief, it slightly undermines the power of the establishment. So it was fundamentally an anti-establishment character where we’re pricking the assuredness of the establishment by saying, “Listen, these people aren’t that smart. They believe that Channel 4 or HBO could have sent one of the most stupid people in the world to interview them.”
What do you make of the argument that not everybody recognizes the absurdity and so the stereotypes being presented can have dangerous ramifications?
Everyone is entitled to their own view. And a lot of the stuff on social media is orchestrated, and not necessarily orchestrated by people who really believe in what they’re saying.

But when I did Da Ali G Show in America, the first people who gravitated to it were the Black hip-hop community. The first GQ Award that I was given was given to me by Method Man and Redman. I did a series of adverts for the NBA directed by Spike Lee, who’s not naive about racial issues. They recognized these characters, these white cultural appropriators, and they found them funny. So, this notion of it being problematic hadn’t been raised for 20 years.
OK, but you seemed to know it would be this time around?

Yes. I knew, and I wanted to make sure that this was an anti-racist movie, which is why we were so concerned with having absolutely brilliant Black writers on board and consulting with brilliant Black cultural commentators.
As I believe you were referencing, there was a pretty sizable social media campaign to boycott the movie, and some have speculated that the campaign is tied to your pro-Israel stance —

Well, I haven’t said anything about Israel. [Baron Cohen voiced his support for Israel and the hostages immediately after the Oct. 7 attacks but has been quiet on the Gaza war and Israeli politics in the years since.] I think people are being portrayed as things that they are not on social media and it’s problematic. We are in a world where people can’t distinguish between facts and lies, and that’s something that I’ve spent a lot of the last few years trying to fix. For example, I co-founded a group called Stop Hate for Profit with the NAACP and Color of Change and the ADL and certain other civil rights groups to stop the misinformation and incitement of racism on social media. So, I’m not surprised that prominent Jews are being targeted. I knew that this was going to happen. The level of organization is surprising, but this is a trend of Jews being portrayed in certain ways and trying to be silenced.
You’ve been vocal about the rise of antisemitism, broadly speaking. Have you felt any difference in your own Hollywood career after Oct. 7?
No, not really. I mean, maybe it’s because I don’t do much, but I haven’t.

Well, you’re about to make your West End debut in a Quentin Tarantino play, which feels like a big leap, going from this film, in which you’re in complete control as the writer, director and star, to being a puppet in Tarantino’s theater. How did that come together?

I’ve never had a career plan, but I have this kind of no-brainer rule, which is if one of the best directors in the world asks me to do something, I’ll say yes, even if it’s instinctively the wrong project. So when Martin Scorsese says, “I’m doing a kid’s film, will Sacha play the villain in it?” And I read the book and the character’s not that interesting. I actually had a lot of arguments with [screenwriter John] Logan about it [Hugo]. But I say yes because I want to learn how to make better films. And so if Quentin comes along and says, “I want to do a play,” I say yes. Then I actually read the play and I thought it was fantastic. And I felt, why not? So currently, I’m doing nine hours of sword-fighting training a week. And I would just clarify, rather than be a puppet, Quentin did suggest that there would be some element of collaboration.

A little bit, yes. But Quentin and I have been talking about doing a project for at least 20 years. We talked about doing The Scarlet Pimpernel about 20 years ago. Borat came out and Quentin and I would have dinner monthly and I almost did a part in [his 2012 Western] Django Unchained. In the end, I had to drop out because I ended up doing Les Misérables. But I came very close to doing a scene with Kerry Washington. I even had a prosthetic chin made because Quentin was very adamant that I would resemble this character he’d liked from the ’40s.

Ant Hines, one of your longtime collaborators, suggested you’ve tussled with Amazon in the promotion of this new film. “We’re giving Amazon panic attacks on the daily,” he told me. “They’re used to Timothée Chalamet eating some chicken wings; they’re not used to 300 Timothée Chalamets attempting to take part in the London Marathon, which is a thing they shut down.”

This is why it’s best not to talk to somebody like Ant. (Laughs.) You know, they’ve actually been great in terms of the marketing. But it’s not a traditional process when you work with me and you’re marketing a movie.
You did end up with 300 Ali G look-alikes following you around London. That had to be validating, if a little overwhelming.

The really concerning thing was that these fans were coming out with catchphrases that I’d completely forgotten. I was like, “Wait a minute. I recognize that … What is that from?” And they’d go, “It’s you!” And some of them were doing better Ali G impressions than me. There was one guy there, an Ali G impersonator, and I had to explain, like, “Listen, you’ve been doing this at weddings and bar mitzvahs every week for the last 20 years. I haven’t been doing this.” I’ve actually had that happen before. We did a movie called Bruno, and Jonah Hill was one of the writers. And in the writers room, he was doing impressions of Bruno, and they were better than Bruno. Then when I started shooting the movie, I realized that I was doing an impression of Jonah Hill doing an impression of me.

In any genre, there’s always an “It” person, and at various points, you’ve employed those people shortly before they reached that status: Jonah, Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg and, most recently, Nathan Fielder, who worked on your Showtime series, Who Is America? What do you think of what Nathan has done in the eight years since you worked together?

Oh, I think he’s a comic genius and he reinvented the genre that I, I suppose, created or developed. And he had a rule, really, which was to not do anything that I had done. But he’s a brilliant, brilliant mind, and absolutely hilarious. I think his documentary [You Can See Everything] is going to be huge, so I’m very excited for him.

But it’s been an honor to have all of these incredible people come and work with me. Seth and Evan, the story with them was, it was the Ali G Show, and they came in with an idea for Bruno — instead of Girls Gone Wild, it was Boys Gone Wild. I said, “OK, you’re hired, but I’ve only got enough money for one writer, so unless you want to share a hotel room and a bed and a wage, I can only hire one of you and it’s going to be Seth.” They came back and said, “We’ll split the wage.” And basically they would write in a double bed in the Best Western hotel we were in. They had beers all around them. They were smoking and they’d write in bed.
That’s fantastic. For you, what do the incoming calls look like these days?
I think they’re kind of what comes in to everyone. I get the traditional comedies, kernels of comedy ideas, and then dramas.
Is one genre more appealing than the other right now?

No. I want to do stuff that challenges me. So again, I’m not doing Borat 3, which also would be incredibly challenging. Again, this movie I just did is the most challenging movie I’ve ever done, but I’m not doing more.
No, no, I really have had enough. I know you don’t believe me.
Oh, I really pray that in six years’ time, you don’t come to me and quote me to myself.
This story appeared in the Oct. 21 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine. Click here to subscribe.

items.title: Disney and Netflix Are Courting Creators. YouTube Is Playing Hardball to Keep Them
items.description: On Sept. 23, YouTube gathered a couple hundred of its top creators at Pier 57 in New York City for its annual “Made on YouTube” event. The showcase is where YouTube reveals new initiatives for its creator community, giving attendees a sneak peek at what the vi
items.author: Alex Weprin
paragraphs: On Sept. 23, YouTube gathered a couple hundred of its top creators at Pier 57 in New York City for its annual “Made on YouTube” event. The showcase is where YouTube reveals new initiatives for its creator community, giving attendees a sneak peek at what the video platform has been cooking up in its Skunk Works, like new AI video editing tools. But this year, YouTube wasn’t the only platform on their minds.

Netflix, Disney+, Tubi and others are aggressively cutting deals for top creators, in some cases securing wholly original programming or day-and-date releases with YouTube, offering millions of dollars in the process. The Google-owned video platform is not taking it lying down, launching a carrot-and-stick approach to try and keep its place as the primary home for top talent. “It’s a very good time to be in the creator business,” says Adam Wescott, CEO of Home Game Studios, noting the demand for their work. With creator-owned studios proliferating nationwide, it’s a battle that could portend the future of streaming entertainment.

It started with kids and family content. Netflix, seeking to bolster its kids programming, inked deals for YouTube native content from CoComelon, Ms. Rachel and Mark Rober. It worked, with all three becoming among the most watched programs in the category. The streamer subsequently ordered originals from them and began to reach out to creators in other genres, spanning food (Nick DiGiovanni), talk (Good Mythical Morning with Rhett & Link) and teen content (Alan Chikin Chow).

Rich Greenfield, the LightShed analyst, believes Netflix has committed upward of $1 billion on creator and podcast programming over the next three years (still, admittedly, a very small slice of its $20 billion annual content budget).

But Netflix only started the current war. Disney has long worked with creators, but recent months have seen wide-ranging deals with the likes of Dhar Mann, Dude Perfect and Like Nastya as it seeks out family-friendly and on-brand creators who can live on Disney+. And the company recently hosted a creator event at the El Capitan Theater and Disney Studios Lot, with some 350 creators to further forge those relationships. Tubi, the Fox-owned streaming service, has inked deals with dozens of creators for both originals and library fare.
There’s already hope in the creator community that Skydance is about to follow them, with new co-CEO Ynon Kreiz having served as the CEO of Maker Studios.

But why are these other streamers so eager to get in the creator business? Multiple sources paint a picture built around audience, money and speed. The larger studio platforms and streamers desperately want to have a product that appeals to the younger, digitally native audience that religiously watches creator content on YouTube.

“I think creators really do value, in the right circumstances, the elevation and amplification of being on a main channel platform like a traditional media company,” says Akshay Mehta, the CEO of Lighthouse Studios, a creator entertainment studio. “Creators are creatives fundamentally. They just discovered that in the last 15 years, for a lot of people, the best way to be creative is to go make stuff on YouTube.”

The money certainly helps. Multiple sources on the creator side stress that they need funding to help pursue some of the ideas they have, and such places as Netflix, Tubi and Disney are helping them do that. The big streamers are funding original shows and offering help to break into areas like consumer products or live experiences (that was a key piece of Disney’s Dude Perfect deal).

Streamers also are banking that creators can not only bring their audience with them but fill their libraries with content that is, frankly, dramatically less expensive than traditional fare and that is produced at a more rapid clip. “These platforms have seen this shift, and they can’t ignore it,” says Nic Paul, the president of the creator services company Spotter. “They all have subscriptions, they all have ad-supported products, even at Netflix, the ad-supported product is becoming a lot more of the focus. There’s a lot of churn. Everyone is like, how do I create enough content fast to keep audiences engaged? Because if you think about it, Stranger Things on Netflix, I’ve got to wait a year plus for a season, and creators are obviously very fast at putting out IP.”

Indeed, one top creator who has a deal with a streaming platform says they told their new partner that they can produce an hour’s worth of programming at perhaps 10 percent of the cost (or less!) of a traditional comedy, drama or unscripted concept, all at a faster pace.

But what has surprised creators more than anything is how hard YouTube is fighting back. The platform is a juggernaut, and it would be just fine if it lost top creators to other places. But it is waging a multipronged effort — with both incentives and threats — to try and convince creators to make YouTube their primary home. Many of the incentives focus on brand deals, with YouTube significantly increasing its resources in the space. Some creators see YouTube’s brand deals as a way to subsidize or pay for content that they want to make, given that YouTube does not pay to license content in the same way platforms like Netflix do.

“Given the cultural phenomenon that YouTube creators are, and this sort of juggernaut that they are in the culture out there, of course other streaming platform services have taken note,” YouTube CEO Neal Mohan told the Big Technology podcast after Made on YouTube when pressed on the dispute, adding that even as MrBeast produces his Beast Games for Prime Video, he still keeps YouTube as his home base. “And, frankly, I think that’s flattering to our creators.”

But YouTube also has played hardball, with one creator telling THR that they were “shocked” at the platform’s approach. On the one hand, some of the threats are reasonable: YouTube selects a handful of creators to appear onstage at its annual Brandcast upfront event, a high-profile stage that can lead to major deals. And it has supported Emmy campaigns for creators in certain categories. Those would stop for creators who shift their allegiances to other platforms. (Netflix and Disney already have promised to bring creators to their own upfronts next year and fund some Emmy efforts, according to sources.)

And they have even suggested that creators may not be eligible for YouTube Select, an ad program for its very top creators. That caught some creators off guard, as it was seen as an objective program based on reach and scale and is built around videos on YouTube. “That was never their approach in the past,” says Wescott. “It was always about supporting creators and reminding them why YouTube was their home.”

The platform still plays that game, though even there the tone has become somewhat combative, as one creator notes to THR. Earlier in October, comedian Lilly Singh returned to YouTube after a years-long hiatus, once again creating original content after working in Hollywood. In an interview YouTube posted to its blog, she did not hold back.

“Hollywood has real systemic issues, especially for women and people of color. Over the past few years, I received countless notes that weren’t about improving the project, but about making it ‘more palatable,” ‘more marketable,’ or ‘less niche.’ That is fundamentally anti-creative. Our job is to tell our stories unapologetically,” Singh said. “On YouTube, there are no gatekeepers demanding I make my brain baby more palatable for the masses. That authenticity is why my channel worked in the first place.”
But why is YouTube seem so interested in keeping creators on-platform? Especially because, as Mohan notes, it’s a good thing for the ecosystem when others are interested?

“On the surface, YouTube should not care. Creators are not launching their careers on Netflix or Disney+,” LightShed analyst Greenfield wrote on Oct. 9. “We suspect YouTube is concerned because the top 20-50 creators have an outsized importance to its major brand advertising commitments each year. Most brands only know a select group of high-profile creators. If brands start to see those creators appearing on Netflix… does a brand start to ask why it is paying YouTube for creators it can find in a curated, brand-safe environment elsewhere?”

Advertising is at the heart of the battle, with the ad-supported Tubi competing with Netflix and Disney (each of which is leaning into ads) for creator deals. Creators, of course, are used to working with brands. “A dirty little secret of our space is 90 percent of the revenue is brand endorsements, influencer marketing,” Wescott notes.

Still, none of the creators (or those who worked with top creators) suggest that they will completely leave YouTube, even if they may still cut deals to develop original ideas elsewhere. And it isn’t just out of loyalty to the platform that made them or that funds them (Instagram and TikTok, they note, pay basically nothing).

“I think you’ll be hard pressed to find a successful YouTube creator who’s willing to walk away from that platform, because it’s what they know, it’s where their audience is, it’s where they grew their business, and it’s where they have the most direct control,” says Wescott. “You’re still playing on someone else’s playground, but YouTube is not telling you what to post on your channel. The other guys are going to have some sort of opinion on what you create on the original side.”
For an ambitious creator, it may mean taking a more strategic approach to how, when, and where they choose to produce content.

“I’m distributing on [YouTube], I’m paying for everything, I’m getting paid, which is amazing, but now I’ve got to start thinking like a CEO and be like, wait, hold on, strategically, what is my distribution? Where is my next thing coming from?” says Paul.
It’s a question that will be felt across the entertainment world.
This story appeared in the Oct. 21 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine. Click here to subscribe.

items.title: ‘Nobody Wants This’ Season 3 Explained: Does Joanne Finally Convert to Judaism? What Happens to Morgan and Sasha?
items.description: [This story contains MAJOR spoilers from Nobody Wants This season three.]
items.author: Lexi Carson
paragraphs: [This story contains MAJOR spoilers from Nobody Wants This season three.]
Like clockwork, fall means another new season of Nobody Wants This — and after three seasons, we finally have an answer to what happens with Noah and Joanne’s interfaith relationship.

The Netflix rom-com has returned with all 10 episodes of its third season currently streaming, picking up with the couple more serious than ever. They’ve moved in together, and Joanne is attending Jewish conversion classes as she and Noah look to build a future together.

Below, The Hollywood Reporter breaks down the season’s biggest moments, from surprise cameos and new relationships to romantic twists that threaten to complicate things. Read on to find out what happens in season three of Nobody Wants This.
Noah and Joanne Get Engaged

In episode four, Noah (Adam Brody) and Joanne (Kristen Bell) take the next step in their relationship by attending their first wedding together. Noah tells Joanne he has to officiate his friend Brian’s wedding, so she accompanies him as his plus one. However, they nearly miss their flight when Joanne offers her seat to a superfan, Nicole (played in a cameo by series creator Erin Foster). They meet at the airport because the woman reminds her of herself.

Ultimately, they make their flight and head to wine country, where Noah reveals that Brian isn’t real and the wedding was a ploy to get Joanne there so he could propose. With Taylor Swift’s “Lover” playing in the background, the two are officially engaged!

Foster told Netflix Tudum that she was inspired by her own 2019 engagement to her now-husband, Simon Tikhman. “I thought I was going to [another couple’s] vow renewal, and I wasn’t. I was going to my own proposal,” she said. “All roads lead back to me every time.”

The moment some viewers have been waiting for all season finally happens in episode seven: Morgan (Justine Lupe) and Sasha (Timothy Simons) cross the line from friends to lovers. Their relationship reaches a turning point when, at Morgan’s request, Sasha joins her on a trip to New York City, where she appears on Watch What Happens Live With Andy Cohen for her new podcast segment, “Make Them.”

The pair go to dinner, which Sasha calls a date — and Morgan doesn’t correct him — before taking a walk, where Morgan opens up to him more than ever before about her former marriage. They nearly share their first kiss, but Morgan pulls back, insisting that once they cross that boundary, there’s no going back. After all, their siblings are now engaged.
But when they return to the hotel, a few more attempts to resist their chemistry prove futile and they finally give in. However, the morning after changes everything (more on that below).

Following her separation from Sasha, Esther (Jackie Tohn) begins exploring life outside her marriage. Although she initially tells him that dating isn’t her priority, that changes as the season progresses. When Morgan tries to help Sasha move on by creating an online dating profile for him, he discovers Esther is on the app, too, making it clear that she’s putting herself out there and that he should do the same.
Esther also pursues a career in real estate, earning her license and meeting Julian (Steven Weber), a wealthy, older client. The two hit it off and eventually decide to date exclusively.
Morgan, Esther and Sasha’s Love Triangle Is Back

After their romantic night in New York City, Morgan walks out on Sasha the next morning, leaving a note saying she caught an earlier flight. After some time to process her feelings, she realizes she made a mistake and tells Sasha she wants to give their relationship another chance. However, he rejects her, explaining that he isn’t emotionally ready to risk their friendship.

The rejection leaves Morgan unable to stand being in the same room as Sasha, making Noah and Joanne’s wedding planning even more complicated. But that’s not the only relationship drama brewing. In the finale, Esther visits Sasha at his home to drop something off for their daughter and the estranged couple ends up hooking up. The encounter threatens Esther’s relationship with Julian and adds another layer to the already messy Morgan-Sasha dynamic.
Hello, Bravo! Andy Cohen and Ciara Miller Cameos

The Bravo love is strong in season three. Early on, Noah mentions Summer House when he interrupts Joanne while she’s bed-rotting and tells her to stop bingeing the beloved reality series so they can talk.

A few episodes later, Morgan appears on Watch What Happens Live With Andy Cohen for her new podcast segment, with Cohen himself making a cameo in a taped segment of his talk show. Her fellow guest is none other than Ciara Miller, who has starred on Summer House since season five. Miller has also made headlines this year amid the drama surrounding her best friend and castmate Amanda Batula’s relationship with West Wilson, Miller’s ex and another Summer House star.
Christmas Episode Without Chrismukkah

With the penultimate episode of the season centered on Christmas, it seemed like the perfect opportunity to celebrate Chrismukkah — the hybrid Christmas-and-Hanukkah holiday popularized by Seth Cohen (also played by Brody) on Fox’s hit early-2000s series The O.C.

Instead, the episode focuses on Noah trying to make sure Joanne has the best Christmas possible. With her conversion to Judaism approaching, he wants to make the holiday special for her as she prepares for a new chapter in her life. The Christmas episode offers a sweet moment for the couple before the season’s emotional finale.
Joanne Finally Converts to Judaism

One of the biggest questions hanging over the series since season one is finally answered: Will Joanne convert to Judaism? Throughout the season, Joanne takes conversion classes taught by Rabbi Eden (Sarah Silverman), alongside Sebastien (Andrew Rannells). In the finale, she reaches the final step: the mikvah, a ritual immersion that marks her conversion.

The emotional moment takes place in the ocean near the Malibu Beach house where the two families have gathered. As Joanne enters the water and emerges following the ritual, Noah watches with tears in his eyes, moved by the milestone she has reached. After all the questions and uncertainty surrounding her conversion, the moment marks a major turning point for the couple. Rabbi Eden jokes that the next step is for Noah and Joanne to start having kids as they build their Jewish family.
Noah and Joanne Are Married

As if the engagement wasn’t enough of a surprise, Noah and Joanne take their relationship one step further in the season three finale: They get married! After Joanne completes her conversion, the couple reflects on the sacred moment they’ve just shared. But as drama between their families reaches a boiling point — particularly Morgan’s inability to be in the same room as Sasha and Noah’s mother trying to control their wedding plans — they realize they’ve lost sight of what matters most: each other.

Instead of continuing to plan a wedding amid the family tension, Noah asks Rabbi Eden to marry them right there on the beach. Joanne agrees to the spontaneous idea, and they find a stranger walking his dog who happens to be Jewish and can serve as their witness. With Rabbi Eden officiating, Noah and Joanne tie the knot in an intimate beach ceremony, becoming Mr. and Mrs. Roklov.
All 10 episodes Nobody Wants This season three are now streaming on Netflix. Read all of THR’s coverage here.

items.title: Where Do Trends Come From Now?
items.description: A few years ago, during a fit of self-actualization, I got my ears pierced. I don’t have any tattoos, and I’ve never even dyed my hair, so the decision to pierce my ears felt both exciting and personally out of the ordinary. I still don’t quite understand why
items.author: Zack Hauptman
paragraphs: A few years ago, during a fit of self-actualization, I got my ears pierced. I don’t have any tattoos, and I’ve never even dyed my hair, so the decision to pierce my ears felt both exciting and personally out of the ordinary. I still don’t quite understand why I did it. Men have been piercing their ears for centuries, but I suspect, as with so many things we guys also do, particularly where clothes and accessories are concerned, my decision had something to do with tiny hoops being trendy.

Trends are as old as civilization itself, but the speed at which they move in the age of TikTok and AI-driven algorithms has never been faster. Likewise, with a good portion of the global population on some kind of social media, a trend’s reach has never been farther. These changes—exemplified by my sudden, inexplicable desire for hoops—begged a couple of questions: Where do trends come from now? And how do we know when they’ve run their course? For answers, I turned to the people who study trends for a living.

Nick Paget, the senior menswear strategist at trend forecasting company WGSN, believes that “it will be increasingly hard to look back on this decade and say, ‘Ooh, it was all about this kind of styling, this look’ in the way that we used to be able to say about the ’90s, ’80s, ’70s or ’60s.” Nowadays, it’s like every era-based trend has been chucked into a blender and blitzed into oblivion. Institutional tastemakers, including high-fashion designers and magazines such as this one, seemingly have less say than ever.

To understand what consumers want and where they are headed, WGSN has its own methods of analyzing data. According to Paget, the company uses TikTok metrics to monitor various algorithms (a platform they aptly call “TikTok Dashboard”) to get a more holistic view of what users are interested in. “We neutralize the algorithm bias that someone might have if they just use their own account,” he explains. Via this mechanism, they can effectively watch a fashion trend be born on the runway and transform, grow, and die across social platforms.

Take, for example, the recent resurgence of skinny jeans. In this case, Paget casts a wide net about how we got there: “A darker aesthetic has come out of the geopolitical mood,” he says. “And then something happens like designers start talking about skinny jeans again, and we start thinking, well, could the Hedi Slimane kind of dark, grungy, but slightly glamorous rock star be relevant again?”

As any dogged menswear aficionado knows, slim silhouettes and skintight jeans defined Slimane’s tenure at Dior Homme in the early aughts. Slimane’s punky aesthetic, which helped define the decade’s look, is now a key reference in the indie sleaze revival trending on TikTok; their return is also a reaction to the big-pants trend of the last five years.
