items.title: Why I wrote mad letters to celebrities on my mother’s behalf | Psyche Turning Points
items.description: My mother paced the patio, working through that week’s crisis aloud. An office mate, she was certain, was a CIA operative sent to spy on her.
items.author: Joe Mullich
paragraphs: My mother paced the patio, working through that week’s crisis aloud. An office mate, she was certain, was a CIA operative sent to spy on her.

I paced back and forth with her, hoping to shift her attention by describing what happened in my third-grade class. When none of my attempts landed, I went to our mailbox to retrieve the monthly issue of Reader’s Digest. At age eight, I was in love with the English language. I tore open the magazine to a feature called ‘It Pays to Increase Your Word Power’, a list of 10 little-used words. The third item stunned me – ‘sesquipedalianism’. I laughed when I read the definition: using a big word when a small one would do.
Before I realised it, my mother was looming behind me, ever-present cigarette dangling from her mouth. Peering at the long, odd, winding word, she nodded with satisfaction.
‘Al Pacino would understand that word,’ she said. ‘We should write a letter to Al Pacino. He will be able to put a stop to this. And be sure to use that seis-qui-whatever word.’
‘You think Al Pacino would know sesquipedalianism?’
‘Without a doubt! He’s an artist. If we use it in the letter, he’ll know how serious we are.’

I ran to my room. It was always a big moment when my mother came out of her walking fits. The next few minutes were critical in how the rest of her day went. I grabbed a handful of the #2 pencils I always kept sharpened and at the ready.

Initially, my mother simply had me proofread the letters she sent to celebrities asking them to intervene in the vast and ever-expanding conspiracy that was orchestrated against her. We wrote to Neil Armstrong, Walter Cronkite, Sean Connery and many people I did not recognise. Over time, my edits to her letters became so extensive that she decided to just dictate her thoughts and let me compose the missives.
When I came back, she was sitting at the breakfast nook, hands clamped at the edges of the table so tightly her knuckles turned white. I sat across from her.
My mother’s ramblings seemed like radio static while she spoke, and I understood her paranoia only when I translated it onto the page

She took a deep drag from a cigarette. When she looked down at the notebook, with my crisply sharpened #2 pencil hovering over it, her eyes turned into slits. She contemplated how to describe the full array of the injustices against her. In such moments, I would wait silently, sometimes for a few seconds, sometimes for 15 minutes, until the dam burst. At some point, words and thoughts would tumble out of her in turbulent currents. Sometimes the thoughts would contradict and bounce off each other, which only increased the frenzy of her telling.
When she finished, her eyes would be glassy but then focus. ‘You think we have it?’ she asked.
She took a deep drag on her cigarette and then snuffed it out. ‘I need to go lay down. Let me know when it’s done.’

I never took actual notes when she spoke. I just doodled on the notebook. I had learned that my mother’s meaning was never in the words themselves but in-between the words, in the tone, in the pauses, in the way her voice raised and lowered. Random and wild thoughts would fly by me like objects swirling in a tornado.

Her word salad never made sense when she was speaking. However, when I paused to put the jumble into a letter, one stray fact would jump out to me, and immediately lead me to another stray fact, forging a connection I had not noticed until then. My mother’s ramblings seemed like radio static while she spoke, and I understood her paranoia only when I translated it onto the page. In the middle of the tornado that was her mind lurked an eerily calm coherence – one I could reach only by listening and writing my way to its centre.

When I finished the letter, I called to her. She came out of the bedroom and plopped herself on the Naugahyde seats, looking both fascinated and sceptical at the paper I held in my hands. Then I read it aloud:

Only you can help me! This is a FEDERAL matter. They plot against me. I am a single MOTHER with 3 small children. No one is on my side. The father (mama’s boy) does nothing. Please use your connections. I am begging you. All I want is what everyone wants, to be left in peace.
PS You are very handsome! (wink, wink)

Stripped of the frantic energy in her voice, her plea made a kind of sense. She was always complaining about how her co-workers at the US Postal Service were ‘getting in her business’ and how her supervisors would ignore her complaints. I added the underlines, capitalisation and exclamation points because I knew from past letters that she particularly liked how they looked on the page.
‘How did you know all that?’ she asked.
She was not one for affectionate hugs, although she would occasionally goose me or my brothers

She took the yellow legal paper and held it as though it was a Gideon Bible. I had the sense that my mother didn’t really understand what she thought until I wrote it down. When it was read back to her, the magnitude of the situation would awe her. At this moment, we had the deepest connection – perhaps the only true connection – we would have in my lifetime. She stared at the letter in amazement that her pain and suffering could be made comprehensible.
‘You understand!’ she said.
‘It’s really not complicated when you get to the heart of it.’

She tipped her cigarette to me in a kind of salute and gave my hand a squeeze, a gesture that shocked me. She was not one for affectionate hugs, although she would occasionally goose me or my brothers, jabbing a middle finger into our blue jeans as we passed by. ‘Better watch out,’ she would direct. We were all very careful before entering any long, cramped hallway to make sure she wasn’t on the other side.
‘This is an excellent letter,’ she said. ‘I can’t imagine how Al Pacino won’t want to get involved. We need to get him this letter asap!’

She chuckled at the foolishness of my question. ‘Oh, if Al Pacino wants to help, he can help, believe you me. The government isn’t afraid of the little people, like you and me. They piss on the little people. But if the Godfather speaks, they’ll listen.’

I dragged my chair to the closet where we kept the brooms and mops. I stood on the chair to reach the upper shelf, which held a stack of phone directories. I opened up to the P section. There was a long string of Pacinos: A. Pacino, Alberto Pacino, Albert Pacino. I picked one at random.
When I wrote ‘Mr Al Pacino’ on the envelope, she said: ‘No. Make it ‘Senor Al Pacino.’ And put a little wavy thing over the N.’

She wrote ‘personal and confidential’ at the bottom of the letter, added three exclamation points, and circled it twice. She never put her return address on the envelope – ‘for security reasons’. Mrs Bottomfield, the neighbour my mother frequently threatened to kill for spying on her, was watering her lawn. She froze in terror at the sight of my mother. However, my mother was in such a happy mood that she let out a boisterous ‘Good afternoon, Beverly!’ and waved at her nemesis. Mrs Bottomfield waved back warily and slowly backed into her house, peering at us through the screen door until we were a safe distance away.
We walked to the mailbox three streets over. My mother believed it was safer to use ‘anonymous mailboxes’.
After depositing the letter, my mother said: ‘Al Pacino is going to lose it when he gets that letter. All hell is going to break loose. They won’t know what hit them. Let’s go get some ice cream.’
I was in the bubble of her madness, but my notebook – my words – shielded me from becoming consumed
‘Thrifty?’ I said excitedly, referencing the nearby drugstore where they would let you sample several flavours of ice cream before choosing one.
‘You bet! Don’t mention any of this to your brothers. They wouldn’t understand like you do. Let’s keep it just between us.’
Another day, another secret.

When I wrote the letters for my mother, it was the only time I felt we occupied the same plane of reality. I was in the bubble of her madness, but my notebook – my words – shielded me from becoming consumed. I cared about her, but I watched from a distance, and that distance made her trust me, if only for a few minutes since trust was not something she could extend to anyone for a long period. When I started to write a letter from her perspective, everything she said made perfect sense, and it made me sorry for what she was going through.

My mother always made Don Quixote relatable to me. If you saw windmills as hulking giants out to destroy you, tilting at them with a lance was survival, not folly. Everything makes sense if you find the proper angle to view it from.

I had always been a quiet child, who liked to keep to the edges of a room or sit under a table and listen to adults talk at a party. But sitting across from my mother in that breakfast nook, I understood for the first time what I actually was: a translator. My gift was being able to listen to people and understand what they said and what they actually meant. That was the moment I found my calling.

items.title: Living in community is where self-illusions go to die | Aeon Essays
items.description: Earlier this year, I surfaced from sleep to a strange noise, a loud, human singing reverberating through our bedroom ceiling, then a low, almost animal groaning. My husband and I looked at each other. ‘I think Hatty’s in labour,’ he said.
items.author: Elizabeth Oldfield
paragraphs: Earlier this year, I surfaced from sleep to a strange noise, a loud, human singing reverberating through our bedroom ceiling, then a low, almost animal groaning. My husband and I looked at each other. ‘I think Hatty’s in labour,’ he said.

The rest of the day proceeded in the usual way, getting breakfast for our children, dropping them off at school, meetings, emails, booking in the car for an MOT, but these activities were interspersed with opening the door to midwives, making cups of tea for Hatty, and finding towels to drape around the birth pool that had appeared in our living room. Towards evening, our eighth housemate appeared in a rush of fluids. Two ambulance-loads of paramedics stood around like a flock of green and yellow London parakeets, blessedly unrequired. At one point, there were nine medical professionals, seven housemates, two grandparents of the new arrival and a cat in our terraced London house. It didn’t even feel that full, I thought later, as I poured bleach on bloodstained towels and binned a discarded catheter that had been overlooked in a corner.

I am 42, and I did not expect to end up here. Like most of my peers, I was handed a vision of a home worth striving for with far, far fewer people in it and, to begin with, I followed that script. A middle-class 1980s child, I did well at school, moved away from my home county dormitory town for university, and never went back. London, jobs at the BBC, running a think tank all followed. I lived with good friends, and juggled seeing others between our clashing personal schedules. Then people began to pair up and procreate. I met someone, followed suit, and we clawed our way onto the very bottom of the housing ladder. It was a lovely life. A bit relentless, perhaps, a bit lonely around the edges, too, as the schedules got ever harder to tessellate, the work and care burdens heavier. But we had done it. Our little dyad, with dependants, was standing on its own feet, even if something felt decidedly unstable underneath.

More space, more privacy, more control – all are sold as natural, unquestioned goods to be sought in the unconscious script that most of us carry. For the nuclear family, they are tokens of success and maturity, whereas forgoing these ‘goods’ and living with people you are neither shagging nor parenting has an association with low-status, studenty seasons. Not for proper grownups. My husband and I began to feel the strengthening drag of this story. I sometimes saw it in my mind’s eye as a tide, washing young adults from their family homes into temporarily intertwined clusters (largely in cities), then out again, to the suburbs and beyond, in pairs or alone, in search of a garden, a bigger kitchen, storage space for the mountains of stuff we inevitably accumulate. Swept away from each other, everyone further and further apart.

Every policy issue we researched at the think tank led back inexorably to disconnection. It was labelled different things (overconsumption, fraying trust, the corrosion of democracy, crises of loneliness, mental health, care, climate, housing). But a thread linked them all: our inability to bear each other, to share (our stuff, space, skills, and deepest selves) was actively making the world worse. I came across thinkers who shared my intuition that something largely invisible but all-encompassing was getting in the way of our being together as healthier cultures remembered how to do. Some called it individualism or modernity. Others blamed ‘the machine’ of late-stage capitalism. I never settled on a name I liked, but I felt the disquiet of it. Still, all the intelligent analysis and critique never quite seemed to lead to progressive action, but instead to a conservative turn that half-appealed in its communitarianism and rooted localism, but not in its approach to women and ‘outsiders’.

The message seems to be that the price we pay for the freedoms of liberal individualism is loneliness. You can have personal autonomy, privacy and endless choice; you can outsource most of your needs to the market rather than navigate complex non-transactional relationships with other people that tie you into reciprocity; you can optimise your surroundings, appearance and experiences to your exact preferences, but what gets bundled in for good measure is a sense of existential weightlessness.

I rebelled. Surely there was something between atomisation – what the philosopher Charles Taylor calls the ‘buffered self’ – and hierarchical, authoritarian community; between girl-boss and trad-wife. The final push to try and find it, ultimately, was fear. When my first child was born, the reality of the climate crisis moved from a theoretical policy problem to one that bubbled acidly in my belly, settled itself in my bones. I had brought this powerless being into a world on fire, and the idea that hard work and individual accumulation could keep her safe stopped making sense. The need to be part of a thick web of humans who would not play a passing role in each other’s lives but commit to costly mutual care felt urgent as the ground bucked and roiled beneath our feet. I wanted ‘a village’, as we say now, not for the golden Instagram images of laughing friends around a photogenic table, but because, in my bleakest moments, I thought it might be essential for survival.

It is a truism that early parenthood is isolating and relentless, but does it have to be? We started questioning accepted norms, not idly fantasising about building a commune but taking serious steps. I wanted to live this season of our lives up close with others, witnessing each other, supporting each other. Not uploading the tidied-up details into group chats, after the fact, or smoothing the misery into memes, holding back the joys for fear of sounding smug. This realisation cracked outwards, connecting with a deeper intuition: I wanted all of life to be like that. I wanted to see and be seen. It felt wrong that everyone didn’t live this way, like something important had been lost in the rush to accumulate stuff and protect our security, status and autonomy by disappearing behind our own front doors.

Whether you call the present a polycrisis or just a gigantic roiling clusterfuck, I became more convinced that the medicine for most of our ills is to actively and counterculturally move towards other people. To resist the powerful forces driving us apart. There are lots of ways of doing this, of course. But letting go of the idea that our homes must be private retreats from other people seemed a decent place to start. I believe that our homes can be places to relearn the habits of reciprocity, sharing and mutual care that for most of history (and, in many parts of the non-Western world, still) are the defining characteristics of a culture worthy of the name. A culture we are urgently going to need.
This sounds much, much simpler and easier than it is.

For us, it took years of intentional conversations, initial enthusiasm from others that then petered out, bureaucratic wrangling, and research. We eventually found people who were equally committed (who were not, interestingly, friends already), and rented together to test it. We learned to navigate sex noises and bathroom smells (sound-proofing and background music helps a lot with the first). We had tense conversations about kitchen storage, our different expectations around spending and cleanliness. It surfaced stuff from our childhoods, which we then had to be honest about and confront. The process (much of which happened during COVID-19 lockdowns, which I’m sure accelerated it) was challenging and exposing, almost unbearably uncomfortable at times.
As I held him at 4 am, my son asked: ‘Why couldn’t we stay in our flat, just us?’

We also practised rupture and repair, realising that, even as we saw the most ridiculous, fragile, defensive parts of each other, we were not running away. In his play The Real Thing (1982), Tom Stoppard aptly defined love as ‘Knowledge of each other … knowledge of self, the real him, the real her, in extremis, the mask slipped from the face.’ In the course of our building trust, it did feel a lot like love. Not love based on surface similarities or romance, but on a mutual commitment to each other. It felt like growing up. The existential emptiness, the unsteady sense of vertigo eased.

Having tested the concept, we embarked on a labyrinthically complex joint house-purchase. It fell through on the day of a long-delayed exchange, after we’d reached the end of the notice period on our rental. For months, we had no fixed address and scattered to the sofas and spare beds of friends and family. My youngest child began having nightmares. As I held him at 4 am, he asked: ‘Why couldn’t we stay in our flat, just us?’ The script glowed temptingly. If living with others was the answer, surely it shouldn’t be this difficult. We held our nerve.

To date, we have lived up close – bodily fluids close – with people we are not related to for nearly six years. We share all the space in our jointly mortgaged home except the bedrooms. We pool most of our money, cook, shop, pray and host hundreds of guests a year, together. And we manage countless petty conflicts, over the milk or the dishwasher or the crumbs on the side, conflicts that often mask deeper questions: who do I belong to? Where can I be really at home, be really myself? Who am I becoming, alongside these people? And are we able, when it comes down to it, to be each other’s safety?

There are very few models for what we are doing. Perhaps the most robust is the monastic tradition. Most orders of religious Sisters or Brothers see the proximity of living up close with each other as essential to spiritual growth. It is precisely in the discomfort of being witnessed, up close, at our worst, in being asked to compromise preferences, to share and serve others, they argue, that we really grow up.
Living with others has shown me things in myself that I would prefer to ignore

My policy-wonk brain knew there were systems keeping us apart. Not just social scripts but monetary policies, mortgage terms, HMO (house in multiple occupation) legislation. Yet living communally has taught me that it is also what is inside us that makes it hard to be together. My romantic ideas about cultures worthy of the name, marked by interdependence and mutual care, clearly also require certain kinds of people – with emotional skills, developed character, an ability to make lasting commitments. None of which my individualistic formation had gifted me an abundance of.

Living with others has shown me things in myself that I would prefer to ignore. How much of me is still a child, wanting my way, quick to cry ‘it’s not fair’. I have been learning all this as the world around us unravels. The contrast is disconcerting. If it really is the end of the world, at least as we have known it, then what kind of people will be needed? What would it take to be braver, more resilient and flexible, more joyful, creative and free? A person who could, at bloody least, wait patiently to go in the bathroom, or let someone else use a favourite mug. Someone able to sacrifice sleep to care for another’s child, and have the hard conversation about a failure to mop the kitchen floor, rather than avoiding it. I want to learn these habits. I have a hunch that much more than this might be asked of me. Of all of us.

This project finds faint echoes in the self-improvement, self-development, self-optimisation we are all constantly hectored into – therapy (or psychedelics, or stoicism) for the mind and Hyrox (or reformer Pilates, or yoga) for the body (with those who are not working on themselves in some way being the exception). Interestingly, the unconventional way our household lives is rarely recommended to those seeking self-knowledge or self-development. The standard advice is an inward turn in order to facilitate a private excavation of an authentic self, along with strong personal boundaries that draw distinct lines between that self and others. Porousness tends to be framed as deleterious to Project Self. Most monastic orders encourage periods of solitude and silence, to be sure, but much of daily life is spent in an exposing proximity to others, the very idea of which would bring most of us out in hives.

This difficult proximity, where we witness and are witnessed without our protective, polished personas is an immensely powerful change agent. You can see it in action in group therapy, the recovery movement and some short-term intensive self-development programmes, but this powerful ‘technology of the self’, to use Michel Foucault’s phrase, is vanishingly rare. This kind of witnessing (during my housemate’s labour, for example, I witnessed parts of her that only her partner otherwise sees) is effective because change requires us to be honest about who we currently are. Living in community is where illusions about the self go to die!

One of the phrases we use a lot in our household is ‘We are made for each other and we are made by each other.’ Marxists such as Silvia Federici call this ‘social reproduction’. Neurologically, this makes sense: human interaction shapes our brains from our very earliest moments. Every human comes into the world in search of a gaze.

The day the baby was born, while their mother was being stitched up and I was moving bins for the paramedics, my primary-school aged son was one of the first people to hold the tiny form. They’d wrapped the baby in a yellow foil survival bag, and he gazed down for long minutes with as much attention as if he was indeed holding a giant Quality Street toffee. This baby had moved from deep bodily entanglement, hidden in just one of us, to a less visible but no less profound interdependence. They have now been held by more arms than your average Western infant, and whether it’s mum, dad, us housemates, family, neighbours or church friends, we all adopt the same posture as my son. Face turned towards face. Eyes meeting eyes. The baby makes noises, and we make noises back. And as we gaze and gurgle, the mycelia of their brain are forming.

Dan Siegel, the clinical psychiatrist and founder of interpersonal neurobiology, says that our earliest relationships ‘shape the very neural structures that create representations of experience and allow a coherent view of the world: Interpersonal experiences directly influence how we mentally construct reality.’ The connections formed by the face-dancing we all instinctively do with babies help create the conditions that enable them to experience what is real. More than this, these gazes are where their sense of self comes from. Siegel says that, beyond these earliest experiences of connection, relationships shape, throughout our lives, ‘how we feel, how we think, how we remember things, how we tell the story of who we are, the sense of self … what gives you a sense of purpose.’ We become who we become because of who we gaze on, and who gazes back at us.
We talk a lot about exits, about the fact that we will probably not live together forever

The porousness of babies to their caregivers, and especially their need for face-to-face connection is widely understood. The neuropsychologist Allan Schore calls a baby an ‘open dynamic system’. What our house is helping me see is how much humans remain ‘open systems’, and how much mind/self/soul (all translations of the word ‘psyche’) arises within and between us. We are not closed selves, semaphoring information to each other and making free rational choices. We are always makers of each other – the act of mutual witnessing, or its lack, moulding us like wet clay.

One way of thinking about our unconventional living situation, then, is that it offers a way of choosing who we want to be formed by, as if consciously curating the powerful gaze of others. Our bet is that the real costs, in control, convenience and comfort, the exposure of being seen and known ‘with masks slipped from faces’, are worth it. I believe that it is a demanding but effective method of becoming the kind of people the world needs now.

I could be wrong. I am not rosy-tinted about the realities of experiments like these, how badly they can hurt people if done poorly. The way we live may not last. We commit, unlike monks and nuns, only in five-year increments. This season has been the most meaningful, the most beautiful and the most fun of my life, despite the challenges. It has made me braver, and freed up swathes of time and energy that I would have otherwise spent on home admin in a household of only two adults. It is working, really working, for now, but we are realists. We talk a lot about exits, about the fact that we will probably not live together forever. Perhaps we’re trying to have our cake and eat it, keeping one foot in the autonomy of liberal individualism even as we experience the benefits of rooted, committed mutual care. Our experiment is imperfect. My hunch, though, is that we are going to need more of them.

As a society, we are still largely in denial about the scale of the existential threats facing us, and against which individualism cannot keep us safe. In times of deep ecological, technological and political crisis, we may be forced to remember how to be each other’s safety. To unpick, laboriously, the conditioning of the weird, prosperous West and call bullshit on the lie that control, accumulation and a frictionless, precision-optimised life was ever going to make us happy. Though I know it’s a lie, a lot of me still wants it. However, as I learn every day how deeply the script of individualism has formed me, I also see how poorly it serves us.

Each day that I wake up in this house, I am choosing to enact a different script, one in which other people’s concerns are more real to me. My housemate’s labour pains, this baby’s cries, are my business. Conversely, my occasional existential terror or my children’s school struggles are tangible to a wider group of people than they would otherwise be. We have a stake in each other. There is a fierce tenderness in it that often brings me to tears. Iris Murdoch describes something like it in ‘The Sublime and The Good’ (1959) when she writes:

Love is the extremely difficult realisation that something other than oneself is real. Love … is the discovery of reality … The exercise of overcoming one’s self, of the expulsion of fantasy and convention … is indeed exhilarating. It is also, if we perform it properly which we hardly ever do, painful.

Isolation allows us to maintain all kinds of illusions about ourselves and about others. In contrast, remaining tethered to a shared reality requires us to really see others, not in the refracted fun-house mirror of social media, but in regular, embodied ways. We triangulate the world via other people, taking readings from a range of perspectives to build a more accurate picture of things. My image of this process is of humans echolocating like bats, where the objects sounding back are the voices and faces of other people. René Descartes might have thought he needed to withdraw from society completely to find truth but, respectfully, he was wrong. Turning in, pulling away disorientates us. The social theorist Sarah Stein Lubrano argues that the more time we spend alone, the more prone we are to delusion. Communities like ours are often laughed at, written off as naive, but if our minds do indeed require a thick web of strong relational connections in order to grasp reality, then we weirdos are possibly learning to see the world more clearly.
Our community (and other lasting ones) hold together by turning attention beyond ourselves

Why, then, are experiments like ours so rare? Why do I, a public advocate, a recipient of the very real benefits of communal living, still feel conflicted about arguing more strongly for it to become the norm? It is partly that such a life is, as Murdoch says, painful. Decentering my preferences, letting go of my self-aggrandising illusions hurts. These are growing pains, every one worth it – but still. Inviting others into something this rigorous, and costly, is not in fashion.

There is another reason. The community we live in offers mutual witnessing, mutual recognition, increased capacity and care, and economies of scale, but this alone is not enough to hold us when it all feels too much. When people come to our home wanting advice about setting up something similar, we always tell them: community for the sake of community doesn’t work. Communes might be highly effective sites of self-formation, but the ones designed primarily to do that will likely collapse. My experience is that our community (and other lasting ones) hold together by turning attention beyond ourselves. The ability to locate the project in a vision of the good – political, ecological, philosophical or other – is an essential foundation.

There is something about our house I have not mentioned much. You may have caught that throwaway line about praying together. One of the arguments made by Charles Taylor and others about the isolating tendencies of modernity is that it is linked to secularity. He argues that pre-moderns had a much stronger sense of how porous they were, how bound up with each other, with nature, and with divine or magical presences. He links our increasingly boundaried or buffered sense of self to the loss of religion: we moderns are not made by and for god(s), by and for each other, but by and for ourselves. I have some sympathy with the argument, because without a robust, collective wisdom tradition, it is challenging to keep choosing to move towards each other. Despite believing in this way of life for policy reasons, emotional reasons, neurobiological reasons, even goddamn survival reasons, I am not sure I would be able to do it without a powerful, and in our case, religious, reason why.

When asked to sum up his teaching, Jesus offered two, interlinked commands. Firstly, love of the divine (Love the Lord your God ‘with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength’) then, love of the other (‘Love your neighbour as yourself’). No moral prescriptions or religious ritualism, but relationality as The Way. I have spent a lot of time sitting with the work that the word ‘as’ is doing in ‘love your neighbour as your self’. In the same measure you love yourself? At the same time as? Because they are yourself? Even when they have left beard clippings all over the sink?
The petty squabbles between early believers trying to share are there in the New Testament for all to see

Helpfully, Jesus had a lot of other less cryptic things to say about learning to bear each other and be together. The New Testament takes it as a given that humans are messy, dishonest, selfish, misguided, that we will hurt and anger each other. We may be made for and by each other, but it assumes there will be days when we wish we were not. This tendency to disconnect, this almost gravitational pulling away from each other led Martin Luther, building on Augustine, to call us ‘Homo incurvatus in se’: humanity turned in on itself. I find it one of the more useful definitions of sin.

The New Testament is largely a set of letters between what we might see as communitarian experiments, and reckoning with our inward-turning tendencies. The petty squabbles between early believers trying to share their lives and possessions are there on the page for all to see. The difficulty was part of the point, not a reason to avoid it.

This realism might be why, despite its very real benefits, this is not a full-throated advertisement for communal life. The costs are real, so you need a powerful story to hold you. A completely different script of what a good life looks like. I don’t think it necessarily has to be a religious one, but it does need to be powerful, and go beyond individual interest. Setting up my life for mutual care and reciprocity is the best thing I have ever done, but its chafing against the script I was born into still leaves blisters sometimes. On days when it asks more of me than I am receiving, it is the ‘why’ that makes me stay.

I hope that, collectively, we can (re)discover some big whys, that more people are inspired to experiment with moving towards each other. I think the upending of the world by climate change, AI and all their currently unforeseen effects will likely force us into it. It is, ultimately, soul work. Our household has had a few years’ head start, no more than a foundation course, yet it is getting easier as the vestiges of the old script become threadbare. I think – I hope? – that I am more patient and less petty; more steady and less resistant to sharing. More oriented towards a rigorous love, and so a tiny bit more of use in this hurting world. Whether that is in fact reality or self-delusion is a question you would have to ask my housemates.

items.title: Jordan Casteel on Hilma af Klint’s Watercolours, Nature and Mothering
items.description: Artist Jordan Casteel is known for her luminous, large-scale portraits, still lifes and landscapes. Winter Sun, an exhibition of her work, opens today at Thaddaeus Ropac’s Marais gallery in Paris
items.author: Laura Allsop
paragraphs: Artist Jordan Casteel is known for her luminous, large-scale portraits, still lifes and landscapes. Winter Sun, an exhibition of her work, opens today at Thaddaeus Ropac’s Marais gallery in Paris
This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:

“I found this watercolour in a book from my studio library – Hilma af Klint: What Stands Behind the Flowers. It’s been open to this page for the past few months as I paint and it stands out among the other works I’ve been looking at for its documentary quality. I was drawn to the sensitivity that af Klint brings to the relationship between nature and observation. The composition feels similar to a diagram but still rooted in what was directly in front of her. She’s gathering multiple ways of seeing into a single image, paying close attention to colour and form, adding handwritten notes. The subjects begin to carry something more interior or symbolic. That combination speaks to the way I work in my own paintings, bringing together multiple images, observations and memories to arrive at a final point of view. My son was born in April of this year, so nearly everything I’ve engaged with since then has had him in mind as I shift perspective and take on this new role of mother. A lot of mothering, I find, is the observing and record-taking that is essential to care. It’s possible I was drawn to af Klint’s studies and her notes for their similarity to the notes I’m taking regularly of my child’s development. Seeds and newborns are wildly different, don’t get me wrong, but both involve paying attention to small changes over time and responding to what is needed.”

In Hilma af Klint’s 1919 botanical painting Convolvulus arvensis (Field Bindweed), Monotropa hypopitys (Pinesap), trailing bindweed and earthy pinesap frame a pair of curious celestial objects that hover in the centre of the composition. The piece is part of the pioneering Swedish artist and mystic’s Nature Studies portfolio (1919–20) – drawings of flowering plants accompanied by esoteric diagrams and a related notebook ascribing a spirit to each specimen. Nature Studies has kept the artist Jordan Casteel company as she prepares for her autumn exhibition, Winter Sun, at Thaddaeus Ropac’s Marais gallery in Paris – a reminder “that subtle examinations of environments can capture the essence of the human condition”. Casteel is known primarily for her luminous, large-scale portraits of her community, producing still lifes and landscape paintings that shimmer with the same attention to detail and interiority. Based in New York, the artist captures her surroundings with a loving sensitivity to their subtleties.

This story features in the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue, marking 25 years of AnOther Magazine, on sale internationally now. Order here. Winter Sun is on display at Thaddaeus Ropac Paris Marais until 23 December

items.title: Inside Lego x Daft Punk – a new partnership inspired by fans
items.description: Lego’s regular forays into the infinite realms of pop culture are becoming more and more involved. Aside from the big-ticket licensing tie-ins – Minecraft, Star Wars, Pokémon, Harry Potter, Lord of the Rings, etc – there have also been high-profile collaborati
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: Lego’s regular forays into the infinite realms of pop culture are becoming more and more involved. Aside from the big-ticket licensing tie-ins – Minecraft, Star Wars, Pokémon, Harry Potter, Lord of the Rings, etc – there have also been high-profile collaborations with Pharrell Williams, Olivia Rodrigo, as well as various football and F1 stars.

Now the brick builders have reached out and added another creative to their closet. French electro duo Daft Punk are the newest sign-ups to the world of Lego, promising a fresh take on Lego’s blend of ‘music, culture and creative experimentation’.

So what will Daft Punk bring to the party? After all, Thomas Bangalter and Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo officially disbanded their act back in 2021, having founded Daft Punk in 1993. The duo enjoyed a career that mixed highly performative anonymity, stunning live and video visuals, not to mention hit after hit after hit.

Few modern artists – let alone those working in the realm of dance music – have shaped, projected and sustained such a well-curated image as Bangalter and de Homem-Christo. It’s therefore unsurprising to find that Daft Punk™ (note the trademark) is very much a going concern, with creative director Cédric Hervet overseeing a host of posthumous projects that includes remixes, reissues, soundtracks, and high-profile partnerships with the likes of Fortnite.

Lego is the latest brand to come knocking. The collaboration was made concrete by a film featuring Daft Punk’s tracks ‘Voyager’ and ‘Human After All’. It’s a pairing that has its origins in a couple of Lego-related events, starting with the duo’s minifig cameo in the Pharrell Williams 2024 brick-built biopic Piece by Piece, followed by an appearance on the Lego Ideas fan creation site, with Daft Punk Concert, a set suggested by super-fan Patrick Harboun and his son.

That representation of the Daft Punk ‘pyramid’ stage set (from the 2007 Alive tour) will go into production next year, the first in what is hoped will be a series of related sets. It's only hinted at in today's launch film, which follows the Daft Punk robotic minifigures along a holographic red brick road through a neon-streaked landscape, leading to a concert venue that builds itself around them.
Wallpaper* spoke with Cédric Hervet about the scope and scale of the collaboration and what it means for the enduring power of the Daft Punk name.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.
Wallpaper*: What can the Lego Universe do for DP's legacy, given that the group only exists as a cultural force and not an active music duo these days?

Cédric Hervet: To me, Daft Punk never stopped existing. A legacy doesn't end when you stop making new work. Our creative outset with the Lego team has been to look at legacy not as something static, but an invitation to innovate and create. The music, the robots, the pyramid all live on through the fans, who keep making them their own. My role today is to look after that world and open up new territory for it. And that's exactly the spirit of Lego creativity: you build, you take it apart, you build again.
W*: Do you see any parity between the technology of the Lego brand and the way DP presented themselves over their career?

CH: For me, the common ground is imagination. Lego bricks are an extraordinary tool for creativity: you're handed some bricks, and it's up to you to build whatever is possible with them. That's also how Daft Punk started. Thomas and Guy-Man wanted to make electronic music, so they bought a bit of gear, figured it out, and created with what they had.

As a kid, just the Lego packaging or the pages of the holiday catalogues made me feel like I was stepping into another world. You wanted to know what was hiding behind a Lego City building. With Daft Punk, we always played on that: leaving people room for their own imagination, their own interpretation.
W*: What are you most excited about with this collaboration? The sets? The technology? The new audience?

CH: First, something very personal. I've always loved Lego toys, and I dreamed about this collaboration for years. I still have to pinch myself. I played with Lego bricks as a kid, I spent many hours being creative with my children using them and as recently as last winter I was still giving them Lego Advent calendars. They're 20 and 19 now, which tells you it hasn't aged a day.

I also sometimes ask them whether Daft Punk's music sounds dated, because when you're inside it, it's hard to have perspective. Apparently it still feels very current to them. And then there's the pyramid. I was lucky enough to work on the stage design for the Alive 2007 tour.

Every night, I watched the show from the side of the pyramid. I was the audience's audience. Seeing thousands of people dance with smiles on their faces for an hour and a half was the greatest reward. So, seeing that pyramid come back in bricks, imagined by a father and his son during lockdown, is the link between generations I'd been dreaming of.
W*: How did the collaboration come about - who approached who?

CH: To be honest, on our side, we had tried to approach the Lego Group several years ago. To me the connection was obvious, but the timing probably wasn't right yet. What really unlocked it was the fans.

The Lego Ideas Daft Punk Concert project won the Music to Our Ears challenge in 2020, then reached 10,000 supporters. This gave us an opportunity to see how naturally the two worlds fit together: ethically, aesthetically, culturally. The fact that fans made this collaboration possible is wonderful to me. Daft Punk's story is also a story of fans inspired by other artists.
W*: How do you see the partnership with the Lego Group evolving over time?

CH: We're only at the first few bricks. The Lego universe is vast, and just seeing the two little robots, GM08 and TB3, step into it means a lot to me. They'll get to live their own lives there. I really love the Lego tone, especially in its animated content. It's a lot of fun, and it reveals a different, slightly offbeat side of the characters.

You get a first glimpse of that in the AV. The pyramid set is a first step. Beyond that, I can't say more for now, but I can’t wait to see this partnership unfold based on what brought it to life: fans sharing with each other and passing on creative experimentation from one generation to the next.

Jonathan Bell has written for Wallpaper* magazine since 1999, covering everything from architecture and transport design to books, tech and graphic design. He is now the magazine’s Transport and Technology Editor. Jonathan has written and edited 15 books, including Concept Car Design, 21st Century House, and The New Modern House, and co-edits the long-running things magazine weblog.

items.title: Best of Design Miami Paris 2026 – it’s aglow with highlights
items.description: 'What a relief to see the Americans showed up,' murmured a Parisian art dealer at the opening of Design Miami Paris 2026, just days after rioting shook the capital. Indeed, both the fair organisers themselves and a number of deep-pocketed collectors came, unda
items.author: Amy Serafin
paragraphs: 'What a relief to see the Americans showed up,' murmured a Parisian art dealer at the opening of Design Miami Paris 2026, just days after rioting shook the capital. Indeed, both the fair organisers themselves and a number of deep-pocketed collectors came, undaunted, for the fourth edition at L'Hôtel de Maisons, displaying 140 years of design and decorative arts from around the world.
Take a tour of Design Miami Paris 2026

The show starts in the courtyard with a huge bronze bear by François-Xavier Lalanne from Galerie Mitterrand, a delightful wooden pavilion with three faces designed by Volumnia's Michele De Lucchi, and 'Arabesque', Pierre Renart's monumental bench crafted from a 17m-long twisted ribbon of weather-resistant moabi wood, winner of the Best Design at Large Presentation award (from Maison Parisienne Gallery).

In the vast gardens behind the 18th-century mansion where Karl Lagerfeld once lived, visitors marvel at the 1944 6x6 Demountable House by Jean Prouvé, clad in timber and decorated like a Japanese tea house, presented by Galerie Patrick Seguin.

This year's Best Gallery Presentation award went to Salon 94 Design, which juxtaposes sculptural works by Alberto and Diego Giacometti with antler stools and other brutalist furniture by contemporary designer Rick Owens.
Director Jackie Greenberg says, 'We knew we were bringing the Giacometti, and we've worked with Rick for a very long time, so it just seemed obvious for them to coexist in the space together.'

'It came out beautifully,' said Owens of the stand as he wandered through the fair with his wife, Michèle Lamy. 'They're opening the Giacometti Foundation next to our house. I always thought, Alberto Giacometti – he lived in squalor, in that artist's studio, and that's what I want our house to look like.'

Italians are prominent at this year's fair. Milan's Nilufar is showing a mix of vintage pieces by the likes of Carlo Bugatti and Gabriella Crespi, alongside contemporary collectible design. Hanging above their stand is the newest version of an annual favourite, a sinuous ceiling lamp in bronze and coloured Murano glass by Christian Pellizzari, this year with seashells at the tips rather than flowers.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

Nearby, StudioDanielK's paravent in white parchment and solid bronze opens to reveal a bar in high-gloss Brazilian rosewood. 'It has a little table so you can prepare your cocktail here,' says designer Daniel Kolodziejczak. First shown at Salone del Mobile, it comes in a limited edition of six, customisable with different parchments and woods.

The Paris-based Galerie Pron, formerly Galerie Italienne, is presenting a colourful and eclectic assortment, including a cabinet with a signature tartan pattern by contemporary ceramic artist Alice Gavalet, and a hammock woven in Nicaragua in 1974, based on an Alexander Calder design. 'This is one of the few in very, very good condition,' says director Matteo Da Dalt.

Scandinavians are well represented, too. Galerie Maria Wettergren brought a new wall installation called ‘Jade’ by Norwegian fibre artist Gjertrud Hals, woven in green and turquoise threads, like jellyfish attached to the wall. Nearby, Mathias Bengtsson's cast and polished stainless steel ‘Membrane’ chair won the fair's award for Best Contemporary Work. 'He conceived it by using a computer program where a digital seed makes the form grow as a living organism,' says Wettegren. 'So it's no longer an imitation of an organic form, it's actually a simulation.'

The New York gallery Hostler Burrows is showing an oversized hand-tufted carpet by Louise Hederström, ‘September’, a tapestry in autumnal shades with various layers of pile. It was woven at the venerable Kasthall mill in Sweden, using materials from the archives of its former lead designer, Gunilla Lagerhem Ullberg.

The Stockholm gallery Modernity makes its fair debut in a spacious pale blue room that happened to be the perfect size for a seven-metre-long knotted pile rug in forest and river shades, crafted in 1952 by Swedish artist Margareta Sundbom-Eichenholtz.

The stand also brought Uno Åhrén's high-backed easy chair with sweeping mahogany lines, first shown at the 1925 Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels (the centenary of which was celebrated last year). 'The exhibition in Paris was Sweden's breakthrough in design,' says Andrew Duncanson. 'Sweden won 26 prizes there, only second to France.'

Of course, French 20th-century design is also plentiful, with exceptional pieces by masters from Robert Mallet-Stevens to Le Corbusier, along with Thomas Fritsch's impressive collection of post-war ceramics. At the Galerie Scène Ouverte, a contemporary French ceramicist, Adélie Ducasse, is showing her first piece in glass, a spherical dark blue lamp made with Venini in Murano.

The one-year old Dubai gallery The A/P Room stops visitors in their tracks with Rogan Gregory's furry biomorphic chandelier and floor lamps, mixing goat fur or horsehair with bronze, ceramic and alabaster, light peeking through the strands of hair. 'It's like a creature. I love the ambiguity between the object and a living thing,' says the gallery's founder, Christelle Basilla, who contrasted the lamps with Brazilian modernism.

Meanwhile, a French-American trio of veteran dealers, Oscar Graf, Robert Kaplan and James Zemaitis, have joined forces to present masterworks of modern design from the 1870s to the 1960s. Their stand is small but packs a punch, with a Joseph Hoffman chair designed for the dining room of the Purkersdorf Sanatorium in Vienna, De Stijl architect Gerrit Rietveld's asymmetrical ‘Berlin’ chair (which belonged to artist Donald Judd), and a Frank Lloyd Wright living room chair from the Ward W Willits house in Highland Park, Illinois.

The Wright chair won the fair's award for Best Work of Historical Design. 'The house was considered Wright's first masterwork of Prairie School design, and he did almost all the furniture,' says Kaplan, adding that most of the pieces are now in museum collections, aside from this one, which formerly belonged to the visionary collector Daniel Wolf. 'It was one chair, not repeated in the house, and not repeated in another commission, so it is truly unique.

Artists' jewellery is another important theme. Elisabetta Cipriani Wearable Art brought new pieces from the Cosmic Jewelry collaboration with renowned textile artist Sheila Hicks, first presented earlier this year at the Venice Biennale. Hicks, who often works at architectural scale, shrank her weavings down to wearable size, wrapping precious stones, vintage pearls, fossils and coral from Cipriani's own collection in colourful silk and wool threads, for round Boules brooches and loom-shaped pendants.

MiniMasterpiece deals in jewellery made by artists, designers and architects; recently, owner Esther de Beaucé convinced the 85-year-old German minimalist artist Franz Erhard Walther to try his hand. The result is a stunning ladder of three half-circles in gold-plated brass, in a limited series of 50. The gallery also has a rare pair of necklaces by Argentine sculptor Luis Quesada, layered from slices of precious woods in the 1960s and 1970s. 'He never made them before or after,' says de Beaucé, who acquired these from the artist's daughter.

This is the second year for the initiative Designers of Tomorrow, sponsored by Apple to spotlight emerging design studios. While the four projects here used a certain amount of tech to produce, they all revealed an astonishing quantity (and quality) of handiwork, from Isabel Rower hand-rolling hundreds of ceramic beads to Yoonjeong Lee meticulously layering 5,000 thin sheets of wood veneer.
Even in our fast-paced, tech-fuelled world, it's evidence that young designers are firmly wedded to the idea of craftsmanship, for pieces that may one day be vintage collectibles in their own right.
Design Miami Paris is on view until 25 October 2026, L'hôtel de Maisons, 51 Rue de l'Université, 75007 Paris

Amy Serafin, Wallpaper’s Paris editor, has 20 years of experience as a journalist and editor in print, online, television, and radio. She is editor in chief of Impact Journalism Day, and Solutions & Co, and former editor in chief of Where Paris. She has covered culture and the arts for The New York Times and National Public Radio, business and technology for Fortune and SmartPlanet, art, architecture and design for Wallpaper*, food and fashion for the Associated Press, and has also written about humanitarian issues for international organisations.

items.title: Hannah Einbinder wants you to scream - A Rabbit's Foot
items.description: The star of Hacks returns as the lead in Jane Schoenbrun’s Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, the year’s most hyped indie film. Kitty Grady meets Hannah Einbinder in New York—with an accompanying shoot at Collier Schorr’s Brooklyn studio—to discuss Gillian
items.author: Kitty Grady
paragraphs: The star of Hacks returns as the lead in Jane Schoenbrun’s Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, the year’s most hyped indie film. Kitty Grady meets Hannah Einbinder in New York—with an accompanying shoot at Collier Schorr’s Brooklyn studio—to discuss Gillian Anderson, unconventional love stories, and Hollywood’s political consciousness.

The day after I speak to Hannah Einbinder, she goes on the Today Show—one of America’s biggest daily talk programmes—and invites the nation to scream. Dressed in a bright red Loewe top, the actor and comedian, 31, tells an anecdote about how she saw a reiki healer in Ojai, California, who encouraged her to rechannel emotion towards her lungs, to convert feelings of sadness into the more cathartic act of yelling. At the count of three, Einbinder, a perfectly coiffed host, and a live audience, yell in unison. “It feels like I’m the only one who did it,” says Einbinder.

The interview is part of the press tour for Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, beloved auteur Jane Schoenbrun’s latest film about a young queer filmmaker called Kris (Einbinder) tasked with rebooting a cult 1980s slasher franchise. Kris heads to an abandoned summer camp, where Billy Presley (Gillian Anderson), the “final girl” in the original film, still resides. A Norma Desmond-esque recluse, she is loomed over by the spectre of Little Death, the franchise’s “monster”—a former camp kid who oscillates between genders. A psychosexual two-hander, in the film Kris’s artistic journey intertwines with a journey to explore their own sexuality with Billy. Like Schoenbrun’s previous work (I Saw the TV Glow (2024), We Are All Going the World’s Fair (2021)), the film is intricately metatextual, with Lynchian cameos, campy product placement, and fantastical cinematography, crescendoing into a maelstrom of blood, sex, and violence.

When Einbinder—who broke out with her role as outspoken, chaotic comedy writer Ava Daniels in HBO’s Hacks (2021–26)—walks into the hotel bar in the Lower East Side of New York on a Sunday morning, her aura is quieter than I had expected. Dressed in a slouchy baseball T-shirt and sweatpants, with a bookstore tote bag on her shoulder, Einbinder, a softly spoken Angeleno, is struggling with the humidity. “I can deal with a dry heat, but humidity? No bueno,” she quips, before congratulating me for avoiding “poisonous” American milk in my coffee order and telling me, semi-jokingly, about the quantities of microplastics an average citizen swallows each year. It’s as if she’s doing a bit: stereotypical Cali girl adrift in New York.

Her manicure, however, stands out. Her nails are streaked with varying patterns of red polish that reference the bloody film and the metal mask made up of concentric squares worn by Little Death. It’s another guise for the press tour—which saw Einbinder return from upstate New York the previous day for a screening of Camp Miasma at Schoenbrun’s hometown cinema in Westchester. Days before that too, Einbinder and Anderson got on stage at Wallis Annenberg Center for the Performing Arts in Beverly Hills for a live read of Secretary, Steven Shainberg’s 2002 adaptation of Mary Gaitskill’s BDSM novel (Einbinder played Maggie Gyllenhaal’s secretary, while Anderson took on James Spader’s lawyer). It was selected for its influence on Camp Miasma. “It’s a story about two people who think they are alone in their desire to find companionship,” says Einbinder. “Both movies act as a blueprint for self-acceptance and liberation from shame as an unconventional love story.”

Odd-couple relationships are familiar terrain for Einbinder. In Hacks, she stars alongside Jean Smart’s Deborah Vance—a glamorous veteran comedian in Las Vegas—who Ava is enlisted to work for after getting cancelled for an inappropriate Tweet. While less Tom and Jerry than Hacks (Einbinder jokes that in Mandarin, the title has been translated to The Diva and the Strawberry), there are obvious parallels in Camp Miasma in its portrayal of an age-gap relationship. Einbinder insists this is incidental. “The thing that connects me to any work is the quality and how much I connect to the story—the age gap is an added plus,” she says. “I’m not going to my agents, ‘What’s going on with Nicole [Kidman]?’ Although I wouldn’t say no.”

Einbinder was initially intimidated by the idea of working with Anderson, 57, whose performances, from FBI Agent Dana Scully in The X-Files (1993–2018) to sex therapist Jean Milburn in Sex Education (2019–23), and Margaret Thatcher in The Crown (2016–23), she had greatly appreciated: “She’s so iconic, there’s so much mythology around her, that was a place where reality blended into the film for me.” When shooting the scene where the characters meet early on in the shoot—Billy creeps up on Kris in an abandoned cinema—Einbinder leaned in to her “parasocial” perception of Anderson. “I was still in the place of, who is this person? I didn’t know her,” says Einbinder. “Then she became a full human being. She has a pretty low-key energy so we became cool pretty fast.”

In Camp Miasma, Kris, who is in a polyamorous relationship, is deeply uncomfortable with sex itself, and is obsessed with a particular shot of Billy’s young face at the film’s climax, which shows fear, desire, and pain all at once. For Einbinder, who identifies as bisexual, the film became a vehicle to explore her own sexuality. “I don’t mean queerness when I say sexuality,” she says. “I reflected on the way many young girls are externally sexualised before we identify with our sexuality. I was a late bloomer and I felt all this energy coming in my direction that I didn’t understand. The film has sent me on a journey of self-reflection.”

There were intense, long conversations with Schoenbrun about the personal story behind the film. (Schoenbrun, who is trans, has said that the film is inspired by their own sexuality post-transition.) The director provided Einbinder with a list of films to watch, among them Secretary, David Cronenberg’s Crash (1996), Peter Strickland’s Duke of Burgundy (2014), and Ingmar Bergman’s Persona (1966). “I like to joke that I went to the Jane Schoenbrun film academy,” says Einbinder, who added Fire of Love (2022), a documentary about a couple who go in search of erupting volcanoes, to the list. “These two dreamers who have a love revolving around this strange and dangerous thing,” she adds. “God rest their souls.”

The sequence where—avoiding spoilers—Kris recreates Billy’s expression was technically challenging. “It’s one of the most multi-layered things I had to portray, of fear, resistance, arousal, sadness, orgasm, and death. When we first met, Jane said they envisioned it to have a Gena Rowlands quality to it. I was like, OK, cool, one of the best actresses of all time, no pressure!” The first time Einbinder watched the film—which premiered at Cannes—was on a television in her bedroom with Schoenbrun and a few other friends. “I’d only really seen myself as Ava, and seeing myself in this new way was freaky,” says Einbinder. “I’ve now watched it five times and I’m like, OK, that’s Kris. I’m just watching the movie.”

While there are more complex scenes and emotional grey areas to execute in Camp Miasma, Einbinder believes the groundwork for her acting was firmly set in Hacks. The show’s final season sees Deborah Vance, who gets a cancer diagnosis, planning to head to an assisted dying clinic in Switzerland. On an emotional farewell vacation to Paris, Ava persuades her otherwise. “Over the course of the series, Paul [Downs], Jen [Statsky], and Lucia [Aniello] gave me the opportunity to do deeper and deeper dramatic work, which made it possible for me to approach this.”

When Einbinder started in Hacks in 2021, she had less confidence. Then finding relative success on the stand-up circuit, she was cast because of the improvisations in her audition. “When I got the job, it was literally ‘Operation Don’t Get Fired’,” says Einbinder. “Coming from the stand-up world, it was all new to me. I was learning to act on the fly.” She cites Michael Caine’s 1989 book Acting in Film as her bible. “When I started, I didn’t know what a mark was [the spot where an actor must stand]. It has everything you need to know before walking on set. Michael Caine, he taught me everything I know.”
“When I started, I didn’t know what a mark was. [Acting on Film (1987)], it has everything you need to know before walking on set. Michael Caine, he taught me everything I know.”

Einbinder grew up in Los Angeles in a family with strong comedy credentials—her mother, Laraine Newman, was a sketch comedian on SNL and her father, Chad Einbinder, was a comedian, actor, writer, and director who worked on projects such as Doctor Dolittle (1998) and 3rd Rock from the Sun (1996–2001). “It was a funny household,” she says. “We were all constantly trying to make each other laugh. Some people have to bring their parents good grades to be in good graces, but I just had to be funny.”

Rather than follow in the family footsteps, she enrolled at Chapman University in California and took classes in broadcast journalism after becoming obsessed with television host and comedian Bill Maher. “He’s a Republican-adjacent prick now,” says Einbinder, “but to understand the jokes he was making, I watched the news. I was on a lot of Adderall, so I’d read the newspaper cover to cover, drinking my Irish breakfast tea every morning. It was a different time in my political consciousness, when I was more capital-D Democrat and I thought that’s what I wanted to do. It didn’t even occur to me to perform until my sophomore year of college, when I joined the improv team.”

Although she has some plans to return to the stage, an immediate return to stand-up is unlikely. Her 2024 special, Everything Must Go—which muses on subjects from queer identity to climate change—was the product of seven years of work. “I’m a real slow burner,” she says. “I plant seeds, I water them, I have to wait months and months for ideas to pop up. I can’t spin gold quickly, and acting has given me that luxury, that I can take my time. So many comedians put out an amazing first special and then their next special is about how they were a celebrity, and I just find that so boring. I’m trying to talk about larger concepts. I’m working on a bit right now that is about money and capitalism; it’s not like ‘Oh, I went to the Vanity Fair Oscars party’.”

Today, Einbinder is one of the more radical voices in Hollywood—part of a list that includes Mark Ruffalo, Susan Sarandon, and Javier Bardem, who advocate for Palestine. When she took home an Emmy in 2025 for Hacks, she ended her speech announcing: “Go Birds, fuck ICE, and free Palestine.” I ask why more don’t use their platform in the same way. “We live in a culture that places an outsized importance on celebrity, so people on my side of things draw attention. I’ve seen the [professional] impact that speaking out can have,” says Einbinder, who works closely with Pal Humanity, a humanitarian organisation led by two female doctors in Gaza. “But I’ve seen the way small donations from a lot of people can impact the lives of the most vulnerable, so to me it’s a no-brainer. Why wouldn’t you, with your visibility, feel comfortable standing with marginalised folks? Why is it that the most marginalised are often the ones with the loudest voices?”

As an actor, Einbinder also wants to work with loud voices. “Inshallah,” she jokes. She describes dream collaborators as Canadian filmmaker and activist Sarah Polley, as well as French auteur Coralie Fargeat. “I fucking loved The Substance (2024),” she says of Fargeat’s divisive feminist body horror. “We are living in a time that is totally oversaturated with safety in art and good art requires risk.” Would Einbinder get behind the camera herself? “I think so,” she replies coyly. “I’ve been doing this for six or seven years now, but I’ve only really had three jobs [beyond Hacks and Camp Miasma, she had a feature film role in Victoria Strouse’s Seekers of Infinite Love (2026)]. I would like to continue to get my sea legs and put in my 10,000 hours.” Einbinder starts to do some maths. On Hacks she worked 13 to 14 hours a day, for six months of the year, for six years. We pause to do the calculation. “Someone in a different profession than either of ours can figure that out,” she suggests.

Later, I calculate this would add up to at least 14,245 hours—well beyond the required 10,000. Einbinder is an actor in her stride, with more Emmy success for Hacks’s final season likely in September. “I’m going on the tits and ass circuit for that,” jokes Einbinder. “I just want to celebrate the show that has changed my life in every conceivable way, and it’s an excuse to hang out with everyone again.” For the next week, however, it’s back on the press campaign for Camp Miasma, with the New York premiere at Metrograph the following week, and, more immediately, of course, an appearance on the Today Show. We say goodbye and Einbinder leaves the bar quietly. She’s got somewhere to scream.
