items.title: 10 What I Can’t Live Withouts That Defined Celebrity Shopping
items.description: Our “What I Can’t Live Without” series started with a simple question: What are the everyday things that celebrities actually use and like? Not the red-carpet diamonds or the $6,000 cashmere throw blanket, but the mouthwashes, the ankle socks, the personal fan
items.author: Ambar Pardilla
paragraphs: Our “What I Can’t Live Without” series started with a simple question: What are the everyday things that celebrities actually use and like? Not the red-carpet diamonds or the $6,000 cashmere throw blanket, but the mouthwashes, the ankle socks, the personal fans. In 2016, Common’s answer was Frank Ocean’s album Blonde, Billy Crudup’s was a Hammacher Schlemmer sound machine, and Rachel Antonoff’s was Blistex Lip Medex. Getting celebrities to respond wasn’t easy initially. “It was just us trying to convince people to do it in the beginning,” says New York deputy editor Alexis Swerdloff. But some, like Antonoff, were early gets. (“I don’t remember exactly how it was sold to me, but I love a recommendation,” says Antonoff. “I have this interior Rolodex of like, No, this is the best detergent.”)

In the ten years since, we’ve interviewed hundreds of celebrities and notable people, from New York City mayoral candidates and the stars of the Real Housewives to Amy Sedaris and Jennifer Aniston. And the column has grown into one of our flagship series (and led to offshoots like “What I Can’t Cook Without” and “What My Kids Can’t Live Without”). Now, we’re looking back at ten of the most memorable “What I Can’t Live Without” columns by returning to the celebrities and writers who interviewed them.
André Leon Talley, the unexpected UGG wearer

Longtime contributing Vogue editor André Leon Talley, who died in 2022, was known for his high-end taste — he collected monogrammed Louis Vuitton suitcases and Limoges luncheon plates with drawings by Jean Cocteau — but his 2016 “What I Can’t Live Without,” the first in the series, was less the stuff of a Christie’s auction, and decidedly more down to earth. “He’s one of the most glamorous people in the world, and he’s talking about UGGs,” says Swerdloff of his list, which also included cleaning supplies and an electric toothbrush. It was that toothbrush that inspired the text that for years ran at the beginning of every column: If you’re like us, you’ve probably wondered what famous people add to their carts. Not the JAR brooch and Louis XV chair, but the hand sanitizer and the electric toothbrush.
New! You can now save this product for later.
New! You can now save this product for later.
How Aubrey Plaza became our personal “deodorant guru”

If it wasn’t for Aubrey Plaza, we might not know about Real Purity’s natural deodorant. It turns out that Plaza, whose list was published in 2017, heard about it from Judy Greer, who later included it in her “What I Can’t Live Without” in 2022. “I do everything Judy Greer tells me to do,” said Plaza at the time. Strategist editors followed suit: Swerdloff and Strategist deputy editor Simone Kitchens both still use the deodorant. Several other items from Plaza’s list have become Strategist canon, too: Writer Kitty Guo credits the Oribe Dry Texturizing Spray with saving her bad haircut, alongside Lucas Papaw “miracle ointment,” which has appeared in Dido’s, Erin Wasson’s, Selma Blair’s, and Alison Brie’s “What I Can’t Live Withouts” since.
Fifteen minutes with Debi Mazar turned into two hours

Often, we only get a short amount of time to chat with celebrities about their items — but sometimes they can’t help but gab. What was meant to be a tightly scheduled 15-minute phone call between Debi Mazar and former writer Chloe Anello lasted more than two hours. “She knew who she was. She knew what she liked,” Anello says. “As we were talking about one thing, it reminded her of something else that she loved.” When Anello got off the phone, she had about 60-something items, 50 of which we ran in one of our longer columns in the series.

“I’m a person who tries things for people and gives my opinions. I’ve been given a lot of free stuff because of my job. They let me take home things that I discover on the set. I’m always flying through an airport and I’m like, Oh, what’s this?” says Mazar. When the list was published, “Everyone called me, like, ‘Oh, my God. I love this list. I am so ordering that.’” Five years later, she still wears Chanel No. 5 and agua de violetas, washes her dishes with Palmolive, and drinks Café Bustelo.
It turns out Jason Schwartzman is our biggest (celebrity) fan

“I love the Strategist; I need the Strategist. So many of the things in my life I’ve gotten from the Strategist,” Jason Schwartzman told New York on a red carpet at Sundance in 2024. Months later, senior writer Lauren Ro met with him for his “What I Can’t Live Without” interview. Schwartzman showed Ro the phone case he got for his wife after reading Amelia Meath’s “What I Can’t Live Without” and a Pilot Varsity fountain pen he bought after reading Ottessa Moshfegh’s. The interview went on for nearly three hours over the course of two days, and the post became our most-viewed “What I Can’t Live Without” in 2024. Maybe it was thanks to his enthusiasm: for an airbrush he discovered on the set of Fargo, a light meter that was part of his research for Asteroid City, and Boggle Sit & Solve puzzles. “He’s somebody that loves to learn. You can just see that in the way that he has chosen the items and how he talks about them and how he has thought about using them,” says Ro.
New! You can now save this product for later.
People tell Ottessa Moshfegh they have the same pajamas regularly

When we talked to the My Year of Rest and Relaxation author in 2022, she was newly “pajamas obsessed” and sleeping in J.Crew’s End-on-End Cotton Long-Sleeved Pajama Set, a recent acquisition at the time. Moshfegh was wearing the very same pajamas when we called recently: “I didn’t sleep, therefore didn’t sleep in [them], but have been in my pajamas since last night and have not changed because I’m hopeful to sleep more,” she told us. It was the pair that she bought the same year as the interview, and even now, four years later, she still hears from people about them. “I would say every six months or so, somebody tells me that they wear the same pajamas as me,” says Moshfegh.
Samantha Irby: “You need to know what the real shitters use.”

Similar to Debi Mazar’s multi-hour interview, Samantha Irby’s went from a quick hit to a two-hour call. In the first 40 minutes, she chatted about everything from scam texts to The Real Housewives of Miami. Then she got down to her stuff: There was her Owala (which later led to our investigation into the new status water bottle), the oregano oil a hippie recommended to her at a co-op, and the Lectrofan sound machine she credits with keeping her “marriage intact.” When we spoke to Irby again recently, she told us that she still reads the column and bought the incense Katie Crutchfield of Waxahatchee burns. “In the way that I’m curious about people, I assume people would be curious about me,” she says. “What does a person who has diarrhea all the time wipe their ass with? You need to know what the real shitters use.” (Charmin UltraStrong rolls, in Irby’s case.)
John Derian (still) uses nearly everything on his list

We’ve regularly talked to people with particular, exacting, and exceptional taste over the years — and there might be no better example than designer John Derian. He’s consistent, too: We interviewed Derian in 2017 and again in 2023 and learned that he still used every single thing on his original list, including the Zig Memory System Calligraphy Dual Tip Marker and Tom’s of Maine Unscented Deodorant. “I think probably the first time I was just sort of like, I’m so basic,” jokes Derian. Basic or not, it turns out that he’s in good company with his recommendations: Danny Meyer also seasons with Maldon sea-salt flakes; Ana Gastayer wears the same deodorant brand, Schmidt’s; and Kiehl’s Ultra Facial Moisturizer SPF 30 protects Chloe Bailey in the Caribbean sun.

Sally Jessy Raphael hasn’t read your comments

No “What I Can’t Live Without” has the number of comments that 91-year-old former talk-show host Sally Jessy Raphael’s 2025 column does: 112, as of the publication of this article. (That’s even more than the 87 left for Ballerina Farm’s Hannah Neeleman and Diane von Furstenberg’s 71.) As one reader wrote, “This is the apotheosis of the ‘Can’t Live Without’ column.” Others loved her Coke Zero Cherry and Sharpie markers. Not that Raphael is reading the comments: “I don’t ever look and see what anyone thinks. I never watch a show I’ve done. People say, ‘Well, haven’t you seen any movie you’ve been in?’ The answer is no,” says Raphael.
“I think Lena Dunham always knows what the hook is.”

When we talked to Lena Dunham in 2017 for the column, she had just wrapped Girls. Nine years later, as Dunham’s memoir Famesick was about to come out, we checked back in to hear about her eBay and Etsy search terms — which we ran in our Secret Strategist newsletter — and her latest batch of things she can’t live without. Her updated list included the Ozlo Sleepbuds she learned about from Susan Orlean’s “What I Can’t Live Without” (both go to bed listening to true-crime podcasts) and Four Thousand Weeks by Oliver Burkeman for “making choices about what’s important to you.” Readers took Dunham’s recommendations seriously; they were among the most-purchased items on the site this April. “I think Lena Dunham always knows what the hook is,” says Erin Schwartz, who spoke with Dunham over email, phone, and text. “Like the thing about all of her animals wanting to sit on the crystal infrared mat, I thought it was just such an indelible image of this sort of woo-woo mat and the rabbits flustered on it.”

We saw Tracee Ellis Ross’s “What I Can’t Live Without” onstage

“She really in so many ways, was humbly showing off that she has been on the forefront of a trend, with the Free City T-shirts being on Girlfriends and wearing Ruby Woo, for so long,” says senior writer Liza Corsillo of her call with Tracee Ellis Ross for the actress’s 2026 “What I Can’t Live Without.” Not long after, Corsillo got tickets to Tracee Ellis Ross’s Broadway show Every Brilliant Thing and she recognized Ross wearing a few things from her list, like the Levi’s 1950’s 701 jeans and Asics they talked about. Ross also told us she carried Alex Mill’s Perfect Weekend Tote (monogrammed with her initials, TER) to and from the theater as well. “It makes her feel like she’s part of the Strat family,” says Corsillo. items.title: Parisian art centre Large opens on the former site of a Renault production facility and it was no small feat
items.description: When French business tycoon François Pinault earmarked Paris’s Île Seguin as the new home for his art collection in 2000, he offered a dose of much-needed optimism to the 11.5 hectares of desolate brownfield. Due west of the city, the site was where automobile
items.author: Claudia Jacob; Amelia Edwards
paragraphs: When French business tycoon François Pinault earmarked Paris’s Île Seguin as the new home for his art collection in 2000, he offered a dose of much-needed optimism to the 11.5 hectares of desolate brownfield. Due west of the city, the site was where automobile manufacturer Renault’s flagship production facility once hummed. But when the project fell through in 2005, Pinault penned, with considerable anguish, an op-ed for Le Monde on how he had become disillusioned by bureaucratic setbacks.

Undeterred by his predecessor’s non-success, Laurent Dumas – a French collector armed with patience and significant property knowhow – decided to take on the site. The strip had been heavily polluted by decades of industrial activity and until 2009 was accessible only by two bridges (the municipality has since added three more). But as the CEO of property developer Emerige, Dumas is no stranger to the nuances of urban-regeneration projects – and this weekend, after more than 30 years since Renault’s departure, the doors finally opened on a new art institution anchoring this mini metropolis.

As Monocle exits the Metro in the Boulogne Billancourt suburb and traverses the Daydé bridge (the island is mainly pedestrianised, except for a bus service), an undulating structure of copper-coloured aluminium seems to unfurl from the river bank. Large is the first project in the French capital to be designed by Catalan firm RCR Arquitectes. It is a 5,000 sq m art centre that anchors the Pointe des Arts, the Île Seguin’s mixed-use development that also includes a cinema, hotel and food court. Downstream, a bulbous glass concert hall and recording studios are part of venue La Seine Musicale, which opened in 2017.

“The ambition is to make the Île Seguin the beating heart of Greater Paris,” says Large’s director, Paula Aisemberg. The former curator is sitting at her new desk, which appears to be almost floating; her perch overlooks the calm waters of the Seine. “We would like visitors to come here for a full day, even the whole weekend, hence we have included a hotel.” The island is currently served by Metro line 9, and a second link will be provided by line 15 from Spring 2027.

Louis Renault originally bought the site in 1919. (Prior to the industrialist’s purchase, the island was farmland, then a commercial laundry and tannery.) Though the plant that he built quickly became the largest of its kind in the country, automotive heft wasn’t the only thing that it was known for. The company began accumulating contemporary artworks in the 1930s, and by the late 1960s, it had become a driving force that connected two worlds by giving a string of artists access to surplus materials and the factory’s machinery; Swiss sculptor Jean Tinguely, Venezuelan artist and sculptor Jesús Rafael Soto and American painter Robert Rauschenberg were among the creatives who benefitted from the scheme.

The Renault production plant became an exhibition space, which displayed works including a chromatic mural by Argentine-born artist Julio Le Parc in its café and Hungarian-born French painter Simon Hantaï’s screen-printed Formica panels in the restaurant. “The factory became a creative laboratory,” says Aisemberg. It’s evident that the thread between the manufacturing plant, which was demolished in 2004, and the new facilities is more than just geographical.

“We felt compelled to eulogise this automotive history,” adds Aisemberg. The gallery’s first exhibition, Moteur Imaginaire (The Imaginary Engine), is devoted to the carmaker’s own collection, featuring more than 50 pieces borrowed from the Renault Fund for Art and Culture and 17 new commissions put together by New York-based Italian curator Cecilia Alemani.

On the ground floor is that same work by Le Parc, which features a gradient of colours that seem to sweep past as though in motion. There are also pieces by Jean Tinguely and French painter Jean Dubuffet. The latter’s large-scale sculpture, “Le Mur Bleu”, was created from the factory’s epoxy-resin stocks, while Tinguely’s “Pit Stop” sculpture is constructed with parts from Renault’s RE40 Formula 1 race car. “We hope that engineers who once worked here will come back and see what we’ve created,” says Aisemberg.

And so a new era has begun for the Île Seguin. But Pinault’s influence isn’t entirely invisible. For the inauguration, he loaned the island a sculpture by British artist Thomas Houseago titled “L’homme Pressé” (“The Man in a Hurry”) from his personal collection. Almost eight metres tall, the bronze-hewn figure appears to be striding forwards resolutely. It feels like a cathartic statement for a collector who recognised the potential in this place 26 years ago. If only he’d have been prepared to wait.

items.title: Survivor Recap: Blood Brothers
items.description: Oh, Jeff, you really got me this time. Halfway through the episode, I was planning my screed about three tribes, how sorting people into smaller groups makes for boring, predictable votes where the most obvious thing always happens. I was going to tell Jeff th
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: Oh, Jeff, you really got me this time. Halfway through the episode, I was planning my screed about three tribes, how sorting people into smaller groups makes for boring, predictable votes where the most obvious thing always happens. I was going to tell Jeff that the editing couldn’t fool me, couldn’t make me think that the tribes didn’t know what they were going to do or make me think that there were some explosions at Tribal yet to come. Then we got to the second of two Tribal Councils, and I noticed there was still a lot of episode left. Did that mean that something was…going to happen? Oh boy, did it ever, making this yet another chaotic episode in a chaotic season. (Extremely complimentary.) While it certainly was great to watch, that doesn’t mean that chaos is a ladder that people can use to climb to the top. After all, look at what happened to Littlefinger on Game of Thrones. He got murdered by a teenage girl with a moldable face. No one wants that.

The episode starts with the purple tribe back from Tribal Council, and they all share why they want to be on Survivor. This felt like a throwback to the “New Era” when we would often get sob stories from players, particularly right before their torch was snuffed. Ori talks about his mother immigrating to the U.S. and working at McDonald’s to take care of him and his siblings. Devin talks about having two brothers who died young and how he’s now older than his older brother. He also talks about a dream he had where everyone in his life was sitting around watching a TV screen like some kind of metaphysical version of The Simpsons opening theme. Alexis talks about her years as an addict and how she ended up in jail and had to find sobriety and straighten her life out. She’s now dedicated herself to helping people who run afoul of the law as a defense attorney. Jelly is like, “Um, I guess I’m here because I’m into Ori.” No, not really, but she didn’t get a story.

At the pre-challenge check-ins, all the tribes are talking about “Toka strong” or “Savu strong” as if it’s late in the game, but we’re only on episode five. Isn’t it early to be drawing lines in the sand? Also, poor Dina. No one wants to be strong for Dina. The challenge, shockingly, is not an obstacle course followed by a puzzle. It is an obstacle course followed by shooting three things at a target. Jeff says, however, that there is only one immunity whale this week and two tribes will be headed to tribal council. The yellow tribe wins, which means we will have to hear the word “brodie” multiple times for yet another episode. May the Catholic Jesus spare all of our ears.

Let’s start with tracking Savu, where, because of the tiny tribes, the most obvious and boring thing ends up happening. The editing wants us to believe that it’s a stalemate between Jelly and Devin on one side and Ori and Alexi on the other, the two twosomes from their old tribes. Then it shifts to make us think that Alexis might be able to convince Jelly to vote with her and Ori to get Devin out of the game. Please. We all know this is not going to happen. The best part of this season is that they have once again started casting characters (dare I say villains) and that they’ve done a very good job introducing us to them and how they work in the game. That includes Jelly. The show portrays her as someone who is torn between not wanting to vote another woman out of the game and not wanting to vote out another Black person, particularly from the “helicopter alliance.” We know she is going to choose that chopper every single time. Last episode, Jelly and Devin were out there giggling on the beach like Will and Grace with sand stuck in their coochies. You expect us to think she’s really going to turn on this man? Please. Just as we knew she would, Jelly joins Ori and Devin and sends Alexis back to that great jail cell in the sky. Well, it’s just Ponderosa, but you know what I mean.

Things at Dina are far more exciting. Lewis knows that he’s doomed, and he comes up with some malarkey (he’s Irish, so I can say that) about how he got an advantage called the Blood Ring on Exile Island. He gives it to Sharonda and tells her it means they are linked, and if he goes home, then she goes with him, but after three Tribal Councils it turns into an idol. This is actually an excellent idea for an advantage, and the Open Era should mean that next season we get a “Lewis Blood Ring Advantage” that shits all over the Billie Eilish Boomerang Idol. The four former Savu on their tribe quickly decide it’s bullshit because Christian, a mute with a bowtie collection, says that Lewis described his traditional Irish wedding ring to him previously and it sounded a lot like this Blood Ring he gave Sharonda. Oh, Lewis’s wife is going to be pissed. She’s going to take his U.S. Passport and send him back to the Emerald Island on a raft with only a canteen and a Tupperware full of Mofongo.

While this gambit failed, advantages are about to save his ass. Back at the Toka Beach, there is a sign that says someone needs to miss their reward of soggy donuts to get on a boat. Maggie is selected, and she finds out that she gets to give an extra vote to someone on the beach of her choice. She goes to Dina and talks to everyone individually, hearing that there is no way that Savu is going to break up and that one of her old tribe mates, either Lewis or Kilby, is going home. She gives Lewis the extra vote she got on the boat (the boat vote) and gives Kilby the extra vote that she and Brady found (the brodie vote). Now they have four and can force it to go to rocks. She says if they use them to vote for Linnea, who she doesn’t like because of vibes. Okay. Sure. Any reason is good enough.

This is the point where I prepared my screed against Jeff. Why would Kilby go to rocks? He’s made real inroads with this new tribe, especially his Miyazaki-loving buddy Eric, and if he ousts Lewis, he gets to stay with this tribe that loves him, keep an extra brodie votie, and live to see another day. It would be one thing if they had enough votes to get the majority, but to just force a tie? It seems like there is no way that Kilby would do that. He even tells the majority four about the extra vote. At Tribal, he says that this is his new family and telling them about the vote gave them a reason to keep him. This does not seem like a guy who would betray his tribe.

I have never been happier to be wrong. Jeff reads the votes, and sure enough, there are four for Lewis and four for Linnea. No, I take that back. There are three for “Louis,” one for “Lewis,” and one each for “Lenaya,” “Lenugha,” “Lanayuh,” and “Luneighah.” I mean, it’s one thing to spell her name wrong; it’s another thing for two people to both spell her name wrong two different ways. (I almost forgive Lewis. He’s Irish. To him, the name “Niamh” makes phonetic sense.) Before the revote, I was hoping Linnea would have told them how to spell her name correctly. Thankfully she did not, and there are four votes for Lewis and, like a Saturday Night Live sketch where they just start comically misspelling someone’s name, there are votes for “Lenaya,” “Lenay,” “Lanehah,” and “Lanayyaah.”

They have one last chance to come up with a unanimous decision, and Lewis and Kilby stick to their guns. There’s a reason that Kilby did this and, well, it’s because he’s not a good player. I don’t even know if he’s that smart. Remember when he thought he was Brady’s No. 1 brodie but was also talking shit about him to everyone at camp? Yeah, this guy does not know how to play Survivor, and thank Parvati Shallow for that. For so many of the recent seasons, we had students of the game who would always play safe, and here we have a Canadian improv artist threatening to go to rocks for the LOLs. His rationale makes no sense. He tells the old Savu he wanted to make sure the vote wasn’t him. He says that his odds are better going to rocks than they are at the vote. None of this makes sense. Sure, it’s different inside the game than watching at home, but he was nerding out with the whole tribe while Lewis was pooping his pants on the beach. Didn’t he see he was in a better position? He had the potential to make it through this vote and then convince the old Savu that he’s worth more than Christian, who only brings with him bow ties and a tertiary knowledge of gemology and maybe even made it through another one.

He knows that the “Savu strong” don’t have the guts to go to rocks, though. When Kilby says that he’s willing to, they end the game of chicken and send Linnea home rather than risk any of them pulling the bad rock. This was, for sure, an extremely interesting evening, and I’m grateful that we got as much drama as a bunch of Real Housewives in the back of a Sprinter van, but it does leave Kilby in an even worse position. He and Lewis are still in the minority at their tribe, and now he’s pissed off the majority and forced them to do something they didn’t want to do. If they lost again, I wouldn’t be surprised if they got rid of Kilby rather than Lewis, particularly because Lewis could sell it as, “Hey, that guy is crazy. Look what he made you do?” But, hey, who cares if Kilby blew up his own spot? We got a great episode of Survivor, and the machinations of the game and a set of players that we’ve gotten to know well finally paid off.

items.title: Elon Musk’s Grok Releases First AI-Generated ‘Odyssey’ Episode, Months After Promising ‘Historically Accurate’ Full-Length Film
items.description: Months after Elon Musk promised that his AI tool Grok Imagine would create an entirely AI-generated, feature-length version of “The Odyssey,” the tech mogul has partially followed through on the claim.
items.author: Payton Turkeltaub
paragraphs: Months after Elon Musk promised that his AI tool Grok Imagine would create an entirely AI-generated, feature-length version of “The Odyssey,” the tech mogul has partially followed through on the claim.

On Friday, the company shared the first 7-minute, AI-generated episode of the “Odyssey” series on X. The account also credited the “creative collaboration” to Wonder Studios and director Dev Walker, both of which specialize in AI filmmaking.
In July, Musk announced plans to make a “historically accurate” full-length feature version of Homer’s ancient Greek poem. He noted that his AI “The Odyssey” would be ready by the end of 2026.

“Before this year ends, Grok Imagine will make a full-length movie of The Odyssey that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer,” he wrote, together with an AI-generated 3-minute short of “The Odyssey” posted by an X user.

At the time, “Doctor Strange” and “The Black Phone” director Scott Derrickson pulled no punches and addressed Musk directly on social media to call out the absurdity of the project. “Clearly @elonmusk doesn’t know shit about cinema & he stopped reading in his 20s,” Derrickson wrote on Musk’s social media platform, X. “His opinions on art are worthless.”

While no further statement accompanied the AI-generated episode — or Musk’s original tweet about creating a “historically accurate” version of “The Odyssey” — the move comes after the tech trillionaire repeatedly criticized the film ahead of its release, especially the casting of Elliot Page as Sinon and Lupita Nyong’o as Helen of Troy.

Musk claimed that Nolan cast both actors to satisfy the Academy’s representation and inclusion standards for Oscar eligibility; in March, he wrote that “Chris Nolan is an anti-White racist,” saying he cast Nyong’o only because “He wants the awards.”

items.title: ‘Clayface’ Director James Watkins Explains That [SPOILER] Cameo, Introducing Gotham City to the DC Universe and All the Shape-Shifting Kills
items.description: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for “Clayface,” now playing in theaters.
items.author: Jordan Moreau
paragraphs: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for “Clayface,” now playing in theaters.

Batman fans will have to wait patiently for the next installment in Matt Reeves and Robert Pattinson’s Caped Crusader saga, but they can get a peek at the rebooted DC Universe’s Gotham City in “Clayface.”

“Clayface” is an R-rated body horror that follows the shape-shifting Batman foe. It blends a supervillain origin story with some stomach-churning scares and comes from horror veterans including director James Watkins and a story by Mike Flanagan. Tom Rhys Harries plays Matt Hagen, an A-list actor who is brutally disfigured by a gangster. With his face ripped up and his career destroyed, Matt turns to an experimental procedure from Dr. Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie), which heals him — but slowly turns him into a clay-covered monster.

Matt’s blood cells gain the ability to transform and instantly reshape his body into someone else, such as Corr or the gangster who disfigured him or even his own father (played in a quick cameo by Aaron Paul). He loses control of his own body and sanity as these newfound shape-shifting powers help him enact bloody revenge on the mob who ruined his life. In the end, Matt kills everybody who wronged him (plus several innocent people), and is forced to live as a reclusive mud monster in the sewers.

Clayface has appeared in many Batman comics through the years, and he’s a classic villain who’s made the crossover into animated shows and video games. This version of him has also technically already appeared in the rebooted DC Universe in James Gunn’s animated series “Creature Commandos,” but now the monster gets his own origin story and live-action debut. The movie also gives the first look at Batman’s hometown of Gotham City in the new DC Universe. Gunn’s “Superman” kicked things off in Metropolis last year, but now another one of DC’s most famous cities gets unveiled in “Clayface.”
With Variety, Watkins explains finding the final Clayface monster look, recruiting Paul for his cameo and creating Gotham City.
The Clayface name has been used by several villains in Batman comics. How did you land on the Matt Hagen version instead of the first iteration, Basil Karlo?

It was really landed by Mike Flanagan and the script. I read all of them, Basil Karlo and all, afterward because there are bits and bobs that are kind of cherry-picked from all over the place. But the key journey, and that’s what Mike had chosen, was the Matt Hagen version. If you’d have gone with Basil Karlo, it’s a little bit too gothic or too hard to do in such a modern idiom. The Matt Hagen is a more relatable version. Whether it’s Basil Karlo and Boris Karloff, there are all those characters that it’s referring back to in the Golden Age of Hollywood, that sort of thing. This is something that can sit in our contemporary time. Our Gotham is not entirely contemporary. It slightly steals from a few different genres. We wanted it to be slightly timeless, but it can play as contemporary.
This is the first time we’re seeing Gotham in the rebooted DC Universe. Did you have a specific year or time you wanted to set the world in?

We deliberately wanted it to be a bit muddy. James Price, our brilliant production designer, and I talked a lot about creating the sense of the world, and we wanted it to feel like a character in the movie. We wanted this oppressive world where the buildings really dominate. We looked at a lot of 1930s German expressionist cinema with huge dominant buildings and the odd angles and the noir-ish shadows. We also looked at street photography from New York from the ’70s, the ’80s and the ’90s. It was all before New York had been cleaned up. The lighting is different. It’s a lot of neon. There’s a lot of practical lighting. There’s a lot of dirt and eccentricity on the street. We wanted to definitely frame Gotham as a contrast to Coast City, with the colors, the bright sunshine, the sky, the sea. You see verdant greens and textures and stuff like that, which you don’t really see in Gotham. You barely see the sky, and it’s a very heavy atmosphere.
There are so many face-swapping scares in the movie. How many of them were practical camera tricks vs. special effects?

A lot of it is in camera. The scene in the nightclub where he comes in and he’s on this dark, lethal, vengeful journey, I wanted to give the audience permission to enjoy his payback before it goes too far. There’s a lot of in-camera wipes. We did so much stuff old-school. He takes somebody out, then he goes past a pillar, then I knew that I’d use that pillar as a wipe, then I do the scene again with another actor and they’d come out of the pillar or Tom would come out of the pillar. It was really good fun.
Did you have a contortionist for the nightclub scene too?

My guiding thing is if I can do it practically, I will try and do it practically. So after that fall down the stairs, which is a stunt with two stunt people, then they’re all on the floor, we were like, “Well, should we try it with a contortionist?” for that sense of bodies out of shape. If you can do it in camera, why not, right?
That sequence also has a quick cameo from Aaron Paul, who plays Matt’s dad in one of his transformations. How did you get him to shoot that scene?

It was like, “Who can we get to play Matt’s dad?” And I really, really love Aaron Paul as an actor. I know it’s tiny, but I think he was living in Paris, and so somebody said, “Why don’t we reach out?” He’s such a nice man, and he came in and was just a really good sport and a really fine actor. It’s a tiny moment, and it’s a sort of really an Easter egg, isn’t it? But the idea that Matt’s not his father and sort of thing. It was a pleasure to meet him. He was like, “Yeah, cool DC movie. I’ll show my face for a moment.” It was very nice of him.
How did you decide on the final look for the Clayface monster?

I took everything as a reference and tried to choose, because there are so many versions in the comics. We did about 19 different iterations. You want to honor the comics, but at the same time, you want to make sure it can work as live-action because it’s obviously a different medium. The key thing for me was making sure that it captured the emotion, the man inside the monster. I was particularly obsessed with his left eye and the pain and the heartbreak within that and the scream, the quality of his voice. I first responded in Mike’s script to the idea of the tragedy and the journey of his character and where he ends up and going with him.

It was an awful lot of work and tiny tweaks. Where one fold of flesh goes makes such a difference. It’s sort of unquantifiable, but you just have to look at it and something about that feels good and real. It was a lot of work, but it was fun.
How did you pull off the suffocation scene where Matt kills his friend, Corey, by pulling him into his body?

The actual pulling into the body is practical with augmentation, but he is wearing a rig on his body with a big cavity in it so he could pull Josh [James], who plays Corey, into his chest. It’s like his face in the airplane. That is prosthetic makeup, not VFX. There’s a tactile quality that just reads when it’s on camera, that I think is very hard to replicate.
So the airplane scene, where he has to cut the strips of clay between his eyes with scissors, is mostly practical?

He had contact lenses, and then he had prosthetic makeup on. He actually had five pairs of scissors. We had sharp ones, blunt ones, rubber ones, one with a green screen tip, one without a tip. It was all on a gimbal, so the bathroom could move in real time and create the jolts. I was on the microphone talking everyone through the scene and jolts and Tom’s reactions. Tom figured out a way to — it sounds awful — where he could shove it in slightly above his eye, but the way it reads on camera, you can’t tell. He was quite in control and safe. For the close-ups, we had an eyeball, which was enormous, with a massive pair of scissors.
How many different facial prosthetics did you have for Tom to wear?

We had so many stages. I can’t say how many prosthetics, but we had like 65 stages at one point. That was all with bandages and this and that, but there was an awful lot because there were subtle differences between different melts and droops, and some that can have a pulley that you could tug. Obviously, some of these things you can augment with VFX because Tom can’t literally do that. But always having that base layer again gives you something that has a sort of heft to it.
I kept looking for a bat flying around or some kind of reference to Batman, but there isn’t anything overt. Did you ever plan to include more Easter eggs in the movie?

I actually think there are lots of Easter eggs that I probably don’t even know about because the graphics department was always throwing in posters and stuff. What I really responded to was the fact that it was a standalone story, and so for me to read that and then to try and get too cute or crowbar something in that wasn’t merited to the narrative felt gimmicky, I suppose. There was zero pressure to do it. I signed up to a certain story, which I believed in, and I just tried to tell that to the best of my abilities.
After the movie ends, do you have any plan for where Clayface goes next? Is he getting ready to fight Robert Pattinson’s Batman or another DC hero?

That’s a question for James Gunn. I liked the standalone nature of it. I liked how it felt like it introduced a character. But I wasn’t trying to introduce the character to go, “OK, what next?” I was trying to introduce the character as a full meal in itself.

items.title: ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Emily Osment Requested Intimacy Coordinator Over Age Gap With Montana Jordan: “He Was a Baby!”
items.description: Young Sheldon star Emily Osment recalls requesting an intimacy coordinator during her time on the CBS series because of the age gap between her and co-star Montana Jordan. Osment, who played Mandy McAllister, was 30 when she joined the series in 2022, while Jo
items.author: Lexi Carson
paragraphs: Young Sheldon star Emily Osment recalls requesting an intimacy coordinator during her time on the CBS series because of the age gap between her and co-star Montana Jordan. Osment, who played Mandy McAllister, was 30 when she joined the series in 2022, while Jordan, who played George Cooper, was 18.

Revealed in Jessica Radloff’s new book, Young Sheldon: The (Juicier-Than-Meemaw’s-Brisket) Inside Story of the Hit Comedy, which is a behind-the-scenes oral history of the series, Osment explained that while she and Jordan didn’t share sex scenes, she felt “uncomfortable” because of their age difference.

“That made me uncomfortable. He was a baby! A baby with a mullet,” Osment said. “So I spoke to Tim Marx, and obviously they were not able to get one that late in the day, but for the next few episodes they had one there, since the relationship between them escalates. It made everything easier having one there. I think it’s something that’s really important.”

“I don’t know if Montana even knew if he could ask for that. Like, let’s give him the option, too. Make him comfortable. And he’s such a sweet kid, I think he would just eat his discomfort,” she continued. “But I love those guys, and I’m really happy it got to the point where they were able to do that [for us].”

Elsewhere in the book, director Alex Reid acknowledged that production initially “dropped the ball” and overlooked having an intimacy coordinator, saying that the team’s decision was influenced by the show’s lack of sex scenes.

“I have a photo between takes of them sitting in that car when we shot that, and they’re looking off in other directions. I showed it to Emily and she said, ‘Yeah, that was so uncomfortable for both of us, because we didn’t know each other,’” Reid added. “It wasn’t even about the lack of an intimacy coordinator. It’s just you’re having to make out with somebody you just kind of met. Obviously they worked that out, and they have a great chemistry now, but that was kind of embarrassing.”
Now, Osment and Jordan star in the Young Sheldon spinoff Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage, which is in its third season and airs Thursdays at 8 p.m. ET on CBS.

items.title: ‘Miami Vice ’85’: Man Arrested After Pulling Out Knife During Dispute on Brooklyn Set
items.description: A man was arrested Friday night after displaying a knife during a confrontation with a crew member on the Brooklyn set of Miami Vice ’85, starring Michael B. Jordan and Austin Butler.
items.author: Lexi Carson
paragraphs: A man was arrested Friday night after displaying a knife during a confrontation with a crew member on the Brooklyn set of Miami Vice ’85, starring Michael B. Jordan and Austin Butler.

The individual, 23-year-old Alex Perez of Brooklyn, was arrested shortly after 11 p.m. in the vicinity of Avenue N and McDonald Avenue, near Washington Cemetery, according to the New York City Police Department. The Hollywood Reporter confirmed that the incident occurred on the Miami Vice ’85 film set.
A 42-year-old man reported that he had a verbal dispute with an individual who displayed a knife, an NYPD spokesperson told THR.
Perez was taken into custody without further incident, and the knife was recovered, police said. No injuries were reported. Perez was charged with menacing and criminal possession of a weapon.

In footage obtained by TMZ, Perez is seen being escorted away by a production staffer before pulling a large knife from his sweatshirt. According to TMZ, Perez also has five prior arrests involving alleged gang-related activities, assault with a firearm and burglary, among other offenses.

Universal Pictures released the first-look images of Butler as Sonny Crockett and Jordan as Ricardo Tubbs earlier this month. The actors have since been spotted filming in New Jersey and New York City. Jordan was also seen filming in New York on Friday.

Miami Vice ’85 is a reimagining of the 1980s NBC crime drama, which starred Don Johnson as Crockett and Philip Michael Thomas as Tubbs. Directed by Joseph Kosinski (Top Gun: Maverick, F1), the film also stars Alden Ehrenreich, Whitney Peak, Camila Morrone, Danny Ramirez, John Leguizamo, Andrew Schulz and Walton Goggins, among others. It is scheduled to hit theaters May 19, 2028.

items.title: The Boys in the Baths
items.description: The hottest party in the East Village is kept at a temperate 194 degrees Fahrenheit. The Russian & Turkish Baths, at 268 East 10th Street, is open seven days a week serving sweat, shrimp, and borscht. It has been going, at least according to lore, since 1892.
items.author: Ryan McGinley
paragraphs: The hottest party in the East Village is kept at a temperate 194 degrees Fahrenheit. The Russian & Turkish Baths, at 268 East 10th Street, is open seven days a week serving sweat, shrimp, and borscht. It has been going, at least according to lore, since 1892.

A hundred-plus years is plenty of time to see your fortunes rise and fall and rise again, and the Baths’ has. There were the émigré years, the second-generation years, the gay years, the Mafia years, the flophouse years. When the current ownership, the result of a détente between the Shapiro and Tuberman families, took over in 1985, the 10th Street Baths, as it was known, was down on its luck. “To be honest, we were probably the worst bathhouse in 1985,” says Dmitry Shapiro, who runs it on alternating weeks. Today, it’s the only bathhouse in the East Village that has survived.

But shvitzing (a Yiddishism for “sweating”) is a hardy tradition, wet-sculpting its own acolytes. Besides the remaining Russian baths in Brooklyn, there’s a flourishing scene of Korean baths in midtown and Queens, not to mention a sudden influx of trendy latter-day inheritors such as Bathhouse, Othership, and Lore. At the Russian & Turkish Baths, you pay a daily entrance fee — currently $60, each price hike attended by kvetching — and from there, the day is yours. You can alternate hot and cold, wetter (Turkish) and drier (Russian), get therapeutically beaten with oak leaves (a platza, which the previous owner, Al Modlin, is said to have dropped dead immediately after administering). You can have a Russian snack and a beer in the restaurant — John Belushi liked it so much he used to order takeout — or lie out on the roof with a smoke.

Today’s steamers attract a wider swath of society than the predominantly Ashkenazi Jews of yore. “You go to synagogue to clean your soul, and you come to the shvitz to clean your body,’’ a High Holidayer told the Times back in ’82. Now, you come to the Baths not to get clean but to get well — but not too well. Unlike its nouveau competitors, and the steam room at your local Equinox, the Baths retain some of its ancestral grit. It’s an oddly alluring patina. New York notables have always visited — Jean-Michel Basquiat and Jackie Mason, strange bathfellows — but even today, when celebrities live in fear of phone cameras and Deuxmoi reports, you can still encounter Bobby Cannavale or Mark Ruffalo, the chef Eddie Huang or his friend the artist Rashid Johnson, and Sam Nivola.

Steam’s adherents cut across class and caste, celeb and plebe, man and woman — the real innovation of the Russian & Turkish Baths, dating back to the current owners’ acquisition, was establishing co-ed bathing. (“Considering that a Turkish baths in New York now has a women’s night … almost anything is possible,” the great gay poet Thom Gunn once wrote to a friend.) The Baths still have dedicated men’s-only hours on Sundays and Thursdays, which have become gay meetups.

Then there’s the famous cold (hot) war. David Shapiro and his business partner, Boris Tuberman, both Soviet émigrés, had a falling-out sometime in the late ’80s. Dmitry, David’s son, mostly shrugs it off; just different management styles, he says. The unusual solution, like the Judgment of Solomon uninterrupted, was to split the baby down the middle: There are now “Boris weeks” (though Boris retired to Miami before COVID and his daughter and grandson run them now) and “David weeks” (though David died in 2020 and Dmitry runs them now). Entry passes are specific to whoever’s week it is and aren’t mutually legal tender. The arrangement makes more sense when you hear David was a New York City taxi driver first: Splitting a medallion and taking in all the cash one day before handing it off the next was standard practice. Forty years later, the system stands, though the families insist talk of a feud overstates the case. “It’s been generations; it’s not up for question,” Dorina Tuberman-Solon, Boris’s daughter, says. “We get along just fine,” Dmitry says.

The bathhouse culture that survived AIDS (“It would need Burroughs to do justice to the ghosts found in ruined bath houses, wouldn’t it?” Gunn wrote) and COVID has found itself ascendant again. The Baths has launched itself into the modern era, playing up its big-name guests on social media (albeit with two separate, parallel Instagram accounts). Its competitors in the new guard lean more direct-to-consumer than dynastic, but Dmitry says there’s no animosity between them. A rising tide lifts all shvitz. Dmitry is advising some newcomers, such as an upcoming female-founded bath in Tribeca; he has even invested in a few.

“There’s a ton, ton, ton of competition now, but I believe New York can meet the demand,” Dmitry says. There will always be some for whom it seems unthinkable: to strip down to your swimsuit (or, for single-sex hours, nothing but a towel) among strangers and sweat till you stink. Yet to its devotees, it’s a temple. “A perfect and disgusting place,” a friend of mine, a regular, told me.

So around Labor Day, we invited a mix of Baths regulars and a few first-timers — Troye Sivan, who’d just moved to the city; Marlon James, days after getting the book review of a lifetime; Francesco Clemente, who used to come with Basquiat in the ’80s — to wear some fashion. But hardly any.

items.title: Kojima Productions x F.C.Real Bristol Teases a Collab That Puts Hideo Kojima’s Studio on the Pitch
items.description: Kojima Productions x F.C.Real Bristol Teases a Collab That Puts Hideo Kojima’s Studio on the Pitch
items.author: Sophie Caraan
paragraphs: Kojima Productions x F.C.Real Bristol Teases a Collab That Puts Hideo Kojima’s Studio on the Pitch
SOPH.’s fictional football club is partnering with the game studio, with product details still under wraps.
Hideo Kojima’s Japanese game studio KOJIMA PRODUCTIONS has announced a collaboration with F.C.Real Bristol
F.C.Real Bristol is the imaginary football club brand run by SOPH., making this a crossover between game development and fictional sports fandom
No lineup, imagery or timing has been revealed yet, with more information promised in later updates

Kojima Productions has confirmed an upcoming F.C.Real Bristol collaboration, linking the Japanese game studio founded by creator Hideo Kojima with the fictional football label operated by SOPH. The announcement arrives as a teaser, marking the partnership as “coming soon” without laying out what the two sides have made together.

At this stage, the reveal is a pairing of names rather than a look at finished pieces. Neither partner has detailed the items involved, so materials, silhouettes, graphics and construction all remain unknown, and the announcement points readers toward future updates for the full breakdown.

What is clear is the unusual makeup of the collaboration itself. On one side sits a studio built around a single game creator’s vision, and on the other a football club that exists only as a brand, which means the eventual product will be shaped by two outfits whose identities are rooted in invented worlds.
“F.C.Real Bristol × KOJIMA PRODUCTIONS” coming soon.

items.title: The NEEDLES x Pendleton Collection Puts Six Pieces of Archival Wool to Work
items.description: NEEDLES and Pendleton link up for the first time on a six-piece capsule cut from Pendleton’s traditional plaids and wool fabrics
items.author: Sophie Caraan
paragraphs: NEEDLES and Pendleton link up for the first time on a six-piece capsule cut from Pendleton’s traditional plaids and wool fabrics
A boxy shirt, a jacket with leather elbow patches and a coat in an archival Pendleton pattern lead the outerwear and shirting
Plaid trousers, a mohair sweater in Pendleton’s signature Native-inspired motif and a fully lined Cowichan knit round out the lineup

NEEDLES is teaming up with Pendleton for the first time, debuting a six-piece NEEDLES x Pendleton collection that reworks the American mill’s classic plaids and wool cloth. Every garment starts from Pendleton’s fabric vocabulary, then gets recut through NEEDLES’ lens across shirting, tailoring, trousers and knits. The result is a tight capsule where the textiles do the talking and the construction choices tell you how each piece is meant to be worn.

The shirt sets the foundation for the collection with a relaxed, boxy silhouette that gives the plaid wool room to drape rather than cling. That easy cut turns a traditional flannel-weight top into something closer to a light overshirt, built for layering through the colder months. The jacket builds on the same fabric language but adds leather patches at the elbows, a reinforcement detail that nods to hard-wearing workwear and protects one of the first areas to wear through on a wool garment.

The coat is the statement piece of the drop, cut from a pattern pulled directly from Pendleton’s archive. Pairing that historical print with a full-length outer layer gives the design the most surface area to show off, making it the clearest showcase of the partnership’s archival focus. Plaid trousers complete the tailoring side, carrying the check pattern from top to bottom so the pieces can be worn as a coordinated set or broken up across a look.

The knitwear leans into texture and structure. Pendleton’s staple Native-inspired pattern appears on a sweater knit with mohair, which brings a soft, slightly brushed hand and extra warmth to the fiber blend. The Cowichan sweater, a chunky knit style with deep roots in outdoor dressing, gets a full lining throughout, a finishing step that smooths the interior against the skin and adds an extra layer of insulation.
The NEEDLES x Pendleton collection is available at Nepenthes stores and the Nepenthes online store.

items.title: The Nike Air Max 90 “Light Orewood Brown” Is All Patent Shine and See-Through Panels
items.description: Name: Nike Air Max 90 “Light Orewood Brown”
items.author: Sophie Caraan
paragraphs: Name: Nike Air Max 90 “Light Orewood Brown”
Colorway: Light Orewood Brown/Blue Tint-Sail-Neutral Olive

Nike is giving the Air Max 90 a material-driven makeover with the “Light Orewood Brown” colorway, pairing translucent overlays with high-gloss patent leather. The palette stays deliberately muted, sticking mostly to Light Orewood Brown and Sail so that texture and transparency become the main event. The result is a quiet take on Tinker Hatfield’s runner that rewards a closer look.

The upper is built in layers that play off one another. Textured mesh forms the base across the toe box and collar, while translucent panels sweep along the sidewalls and frame the lacing system, letting the mesh show through from beneath. Down low, the mudguards are finished in glossy beige patent leather, adding shine and contrast without breaking from the tonal color scheme.

Nike carries the see-through concept into the branding as well. The tongue labels and heel tabs are rendered in the same clear material, so the logos underneath remain visible through a glassy top layer. Cream laces and a matching lining keep the interior and lacing in step with the exterior, while a tonal midsole houses the silhouette’s signature visible Air unit in the heel.

Underfoot, a semi-translucent outsole continues the theme from top to bottom. The standout accessory is a metallic Swoosh hangtag clipped to the laces, engraved with an intricate pattern that is echoed on the printed insoles. That artwork links the pair to a wider set of releases, with forthcoming Air Max 95 and Air Force 1 styles set to carry the same engraved motif alongside their own patent leather and translucent details.

items.title: A. Lange & Söhne Marks 20 Years of the Datograph Perpetual in Platinum
items.description: A. Lange & Söhne marks 20 years of the Datograph Perpetual with a new platinum edition.
items.author: Zoe Leung
paragraphs: A. Lange & Söhne marks 20 years of the Datograph Perpetual with a new platinum edition.
The black dial features 11 baguette-cut diamond hour markers.
Its hand-wound L952.1 calibre combines flyback chronograph and perpetual calendar functions.

To celebrate the 20th anniversary of the Datograph Perpetual, A. Lange & Söhne has introduced a highly exclusive 50-piece limited-edition update to the iconic grand complication model. First launched in 2006, the Datograph Perpetual was the brand’s first wristwatch to seamlessly integrate a classic column-wheel flyback chronograph with a mechanical perpetual calendar and an outsize date.

This new iteration elevates the original design by pairing a 41mm 950 platinum case and matching platinum bracelet with a striking black and rhodié-colored 925 silver dial. Further enhancing its prestige, the dial features eleven manually applied baguette-cut diamonds serving as hour markers, omitting indices at 4 and 8 o’clock to accommodate the prominent rhodié auxiliary dials.

The dial is anchored by the signature Lange outsize date at 12 o’clock, which forms the tip of an equilateral triangle with the two main subdials. The subdial at 9 o’clock tracks small seconds, the day of the week, and a day/night indicator, while the 3 o’clock subdial displays the jumping minute counter, the month, and the leap-year cycle. A precise moon-phase display sits at 6 o’clock, completing the triangle.

The perpetual calendar mechanism is programmed to remain accurate until March 2100, while the moon phase will deviate by a single day only after 122.6 years of continuous operation. Adjusting these displays is remarkably simple, utilizing a single rapid-correction pusher at 10 o’clock or individual recessed correctors.

Driving these dual complications is the meticulously crafted L952.1 manually wound manufacture caliber, visible through a sapphire-crystal caseback. Assembled twice by hand, the 556-part movement features plates and bridges made of untreated German silver, a hand-engraved balance cock, and a classic column wheel to coordinate the chronograph’s precise switching sequences. The complex architecture provides 36 hours of power reserve while operating at a frequency of 18,000 semi-oscillations per hour.
For more information regarding the timepiece’s price and availability, head over to A. Lange & Söhne’s official website.
