items.title: New York’s AMC Kips Bay Theater Closes on Jan. 3; CEO Says ‘AMC Wants to Stay’ but NYU Langone ‘Wants Us Gone’
items.description: AMC CEO Adam Aron has spoken out on the closure of New York City’s popular AMC Kips Bay 15 movie theater, which will shutter on Jan. 3.
items.author: Jordan Moreau
paragraphs: AMC CEO Adam Aron has spoken out on the closure of New York City’s popular AMC Kips Bay 15 movie theater, which will shutter on Jan. 3.

Aron wrote a letter to the Kips Bay community and addressed how the nearby hospital NYU Langone, which plans to grow its medical facility, has not engaged with any of AMC’s alternatives to share the space. In addition to the 15-screen AMC theater, the building also houses a Fairway supermarket and bank, which are also expected to close.

“Unfortunately, the decision to retain or end AMC’s tenure in Kips Bay is not ours to make. The nearby NYU Langone Health facility wants to expand, seems to be in the process of buying the building in which your (our) theatre now operates, and it wants us gone. In anticipation of such a transfer to NYU Langone, the current building’s owner has terminated our lease,” Aron writes. “We have engaged with NYU Langone, suggesting any number of alternatives — including that it enlarge the current low-rise building to satisfy its desires for a growth of its medical facility but also leaving a theatre in place for you. Or alternatively, we offered that our theatre could get smaller, so that at the very least we could leave something remaining in place to continue to serve you. Sadly, any and all variations that we have proposed have fallen on closed minds.”

On Aug. 24, Variety reported that the Kips Bay theater would close at the end of 2026, ending a 27-year run at the location. AMC took over the theater in 2006, which became the chain’s second-largest multiplex in the city (after Times Square’s Empire 25 theater). The Kips Bay location has become adored by local residents, who staged a protest in September in an attempt to stop the closure.

“Every day, thousands of guests watch a movie at AMC Kips Bay 15,” Aron wrote. “It has become so popular of late that on several days this past summer, AMC Kips Bay 15 was repeatedly among the 10 most attended movie theaters across the entire United States, out of the more than 500 theaters operated by AMC nationally.”

The theater closure comes after a record-breaking summer box office, which saw movies like “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” “The Odyssey,” “Toy Story 5” and more collectively gross $4.67 billion domestically. There are also major upcoming movies like “Avengers: Doomsday” and “Dune: Part III,” which Kips Bay residents will now still get a chance to see at their beloved theater before it closes for good.
Read Aron’s full letter below.
“To the Kips Bay Community,

Since news first broke that our popular AMC Kips Bay 15-screen movie theatre located at 570 Second Avenue in Manhattan will soon be forced against our will to close its doors, I’ve been struck by the extraordinary support that this AMC theatre has received from within the local surrounding community.

So many moviegoers and neighbors, and importantly so many of your elected officials, have rallied around our theatre. (Given the central role that movie theatres play in the lives of so many New Yorkers, perhaps it is much better and more accurate to say that so many of you have rallied around YOUR theatre.)

On behalf of everyone at AMC, thank you. Your support means a great deal to us, and especially to our theatre team members at AMC Kips Bay 15 who work tirelessly day-in and day-out to put smiles on your faces.

In thinking about this theatre, which has been a cultural icon and entertainment lifeline to so many nearby residents for decades and decades since its opening on May 14 1999, I want to make one thing absolutely clear:
AMC Theatres does not want to go. Not one little bit. AMC Theatres wants to stay in Kips Bay.

Operating under long term leases, there was a time that the monies headed each month to the theatre’s landlord had risen to become so high that the theatre’s long-term viability was uncertain. But, we were fortunate to have been successful in addressing those concerns in recent years. Today this theatre (one which has been in continuous operation for more than 25 years) has a bright future — if we would be allowed to keep it.

Indeed, every day, thousands of guests watch a movie at AMC Kips Bay 15. It has become so popular of late that on several days this past summer, AMC Kips Bay 15 was repeatedly among the 10 most attended movie theatres across the entire United States, out of the more than 500 theatres operated by AMC nationally.
In that light, this is a theatre that should not be even close to a permanent shutting off of its lights.
Of course, AMC wants this AMC movie theatre to stay in place.

And remembering how much and how often Americans love watching movies in theatres, a tradition in Manhattan that dates back more than a full century, we have heard from so many of you that you too want us to stay open for your benefit.
Apparently, NYU Langone Health does not share that view, not ours or not yours.

Unfortunately, the decision to retain or end AMC’s tenure in Kips Bay is not ours to make. The nearby NYU Langone Health facility wants to expand, seems to be in the process of buying the building in which your (our) theatre now operates, and it wants us gone. In anticipation of such a transfer to NYU Langone, the current building’s owner has terminated our lease.

We have engaged with NYU Langone, suggesting any number of alternatives — including that it enlarge the current low-rise building to satisfy its desires for a growth of its medical facility but also leaving a theatre in place for you. Or alternatively, we offered that our theatre could get smaller, so that at the very least we could leave something remaining in place to continue to serve you. Sadly, any and all variations that we have proposed have fallen on closed minds.

We call on NYU Langone Health to open their minds, to think creatively, and come up with a solution that will give the Kips Bay community BOTH of the two things that is wanted most of all: expanded facilities offering the world class medical care that is the hallmark of NYU Langone Health AND a fully functional AMC Theatre on Second Avenue.

It isn’t true that New Yorkers can be prevented from having your cake and eating it too. Indeed you can. But only if people of goodwill think out of the box a bit. After all, the ubiquitous proverb “where there is a will, there is a way” is one that is believed to have first been published in the year 1640 — that’s three hundred eighty six years back to be precise.

Speaking of people of goodwill, I especially want to express gratitude to Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal and New York State Assembly Member Keith Powers, for their leadership and tireless advocacy on this matter. Reinforcing and speaking for the local community’s clear desire, they have energetically brought attention to the importance of keeping an AMC movie theatre open and operating in Kips Bay.
In summary, this is a theatre that you in Kips Bay want to continue to be at your beck and call, and one that we at AMC unequivocally also want to be allowed to continue within our theatrical fleet.

But time is short. Unless NYU Langone Health lets us delight the Kips Bay community beyond then, to comply with our terminated lease, the lights on AMC Kips Bay 15 will forevermore see their final sunset on January 3, a mere two and a half months from now.
Hopefully, there is an outcome in which a wise workable solution is devised, one that will benefit and please the entire neighborhood. What say you NYU Langone Health?

Whatever happens, I want you to know how much AMC appreciates your support, your efforts and your voice. We are proud to have been part of the Kips Bay community since 1999, and I sincerely hope that we can continue to be part of it for years to come.
Adam Aron, Chairman of the Board and Chief Executive Officer AMC Entertainment

items.title: Why Olivia Colman Didn’t Get Splinters From Getting Intimate With Alexander Skarsgård’s ‘Wicker’ Costume
items.description: Believe the hype. “Wicker,” now in theaters, is every bit as horny, romantic and wonderful as the trailer leads you to believe.
items.author: Jazz Tangcay
paragraphs: Believe the hype. “Wicker,” now in theaters, is every bit as horny, romantic and wonderful as the trailer leads you to believe.

Olivia Colman plays a spinster fisherwoman in a medieval community where marriage is what gives a woman worth. Although she is a fierce independent woman, the village mocks her as she goes about making her living. One day she goes to the local basket weaver, played by Peter Dinklage, and asks him to make her a wicker husband.
Enter Alexander Skarsgård — yes, that is him under all that makeup — wearing a practical suit and prosthetic makeup to transform him into a basket man.

It began with Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson, who were adapting Ursula Wills’ short story “The Wicker Husband.” Weta Workshop artists, prosthetic makeup designer Joe Dunckley and lead makeup FX artist Sarah Rubano received the script and a call from the writers and directors who told them, “We want to make this practically,” says Dunckley. “They wanted a piece of beautiful concept art that showed their vision.”

The pair spent 18 months in research and development alone. Because prosthetic makeup materials are manufactured to imitate human flesh and skin, it posed a challenge. “This guy is made of wicker, so we had to do it a different way,” Dunckley says. He continues, “We tested our theory. We thought that if we could get the strands of the weave to be individual and get them to move as if they were individual muscle fibers that drove his movement, then he could be a believable sentient wicker being.”
But they couldn’t mold it, so the pair were pushed toward modern innovation using 3D digital sculpting and 3D printing.
They began with a full-body scan of Skarsgård so they could sculpt pieces specific to him.

The intricate basket weave was created using a relatively new powder-bed laser-sintered printing process. Dunckley explains, “It’s a volume of thermoplastic elastomer; you shoot a laser into it and where that focal point of the laser is, it fuses the powder and you can build intricate weave and complex geometry. The powder in the bed holds the strands apart while they set.”
And why didn’t Colman get splinters during the film’s steamy bonking scenes?

Nearly all of Skarsgård’s costume was made up of 50 individual 3D-printed appliances that were painted to look like wicker before being stitched onto a suit made out of soft, flexible spandex — so no actual straw was involved.
Dunckley says, “It’s a semiflexible material, not too dissimilar to the feeling of touching proper wicker weave.”
As for the prosthetics, Rubano focused on the makeup, which comprised 10 individual pieces.

Rubano says, “He would get into this very fitted suit and we would bounce between the makeup chair and getting him ready in the suit, depending on the different stages.” She goes on to say, “We had ears, eye bags and lips. We had an underlip piece and a jaw piece, and the larger forehead, nose, cheekbones and there was lots of hand painting around his eyes.”

His facial hair — beard, hair and eyelashes — was constructed from muka, a silky-soft fiber extracted from the harakeke plant. This material allowed them to knot the individual strands onto the weave itself so they could cut and style it like human hair.

The key was not to lose Skarsgård under the makeup. Dunckley says the team used 3D animation software: “We could track the expressive range of the face so that we could engineer into the weave the ability to move for his expression.”
In all, it took under two hours to transform Skarsgård into the wicker husband. “90 minutes is where we were by the end of it,” Rubano says.

Dunckley adds, “The other big piece to the puzzle was Alexander himself. What a wonderful collaborator and team player! He was resilient. He was funny. He was so invested. He would sit as still as a statue in the chair.”
They encountered one small issue. Rubano reveals, “He runs hot; the suit’s kind of hot and it was a hot Hungarian spring.”
And what about the wicker penis?

“There’s been a lot of speculation about just the mechanics of how this would work and about the potential danger of a wicker penis,” Dunckley says. “I think the basket maker, he’s skilled. He’s traveled the world. He’s learned from every culture how to weave, and I think he would know exactly how to weave a wicker ween so it’s user-friendly.”

Rubano credits the film’s costume designers András Dániel Tóth and Attila Godena-Juhász for that detail. “They fabricated the wicker ween for the full-body river shot. They did such a great job because it was very last minute, but it’s puff spandex. The weave was 3D, so there was dimension to it. From a distance, they color-matched it so beautifully.”

items.title: The Emancipation of Charli D’Amelio: How the TikTok Queen Took Back Her Life
items.description: Charli D‘Amelio — the reigning queen of TikTok — loves to dance. Whenever a new song comes on at this photography studio in L.A., Charli is shimmying her shoulders, shaking her hips. Now she stamps and turns like a flamenco dancer, swishing the skirt of her ru
items.author: Nancy Jo Sales
paragraphs: Charli D‘Amelio — the reigning queen of TikTok — loves to dance. Whenever a new song comes on at this photography studio in L.A., Charli is shimmying her shoulders, shaking her hips. Now she stamps and turns like a flamenco dancer, swishing the skirt of her ruffly black gown. “So pretty, stunning,” says Emman Montalvan, the photographer snapping her. “Gorg!”

With her glossy black hair and sparkly smile, Charli is gorg. She’s the girl next door drawn by Disney; she’s the bright and shiny face of social media, making it all seem benign. “This is her before she becomes jaded,” Montalvan observes. “Nothing calculated. Natural. She reminds me of when Britney Spears was young.”
Rihanna’s “Breakin’ Dishes” begins to play. Charli mouths the words: “I don’t know who you think I am —”

“Are you having fun?” I ask, finding myself smiling. Because when Charli is happy, you feel happy — which is no doubt part of her appeal. You want to believe that a life spent dancing around in fabulous clothes and opening yourself up to a dizzying 160 million-plus followers (the second most on TikTok) really is as wonderful as it looks.

But a flicker of annoyance crosses Charli’s brow, as if the question touches a nerve. Maybe that’s because of how the algorithms are always demanding she offer up the semblance of a perfect life, the performance of joy, no matter the reality.

“Are you having fun?” she asks, flashing her diamond bracelet smile. Then she’s running gleefully down the hallway of the studio, followed by her social media manager, Alexa Davis, who films her nearly constantly with a DJI Osmo Pocket. When Charli’s having fun, there’s someone there to capture it.

Coming off a 10-month run in Broadway’s & Juliet — in which she sang and danced in the ensemble cast, earning some good reviews — Charli moved into a house in Valley Village, California, all by herself, earlier this year. The place represents something more than just a first home: At 22, Charli has separated herself professionally and financially from the family with whom she built her extraordinary career.
“I’m figuring out who I want to be,” she tells me, “and that’s what I’m really excited for.”

For years, Charli and her parents, Marc and Heidi D’Amelio, and her older sister, Dixie, seemed inseparable. They moved to L.A. together, signed with the same talent agency, started businesses, starred in a Hulu reality show. Charli was always the main attraction, the engine of an empire — consisting of brand partnerships, media ventures, a clothing line and more — all built on the image of a close-knit family. Now, amid public speculation that her parents mismanaged her money — which her father has denied — she’s trying to find out who she is apart from them. (None of the D’Amelios responded to requests for comment.)

The new place is her first house of her own. It doesn’t quite look like what you’d expect of a young woman who earns an estimated $18 million a year annually, according to Forbes. It’s a modest, almost nondescript two-story house on a tree-lined street, with a gate and security door, but nothing that screams “TikTok star.”

But then you get to the secluded backyard with its shimmering pool, immaculate lawn and big stone grill, and you see the dance studio with the neon sign: RED BULL DANCE YOUR STYLE. Red Bull, one of Charli’s sponsors, built it for her. She grew up promoting brands; now even her backyard comes with one.

“This is a very much a home,” Charli says, her voice soft and gentle as ASMR. She’s sitting cross-legged on the oversized wraparound couch in her big, open living room — her “safe space,” she tells me. She’s wearing Levi’s and a long-sleeved black Prada top (she’s an official friend of the house, so there’s Prada, Prada everywhere around her). Seventeen silver studs and hoops glint at her ears.

“Sometimes I just fall asleep here,” she says sleepily. “It’s so comfy, it’s a slippery slope.” She spends a lot of time alone, just being on her phone or watching her giant, wall-mounted TV. On the couch, there’s a pillow that says: JUST A GIRL WHO LOVES ORCAS. Charli says she likes the way they always win in a fight with sharks.

“Lame of a life as it may be sometimes, I love just to be at home and do nothing,” she says. “I’m surrounded by a lot of peace, which is something it took me a long time to realize I need to be comfortable.”

She’s been a bit of a “hermit” over the past year, she says, retreating from a life in which almost everything she did was potentially something to be shared. “I took my first break off of social media” between October and February, “which was a really tough decision — I was always told, ‘If you take a break, you can never come back’ — but I think mentally I was just in a place where I needed to stop working and figure out who I was.

“I started working full-time when I was 15,” she continues, “and once I started, it was, ‘OK, this is my life now.’ But the other side of it was, ‘This is all I’ve ever known.’ And I think it took me, really for the first time, taking a step back and being like, ‘Who am I? What am I? Do I have a favorite color? Do I have a favorite anything?’ I realized I didn’t really know anything about myself, and so I had to sit with the hard truth of like, ‘Who am I at night when everyone leaves and no one cares that I’m Charli D’Amelio,’ you know?”
Her dog, Rebel, a 12-year-old chocolate lab, stares up at her worshipfully.

The bloodshot eyes of the internet noticed, of course, when Charli took a break — not just from social media but seemingly from the family that had been so central to her identity. She hasn’t appeared publicly with her parents or her sister for about a year, adding to speculation of a rift.

In May, the gossip website Deuxmoi published allegations that Marc and Heidi had mismanaged Charli’s money. In June, Marc took to TikTok to deny these claims. “So a website said … we took money and put it offshore,” said Marc, sounding frustrated. “I wouldn’t even know how to do that. Come on, dude. This was never about money, it was about having this crazy, awesome experience with my family.”

And then in September, appearing on creator Quenlin Blackwell’s YouTube cooking show, Feeding Starving Celebrities, Charli was asked how much money she had made from a certain item of merch. “Mmm, ain’t that the question,” she responded, deadpan. “Wouldn’t I like to know.” The moment went viral, becoming a GIF. “Charli D’Amelio family drama” trended on TikTok.

Charli was just your average upper-middle-class girl, growing up in Norwalk, Connecticut, when TikTok made her famous overnight. She’d been dancing competitively for nearly a decade when, in May 2019, at age 15, she began posting videos of herself doing popular routines, “just like everybody else was doing.”

“My dream in life was to be a backup dancer,” she says. “I was like, ‘I want to go to the University of Nevada at Las Vegas and join their dance team,’ because they’d won nationals. I’m a very type A person. I had a vision board — I had a whole plan. But then the plan went sideways.”

Five months after she started posting on TikTok, she had a million followers. By November 2020, she’d become the first TikTok creator to reach 100 million. Why her? Even Charli can’t explain it. “I think it was a mix of things,” she says. “Happy accident.” People watched her videos repeatedly to learn the choreography. “Also, when I started, I got just as much hate as I got love, so people were talking, arguing with each other.”

Enragement, as they say, drove engagement. People argued about Charli’s looks, her dancing, whether she deserved her fame. In 2019, she drew criticism for performing the viral “Renegade” dance to K Camp’s song “Lottery” without crediting its 14-year-old Black creator, Jalaiah Harmon. (Charli and pop star Addison Rae later performed the original choreography with Harmon, giving her proper credit.)
Then COVID-19 drove young people inside, where they were more often on their phones, and what better way to distract oneself from a pandemic than watching pretty Charli D’Amelio dance?

For a generation of girls, Charli represented the ultimate social media success story. You didn’t need a Hollywood agent — you could become famous in your bedroom, just by being yourself. The catch: Once being yourself became your job, you might never get to stop working.

Charli was about to become one of the most famous teenagers in the world while remaining remarkably powerless over her own life, she says: “I was a child, which I didn’t really get the significance of at the time, but I can see it very clearly now.”

In summer 2020, Charli moved with her family into a rented mansion in the Hollywood Hills. The relocation was her idea; she felt “there was a lot more I could be doing,” though she’d already appeared in a Super Bowl commercial and an ABC special. She and her family signed with UTA as a package.

Marc came from the apparel industry and had an unsuccessful run as a Republican candidate for the Connecticut State Senate in 2018; Heidi was a former model and personal trainer; and Dixie, three years older than Charli, was an aspiring singer. The family seemed to envision a Kardashian-esque enterprise, with Charli as its teenage Kim. Marc and Dixie launched their own TikTok accounts after Charli went viral. Everyone had a part to play in Charli’s newfound fame.

There’s a family story here that predates TikTok: A gifted child gets flooded with opportunities, and the adults around her see ways to capitalize on her appeal. Their involvement in her career, no matter how well-meaning, also gives them a say in her image and her decisions.

In the pilot episode of The D’Amelio Show (2021-2023), the family sits down to hear the business plan for the upcoming year. Greg Goodfried, a former UTA agent who became their manager, holds forth enthusiastically. On the floor are 23 binders — 23! — containing proposals for a slew of new business ventures.
“Where is the binder where she gets to be a kid?” Heidi asks.
“I still have those binders,” Charli tells me wryly. “Twenty-three major projects in a year were agreed to. I had just turned 16.” (Goodfried did not respond to requests for comment.)
“I’m always grateful. I know I’m very lucky,” Charli says. “I don’t know what doing this without them would have looked like; I don’t know if I would have had this life.”

It’s a refrain she returns to, almost as if she fears that questioning what happened will be mistaken for ingratitude. One of the peculiar cruelties of fame for young women is that they must be grateful for it, no matter how much it hurts.

But lately she’s been reassessing what it meant to be a working child in the entertainment industry. “I was the youngest in every room I was in,” she says. “I was surrounded by people who were the best in the business, so you trust because that’s all you have — these people who are supposed to be guiding and helping you. But people are selfish, and that’s the sad reality.
“And people have bad intentions, too,” she adds. “You can’t be a trusting person. I’ve learned that the hard way.”
Rebel presses her nose against Charli’s knee. Charli pats it.

“There are not a lot of rules and regulations when it comes to people who do what I do,” says Charli. “I didn’t start learning about and getting involved in my financials until I was about 21. I’m very fortunate to be able to be living the life that I am, but I’ve also been working nonstop since I was 15, so I should have stuff to show for it.”

The laws protecting children in film and television evolved over decades in response to cases of exploitation. But the business of children making money on social media has grown faster than the rules protecting them. When parents are also business partners, who is looking out for the child?
Are the rumors true, I ask, about her parents mishandling her money?
“No, they’re not true,” Charli says. “I wouldn’t say that they stole my money.”
“I think we did a lot of things as a family,” she says carefully.

Recently, Charli has been watching The D’Amelio Show for the first time. “It’s kind of like watching something I never lived,” she says. “It’s almost as if I’m figuring out what has happened in my life over these last few years. I was so disconnected in so many ways.”
I mention how flat and monotone she seems onscreen, nothing like the person talking to me now.

“I was like that. For years,” she says. “I kind of stopped talking. I stopped having a personality. I stopped doing much of anything because I had so much scrutiny from the outside world. It’s taken me to now to realize maybe I was dissociating through a lot of it.”

All 28 episodes of The D’Amelio Show come with mental health trigger warnings. Charli and Dixie are seen struggling with the unceasing abuse that comes with online fame. At one point, a viral post predicts Charli’s death. Grown men make vulgar, sexualized videos about her when she’s still a teenager. “It’s a scary world, and it was hard on me,” she says.

Her experience wasn’t so different from that of millions of girls negotiating a world of constant comparison and judgment — it was just on a much larger scale. Charli was the smiling face of a platform that amplified those pressures, twerking and twirling like the girl in The Red Shoes who couldn’t stop dancing.

To many of her fans, she represented the fantasy: beauty, popularity, incredible clothes, a seemingly perfect family, wealth that came from doing what she loved. Behind it was a girl overwhelmed by scrutiny. Adolescent girls had always been judged on their looks and popularity; what was new was the technology that could make the judgment relentless, public and profitable. Charli was both a victim of social media culture and one of its most effective advertisements.
“Have you ever seen The Matrix?” I ask.
“Is that the one where Keanu Reeves goes like this?” she says, doing the move where he dodges bullets in slow motion.
I tell her about the main character, Neo, who discovers his world is a simulation controlled by machines. “And then when he wakes up, he starts fighting back. You should watch it.”
“I love that, you’re giving me homework,” she says with a little laugh.

Charli had suffered from anxiety even before TikTok. “I was a kid when I started having severe anxiety,” she says. In third grade, bullies pulled her hair and shoved her into a bathroom stall, breaking two of her fingers. “That was the same age I started having anxiety, so maybe they are connected,” she says. “I never really thought about that before.”

On her reality show, her anxiety becomes a storyline. She describes having up to 15 panic attacks a day; viewers see her sob and break down in response to online hate. “But then I would get hate for showing my feelings,” she says. “You’re not allowed to be upset, you’re not allowed to cry, you’re not allowed to have any emotion, you can’t be angry.”

Part of the concept of the show was to expose the dark side of influencer fame — even as it made its underage star more famous. But while the show urged viewers who were struggling to seek treatment for their mental health, Charli feels she didn’t always get the help she needed.

“I went untreated for most of my life,” she says. “I had a life coach” from ages 16 to 19, “but I didn’t have a therapist. I probably should have had a therapist. I wasn’t medicated at all, even though I had ADHD, which I didn’t get diagnosed with until I was 18.” She was later also diagnosed with OCD and trichotillomania, a hair-pulling disorder associated with OCD and anxiety.

Her life was work. Due to her professional commitments, she dropped out of high school at 16, though friends back home in Connecticut made sure she went to prom. Meanwhile, she was having experiences some kids dream of, such as winning season 31 of Dancing With the Stars (along with her dance partner Mark Ballas) in 2022, when she was 18.
Her mother, Heidi, also competed that year. She came in eighth place.

Charli has been seeing a therapist lately. “I told my therapist,” she says, “one thing I don’t want to be is another statistic. I don’t want to be another kid who got thrown into Hollywood and let that ruin their life.”

The cautionary tales of child stardom, from Judy Garland to Britney Spears, have found a new breeding ground online. Charli’s generation doesn’t need studio executives to make them famous anymore, but the disappearance of the old gatekeepers hasn’t made children any less vulnerable to exploitation.
I ask what finally made her reconsider how she wanted to move forward?

“This is probably going to sound really crazy,” Charli says, “but I was doing Broadway” — & Juliet, a gig she’d chosen herself — “and it was the easiest thing I had ever done. And I did a good job. I showed up every day with a smile on my face, and I loved every second of it. And it reignited something in me, this love that I used to have” for dancing, performing.

She had moved to New York — without her family — and was living in Columbus Circle to be near the theater. After years of being the star, it felt like a “relief” to be part of an ensemble of dancers, some of whom became friends. For the first time in her life, she was on her own, and it felt good.

But then, when her run ended in September 2025, she says she became “the most depressed I’d ever been.” She rarely left her apartment and “didn’t see another human for a few months.” She went off social media and decided it was time to “take a look at myself.”

Her team continued pitching projects that felt uncomfortably familiar. She started saying no. In December, she parted ways with Goodfried, her former manager. She doesn’t have a replacement manager yet, “but I’m OK with that,” she says. “I like it. I’m in charge. Now I say what I’m doing and not doing.” She sits up a little as she says this, her drowsy voice suddenly more alive.

She also separated herself from the D’Amelio family business. Now, she oversees her own finances. For most 22-year-olds, independence means getting a job and supporting oneself; for Charli, it has meant taking command of an empire she helped build before she was old enough to vote.

The internet took note again when she and her parents unfollowed one another on Instagram. Marc said on TikTok that he now communicates with Charli “through her lawyer.” As for Dixie, Charli says, “I mean, that’s my sister. I’m going to love her till the day I die. But there are times where you’re figuring stuff out.”

Charli’s still making TikToks, still dancing around, smiling, in cool clothes; and she’s vlogging more on her YouTube channel, which has around 9 million followers. “Sometimes I want to record my entire day,” she says. “And sometimes I talk about whatever people are asking for. People like to feel included.” She’s still looking for ways to monetize her platform, still promoting Dunkin’, which has named two drinks after her: The Charli (2020) and The Charli Cold Foam (2021).
Charli isn’t trying to bring down TikTok or renounce the fortune that brought her here. She isn’t trying to escape the machine. She just wants to be the one at the controls.

“I’m taking the last few months of 2026 to work on getting to a place where I’m doing things I’m really proud of,” she says. She has a major project to announce in November, something that “I hold dear to my heart.”

She continues: “Because of being told so often I didn’t deserve where I was, I felt that way for a really long time. But I’m at the point now where I can see that, like, I’ve lived a pretty amazing life, and I’m getting what I feel is like my second chance to do this the way that I want to do it.
“I love what I do,” she says. “I love the person that I’m turning out to be.”

Charli’s publicist, Nicole Perez-Krueger, comes in the room and says it’s time to stop. Charli’s dinner guests are arriving — her social media manager, Davis; her day-to-day manager, Alison Scoon; her stylist, Carlee Barrow; her agent, Ali Berman, and Berman’s 7-year-old daughter, June.
They really are her friends, Charli says. They bring the sides. Charli’s going to grill them steak.
“How do you do your TikToks and stuff?” June asks.
“I just dance what I feel and say what I feel,” Charli says with a smile.
Her social media manager is filming again.
This story appeared in the Oct. 21 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine. Click here to subscribe.

items.title: With ‘Phony,’ Nick Paley Poses a Horrifying Question — But Makes It Funny
items.description: There are TV moms. And there are TV moms played by Connie Britton, a God tier performer who can pull off a legitimately cool parent unlike anyone else. (Apologies to Amy Poehler’s Mean Girls character.) So, if you’re a showrunner wanting their audience to imme
items.author: Mikey O'Connell
paragraphs: There are TV moms. And there are TV moms played by Connie Britton, a God tier performer who can pull off a legitimately cool parent unlike anyone else. (Apologies to Amy Poehler’s Mean Girls character.) So, if you’re a showrunner wanting their audience to immediately buy in on a bonkers maternal premise — a son wakes up from a coma and decides that his mother/best friend has been replaced by an impostor — who but Friday Night Lights‘ Tami Taylor would you cast to play the mom and her alleged doppelganger?

Fortunately for Phony creator Nick Paley, he never had to answer that question. “I wrote this letter to her telling her how big a fan I was,” Paley says of his initial ovation. “She was freaked out by this idea of playing two people. This is somebody who could rest on her laurels if she wanted to, but she’s taking a big creative risk.”

He says “two people,” though whether that’s even true or not is the mystery part of this mystery-comedy. Phony, which saw its first two episodes arrive on Hulu on Oct. 20, stars Sam Nivola as Sonny. Over the course of that first episode he goes from earnest teenager, a mama’s boy but not in a gross way, to a rebel on the rise. His belief that something horrible has happened to Ellen (Britton) and that he now shares his home with an alleged stranger (also Britton) is bolstered by a curious shift in Ellen’s behavior. Co-workers ask her what she’s done with her hair. She’s even smoking. It’s a dark idea, but the show never avoids the humor to be found in the surreal.

Paley previously edited on Inside Amy Schumer, directed for Broad City and co-wrote the script of Oscar-nominated Marcel the Shell with Shoes On. Phony is his first time as a series creator and showrunner, so the inspiration of the project goes way back. Way, way back.

“When I was in kindergarten, I was obsessed with the idea of my mom disappearing or dying,” he says. That Paley laughs as he explained all of this tells you something about the tone of his show: “She would drop me off at school, and I would tell her to drive safely. If she didn’t pick me up on time, I’d just assume she was a goner. Around that time, I found out my mother’s sister was her nonidentical twin. This was a new concept to me, and I was very freaked out by it.”

What helped turn this childhood quirk into a pilot script was a little research into Capgras syndrome, one hell of a delusional disorder that affects the rare patient who firmly believes a family member or close friend is an impostor. This naturally brings up the “unreliable narrator” issue that tends to misdirect mysteries — and has been deployed by more than one best-selling novel in 2026. Paley has purposely avoided this term. “Obviously that’s been coming up a lot in the press, but I told Sam, ‘You are reliable because it’s your narrative. You’re the reliable narrative.’”

And speaking of narratives, mom confusion seems to be in the cultural ether. After the viral trailer for horror feature Other Mommy dropped before those first screenings of The Odyssey, it was weeks before Paley even heard that dueling Jessica Chastains would traumatizing a child in cinemas weeks before his show premiered. Content wise, the two projects couldn’t be more different, but that hasn’t stopped Instagram users from commenting “It’s Other Mommy season!” below the Phony trailer. Rest assured, the only demons in Phony appear to be figurative. Even if you eighty-six the possibility of anything supernatural, though, clues about what’s really at play in Phony, if there are any, are not obvious. Though there is a plan.

The Phony pilot filmed way back in December 2024, before the third season of White Lotus landed and minted Nivola an instantly recognizable face to many TV viewers and the writers room didn’t gear up until fall 2025. Paley and his team have had time to put a lot of thought into the tone of the show and, pivotally, how he wanted to pace it. It’s not a limited series. And there’s no guarantee of a second season, so viewers looking for answers may wonder if they’ll even get them when the eight-episode run wraps in December. In hopes of wedding out any future frustrations, Paley is not being coy about that subject.

“I hate an endless mystery that just keeps compounding,” he says. “From the pitch, we said we were on a path could carry us through two more seasons. So, there is resolution coming to this mystery, the mystery you experience in these first episodes. That story gets answers… and then there’s a huge cliffhanger at the end of the season that kicks off into a new story.”

items.title: LUCIEN PAGÈS - FANTASTIC MAN
items.description: Fashion brands and media could barely exist without PRs as their dogged middlemen, and nobody in Paris does it with as much spirit as Lucien Pagès. Over the last 20 years he has built his company Lucien Pagès Communication into a publicity empire that’s behind
paragraphs: Fashion brands and media could barely exist without PRs as their dogged middlemen, and nobody in Paris does it with as much spirit as Lucien Pagès. Over the last 20 years he has built his company Lucien Pagès Communication into a publicity empire that’s behind everything cool and exciting in fashion today. The ever-present Frenchman is known for being a fixture at nearly every event and show he organises. Thanks to his knack for social media, he’s now more famous than many of his clients. However, last year Lucien suddenly disappeared from the fashion circus. Perhaps it was because he’d recently sold his business to a wealthy investor? Or maybe there were other, more personal, matters at play? The very welcoming PR mogul is now back, and ready to tell all.
From Fantastic Man n° 43 – 2026
Photography by PAUL KOOIKER

One of the first things Lucien Pagès does when we meet is give me a copy of ‘Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes’ by Robert Louis Stevenson, in which the future author of ‘Treasure Island’ goes hiking with an ass named Modestine. The book was last year’s Christmas present to clients and friends. Its cover – designed and printed by Benoît Astier de Villatte, founder of highbrow ceramics, perfumes and stationery brand Astier de Villatte – depicts Lucien leading a donkey forward along the road, an arm wrapped affectionately around its neck. Lucien is from the Cévennes, which is the key context at play. He grew up in the small, remote village of Vialas, and went on to become the most influential fashion publicist of his generation.

Today Lucien, who is 51, is sat at his desk in the Paris office of Lucien Pagès Communication. It’s in the 2nd arrondissement, not far from where Boulevard Poissonière turns into Boulevard Haussmann (at which point everything suddenly seems part of the same luxury shopping wonderland thanks to department stores Galeries Lafayette and Printemps, for whose product universe some portion of supply and demand has been driven by, or at the very least ambiently massaged by, Lucien’s work). His grey hair and beard are at the longest point where the word “shaved” is allowable. He’s wearing a black T-shirt, white trousers, white Nike trainers and a Rolex watch. His thick, slightly tortoise-shell glasses point, quite exactly, to a close proximity to the worlds of fashion and design.

Lucien’s 140 or so clients include fashion brands like Calvin Klein, JW Anderson, Loewe, Sacai, Saint Laurent and Schiaparelli; beauty brands like Aesop and Humanrace; luxury hotel brands like Pellicano; silverware brands like Puiforcat; restaurant brands (okay, just restaurants) like Le Voltaire; and perfume-slash-scented-candle brands like Byredo and Diptyque. What “client” means here varies quite a lot. A PR agency’s output might involve events, press releases, dinners, shows, presentations, influencer outreach, openings and showroom invites, plus a host of intangible actions that can’t be defined or quantified. Whatever Lucien is doing, he’s always communicating. “Did you know that calling came back?” he asks. “People receive too many emails so now you have to call.” Just out of the blue? “No, I send a message. ‘Can I call you? Do you have five minutes?’”

You imagine most people would have five minutes. Leaning against a wall in the office is a framed graphic entitled ‘Lucien Pagès in one word’: a series of Yves Klein blue squares (the calling card of its creator, the Instagram account Style Not Com) containing words supplied by some of Lucien’s acquaintances. Sarah Andelman goes with “chic.” Nicolas Di Felice offers “magician.” Anthony Vaccarello contributes “malin” meaning smart, shrewd, clever.

Courtesy of the book-prompt, our first conversation is almost entirely about Lucien’s childhood, his origin story. “My grandparents had a hotel and restaurant and my parents took it over, so I grew up there,” he says. The hotel was called the Chantoiseau, or birdsong, and despite its remoteness it attracted very interesting guests. The singer Yves Duteil wrote a song about it, ‘My Cévennes Friend’ (1983), that still goes out on the radio sometimes. Lucien’s father, Patrick Pagès, had a Michelin star and was a master sommelier. President François Mitterand came for lunch once, arriving by helicopter.

Much of Lucien’s sense of fashion and popular culture came via the three TV channels then available in France: “I was obsessed with ‘Dynasty’. It was on every Saturday night. We never had an apartment inside the hotel. We had a little room. I’d see strangers in the corridor. My mum would bring me the dessert that people didn’t want and I’d eat it in front of ‘Dynasty’. It was heaven.”

One day Lucien came across a list of the best fashion schools in the country and decided he would like to go to one. The École de la Chambre Syndicale de la Couture Parisienne (now the French Fashion Institute) was a place dominated by those you’d describe as “BCBG” or “bon chic, bon genre”: members of the French upper middle class, adherents of a certain conservative-coded chic. “I showed it to a friend of my parents because I didn’t dare talk to them about it,” Lucien remembers. “My dad was so scared I was gay. Saying I wanted to be a grand couturier would be to basically say: ‘I am indeed gay.’ So I talked to this friend and was thinking she’d help me to convince them, and she said, ‘They will never take you because you’re not BCBG.’”

They did take him. He learned about fashion history, needlework and draftsmanship, and he assumed he would be a designer. He took some internships, including a stint at Yves Saint Laurent and multiple spells at Dior in the final years of the Gianfranco Ferré era. Lucien’s first real job was with art director Marc Ascoli. “It was communication, but more the image side. We worked on Chloé’s first four campaigns with Phoebe [Philo].” He also helped organise shows for French designer Martine Sitbon, with whom Ascoli shared an office.

It was for Sitbon that he pulled off his first PR coup. “I found this fax asking for one of her dresses for Cate Blanchett, to promote a movie. I found it funny and I went to the atelier, because there were some duplicates, and I sent some dresses to the stylist without asking anyone. Cate Blanchett wore all of them, and there was a particularly bright yellow one. Everyone wrote articles about it because it was a very daring colour. It was my first PR action on my own. Because of the fax machine.”

The second time I visit, I bump into Lucien downstairs and we get into the lift together. “Can you give me ten minutes?” he says. “I have to call the New York office. There’s a bit of drama. I hope it’s not like Friday. That was just…” He imitates a fighter blocking strikes from all directions. “I just don’t want it to escalate.” I wait on one of the chairs by his door, opposite the receptionist and a vintage portrait of Kate Moss. Around 50 people work here, and Lucien is on the phone to one of the 15 in the New York branch. The London office – formed from a merger with British PR firm AIPR – has 25 staff.

When I am allowed to enter, I ask what it was about. He declines to say anything other than that today was “internal” and Friday was “external.” His office contains, by the way, around 200 oversize perfume bottles, which are part of a collection that totals nearly 400. Back in 2020, Lucien acted on a long-standing urge to own a giant classic-shaped bottle of Chanel No. 5, which led to wanting a giant heart-including-the-aorta-shaped bottle of C’est La Vie! by Christian Lacroix. He ended up finding ten of these in sizes ranging from ridiculously tiny to impractically huge (they sit Russian doll-like on the mantelpiece behind his desk), and it escalated from there. For a time he shared the bottles on TikTok, attracting as many as 600,000 views per video: there are people who know him as a fragrance collectibles influencer, nothing else. Even so, it all relates to his day job. “I’m not doing TikTok for fun,” he says. “I do TikTok to understand it.”

A publicist’s work used to be mostly about machinating behind the scenes – schmoozing editors, browbeating journalists, gatekeeping talent – but social media changed the equation. Lucien goes to almost every event the agency is involved with, then shares perfectly captured images of them via his Instagram account. With approximately 140,000 followers, including much of fashion’s core elite, that account is arguably more influential than quite a lot of the conventional media coverage he achieves. He runs through some imminent fixtures: the opening of a Paris flagship by lux-casual brand James Perse; a dinner hosted by Snapchat in honour of the wrapping-up of Pont Neuf (the bridge) by street artist JR; and a philanthropic dinner for the Pompidou Centre for which they are expecting around 1,000 guests and have commissioned an enormous flower arrangement that will resemble the tubes on the museum’s exterior. What does success look like for something like that? “That it’s open on time and it goes smoothly. Everyone’s changing their table until the last minute. You need to be sure that the new name is written by the calligrapher. You need to be sure the tables match the most recent changes.”

In a phone call, Business of Fashion editor-at-large Tim Blanks places Lucien in a small tradition of fashion PRs who become almost as well known as the clients they represent. “There is a PR person at any given moment whom everybody wants to be their PR person,” he says. “Before Lucien was Karla Otto. Before that there was Ed Filipowski at KCD. And in the ’90s, Michèle Montagne had all the cool people.”

Blanks – a friend and contact of Lucien’s from the early days – admires his “nose for the new and interesting,” which was evident from the beginning. Lucien founded the agency in 2006. His first client was American designer Adam Kimmel, with whom he shared an office in the Marais (Kimmel later became chief creative officer of WeWork, so office sharing is a theme for him). Other early clients included Jonathan Anderson and Simon Porte Jacquemus.

“He had a very small but amazingly interesting client list and it was already sort of global,” says Blanks. “Adam was from New York. Chitose Abe [the Sacai founder was Lucien’s second client] was from Tokyo – people that you actually wanted to cover. He has this very winning way of actually making you take interest in his clients because you want to. This is an asset for a PR person because you love him and you want to do something for him. So you will go to the thing that he wants you at without dragging your heels and going, ‘Oh, do I have to?’ If you really, really trust their taste and they’re telling you about somebody you haven’t heard about, somebody new that they’re representing, there’s obviously a much stronger chance that you listen.”

It’s the first day of Paris Fashion Week Men’s and, as ever, a driver will ferry Lucien between events and appointments. We find the car, a Mercedes, out on the boulevard and climb into the back. A bag has been stashed there containing a change of clothes in case needed. We’re on the way to the SS27 show of the label Rescha, by emerging designer Charlotte Chowdhury (formerly with Jacquemus).

As we drive across town Lucien mentions a piece ‘Architectural Digest’ published last year about his relationship with the Chantoiseau hotel. His father died 15 years ago, and although his mother, Christiane, tried to run it as a guest house for a time, that project proved short-lived. “It was costing more than it was bringing in, with some very strange people passing by,” he says. “I was, like, ‘Enjoy your house if you want to stay there, but I don’t want you to be in danger. I don’t want you to work for nothing.’” So now the 20-room hotel is simply his mother’s house but filled with the paraphernalia of Lucien’s universe: ceramics by Astier de Villatte, cushions and vases by India Mahdavi, a library of magazines in the former wine cellar.

But the point about the ‘Architectural Digest’ piece is that Lucien partly credits the memories it dredged up – his father died from cancer – for his noticing, the day after he did the interview, an irregularity in his testicle that turned out to be a tumour. “Maybe thinking about my dad saved me, because I paid attention to it.” Lucien had surgery but the cancer spread and he went through four rounds of chemo before getting the all-clear.

“It’s a trauma, in my life. My dad died from cancer at 62 and me, I got it at 50. He was treated and, without going into detail, it was very, very tough for him… So I was, like, ‘Okay, now it’s happening to me,’” he says. Did it make him want to change anything? “No. I wanted my life to be back as it was. Not because it was perfect but because I didn’t want what happened to exist, so the way for me to erase that moment was to go back to how things were.” Even so, after the first round, Lucien married his boyfriend of nine years. “It was just, ‘Okay: maybe it’s time to arrange your life.’”

We arrive at the Musée Guimet, France’s national museum of Asian art, an ideal backdrop for Rescha’s Franco-Indian aesthetic. Lucien receives a briefing. “We have ‘Le Monde’ coming through… Angelo Flaccavento…” He and Charlotte take a selfie together and confer for a while, then she’s summoned away by the guy who does TikTok for ‘Le Figaro’, France’s leading centre-right broadsheet. Lucien tells me Vogue Runway have pledged to attend, which is great as they’ve never covered Rescha before, though they haven’t decided whether or not to write a review. He heads backstage, asking if anyone knows where the whiteboard is: he wants to check the final looks. It’s the first time the agency has worked with Rescha. “It’s a special moment: the first one,” he says. “It’s the one I always remember.”

The moment approaches to allow guests in, and the room thins out. It’s important that people aren’t left waiting outside (it is the hottest day in history, heading towards a high of 39ºC), but a shoot has just finished and there are still a couple of models around who should not be seen off duty. I am shown to my allocated chair, where I sit next to Iris de la Villardière, co-founder of jewellery brand Viltier. She lights up warmly at the mention of Lucien’s name. The show starts. A few chiselled men – in sparkly sarees and cotton poplin shirts – appear among the largely female cast.

By the time I re-enter the entrance area, Lucien has left for the Saint Laurent show, shortly to start in the rotunda of the Bourse de Commerce. Near a giant Cambodian statue I run into Louise Chen, the famous DJ. “Lucien’s a sweetheart,” she says. “He’s everywhere, involved in everything, yet still manages to be charming to someone like me.”

Later, the Rescha Instagram account is filled with story reposts from fashion media and notable guests including South Asian community platform Diet Paratha (“She Worked at Jacquemus + Wales Bonner so OFC her PFW Show Was Beautiful”), ‘Women’s Wear Daily’ (“Ones to Watch for Men’s Spring 2027”), ‘Purple’ (“Backstage Rescha S/S 2027, PFW”), ‘Numéro’, ‘Grazia’, ‘L’Officiel’ and ‘L’Etiquette’. Tableware entrepreneur Alice Moireau self-identifies as “a @rescha.paris girl” to her 125,000 or so followers. Vogue Runway, alas, do not show.

The launch party for the new issue of ‘Acne Paper’ at the Jardin du Palais Royal is packed. Everyone is waving identical black fans to cool themselves down, making it feel like the summer party of an influential secret society. There’s an exhibition in the shop – images of a woman lying in multicoloured paint – but most guests are spilled out into a cordoned-off area in the gardened square. The theme is “Autoportrait,” described in a blurb as “where the magazine turns the gaze towards its publisher for the first time exploring the ideas that have shaped the house over three decades.”

Lucien’s agency has been helping to compile the American names on the guest list. I find him standing in front of the gate, talking to four people who are facing him and not each other. He is friendly and warm but there’s an inscrutability to him as well, a perennial sense there’s more he could theoretically say but won’t. About what, you’re not sure. He greets a revolving cast of interlocutors: a shinily black-clad Lauren Sherman from Puck, then Edouard Benadava, chief content officer at communications and production group The Independents. “I’m building our content vertical,” Edouard says.

The Independents acquired Lucien Pagès Communication back in 2024, adding it to a communications “vertical” (i.e. companies sharing an industry or theme) that also includes Karla Otto and AIPR. But although Lucien no longer owns the agency, the operational side remains the same. “There is more financial reporting, of course, so you feel the numbers more, but that’s why they leave me very free,” says Lucien. “People have fantasies about the group. It looks powerful, but in the end we do the same job. They just want me to perform in the best way possible.”

It’s a 40ºC evening. Desperate for hydration, I walk over to a bar surrounded by people with five-or six-figure Instagram followings: Syrian-Swedish painter Jwan Yosef, avant-garde surfer Michael February. I spot Lucien heading away along the ornate arcade. Is he leaving? “Yes!”

Lucien’s agenda this week also includes the launch of a “queer library” by Aesop, a cocktail reception for Meta, and shepherding guests through showrooms from relevant brands such as Our Legacy, God’s True Cashmere and JW Anderson. The latter is on the Rue du Louvre. It’s laid out and organised as if a retail outlet, and indeed it will be a pop-up store a little later this year. There’s a pair of floral Chelsea boots, a sweatshirt displaying the phrase “Anonymous Nude,” and a soft, brown replica of a squirrel. Lucien arrives, checks in with his door staff, then introduces me to Adam Iezzi, founder of AIPR, who merged with Lucien’s UK operation just over a year ago. “When you’re a PR you meet a lot of other PRs, but there’s no one else that I wanted to get into bed with,” Adam says.

The presentation for the new collection of Californian brand ERL is in a completely pink room with flowers painted onto the walls. Models lounge on cuboid blocks. On one plinth is a small pile of paperbacks. There is an Old English Sheepdog in the room, which seems to be part of the show. ‘Candy Girl’ (1963) by Frankie Valli & The Four Seasons, a proper diner-after-high-school number, is playing.

Is it meant to feel a bit David Lynch? “Maybe a bit Barbie,” says Lucien. It’s our last encounter. On Sunday, he’ll fly to Corsica for Jacquemus. Earlier this week, he tells me, ten influencers got trapped in the lift to his office. This doesn’t surprise me: it felt relatively full with two of us in it, and so certainly wasn’t designed to take that many people, or influencers. “Now nobody can use the lift in our whole building. I’m quite ashamed.” A guest kisses him on both cheeks. Another squeezes his arm: “C’est magnifique! C’est beau, eh?”

Does Lucien have an armoury of solutions for dealing with sticky situations? “When there’s a problem, we have to find a way for everyone to save face so we can move on. For a long time you could say, ‘It was a misunderstanding.’ But we’ve used it too much. People are starting to say, ‘No, it’s not a misunderstanding.’ And you’re, like, ‘Fuck, I tried the “misunderstanding.” It didn’t work.’”

Collaborative guest lists are a hornet’s nest. Lucien remembers an event “for someone very rich” where they were asked to get rid of a guest who’d slipped onto a supplementary list compiled by someone else. “They’d received the invitation and !SVP’d so what could I do? I couldn’t disinvite her. So I created what looked like a mass mail-out, saying that due to unfortunate circumstances, and because of security, we weren’t actually allowed to invite any more people and please accept our apologies. But in fact only one person received it. The person wasn’t offended because she imagined she was one of many.”

Lucien left hospital on 20 December 2025 and was back in the office on 8 January. “It was difficult for me because I work in fashion and I came back with no more hair and a fat face. I decided I didn’t care. I went to events.” It had been a lot thanks to his non-attendance that people caught wind of his illness. If his job had only involved emails, they wouldn’t have noticed: he never stopped replying to them. The idea to make a new edition of ‘Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes’ came during treatment. “I was finishing a journey, and it made me think of Stevenson, you know?” But despite the Cévennes coming up a lot, Lucien wants to disavow the appearance of hanging on to the past. “I’m not nostalgic for my childhood. I wouldn’t go back there for anything.”

As for actually reading the Stevenson book, the instinctive reaction is to think, “Well the contrast couldn’t be bigger could it?” Travelling around small villages in the 1870s versus achieving visibility for luxury brands in the 2020s. Another way of looking at it though is that it’s a powerful testimony to the power of PR, simply given how many people go to the region because of it. I’m not saying a press officer called Stevenson in 1878 to invite him on a “trip,” just that cultural gestures can have a long-lasting impact. There is a business in Vialas, near the Chantoiseau, where you can rent a donkey and follow Stevenson’s route. Vaguely related, the grandson of Yves Duteil, who wrote the song about the hotel, is now doing an internship with Lucien.

items.title: White Mountaineering x Alpha Industries Splice Three Military Classics Into Two Hybrid Jackets
items.description: White Mountaineering and ALPHA INDUSTRIES return for a third collaboration, built around two military-derived outerwear styles
items.author: Sophie Caraan
paragraphs: White Mountaineering and ALPHA INDUSTRIES return for a third collaboration, built around two military-derived outerwear styles
A hybrid coat starts from the N-3B and borrows details from the MA-1 and CWU-45P, while a hybrid flight jacket pairs an MA-1 silhouette with N-3B elements
Both styles combine water-repellent, high-density shells with a breathable, windproof WINDSTOPPER lining

White Mountaineering and Alpha Industries have reunited for their third collaboration, a two-piece outerwear release that blends the American military outfitter’s archive with the Japanese label’s functional design. Rather than reissuing a single classic, each jacket mixes elements from several military flight and cold-weather styles into one hybrid build.

The hybrid coat takes the N-3B as its foundation, keeping the longer, cold-weather proportions of the original while adding details drawn from both the MA-1 and the CWU-45P. Combining three distinct references in one garment gives the coat a familiar military feel without tying it to any single archival piece.

The hybrid flight jacket works the same idea in reverse. It keeps the shorter, instantly recognizable silhouette of the MA-1 and layers in details from the N-3B, bringing some of the parka’s practicality into a more compact flight-jacket shape.

Both styles share the same technical foundation. Each is cut from a densely woven fabric treated with a water-repellent finish to handle wet conditions, while the interior is lined with WINDSTOPPER, a membrane that blocks wind while letting moisture escape. That pairing allows both jackets to protect against the elements without trapping heat and sweat inside.
The White Mountaineering x Alpha Industries collaboration drops October 31 via White Mountaineering stores, the White Mountaineering online store and select stockists across Japan.

items.title: Matt Hui's SS27 “Live to the Fullest” Collection Reimagines the Uniforms of Childhood
items.description: Matt Hui's SS27 “Live to the Fullest” collection explores childhood nostalgia, freedom and self-discovery.
items.author: Zoe Leung
paragraphs: Matt Hui's SS27 “Live to the Fullest” collection explores childhood nostalgia, freedom and self-discovery.
School uniforms, scout attire and workwear inspire reconstructed tailoring, delicate knitwear and floral embellishments.
A dreamlike campaign explores identity through playful contrasts between reality and illusion.

What if growing up didn’t mean leaving behind the freedom and fearlessness of childhood? Hong Kong-based designer Matt Hui explores this question through his Spring/Summer 2027 collection, “Live to the Fullest,” a nostalgic yet forward-looking study of identity, self-expression and the possibilities of rediscovering one’s younger self.

Following his debut collection, which drew from old family photographs and childhood drawings, Hui continues his introspective approach by revisiting the uniforms and everyday clothing that shaped his formative years. School uniforms, physical education kits, scout attire, workwear and even pajamas become the starting points for a wardrobe that challenges the boundaries between discipline and individuality. Hui reinterprets these underlying codes through unexpected proportions, softened tailoring and playful construction, exploring how the conventions of adulthood might coexist with the uninhibited spirit of youth.

Throughout the range, traditional wardrobe elements are reconstructed into unconventional yet understated silhouettes. Scarves and ties are incorporated directly into garments, transforming accessories typically associated with formal dressing into integral design features. Classic pinstripes recur across the lineup, referencing the rigidity of uniforms while taking on a more relaxed, contemporary character. Hui balances structured tailoring with lightweight cotton lawn, soft cotton jersey, paper yarn and fine cashmere, introducing tactile contrasts that lend the pieces an effortless, lived-in quality.

Delicate floral embroidery, pointelle lace knitting and fully fashioned construction further soften the collection’s minimalist aesthetic, while hand-crocheted floral accessories introduce a sense of warmth and personal sentiment. Building on the one-size-fits-all philosophy of his previous season, Hui continues experimenting with adaptable proportions and considered craftsmanship, allowing familiar garments to take on new expressions without losing their original references.

The collection’s themes of memory and self-discovery extend into its accompanying campaign, which reunites Hui with stylist Perpetua Ip and photographer Feicien Feng. Conceived as a dreamlike game of hide-and-seek, the imagery moves between reality and illusion, following an ambiguous journey of searching, pursuit and awakening. Scenes of childhood play are juxtaposed with restrained interior settings, reinforcing the contrast between youthful spontaneity and adult introspection.

items.title: Maison Margiela Celebrates 20 Years of Its Ebisu Tokyo Store With New "Folders" Chapter
items.description: Maison Margiela has introduced a new chapter of its documentation project titled Maison Margiela/folders to honor 20 years of its Ebisu Tokyo flagship
items.author: Joyce Li
paragraphs: Maison Margiela has introduced a new chapter of its documentation project titled Maison Margiela/folders to honor 20 years of its Ebisu Tokyo flagship
The project highlights the building's evolution from a former electrical products factory alongside interviews with local Tabi collectors and original staff
The rollout includes a limited-edition zine and an in-store Line 2 cultural dialogue installation open to the public from November 5 to November 15
Maison Margiela has officially unveiled a new chapter of MaisonMargiela/folders, celebrating 20 years at its foundational Tokyo boutique located at 2-8-13 Ebisu Minami.

In September 2000, 12 years into the house’s history, the brand opened its first-ever standalone store not in Paris or Belgium, but in a traditional residential home in the Tokyo suburb of Ebisu at 3-3-3 Ebisu Minami. When required to relocate in 2006, the label avoided commercial strips and instead deepened its commitment to the neighborhood by acquiring a former electrical products factory just five minutes away at 2-8-13 Ebisu Minami. Retaining team members who have worked at the location since its inception, the space has served as the physical anchor for the brand’s identity and creative milestones in Japan for the past two decades.

Titled “Maison Margiela Tokyo: 20 Years at 2-8-13,” the documentation project records oral histories from staff, investigates the district’s creative landscape, and spotlights the local community of Tabi collectors. Alongside the historical survey, the initiative documents “Line 2: Unravelled Memory, Rewoven Future,” which captures a cross-cultural collaboration between Japanese artist Mio Suzuki and French tapestry fabricators Les Manufactures Nationales – Sèvres & Mobilier National.

The initial archive preview is accessible now via the Maison Margiela website, while the physical limited-edition ZINE will distribute across Ebisu on November 5 alongside the Line 2 installation, which remains on view in-store through November 15.

items.title: Marmot x CITY COUNTRY CITY’s “Everywhere” Capsule Layers Up for Winter
items.description: Marmot and CITY COUNTRY CITY reunite for their sixth capsule collection, titled the “Everywhere” series
items.author: Sophie Caraan
paragraphs: Marmot and CITY COUNTRY CITY reunite for their sixth capsule collection, titled the “Everywhere” series
A puffer jacket pairs PrimaLoft insulation with a Pertex Quantum shell, while a Polartec 100 fleece jacket comes with matching pants and a cap
Long- and short-sleeve tees feature archive-inspired graphics on a cotton-like, moisture-wicking body

Marmot and CITY COUNTRY CITY have teamed up again on the “Everywhere” series, their sixth collaborative capsule. Designed for the cold months ahead, the collection centers on technical insulation and fleece layers, rounded out by a pair of graphic tees that bring the same performance focus to everyday basics.

The puffer jacket leads the lineup, built from two well-known performance materials. PrimaLoft synthetic insulation provides warmth, while the outer shell is made from Pertex Quantum, a lightweight fabric designed to pack down small. Together, they give the jacket substantial insulation without excess bulk.

A fleece set offers a lighter layering option. The jacket is cut from Polartec 100 fleece and loaded with an array of pockets for storage, and it is joined by pants and a cap made from the same fabric, allowing the three pieces to be worn as a matching outfit or mixed into other looks.

The capsule closes with two T-shirts, offered in long and short sleeves. Both carry graphics inspired by archival designs, printed on a body that feels like cotton but absorbs moisture and dries quickly. The choice extends the collection’s technical approach to the most basic layer in the range.
The Marmot x CITY COUNTRY CITY “Everywhere” capsule drops October 24.

items.title: В ноябре россияне увидят метеорный дождь, парад планет и суперлуние
items.description: В ноябре россияне увидят метеорный дождь, парад планет и суперлуние
items.author: Иван Адоньев
paragraphs: В ноябре россияне увидят метеорный дождь, парад планет и суперлуние

Жители России в ноябре смогут наблюдать несколько астрономических событий, в том числе метеорный поток Южных Таурид, выравнивание четырёх планет и суперлуние. Об этом РИА Новости рассказал руководитель обсерватории Университета Решетнева Сергей Веселков.
В ночь с четвёртого на пятое ноября ожидается пик Южных Таурид. Активность потока составит около 5–10 метеоров в час, при этом он известен медленными и яркими болидами.
Условия для наблюдения в этом году будут благоприятными. Луна будет находиться в фазе убывающего серпа, а её освещённость составит 14%, поэтому она практически не помешает наблюдать за метеорами.

14 ноября на небе выстроятся Меркурий, Венера, Марс и Юпитер. Все четыре планеты можно будет увидеть невооружённым глазом. В Северном полушарии их следует искать в юго-восточной части неба: Венера и Меркурий окажутся ближе к горизонту, а Марс и Юпитер поднимутся выше.

24 ноября наступит полнолуние, которое в народной традиции называют «Бобровой луной». Оно совпадёт с суперлунием, поэтому спутник Земли будет казаться больше и ярче обычного. Полная фаза наступит в 17:53 по московскому времени.

30 ноября Луна с освещённостью 60% пройдёт по созвездию Льва и окажется почти посередине между Юпитером и Марсом. По словам Веселкова, наблюдать это явление будет легко благодаря яркости обеих планет.

items.title: Пыщ-пыщ! Помните ли вы рунет нулевых? Сложный тест для тех, кто учил олбанский
items.description: Только два из этих фактов про 2001 год правдивы. А какой мы выдумали?
items.author: Афиша Daily
paragraphs: Только два из этих фактов про 2001 год правдивы. А какой мы выдумали?
* Олег Куваев внесен Минюстом в реестр иноагентов.
А эти три события произошли в 2002 году… Или нет? Найдите неправильный.
2003 год — отличите событие, которого на самом деле не было?
Почти все эти факты про 2004 год правдивы. А в каком есть неточность?
Хорошенько вспомните 2005 год: какое событие в нем не случилось?
Присмотритесь внимательно: в одном из этих утверждений про 2006 год есть ошибка. В каком?
Возвращаем вам 2007 год — и снова один из фактов мы выдумали. Отличите его?
Непростой вопрос: в одном из этих фактов про 2008 год есть ошибка — всего в одно слово. Отличите?
Предпоследний вопрос — про 2009 год. В какое из утверждений закралась совсем маленькая неточность?
Последний вопрос, про 2010 год, совсем простой. Но будьте внимательны: что мы выдумали?

items.title: «Чувствую себя Николь»: как Адела превратила Николь Кидман в бимбо-икону тиктока
items.description: Адела — гламурная и смешная славик-бимбо с розовыми волосами из Братиславы. В детстве она занималась балетом, учила английский по ютуб-шоу и Disney Channel, мечтала стать певицей и в итоге оказалась первой словацкой артисткой в истории американского Billboard
items.author: Афиша Daily
paragraphs: Адела — гламурная и смешная славик-бимбо с розовыми волосами из Братиславы. В детстве она занималась балетом, учила английский по ютуб-шоу и Disney Channel, мечтала стать певицей и в итоге оказалась первой словацкой артисткой в истории американского Billboard Hot 100.

В сентябре Адела выпустила дебютный альбом «Prima». На нем была и песня «Nicole Kidman», которая стала хитом тиктока. В припеве певица повторяет: «I feel like Nicole» («Я чувствую себя Николь»). Идея песни пришла к ней, когда она собиралась на вечеринку «Золотого глобуса» и затягивала на себе тугой корсет. В этот момент Адела почувствовала себя такой гламурной, что к ней пришла мысль: «Сейчас я чувствую себя как Николь Кидман».

Песня превратилась в гимн гламура и уверенности в себе. Пользователи стали снимать ролики под трек, показывая моменты, когда чувствуют себя настоящими звездами. Достаточно лишь надеть любимую одежду, сделать удачную прическу или просто поймать нужное настроение.

Перед релизом Адела связалась с командой Кидман, чтобы получить разрешение использовать ее полное имя. Актриса согласилась, а в августе на лондонской премьере фильма «Практическая магия-2» рассказала поклоннице, что знает о певице и собирается сходить на ее концерт в Нэшвилле. После этого Кидман дебютировала в тиктоке, выложив ролик под песню Аделы «Ain’t in LA».

С сентября тикток разрывала песня про актрису. Тренд достиг пика 5 октября на показе Chanel весна-лето в Париже. Кидман записала липсинк под «Nicole Kidman» вместе с Дуа Липой, Педро Паскалем и Кристен Уиг. Видео мгновенно разошлось по соцсетям и только в тиктоке набрало 38 млн просмотров.
«Адела, детка, ты справилась».
«Тот факт, что сама Николь Кидман непринужденно подпевает песне, которая буквально называется „Nicole Kidman“, меня просто убивает».
«Адела официально поп-королева».
«Всегда любил Николь Кидман. Она одна из самых красивых женщин в мире».
«Теперь никто не сможет остановить Аделу. Она собирается покорить мир поп-музыки».

Популярности трека помог и клип, вышедший вместе с альбомом 4 сентября. В нем Адела отсылает сразу к нескольким фильмам Кидман: «С широко закрытыми глазами», «Плохой девочке», «Рождению» и «Мулен Руж». Актриса похвалила видео и призналась, что уже сама забыла некоторые ленты из своей фильмографии.

Есть у Аделы еще один вирусный трек — «Ain’t in LA» (да, именно под него в тиктоке дебютировала Кидман). Под него пользователи показывают родные города и районы, напоминая, что не обязательно жить в Лос-Анджелесе, чтобы быть интересным и чувствовать себя звездой. Этот трек, к слову, первым в карьере певицы попал в Billboard Hot 100.

items.title: “History Will Judge”: Bret Baier on Trump, Fox News, and the Perilous State of the Press
items.description: Bret Baier and I arrive at Cafe Milano and slip past the heavily armed Secret Service detail idling out front: Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, is having dinner in the back room. “This is kind of my clubhouse,” says the chief political anchor of Fox News
items.author: Aidan McLaughlin
paragraphs: Bret Baier and I arrive at Cafe Milano and slip past the heavily armed Secret Service detail idling out front: Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, is having dinner in the back room. “This is kind of my clubhouse,” says the chief political anchor of Fox News as we settle into a corner table. Franco Nuschese, the Georgetown restaurant’s proprietor, comes over to say hello. “I’ve known Franco for a long time, 25 years,” says Baier. He takes friends to dinner here and interviews subjects in the establishment’s dining room. After the Alfalfa Club dinner earlier this year, Milano hosted the after-party, and I ambled out sometime after midnight, faintly proud of my stamina. I learned the next day that Baier held court at one of its back tables until 3 a.m.

Tonight he’s on better behavior, waving off wine and sticking to soda water. “I have an election diet,” he tells me, explaining that he drops around 15 pounds every October of an election year. He recommends the beef tenderloin but orders the branzino for himself.

Tucked into a corner seat at the best table in the room, Baier is in his element. He pats down his hair, which is short and sculpted and appears totally immovable, like the top of a Playmobil figurine. He’s just come off set, and his face remains brushed with the tan makeup that ensures its uniformity and consistency through time and space and episodes of Special Report, the daily news program he has anchored for the last 17 years. The job—that is, serving as the face of the mighty conservative network’s news operation, which is celebrating its 30th year in business this month—has grown more challenging over the years as the institution has become increasingly intertwined with Donald Trump’s political movement.

We’re discussing the president’s attacks on the press, which recently culminated in an unprecedented attempt to ban certain news outlets from the White House over their coverage. “We made our feelings clear the second it happened,” Baier tells me. Privately, Baier lobbied Trump to reverse the ban, I’d been told by a source with knowledge of the conversations. Publicly, Fox News joined the rest of the media in pulling its coverage from the White House press pool. “There are die-hard MAGA folks who say that it was the wrong move, but there was no doubt,” he says. “There was never even a split second of thinking about it.”

It isn’t the only measure Fox is taking against the Trump administration: Internally, the network has for months paused booking interviews with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a former Fox News host, following his ejection of journalists from the Pentagon. “I always had a good relationship with him at Fox,” Baier says of Hegseth. “Obviously, I’m not a proponent of what he did with the Pentagon press pool. And I see…[the president] talks about him all the time as central casting.”

I ask whether he would host Hegseth on Special Report. “If I get clearance to, I would,” he says. He’s not getting clearance right now? “No, I mean, I think we made another decision as a news organization once we left the premises and got kicked out, and that was the decision that was made.”
It’s an early taste of the anchorman’s studied posture of neutrality—though Baier does, for a moment, betray a point of view. “I hope he lets the press back in,” he says.
