По словам руководителя арт-галереи Ельцин Центра Светланы Усольцевой, все участвующие в проекте заведения так или иначе связаны с современным искусством: молодые авторы, например, разрабатывают для них принты (для обложек меню и открыток).
Приобрести тиражное искусство в коллекцию

Специально к октябрьской выставке екатеринбургский бренд одежды Éclata вместе с художником Филиппом Олиефом создал платок «Плюша любит цветы» с принтом, композиция которого строится вокруг образа кошки с вазой цветов на спине. Носить его дизайнеры предлагают как топ, юбку или платье-бандо, а также использовать для создания сумки.

Стоимость аксессуара — 8 600 рублей. Купить можно в бутике Éclata в Екатеринбурге — на улице Хохрякова, 48, и в сувенирных магазинах Ельцин Центра. С 23 октября коллаборация появится во флагманском бутике бренда на Петровке в Москве.

items.title: Is God Another Addiction?
items.description: “God does not and cannot exist,” Iris Murdoch once wrote, “but what led us to conceive of him does exist, and is constantly experienced and pictured.” You could hang that sentence—epigraph, baleful blessing—over Meghan O’Gieblyn’s memoir, “Will and Attention”
items.author: James Wood
paragraphs: “God does not and cannot exist,” Iris Murdoch once wrote, “but what led us to conceive of him does exist, and is constantly experienced and pictured.” You could hang that sentence—epigraph, baleful blessing—over Meghan O’Gieblyn’s memoir, “Will and Attention” (Doubleday). In some ways, it resembles a conventional addiction memoir: an alcoholic in her twenties, O’Gieblyn got sober, flourished for more than a decade as an essayist and critic, and then started drinking again during the pandemic. She vividly recounts her year of secrecy and collapse, followed by rescue and restoration. The fractions of fall and rise are in order: the book’s existence attests to the recovery.

But “Will and Attention” is more complex and surprising than its form suggests. An anguished engagement with theological and philosophical texts, above all the writings of Simone Weil, it is closer to an unfinished spiritual diary than to the familiar sort of sculpted redemption story. O’Gieblyn was raised in a fundamentalist Christian community on Lake Michigan and intended to enter the ministry. She lost her faith in her early twenties, relatively late for a loyalist. (Losing one’s faith, like discovering an aptitude for music or sports, tends to happen early or not at all.) You may wonder whether she only mislaid it. She certainly does: “I want very much to live a good and virtuous life, without alcohol and drugs, which have made my life miserable. And I still long to believe in God, despite the resounding silence that suggests that he does not exist, or is not interested in us, or in me specifically.” Perhaps her book is really a memoir of her addiction to God. More anguishing, to a God who does not and cannot exist.

A sentence of Weil’s provides the book’s title. On the wall above her desk, O’Gieblyn tells us, is a line from the French thinker’s notebooks, collected in “Gravity and Grace”: “We have to try to cure our faults by attention and not by will.” O’Gieblyn is in pained and plaintive agreement with Weil, who goads her throughout the book. She shares Weil’s suspicion of the will, but has doubts when it comes to her own powers of attention. Her account opens with an acute examination of the paradoxes of willing (an example of how boldly this memoir follows its philosophical interests). Experience has taught her that you cannot will yourself out of addiction, or into religious faith. At twenty-eight, she started treatment for alcoholism, but only when she had reached the very bottom—she was living out of her car, having “lost basically everything and having refused the interventions of everyone who’d previously tried to help.” This turn to sobriety felt less like determination than like surrender, a failure of will. She notes that “will” means both desire (to want something, to will it) and the faculty used to control or cancel desire (will power). So “the will is both the problem and the solution to the problem.” O’Gieblyn considers her alcoholism and her loss of faith to be failures of will, yet she grew up hearing worshippers testify that their conversion to evangelical Christianity came through a surrendering of the will, a submission to God’s grace. At the wooden tabernacle where congregants gathered on summer evenings beside Lake Michigan, the pulpit bore a sign that read “LET GO AND LET GOD.” She remains “fascinated with this idea, despite having no metaphysical beliefs to support it.”

If O’Gieblyn’s self-diagnosis is right, the collapse of will that led to her loss of faith is awkwardly close to a collapse of will that might lead to her return to faith. A failure of will is not quite a surrender of will; a voluntary submission might be seen as some noble version of willing, a willing away of will. Nevertheless, we seem to be in a strange twilight realm in which religious success may resemble secular failure.

In 2018, this former evangelical Protestant, who had studied at the Moody Bible Institute, in Chicago, found herself wandering into the Catholic St. Mary’s, “a large and beautiful church on our side of town.” (O’Gieblyn lives in the Midwest but does not name the town.) She is winningly honest about classic conversion narratives that somehow fail to persuade, and modest about her ability to account for her own urgings. So she cannot say exactly why she started attending Mass, except that she remembers being “overcome one spring with an inarticulate but decisive need to worship something.” The nature of the object wasn’t especially important; she simply wanted to kneel before something beautiful, to lose herself in it. The large Catholic church was drowned in golden light, and she was transfixed by the priestly mummery (her word is “pageantry”—a moment when the author and a certain kind of reader may diverge at supersonic speed), by “the senseless, hexlike redundancy of the Nicene Creed.” This worship began to take on the shape and the dynamic of her former alcoholism: she kept the visits secret, as if they were shameful, from her husband and her closest friends. By the fall, these services became “the most intensely sensuous experience” of her week; “there was nothing more desirable, more perfect, than to lose myself in a trance of senseless movement.” There’s a deliberate hint here, I think, of Emma Bovary’s secret raptures, her own wayward Catholic sensuousness.

As O’Gieblyn started going to church, she stopped going to the recovery meetings that had sustained her for years. She collapsed back into religion and then into drinking. When she eventually tells her husband, Barrett, that she has started drinking again, he calls her secrecy a kind of “infidelity.” Attending Mass had been the first infidelity. The “success” of religion led to the “failure” of alcohol. She now sees that the return to church “was just a veiled desire for intoxication, that the experiment with Catholicism served as a gateway back into drinking.” She was returning to “the things that had ruined my life before: alcohol and institutional religion.”

As in “Madame Bovary,” the priests are a mite disappointing, even if the cloaks and swirling stoles enchant. O’Gieblyn starts talking to the church’s pastor, whom she calls Father Aaron. He is intelligent, well read, respectful of the writer’s doubts. Shrewd, too: he gently parries her desire to become “a Catholic atheist,” and asks, “Why would you have a desire for something that doesn’t exist?”—the very question that O’Gieblyn can’t stop asking herself. It’s a version of C. S. Lewis’s insistence that an unappeasable yearning points to the existence of something beyond this world. O’Gieblyn concedes that this “shapeless longing for nothing I could locate, which I took to be a yearning for God,” has intermittently possessed her all her life—“and religion has never cured it.” Nor does religion offer a cure at St. Mary’s. She and Father Aaron get bogged down in orthodoxies both doctrinal and political (he asks her about the Catholic sacraments, and why she hasn’t had children), and the fever slowly cools. She confesses her secret churchgoing to Barrett, who calls it “addict behavior.”

This particular “addict behavior” is a heart murmur against the turbulent pulse of the actual addict behavior. Unappeased by religion, O’Gieblyn’s “shapeless longing” restlessly seeks its familiar object, its proper location, its old home. Soon, the pandemic brings its own kind of turbulence, vitally evoked here in bold Didion-like strokes: “I remember thinking that we were all slowly losing our minds. I remember the day that the heat broke and the entire city was loosed into the streets . . . . The evening when all the businesses downtown simultaneously boarded up their storefronts and tacked BLM posters to their doors, as though it were calf’s blood, hoping to be passed over.” In 2021, she publishes a book, resumes travelling, gives talks and readings. Airport bars, foreign cities, lonely hotel rooms: the sour reek of temptation. In Helsinki, she falters; at the Nashville airport she goes under and drinks three white wines, followed by vodka at O’Hare. The degradation is shameful, and shamefully compelling to read about. O’Gieblyn falls back into old tricks that come as easily as “riding a bicycle.” Drinking at home, she knows how to disguise her flushed cheeks and the smell of booze before Barrett returns: she takes a hot bath. One night, while he is sleeping, she slips out of the house to find another drink—or thinks she did, because the next morning she can remember only standing at the door, about to leave. But Barrett heard her, and he asks what’s going on. The culminating scene of confession and forgiveness is at once domestic and utterly religious. She’s on the threshing floor, saved and abased: “It is the only moment in my life when I have felt loved so completely, loved in the depth of my wretchedness and failure.”

One fascination of this brave book—brave in its disclosures but more so in its demands, its spiritual rigor, and its ardent intellectualism—lies in watching the eloquent, intelligent sufferer steadily entrapping herself. I don’t mean the obvious entrapment by her twin poisons, alcohol and institutional religion. I mean something more fundamental and less fathomable: her theology of alcoholism. The association of intoxication with religious ecstasy has a long history; its terrible force here comes from O’Gieblyn’s sense that the substance that has ruined her life also grants the surrender she was unable to achieve through worship. When she was young, she writes, she could never relax into God’s presence. The bustling ego, the barging will, always got in the way. “Alcohol is the only thing that has ever allowed me to rest happily in the presence of God,” she writes. Her drinking days in her twenties, and their morning hangovers, “were the closest I have come to the experience of enlightenment.” Her recent relapse, despite the secrecies and shame, was also a time of bliss. Alcohol offers her mystical release. Drinking, she can annihilate the self as the ancient mystics did, and as a modern one, Simone Weil, commands. The will recedes, peace and freedom suffuse her soul, and she glimpses the “nothing”—the God, the absent God—that her “shapeless longing” is always seeking. She experiences not the warm secular blur that most of us feel but “a bolt of religious rapture that makes you want to sell all your possessions and hole up in a cave with your one precious pearl.” In this theology, alcoholism represents not just fallen addiction but also religious application; she reminds us that “addiction” descends etymologically from the Latin verb addicere, to devote.

On this point, O’Gieblyn is movingly, almost repetitively, adamant. I should say that I’m largely immune to seeing alcohol or drugs as vehicles of religious insight: I think spilt religion should be cleaned up. Shouldn’t we avoid trading in substitutes, in transferences? But, as someone who, like O’Gieblyn, grew up in and came through an evangelical upbringing, I comprehend the longing that compels her to seek a godly non-God, a presence that may be an absence.

Still, the cost of persistently naming these experiences as religious would seem to be very high. If you can encounter God only by drinking to oblivion, every religious success is an abject secular failure. So is drinking O’Gieblyn’s problem, or is God? Which intoxication comes first? O’Gieblyn recognizes this dilemma (though she wouldn’t put it exactly like this) but remains in thrall to the longing that sustains it. Although she presents herself as having lost her faith, she can’t help wanting to return to it. Just when she thinks she’s out, God pulls her back in.

There is a telling moment when she considers her religious youth and ruefully wonders whether she ever had any true faith “in a heavenly Father.” “I had not been born again,” she wittily decides. “I had only been born.” But, a page later, she writes, “A friend of mine who left the church says that every liberatory deconversion narrative obscures a tragedy about failing to believe.” Does it? Can’t it just be liberatory? Surely O’Gieblyn sees that her friend is ruling out what we might call good-faith faithlessness. It’s as if we catch her revising her jest: I had not been born again, but it’s a tragedy that I wasn’t.

A tormenting syllogism seems to grip the author: she longs to encounter God; to do so, she must escape her will; to escape her will, she must drink. Therefore she drinks. Or she drank: this beautifully sober book describes her release from that prison. But her tradition does appear to have bequeathed her a powerful suspicion of the will. As she concedes, Christianity has reasons to denigrate human will, making it the source of disobedience and an explanation for much of the world’s evil. Salvation comes instead through God’s grace, the unearned gift that saves us from ourselves. Assigning responsibility for evil to human will also helps to absolve God. Yet understanding this religious inheritance, as O’Gieblyn so lucidly does, offers little assurance that one can escape its hold.

In practice, she treats the will, even the ego, as a sly old enemy to be outwitted or annihilated: “What I drank for was the peace and freedom from my own will.” Weil offers an extreme version of this hostility to the self. She was a daring mystic, but her pursuit of selflessness assumed the punitive intensity of a kind of ego-starvation: literally and theologically, the self was always too large. “Gravity and Grace” presents an exacting vision of kenosis, or self-emptying, in which an ideally voided ego will learn how to worship an ideally voided God. “To empty ourselves of the world,” Weil writes. “To take the form of a slave. To reduce ourselves to the point we occupy in space and time—that is to say, to nothing.”

O’Gieblyn’s memoir ends with a glimpse of serenity in freedom and something like redemption—a renewed sobriety, rooted in attending to the good, to the beautiful, to the world. (She uses Iris Murdoch’s writing about the good to soften some of Weil’s religious ferocity.) “Attention” replaces the feeble or malevolent “will,” as Weil says it should. For O’Gieblyn, “the good” also seems to replace “God.” On holiday in Italy, swimming regularly, alert to herself and to the beauty of her surroundings, she hopes that she is “no longer trying to obliterate my ego,” and begins to doubt “whether this was really the goal of spiritual life.” The reader who has journeyed this far with O’Gieblyn hopes that it is indeed a release and not merely a reprieve, that the old grinding syllogism will not return. Yet this reader can’t help noting that O’Gieblyn’s “attention,” which she and Weil offer as the alternative to will, sounds an awful lot like willed attention: “I was attuning my mind to the good. I was teaching myself, through daily acts of attention, to want it.” It’s one of the many ways that this remarkably honest spiritual journal seems alarmingly open and unfinished. ♦

items.title: Itinerary for Your First Couples’ Vacation
items.description: You and the love of your life are planning an international holiday together. It’s special! It’s exciting! You’re calling it a “holiday” because it’s more European that way! This guide will help you make the most of your whirlwind adventure.
items.author: Grace Henes
paragraphs: You and the love of your life are planning an international holiday together. It’s special! It’s exciting! You’re calling it a “holiday” because it’s more European that way! This guide will help you make the most of your whirlwind adventure.

Lie extensively about what you enjoy doing on vacation. Say things like “I just love wandering around and taking it all in,” when the activities you really love are getting drunk in the general vicinity of a body of water and reading bad novels about sexy enemies. Book the cheapest ticket you can find on an airline whose baggage policy seems designed for minimalist schoolchildren. Pack eight times the amount of underwear that you will need and zero shoes with arch support.

Upon arrival, check into the rental home, which will be both smaller and darker than the photos online. The toilet will be separated from the bedroom by a wall the width and consistency of a Communion wafer. Consider how long the human body can go without expelling waste. Gaze out the window and indulge in a brief cinematic fantasy about what it would be like to leave everything behind and move to this city with your partner, immediately triggering your preferred attachment disorder.

After spending five full business days curating a list of restaurants, learn that none of them are restaurants your partner is interested in. Be totally fine with that! Try to find a restaurant you both want to eat at that isn’t too touristy, expensive, loud, or busy, but which also exists. Walk to the restaurant your partner decided on, laughing thirty per cent less than usual at their jokes to punish them. Once you sit down, receive a menu that doesn’t believe in I.B.S. Panic-order a dish with a name that you don’t fully understand. When the food arrives, learn that it is a pig’s trotter. You are both vegetarian—fill up on bread.

Go to a famous, cold museum, full of art that is both pretentious and boring. Lie sophisticatedly about how much the art speaks to you. Stare at a painting of a sad, buxom peasant next to a horse, and think about how you once puked during a screening of “Wreck-It Ralph,” and how this moment is much worse than that. Sit on a bench while your partner painstakingly reads every plaque, resenting their childlike sense of wonder, then quietly devour a granola bar in the bathroom because you are still hungry from not eating your expensive hoof.

Attempt the kind of athletic sex that you imagine people have on vacation (uncomfortable, but visually impressive). Accidentally puncture a hole in the wafer wall. Apologize to each other profusely. Realize that you packed the wrong adapter, and now must jerk each other off manually, like it’s the Middle Ages. Take a cursed nap for five hours and miss the romantic candlelit dinner that you booked two full months in advance. Wake up disoriented and spend your evening watching dubbed reruns of “Boy Meets World” while eating the local equivalent of Cheetos.

Pay more than is reasonable to walk through a building that is old, but doesn’t appear to be doing much else. Stand alone in a room where a child tyrant used to do religious persecution and wonder if you would be less anxious if you lived in ancient times and only had to worry about dying of feudal warfare. Wait on another bench while your partner reads another plaque, and get a slow and painful sunburn that you won’t notice until later because it is overcast and you never learn.

The last day is the perfect time to have your breakdown. Walk to the breakfast place that Instagram told you you must visit if you don’t want to be a fucking loser. It will be closed because it is a public holiday, just like every other day in this country. Burst into tears in front of a gelato stand, then have a long conversation about your parents and why it is their fault that you are not able to hold hands in front of a famous statue. Agree never to visit this city together ever again.

Much like a person’s body will trick them into forgetting the pain of childbirth, amnesia will set in as soon as you arrive back home. Post a story of your amazing, romantic vacation, and patiently wait for your high-school nemesis to watch it while you start preliminary research for your next couples holiday—would it be crazy to go to Paris? ♦

items.title: Never Going to Italy
items.description: One of my lifelong ambitions is never to go to Italy. When I was a boy, in Ohio, my parents urged me to wish for something more realistic, such as never going anywhere in Missouri (several states away). Mom and Dad knew that never going to Italy would be unatt
items.author: Ian Frazier
paragraphs: One of my lifelong ambitions is never to go to Italy. When I was a boy, in Ohio, my parents urged me to wish for something more realistic, such as never going anywhere in Missouri (several states away). Mom and Dad knew that never going to Italy would be unattainable for people like us. But I kept dreaming, as I pored over my lists of places in Italy I dreaded to see, foods I hoped not to eat, and famous cathedrals I did not want to go on tours of. After all, a big part of the fun of never travelling somewhere is in the planning. My folks had the wisdom to allow me that, though they knew the disappointment sure to come.

My own inborn artistic temperament created an additional problem, because I happen to be highly susceptible to the visual arts. Much as I try to scrub my brain of all knowledge of painting and sculpture, I can’t. With great effort, I got rid of every word in the art lover’s vocabulary except for one pesky holdout: “provenance.” Even today, if I find myself at a cocktail party and a particular work of art comes up in conversation, out of my mouth always leaps the question “Yes, but what is its provenance?” As it turns out, “provenance” is the only word you need in order to fall into a bottomless pit of art-related discussion that always seems to lead to Italy (usually by way of Vasari). For me, in this direction lies madness.

I also have a strange and regrettable weakness for inventing catchy acronyms for art museums. Even if I firmly resolve to use a museum’s entire name whenever that museum comes up, my natural bent betrays me. For example, I faithfully try to say “the Museum of Modern Art,” but what I blurt out instead is “MOMA” (an acronym I invented some years ago). Similarly, I always want to refer to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art by its full name, and never say “LACMA,” the popular acronym I came up with (though it is, I admit, much shorter and handier). And not many people know that I’m the person who thought of calling the famous Musée du Louvre, in Paris, “MUDULOU” (pronounced “moo-doo-loo”). In these now widely adopted coinages of mine, I discern a vague, threatening spectre somehow inexorably drawing me toward Italy—and I tremble.

I had a close call the other day. I was on an airplane that was diverted from Heathrow to Italy, because of bad weather. Now, I consider Heathrow my second home. As a citizen of the world (except for Italy), I would have preferred that the flight brave the storm so that I could relax in Heathrow’s Citizens of the World (Except for Italy) V.I.P. Lounge. But the pilot of the plane was the rugged type who looks like a male model and therefore seeks the male model’s natural habitat—i.e., Italy. The plane kept on going, Italy bound, while I sweated in my seat. The dream of a lifetime was about to come to an inglorious end. Then, ten minutes before we entered Italian airspace, the weather over London cleared and the plane turned around. My dream still lived! I began to weep quietly. I told myself, “Hold on to your dreams! You will never go to Italy, if only you believe you won’t!”

This near-Italy experience has only made me more determined. Never going to Italy might take a lot of sloth, but I believe I am up to it. First, I’ll need to be in the very worst physical condition. That way, when someone interrogates me about why I haven’t yet gone to Italy, I’ll answer, “Can’t! Too out of shape!” Second, I’ll have to write a book exposing organized crime in every major Italian city. Then the Italian government will not allow me to cross the border, because of the potential costs of heightened police protection. And, third, I’ll lose my passport! The beauty of that strategy is in its simplicity. I’m surprised I’ve never thought of it before.

I can hear the Italy-goers, in their multitudes, telling me that I’m only cheating myself. But look at it this way: I’m also not carrying around a small flag, leading a tour group into one basilica or another and bumping into you as you try to get a better look at that gorgeous-whatever Vasari. In the busiest Italian places, check out the one less-crowded corner. The person helpfully not standing there is me. ♦

items.title: The second edition of our ‘Design Directory’ is a reminder that there is more to the sector than meets the eye
items.description: They say a musician’s sophomore album is always the hardest: after the critical acclaim of a breakout debut, expectation weighs heavy on an artist and production team. The same could be said for the follow-up edition of a magazine. Which raises the question: f
items.author: Nic Monisse; Kate Lucey
paragraphs: They say a musician’s sophomore album is always the hardest: after the critical acclaim of a breakout debut, expectation weighs heavy on an artist and production team. The same could be said for the follow-up edition of a magazine. Which raises the question: for the Monocle Design Directory’s second outing, how could we step it up? We didn’t want this issue to simply be a showcase of good-looking design – a round-up of handsome products and projects. Rather, we wanted to seek out people and places that demonstrate the impact that design can have beyond aesthetically pleasing architecture, and how it shapes communities and cultures.

To do so, we touched down in Baghdad to trace the work of Le Corbusier and Walter Gropius. Commissioned by the country’s ruling powers in the mid-20th century, the duo played a part in transforming the Iraqi capital into a major Western-style city. The ambition? To distinguish it from other Arab metropolises that were looking to the Soviet Union for inspiration. It was architecture intended to empower and embody a young nation, though it was ultimately co-opted by dictators. Yet it shaped a generation of Iraqi architects, including Rifat Chadirji. “I thought it imperative that, sooner or later, Iraq create for itself an architecture that is regional in character,” wrote Chadirji. The architect would go on to do exactly that.

We also saw how architecture can influence artistic experience, visiting the Fondation Beyeler near Basel, which has been newly expanded with three structures by Peter Zumthor. “Let’s not make museums too didactic,” he told Monocle’s Blake Matich. The result is a set of buildings that prioritise the viewer’s experience: there’s no artistic preamble, wall labels are spare and art is positioned so that visitors encounter it immediately. Large windows and abundant light put the galleries into conversation with the surrounding landscape. It’s a welcome reaction to screen and information saturation.

Design’s ability to transform economies is also on show, with the municipality as patron and dealmaker in Saint-Étienne. The French city is offering affordable studio space to creatives and grants to businesses that hire designers in a bid to supercharge its economy. In a similar vein, Brussels-based Rotor is building circular economies by reviving reuse, a practice that was the norm until industrial materials made new products cheaper than those that exist already.

All of this is rounded out by visits to communities in Kyoto, New York and Florence, where makers and quality of life go hand in hand. It’s a reminder that we can design the lives that we want, with creatives marching to the beat of their own drum.

items.title: A tour of the world’s best autumn/winter menswear collections and collaborations
items.description: Menswear brands have dropped trousers and more. But what has caught the eye this season? It seems that clothiers have fallen for popped collars again and – encouragingly – remain certain that quality fabrics are a non-negotiable. And for those who have also fl
items.author: Jack Simpson
paragraphs: Menswear brands have dropped trousers and more. But what has caught the eye this season? It seems that clothiers have fallen for popped collars again and – encouragingly – remain certain that quality fabrics are a non-negotiable. And for those who have also flicked through hundreds of brands’ lookbooks this autumn, I ask you this: why is every collection being shot in Scotland this year? Seriously, the Hebrides have never been better dressed – or better-looking. But before trekking up there, let’s start off by checking in with the Antipodeans:
Pick up fine fabrics from Asha Jasper

When it comes to building the best menswear collections, sourcing deadstock threads and knowing the right mills have become just as important as fashioning a well-crafted garment. Asha Phillips, founder and creative director of Sydney-based brand Asha Jasper, designs collections from the weave and weight of textiles hand-picked from Japanese and Italian mills. With the perfect fabric to hand, Phillips shapes pieces using classical tailoring methods and modern utilitarian references. We particularly like Asha Jasper’s straight-cut, made-in-Australia trousers that would fit everything from a boardroom to a bar.
Ride on Japanese clothier Niceness’s coattails

Tokyo-based Niceness has, for yet another season since its 2017 debut, produced a range of outwear that’s the envy of all those who thought last year’s coat would do. Among rails of beautiful wool suiting, silk shirting, knits and accessories for men and women, it is the outerwear pieces that form the new collection’s coat stand of showstoppers.

The E Calder coat is one of many (do check out the Rowan and Dieter shapes too) that takes traditional silhouettes a little further. Inspired by British military macs and made from US Sea Island cotton, it’s a nod to 1950s and 1960s design, with side slits to access trouser pockets. Last year’s coat will not do.
NN07 and Fracap’s latest collection has a foot in many camps

Danish clothier NN07 and Italian bootmaker Fracap have been in lockstep for years. In their third collaboration, the brands reimagine Fracap’s M127 silhouette with three new boots that, for the most part, reflect NN07’s penchant for pared-back aesthetics.

Two of the designs, which come in traditional brown and black leathers, are quite at home on a steep alpine edge, pounding inner-city pavements or mucking out the stables in the country. The third pair – though it wouldn’t struggle with these tasks – might make you forever conscious of scuffing your prized, dark-grey ponyhair shoes. The choice is yours.
Stone Island Ghost will blend seamlessly into your wardrobe

Stone Island’s Ghost collection draws on the brand’s extensive material research and garment-dyeing capabilities to create pieces inspired by the art of camouflage. Its approach is pared-back but delivers striking monochromatic and tonal looks.

The David-TC is a padded jacket with an inviting shearling-trimmed collar, woven from a star-shaped Japanese polyester that mimics vintage military motifs. It’s one for cooler months, to be worn for years to come.
Stride into the new season with Tarvas hiking shoes

Finnish shoemaker Tarvas has found its footing at the top of the crossover between hiking boots and trainers. With its topographical layering of leather, rubber and mudguard, the brand’s Easy Hiker is now a recognisable silhouette on the streets of Paris, Tokyo and beyond.

The Wanderer is the Hiker’s slender cousin. With a generous Vibram sole and a Jacques Solovière-like upper side that forms a calfskin pleat through its centre, it’s ideal for both the fleet-footed city flâneur and the forest trail explorer. If you can’t decide, the Explorer and new Derby shapes provide a middle ground with a more classic look. Picking which style to buy might be your only uphill battle for a while.
Toast the season in classic, warm-toned pieces from Forét

Without wishing away the ease of summer styling, we’re now in the sartorial “good bit”. The part of the year when layered pieces form pleasing depths and contrasts in outfits. Wardrobe staples form new affinities: that old woolen jumper pairs rather well with that new, popped checkered collar.

Forét’s autumn collection picks a perfect country colour palette of cumin, sage and wooded hues to complement city silhouettes and styling. Outerwear ranges from Harris Tweed macs to lighter twill and herringbone jackets made in Portugal. And we particularly like its high-necked, ribbed knit in thyme and flannel shirting in navy and rust.
Put down your roots in attire from Nikawi and YMC

Our Chiltern Street neighbours Niwaki do much more than make the perfect set of secateurs. The gardening brand also creates thoughtful pieces of kit for everyday life, from lunchboxes to stepladders. And, on this occasion, it’s a limited-edition clothing collection in partnership with UK label YMC that has caught our eye.

The Gardener’s Jacket is a reinvention of one of YMC’s staple silhouettes, featuring a water-resistant shell, a more generous hood and a reconsidered pocket placement for tools. The Suedehead Jumper is made from Scottish lambswool and comes in alluring pink and understated pine colourways. Naturally, there’s also a set of YMC x Niwaki Higurashi Secateurs with a leather belt and holster. Whether you’re working on the allotment or tending to your monstera, it’s a collection that celebrates urban gardening.
nikawi.com; youmustcreate.com
Mix up your wardrobe with Auralee’s two-sided coat

Running gear by District Vision or Satisfy might be the best kit while you’re on a run – but what if you’re on the run? If a leather jacket is too conspicuous, Tokyo’s Auralee has a reversible coat that enables you to switch up your look fast.

But it also suits a stand-up citizen wanting to turn heads, with its two-sided, stand-up collar. One side boasts a smooth Pakistani sheep leather, while the other comes in either a khaki or brown chambray for a more elegant, draped finish. For something a little more traditional, opt for a blue tweed blouson jacket or the brand’s ultrafine, wool twill trench coat with detachable lining.
Layer up in fine fabrics by Oliver Spencer

Oliver Spencer’s autumn collection is a nod to the brand’s city origins. Elegant trenches feature rear-dart detailing, allowing the coats to drape and move as you walk. Softly tailored suits create a less stuffy silhouette that won’t look out of place during an alfresco business lunch or the commute home. For layered looks with texture and depth, try checked wool coats, bright alpaca knitwear and shirts in corduroy and brushed cotton. It’s a range that you’ll fall for.
Look sharp on hairpin bends and out of the saddle too in Pas Normal Studios

Copenhagen’s Pas Normal Studios makes cycling gear Copenhagen’s Pas Normal Studios make cycling gear that looks good even when you’re just a blur, clocking 45km/h on a steep descent in Palma de Mallorca. But the brand’s racing jerseys and speedsuits can look a little too taut once you’re back in the city.

Its new Off-Race collection is designed for all of those quieter moments when you’re not pedalling to your destination: think lightweight jackets made from Japanese seersucker, boiled-wool fleeces, musette bags and packable down jackets. One standout is a merino-wool half-zip made in tandem with fellow Danish brand and knitwear specialists SNS Herning.
Stride out in a pair of Jacques Solovière

This season’s grained leather Raymond shoe adds even more depth to an iconic silhouette that already folds and puckers just so. Unlike many French-made leather shoes, Jacques Solovière’s kicks are extraordinarily light to keep you fleet-footed through the winter if a boot isn’t your thing. And if the calf leather and single laced eyelet makes too subtle an impression, the Boldie offers a perforated, brogue version for a little more bulk.
CDLP are an underwear brand that gets the brief
Not all men are underwear models and most work in industries where trousers are encouraged. So it’s odd that the majority of brands seem to approach boxer-short design like an advertising campaign.

Stockholm’s CDLP, however, makes drawers that put fabric and feel before all else. Its Tencel Lyocell boxers are silky and tailored for comfort. And if you’re one for a Y-shaped brief or baggier short, CDLP will have you covered.
Upgrade your journey with DB’s new Rameverk luggage range

Are you off anywhere chasing sun or embracing the elements? Well, Oslo-based baggage experts Db understand how to cart your kit from A to B in one piece. The brand’s Rib-Cage Construction technology means that its luggage proudly holds form, no matter which bellboy or air steward is hoiking it around. Db’s new Ramverk aluminium range has a zip-free frame that’s built to protect your belongings – including all of these new purchases – for a lifetime. But better than that, isn’t it rather fetching?

items.title: Costume Sketches from ‘The Devils’
items.description: What did you get up to during your school vacation? In the summer of 1970, an 8-year-old Vicki Russell was “playing a slave girl, pushing a great big truck full of plague victims.” Her parents? The visionary director Ken Russell (Altered States, The Boy Friend
items.author: Douglas Greenwood
paragraphs: What did you get up to during your school vacation? In the summer of 1970, an 8-year-old Vicki Russell was “playing a slave girl, pushing a great big truck full of plague victims.” Her parents? The visionary director Ken Russell (Altered States, The Boy Friend) and his frequent costume designer collaborator Shirley Russell. While her classmates were at the beach, or running around play parks, Russell, now a costume designer herself, was getting a front-row seat to an industry she’d soon be a part of. She was on set of The Devils—a controversial, ecclesiastic horror movie that, 55 years later, is about to be seen by a whole new audience.

The film, loosely based on the real life demise of a priest accused of witchcraft after a collective of nuns become “possessed” by his spirit, starred Oliver Reed and Vanessa Redgrave, and, until recently, has never been seen the way its director intended. But now, in a 4K remastered version (released this Friday in the US, and from October 30 in the UK), sequences deemed so controversial that they were left on the cutting room floor have been salvaged and re-added. They contain things that would make any modern horror auteur wince.

Thankfully, 8-year-old Vicki didn’t witness the horror of what her family was making as she dotted around the set. “It was like Disneyland to me,” she tells me over the phone, recounting memories of learning how to ride horses at the guidance of the film’s horse wrangler. In addition to her brief on-screen appearance, Russell spent a lot of time on the set of The Devils with her mother in the costume department, poring over the wildly designed and cultivated garments that captured the 17th century French era the film was set in.

But it all began months earlier, in the Russell family home in Portobello Road. “Half of their bedroom was mom’s studio where she would be drawing [these garments],” Russell says. “You could just see them coming together from these historical references.” She’d sketch them out in ink, dissect each piece and hone in on the details. You can see it in these sketches, presented here for the first time ever.

“She was fast because she knew her history of fashion so well,” Russell says of her mother’s process. “I think she just had to understand the character and what drove them.” The Devils had plenty of bombastic outfits to balance out the plainness of plague victims and peasants. Even then, the outfits were striking: regal dresses, pompous religious wear, and costumes for dancers that made them look like stars and birds. In the restored version, framed by sets from the master of British cinema Derek Jarman, you can see all of them in perfect detail.

After working on a project, the costumes Shirley Russell created would end up in a costume house of her own making: The Last Picture Frock in Shepherd’s Bush, West London. Russell recalls it being known as “one of the best in Europe.” Inevitably, some of the costumes in The Devils were destroyed during the fiery and untameable shoot; existing only on celluloid and in these sketches. A handful, including the regal red dress worn by Georgina Hale (seen below), will be included in an exhibition coming next year, to mark what would be the 100th birthday of Ken Russell.

It’s the blessing of Russell’s life to have followed in the footsteps of her artist parents, working alongside her mother in the costume department on several films, and eventually collaborating with her father as the lead costume designer on the 1986 film Gothic. “I’ve worked with him since I was 18-months-old, playing Oliver Reed’s daughter in Debussy, wearing period costume. Okay, he had a temper, but I knew it was just a rage and it would pass. But he absolutely loved the creative process, and he really loved costumes and set design.” He might have been her dad, but he also, she says, was “a very funny and brilliant man to work with.”
‘The Devils’ is in US cinemas for a one week engagement from Friday October 16. It opens in the UK on October 30.

items.title: Jamie Lee Curtis Leaning on “Love and Service” in Honoring the Late Rob and Michele Reiner: “Every Day With Them Was Activism”
items.description: Suit up, show up and celebrate the lives, activism and legacy of Rob and Michele Reiner.
items.author: Chris Gardner
paragraphs: Suit up, show up and celebrate the lives, activism and legacy of Rob and Michele Reiner.

That’s how Jamie Lee Curtis is approaching the night of Nov. 8, a date that will find her become the inaugural recipient of the Michele and Rob Reiner Champion for Change Award during the Children’s Institute’s Cape & Gown Gala. It’s an honor created in partnership between the Children’s Institute, its president and CEO Martine Singer (Michele’s sister) and the couple’s children, Jake and Romy Reiner, to recognize the Reiners’ “lifelong commitment to improving the lives of children and families and strengthening communities across Los Angeles, throughout California and beyond.”

When news broke of the honor and that Curtis would be its first recipient, the Oscar winner said she was “deeply honored” to be selected as it’s a testament to the legacy of the late Reiners, a couple she had known for decades and with whom she shared a duty for activism. (She and her husband, Christopher Guest, were also married at Rob’s home in 1984, and he served as the best man.) “They didn’t just create together. They lived a life of service, building something greater than themselves and giving so much to the world around them. And that is something worth honoring again and again,” Curtis said in a statement when she was announced as the award recipient. “The world needs so much more of what they gave us: their love, their courage and their joy. I am forever grateful to carry a small part of their legacy forward.”

She’s hoping that joy surfaces at the upcoming gala. “Rob and Michele’s [lives are] celebratory. They would not want this [event] to be morbid and funerallike. It has to be a celebration,” Curtis told The Hollywood Reporter in a new interview about the award and the Reiners. “So, I’m going to suit up, show up, do my thing, stand there in community and say thank you to them.”

Below, she opens up on how she’s walking through this emotional time by placing a focus on “love and service,” how her appearance at the recent Emmy Awards came to be and the indefatigable nature of the Reiners’ work on a variety of causes: “Every day with them was activism.”
(Read an edited transcript of the conversation below, or listen to an audio version here.)
We’re sitting here at the Children’s Institute on Temple Street in Los Angeles for a special reason.

First of all, this institution has been around for 120 years. They’ve been raising money to help children in the City of Angels for 120 years. That alone is enough to kind of be like, “Whoa.” And, of course, we’re here because the Children’s Institute is run by Martine Singer, the sister of Michele Singer Reiner and sister-in-law of Rob Reiner. We are here at the Children’s Institute specifically because Martine runs the institute and was the sister of Michele Singer Reiner and the sister-in-law of Rob Reiner. Rob and Michele were big supporters of the Children’s Institute, and Martine has been a beautiful, beautiful aunt after that awful experience in December.

Rob and Michele supported the Children’s Institute for years. The institute is having its big event on Nov. 8 and is naming an advocacy award in Rob and Michele’s name. I am the inaugural recipient of that award, and I’m very moved to be so. Today, we came to the institute to be with the children, see more of the programs and have some public conversations about the institute, Rob and Michele and their advocacy for children. Jake Reiner was with me today and did a few press interviews. We’ve been talking about Rob and Michele all day long.

Very emotional. We haven’t had a big public group hug yet. There’s the very small circle of family, then their very closest friends and then the concentric circles that go out from there: friends, colleagues, advocates and, finally, the public: people who just loved his movies, loved his television shows and loved his father. The circle gets wider and wider, and none of us have come together yet to grieve this terrible loss. It’s been an emotional day because I’ve been talking about my relationship with them and talking about them in the past, and it’s only nine months later. It’s been difficult but important because we just want to carry on their work.

We’re also sitting here right after the beautiful moment at the Emmys when you offered some remarks about Rob, and the camera panned to the audience to show how touched people were. And we could see how emotional you were. Now feels like a good time to have this conversation.

I’m obviously a close friend of theirs; we got married at Rob’s house on Dec. 18, 1984. Rob was the best man. My late sister Kelly was my maid of honor. So we are close. Rob is our daughter Annie’s godfather. When Michele married Rob, she and Rob became my daughter’s godparents. We have a closeness, of course. What I’m trying to say is that I felt a responsibility to represent everyone — strangers, fans, colleagues, friends, close friends and family — in that moment at the Emmys. I was fine and happy to do it.

I went to the rehearsal, and they were playing “Bridge Over Troubled Water.” There’s an exercise in grief about desensitizing yourself, so I listened to that song for the next day, trying to get used to it. It’s so moving to me naturally, and then it was sung live. It was very challenging because it was challenging enough to represent everyone and try to honor, in this case, particularly Rob’s passing, but I also have feelings of my own.

I was happy to do it, but it was a little tougher than I anticipated. The way media works, words like “breaking silence” and “first comments after” start being a little strange. I’m here for the Children’s Institute. I’m here to support their work. I’m going to be at the event to support the work that Rob and Michele did, and it shouldn’t be about me. And yet I’ve been the one talking a lot about them. So it’s been a little strange because it’s a very private grief, and yet I’m a public-facing person. I’m trying to walk that line a little bit.

The work of the Children’s Institute is focused on so many pillars of lifting up children and families, with education and literacy chief among them, issues that are also very important to you and your work as a children’s author. How do you wrap your head around the way all of these threads are connected?

Love and service aren’t compartmentalized. They’re expansive. It’s not about me at all. I just read a beautiful book by Ann Patchett called Whistler — the new novel. It’s about impermanence at its core. I’m not a particularly religious person, but I’m sober and it can’t be about me. It has to be about love and service. If we’re just expanding love and service in whatever way we can, that’s what they did, that’s what I try to do, that’s what you try to do. It’s just what we do. It’s what these people do. It’s what Martine does here in this office.
And that’s what you’re doing. I’ll point out that you’re wearing a “Love and Service” pin right now.

I wear it often, particularly when we need to be reminded: What are we doing? What are we doing? I don’t need more attention. I’m pretty comfortable with who I am, and I know who I am pretty honestly. I’ve reached a ripe old age, I’ve had a good amount of psychoanalysis, I’m sober and I’m a grandma. I’m pretty clear that if love and service is at the center of what I do, then I’m good. I can take a little of the energy and appreciate it, and really want to reflect it back onto Rob and Michele and what they dedicated their lives to — the betterment of the world because they were in it.
Do you remember any conversations you had with them about service or activism?

Every day with them was activism. They were enraged at the way the current administration had decimated progressive policies toward children, women, people of color, gay people and transgender people. I mean, don’t even get me started. Rob was a firebrand. I can talk a good game, and I’m a passionate advocate, but Rob had the acumen and the political savvy. I don’t have political savvy. He was able to find common ground with people he disagreed with and was a powerful leader.

Many of the times Rob stepped into that position of power were because Michele Reiner said, “Rob, come on. You can do this. You need to do this.” Much of that advocacy was fueled by Michele saying, “You need to do this.” She was the lighter of that firebrand. She got it hot, and then Robbie took it. That was his great skill, but it was a partnership and that’s just impressive.

Some of the work you do with Children’s Hospital Los Angeles overlaps with the institute. How did you decide that CHLA would be one of the focuses of your activism and advocacy? You’ve raised millions for CHLA through My Hand in Yours, and it’s a hospital you’ve supported for many years.

I was working on a forgettable movie called Grandview, USA, about demolition derby in Pontiac, Illinois. We shot there, and I was in town for 12 weeks, which is a long time. In Pontiac, there was a family whose daughter, Lori Tull, [had one of the first successful heart transplants]. The town was putting on a fundraiser for Lori and her family because, at the time, the insurance company said it was experimental surgery and wouldn’t pay for it. It was an enormous amount of money.

The movie company joined forces with the town because we were there for 12 weeks. We sold kisses at booths; it was like a fair. Lori and I became friends. She ultimately had a second heart transplant at Children’s Hospital of Pittsburgh and died at 19, but we stayed close. I made a connection to that hospital in Pittsburgh and, for many years, went back to work with them. I became friends with another patient named Katie Westbrook, who had bone cancer.

If you’ve ever seen a picture of me in a pink wig, I wear a pink wig when I do children’s hospital work. That was Katie’s wig. She wore it when she lost her hair because of chemotherapy. When she died, her mother gave me the wig. I wear it to remind people: This is what this young girl wore while she was fighting for her life. She was saying to everybody, “Look at me,” because if you’re looking at me in this, you understand that I’m fighting for my life here.

I helped them raise a lot of money at the hospital. When I came back from one of my trips to Pittsburgh, I realized, “Wait, I live in Los Angeles.” I cold-called Children’s Hospital Los Angeles and said, “My name’s Jamie Curtis. I’ve been going back and forth to Pittsburgh and working with them for many years, and I live here. I was born and raised here in the City of Angels. What can I do to help you?”

It was right when one of the propositions was going to be on the ballot — one of the children’s hospital bond acts — and I became the face of it. I said, “Yes, I’ll do whatever you want. Commercials? Sure, let’s do commercials for the children’s hospital bond.” It passed, and it raised hundreds of millions of dollars for various children’s hospitals, including CHLA. That began my advocacy with them.
Can you take me back to getting the call for this award?

Martine, Jake and Romy called me this summer when I was away with my family. Martine had texted, “Can you talk? The kids and I want to talk to you about something.” I didn’t know what it was, obviously, but I said, “Yes, of course.” When I called them, the three of them said, “We want to support Martine and the Children’s Institute in the name of our parents and we would like you to receive the inaugural award in their name.”

Obviously, I said yes. When I got back home, it was about trying to connect more dots here at the institute in a way I hadn’t been able to. I’ve been working a lot, so it’s taken me a minute. But, again, we haven’t had a public gathering. This will feel a little bit like that. By the way, this award conversation predated the Emmys. The Emmys happened about a week after the award was discussed.
How did the Emmys appearance come about?

I don’t think they had really thought it through. The weekend before, Rob won an Emmy, and the entire room stood up. So I think they must have been thinking, “Oh, we haven’t really addressed this yet. It’s tricky.” There were so many people lost this year, particularly in television, who had big careers. It was unexpected. I hadn’t planned on that.
The fact that he got it for The Bear, on which you were ferocious, award-winning and incredible — what a moment.

It was. Rob called me and said, “I’ve been offered a part on The Bear. Should I do it?” And I said, “Yes, Robbie, you should absolutely do it.” I didn’t know how that character was going to fit in or who he would be, because obviously I didn’t know any of that. But my experience on the show was transformational. It was a fantastic writing opportunity and something I had never had the opportunity to do before. So I said, “Yes, you should do it.”
You’ll accept the inaugural Michele and Rob Reiner Champion for Change Award in November. How do you approach a speech?

I’m not that girl. I have a poem I may read. It was given to me as a gift by Moye Thompson, a ceramicist whose work I collect. The poem is called “To Be of Use,” by Marge Piercy. Moye imprinted the words of the poem on a bowl, all the way around it — individual letters, the whole poem. Then she took the poem and broke it into individual words and printed those on little pieces of porcelain. It’s a beautiful art piece: the collective poem, with each individual word inside the bowl.

It’s a beautiful poem about activism, about being of use as a person and about the kind of people I like to know. I looked at that beautiful piece of art the other day and thought, “That’s Rob and Michele right there: to be of use.” Stay out of the way. Be of use. Link up and get dirty. Do your work. Get sweaty.
Is that what you think of when you think of them?

Yes. Just to be of use. It brings back to me the song “That’s Why I’m Here” by James Taylor, where he basically says, “That’s why I’m here.” I think, “Why am I here?” I’m here to be of use, to connect people, whatever it is. It’s just service. Love and service. It goes back to love and service. It always will. At the end of the day, it really does.
Congratulations again on the honor.
Thank you. I’m honored — truly honored. I also have to crack jokes. I want to crack some jokes. I don’t want to …

But it doesn’t have to be. It’s not a memorial. This is a celebration of 120 years of an institution showing up for people from ZIP codes that you and I may never visit in the City of Angels. There are probably areas of this city I’ve never been in, you’ve never been in and may never be in, whose residents can come here and get the services and support the Children’s Institute offers. That alone makes it very important that this is a celebration: a celebration of all the years of people like Martine, all the staff and all the teachers I worked with today in the classroom — everyone coming together to help these people.

Rob and Michele’s [lives are] celebratory. I want to make sure that’s included, too. They would not want this to be morbid and funeral-like. It has to be a celebration. So I’m going to suit up, show up, do my thing, stand there in community and say thank you to them.
Beautiful. And John Mayer is going to perform.
John Mayer’s going to perform, and he’s a great communicator, a great singer and a great lyricist.

Knowing he was going to be there made me wonder what Jamie Lee Curtis listens to when she wants to roll up her sleeves. You mentioned James Taylor, but when you’re either doing the work or want to shut off, what music do you turn on?

I’m eclectic as hell. I listen to everything from John Coltrane to yacht rock. You have to remember, I came of age in 1976, ’77 and ’78. ’70s music — the Eagles. Are you kidding? I’ve seen the Eagles documentary 25 times. It’s three hours, by the way. But I’m eclectic: yacht rock, Coltrane, the Eagles and Wyclef Jean. That was two weeks ago. I randomly listened to Sam Sanders and Wyclef Jean was interviewed by him. I want you to download the Sam Sanders podcast — or whatever radio show it is — and listen to his interview with Wyclef Jean.

Drive back to Santa Monica and listen to it. Then download all of the albums Wyclef Jean has just released. You’re going to hear someone with wildly deep, immersive talent. It knocked me sideways. I’ve been obsessed with Wyclef Jean ever since.

items.title: Size Really Does Matter: How Alexander Skarsgard’s ‘Wicker’ Man and Member Came to Life
items.description: [Warning: this story contains spoilers for Black Bear’s Wicker.]
items.author: Carly Thomas
paragraphs: [Warning: this story contains spoilers for Black Bear’s Wicker.]
The internet went feral over Alexander Skarsgård’s wicker penis in the highly anticipated romantic fantasy Wicker that hit theaters on Friday. However, it almost didn’t make the cut.

“The wicker man was already designed, the prosthetic face and the upper body,” costume designer Tóth András Dániel recalls. “And just one week before the shoot started, the directors [Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer] came up with this idea: ‘He’s so sexy. We should see him naked.'”

Fans clearly agreed. After a Wicker teaser dropped in August, the internet instantly got hot and bothered over this attractive man made from wicker. The film, based on author Ursula Wills-Jones’s short story, The Wicker Husband, follows a fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) who commissions the local basketmaker (Peter Dinklage) to weave her a husband (Skarsgård), sparking jealousy and chaos in the quiet village.

The character’s masculine build initially caught the horny BookTok girlies’ attention, but it was the thought of what’s underneath Skarsgård’s tailored suit that had them really drooling. “Hell yeah! 50 shades of Pinocchio!” and “The bar is so low for men we’re romanticizing baskets” were among thousands of similar comments shared on social media at the time.

Wētā Workshop, which designs specialty costumes for film and television, worked with 50 people for a year to build the upper half of Skarsgård’s wicker suit. The attention to detail was evident from the way the suit moved to how it blended in with the prosthetic face.
However, Dániel and fellow costume designer Attila Godena-Juhász had a much harder task when it came to creating the lower half, as time wasn’t on their side.

“There was no time for Wētā to prepare the whole bottom part of [Alexander’s suit], including the wicker penis, which was such a big subject about the size and everything,” Dániel says, adding, “We had one week with four people in the workshop to seamlessly continue the wicker bottom part.”
Given that the costume designers had different materials to work with than Wētā, Dániel says they “had to experiment and invent a kind of new technology” to mimic what was already created.

“Attila came up with this idea that we should use this special paint that you can see printed on textile, and if you treat it with heat, it gets three-dimensional,” he explains. “So it’s really giving you this woven textile feeling, but that was still [the color] white. So every little detail we had to hand-paint with tiny brushes and shade it and match it with the color that was used for the whole upper prosthetics.”

Unfortunately for fans who had been eagerly hoping to see Skarsgård’s wicker member up close and personal in the film, they might be slightly disappointed. The only full frontal is when the fisherwoman (Colman) is looking at the nude wicker man off in the distance in the water.
That was intentional. “That was a decision from the directors,” Dániel says. “They just wanted to give the audience a peek of him being naked, but they don’t want it to show everything.”

However, for audiences still pondering, this writer — who got a close-up look at the lower half of Skarsgård’s costume before it was painted, via a photo from the costumers — can confirm Colman’s fisherwoman definitely wasn’t complaining about size.
Skarsgård’s wicker willy wasn’t the only thing that was impressive, but rather his whole physique. And Dániel and Godena-Juhász took that into account when dressing him.

“Because Alex is such a huge guy, with the prosthetic on, it made him even bigger and more muscular. So the idea was that his costumes shouldn’t fit perfectly because nobody was prepared that one day a wicker man would knock on their door and ask for a suit,” Dániel explains to THR. “The lengths are shorter on purpose because it really gives you the feeling that at first he’s such a huge man.”
Going into the film, it was important for the filmmakers to create “this sexy beast as realistic as it can be,” Dániel says.
Ahead of release, multiple people on social media posed a question about the logistics of having sex with a man with a wicker penis. One wrote: “Can you imagine the splinters?”

These are obviously fictional problems, but Dániel reassures that “the bottom part was 3D printed in a special rubber-like material,” with Godena-Juhász adding that it’s “obviously softer than the real wicker.”
The costume designers also got a kick out of the film and their creation transcending into the mainstream. Even IKEA got into the game, marketing its rattan furniture as “husband material.”
Dániel says, “That was our goal: to do something that can inspire mainstream fashion. But it was still a surprise that the hype is so big around the movie.”
Wicker, also starring Elizabeth Debicki and Richard E. Grant, is currently playing in theaters.

items.title: What to Know About Shamonda Virus Following the First Reported Human Infection
items.description: France confirmed the death of the first person infected with the Shamonda virus, which is known to affect cattle, sheep, and goats and was previously considered non-transmissible to humans. The French government asserts that, based on current knowledge of this
items.author: Fernanda González
paragraphs: France confirmed the death of the first person infected with the Shamonda virus, which is known to affect cattle, sheep, and goats and was previously considered non-transmissible to humans. The French government asserts that, based on current knowledge of this pathogen, there is no risk to the general public. It emphasized, however, that health authorities are continuing to investigate.

The report specifies that the case occurred in Lyon. The patient, who died earlier this month, suffered from severe immunosuppression, making this likely an exceptional case. “The neurological complications observed in the immunocompromised patient prior to his death were most likely related to infection with the Shamonda virus,” the official statement notes.

According to preliminary evidence, the patient contracted Shamonda virus from an insect bite. A tiny gnat known as the biting midge is known to be the primary route of transfer between animals. Since the virus was first identified in Nigeria in the mid-1960s, sporadic infections have been reported in livestock across Africa as well as in Japan. Cattle are considered the primary host because they develop visible symptoms. (Although sheep and goats can become infected, no obvious clinical signs have been documented in these animals.)

After animal is bitten by a midge carrying Shamonda virus, the infection has an incubation period of two to three days. Symptoms observed in animals include fever, diarrhea, and a decrease in milk production. When pregnant cows have become infected, the virus can cause miscarriages or severe deformations in the calf.

To date, there is no vaccine, so prevention and control measures rely on the use of insecticides and repellents. That doesn’t mean you should panic. Public health authorities are considering the case to be “exceptional,” because the deceased patient was severely immunocompromised.

Still, several European countries are on alert, because until a few months ago, this region was considered free of the virus. However, this summer, a new variant known as Shamonda-Europe was detected in livestock in Switzerland. Other cases were subsequently identified in Germany, France, Austria, Belgium, the Netherlands, Liechtenstein, Italy, and Spain.

Spain’s Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, and Food states that two genetically distinct forms of the virus, known as Shamonda Type 1 and Shamonda Type 2, have been identified circulating in Europe. It adds that, in early September, infections of both types were confirmed on livestock farms in 37 provinces across France.
The case documented in France constitutes the first known infection in a person.

“This is an important scientific finding. However, it is important to put this into perspective. The patient had a serious underlying illness that left them particularly vulnerable to infections, and we do not yet know whether Shamonda virus contributed to their death,” Ben Brennan, professor of virology at the University of Glasgow, said in a statement.

It’s premature to draw conclusions about the virus and it’s potential to infect humans, agreed David Roiz, a scientist Institute for Game and Wildlife Research in Spain. Many viruses “circulate naturally amongst mammals in tropical regions and cause sporadic cases in humans,” he said. “In a globalized world, where animals and goods are on the move and the climate is changing, it is not unusual for cases of human transmission to occur, and we should not be concerned; we simply need to monitor the situation, remain vigilant, and be proactive in addressing potential health risks.”
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: October 23, 2026
items.description: This morning, the sun leaves Libra to enter Scorpio. For the next month, you may find yourself placing less value on social harmony and more on candor. Right now, avoiding sensitive subjects or “agreeing to disagree” in the name of good manners will seem deepl
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: This morning, the sun leaves Libra to enter Scorpio. For the next month, you may find yourself placing less value on social harmony and more on candor. Right now, avoiding sensitive subjects or “agreeing to disagree” in the name of good manners will seem deeply unsatisfying, if not outright unfair. You’d rather have a conversation that gets heated over one that tiptoes around the important stuff. Your instinct for honesty is a good one, but remember that your interactions don’t have to be contentious to be authentic and interesting. Particularly as Venus aligns with the sun tonight, you have a good chance of finding people who are on your wavelength — and who are willing to go deep with you.

You aren’t generally interested in cultivating an air of mystery. You are who you are, and you’d rather be honest about it: You make it clear what you do (and don’t) bring to the table and then let others decide how they want to proceed. Today, though, consider this: You don’t owe it to anyone to put all your cards on the table right away. Keeping some information to yourself, at least for now, could motivate people to put more effort into getting to know you on a deeper level.

Sometimes, you feel pressured to resolve conflicts as quickly as possible — regardless of whether the outcome is satisfying. But today, refuse to accept solutions that don’t work for you. If you’re going to accept a compromise, make sure it’s one that genuinely feels fair. It might be tempting to agree to a bad deal just because you’re tired of arguing, or because you’re being pushed to relent, but don’t do it. You can’t expect to get everything you want, but you shouldn’t feel bullied or taken advantage of either.

You often feel safest when hiding your opinions behind multiple layers of irony. That way you can always backpedal if you change your mind about something; you’ll have plausible deniability if your words provoke a reaction you don’t like. But today, trying to be cagey or clever won’t get you anywhere. There’s room for humor in your conversations, but it shouldn’t act as a substitute for saying what you really mean. It’s better to be honest — even if you know some people will disagree — than to worry excessively about being liked.

When people express a desire to get to know you better, you have a hard time not feeling suspicious. If it’s not immediately clear why they’re interested in you, you tend to assume they must have some kind of ulterior motive. But today, give yourself a little more credit than that. You have lots to offer; it shouldn’t be surprising that others might want to spend time with you. You don’t have to let your guard down completely, but give people a chance.

Today, you might wonder — even more than usual — why the people around you act the way they do. You’ll want to dig into the deeper feelings and past experiences that motivate them, to understand what’s going on beneath the surface. But be careful not to get too swept up in your own musings. Your theories might sound compelling, and they might even be accurate. But you won’t actually know what’s going on in someone else’s head unless they tell you. So if you’re curious about someone, don’t just study them. Talk to them.

You might feel as though you need to rush through your day today. Especially if other people try to convince you that your usual routines are “inefficient,” and that you should instead do things the way they think is best, you’ll be inclined to believe them. But take a step back and realize you’re allowed to set your own pace. You have no obligation to speed up just because other people are in a hurry. Rushing will only lead to stress and avoidable mistakes, so keep things slow and steady for the time being.

In general, you want to give everyone a fair chance. You always try to hear people out, even when you suspect you won’t agree with them. You do your best to offer grace even when it’s not deserved. But privately, you worry people think you’re a pushover. Today, you’ll have the opportunity to prove them wrong. You know you have deep reserves of conviction and determination, and this could be the time to let others see them. As much as you value kindness, you occasionally need to make it clear that you shouldn’t be underestimated.

More often than you might realize, you hide the parts of your personality you worry might repel people. You want to be successful and liked, and so your strategy is to amplify your most charming qualities and conceal the ones that embarrass you. But this is a stressful — and ultimately lonely — way to live. Today, give yourself permission to relax. Stop working so hard to maintain a polished façade, and just do what feels natural, what feels right. Maybe some people won’t like it, but others will like you more for your honesty.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

Generally, you’re willing to change your mind when presented with new information. You’d rather be adaptable than stubborn; you’d rather learn and grow than double down on a wrong idea. But today, don’t automatically assume that everyone else must know more than you do, and therefore you should be the one to fall in line. If you know in your gut that you’re right, then now is the time to be brave and stay true to yourself, regardless of what anyone else has to say.

You’re someone who’s caring but also strategic with your relationships. You understand that sometimes it’s important to maintain positive connections even with people you don’t particularly care for. Being civil and helpful can make everyone’s lives easier — and you never know when you might need a friend. But today, remember that there are some relationships that aren’t worth the stress, frustration, or heartache. If someone is being cruel, difficult, or draining, consider whether it’s best to distance yourself, at least temporarily. There’s no shame in taking care of yourself.

You occasionally convince yourself that if you don’t actively seek attention, you’ll be able to fade into the background. There, you can observe and behave as you wish, unnoticed. Today, though, the people around you are probably paying closer attention than you realize. Don’t assume that no one’s watching just because you haven’t sought the spotlight. Try to carry yourself in a way you can be proud of, because even if it seems like nobody’s got an eye on you, chances are, someone does.

When you’re afraid you won’t like the answers to your questions, you often avoid asking them at all. The less you know, you imagine, the simpler things will be! If you can avoid learning unpleasant or inconvenient facts, then you won’t have to figure out what to do about them. But today, knowledge will only help you. The clearer a picture you have of what you’re dealing with, the more effectively you’ll be able to navigate it. Follow your curiosity where it leads you. You’ll ultimately be glad you did.

items.title: Fender x Paul Smith Telecaster brings sound, style and stripes
items.description: A meeting of two brands that are never too far away from their next collaboration, the Fender x Paul Smith Telecaster is a new guitar out of Fender Japan, a limited-edition model due to ship in 2027 and created to mark the 80th birthday of Sir Paul Smith and t
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: A meeting of two brands that are never too far away from their next collaboration, the Fender x Paul Smith Telecaster is a new guitar out of Fender Japan, a limited-edition model due to ship in 2027 and created to mark the 80th birthday of Sir Paul Smith and the 80th anniversary of the founding of the Fender Musical Instruments Corporation.

Why a Telecaster? This minimal, timeless form was designed by Leo Fender in 1949 and went into production the following year. The form has remained essentially unchanged ever since, with an infinite palette of variations keeping the Tele fresh and relevant for each successive generation. The Made in Japan series offers some of the most stylistically eclectic and finely crafted models in Fender’s range; it’s also a market with a long history of Paul Smith fandom.

The result is this Made in Japan Paul Smith Telecaster, a guitar that is instantly recognisable as a product of the Paul Smith school of bold but tasteful polychromy. The Signature Stripe pattern covers both front and back of the alder body, paired with a tortoiseshell pickguard. A light-coloured Maple Modern neck and dark Rosewood fingerboard (the neck is shaped in Fender’s shallow C-shaped profile).

The guitar also features two specially modified pick-ups in the Telecaster’s signature bridge and neck positions, along with a brass barrel bridge and a custom neckplate bearing the Paul Smith logo. Each guitar is individually numbered and comes with a specially designed hard case. Orders are open now for delivery next year.

In addition to the guitar itself, Paul Smith has collaborated on a new 16-piece capsule collection of clothing and accessories, running from ready-to-wear pieces to fine tailoring. One item that’s a must-have for buyers of the Telecaster is the Signature Stripe Paul guitar strap, made in Japan with co-branded leather trims and a polyester weave that perfectly matches the guitar itself.
Fender x Paul Smith Telecaster, £1,999, UK.Fender.com, @Fender
Paul Smith x Fender Signature Stripe Guitar Strap, £150, PaulSmith.com, @PaulSmithDesign
