paragraphs: Гонка за фигурой после родов: Ксения Дукалис — о показе Victoria’s Secret
Барбара Палвин на шоу Victoria’s Secret в октябре 2026

18 октября в Лос-Анджелесе прошел показ Victoria’s Secret. Одной из его участниц стала 33-летняя венгерская модель Барбара Палвин, которая вышла на подиум через шесть недель после рождения первого ребенка. В интервью Good Morning America Палвин подчеркнула, что все еще продолжает восстанавливаться, а также рассказала о помощи родителей и друзей. Ее возвращение спровоцировало дискуссию в соцсетях: пользователи обсуждали ожидания, которые подобные случаи формируют у зрительниц. Критике подвергся и сам показ — в колонке для Allure журналистка Даниэль Пергамент обратила внимание на преобладание экстремально худых моделей на подиуме и усомнилась в том, насколько шоу соответствует идее инклюзивности.
Ксения Дукалис, блогер и предприниматель, мама сына Григория (1 год и 10 месяцев)
Материнство на профессиональном подиуме
«Сейчас действительно появляются новые образы для женщин — их мышления и существования. И я, хотя и фанат репрезентации, не могу сказать, что все они однозначно прекрасны.

Есть тенденция, которая мне безумно нравится: женщины старше 50 лет продолжают работать в публичной среде. Николь Кидман, Сандра Буллок, Мэрил Стрип — все они по-прежнему с нами. Идея о том, что после 30 лет "женщина должна уйти в лес", отживает свое.

Казалось бы, с матерями на подиуме — та же история: нам показывают, что после рождения ребенка публичная жизнь и карьера продолжаются. Но к ситуации с Барбарой Палвин и вообще со всеми, кто родил и через 20 минут побежал по своим делам, много вопросов. В показе участвовали женщины старше 40 лет, среди них было много мам. Это преподносится так: "Вот какие они крутые — у них есть дети, но они здесь". Но это не рядовые матери — организаторы шоу не пришли в детскую консультацию и не пригласили оттуда женщин. Это профессиональные модели Victoria’s Secret. Даже среди них это — особая категория: девушки проходят амазонские испытания, чтобы попасть на подиум. Считать их зеркалом для всех остальных невозможно.
Идея о том, что после 30 лет «женщина должна уйти в лес», отживает свое.

При этом сама Барбара Палвин не вызывает у меня негативных эмоций. В интервью она — в полном контакте с реальностью. За кулисами показа модель обращала внимание на то, что многие американки тоже возвращаются к работе вскоре после родов. Мол, она сейчас пройдется по подиуму, а другая женщина должна отправиться на свою работу. Честь ей и хвала за то, что подсвечивает эту проблему.

Но я вспоминаю себя спустя шесть недель после родов — ни о каком подиуме мыслей тогда не было. И мне не кажется здоровой модель, которую нам продают: "Ты должна максимально быстро вернуться к тому виду, который у тебя был до родов, будто осталась тем же человеком".
Барбара Палвин на шоу Victoria’s Secret в октябре 2026

Роды действительно меняют. Более того, вы меняете свою роль — особенно если это первый ребенок. Из абсолютно самостоятельной единицы вы превращаетесь в единицу в связке с кем-то еще. Я говорю не про бытовой уход, а про психологическую связь. Вы навсегда мать.

Изменения в теле тоже связаны с этой новой ролью. Например, шрамы от кесарева сечения не кажутся мне чем-то постыдным. Это напоминание о новом статусе, о большой боли и смелости, которые потребовались, чтобы появился новый человек.

У меня есть вопросы к самой формулировке "вернуться в форму". Много раз я наблюдала, как и без того прекрасные девушки обозначают себе проблему: они немного набрали, и теперь нужно как можно скорее вернуться назад. Это преподносится как катастрофа.
У меня есть вопросы к самой формулировке «вернуться в форму».

Я не вижу проблемы в том, чтобы заниматься спортом после родов, когда это уже разрешено, и воспринимать его как вклад в здоровье и собственную функциональность. Но совсем другая история сводить все исключительно к сантиметрам и внешней привлекательности. В частности, к привлекательности в социальных сетях.

Помимо реального стандарта красоты у нас есть еще 2D-стандарт: как ты будешь выглядеть именно на фото. В этом смысле культура TikTok подает мне надежду — там есть место для уязвимости, неидеальности. Мамы, которые рассказывают, как они выглядят после родов или как вынашивают двойню, на мой взгляд, делают для женщин гораздо больше, чем Victoria’s Secret.
Уязвимость после родов и ловушка сравнения

Женщинам годами объясняли, что вся их ценность связана с худобой, субтильностью, привлекательностью для мужчин. Конечно, партнер не должен говорить женщине, которая только что родила, что ей нужно скорее похудеть. Или убеждать ее не кормить грудью, потому что пора "возвращаться в форму". Но мы живем не в самом здоровом обществе, и периодически приходится себе об этом напоминать.

Когда видишь истории таких преображений, после десятилетий навязывания стандартов красоты начинает шевелиться червячок внутреннего недовольства: «Иди худей». Послеродовой период — очень уязвимый. Меняется образ жизни, режим сна. Накапливается усталость, появляется чувство вины. И мысли, которые в другое время вы бы к себе не подпустили, начинают звучать убедительнее.
Мы живем не в самом здоровом обществе, и периодически приходится себе об этом напоминать.

Если вы и так склонны тревожиться и катастрофизировать, легко подумать: «Все, я теперь навсегда останусь непривлекательной, ненужной. Надо срочно взять себя в руки». Мне кажется, стремление похудеть и измениться очень часто связано с контролем. Когда его не хватает в других сферах жизни, пытаешься обрести его хотя бы таким образом. И это далеко не всегда полезно.

Конечно, исключительный пример может превратиться в представление о норме. Тем более что модели в соцсетях стараются показать себя своими, родными. Мы вступаем с ними в парасоциальные отношения, начинает казаться, что мы их знаем. С одной стороны, это недостижимый идеал красоты, который боготворят. С другой — если эта девушка такая же, как я, почему я не могу добиться аналогичного результата?
Вы же не станете сравнивать свои прыжки с шестом с результатами Елены Исинбаевой. Почему тогда выход профессиональной модели должен становиться меркой для вашей жизни?
Шоу Victoria’s Secret в октябре 2026

Есть большая ловушка, которую стоило бы обсуждать в рамках феминистского дискурса, — рассказы о том, что вы можете получить все. Да, действительно, мы можем быть матерями и еще очень много работать. Но какой ценой? Насколько этот ресурс восполняем? Вопрос риторический.

Большая роскошь после того, как вы стали матерью, — дать себе возможность не соответствовать навязанным внешним стандартам. У вас вполне могут меняться приоритеты, и это окей. При этом у меня есть ощущение, что общество все еще функционирует так: пока ребенок внутри тебя и ты беременна — мы все тебя любим. Но как только ты родила, будь добра в течение двух дней снова стать звонкой и тонкой. И мне кажется, в России это особенно заметно.

Я считаю, что это мизогиния, которая проявляется как псевдозабота. Восхваляя беременную женщину, а спустя неделю, две или даже год после родов осуждая ее тело, мы показываем: когда она носила ребенка, мы ценили лишь ребенка, а мать была для нас только его хранителем.

Гораздо лучше в такие моменты напоминать себе про концепцию Дональда Вудса Винникотта "достаточно хорошая мать" и про то, что тело с годами меняется (британский педиатр и детский психоаналитик считал, что матери не нужно быть идеальной — достаточно оставаться внимательной к потребностям ребенка, не стремясь оградить его от любых разочарований). Взрослая женщина не обязана оставаться субтильным подростком.
Реалистичные примеры и красота без ретуши

Люблю, когда женщины с обычными работами показывают, как, занимаясь силовыми тренировками, они за год или два вернулись к форме, которой хотели добиться, а иногда даже улучшали ее. Мотивация для меня — там, где видны время, усилия и реальная жизнь.

Я вижу большое количество знаменитостей вживую, а потом могу посмотреть, как они показывают себя в социальных сетях. И это большая разница. Если человек не сталкивается с такой реальностью, у него возникает ощущение, что все вокруг красивые, а он один — ужасный. Поэтому я люблю фотографии знаменитостей крупным планом, без ретуши. Для меня это очень терапевтично.
Мотивация для меня — там, где видны время, усилия и реальная жизнь.
Помощь, которая остается за кадром

Если вместе с результатом человек показывает, какая помощь за ним стоит, это как минимум честно. Когда женщина рассказывает: у меня есть няня, повар, другие помощники, — становится понятнее, почему наши возможности различаются. Самое неприятное, когда очень многое остается за кадром, а нам предлагают сравнивать только результат.
Надеяться, что медиа и бренды в массе своей будут ответственными, не приходится. Каждому из нас приходится наращивать собственную броню, которая позволит не падать ни в идеализацию, ни в демонизацию.
Право жить на своей скорости
Женщине, которая только что родила, смотрит на показ Victoria’s Secret и думает: "Как же так, они смогли, а я нет", — мне хочется напомнить: вы родили человека. Это невероятное, огромное достижение.

Большая роскошь — быть здоровой в своем теле. Большая роскошь — радоваться еде. Большая роскошь в современном тревожном мире — иметь возможность жить на своей скорости. И большая роскошь — иметь стержень, чтобы сказать "нет" навязываемым стандартам.

Многие стандарты красоты создаются для того, чтобы что-то продать. Они концентрируются на нашей неуверенности, на слабых точках. Поэтому можно попросить близких напоминать вам — или самой записать себе аудио на повтор: вы замечательная, вы супер. Вы не Барбара Палвин, вы не Эльза Хоск (шведская модель, одна из «ангелов» Victoria's Secret, в 2021-м родила дочь). Вы — это вы. У вас другой путь и свои крутые качества.
Даже если бы вы похудели до тех же параметров, это само по себе не сделало бы вашу жизнь лучше. Это не ваша работа и не гарантия побед в жизни».

items.title: Fear and Loathing Are All the GOP Have Left
items.description: The closer we get to the midterm elections, the clearer it has become that Donald Trump has decisively failed to convince anything like a majority of Americans that he’s doing a good job. The more he insists that his success is brilliant and self-evident, and
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: The closer we get to the midterm elections, the clearer it has become that Donald Trump has decisively failed to convince anything like a majority of Americans that he’s doing a good job. The more he insists that his success is brilliant and self-evident, and the more he exhibits resentment of Americans for their ingratitude, the worse his job-approval numbers get. And while a lot of things are going on in this (and every other) election, midterms are almost invariably a referendum on the job performance of whoever occupies the White House. The only presidents whose parties made midterm gains dating back to FDR were those with very high job-approval ratings (Bill Clinton in 1998 and George W. Bush in 2002). It just isn’t happening for Trump, who is experiencing the worst job-approval numbers since Bush’s popularity fell apart in 2006 and perhaps since Harry Truman became the scapegoat for post–World War II discontent in 1946.

So with time clearly having run out for persuading voters they’re totally wrong about Trump, Republicans are now focused on mitigating their losses — and that means convincing their own partisan voters to show up despite their own misgivings about their president. They are a distinct minority of the electorate nationally, but they have majorities (at least if they vote in robust numbers) in many of the red states where their Senate, House, and gubernatorial candidates are deeply in trouble. If the GOP can motivate them to turn out in number matching their very enthusiastic Democratic counterparts, who are psyched up about limiting Trump’s power and reversing policies and practices they intensely dislike, perhaps the bleeding can be staunched. But that involves something much simpler than the usual tools of persuasion: It requires emotional appeals to past Trump voters to turn out again to help themselves and the country avoid a fate worse than the current malaise (under Trump).

For Republicans, that has dictated two specific tactics: First, it means convincing hard-core Trump voters that their loyalty to The Boss requires getting off their butts and voting anyway (“pretend I’m on the ballot,” the president has said again and again). And second, it means convincing even voters who are lukewarm about Trump and his party that the success of individual Democratic candidates (or all of them combined) will threaten or violate everything they hold dear. Fear and hate, lathered in lies, has sadly become the order of the day for the GOP as Election Day grows near.

The sanitized way to talk about this descent into the gutter is that Republicans are seeking to change a “referendum” election (which is what midterms typically are) into a “choice” election where voters weigh the pros and cons of both parties instead of reacting viscerally to conditions in the country and laying them on the feet of the presidential party. But what it really means is exploiting, and if necessary creating, terrible doubts about Democratic candidates specifically and the opposition party generally.

The nationwide name-calling of Democrats as “radical liberals,” “socialists,” or “communists”; the attacks on Muslims like Abdul El-Sayed as “jihadists” or “terrorists”; the labelling of clerics like Adam Hamilton and James Talarico as “heretics” or “anti-Christians”; and the wholesale association of every Trump critic with “illegal alien criminals,” noncitizen voting, and forcible gender-affirming care for minors are already notorious. Down the midterm homestretch such new outrages as insinuations that Maine Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson is guilty of incest and use of Ohio Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton’s estranged mother to label her a “liar” have reached new lows.

Worse than the attacks are the rationalizations for them. Instead of demanding that Ohio GOP candidate Vivek Ramaswamy take down or repudiate the ad featuring Acton’s mother, Vice-President J.D. Vance went after Republicans who expressed dismay over it, as the Associated Press reports:
“Politics is a tough business,” Vance said to reporters.

In Cincinnati, the vice president said it was “not really my concern” whether the controversial 60-second spot was appropriate, and said he was focused on supporting Republican candidates in their midterm races.

“I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America,” Vance said in his first public comments on the ad, which has roiled one of the most contentious and expensive governor’s races in the country.

The end justifies the means, you see, and Vance is faithfully echoing his boss’s claims that a Democratic midterm win wouldn’t just be an electoral setback but a horrifying catastrophe that will usher in an “economic depression, much like 1929” and make America a fiery hellscape. Campaigning in Kansas earlier this week, Trump pointed to riots in France and said that’s what Democrats stood for:

Globalist left-wing have treasonously imported millions and millions of third world migrants who are totally incompatible with the West, and they are incompatible with Western values. They despise everything about France, and they’re destroying that country, and we’re not going to let that happen to this country. … When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to do to America.

There’s no line of attack too implausible or shocking for Republicans who are on the run. There are hard cold numbers behind this red-hot rhetoric, as the New York Times’ Nate Cohn observes in explaining the results of the final Times-Siena poll of the midterm cycle:

Democrats lead by nine points among registered voters who have actually voted in a prior midterm or a primary. On the other hand, Democrats could win by even more if only those who say they intend to vote show up: Democrats lead by 14 points among those who say they’re at least “very likely” to vote or have already done so.
The Republicans lead among only one group by likelihood of voting: those who said they were “not at all likely to vote.”

So these potential voters need to be scared out of their wits, or driven out of their minds with fury, to ensure they show up by November 3. That’s the only ammunition the president and his party have left, and they are not about to let scruples keep them from using it.

items.title: Who Is Alina Habba, the Ex-Trump Lawyer in the Thick of Multiple Scandals?
items.description: Donald Trump has churned through a lot of lawyers during his time as president — constantly suing people, being sued, getting impeached (twice!), and taking an elastic view of what constitutes a crime will do that to you — but some have been more memorable tha
items.author: Bess Levin
paragraphs: Donald Trump has churned through a lot of lawyers during his time as president — constantly suing people, being sued, getting impeached (twice!), and taking an elastic view of what constitutes a crime will do that to you — but some have been more memorable than others. Former NYC mayor turned national embarrassment Rudy Giuliani. Sidney “Release the Kraken” Powell. Todd Blanche, the personal lawyer he made attorney general. Michael Cohen!

Then there’s Alina Habba, who joined Trump’s legal team during his first administration, was disqualified from the job he gave her during his second, and has been in the news a lot lately. See: the “blood feud” between her and Trump ally Richard Grenell over millions of dollars that were allegedly meant for the Kennedy Center but were allegedly misappropriated; or the $50 million deal she reportedly struck with the family of a billionaire banker who was seeking a pardon from Trump — which came through weeks after she was hired.
Anyway, if her name is not ringing any bells, here’s a quick primer.
She met Trump at one of his golf clubs

A New Jersey native, Habba met the president at Bedminster, which was a short distance from her law firm at the time. When he hired her, her experience included serving as the general counsel of a parking garage and representing a cast member of The Real Housewives of New Jersey in a fight with Facebook. His allies were not impressed, and told the press as much, saying: “He has some lawyers that are very sophisticated with years of experience litigating, and he has now fallen prey to inexperienced lawyers who are just telling him what he wants to hear.”
She was sanctioned for her legal work involving Hillary Clinton

In 2022, Habba brought a suit on behalf of Trump against Hillary Clinton, John Podesta, Jake Sullivan, Debbie Wasserman Schultz, and other individuals and entities he wanted damages from in connection with the 2016 election. That suit and all of its claims were dismissed, and Habba along with four other attorneys representing Trump were sanctioned and ordered to pay the legal fees of 31 defendants, including Clinton. Of the suit Habba brought, a judge wrote, “No reasonable lawyer would have filed it. Intended for a political purpose, none of the counts of the amended complaint stated a cognizable legal claim.”
She was the lead attorney on the E. Jean Carroll v. Donald J. Trump trial

That also did not go well, both from the perspective of Trump losing and being ordered to pay Carroll $83.3 million in damages and Habba being repeatedly reprimanded by the judge presiding over the case. (At one point, he threatened to send her to jail.)
She was disqualified from the job Trump gave her at the start of his second term

In March 2025, Trump named Habba interim U.S. attorney for New Jersey. Months later, a panel of federal judges gave someone else the job, and despite then–Attorney General Pam Bondi firing the woman in an attempt to keep Habba in place, the court found Habba had been unlawfully appointed and ultimately disqualified from serving.
She and one of Trump’s special envoys are at war

Earlier this month, Habba reportedly went directly to Trump to accuse presidential envoy for special missions Richard Grenell of convincing her husband — more on him later — to wire $17.6 million to a Texas defense company, with some $6 million meant to go to the Kennedy Center. According to Habba, the wire transfer went through, but the money never went to its intended recipient. (Grenell has called the claims “absurd,” adding: “I’ve never asked for one cent to be sent somewhere else pretending it was for the Kennedy Center, and I’ve never received any payment from him at all.”) The White House general counsel is said to be investigating.
She and one of Trump’s close allies are at war

Late on Tuesday, the New York Times reported that last fall, the family of billionaire banker Julio Herrera Velutini hired Habba, with a package of $10 million a year for four years, plus bonuses, for a guaranteed $50 million over four years. The hire happened around the same time Herrera was seeking a pardon from Trump, which had thus far proved elusive. Then, weeks after Habba began working at the firm set up by Herrera’s daughter — while also working as “a senior adviser to Attorney General Pam Bondi” — Trump issued Herrera “a full and unconditional pardon.”

Habba has denied playing a role in the pardon, telling the Times in a statement, “Any insinuation that my employment — all of which has been vetted and disclosed to the D.O.J. — had anything to do with securing a pardon is false.” Both Julio Herrera Velutini and his daughter did not respond to requests for comments from the Times; the DoJ said Habba did not discuss a pardon with anyone.

Last month, Habba married Turkish businessman Turhan Mildon — the one she claimed Grenell swindled — at the Waldorf Astoria. The affair reportedly cost approximately $10 million, and the guest list included Bondi, Blanche, Kash Patel, and Mike Tyson.

items.title: MCM and PAPER Team Up for 'Festive' Campaign
items.description: MCM is rolling out a highly anticipated new collection this season, and it's pulling out all the stops to mark the occasion. The luxury brand is debuting its first full-fledged line-up of ready-to-wear and accessories under its global creative director, Dirk S
items.author: Mario Abad
paragraphs: MCM is rolling out a highly anticipated new collection this season, and it's pulling out all the stops to mark the occasion. The luxury brand is debuting its first full-fledged line-up of ready-to-wear and accessories under its global creative director, Dirk Schönberger, who joined in 2018 after a highly successful eight-year stint at Adidas.

To coincide with the worldwide drop of their Spring/Summer 2020 line, PAPER teamed up with MCM to produce its "Festive" campaign, which was filmed at the TWA hotel in New York City's John F. Kennedy Airport. As the German brand's roots are in travel, the video fittingly captures the jet-set experience.

Globe-trotting influencers Tanner Reese, Vanessa Hong and Sami Miro hang out in the international departures lounge decked out in MCM-branded gear, including logo tracksuits, sneakers, and the brand's iconic Visetos-print luggage. Once they board the plane, their flight turns into a full-on dance party complete with a live DJ and glasses of champagne as the passengers await their next destination.

The collection drops this month just in time for the holiday travel season. Each piece is designed with a nod to the brand's travel and music heritage, which dates back to the disco days of 1976 Munich. Some of the standout looks include all the oversized monogram detailing as well as a leopard floral tracksuit. MCM's signature accessories like their backpacks, weekender beltbags and crossbodies also feature throughout.

In addition, new bag styles such as the Milano series reappear this season. A color palette of black is paired with flashes of bright red and shimmery metallics, as well as a base of pale neutrals offset by lively prints. The brand's go-to legacy heritage trunks and rolling luggage round out the assortment.

items.title: At the NBA Finals, Celebs and Fans Make It ‘Knicks But Fashion’
items.description: Taylor Swift, Timothee Chalamet, Kylie Jenner, Spike Lee and Walt Frazier aren't the only ones making fashion statements at the Knicks games. As New York's best comeback story advances in the playoffs with three wins against the San Antonio Spurs, the city is
items.author: Joan Summers
paragraphs: Taylor Swift, Timothee Chalamet, Kylie Jenner, Spike Lee and Walt Frazier aren't the only ones making fashion statements at the Knicks games. As New York's best comeback story advances in the playoffs with three wins against the San Antonio Spurs, the city is welcoming a different kind of fashion week: looks that would make even WAGS turn their heads.

Swift donned a "punny" tee simply saying Steve Knicks, alongside the Haim sisters wearing Knickleback and Knickole Kidman, too. (Swift even gave her longtime friend, Law and Order: SVU icon and the inspiration for her two cats' names, Mariska Hargitay, a matching tee). Chalamet and Jenner continued their courtside runway reign in complementary Chrome Hearts denim fits, and Jordyn Woods brought her lucky orange purse back to Madison Square Garden to watch her fiancé Karl-Anthony Towns continue his winning streak.

But we have to look outside the Garden for some of the best street styles that bring fashion to the fandom. Celebrity stylist Tania Ali tapped into her lifelong love of the Knicks when dressing certain buzzy "die hard" Knicks fan clients, one of whom (Natalie Dougherty) renamed the Staud Wells dress -- a blue frock with orange railroad stripes -- the de facto "Knicks Dress" for the season while attending the luxe Frick Garden Party on a game day. Ali herself locked in for Game 3 with Mother Denim Lemon Twist wide leg jeans paired with a grey Hanes tank, official Knicks hat, an orange Desigual bag, and a NBA orange Knicks hooded sweatshirt tied around her shoulders.

"I think this series has brought out the best fashion because everyone is incorporating Knicks gear and colors into their individual style," Ali told PAPER. "Everything feels authentic and fun at the same time. You see personal style effortlessly blending with fan support."

Ali added, "I think the celebrity buzz has definitely elevated the fashion buzz. New York has always been integral to fashion and then add in the variety of celebrity looks, and it’s the perfect mix of fashion and sports."

Casey Kohlberg, fashion writer and founder and CEO of Phoenix Rising Productions, admitted that she is fully "jumping on the bandwagon" for the playoffs. "I'm loving the energy New Yorkers are bringing to the finals," Kohlberg told PAPER. When dressing for game day watch parties, Kohlberg has the classic Knicks hat in tow; she cites the Moda Operandi cobalt blue Made Some mini skirt and a blue suede Alberta Ferretti bag as other staples of her playoff wardrobe.

Drag performer CT Hedden won't say he's quite a bandwagon fan because his knowledge now runs deep: as a performer, Hedden channeled his cosplay tactics to that of the Knicks history. "I’m locked in now, and a new forever fan," Hedden told PAPER. He even brought out the orange and blue for Madonna's party at Macy's Herald Square to represent the team during the Wednesday game. "I wanted to make sure I dressed up to show Knicks support," Hedden said. "I somehow have come to realize just how many Knicks-appropriate outfits I own from collecting designer pieces for years."

As Hedden captioned on Facebook for his blue Jonathan Simkhai suit and neon orange Louboutin bag with matching heels, "Knicks but make it fashion." He later teased his one fashion requirement to PAPER: "Game Days require a minimum of 120mm heels. Period!"
But has the celebrity row element for the series elevated Knicks fans' fashion tastes, or is it vice versa?

"If anything, the celebrities are trying to look like New Yorkers and not the other way around," culture writer Shamira Ibrahim told PAPER. "The one thing about Knicks fandom is that it really is a fandom that belongs to the people, and we have always dictated the direction of how we move and how we like to show up and show support. We are a fandom that travels with our team, that carries New York on our chest. It really is a source of New York pride."
Ibrahim added, "That said, shout out to Jordyn Woods and her lucky orange purse. I hope that [her] bag line thrives forever and ever as we take this to the next championship."

There is also a wider level of Woods-esque superstition throughout the fandom, though. Auteur filmmaker Spike Lee had Pope Leo bless his Knicks jersey, and Knicks supporters everywhere are hoping to close out the series in five games which means rewearing key pieces to keep the good juju flowing -- and tossing out the outfits they wore during the single loss to the Spurs.

"On Monday, I wore a blue bandanna, a white crop top, orange pants, and white and orange Nikes paired with my Knicks tote bag. Then we lost so of course I’m never going to wear that outfit again," Ibrahim, a Knicks fan for three decades, said.

Former Jezebel columnist and author Ashley Reese broke it down: "The hope is that a good fit will add some good luck for the Knicks," Reese said. "I can’t explain the logic of it, it’s just not logical. [But] I don't think I can support a sports team without getting a little superstitious, and I definitely get superstitious about what I wear on game day."

Reese had to similarly shelve her blue and orange Hokas after Monday's Game 3 loss, saying, "Now I'm not going to wear those shoes to another finals watch party. I just can't." At least she still has another outfit option: blue Prada sneakers that proved to seal the deal for the team during Game 4 ("I will be wearing those again for Game 5," Reese promised).

As Jordan Frazes, founding publicist at Frazes Creative, described, "The stakes are higher, and so are the outfits." When asked who the best dressed player on the team is in her opinion, Frazes quipped, "Since Timothée Chalamet is convinced he’s on the team, we’re courting him: stylish, slightly unhinged and completely committed to the bit."

Frazes herself is committed to showing her team support for the NBA championships. Frazes started the playoff series in "full Knicks uniform mode," which meant pairing Knicks jerseys Tibi or Adam Selman mini skirts and later incorporating orange and blue into her eye makeup.

Food influencer Sarah DelRosso, who recently became a Knicks fan after witnessing the playoff run during the 2024-25 season, also leaned into Knicks-inspired makeup looks: She got a manicure with Knicks colors alternating per each nail. As for accessories, her NY or Nowhere bracelet has been a "good luck charm" for the series, and like Frazes, DelRosso added Tom Ford eyeshadow with two shades of orange on her lids. "Any creative way you can wear orange and blue, I'll support it," DelRosso said. She even made an inaugural visit to the NBA store to snag a shirt that has the Knicks Eastern Conference Champions logo on it.

Culture writers Ibrahim and Reese opted to emphasize bootleg or custom merchandise instead of NBA branded gear. "Sorry, I know people were scrambling to get the official merch when the Knicks got into the finals, but something feels way more legit about getting a bootleg shirt that will absolutely shrink 4 sizes as soon as you wash it," Reese told PAPER. "There's an old school camaraderie about it that I love, and I think it really taps into the spirit of the city right now."

And that bootleg spirit was brought to the court for Game 4 in a very A-list way with Alana Haim making DIY screen printed tees for Swift and her sisters. We're primed for even more big fashions swings from tunnel fits to fanwear.

Reese added, of the trend of fashion statements: "The Knicks haven’t been in the finals in over a quarter of a century. Look, I'm all about positivity but we're not guaranteed to do this well again next year. Might as well go all out now while you can!"

items.title: John Mayer Launches New Label Sob Rock Records
items.description: John Mayer has launched his own label entitled Sob Rock Records. Named after his latest album, the musician has teamed up with Mercury Records for the endeavor.
items.author: Althea Legaspi
paragraphs: John Mayer has launched his own label entitled Sob Rock Records. Named after his latest album, the musician has teamed up with Mercury Records for the endeavor.

“Working with [Mercury Chairman and CEO] Tyler Arnold and the talented team at Mercury Records has already proven to be a great partnership,” Mayer said in a statement. “The path from creative vision to execution has never been easier or more rewarding. I feel very inspired, and I’m excited for what’s to come.”

Mayer will be releasing his first new single, “Tom and Jerry,” since dropping his 2021 album Sob Rock, this Friday. Produced by Blake Slatkin and Mayer, the musician will premiere it on his Sirius XM channel “Life With John Mayer” on Thursday where it will be played throughout the day, before it arrives at midnight.

Mayer has been teasing the track the last few days. On Instagram Wednesday, he shared its cover art and revealed guests bassist Pino Palladino, drummer Aaron Sterling, percussionist Lenny Castro, and organ player Larry Goldings. It was recorded at Chaplin Recording Studio.

“’Tom and Jerry’ was the name I used when saving my first voice memo with this song idea. ‘And if you ever come through, which I doubt you’ll do, I’ll run away with you,’” he captioned the post. “From that moment on, the adventure began in bringing that feeling to life. I’ve said it before, but it bears repeating every time – I get to work with a group of incredibly talented and deeply dedicated artists who will stop at nothing until the sound comes into focus and becomes a picture. I can’t wait to tell you more about it, but first, it’s important that you know who contributed to this track.”
He also shared a snippet of him singing along to the track while in the studio, another featuring a different lyric selection of the song, and also an instrumental section.

“John Mayer is one of the greatest artists of all time, and I couldn’t be prouder to welcome him to Mercury Records,” Arnold said in a statement. “We’re excited to be part of his next chapter and to partner with his label, Sob Rock Records, to help bring his creative vision to life.” Mayer signed with Mercury himself after parting ways with Columbia in 2022, as Billboard notes.

In other Mayer news, the musician is returning to the Sphere in Las Vegas in 2027 for a run of show featuring three different sets. The April 2027 residency will feature Mayer performing as a solo artist, with a full band, and with the John Mayer Trio.

items.title: The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City Recap: Candid Camera
items.description: The ladies are back from their trip to San Francisco, which means Mary is thankfully back on our screens. She gets tea at Angie’s house, and by tea I mean that they’re drinking wine out of a teapot and eating what seems to be pickles off of plates with the pri
items.author: Tom Smyth
paragraphs: The ladies are back from their trip to San Francisco, which means Mary is thankfully back on our screens. She gets tea at Angie’s house, and by tea I mean that they’re drinking wine out of a teapot and eating what seems to be pickles off of plates with the price tag still on them. Mary sees that they cost “499,” but it’s unclear whether that’s $4.99 or $499, and I, honest to God, have no idea which it is. I can’t imagine Angie paying five bucks for a plate, but I also think anybody who would pay almost $500 should be institutionalized, so I can’t take this on.

In any case, soon enough Angie is giving Mary a rundown of what she missed on the trip beat for beat like she’s doing a “And that’s what you missed on Glee.” All of that, and I truly mean all of that, leaves Mary confused because the last time she saw all of the women was during the moment of peace they all found at her place. So in an attempt to get back to that place, Mary decides she has to gather them — both figuratively and literally — to get things back on track.

But before that, Britani is hosting a 21st-birthday party for her daughter Olivia, where she faces yet another indignity when one of her daughter’s friends mistakenly calls her “Brooklyn.” This poor woman will never know peace nor respect, but how fun is it to watch? And besides, it’s just a miracle that this event is even happening at all, given how tumultuous her and Olivia’s relationship used to be. They were once totally estranged, and now she gets to be there for Olivia’s first drink, which I would think was a lie if it weren’t for the Mormonism of it all. Having grown up Catholic, it’s always so fascinating to see a religion that’s conversely against drinking alcohol. I can’t relate.

At the party, Bronwyn fills them in some more about selling her house, to which Britani quickly asks how much it sold for. God bless her and her lack of shame. But the real development comes when Britani says that because Todd can still see her credit card statement, he caught on when she went down to Florida to meet Brandon’s parents. The women all agree that it seems a little soon, but maybe Bronwyn just needed someone to reminisce with about the ’80s.

Then it’s on to Mary’s “boss brunch,” where she’s intent on getting these women’s lives together. First up is Whitney, whom she pointedly thanks “for being responsible” upon seeing her take a sip of water instead of alcohol, and Whitney once again acknowledges her public intoxications, saying that she’s going through a lot at the moment. But what is “a lot,” Lisa wonders? Since Whitney isn’t ready to share about her separation, Lisa thinks she’s yet again alluding to some vague personal struggle as a “Get Out of Jail Free” card. Even though we do know that Whitney is being very honest, I get Lisa’s frustration, even though I wish she’d say the same when Meredith pulls that same trick. It’s a little bit of hypocrisy if you ask me … maybe someone should write a song about that.

Speaking of Lisa and Meredith’s song, it doesn’t take long for that to come up, but Meredith very firmly asserts that it wasn’t directed at Bronwyn. Bronwyn isn’t so sure about that, and when she interrupts to say as much, Meredith fires back with, “Can you seal your mouth like your lawsuits?” See, this is a perfect example of a read still landing beautifully, even though it was clearly written and rehearsed in advance. There’s an art to these things, and Meredith always knows how to deliver a line without it sounding canned or forced.

While they maintain that they thought Bronwyn would find it funny, Meredith shockingly ends up delivering a genuine apology for hurting her feelings, and Mary couldn’t be prouder. Whitney, on the other hand, is jealous, since she’s never been able to get an apology out of Meredith once in the past seven years. She says that aliens will invade, dinosaurs will come back, and we’ll have a female president before Meredith would ever apologize to her. God, I at least hope that last one is true.

Then everybody turns their attention to Lisa, but she doesn’t have any apology to offer. “I’ll write a check; I’m not giving an apology,” she says, and if Bronwyn were a more interesting Housewife, she’d ask for the check. The way this divorce is going, I think she might end up needing it. When she fires back at her, Lisa then mocks her for bumming a cigarette on the cast trip to look like a bad girl, which is such a devastating read because that’s exactly what she was doing. Eventually, Mary shuts the back-and-forth down, saying that you “can’t squeeze blood out of a turnip.”

Besides, we apparently have a much bigger issue at hand, with Meredith taking the floor to accuse Whitney of assembling “a team of 50-year-old women” to take her down. Marvel should take note; this is what it needs to do to get me to watch an Avengers movie. But where did Meredith even get this idea from? “Me, right here,” Quai says. Oh, now this is television. Quai admits that she lied in San Francisco and was, in fact, talking shit about Meredith, but has since come clean and, as a beautiful apology gift, offered up some gossip about Whitney. Quai told Meredith that Whitney told her, “We wanted you in the group to get Meredith out.” But who is “we”? By process of elimination, Lisa surmises that it’s Whitney, Britani, Heather, and Angie — and the drama harkens back to the good old days of “taking down the Dubrows” and the RHONY girls teaming up to end Bethenny.

At some point during all of this, Quai claims that Whitney recorded their conversation — which explains why she ended up coming clean to Meredith. Apparently, she got this idea because when the conversation was first being debated in San Fran, Angie told her that she has to come clean because Whitney has cameras in the house. Angie, of course, just made that up and now clarifies that she meant that in today’s world, we live in a constant surveillance state. “The last time I got a pap smear, there was a tape recorder in there,” she says … for some reason. But I think what Angie was actually doing was the same trick you pull when you’re trying to get a lying toddler to tell the truth — threatening to check security cameras that don’t exist. Next week, I expect someone to threaten to call Santa.

After all this fighting, Mary is completely disappointed in them and tearfully tells them that she expected more from all of them. Rookie mistake, Mary. She gives talking-tos to Lisa and Whitney specifically, encouraging everyone to get to a better peace — and whether or not she’s successful, I do love Mary in this role as the mediator that they all want to do right by.

To her credit, Whitney actually takes Mary’s advice seriously and later tries to smooth things over by inviting Quai over to her home, showing her that it is not filled with hidden cameras. It is, in this instance, filled with reality television cameras. But when it’s just the two of them, the vibe is completely different, and they’re able to make peace with ease. Clearly, the problem is when other people get involved, particularly when Quai is caught between feuding parties — so they vow to keep their friendship separate from all the crossfire in order to maintain it, and based on how this meeting went, I have hope.

Heather and Angie, meanwhile, go to the aptly named “Gossip Kitchen” with Mary and Lisa to do just that. Mary tells them that Britani left her event with not one but THREE floral arrangements, which included the one that Mary gifted her, one right off the table, and the one that Britani herself brought as a gift. I will say, I don’t actually know how that’s even physically possible, but who am I not to believe Mary. Plus, she has some photo evidence, given that Britani sent her a photo of her delivering one of the bouquets to a nursing home like a middle-age candy striper. This prompts Angie to share a theory she’s been sitting on: “I feel like she goes to rest homes to try to get into their will,” she says, and I almost fell to the ground. It’s simply one of the funniest things I’ve ever seen a woman be accused of on Housewives, and yet they move right past this I Care a Lot–esque assertion as quickly as it was brought up. Maybe Britani was pinching those people in the airport to get in their wills too.

When they move on, and Mary asks Angie how she and Shawn are doing, Angie clams up and, not ready to come clean just yet, breezes right past the question so they move on to Heather instead. She says that she’s nervous to bring her new man around the women, but Lisa assures her that they’ll be nice. The camaraderie and banter in this last scene, particularly between Heather and Lisa, fill me with so much joy. Seeing the two of them joke around gives me hope for peace on earth, and ultimately this sisterhood — though it’s often buried deep under endless drama and bickering — is the lifeblood of the show. It’s even more apparent when the whole group giddily gossips about Britani’s mission to uncover information about Bronwyn, who they all agree is a complete phony. Everything about her is a ruse; it all feels put on, and this new boyfriend undeniably feels like a PR relationship. The gossip fills them with a childlike glee that, quite frankly, I find beautiful.

items.title: Rome MIA Market Takeaways, From Bracing for Netflix Fallout to Italy’s Production Slump and European Producers Fighting Back
items.description: The 12th edition of Rome’s MIA Market came to a close on Friday with market head Gaia Tridente heralding “a stronger, renewed edition of MIA, with a more ambitious and expanded program,” that saw a high-powered cohort of European and global industry guests — i
items.author: Christopher Vourlias
paragraphs: The 12th edition of Rome’s MIA Market came to a close on Friday with market head Gaia Tridente heralding “a stronger, renewed edition of MIA, with a more ambitious and expanded program,” that saw a high-powered cohort of European and global industry guests — including Banijay Entertainment CEO Marco Bassetti, Studiocanal CEO Anna Marsh, Bad Wolf CEO Jane Tranter, and filmmakers Edward Berger (“All Quiet on the Western Front”) and Asif Kapadia (“Amy”) — arriving for a lively week in the Eternal City.

This year’s market expanded its footprint beyond its traditional home in the Palazzo Barberini and adjacent Cinema Barberini, incorporating several new venues along the elegant Via Veneto — of “La Dolce Vita” fame — and in the process “making the city itself an integral part of the market’s identity and experience,” according to Tridente.
She went on to say that those changes represented “probably been one of the biggest transformations of MIA, and certainly one of the most challenging from an organizational perspective.”

“We have completely reimagined the geography of the market, creating a new industry district in the heart of Rome, with Palazzo Barberini as our main hub and a network of venues along Via Veneto,” she said. “The idea was not simply to accommodate a growing market. We wanted to create a different experience for our participants, with dedicated spaces for the different activities, while keeping everything within walking distance.

“In many ways, the entire neighborhood becomes part of the market. I believe this new structure gives MIA a much stronger identity and offers us room to grow,” she continued. “And I have to say, being able to experience Rome in this way is something quite special. The city is not just a backdrop for MIA; it is part of what makes the market unique.”

This year’s event witnessed several other significant changes, including the introduction of a new gap-financing market for animation series and the launch of a dedicated strand showcasing the range of financial tools available to European producers and the growing role of equity capital in film and television production (more on that below).
The market also shifted its dates to take place alongside the Rome Film Festival, as well as Alice nella Città, an autonomous festival that runs parallel to the Rome fest.

“The decision was primarily part of a broader strategy to strengthen Rome’s position as an international hub for the audiovisual industry,” said Tridente, by “bringing these three events closer together in the calendar and creating greater opportunities for collaboration and synergies between the industry and the festivals.

“MIA remains an independent international industry market, with its own identity and objectives, but I believe that having the market and the two festivals taking place at the same time can generate additional value for the entire industry, from producers and distributors to filmmakers and international buyers,” she added.
Here are Variety’s takeaways from a busy week in Rome:
Unprecedented turbulence, untapped potential

The 12th edition of MIA marked the first industry confab to take place since the Red Wedding-style bloodbath at Netflix, which saw the Los Gatos-based streamer ax 1,000 employees — around 6% of its workforce — including chief content officer Bela Bajaria and head of film Dan Lin, whose firing was announced on Monday just hours before MIA attendees gathered for an opening reception in Rome’s lavish Palazzo Barberini.

The firings were the latest in a series of shake-ups, retrenchments and mergers — including Paramount Skydance’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery to form Skydance Corp. — that are recasting the shape of the industry, with many still puzzling over what such seismic shifts will mean for the landscape of production and distribution moving forward.

For some execs in Rome, such turbulence invites a chance to think outside the box — and seize the moment. “In my world, mergers represent opportunity. Contraction represents opportunity,” said Roeg Sutherland, who is co-head of CAA’s media finance department and its international film group. “Financiers see that as a moment where people will be opportunistic.” Anna Marsh, the CEO of Studiocanal and the deputy CEO and chief content officer for Canal+, which in the past year alone has swooped up several companies across two continents, insisted such M&As are essential for survival amid the disruptions of corporate consolidations, shifting consumption habits, emerging technologies and other industry turbulence.

“The audience is so tough that we constantly need to be looking at ourselves in the mirror,” she said. “It’s really important to have a fresh perspective. People that are going to challenge the status quo. Because the business is moving so fast.”

For European producers, there’s also an upside when pan-European studios like Banijay, Mediawan and Vuelta go on a buying spree. “In an ideal world, a group gives you business affairs, cash flow, finance,” said Lorenzo De Maio, president of De Maio Entertainment. “Because the market is so challenging, being part of a group does give you a little bit more support. And usually, the creative stays with the producer.”
European producers digging in

In a keynote speech in Rome, Marco Bassetti, CEO of London-based Banijay Entertainment, the world’s largest independent studio, said that “the major debate currently taking place in Europe … is about recognizing and providing compensation for creativity.” That debate is taking different forms, from the ramped-up efforts of European producers to retain IP rights to the ongoing calls for quotas that would require global streamers to invest a portion of their revenues into local productions. “The reality is that we have no ownership, and it’s extremely difficult to secure any, though things are starting to open up a bit,” Bassetti said. “Ultimately, [the studios and the streamers] still have total control.”

Across the board, producers are feeling the squeeze. “We all know that the business has gotten quite challenging right now,” said De Maio. “Distribution advances have gone down. Gaps are harder to finance …. Buyers, both in film and TV, have become very specific with their mandates. Production costs are going up.” Meanwhile, the dizzying pace of shake-ups in C-suites and boardrooms has made it harder than ever to shepherd a project from script to screen; the commissioner who greenlights a project one day might be pink-slipped the next. “Sometimes the decision is made for you,” said Andrea Calderwood, of the U.K.’s “Die My Love” producer Potboiler Productions, on learning to adapt to uncertainty. “Sometimes you might think you’re choosing, but often the circumstances choose you.”

“Tenacity” is key, said Calderwood, while Daniel Campos Pavoncelli, partner and producer at “My Brilliant Friend” outfit Indiana Productions, said that in a fickle market, producers need to identify the “one big selling point that will make a difference” — whether it’s an A-list star, a bankable director or an irresistible IP.

Still, some aspects of a historically chummy industry remain unchanged. “What we’re trying to do is leveraging relationships more than ever,” said Pavoncelli. “And that’s relationships with talent mostly, but also co-producers, buyers, broadcasters. Those relationships, which in our business are so important, then become vital.”
Italian production spend drops for first time since 2018

Investment in content production destined for Italy’s film, TV and streaming industries dropped 7.4% to €2 billion ($2.24 billion) in 2025, compared with the previous year, with the scripted sphere suffering most amid uncertainty over government support of the country’s tax credits and the ongoing transition in viewership from linear to streaming.
That was the main takeaway from a report issued by Italian TV producers’ association APA, which noted that this was the first decline in spend since 2018.

After reaping the rewards of a protracted growth spurt, Italian producers in 2025 faced a forced slowdown as the country’s right-wing government dithered with ongoing regulatory modifications to tax incentives for domestic film and TV production. The domestic tax credit modifications impasse did not impact Italy’s international production rebates, which remained firmly in place.

The report underlined that Italian scripted content continues to reach broad and demographically diverse audiences. In the linear broadcasting sphere, Lux Vide’s “Sandokan,” a modern take on the classic pirate tale adapted from Italian author Emilio Salgari’s iconic book series, and BiBiFilm’s “La Preside,” about a feisty female principal of a school in a crime-ridden Naples neighborhood, both drew a hefty average of over 4.6 million viewers per episode. In the streaming space, Picomedia’s Naples-set prison drama “The Sea Beyond” is still a big hit on state broadcaster RAI’s streaming and linear outlets, as is Aurora TV’s period drama “Il Paradiso delle Signore.”

The standout Italian original on Netflix is serial killer series “The Monster of Florence,” directed by genre specialist Stefano Sollima that launched from the 2025 Venice Film Festival and garnered 9.7 million global views in its first week in October 2025.
Finding the audiences — wherever they may be

Audiences are arguably consuming more content than ever before — just not in the ways that they used to, with YouTube, TikTok and other platforms competing for eyeballs alongside old-fashioned TV shows. So where does that leave drama producers? “Audiences are being really choosy about how they invest their time, and we need to up our game,” said “Black Mirror” and “Sharp Objects” executive producer Jessica Rhoades. “It is harder and harder to hit the bull’s eye,” agreed Anna Marsh, the CEO of Studiocanal and the deputy CEO and chief content officer for Canal+. When it comes to Gen Z audiences in particular, “there’s just no room for error.”

Gauging audience habits to thread that needle can be both art and science. Jamie Lynn, exec VP of co-production and distribution at Fremantle, expects to see more “razor-specific audience targeting” that will allow companies to develop projects for specific demos “at the right size and scale.” But producers and commissioners are bombarded with more viewing metrics than ever before; as Rhoades put it, “Listening to the audience too much is a fool’s errand.”

“We have a lot of data,” said Emanuele Marchesi, the director of Sky Studios Italia, the original programming and scripted television division of Sky Italia. “We have to find the courage to create new audiences.”

How to do that could just come down to good old-fashioned storytelling. “I like to think that we have the courage of our convictions,” said Andrew Plotkin, executive VP and head of drama development at Sony Pictures Television. “You never quite know how something’s going to be received, so all we can do is take something on that we feel passionate about. The audience is fickle. You never know what they’re going to connect with.”

This year saw the first edition of the MIA Market’s new European Investment Hub, which aims to help European industry professionals navigate the wide range of financial tools at their disposal and “foster direct contact between producers and representatives from these various entities who can provide guidance,” according to Tridente. Right on queue, Rome witnessed the launch this week of a €100 million ($112 million) fund — backed by Media Capital Technologies and Italy’s RP1 Holding — to finance audiovisual productions and film distribution in Italy and boost the country’s flagging indie sector.

From institutional investors and private-equity groups to brands and family offices, “there’s definitely more money in the marketplace than there ever has been in the 25 years I’ve been doing this,” said CAA’s Roeg Sutherland, who’s co-head of the agency’s media finance department and its international film group. For investors, the emergence of new formats and the booming creator economy offer inroads into the industry beyond the traditional realms of film and television. For producers, “I think we’re finding right now there are a range of international financing opportunities…[that] give you opportunities beyond the main U.S. and U.K. gatekeepers,” said Andrea Calderwood, of “Die My Love” producer Potboiler Productions.

Those opportunities can take myriad forms, from financing for an individual project or slate to an investment in a company that can catapult it to the next level. There’s no one-size-fits-all solution — either for the investors or their creative partners — and such arrangements, like any marriage, require give-and-take from both sides. Due diligence not only means having “your books ready” and being “realistic about your prospects” for a return on investment, according to Christopher Borde, managing director at the U.K.’s Media & Investment Advisors. It also means finding the right partner that’s aligned with your goals as a creative. “Know who you are and what you want to do,” said Celine Dornier, a content executive at Finland-U.K. based film investment fund IPR.VC.
European verticals ready for lift-off?

It’s still early days for vertical content in much of the world, though a recent study projected that the format will generate $150 billion in revenue in global markets outside of China this year. In Europe, the interest — and investment — is rising, with German powerhouse Constantin Entertainment among the continent’s players entering the vertical market earlier this year. “Are we at an inflection point? I think the answer is yes, in terms of people’s cultural habits and why this might work now versus just 18 months ago,” said Andrew Plotkin, executive VP and head of drama development at Sony Pictures Television.

Digital platforms like YouTube and TikTok are beginning to invest in original vertical content, while legacy media companies are also leaning in, said former Netflix exec Kelly Luegenbiehl, founder of vertical video and microdrama outfit Shorties Studios. “Ultimately, what is their strategy going to be in this vertical space?” she asked, acknowledging that the burgeoning market is “definitely not for the risk-averse.” “It is definitely the Wild West. I think that there is no clear path for profitability — there’s no exact roadmap yet.”

It’s the prospect of getting in on the ground floor that makes vertical content so enticing, not only for investors but for creators. “Creativity is alive and well in the vertical space,” said Luegenbiehl, noting that without a playbook, her company has been “able to try things and take risks and move pretty quickly.” “In the vertical space, I like to say we’re in the business of yes,” she said, noting that the people driving the format’s growth are laying the groundwork for the successful industry to come. “If you build it, the audience will come.”

It’s been decades since the golden age of Dario Argento, Lucio Fulci and Mario Bava, but if there’s any doubt that Italian horror is enjoying a renaissance, look no further than Paolo Strippoli’s high-concept thriller “The Spiral,” which is repping Italy in the best international feature Oscar race. The talk during a lively MIA panel centered on some of the trends driving the current horror boom, from the rise of digital-native content creators to the eventizing of the theatrical experience and the “broadening beyond the elevated, arthouse horror that perhaps was only for a certain audience,” said Rachael Labes, manager of acquisitions and productions at horror streamer Shudder.

Savvy distributors are honing in on how to “create an aesthetic or a brand or a character that people want to seek out,” said Peter Kuplowsky, a producer and independent programmer for TIFF’s Midnight Madness strand. “You’re not just selling the one individual horror film. You’re selling the next film as well, and the idea that you want to create a brand around the filmmaker.”

Horror has always been a way to “discover new voices and [do] good business,” noted Andrea Romeo, founder and CEO of I Wonder, which released “Backrooms” and “The Substance” in Italy. So how to find the next “Backrooms”-style breakout? “TikTok’s definitely driving a lot of the conversation,” said Jonny Bunning, of “Faces of Death” and “It Ends” U.K. distributor Signature Entertainment. Kuplowsky said there’s a “gold rush” for YouTube and other online creators — “No one wants to get blamed that they missed something” — while Labes described “a frenzy toward finding the next Kane Parsons.” Still, “you can’t acquire a trend; you can only acquire a specific film or a specific director,” the Shudder exec noted. “Seeing the success and learning the lessons and investing in talent and letting a voice come through: That’s the lesson.”
Nick Vivarelli contributed reporting to this story.

items.title: Amy Winehouse West End Musical in Development (EXCLUSIVE)
items.description: A musical based on Amy Winehouse is officially in development, Variety has exclusively learned.
items.author: K J Yossman
paragraphs: A musical based on Amy Winehouse is officially in development, Variety has exclusively learned.

The project is in early days although legendary Broadway producer Catherine Schreiber, who has produced shows including “Cabaret,” “Rent” and the stage adaptation of “High School Musical,” is understood to be involved and casting is said to be underway.
One source described development of the musical as “the worst kept secret in theater.”
Winehouse’s father, Mitch Winehouse, who oversees the late singer’s estate, is also believed to be involved in the project, which will likely mean it involves some of her best-known songs.
Winehouse released only two studio albums before her untimely death in 2011 at the age of 27 although they generated numerous iconic tracks such as “Back to Black,” “Valerie” and “Rehab.”

It is unclear if the musical adaptation would be based on Winehouse’s life, like the biographical Tina Turner musical or more in the vein of “Mamma Mia!” which uses ABBA’s songs to accompany an original story.

The possibility of a musical about Winehouse’s life and featuring some of her best-known songs has been floated before, with Mitch reportedly discussing the prospect as far back as 2017. But with Schreiber’s involvement it looks like the project may finally come to fruition.
A biopic about the singer, “Back to Black,” was released to mixed reviews two years ago. The film starred “Industry’s” Marisa Abela as Winehouse and was directed by Sam Taylor Johnson.
Jukebox musicals have become West End staples in recent years, ranging from ABBA-inspired “Mamma Mia!” and “Tina – The Tina Turner Musical” to the more recent “MJ the Musical.”
Not every musical is a guaranteed hit, however, with the recent Chaka Khan musical “I’m Every Woman,” which opened in London earlier this year, receiving less than stellar reviews.
Reps for Schreiber and Mitch Winehouse did not respond by press time.

items.title: You Only Audition Twice: Watch Henry Cavill, James Brolin, Sam Neill and Others Screen-Test for James Bond
items.description: Right now, somewhere on a soundstage at Pinewood Studios, several young British actors are lining up to have their dreams crushed.
items.author: Benjamin Svetkey
paragraphs: Right now, somewhere on a soundstage at Pinewood Studios, several young British actors are lining up to have their dreams crushed.

Rumor has it that Amazon execs and director Denis Villeneuve are finally holding screen tests to determine who will succeed Daniel Craig as the seventh James Bond. Not even M knows the full list of potential 007s, but Jack Lowden, Callum Turner and Josh O’Connor are widely presumed to be among the top contenders. One of these hopefuls, and only one, will end up inheriting the most coveted male lead in cinematic history. The rest will experience the emotional equivalent of being ejected from an Aston Martin passenger seat.

Luckily for the losers, there is one consolation: They aren’t alone. Pinewood is littered with the dashed hopes of would-be Bonds going back decades — many of whom went on to become household names for other reasons. And, even more luckily for the rest of us, some of the footage from their 007 screen tests has survived intact and leaked onto the internet.

With Roger Moore making noises about retiring after For Your Eyes Only, Bond’s producers did something unthinkable: They seriously considered casting an American. James Brolin, then 42 and best known for The Amityville Horror, tested over several days, even adopting something almost resembling an English accent. His Octopussy audition included the seduction scene from From Russia With Love — a sequence Bond producers had long used to test would-be 007s — as well as a specially staged fight to test Brolin’s physical chops. He nearly got the part, until Moore agreed to return.

When Moore finally did retire after A View to a Kill, the producers went looking for a new 007 for The Living Daylights. Among the contenders was the 38-year-old New Zealander then best known for the miniseries Reilly, Ace of Spies and Omen III — and still seven years away from Jurassic Park. Neill performed the same From Russia With Love seduction scene Brolin had tackled four years earlier. Director John Glen reportedly favored him, but producer Cubby Broccoli wasn’t convinced. The role ultimately went to Timothy Dalton.

Seven years before he put on Superman’s cape, a 22-year-old Cavill came remarkably close to slipping into Bond’s tuxedo for Casino Royale. Director Martin Campbell later said the young Brit gave a “tremendous” audition but was simply too young for the role. For his test, Cavill traded the old From Russia With Love bit for a more recent Bond encounter: Pierce Brosnan’s double-entendre-packed first meeting with Xenia Onatopp at the casino in GoldenEye. The role, of course, went to Daniel Craig.

The New Zealand actor was 29 and virtually unknown to American audiences when he joined the Casino Royale Bond hunt. Starr performed the same GoldenEye scene as Cavill, but in his native Kiwi accent — an unusual sound coming out of 007’s mouth. He eventually found international fame playing the considerably less suave Homelander on The Boys.

Friend had exactly one movie on his résumé — The Libertine, opposite Johnny Depp — when the 23-year-old Brit found himself auditioning to become Bond. His test used the same GoldenEye bit as Cavill and Starr — but he obviously didn’t get the part, either. Still, Friend soon landed Pride & Prejudice and eventually got to play a CIA operative on Homeland.

Before Pandora came calling, the 29-year-old Australian actor came surprisingly close to winning the Casino Royale sweepstakes. Worthington was flown to London, fitted for a tux and screen-tested with the usual GoldenEye material. Worthington later admitted he could handle Bond’s physicality but struggled with the suave stuff — especially the accent. Four years later, Avatar turned him into an international star.

items.title: ‘MobLand’ EP Teases What Season 3 Holds for Tom Hardy as ‘Laird’ Star Peter Sarsgaard Shares How He Feels About Playing a “Malevolent U.S. Billionaire”
items.description: Peter Sarsgaard infused a Paramount U.K. upfront event in London on Thursday evening with some political commentary, while the executive producer of his upcoming Paramount+ series Laird and the streamer’s MobLand teased what season 3 will bring for star Tom Ha
items.author: Georg Szalai
paragraphs: Peter Sarsgaard infused a Paramount U.K. upfront event in London on Thursday evening with some political commentary, while the executive producer of his upcoming Paramount+ series Laird and the streamer’s MobLand teased what season 3 will bring for star Tom Hardy.
Sarsgaard appeared during a discussion with fellow Laird star Kenneth Branagh and executive producer David Glasser about their upcoming family drama series set in the Scottish Highlands.

Sarsgaard told the audience that he is playing a “malevolent American billionaire,” who is looking to take land from Branagh’s proud Scot, who is defiant. “It’s an interesting time to be an American in the world,” he shared. “When I grew up, you watched Raiders of the Lost Ark, and the Nazis were the bad guys. But I don’t feel conflicted right now [about taking on this role]. It feels right.” The star concluded: “I’m really enjoying that aspect of it.”
Branagh said about Laird: “It’s a great world and has lots of riveting characters made by people who know how to put these things together.”
Branagh and Sarsgaard called the production in the Scottish Highlands demanding, comparing it to an 800-meter run.
Executive producer and 101 Studios boss Glasser shared that his team is focused on making the show really “epic.”

About MobLand, he shared an early tease for the recently confirmed season 3 and what it will bring for one of its main stars. “Someone will challenge Tom Hardy,” he said to cheers, but he didn’t share more.
Thursday evening’s London event also featured video messages from Samuel L. Jackson and David Beckham, along with a live appearance by Yellowstone and Dutton Ranch star Kelly Reilly.

A video touting the combined star and content power of the merged Skydance and featuring various Paramount and Warner Bros. brands and ending with Tom Cruise sitting atop the company’s iconic water tower, closed the event’s formal part. “We’re only getting started,” Paramount international ad sales president Lee Sears concluded. “And the best is yet to come.”

items.title: ‘Clayface’ Aims to Give DC Studios a Box Office Win as ‘You Can See Everything’ Stays Strong
items.description: Clayface looks to give the DC Studios team a reason for a happy face in its opening weekend at the box office, although it will encounter competition from the second frame for A24’s You Can See Everything, which continues to get audiences pumped.
items.author: Ryan Gajewski
paragraphs: Clayface looks to give the DC Studios team a reason for a happy face in its opening weekend at the box office, although it will encounter competition from the second frame for A24’s You Can See Everything, which continues to get audiences pumped.

Warner Bros. projects a launch between $25 million and $30 million domestically for Clayface from more than 3,400 North American theaters, along with an additional $20 million to $25 million internationally. Director James Watkins’ $44 million-budgeted body-horror feature stars Tom Rhys Harries and Naomi Ackie in the story of Matt Hagen (Harries), an actor who turns to a scientist (Ackie) for assistance after his face becomes disfigured.

This marks the third feature release in the planned slate for DC Studios bosses James Gunn and Peter Safran. Superman kicked off the DC Universe’s film side with a strong start last year, while Supergirl sputtered over the summer, with the $170 million-budgeted movie debuting to a soft $37.1 million domestically before ending its run with $126 million worldwide. Clayface has the benefit of a far more modest budget.

Clayface has fared better with critics than Supergirl, holding a 75 percent approval from Rotten Tomatoes reviewers, as opposed to the 52 score for the summer’s Milly Alcock-led release. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter, critic Frank Scheck called Clayface “a big swing that definitely pays off.”

Offering potential competition for the weekend’s top spot is A24’s buzzy Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything, which expands to 2,600 North American theaters after playing in 855 in its debut frame. Directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim‘s film about the disgraced Theranos founder’s life before beginning her prison sentence was a sensation in its opening weekend, overperforming to the tune of $15 million as it placed second behind Paramount and Legendary’s Street Fighter.
You Can See Everything is projected to gross at least $18 million for the weekend and could likely go beyond that.

Hitting theaters this weekend is Laika’s animated stop-motion feature Wildwood from director Travis Knight. It is set for 2,926 North American theaters and holds a sterling 100 percent approval on Rotten Tomatoes.

Additionally, Sony’s Klara and the Sun, with Jenna Ortega and Amy Adams starring for director Taika Waititi, debuts over the weekend. The same is true for Amazon MGM Studios’ Ali G: Who Iz I?, as Sacha Baron Cohen‘s comedy hits theaters for just one week ahead of its streaming launch on Prime Video.
Another newcomer is Black Bear’s Sundance standout Wicker, with directors Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson’s romantic fantasy starring Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård.

items.title: J-Hope and Nigo Teamed Up to Make Sneaker Dynamite
items.description: By many metrics, it doesn’t get bigger than the Bangtan Boys. The members of BTS have been on a roll this year, dropping their reunion album Arirang in February and then taking the show on the road for one of the highest-grossing stadium tours of the year. Alo
items.author: Tres Dean
paragraphs: By many metrics, it doesn’t get bigger than the Bangtan Boys. The members of BTS have been on a roll this year, dropping their reunion album Arirang in February and then taking the show on the road for one of the highest-grossing stadium tours of the year. Along the way, each member has taken on a compelling sidequest or two, from Jung Kook stepping in as Hublot’s newest brand ambassador to RM loaning his art collection to SFMOMA for a recently opened exhibition. And then there’s J-Hope, the crew’s resident sneakerhead. After the band previously teamed up with Nike for a line of tour merchandise, J-Hope circled back to the Swoosh for his first-ever sneaker collaboration. And this time, he’s working alongside one of the biggest names in streetwear with him: Nigo.

Nigo is the man behind BAPE and, in a sense, streetwear as we know it. His iconic Bapesta—which bears an uncanny likeness to the Air Force One—upended the sneaker world, and he’s been working with Nike in a much more official capacity these days. Collectively, Nigo and J-Hope—who are also, respectively, a close collaborator and ambassador of Pharrell’s Louis Vuitton—surely have a good sense of what gets people riled up, whether about sneakers or otherwise.

The fruits of the collaboration are ripe. They’ve kitted out a AF1 silhouette from 2001 in a glossy gold and burnt auburn upper, with turquoise accents and chunky knit laces. The left and right shoes feature, respectively, unique “NIGO AIR” and “J-HOPE AIR” branding on the tongue tags, sockliner, and heel, where the traditional embroidered “NIKE AIR” logo usually sits. And for Nigo, it’s the first of many to come—J-Hope is the first collaborator in the designer’s ongoing series of Air Force Ones he’s planning to release with a global lineup of collaborators.

Those looking to cop a pair of the Nigo x J-Hope Air Force One best set their alarms accordingly—civilian sneakerheads are going to have to compete with ARMY for these joints. The shoe goes on sale for $150 on Thursday, October 22via the SNKRS app and select retailers.

items.title: Alexander Skarsgård Is Rocking Custom Olivia Colman Merch
items.description: Buying flowers is nice. Booking a restaurant is good, too. But if you really, really like someone, Alexander Skarsgård has a suggestion: get their face printed on your shirt.
items.author: Adam Cheung
paragraphs: Buying flowers is nice. Booking a restaurant is good, too. But if you really, really like someone, Alexander Skarsgård has a suggestion: get their face printed on your shirt.

Last night, at the Los Angeles premiere of Wicker, the actor pulled up with a photo of Oscar winner Olivia Colman across his chest. In the film, she plays a fisherwoman who gets a husband made out of wicker (that's Skarsgård). But apparently, being handcrafted specifically for someone isn't enough anymore—you also have to wear their merch.

Skarsgård—who has been working with Harry Lambert, the longtime stylist of Harry Styles—was wearing a custom look by the London-based brand Chopova Lowena. Printed on the beaded jersey was a portrait of Colman as the fisherwoman, with little spiky embellishments framing her face. It was quite sweet, actually. The sorta thing your mom might have on the mantelpiece, only that in this case, it was stretched across a six-foot-something Swedish man.

He wore it with the brand's signature taffeta midi skirt in green and pink tartan, complete with pleats and silver carabiners. Plus, black socks. Black shoes. An Oscar-winning actress on his torso. And to think that getting dressed for a red carpet used to involve calling someone about a tux.

And look, this does make the rest of us seem a bit lazy. There are guys out there who won't even put their girlfriend on their main grid. Skarsgård has put his on-screen wife right there on his chest—with beading! Your anniversary Instagram story with the tiny heart in the corner is looking a little half-assed now, isn't it?

Imagine going for dinner with someone wearing this. You're sitting opposite them, trying to work out what you want, and there you are again, just below the bread basket. They take their jacket off. More you. The waiter comes over and immediately knows who's paying. (There would also be the question of which photograph was chosen, because “I had a top made with your face on it” is lovely, in theory. “I had a top made with that picture of you that you've asked me to delete six times” is a very different evening.)

For Skarsgård, though, it helps that Colman was right there beside him, looking very pleased with the whole thing. Which is probably the response you'd want after going to all that trouble. Especially if the top's custom. You're not getting a refund on Olivia.
A version of this story originally appeared in British GQ.

items.title: Belts Were All Over the Spring 2027 Runways—and Not Just Around Waists
items.description: For most of their history, belts have had a simple practical purpose: to hold up your pants. The biggest style advice given about them was equally as utilitarian: they should match your bag and shoes. But the belts shown across the spring 2027 runways aren’t q
items.author: Natalie Michie
paragraphs: For most of their history, belts have had a simple practical purpose: to hold up your pants.
