The biggest style advice given about them was equally as utilitarian: they should match your bag and shoes. But the belts shown across the spring 2027 runways aren’t quite like their predecessors. They were often comically large or ironically itty bitty. They had secret uses, and they crept onto other areas of the body like an invasive vine. They were replacing chokers, embellishing necklines, and sitting aimlessly, though chicly, below the hips. They’re made to be seen, and they are, for better or worse, the breakout accessory of the moment.

Is it a response to shrinking waists in the age of Ozempic? Is it symptomatic of the death of quiet luxury? Or are fashion houses simply trying to hype up another class of ‘It’ accessories to compliment their bag and shoe sales?
Whatever the case, they’re certain not boring. Here, the wildest belts from the spring 2027 runways.
MM6 Maison Margiela’s New Necklines

For spring 2027, MM6 championed clothes that just seemed “wrong.” Sweaters became skirts. Pants morphed into minidresses. Collegiate collars were turned on their side and used, rather effectively, as arm loops. The belt, too, was given a new look. It was brought way up past the waistline to the chest, where it became a bust decoration instead.
Givenchy’s Covert Compact Mirrors

Sarah Burton is a designer who thinks about women’s bodies. Beyond what looks good, she asks what feels good, with tailoring techniques and design details that serve the wearer in unseen ways. This came through in her belt offerings this season, which featured medallions with a secret second purpose. The statement disks opened to reveal compact mirrors—lightening the load of purses everywhere.
Alexander McQueen’s Heavy Metal

Is it a collar? Is it a harness? Is it a metallic suspender of sorts? The belts at Alexander McQueen delivered all of the above. Seán McGirr’s part Victorian gothicism, part rave-wear employed heavy-duty adornments with multiple straps. While the runway also had classic house suiting, it was the soft, silky evening gowns that got the belts. An effectively off-putting choice.

This season, Michael Rider’s joyful runway played with the extremities of the belt. Most talked-about were the thick leather iterations with supersized gilded buckles. On the opposite end of the aesthetic spectrum? Wiry cords that appeared almost as an afterthought. Both, however, were successful in drawing eyes to the waist.
Christopher Esber’s Ode to Elvis

Elvis Presley was on the mood board for Christopher Esber’s spring 2027 collection. Specifically, the designer looked to the flashy, studded belts that embellished the superstar’s suits in the 1950s. On the runway, that manifested in modernized takes on the rock-n-roll accessory, with belts that stretched up the torso before wrapping around the neck. Though these were presented with shift dresses instead of fit-and-flare jumpers, they still evoked Presley’s Las Vegas-era costumery.

Protective dressing was top of mind at Acne Studios, where belts were strapped across waists, chests, collars, and sometimes trousers for a small taste of traditionalism. Even with non-utilitarian designs, like warped Rococo ballgowns and loosely draped blouses, the idea of belts was never far—as buckles adorned tote straps and pointed loafers.
Ferragamo Does Double Duty

Maximillian Davis leaned into Ferragamo’s statement-belt legacy by finishing almost every look with a belt (or two). Suede capes and boxy blazers featured stacked leather straps, as did latex sheer sets and sexy going-out dresses. The result was a hit of polished hardware befitting cashmere-swathed dignitaries and skin-baring It-girls alike. Case in point: the collection looks right at home in the wardrobes of both Celine Dion and Dua Lipa.
Valentino’s Hourglass Drama

From 2010s-era studded straps to colorful fabric cummerbunds, Valentino’s spring 2027 show delivered Alessandro-Michele-level drama by way of cinched waists. High-rise pencil skirts, peplum tops, and cardigans tucked into trousers emphasized the hourglass silhouette. But big belts got the message across best.

Demna’s contribution to the belt renaissance came via his signature runway irony. Models with knife-sharp shoulders and smudged eye makeup balanced corporate dressing with vampiric edge, and thick belts offered a final touch of intensity. Whether worn high on midsections or slung below the hips, the multi-buckled, bondage strap was an unmissable attraction that winked at Tom Ford-age sexiness.
Dries Van Noten’s Ageless Accessories

Grandmotherly codes—like strings of pearls, bedazzled brooches, and knee-length skirts—were supercharged with saturated palettes and cartoonish proportions. Belts were central to creative director Julian Klausner’s vision of practical, offbeat femininity, with patterned waistbands on everything from floral sack dresses to wrinkled bubble skirts.

items.title: Every Must-See Look From the 2026 Academy Museum Gala
items.description: The sixth annual Academy Museum Gala is here, and once again, it’s living up to its reputation as one of Hollywood’s most glamorous nights. Dubbed the “Met Gala of the West,” the star-studded affair raises funds for the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and su
items.author: Natalie Michie
paragraphs: The sixth annual Academy Museum Gala is here, and once again, it’s living up to its reputation as one of Hollywood’s most glamorous nights. Dubbed the “Met Gala of the West,” the star-studded affair raises funds for the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and supports its mission to preserve cinema through special exhibitions, public screenings, and educational initiatives.

This year’s ceremony will honor Oscar-winning actor Charlize Theron with the Icon Award. Filmmaker and composer John Carpenter will receive the Luminary Award, while Colman Domingo will take home the Vantage Award. For the first time, Taylor Swift will not only attend, but also perform. The gala is a major stop for Oscar hopefuls, and Swift’s presence marks her continued involvement in cinema amid the success of her original song from Toy Story 5, “I Knew It, I Knew You.”

Its October timing, right after Fashion Month, means the evening always delivers looks straight from the runways. Expect to see plenty of Matthieu Blazy’s Chanel, Jonathan Anderson’s Dior, and Anthony Vaccarello’s swan song for Saint Laurent. With a host committee that includes Teyana Taylor, Demi Moore, Kirsten Dunst, Greta Lee, Adrien Brody, and Kate Hudson—as well as a star-studded guest list spanning sports, music, art, and television—the 2026 Academy Museum Gala offers a first taste of awards-season trends. Plus, with Rolex as the presenting sponsor, there will certainly be some exquisite timepieces on display.
Below are all the must-see celebrity fashion and jewelry moments from the 2026 Academy Museum Gala.
In Valentino and Cartier jewelry.
In Dior and Chopard jewelry.
In Tom Ford by Haider Ackermann and Boucheron jewelry.

items.title: Airbnb Hosts Are Furious They Can No Longer Make Guests Do Their Chores
items.description: Airbnb hosts are melting down over a new policy banning them from making guests complete tasks that “would typically be performed by a cleaner,” like “stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes.”
items.author: Caroline Haskins
paragraphs: Airbnb hosts are melting down over a new policy banning them from making guests complete tasks that “would typically be performed by a cleaner,” like “stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes.”

The change, which applies to all bookings made on or after November 20, quickly sparked outrage after it was announced in an email to Airbnb hosts on Wednesday. Many began fuming online about losing the right to make their guests clean up after themselves.

“As hosts, we have a responsibility to protect our investments, our homes, and, in many cases, our personal living spaces,” one person wrote in Airbnb’s official forum for hosts. “The problem is that Airbnb increasingly expects hosts to accept the risks while limiting our ability to protect ourselves.”

“Airbnb is like an abusive partner,” wrote one user on the Reddit community r/airbnb_hosts. “I'm alive long enough to recognize how truthful those few words are,” another person replied. “Until and unless I see substantive changes, I'm finally out.”
A different self-described host declared that going forward, the kitchens in their rentals will be “stripped down to only bare essentials.”

Many guests, meanwhile, are celebrating. For years, travelers have complained about having to pay hefty cleaning fees as part of their Airbnb bookings, only to be required to complete a list of chores before checking out.

“The guest experience has become total ass,” one person said in a subreddit for Airbnb hosts. “Clean dishes and run in the dishwasher. Strip the beds, put all linen in the laundry room. Take out all garbage, put in garbage can, take to the curb. Honestly, knock it off.”

Airbnb noted in its Wednesday announcement that hosts can’t get around the new policy by putting cleaning tasks in the “Requests” section of their listings instead. Airbnb spokesperson Simon Letouze tells WIRED that hosts can still make “reasonable” requests, such as asking guests to put dirty dishes in the sink. Other examples Airbnb cites include asking guests to take short showers in areas with drought-related water restrictions, or telling them to place trash in bear-proof containers.

In a Facebook group for Airbnb hosts, one person posted what they claimed was a screenshot of their failed attempt to edit their property’s “Requests” section. They tried to ask guests to wash and air-dry dishes, put dirty towels in the laundry room, and take trash to a dumpster at an RV park they could find using a map on the refrigerator. But they realized they couldn’t hit Save. Airbnb's interface had underlined and highlighted the requests in red and displayed a pop-up that read “Guests shouldn't be asked to do this task.”

Hosts also can’t circumvent the new policy by giving guests a printed list of rules and asking them to sign it when they check in. On November 20, Airbnb is also banning hosts from requiring guests to sign separate contracts, with limited exceptions for local legal requirements, longer stays, or accessing “an optional amenity” like a “golf cart rental.”

If one of these situations applies, hosts have to mention it in the dedicated section of their listing. Airbnb adds that it “doesn’t help enforce the terms of these contracts.” Hosts who violate either policy, Airbnb warns, may receive warnings, or in severe situations, have their listings removed or be banned from the platform entirely.

In a Facebook group for Airbnb hosts, one person posted a letter they claimed to have sent to company executives, demanding the ability to set their own “common-sense expectations” for guests. They encouraged others to send their own versions. Another asked if they should raise their prices, while a third called for hosts to organize a platform-wide strike.

“Even if we all unlist our properties for just a day or two, we can send a powerful message,” they wrote. “Airbnb built its empire on OUR properties. It’s time we reminded them who actually holds the power.”

Some hosts haven’t given up on finding a way to ignore or get around the changes. On Reddit, one person said they would simply move their rules to other sections of their listing, like “Guest Access.” (Airbnb did not immediately respond to WIRED’s inquiry about whether this would work.) Another person said they would give the guests a “house manual,” require the guest to read it, and provide a “codeword” as proof. (Several pointed out that this is not only unenforceable but against current Airbnb policy.)

“First sentence of my requests section will now state ‘Here are my house rules!’” another person said, though it’s unclear whether Airbnb’s interface will allow this. They named “not smoking” as an example of one of their house rules, but Airbnb has said it enforces host-imposed smoking bans.

Unwanted smoking and other serious scenarios—like letting dirty dishes become “health hazards,” leaving “permanent stains on sheets,” and creating “mountains of rotting garbage”—were invoked by several hosts. But these policy adjustments, seemingly, will not change how any of these things are treated.

Airbnb already has its own ground rules that all guests must agree to. The general credo is to "treat your host’s home like your own," which translates to things like putting trash in the trash can and not leaving moldy dishes.

If a host finds that anything was damaged or went missing during a stay, guests are expected to pay a “reasonable” amount to repair or replace it. Hosts are also protected through the platform’s protection program, AirCover, which will reimburse up to $3 million for certain property damage caused by guests, including furniture, cars, and other belongings.

Additional cleaning costs, such as performing "smoke odor removal" or handling "pet accidents” are also covered by AirCover. Airbnb notes that the cleaning fees hosts are allowed to set are only meant to cover standard guest turnover tasks like laundry and vacuuming. Hosts can’t “charge guest fees for failing to perform specific cleaning or checkout tasks,” though they can still leave guest reviews “based on cleanliness.”

In the Airbnb Hosts subreddit, a few lurking guests were quick to bring up the cleaning fees, which are famously the subject of their ire. One self-described “mostly guest” said they’re not opposed to running the dishwasher or stripping the bed. “Just don’t charge me a cleaning fee over $100 then,” they said.
“Truth nuke,” another person replied. “Why would I have to pre-game the cleaners?”

items.title: ‘Is There Any Good Advice for First-Time Parents?’
items.description: I’m getting ready to become a new mom, and I’m worried I’m not prepared. I know there’s probably not any sure way to be prepared — at least not completely — but still. I’m someone who likes to have a plan, and it feels like there’s so much I still need to lear
items.author: Amil Niazi
paragraphs: I’m getting ready to become a new mom, and I’m worried I’m not prepared. I know there’s probably not any sure way to be prepared — at least not completely — but still. I’m someone who likes to have a plan, and it feels like there’s so much I still need to learn before the baby arrives. I’ve tried looking for guidance in books or on the internet, but every time I do, I’m totally overwhelmed by how much advice is out there, and so much of it is contradictory or unhelpful. (I had to stop watching parenting TikToks because it was giving me so much anxiety.) I’ve also had multiple friends who are already parents tell me that most of the advice I’ve read isn’t good advice anyway and it might not even apply to me and my baby. It’s so frustrating. Is there any good advice for first-time parents? And if so, how do I find it?

When new parents — and in this case, new mothers — look for advice, there’s inherently a funny dichotomy at play. On the one hand, you’re right: Anything you could possibly wonder about matrescence or the postpartum experience has already been documented. It’s all, as you put it, “out there.” We are privy to thousands of years of hard-earned, tried-and-true matriarchal knowledge passed down to us through our mothers and grandmothers, sisters and friends. There are entire libraries full of books about motherhood, endless threads on social media, and so, so many blogs.

Yet, as common an experience as becoming a mother is, it’s also entirely singular. Each of us spends hours levitating in the space between life and death, birth and rebirth, then we come out the other side shattered, feeling around in the dark, tasked with putting ourselves back together — now with a baby on our breasts. The person who emerges from this experience does so in a way that’s uniquely her own. No wonder so many of us end up asking some version of, “Why didn’t anyone tell me it would be like this?”

Nevertheless, we persist — in both the soliciting of first-time parenting advice and in the giving. And there is a lot of really good, really accessible advice out there worth taking, a lot of which I wish I’d followed with my first baby and some of which I was able to use with my second and third. So in the spirit of this column, I took the pleas for advice and … asked for some advice of my own.

Putting out a call on Instagram, I asked my followers to share what guidance they wished they’d had as first-time parents as well as some of the advice that drove them crazy. Within a few hours, I was inundated with messages. I wasn’t surprised. I think once any of us have gone through something so radical, so upending, it’s hard not to want to scream what we’ve learned from the mountaintops.

Many moms wrote to me lamenting how much cliché and unhelpful parenting advice is out there. One frequent source of ire: the recommendation to “sleep when the baby sleeps.” As a new mom, I hated that one too. The baby’s nap time was my alone time, my stare-at-the-phone-or-TV time or my talk-to-my-husband time. But admittedly, this advice was useful to me eventually: By the time I’d delivered my third baby, I was sleeping when the baby sleeps all the damn time.

One woman, Erin, shared another commonly cited tip: Don’t load up on “baby stuff” until you know “what you actually need.” Wait to buy any extras, such as bottle warmers, changing tables, or any kind of expensive rocker or swing. I remember feeling pressure from social media to stock my Amazon cart with every fancy rocker and swaying seat and $200-plus baby lounger (that later failed federal infant-sleep standards.) Then it turned out my son didn’t like a single one of them and they languished in our small living room, gathering dust as I held my newborn who hated to be put down. And as much as I loved the look of our changing table, so carefully organized with wipes and diaps and all kinds of bum creams, only to end up changing the kids wherever I could get them to stop wiggling long enough to throw on a diaper. Now we keep essential supplies all over the house and we sold the changing table.

Most of the best advice in my DMs wasn’t even practical; it was emotional. Another mom, Meg, cited a 2013 article from The Atlantic, which reassured readers that “no one should expect a woman with a newborn to be ‘on cloud nine.’” She screenshotted the essay when she first read it and says it helped her realize she needed to give herself grace until she was out of the postpartum period. With its help, she was able to see that not every moment needed to be a “happy” one just because she was grateful to have a new baby. I saw her anxieties reflected in many other responses I received: new moms who had felt they needed to make everything perfect and be perfect in the immediate wake of their child’s birth. Advised Elise, “Most things work themselves out with time. You don’t have to rush to fix it.”

Versions of this guidance popped up again and again: Elzear loved being told to “let go of all expectations.” (She admits that’s obviously easier said than done but says a good way to put that attitude into practice is to remind yourself to stop “rushing.”) Similarly, Eva’s best advice was to “lower the bar for everything else.” Even though your house isn’t clean and sometimes “you may look like shit,” as long as your kid is “happy, healthy, fed, and loved,” that’s all that really matters. Amy, a midwife who doesn’t have kids herself but has delivered over 1,000 babies, offered the same guidance, which she gives to all of her patients: “Love it, keep it clean, and keep it fed.”

When I was pregnant with my first kid in 2017, there was almost no advice I was interested in hearing. My mom kept telling me to slow down, that I’d need time to heal after giving birth. She strongly advised me not to do things like book a three-hour flight to see my in-laws at Christmas seven weeks postpartum. Despite her experience raising three kids, at six months pregnant, I thought I knew better. I was feeling healthy, round, confident, and, yes, a little smug. I was going to be the first person to really nail parenting right out the gate! I took the birthing classes, I practiced my breathing, I read Expecting Better and some books (okay, some chapters of some books) on gentle parenting.

A few months later, I spent nearly 24 hours in labor and had a fairly significant vaginal tear that required stitches. Oxytocin still coursing through my veins, I again refused to hear any advice. The minute we got home with our baby boy, my husband and I decided to go for a walk to our favorite coffee shop while we basked in the terrifying glow of new parenthood. A few minutes into the walk, I felt like my entire uterus was falling to the floor. Every step became an angry lightning bolt of pain shooting through my crotch. I had torn my stitches and was in agony for the next couple of weeks, rotating through a pile of heavy ice packs I kept between my legs 24/7. When it was finally time to take that flight I’d booked, I was still bleeding into a diaper and carrying an inflatable donut everywhere.
As hard as it was to admit, I think my mom was right.

Part of my reluctance to stop and rest, to slow down at all, was out of a desire to remain myself despite this huge change in my life. I wanted to be me with a baby, rather than what my perception of a “mom” was. I was resisting the inevitable, trying to keep hold of a version of my life that no longer existed. And for a while, that resistance kept me from enjoying the life I now had.

After all that, my advice to expectant parents is to know that you will change and embrace whatever that change looks like — even if it’s uncomfortable, even if it’s not what you expected, even if it’s not what you hoped. Transformation isn’t seamless, and it takes time. Accept that and welcome it. Delete social media for a while, or at least unfollow anyone who’s pretending to have it all figured out. Ignore any advice that’s inflexible or unreasonable and any conversations about “bouncing back.” None of us really know what we’re doing at first and maybe not ever. But when you’re ready to sit in the truth of how messy and joyful and exhausting and funny and heart-wrenching and tender and wild it all is, lots of us will be waiting to welcome you with open arms — and, yes, plenty of advice.

items.title: When a Relationship Ends But the Venmo Requests Don’t
items.description: Breakups are complicated. When money’s involved, they’re even messier. If one person owes the other a debt — or the other claims they do — there isn’t much in the way of protocol: Unlike divorces, regular breakups involving unmarried couples aren’t governed by
items.author: Charlotte Cowles
paragraphs: Breakups are complicated. When money’s involved, they’re even messier. If one person owes the other a debt — or the other claims they do — there isn’t much in the way of protocol: Unlike divorces, regular breakups involving unmarried couples aren’t governed by family law, so exes have fewer apparent ways to settle arguments over who paid for what. Civil court can be an option, but informal IOUs don’t always hold up — and the associated legal fees may not be worth the battle. (Of course, as any fan of Judge Mathis knows, financial disputes between former romantic partners are quite common in small-claims courts.)
Below, four women share their own experiences of owing (or being owed) money after a breakup, how they handled the debt, and what they wish they’d known before the Venmo requests began.
“He drunkenly transferred me all the rest of the money in the middle of that fight, right then.” —a 37-year-old social-media manager from Canada

I met my boyfriend about ten years ago, and over the course of our relationship, his business became increasingly successful. We were traveling nonstop, living in multiple residences, mostly in Europe. I had a really great job working in social-media management when we first got together. But once we started traveling so much, he asked me if I wanted to quit and he would support me. He offered me an allowance of about $4,000 a month, plus the use of a credit card. I said “yes” because the company where I was working had become very toxic.

There’s this stay-at-home girlfriend, trophy-wife dream that you’re sold, and it felt like I’d achieved that. Of course, my dumb ass never thought of how that could turn out badly. I thought it was love. He was always clear that if we ever broke up, he’d make sure that I had some money, too. I wouldn’t just be left hanging with nothing after I’d quit my job to be with him.

You’d think I could have saved money in this situation, but the $4,000 a month went surprisingly fast. It costs a lot to hang out with rich people. They always want to eat at expensive restaurants that I’d never go to in my regular life and have multiday theme parties that require all these different outfits. You waste so much money.

Soon, things started going south. I checked my boyfriend’s phone one night and found out that he was talking to a really young girl on Instagram. We had one big blowout fight and after that he was like, “I’m done.” He sent me an email about our breakup deal — it was basically my severance package. He said he would pay out my allowance for three more months and give me $250,000. Which sounds pretty great, except he never paid me the $250,000.

I moved back into my parents’ house in Canada in the middle of nowhere. I felt like an alien. I understand why people get trapped in these relationships because they get used to a lifestyle. They can no longer imagine living without what they have. And I certainly felt that way. I mean, I didn’t grow up with much. I had worked in factories and at McDonald’s. I really didn’t want to go back to that.

Very luckily, I was able to get a new job with my old company. Still, I couldn’t let it go — like, how am I going to get the money that was promised to me? My ex wouldn’t answer my calls and didn’t want to be in contact. But he also kept telling people that we were still together. It was very confusing.

Eventually, I called a friend of mine who’s a psychologist, and he helped me compose a diplomatic email to my ex. And that actually did work: He sent me a quarter of the money. Then we kept in touch, and a few months later, he gave me the second quarter of it. He was kind of stringing me along, but also, I missed him. We met up in person a few times and hooked up. But I knew I couldn’t trust him.

At one point, we got into a huge argument. He was drunk, and I was so angry at him. I screamed at him, “You don’t keep your promises! You never even gave me the money that you offered.” And he drunkenly transferred me all the rest of the money in the middle of that fight, right then. It would have been a relief if it wasn’t such an awful moment.

From time to time, he now asks me to give it back. I think he feels entitled to it because we still travel together occasionally. In fact, we got back together for a bit and then never officially broke up. I’ve used most of the money to set up an entirely new life — move to a new city, get a new apartment, rebuild my career. I have about $100,000 left at this point, about three years later.
“My friends still call me Judge Judy because I threatened to take him to small-claims court.” —a 29-year-old teacher from New York

I know it was dumb, but I lent my then-boyfriend — now my ex — $5,000 to buy a new car. His old car had just broken down, and he’d gotten a great new job that required him to be in the office, starting right away. Lending him the money was my idea. He told me he’d pay it back in installments, $1,000 a month, once he got his new paycheck.

He was a trustworthy guy, or so I thought. I really wanted to help him out. He’d had a bad run of luck: His mom was sick, he’d gotten laid off, and he just couldn’t catch a break. We’d been together for two years and we were talking about moving in together.

The $5,000 was from my savings account — in fact, it was most of my savings — and I banked on him paying it back pretty quickly. But then, a month later, I caught him texting with an old flame. He swore it wasn’t anything serious, and at first I believed him. But then he did it again, and I could tell from their messages that they’d met up in person. I was devastated.

We broke up, and he said that he would still pay me back. He’d paid me the first month already, and I still have his texts to me saying that he’d continue with the planned installments. But then he didn’t pay the second month. He had excuses: He said his mom needed money for medication, which she probably did. Another month went by. I really didn’t want to deal with him anymore. So, finally, I threatened to take him to small-claims court. I think he thought I wouldn’t actually follow through with it. I’m a teacher, and I didn’t want to have a public court record — it’s embarrassing, and I didn’t want it coming up if someone Googled me. But finally a couple of friends came over with a bottle of wine and helped me fill out the paperwork to file a claim. They still call me Judge Judy because of it.

Luckily, we didn’t actually have to go to court. Once my ex got notice of the claim, he started paying me back. He still hasn’t paid all of it, or even in the amounts that he promised — it’s $400 here, $600 there — but he’s been Venmo-ing me every month. He still owes about $1,500. I’m annoyed, but I also feel like I dodged a bullet. I mean, what if I had kids with him or something? What if we’d actually moved in together? $5,000 is a lot to me, but it could have been so much worse. I don’t want to say that I learned a lesson; I hope to find a guy who I can share finances with someday. But it sucks that I trusted him and it blew up in my face.
“I sent a screenshot of the Venmo requests. And then he just stopped responding.” —a 36-year-old publicist from New York

I have outstanding Venmo requests that my ex hasn’t responded to for over a year. He owes me about $1,000 total. It’s not going to ruin my life if he doesn’t pay me back, but I’m annoyed that he’s ignoring it. He reaches out to me and acts like things are normal, as if there isn’t this outstanding debt.

We were together for over four years when I lived in San Francisco, and we were friends for several years before that. So we have a lot of shared history. During the pandemic, we wanted to move in together, and that’s when mortgage rates were incredibly low. He was like, “Why don’t we just buy a house?” And once he got that in his head — this milestone of being a homeowner — he wouldn’t let it go.

At the same time, I was working at a company that got acquired, so I got a lump sum of cash. That put me in a position where I actually could afford a down payment on a house. My mother definitely thought it was a bad idea. We weren’t married, and we didn’t plan to get married anytime soon.

My ex was incredibly successful financially. He worked in tech, and he never spent aggressively. So he definitely had the means to buy a house with or without me. Eventually, we found a place that we really liked, so we bought it together, put the deed in both our names, and split everything 50-50. When we went through the mortgage process, the bank looked at his financials and told him, “Oh, you don’t even need another person on this mortgage.” They barely even looked at my paperwork because of how good his was. But we split it anyway. The house was $1.25 million. We each paid half of the down payment, which was $115,000. And then we split the mortgage, which was $8,000 a month.

My ex was incredibly resistant to change and confrontation. We were in couples therapy for a while. Finally, I realized that certain issues would always be there, and if I stayed in the relationship, it wouldn’t make me happy. But then I had to figure out how to get out of it. Owning a house with him made that significantly more complicated.

When we broke up, we’d owned the house for two years. I was like, “Okay, here’s the deal. I’m going to do a sublet in New York for a month, and I’ll give you some space. And then, when I come back, we can get ready to sell the house.”He said he could make that timeline work.

Of course, when I came back, he still wasn’t ready to leave. I offered to help him pack.I offered to help him find a new apartment. I’d been paying my half of the mortgage while also paying for a sublet in New York, so I was losing patience. Finally, he showed me all this math he had done in a spreadsheet and was like, “This is how much money we’re going to lose if we sell our house right now. I think we need to wait until it’s a better time to sell.”

I stayed in New York, and he stayed in the house. Once he finally agreed that it was a good time to sell, I did all the work of getting the house prepared. I hired the landscapers, the painters, the flooring people. My ex and I had a shared bank account where we would put our money in for the mortgage and pay for other shared costs, but sometimes he would forget to put his share of the money in, so I would cover it and send him a Venmo request. And there’s still two outstanding things adding up to $1,000. You can only remind someone to pay you one time and then the request just sits there.
He reached out about something recently, and I was like, “While I have you …” and I sent a screenshot of the Venmo requests. And then he just stopped responding.

Then, two weeks later, at 2 a.m. his time, he sent me a playlist on Spotify with no context, a bunch of love songs. I didn’t respond. Then he sent me another song a week later that reminded him of a concert we went to. Again, I didn’t respond. Then, he sent me a picture of a piece of mail addressed to me that got delivered to his new apartment. It was very clearly junk mail, but he was like, “Do you need this?” And I was like, “No, throw it away.” And then he was like, “Oh, hey, how are you?” And I was like, “Listen, I’m not trying to be rude.I don’t like ignoring you. But I did send you a text message asking if you’re going to pay me back, which you ignored, and then you continued the conversation when it was convenient for you.” Which is always what he does.

He scrambled and was like, “Oh my gosh, sorry, it’s my ADHD, I totally meant to go look at our Excel spreadsheet to make sure the calculations were right.” But that was 22 weeks ago at this point. This man still has not gotten back to me.
“I didn’t want to rely on him, but I was living under the poverty line and he was making over six figures.” —a 38-year-old arts teacher from the Midwest

Throughout my life, I’ve worked for different arts organizations and theater companies. I’m also an actor and a playwright. I’m proud of my work, but it’s challenging financially. I’ve been on food stamps and Medicaid. I need social services to cover my basic necessities. I recently got a grant to help pay my utility bills. It’s always been challenging to be an arts worker, but especially in the past couple of years, there’s been a lot of cuts to arts funding.

I met my ex about three years ago and we really hit it off. I was ready for a serious relationship. From the jump, he was very much like, “Oh, just let me take care of everything.” He made so much more money than me that it was hard to say “no.” He was asking me out for dinner and taking me to events and things that I wouldn’t be able to afford on my own. I met some of his friends and they were like, “Just let him do it. He’s rich.”It felt nice to be wined and dined, but it also made me a little uncomfortable. I’m not from a background where I’ve met a lot of rich people — if anything, it’s always been the opposite. But he seemed to really respect my work and want to be supportive of it.

A few months into dating, my rent went up and I had to move. He offered to help me, and I was like, “Oh, sure,” thinking that he’d help me pack boxes and carry stuff. But then it turned out he was offering to help pay for movers. That made me realize that he lived in a different kind of reality. I’ve helped a lot of friends move. I think it’s normal to put in some elbow grease to help people you care about. But he wasn’t actually going to put in elbow grease — he was going to pay someone else to do it for him. I declined.

About a year and a half into the relationship, a couple of my contracts dried up. I was also dealing with an ill parent, and that required some unexpected travel. I was really stressed about my finances, taking on extra gigs wherever I could. And that’s when he was like, “If you need help with your bills or rent or anything, just let me know.” Finally, I took him up on the offer. He paid for a full month of my rent — which was cheap, under $1,000, but still, that was a huge weight off my shoulders. And he said, “You don’t have to worry about paying me back. It’s all good.”

At that point, he had also bought a house and invited me to move in with him. But the house was outside of the city, and I don’t have a car. He offered to get me a car, but I said “no.” He also offered to put me on the deed of his house, and I was like, “Don’t do that. I have student loans and we haven’t been together that long — this is kind of fast for me.” Everyone in my family was like, “He sounds like a keeper!” And I was impressed that he was making his intentions known. But I also didn’t want to move.

A few months later, I was still struggling. I didn’t want him to pay my rent again, but he kept offering. Finally I agreed to let him pay for half. Then a similar situation happened a few months later. And again. He gave it all freely and said it wasn’t a big deal, but to me, it was a lot of money. I didn’t want to rely on him, but I was living under the poverty line and he was making over six figures. I realized that I really needed to find a pathway out of this trap that I’d gotten into. I applied and got into a teacher training program that would give me my master’s degree in education, fully funded, along with a small stipend.

At the same time, we started having some conflicts. If I ever had a concern about something, he would get defensive and behave in a sort of entitled way. Like, “Oh, I take care of you, I look after you, and you’re going to be upset about this little thing?” He seemed to feel like I didn’t have a right to be concerned about anything.

Around that time, a play I wrote got production funding, so I got a space to perform it. The venue was outside of the city, so my ex gave me a ride and helped me set up. But the whole time, he seemed really grumpy about it and was rude to some of the other volunteers. When we got in the car afterward, I was like, “Are you okay?” And he got extremely defensive. He was like, “Why do you care so much about these volunteers? You don’t even know them. Don’t you see I’m doing so much for you?” And then he started bringing up the money. Like, “I just paid your rent for you. You don’t appreciate me.” It was late at night, and he was driving, and I was starting to get scared. So I just tried to de-escalate. I was like, “I’m sorry. I appreciate you, I really do. Can you please just pull over?” I was crying. And that’s when he broke up with me. He was like, “I guess you’re going to say that we’re never going to come back from this.” And I was like, “Yeah.” A friend came and picked me up and got all my stuff at two o’clock in the morning.

In the days after, he was texting me all the time, calling me names, harassing me. He wanted us to get back together. It was just not healthy. That’s when he told his family that he’d been supporting me financially and that I’d emotionally manipulated him. They accused me of financial abuse. And I was so upset about it that I told him I would pay him back. I don’t want this karmic weight on me, feeling like I just took this money.

If I ever knew things would go this way — that it would create this power imbalance where he would feel like he could treat me however he wanted because of his financial situation — I never would have agreed to his help. I would have figured out another way, like I always have before.

I can’t afford to pay him back now. I told him that as soon as I could, I would. I have no idea when that will be, and I feel really conflicted about it. I really don’t want this money between us, hanging over my head. Overall, it’s more than $4,000. To me, that’s so much money, but to him, it’s not. Sometimes, I’m like, Is this a fair exchange?
Email your money conundrums to mytwocents@nymag.com (and read our submission terms here.)

items.title: Habermas’s theory of truth meant he changed his mind | Aeon Essays
items.description: Jürgen Habermas died on 14 March 2026, in the German town of Starnberg, aged 96. Every fall, from the mid-1990s into the late-2000s, he would come to Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois to teach and give talks, a visit that a dedicated group of stude
items.author: Emilie Prattico
paragraphs: Jürgen Habermas died on 14 March 2026, in the German town of Starnberg, aged 96. Every fall, from the mid-1990s into the late-2000s, he would come to Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois to teach and give talks, a visit that a dedicated group of students looked forward to every fall term. The year that has stayed with me is 2004, when he taught what he’d spelled out in Between Facts and Norms (1992), his opus applying his theory to democratic politics. Law, philosophy, history, political science: students spanned many disciplines to come watch the famous German scholar every week, dressed in Wrangler jeans and a tweed jacket, expose his theory of deliberative politics in his unmistakable nasal voice, thick German accent, and impeccable English. Max Weber and the Frankfurt School, which were intimate to him, since he’d been Theodor Adorno’s research assistant in the 1950s, came to life in his speech and then in schemas and figures in chalk as he theorised about them.

I understood almost none of it at first: words I’d read were coming to life in the room, spoken by their author, and still not resolving into sense. After several lectures, the shape came into focus: this wasn’t just Between Facts and Norms being rebuilt in public, but decades of work arriving at a single place. Since The Theory of Communicative Action (1981), Habermas had been arguing that reason survives in modern life only as something people do together, that is, by giving each other reasons and staying open to being moved by them, rather than by force, money or tradition. Between Facts and Norms was that idea turned toward law and democracy directly: a state counts as legitimate only when its laws could in principle be justified to everyone bound by them, through exactly that kind of open exchange. I’d watched that argument take root in a decades-long intellectual history. Thinking is a practice, it involves owing each other explanations, questions, answers. It is not a fast process, and doing it in public, out loud, in front of a room, is what makes it worthwhile.

I attended all of Habermas’s seminars during my time at Northwestern with great interest and, to be honest, a sense of awe. One day, the topic of the weekly seminar was inclusion, and I had argued, with the timid conviction of a green graduate student, that deliberative publics ought to be designed for inclusion, and that entry into these publics required that members accept the terms of deliberation themselves. ‘Well, we can tell that Ms Prattico really is a Catholic in the strict, universalist sense,’ was not the answer I expected – and what took me by surprise wasn’t that he’d made a joke of my religion, but that he’d seen me as a person with a history and a set of unexamined beliefs, something he’d noticed only by teaching me.

After the seminars, the class would sometimes go out for drinks. It was on one of these occasions that I understood where the joke had come from. I’d asked him what it had been like arriving in the US as a visiting professor for the first time, at the New School for Social Research in the autumn of 1967, which decades earlier had served as a refuge for scholars fleeing the same Germany in which he’d grown up. It was the start of a long habit of crossing the Atlantic: Princeton four years later, for the Gauss Lectures where he first tried out the turn toward language that would eventually become his theory of communicative action; then, decades on, Northwestern, where I got to sit in the room.

Habermas answered my question by going back further than any of that. He’d been raised Lutheran. Visiting the US in the 1960s and ’70s, he’d been introduced to the Quakers, and something in their small meetings had stayed with him, specifically the way they sought unity with everyone present. When he came to describe the conditions under which people could reason together as equals, he said he heard an echo of those meetings: conditions that hold only when everyone who could be affected by a norm isn’t just included but has a voice, can object, and speaks with sincerity. In those conditions, which go far beyond mere inclusion, the only constraint left on discourse is ‘the unforced force of the better argument’, as he put it in Justification and Application (1993). It didn’t feel like something he’d have said at the podium.

The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere (1962), his seminal work originally published in German, made an argument about something concrete: 18th-century coffeehouses, salons and journals, where private citizens began treating the affairs of state as something they had standing to publicly discuss and judge, rather than simply obey. That habit, Habermas argued, was where modern democratic legitimacy first took root. The book also identified tendencies that would weaken it, too. He thought that the public sphere had already started to decay, folded back into spectacle by advertising and mass media, the public reduced from participants to an audience. It took almost 30 years for an English translation to appear. By the time it did, in 1989, Habermas had gotten a great deal of mileage out of the book in its original language; indeed, it had already made him a name outside Germany. When Craig Calhoun finally gathered the English-language response into a single volume, Habermas and the Public Sphere (1992), bringing together historians and theorists who challenged the argument, closing with a long response from Habermas himself, he could have easily spent the occasion defending a book that had already proved itself. Instead, he very openly contended with these critiques.
He came to think he’d been too sceptical about one piece of that story. But the warning itself never went away

Two critics stand out. Nancy Fraser argued that the public sphere was never actually open to everyone since it had excluded women and other groups from the start. She proposed replacing one public with many, arguing with each other, including publics formed by the very groups shut out of the first one. Geoff Eley made a related point from history: working-class and plebeian public spheres had existed alongside the bourgeois one all along, not before or after it. Both were extending an argument that Oskar Negt and Alexander Kluge had made back in 1972, that a whole proletarian public sphere existed, which Habermas’s book never accounted for.

Habermas answered these criticisms directly, in an essay called ‘Further Reflections on the Public Sphere’, printed as the closing chapter of Calhoun’s book. Habermas conceded that the exclusion of women was not incidental but built into how the bourgeois public sphere had worked from the start. Unlike the exclusion of underprivileged men, which was a problem of class, and in principle correctable, the exclusion of women, he now wrote, ‘has been constitutive for the political public sphere not merely in that the latter has been dominated by men as a matter of contingency but also in that its structure and relation to the private sphere has been determined in a gender-specific fashion.’ Habermas conceded that other public spheres had existed alongside the one he had taken as foundational. And he softened the warning, without abandoning it. He came to think he’d been too sceptical about one piece of that story, the early stirrings of consumer society. But the warning itself never went away. Sixty years on, he was still diagnosing a public sphere being distorted by commercial and structural forces, only now the culprit was platforms and algorithms rather than advertising and mass circulation.

He did not give up everything. He still wanted to keep the public sphere as something to measure democracies against, even if the history behind it was messier than he’d first made it look. The criticism and his answer to it sit in the same book, printed one after the other. Habermas’s views were open to being challenged, and open for us all to witness his thought in process.

Early in my dissertation work, I wanted to explore the role of experts in democracies through Habermas’s theory of deliberative politics, though I didn’t yet know how – I was, by any measure, stuck. My advisor, Cristina Lafont, one of his most trusted students, arranged a meeting anyway, at the hotel where he stayed during his visits to Northwestern’s campus in Evanston. He didn’t seem to mind that I arrived without a fully formed argument. Over almost two hours at what was then the Homestead Hotel, he had me lay out the problem as it stood, half-formed, and began working through it himself, out loud, testing it against his own theory as he went. He explained the three types of discourse that characterise deliberation – moral, ethical, and pragmatic – and was clear that when it comes to the moral, there are no experts: only individuals working out, together, what’s right in a given context.

Followed to its conclusion, that seemed to leave no room for expertise anywhere in deliberative politics. But he then turned to pragmatic discourse, where expertise does real work: finding the most empirically sound way to reach a goal already agreed on. Experts have no authority over what’s right, fair or worth valuing – only over facts. This was, in miniature, an argument he’d been making since his early work on science and politics: that treating value-laden political questions as though they were merely technical ones corrodes democracy. Decades later, in Justification and Application, he’d given the same worry he’d laid out in the trichotomy that morning sharper philosophical shape.

In later meetings in his office, more routine than that first one, I pushed the distinction further: what did it mean for climate change – a problem almost always treated, in his terms, as a matter of pragmatic discourse, all graphs and targets and carbon budgets, and almost never as a moral one. Who pays? What do we owe the people who pay? How should the resources that caused the damage be used? He didn’t have a ready answer. He asked question after question, testing the case against his own framework as though it genuinely hadn’t occurred to him before.
Justification answers only to the standards we happen to hold now: those standards can be shown wrong later

I’ll never know for sure if he was being generous or if I had shown him something he had not yet thought of in applying his own distinction. What stayed with me wasn’t the answer but the manner of it: a philosopher in his 70s, decades into a settled framework, still willing to test that framework against a case he hadn’t considered, in real time, out loud, in front of a student.

By 1999, Habermas gave up a position he’d held since 1973, the year he’d argued that truth is simply whatever people would agree on if they argued it out under fair-enough conditions. By the end of the century, he’d decided this was a mistake: it confused truth with justification. A claim can meet every test we have for it, survive every objection anyone raises, be about as justified as a claim can be, and still turn out false. That’s because justification answers only to the standards we happen to hold right now, and those standards can later be shown wrong. Truth doesn’t move when our standards do. Moral claims were different, he still thought: what’s right can only ever be what a fair conversation would settle on. There’s nothing else for rightness to answer to. But facts about the world answer to the world itself, not just to our best current agreement about it.

Several people had been pushing him toward this change. The US philosopher Richard Rorty pushed from the side from which Habermas was now backing away: for Rorty, there was no need for truth to answer to anything beyond what an audience could be talked into agreeing on, and he’d been making that case to Habermas for years. Lafont, my advisor, who’d arranged the hotel meeting, pushed from the other side, drawing on the US philosopher Hilary Putnam, who had spent much of his career arguing against exactly the kind of view that made truth depend entirely on human agreement. Lafont had argued since 1994 that Habermas’s own philosophical tradition, in its turn toward language, had drifted into a position where it couldn’t say the world holds firm no matter how we talk about it. When Habermas changed his mind, he moved toward Lafont’s position, not Rorty’s.

What Habermas never spelled out is what this does to moral and political claims once people stop being able to agree at all. Truth, on his revised view, still has somewhere to go even if everyone stops talking: the world doesn’t care whether anyone’s listening. His philosophy of Rightness never had that option. So, when the people who’d need to agree on something splinter into groups that no longer talk to each other, a factual claim can still be true or false regardless. A moral claim has nothing left holding it up, once nobody’s left in the room to agree on it.

Habermas gave up a position he’d held for almost 30 years because the people around him showed him it didn’t hold. He’d spent decades arguing that claims get redeemed when someone can compel you to answer, and then was compelled himself, and answered, in print, aged 70. Those critiques were not meant to be damning objections: they were precisely what his theory called for and was built on, ultimately.

Habermas returned to the subject in ‘Reflections and Hypotheses on a Further Structural Transformation of the Political Public Sphere’ (2022). His starting point is a particular relationship between beliefs and reality. Constitutional democracy runs on citizens holding certain assumptions about their own disagreements, namely that the disagreements are real, that they’re about something, that better reasons could in principle settle them. The system holds together only as long as those assumptions stay reasonably close to how politics actually works. His argument is that a public sphere, run through social media, threatens that relationship and widens that gap.

For Habermas, there are two forces at play in this widening. Platforms drop the editorial filtering that newspapers and broadcasters used to perform, and they turn every user into someone who publishes. For Habermas the deeper problem isn’t the resulting noise; it’s that heavy platform use produces something smaller than a public: semi-public spheres, self-enclosed, silos whose members can no longer perceive the wider public sphere as inclusive at all – claims to universality beyond their own horizon become, in his words, ‘suspect of hypocrisy’. That perception is itself the damage, on his account, as much as anything actually happening out in the general public sphere. He ends by insisting that ‘maintaining a media structure that ensures the inclusive character of the public sphere and the deliberative character of the formation of public opinion and political will is not a matter of political preference but a constitutional imperative.’

A factual claim still has to get the world right, whether or not anyone’s around to check it. Moral claims never did: they answer only to discourse. And discourse is exactly what he’s just described coming apart. He doesn’t draw the conclusion for moral and political claims himself, but it follows from putting his two books next to each other: the very thing a claim about what we owe each other had to answer to is the thing he says is disappearing, in an age dominated by exchanges on social media.
People retreat into whichever group agrees with them and lose their grip on a shared standard of true and false

Around that time, I reached out to my advisor for help asking Habermas for a foreword to a collection I was editing on Habermas and democracy. He was known for guarding his time closely – very few people had his email address, and he accepted only a handful of the hundreds of such requests he received each year. A couple of months later, an email came from an address I didn’t recognise: he had accepted, and written to say so himself. Amid the logistics, he added one condition: ‘You should send me at least a substantive part of the book before I can and would sit down and settle a few ideas.’ At 92, he wanted the material in hand before he’d commit to anything.

What came back was not a review of the interviews that make up the book one by one. He says so himself in the opening lines: it isn’t his task to comment on the conversations directly. Instead, he used the occasion to answer the standing objections to his view of deliberative democracy, and to close with the digital transformation that turned out to run through nearly every interview in the book – a theme he noticed himself, and named as central to the collection. One section was on experts, common sense, and the chain of translation that carries specialised knowledge into public reasoning: the same distinction he’d first sketched over a hotel breakfast, worked out now in far more detail, at the very end of his working life.

At one point, he writes that what’s been lost, in the democracies now regressing, is ‘a conflict of opinions that remains recognisable as a dispute about which position is backed by the better reasons.’ That’s as close as he ever came, in anything he wrote for me directly, to stating my own premise in his own words. He names the same loss again later in the foreword, describing people who retreat into whichever group already agrees with them and lose their grip not just on the public sphere’s inclusiveness but on the idea of a shared standard of true and false. What he doesn’t do here, any more than he did in 1999, is follow that loss when it concerns a moral claim once the discourse behind it comes apart. And that is what I tried to explore in my philosophical work since my dissertation.

He still believed the gap between expert and layperson could always, in principle, be closed by the right chain of translation. It was the one thing he never revised: he revised his theory of the public sphere, his theory of truth, but never the conviction that under the right conditions people can still reach each other. I am not persuaded that these conditions are as anywhere close to being met today – but that’s a disagreement I never got to have with him.

items.title: Swizz Beatz's furniture collection for CB2 was designed to help people 'tune into themselves'
items.description: For Kasseem Dean, the Grammy Award-winning rapper and producer best known as Swizz Beatz, furniture and family go hand in hand. He remembers, as a kid growing up in the Bronx, the squeak of the plastic that covered his grandmother’s couch and the ritual that a
items.author: Anna Fixsen
paragraphs: For Kasseem Dean, the Grammy Award-winning rapper and producer best known as Swizz Beatz, furniture and family go hand in hand. He remembers, as a kid growing up in the Bronx, the squeak of the plastic that covered his grandmother’s couch and the ritual that accompanied her record cabinet, which also conveniently concealed adults-only barware.

‘Furniture’s always been a language of family,’ Dean tells Wallpaper* from his home in Harlem, one of several the mogul owns alongside his wife, fellow Grammy-winner Alicia Keys. ‘For me growing up, it was like, “Come sit down, come have a talk.” But furniture was always to be respected as well.’

All of those memories, not to mention decades spent amassing one of the world’s most significant collections of Black art, have informed Dean’s latest venture, a furniture collection in partnership with the contemporary home decor brand CB2. The collection, which comprises furniture, lighting and decorative accessories, is appropriately named for the producer’s family: Casa Dean. ‘I didn't want to just do something just to do it,’ Dean says. ‘My thing was more like, if we're gonna do it, what's the concept? What hole are we filling? And how can this inspire people?’

Dean’s fascination with design grew as he found success as a teenager, first as a DJ and later, at the ripe age of 18, the producer of DMX’s hit ‘Ruff Ryders' Anthem’. Dean jokingly recalls decorating his first home: ‘At that time there was no taste involved. It was just like, is it expensive? OK, I need that couch. What's the name brand of it? Gucci? OK, let's get it.’

But as his renown grew, Dean began to develop his own taste. ‘My style has grown tremendously throughout the years from travelling and seeing different walks of life,’ he says. ‘I'm just a creature of culture.’

In the Casa Dean collection, those sensibilities manifest in the line’s variety of colours, textures and silhouettes. There’s a curvaceous chair in a woolly taupe shearling; a linear console table topped with red enamel; a green velvet modular sofa with a gently swooping silhouette; artwork created in collaboration with artist Megan Gabrielle Harris; and bubbly barware in smoked crystal.

‘I love where I landed with the diversity of the collection and the colours and the palettes,’ Dean says. ‘That took guidance. That took being open-minded and not just coming in with the fake celebrity energy. I was more of a student.’
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

That’s because designing furniture didn’t come into the picture until recently. Keys’ nail tech, the celebrity manicurist Dawn Sterling, introduced Dean to a mutual connection at CB2. ‘Next thing you know, I was in Chicago looking at fabrics,’ the rapper jokes.

Working alongside designer Evan Jerry of Studio Anansi, the collection began to evolve. ‘Swizz was especially thoughtful about the experience of each piece. How does a sofa sit? How does a material feel? How does the furniture encourage people to gather and connect?’ says Andrea Erman, CB2’s senior director of design and development for housewares. ‘He was equally interested in the emotional experience of a space as he was in the visual impact.’

‘People take furniture so [lightly], but just with this hands-on process with CB2 and their amazing team that they surrounded me with, I really got a front-row seat to the movie called “furniture”,’ Dean adds. The Dean family even got a front-row seat: he and Keys would review drawings and photos at the family dinner table.

Each piece in the Casa Dean collection is meant to foster what Dean calls ‘the creative home’. There are items that especially resonate with him, like the ‘Lam-Louie’ credenza, named for his father, who also worked as a DJ alongside hip-hop pioneer Cool Herc, that doubles as a DJ set-up. And a chair that’s designed exclusively for solo daydreaming. His favourite colour, British racing green, pops up throughout.

‘I just want people to just tune into themselves with this collaboration,’ Dean reflects. ‘The world is moving so fast and there's so much uncertainty that when you sit on this couch, or when you plug your set-up into this DJ set, or put some ice in this amazing bucket, you're doing it to reflect yourself.’

Anna Fixsen is a Brooklyn-based editor and journalist with 13 years of experience reporting on architecture, design, and the way we live. Before joining the Wallpaper* team as the US Editor, she was the Deputy Digital Editor of ELLE DECOR, where she oversaw all aspects of the magazine’s digital footprint.

items.title: CMF bring their playful minimalism into portable audio with Speaker S and Speaker M
items.description: With their milk carton-inspired form factor and on point selection of colour finishes, the new Speaker S and Speaker M from CMF offer up a tantalisingly affordable piece of audio equipment for the younger generation. This is the first time that CMF – Nothing’s
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: With their milk carton-inspired form factor and on point selection of colour finishes, the new Speaker S and Speaker M from CMF offer up a tantalisingly affordable piece of audio equipment for the younger generation. This is the first time that CMF – Nothing’s India-based sub-brand best known for their smartphones, watches and headphones – has ventured into the realm of portable audio.

The two sizes are self-explanatory (half a litre and a litre, for those still thinking about milk), and the speakers play nicely with each other via a special Stereo Mode and Party Mode, encouraging you to acquire a pair. In fact, it’s more of a set, given CMF have lived up to their name and dug deep into their palette bag to conjure up four delightful hues for each size, White, Dark Grey, Orange and Turquoise.

More playful in tone than Nothing, which tends to over-emphasise the tech within, CMF is about reduce functions to the most minimally appropriate forms. Both speakers therefore have simple and swappable front panels and knobs to further mix up the available chromatic options. On top of that, the company is encouraging 3D-printer owners to go while and add another layer of personalisation.

Both speakers include Bluetooth 6.0 connectivity, strong IP68 protection dust and water resistance rating and have an impressive maximum battery life of up to 18 hours in ideal conditions. Naturally, the larger speaker is the louder, with the smaller S targeted at desk workers who want a colourful audio companion that looks good even when there’s nothing on.
Both come with an Ultra Bass mode and can be further tuned through the Nothing X app. Charging is via USB-C, which also offers audio compatibility for ultra-low-latency playback (good for gaming).

The sizing guide suggests a Speaker L might be in the works for even more power, but for the time being you’ll have to make do with the custom-tuned 45 mm full-range driver and dual passive radiators in Speaker S (up to 10W output) and a dual-driver (25W woofer and 10W tweeter) in the Speaker M.

items.title: The Sony Walkman is back – and its latest models cost up to £4,299
items.description: Sony was once the GOAT of all things related to portable audio, a title it’s had to relinquish in the face of hundreds of new challengers. Whilst the Japanese giant made hay in the compact cassette and CD era, it subsequently struggled valiantly with its super
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: Sony was once the GOAT of all things related to portable audio, a title it’s had to relinquish in the face of hundreds of new challengers. Whilst the Japanese giant made hay in the compact cassette and CD era, it subsequently struggled valiantly with its superior but overlooked MiniDisc format and then watched everything go to pot as mp3s rose in popularity and Apple stepped forward to create the definitive player and ecosystem.

It’s not that Sony ever stepped back from the format, or that its mp3 players haven’t been any good, but for two and a half decades the zeitgeist has largely passed it by. With renewed interest in all things mp3, from affordable ultra compact players to a new wave of premium players from the likes of Astell&Kern, Sony wants to be back in the game.

These are updated versions of Sony’s two premium Walkman models, the NW-WM1ZM3 and NW-WM1AM3. They sit at the very pinnacle of Sony’s portable range, with prices to match, and compare only to a handful of other dedicated mp3 players. In short, we’re in true audiophile territory here, and whilst those of not blessed with golden ears will thrill to upgrades like the larger 5.5” touchscreen and 31-hour battery life, the real improvements are under the skin.

Build quality is clearly second to none, and Sony hasn’t scrimped on components either. To minimise noise and maximise sound quality, the company has used materials like oxygen-free copper and gold-plate. This is particularly evident in the NW-WM1ZM3, which uses a precision-machined, gold-plated oxygen-free copper (OFC) chassis (and a gold surface finish to match).

It’s joined by the NW-WM1AM3, which has to make do with aluminium-alloy for the main chassis (with gold-plated OFC on the rear). Improvements to power supply and circuitry is said to bring other big audio quality wins, with Sony’s onboard DSD Remastering Engine capable of upgrading digital files to give them a more analogue quality.

All this is slightly undermined by Sony decision to only cite playback times using low-quality 128kpps mp3 files, anathema to most fans of high-fidelity (although good for over 60,000 songs, given the player’s onboard 207GB of storage). Even if you only use files in the maximum lossless FLAC format, the new Walkmen are still good for around 10,000 songs. Streaming audio abilities also come as standard.

Alas, we’re in the realm of perception now, and while both players have characteristically high-quality finishes, a straightforward interface that combines a touchscreen with physical transport and volume buttons, the positive improvements netted by the circuitry, hand-soldering and absence of oxygen will only make a difference to a very small coterie of hardcore audiophiles.

items.title: What do boxing and architecture have in common? For Tadao Ando, it’s a lot
items.description: Tadao Ando was once a professional boxer. Before becoming one of his generation’s most esteemed architects, he had a brief stint with the punching gloves, aged 17, while living in Osaka, Japan.
items.author: Tianna Williams
paragraphs: Tadao Ando was once a professional boxer. Before becoming one of his generation’s most esteemed architects, he had a brief stint with the punching gloves, aged 17, while living in Osaka, Japan.

‘An architect holding a pencil and drawing, and a boxer wearing gloves and stepping into the ring, are of course engaged in entirely different professions and ways of life,' says Ando. ‘But to me, they are fundamentally the same in one respect: both are battles in which you must overcome your own fears and find the courage to move forward. A boxer endures gruelling training and relentless weight cutting, pouring everything into a single fight. In the end, all you can rely on is yourself. Boxing is a profoundly stoic and solitary sport. Yet it is precisely by pushing your body and mind to their limits that you discover strengths you never knew you had.’

Ando goes on to explain that architecture is very much the same; when a project comes with severe constraints on its programme or budget, it leaves little freedom in the design. But, he adds, ‘those very limitations force you to think deeply about what is truly necessary and what you should create. And somewhere in that process, a glimmer of light begins to emerge’.

It is safe to say that the 85-year-old has certainly lived. Now, he has his first memoir to be translated into English, Towards Light, which explores the stories behind his greatest buildings and other anecdotes along the way.
Towards Light by Tadao Ando

The term ‘starchitect’ seems rather reductive when referring to Ando. While his buildings have become cultural landmarks within Osaka and worldwide, they shouldn’t be reduced to his celebrity. Ando’s work is bold. He blends modernist design with Japanese tradition, and effortlessly plays with light, shadow, and nature.

His humble beginnings emphasise his resilience. Born in a working-class family living amongst the ruins of postwar Osaka, he could not afford a university education. He taught himself architecture at night from books, and founded a practice in a cheap rented room in 1969. Success didn’t happen overnight. His first built work was the single-family residence Tomishima House in 1973. Three years later, he had his first major critical breakthrough: Row House in Sumiyoshi (also known as Azuma House), completed in 1976 in Osaka, Japan.

Ando has gone on to be widely acclaimed, receiving the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 1995, Gold Medal of the American Institute of Architects in 2002, and Grande Ufficiale dell’Ordine della Stella d’Italia in 2015. He received the Japanese Order of Culture in 2010. But the book isn't all architecture, he explains.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

‘Although the book is meant to be an account of an architect's life, as I continued writing, I found myself wandering further and further away from architecture,’ Ando tells Wallpaper*. ‘Readers who pick it up expecting a discussion of architectural theory may be surprised by how much of the book ventures outside of architecture.’

Ando wanted to write as honestly as possible. However, the architect found his thoughts would wander from one subject to another. ‘In the end, I gave up trying to organise my life into a systematic narrative, whether by looking back chronologically or objectively explaining the circumstances behind particular events. Instead, I decided to write freely, following wherever my thoughts took me. That made the process of selection all the more difficult. From the vast accumulation of memories and experiences within me, deciding what to include and which moments to capture in words took some effort.’

Ando says he wants readers to come away thinking, ‘So, that's another way to live a life!’ He concludes, ‘And if, when they close the book, they are left with even a small sense of hope – a feeling that perhaps they, too, might try something new or find the courage to take a step forward – I would be happy.’
Towards Light: A Philosophy of Life and Architecture by Tadao Ando, translated by Polly Barton, is £25 and available to buy from Scribe Publications

Tianna Williams is Wallpaper’s staff writer. When she isn’t writing extensively across varying content pillars, ranging from design and architecture to travel and art, she also helps put together the daily newsletter. She enjoys speaking to emerging artists, designers and architects, writing about gorgeously designed houses and restaurants, and day-dreaming about her next travel destination.

items.title: Twenty-One Conversations with Architects by Arquitectura-G
items.description: Twenty-One Conversations with Architects by Arquitectura-G has been added to your shopping bag
paragraphs: Twenty-One Conversations with Architects by Arquitectura-G has been added to your shopping bag

Twenty-One Conversations with Architects brings together more than a decade and a half’s worth of interviews conducted by Barcelona-based architecture firm Arquitectura-G, published in Apartamento magazine since its very first issue in 2008. Expansive, technical, submerged, the book threads together some of architecture’s most singular minds, crossing decades, archives, disciplines, and countries, and placing multiple generations of architects side by side in a single volume. What started as a takeover of the magazine’s architecture section has now become something else entirely: a portrait of the studio itself, their own obsessions surfacing across every conversation—questions of scale, ambiguity, hedonism, bathrooms, dances, the house as a laboratory. As they open these interviews to the anthology, the architects unfold a series of choices in houses and homes that are deeply personal to those who conceived them, united by their fundamental questioning of universal needs answered by universal forms. What ties these houses together is something beyond architecture—less about having built them, and more about having gone on living inside the questions they raised. Twenty-one conversations later, Arquitectura-G draws each architect into a new one—curated together, and compiled by Moisés Puente, they are now asked to speak to each other across time.

Arquitectura-G is a Barcelona-based architecture studio founded in 2006 by Jonathan Arnabat, Jordi Ayala-Bril, Igor Urdampilleta, and Aitor Fuentes. Their practice spans ephemeral installations, residential projects, retail, and urban planning, with work published widely in international media. In 2015 they received the prestigious 2015 Mies Van der Rohe Award for Emerging Architects. They also teach, returning to the school where they first met. Since 2008 they have edited the architecture section of Apartamento magazine, a collaboration that also traces the development of their critical thinking.
Published by Apartamento Publishing S.L.
