items.title: No One Is More Excited About the Glee-boot Than the Glee Cast
items.description: Glee is officially coming back, and it’s hard to tell who’s more excited: people who still regularly listen to Darren Criss’s version of “Cough Syrup” or the cast of Glee. Variety reported on Wednesday that the Ryan Murphy show is being revived at Disney+ and
items.author: Olivia Craighead
paragraphs: Glee is officially coming back, and it’s hard to tell who’s more excited: people who still regularly listen to Darren Criss’s version of “Cough Syrup” or the cast of Glee. Variety reported on Wednesday that the Ryan Murphy show is being revived at Disney+ and Hulu, which means it’s only a matter of time before we get to hear Lea Michele singing an Olivia Rodrigo song. (I hope it’s “drop dead.”) Sure, there are some questions to be asked about what exactly a Glee-boot looks like — will they have an adult glee club or are we bringing in new teens? — but the former stars of the show have no qualms. Shortly after the news was announced, several members of the cast shared how pumped they were to return to the band room at William McKinley High School.

“Reunited and it feels so good!,” Chord Overstreet, whose character, Sam Evans, took over the New Directions glee club in the series finale, wrote on X. Kevin McHale, who hosts a Glee-themed podcast with co-star Jenna Ushkowitz, quote-tweeted a 2020 post that stated Drake had surpassed the Glee cast for “most Billboard Hot 100 hits of all time.” “Challenge accepted,” he wrote.

Over on Instagram, Jane Lynch shared the news, while Heather Morris posted several throwback photos. “Brittany S Pierce was in fact lost in the sewers for all these years. But I’m here to inform you that she is alive and well … And back for more #Glee,” she wrote.
Ushkowitz also shared a slideshow from her Glee years, captioned “QUEEN T” (a reference to her character, Tina) with a winking emoji.

To be clear, only Michele is 100 percent confirmed to be returning for the reboot. Everyone who posted could just be sending a smoke signal to Murphy. However, the Glee creator previously told Entertainment Tonight that he had been in touch with “around ten of the original cast members,” so I wouldn’t be surprised if Overstreet, McHale, Ushkowitz, and Morris will be coming back in some way.

More interesting is who hasn’t posted. Amber Riley has yet to acknowledge the reboot, which would be a devastating loss to the Gleek community. Dianna Agron is busy filming Industry in London, and Harry Shum Jr. only posts about Dancing With the Stars, so their silence is understandable. Chris Colfer and Criss also haven’t said anything, but the pair did reunite at Criss’s show in London over the weekend to sing “Baby, It’s Cold Outside.” Listen to how loud this crowd is and then tell me that these two aren’t going to be coming back.

Matthew Morrison, who is currently playing Bobby Darrin on Broadway in Just in Time, has also remained mum, although there might be a reason for that. Sources told Deadline that Morrison is not yet in talks to be back on the show but that he’s “hopeful that he will be part of the project.”

Oof. I’ll be honest: I would love for them to make something work with Morrison. I need to see him singing a Sombr song in a high-school gymnasium, and I think if Murphy digs deep within himself, he’ll find that he needs to see that too.

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: October 22, 2026
items.description: The Pisces moon could create a gentler, more compassionate atmosphere today — one that makes everyone feel safe lowering their guard. People will be more willing than usual to see things from other perspectives, so interactions that might normally have grown c
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: The Pisces moon could create a gentler, more compassionate atmosphere today — one that makes everyone feel safe lowering their guard. People will be more willing than usual to see things from other perspectives, so interactions that might normally have grown contentious will hopefully be less stressful. But be aware that by midmorning, the open-mindedness you’re feeling could deepen into impressionability. Take care not to come off as too credulous. Remember that not all opinions are based in truth, and you don’t have to believe everything you’re told.

In most situations, you can act swiftly and decisively. You understand there’s not always time to carefully sift through all the facts and consider all the possibilities; you prefer to go with your gut and hope for the best. But today, you may be uncharacteristically wishy-washy. You’ll be able to see the merits and drawbacks in all the options available to you, and you’ll struggle to make a choice between them. Don’t get too caught up in deliberations. Even if you choose “wrong,” you’ll have time to fix things as you go.

It’s hard to fully commit to your dreams when some part of you believes, deep down, that you don’t actually deserve them. Maybe you’ve convinced yourself the life you want is somehow “too good” for you and thus you need to lower your sights to something more modest. But right now, dreaming big is exactly what you should be doing. There’s no guarantee you’ll get everything you want, but at the very least, you deserve to try. Imagine more for yourself, and don’t be afraid to pursue it.

Today, you may feel particularly invested in others’ perceptions of you. More than ever, you want to make a good impression and come across as competent and likable. But the harder you try to make other people see you the way you want them to, the less likely it is to work. Right now, simply being your authentic self is the best thing you can do. Trust that you’re good enough as you are — and that others will recognize that fact.

Your imagination is likely to run wild today. You have ambitious goals for the future and the motivation to make them happen. But part of you may imagine that you don’t have the skills or resources you need yet and that you can’t get started on your agenda until you do. Consider this: Waiting around is the last thing you should do. You’ve got plenty of knowledge and support at your disposal right now. Don’t dwell on what you feel you’re lacking; instead, figure out how to use what you already have.

Today, you may be more sensitive than usual. And while that could make you more perceptive, it may also prompt you to see problems that don’t actually exist. People’s innocent comments could strike you as veiled insults, or you may read too deeply into situations that have nothing to do with you. Take a breath when this happens. You can’t force yourself to suddenly grow a thicker skin. But you can try to think before you respond so you don’t react in a way you’ll regret.

Usually, you take pains not to mindlessly follow along with what’s popular. You want to follow your own desires, not everyone else’s. But today, you may be deeply influenced by the people around you without even realizing it. You may take on their opinions and feelings as your own. There’s nothing wrong with being shaped by your relationships — everyone is to some degree — but be aware when it happens. You shouldn’t feel as if your own personality is getting lost in the shuffle.

You’re not prone to behaving recklessly. You would rather create a plan and prepare yourself before diving into something new; you want to know what point you’re trying to make before you open your mouth to speak. Today, though, your instincts may tell you it’s time to act — even if you don’t yet feel ready. Don’t worry if this scares you. If your gut is urging you to take action, listen to it.

You may get impatient with yourself today, especially if progress toward your goals feels slower than anticipated. Maybe you’ll even worry that you’ve taken so long you’ve missed your shot. But the truth is you still have plenty of time to achieve what you set out to do. Don’t berate yourself over everything you wish you’d done differently. Instead, focus on using the time you do have productively.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

You want to do right by the people in your life. You’re caring and generous, and you genuinely want to make others happy. But sometimes, you feel guilty for doing what you want to do. You worry that prioritizing your own dreams and desires means you’re being selfish — if you were a truly good person, you would put others first every time! Today, though, cut yourself some slack. You don’t exist solely to fulfill everyone else’s needs; you’re allowed to make some decisions just for you.

You usually don’t change your mind casually. Once you’ve formed an opinion, you’re unlikely to be swayed. You would rather double down (even if you risk seeming hardheaded) than come across as capricious and unreliable. But today, don’t force yourself to defend ideas you no longer believe in. Don’t stick with opinions you’ve outgrown. Being willing to grow and change won’t make you seem fickle — if anything, being honest that you’re still learning will make you seem more trustworthy.

You tend to believe, maybe unconsciously, that your worldview is the only correct one and that everyone who disagrees with you is on some level mistaken. You try to be patient and tolerant of others’ ideas, but deep down, you rarely take them seriously. Today, try not to be overconfident. If only as a thought experiment, assume everyone you encounter has something meaningful to teach you. You may be surprised.

Sometimes, you consider your compassion a hindrance, rather than a strength. Your care for others often seems to create unhelpful emotional baggage for you. You see people acting with total focus, even ruthlessness, to get what they want, and you wish you could do the same instead of always worrying about how your behavior may affect those around you. But today, remind yourself that your empathy is an asset, not a burden. Your awareness of other people’s thoughts and feelings will actually help you get what you want — while helping those around you feel seen and loved.

items.title: The Amazon Coat: An Oral History
items.description: Even with a decade of trendspotting, deal hunting, and expert interviewing behind us, few stories compare to that of the Orolay coat. As the tale goes, in March 2018, former New York fashion director Amy Larocca appeared behind features editor (then–associate
items.author: Bella Druckman
paragraphs: Even with a decade of trendspotting, deal hunting, and expert interviewing behind us, few stories compare to that of the Orolay coat. As the tale goes, in March 2018, former New York fashion director Amy Larocca appeared behind features editor (then–associate editor) Katy Schneider’s desk with a hot tip: “There’s this coat I need you to look into. It’s $89, and every woman I know on the Upper East Side has it.” In the months and years following Schneider’s reporting, the coat became so ubiquitous in the city that it earned its own nickname: “the Amazon Coat.” Here is an oral history of the Orolay coat — from its uptown origins to its eventual banishment to Buffalo Exchanges — according to the whisper network of women who set off the trend, the New York staffers who broke the story, and several folks who covered the coat’s unlikely takeover of the city.
“Women were crossing the street to ask me where I got the coat.”
No one knows exactly who bought the Amazon Coat first, but a daisy chain of women shared the link with friends and strangers until it caught our attention as a thing.

Jessica Reich, teacher: “It was actually in 2016 that I purchased the coat, so it’s been about ten years. It’s crazy. I was planning a trip for a joint 30th birthday with my boyfriend at the time to Iceland. I was just doing what I do whenever I’m going to travel to a new place, which is look around and see what gear I need. I was going in March, so I was really interested to see what type of winter gear I would need, and I found this blog — I don’t know if she’s around anymore, but it was called The Blonde Abroad. This was obviously back when you didn’t necessarily go on someone’s Instagram to find clothes and stuff. You were literally going to their blogs. So I was probably just searching ‘Iceland fashion,’ something along those lines, and she popped up. She had this coat and linked it, and I was like, This is amazing. So I just bought it through her link.”

Kiki Rich, author of The Blonde Abroad: “It came from this picture of me in Whistler. We had helicoptered into this snowy mountain peak, and that picture — this was pre–the term, even, viral, I think — it just got so much attention. Then even my own audience was like, ‘Where’s that from? Where’s that from?’”

Fernanda Niven, founder of homeware brand the Bouwerie: “I found out about it because a friend of mine had one and I saw her in it and nobody else was wearing it. I think she just discovered it on Amazon. I loved it, and I said, ‘Can I find out where you got that coat?’ She told me and I bought one immediately and I started wearing it around the Upper East Side. It was unbelievable. Women were crossing the street to ask me where I got the coat.”

Reich: “I kept wearing it. It just started to become a thing. I was a teacher at the preschool at the 92nd Street Y at the time. So the moms at school and the other teachers were like, ‘Oh, tell me about the coat.’ And then at the time, it was relatively, from my standpoint, inexpensive. It’s funny the article has updated itself to reflect the current price. But I think back when I got it, it was well under $100. It might have been $70, $80 at the time.”
Niven: “I’ve never had anything like that happen to me before, where it was just like girl after girl, woman after woman asking me, ‘Wait, I’m so sorry to ask — where is that coat from?’”
“It was like our Watergate.”

One March morning, then–New York fashion director Amy Larocca was discussing the latest trends with her friend and former market editor Gretchen Fenton. The coat she’d be seeing around, it turned out, was from a then-unknown brand you could find on Amazon called Orolay. When she got back to the office that day, she tipped off Schneider (now features editor, then associate editor) and Alexis Swerdloff (now deputy editor, then Strategist editor), who got right to work.

Amy Larocca: “Gretchen was like, ‘Do you know about this coat?’ I was like, ‘Yes, I have seen this coat.’ And she was like, ‘Do you know the thing about it?’ And I was like, ‘What about it?’ She was like, ‘It’s from Amazon.’”
Katy Schneider: “We immediately knew it was such a great story. We were super freaked out about getting beat.”
Larocca: “I was always telling Alexis and Katy things. I’m sure I probably just got back to the office and I was like, ‘All right, guys. Hot tip.’ I did not think it was gonna be this hot a tip.”
Alexis Swerdloff: “It was like our Watergate.”
Schneider: “It was a perfect daisy chain. Every single person told me someone else to call and gave me their number. It’s not so easy to get this kind of reporting or to get quotes like this.”
Niven: “I felt like if someone was calling to talk to me about it, it meant that clearly she had been noticing it around.”

Schneider: “I was going the next day to Florida for a family trip. I was just like, ‘I am so determined to figure out what’s going on with this Amazon coat that I’m not letting it go.’ I remember I was with my family and I was at the airport sitting at a table on the phone with one or two of those women from the lede, just being like, ‘Tell me where you got the coat.’”
Larocca: “I think it’s the ultimate Strategist thing because it was cheap. I think that was so in the spirit of the Strategist — like, ‘Amazing finds. We do the hunting for you.’”

Schneider: “It was just one of these things where Amy had stumbled upon such a phenomenon. That was evident immediately when I started reporting. Every single person who I called immediately knew what I was talking about, immediately had another person to connect me to. And it came together super quickly.”
“It was so much bigger than anyone could have imagined.”

After our story went live, dozens of publications covered the coat’s unlikely rise to popularity — and more people bought the coat than we could count. One woman even made an Instagram account under the handle @theamazoncoat that accrued more than 10,000 followers as it documented the women and men wearing the coat across the country.

Schneider: “It was so much bigger than anyone could have imagined. I remember it being very strange to see the effect of that in real life over the next couple of not just months but years. For years after that story, seeing people wherever I went in that coat on the street was crazy.”
Swerdloff: “You’d walk down the street and you’d be like, We did this. For better or for worse.”
Larocca: “I always thought, All my years at New York Magazine and my biggest contribution is the frickin’ Amazon Coat.”

Swerdloff: “It was a little secret you’d have. I remember being in a room with all these people being like, Well, you’re wearing this sort of because of me. I mean, not me, multiple people, but it was a very strange feeling to have.”

Lucy Handley, freelance journalist who covered the coat for CNBC: “We had this stand-up meeting with a couple of editors and maybe 12 journalists who wrote for the website, and I remember saying, ‘Oh, there’s this Amazon coat.’ Immediately, my editor went, ‘What’s the Amazon Coat?’ There was this level of intrigue because I guess at the time you might not have associated Amazon with fashion.”
Making its Good Morning America debut.

Reyhan Harmanci, executive director at Wired who wrote about the coat for the Times: “I totally bought it. I couldn’t believe the price. It was so cheap, and it was really, really warm. But it was then a bit uncanny to be wearing the same thing as literally every other woman I could see.”

Handley: “It’s a baggy, kind of casual, a bit oversize style that I think is still fashionable now. I can see the picture I used. The model in the picture was wearing skinny jeans, and that was the big trend. Athleisure was just starting, so yoga leggings with a big top.”

Swerdloff: “This idea of a viral item wasn’t really a thing at the time. The only other thing I could think of at the time that was sort of like that was the Instant Pot. There just weren’t items that went viral on the internet in that way. It was really one of the first that I can remember like that and that you would just see out in the world and everywhere. That happens now all the time.”
Harmanci: “This was before lanternflies, but it had the invasion kind of vibe.”

Larocca: “My kids were pretty little, and they would be like, ‘Mom, the coat, the coat!’ It became a family joke. I remember sitting in the subway and being like, Oh my God, there are multiples in this car. What is happening? That is so crazy. This just sort of blasted in out of nowhere.”

Lauren Posner, creator of the @theamazoncoat Instagram account: “A lot of my friends and people I knew had the coat, so I just thought, Oh, why don’t I just start taking pictures of people wearing the coat? And if they want to answer a question — why they bought the coat, what drew them to the coat, why does it inspire them or something quirky — and just put it on Instagram, it would be fun. But that was also a time when a lot of Instagram accounts like that were coming about.”
Harmanci: “I somehow managed to write about this at least a year after you guys had done multiple stories, so it’s really amazing anyone let me write about it.”

Posner: “There were people who did outrageously creative things. Someone made a cake that looked like the Amazon Coat, and they used the hashtag #theamazoncoat. I would also look for posts that had the hashtag and repost them.”

Harmanci: “Everyone I talked to seemed to have a different way into it. Like, some people had seen the New York Magazine story, but a lot of people just saw it on the backs of their friends or saw a picture of it or it was a hand-me-down coat from somebody. It just seemed like no one really knew where the coat came from.”
“I remember seeing the coat at Buffalo Exchange, and I was like, Okay.”

Over the years, Orolay released ankle-length and cropped versions, a fleece-lined variation, and even a line for kids, but the Amazon Coat was eventually demoted to the back of closets or pawned off to Buffalo Exchange during the pandemic. Still, the original coat has amassed more than 29,000 reviews on Amazon (that’s up from 6,000 in 2019) with an impressive four-and-a-half-star average rating. Every Prime Day when it goes on sale, readers still buy it. Will it ever have a nostalgia-fueled resurgence?

Harmanci: “It was two winters. First winter was early adopters. Second winter was the rest of us. And then it was kind of gone. I do think that all of the new variants helped kill it. One of the fun things about the coat originally was that it was so basic. You had two or three colors, maybe — no other options. It was at a moment where you had these formfitting puffy coats. It was a real choice to be wearing this puffy square, essentially, with these pockets hanging out. It was not an elegant coat, but it was extremely comfortable and extremely warm. I think that helped its lanternflylike recognizability because it was so differently and awkwardly shaped.”
Emily Gould, New York features writer: “When I would first see an Amazon Coat in the wild, I would be like, Oh, she’s got the Amazon Coat. And then it eventually just became ‘the Coat.’”

Megan Reynolds, freelance writer and editor who wrote about the coat for Jezebel: “It’s like the Spider-Man meme — you’re all pointing at each other in the same fucking outfit. To me, that’s kind of what killed the coat.”

Niven: “I wore it so much, and I kind of got sick of it. Then seeing it everywhere, you’re wearing it and you’re seeing it, so it’s overload. But I still love the navy one. I still have it, and every once in a while, I break it out.”
Reich: “It definitely will always have a place in my closet.”
Larocca: “I never wanted to see it again.”
Posner: “Believe it or not, I still wear it occasionally, especially on really cold days. I still see plenty of people wearing it as well.”
Swerdloff: “I remember seeing the coat at Buffalo Exchange, and I was like, Okay.”
Reich: “I wonder if some people will think, Oh, I just came upon this, not knowing that it’s been around for so long. Or other people might be like, Wow, this is a throwback.”
Larocca: “Is the Amazon Coat going to have one of those hilarious revivals of ‘It’s so pre-COVID’ or whatever they decide to call that era?’”
Swerdloff: “Is it gonna come back in style? Is it going to be like suddenly you’re going to see Liana Satenstein wearing the Amazon Coat? I don’t know.”

items.title: Watching 'Clayface' Is Like Eating Play-Doh
items.description: The rogue’s gallery of Batman villains has a deep bench, and given that a certain Clown Prince of Crime received not one but two solo outings and Gotham’s waterfowl-related kingpin got his own prestige-TV drama, it makes sense to start pulling out other MVP ba
items.author: David Fear
paragraphs: The rogue’s gallery of Batman villains has a deep bench, and given that a certain Clown Prince of Crime received not one but two solo outings and Gotham’s waterfowl-related kingpin got his own prestige-TV drama, it makes sense to start pulling out other MVP bad guys for side projects. Personally, we might have gone with a few other first-stringers before landing on Clayface, a character whose name goes back to 1940s Batman comics. The original was simply an actor moonlighting as a criminal; the better-known version was introduced in the Fifties, a shape-shifter who could take on anyone’s appearance but usually presented as a giant, hulking lump of clay. In terms of Hall of Fame status, he’s somewhere between Killer Croc and Solomon Grundy. (IYKYK.)

But Mike Flanagan — longtime Stephen King fanatic, current Carrie reinterpreter, future caretaker of the Exorcist franchise — had the idea of using this DC Comics deep cut to anchor a potential body-horror movie. Brand new co-CEO of DC Studios James Gunn happened to dig Flanagan’s pitch, and greenlit a film that would serve as a showcase and a likely introduction of the malleable maniac to the rebooted cinematic universe’s live-action world. (Clayface is already part of the animation side of the house.) Long story short, Flanagan had to drop out. Writer Hossein Amini (Drive) and director James Watkins (Eden Lake) were brought in. The project went ahead as planned, having the bad fortune to hit screens at a moment when the revamped DC franchise finds itself in a bit of a quality-control pickle.

Clayface is not going to reverse that trajectory. In fact, this attempt to have it both ways — a horror movie set in the DC universe, and a DC universe movie that hopes to attract the horror-fan crowd — may have knocked things down a peg or three. Only time will tell whether this is truly a stand-alone experiment in genre mixing and matching or something designed to thread the big lug into the bigger cinematic picture. Yet we can confirm that watching this intriguing-on-paper chronicle of a Batman supervillain once again recast as a tragic antihero, one who’s dealing with the psychological fallout of his newly batshit physical state, is the equivalent of eating a handful of Play-Doh, and twice as flavorless.

Movie star Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries) is on top of the world. He’s young, handsome, and has just been nominated for an Oscar. Jetting over to Gotham City for a quick talk show appearance to promote an upcoming project, Hagen and his fellow actor/childhood best friend Corey (Joshua James) decide to hit the clubs. A woman in a slinky dress starts dancing with him. She’s Mia (Joana Ribeiro), the girlfriend of Gotham’s current reigning gangster Markos Szabo (David Dencik). Turns out that Matt messed around with the wrong moll. A razor blade gets unsheathed. Soon, pretty boy ain’t so pretty no more.

Hagen’s career takes a nosedive. Everyone is scared to testify against Szabo, so his legal case is dismissed. Broke, friendless, and hideously scarred, Hagen gets a dingy apartment in the bad neighborhood he grew up in, and essentially goes into hiding. He happens to come across an article on Dr. Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie, doing the best she can), a scientist working with nanotechnology. She’s never experimented on humans before, but Corr takes pity on this sad sack. A series of treatments over several months restores Hagen to his formerly gorgeous glory. It’s comeback time, baby!

There are a few side effects, naturally. Hagen seems to have incredible healing powers. When he gets angry, he has the ability to rearrange his appearance and resemble anyone imaginable. His face is once again highly photogenic, but the skin on his matinee-idol mug… let’s just say it’s unstable at times, and occasionally droops, sags, or altogether melts off his jawline like hot wax. Oh, and it’s slowly curdling Hagen’s mind as well, notably when he finds out that Corey sold him out and that his old business manager (Eddie Marsan) is now working for Markos. He has these newfound gifts. Why not use them for some good, old-fashioned payback?

All those Cronenbergian elements — The Fly vibes are strong with this one, especially when things start going south — butt up against the comic-book bits of business in ways that suggest an arranged marriage over a passionate genre hook-up. Watkins and co. set up a few creepy scenes and possibly fertile scenarios, then have a tendency cut away too soon or simply seem to lose interest; why you would not take full advantage of a turbulent flight, a pair of scissors and someone’s eyelids being goopily melded shut in terms of an extended showstopper, as opposed to a blink-and-miss set piece, is a mystery. Every so often, Corr’s police-detective fiancé (Max Minghella) reminds us that he works for Gotham City PD, or someone namedrops Coast City, a.k.a. the O.G. Green Lantern’s hometown. You could easily take those references out, and just find yourself occasionally being grossed out in between Hagen’s pity parties, rage spirals and romantic mooning for his now-quite-concerned scientific savior.

That Clayface must rise and fall on its own merits, and is not necessarily as something attached to some unwieldy serialized narrative arc, becomes both a feature and a bug. At this point, no one needs more superhero films that exist merely to set up some coming-soon chapter. Nor do we necessarily need to suffer through a slightly chintzy horror flick about a guy going full Brundlefly, while changing identities willy-nilly in the name of righteous vengeance. Which is really what you’re left with: a rather generic, cut-rate take on a now familiar formula that still feels like a franchise placeholder. Clayface, the poor, doomed guy destined to give the Caped Crusader a lot of agita down the line (or not!), can transform himself into anything he wants. Clayface the movie can’t even seem to morph into the only thing it needs to be: a mildly satisfying piece of entertainment. Suddenly, Supergirl doesn’t look so bad now, does it?

items.title: ‘Glee’ Reboot Officially Set at Disney+ and Hulu
items.description: To quote Finn Hudson, “The show must go all over the place, or something.” He was right: “Glee” is back.
items.author: Selome Hailu
paragraphs: To quote Finn Hudson, “The show must go all over the place, or something.” He was right: “Glee” is back.

Disney+ and Hulu have greenlit a reboot of Ryan Murphy‘s famous (and infamous) musical dramedy series. “Glee” premiered on Fox in 2009 concluded in 2015 after six seasons of following a group of show choir members from Lima, Ohio as they dealt with the highs and lows of high school and beyond. It was a massive cultural phenomenon that is especially remembered for the blunt, sometimes controversial ways it tackled topics such as sexuality, race, disability, mental health and more — as well as its covers of songs like “Don’t Stop Believin’,” “Teenage Dream,” “River Deep, Mountain High” and “Smooth Criminal,” among others. The series remains popular today, as does its music, which averages 4.1 million monthly listeners on Spotify.

The original cast included Lea Michelle, Cory Monteith, Matthew Morrison, Jane Lynch, Dianna Agron, Chris Colfer, Darren Criss, Amber Riley, Naya Rivera, Heather Morris, Kevin McHale, Jenna Ushkowitz, Harry Shum Jr., Chord Overstreet, Mark Salling and more.

Details about the new “Glee” are scant; Disney shared nothing aside from the fact that the series is being produced by 20th Television and will air on Hulu and Disney+. Casting information is not yet known, though it can safely be assumed that several of the original stars will return. “I’ve been in touch with around 10 of the original cast members,” Murphy recently said in an interview with Entertainment Tonight, in which he confirmed that he’d just written a reboot script with collaborators Brad Falchuk and Ian Brennan. “It’s very sweet, and they all had a lot of questions, but they all were very enthusiastic about the idea.”

Murphy’s comments came weeks after Michele expressed to E! News that she’d be happy to join a “Glee” reboot: “I love ‘Glee.’ I will always love ‘Glee.’ I love Ryan Murphy. It just holds such a special place in my heart for me… I will follow Ryan wherever he goes.”

Speaking to Bustle recently, Colfer pointed out that rebooting “Glee” would be complicated following Rivera’s death, but that he would consider it: “It was a really tough show to do, and it would be really hard to do it now that Naya [Rivera] is gone. But I do know that Glee fans would probably come after me with pitchforks and jazz hands if I said no. So I don’t know, but hopefully I’ll have more information and I can actually think about it.”

Rivera died in 2020 at age 33, tragically drowning in a lake while saving her young son who had fallen into the water. She was the third death among the “Glee” cast: Monteith died from an overdose in 2013, while the show was still on the air, and Salling died by suicide in 2018 after pleading guilty to possession of child pornography.

items.title: Olivia Cooke on Returning to ‘Slow Horses,’ On-Set Injuries and That Shocking Finale Cliffhanger: ‘I Want a Showdown!’
items.description: SPOILER ALERT: The following article contains plot details from “Judgement Day,” the Season 6 finale of “Slow Horses,” now streaming on Apple TV.
items.author: Alison Herman
paragraphs: SPOILER ALERT: The following article contains plot details from “Judgement Day,” the Season 6 finale of “Slow Horses,” now streaming on Apple TV.

Those two fateful words announced Olivia Cooke’s return to “Slow Horses” after a four-season absence from the Apple TV spy drama. Cooke’s MI5 agent Sidonie Baker made a brief but memorable appearance in Season 1, forging a flirty chemistry with inept spy River Cartwright (Jack Lowden) before dying from a gunshot wound to the head — or so River thinks.

Sid’s resurrection wasn’t a total surprise to “Slow Horses” fans: the character comes back in author Mick Herron’s namesake novels, and Apple made little secret of her storyline in the advance promotion for Season 6, which concluded this week. But enough has changed since Cooke’s first stint on the show to make her re-joining the ensemble an event in itself. First, “Slow Horses” itself grew into a hit, with a raft of Emmy nominations (plus a few wins) and an avid audience to show for it; meanwhile, Cooke’s own career has taken off thanks to a leading role in the fantasy epic “House of the Dragon.”

That star power is on full display throughout Season 6, which sees Sid and River on the run from Russian sleeper agents over one incredibly stressful night. Icy MI5 head Diana Taverner (Kristin Scott Thomas) — who once planted her favored mentee Sid in Slough House, a kind of purgatory for screwup agents, as her eyes and ears — used Sid’s identity as a cover for an off-the-books assassination on Russian soil, and now the Kremlin is out for revenge. All of the Slow Horses (a not-so-affectionate nickname for Slough House employees), past and present, are targeted, and Sid goes to River for help.

The pair’s winding route from River’s late grandfather’s country house to Diana’s beach retreat, which Slough House head Jackson Lamb (Gary Oldman) cheekily appropriates as a safe house, is a winding one. Sid and River barrel through a barn, an arcade, and finally an airstrip where Sid is nearly shipped off to Russia as an unwilling sacrifice on their way to a long-awaited first kiss. This being “Slow Horses,” though, their triumph is short-lived: River helps Sid escape and nearly reunites with her at his grandfather’s house, but collapses from an apparent poisoning in the kitchen while she showers upstairs in the season’s final moments.

“River has kept her going, in a sense,” Cooke says now of the star-crossed lovers. Speaking with Variety from the U.K., the actor shared what it’s been like to dive back into the deep end with over a month of night shoots, from an unlikely injury to her collaboration with Lowden.
Your character comes back in the books, but I’m sure when you were first filming, it wasn’t certain we would get to this point. Did you know there was a chance you would return?

We shot [Season 1] towards the end of 2020. It was one of the first projects back after lockdown. I don’t know if the book had come out yet where I make my return, but there were whispers of it. I don’t know. It was such an uncertain time, and it was the first series as well. It just felt, like, an eon away. Who would have thought it would have gone on for so long?

But they kept me abreast of all the things that were going on story-wise over the years. I’ve been admiring from afar, and biding my time. I’d get messages from Jack being like, “You’re coming back!” and I’m like, “Fantastic, when?” And no one could really give me a clear answer. I remember seeing Saskia [Reeves], who plays Standish, at the theater, and she was like, “You coming back? And I was like, “I would love to. I just don’t know. I have no clear answers.” We were all just in a cloud of mystery for a bit.
During that time, what was it like for you to watch this show that you were once a part of, but weren’t for a while?

Really fun, but tinged with jealousy. Because I experienced it, you know? Even though we were all masked up and socially distanced from each other and the crew when we weren’t in the scenes, it was such a fun, charmed environment that I was just desperate to get back to. And it’s so palpable — watching Season 2, 3, 4, 5 — just how much fun everyone’s having on set. It really just glows through the screen. So it’s always bittersweet. I love watching them, and I love seeing how good all my friends are, but I’m also incredibly jealous as well that they’re all having fun without me.
I imagine that, as an actor, having to return to a character that you left behind is a challenge. Is there any work or preparation that you did to reassume this role?

I had to remind myself how I sounded, like what accent I was doing. I had to check back in with that. But also, it was quite nice, because Sid is coming back in a very jaded way. Both her and River have grown up mentally in the interim. They’ve been away from each other, and the events that led up to Sid’s disappearance were really traumatic. So I had a bit of rope to not honor the more jovial, happy-go-lucky version of Sid that we saw in the first season.
We don’t get a lot of detail about what the last three years were like for Sid, because there’s a lot happening in the present. Do you have your own sense of that backstory?

I was asking Adam [Randall], the director, a lot about that. We thought that she’d been in a rehabilitation facility that is kept under wraps by MI5. It’s for ex-spies, ex-Joes, and she’s had to learn how to walk and talk again, basically. It’s been an incredibly lonely process that has, I think, cauterized a part of her, in some non-descript location. We were thinking maybe Cumbria, if you know of it. Sort of like the the Vermont of England — very green, but you can get lost in the landscape. I think it’s just been a very long road of recovery, and also of introspection for her.
You mentioned the FOMO earlier, so I’m also interested in what it was like for you to actually step back into the set. I’m sure the non-COVID version of the show feels different.

Well, it was pretty much the same crew, and also it’s a lot of the same crew that does “House the Dragon” as well. Like on off seasons with “Slow Horses,” there’ll be people that do dailies and things on “House the Dragon” and vice versa. So I know everyone quite well. It was really lovely. It’s like the best high-school reunion possible. As if you went to a high school and everyone’s your friend, which I don’t think is a reality for anyone. It was just really joyous, even though we shot it right before the December break, in the middle of winter, all night shoots for five weeks, because they truncated all my stuff.
I was going to ask about that too — the nocturnal nature of it.

I sort of loved it. Adam has this energy about him where it sometimes feels a bit run-and-gun, which I love. And if a particular stunt doesn’t work out, or when we get to the set, the material doesn’t quite match with how the workings of the set are, he’s like, “All right, let’s figure this out. Let’s improvise.” It’s so lovely for me as an actor, too, because I feel like there’s a real energy to that. It did just feel like we were making an independent film for five weeks, because the majority of my stuff was just with Jack and Adam.
Your storyline this season is almost entirely two-handers with Jack. What’s he like as a collaborator?

He’s my favorite type of man, which is a very silly man. It’s wonderful acting with him, because he just chucks you a curveball, and then you try and grab it. It makes me feel like I’m stretching my mind in ways that I don’t usually get to do with doing this job. And he’s so fun! He wears it very lightly. He’s such a good actor. He’s very funny, and doesn’t take it too seriously either. Which I love, because sometimes, with other male actors, they take it very serious.
In addition to the night shoots of it all, there’s a lot of action on the show. Were there any particularly tricky sequences?

There were, but the one thing that actually did me in was just running. There’s a lot of scenes where I’m just running alongside Jack, who is twice as tall as me, and my 5-foot-5 arse is just desperately trying to keep up. It was like 2 in the morning, and we were being chased by a Land Rover. You’re stretching, you’re trying to keep warm, but I think I’d been a bit static for too long, and we set off and I just felt both thighs go snap. I pulled both of my quad muscles really, really badly. For two weeks, I was hobbling around. Just from a run! But then I thought to myself, “When was the last time I got chased?” Since I was like 12!
You’ve gotta have your people page Tom Cruise’s people and be like, “How do I run onscreen?”
Literally! Climbing fences, shooting, being on the back of a moving truck while there’s all these fire and gas canisters going off — but just running really, really did me in.
I was curious about the barn interlude. I can’t imagine being in a barn full of smelly cattle for hours on end.

The thing is, you can’t really do anything about it. You just have full acceptance 20 minutes in, and get used to it. But we were moving around in and amongst a lot of cows, which was quite scary, actually. They’re really big, and they can kick! I was just remembering old horror stories about people being killed by a stampede of cows, just walking across a field, and I was like, “I’m so close to them!” But it was fine, no one died.
The other action moment that really stood out for me is when you’re on the truck and kicking the oil drum, and it explodes. That looks tricky.

That was a crazy, crazy sequence, just trying to dispose of the Russian agents who had come to collect me, and running and jumping on the truck and then Jack just doing donuts around a plane. And you know, Jack does all his own driving stunts! It was very impressive. That was so fun, so cathartic. I love kicking things, and then having this big old stunt where it blows up — it felt like our own Jason Bourne moment.

In addition to the action, Sid has a whole emotional trajectory. She seems reluctant for most of the season to accept just how ruthless Diana Taverner has been with her. Why do you think Sid clings to that so much?

Because Sid thinks, ultimately, that Diana saved her by getting her out of the hospital, by putting her into some specialized rehab. I think she does genuinely think that she’s only here, she’s only alive because of Diana Taverner. So there’s, I think, some real Stockholm syndrome going on with her. Also, she’s only ever experienced one side of Diana, which has always been very collegial. I think Sid has liked how impressed Diana’s been with her in the past, and hasn’t seen this steely, ruthless side to her that everyone else has experienced.
How do you think she feels once she speaks to Diana on the phone and can’t deny what’s happening anymore?

It’s incredibly clarifying, and almost a relief to know that this is the truth — the cold, hard truth. This person thinks that I’m dispensable, that I’m a pawn in whatever game that Diana is trying to play. Knowing that her life could be forfeit so easily — I think through the shock of it — she’s almost giddy. Like, “Oh shit, this is all so obvious to me now.” She kind of has nothing to lose from that point on, because it’s like, “Well, I’m gonna die regardless, going on this plane with these people, so I might as well just try to get out of here.”

You and Jack have great comedic chemistry. But because it’s a spy show, and especially because of what happens at the end of the season, you’re also meant to be questioning everyone’s motivations all the time. Do you have your own read on how Sid feels about River, and how sincere those emotions are?

I think despite herself, especially in the first season, her feelings for River have really caught her off guard. I think there’s a genuine connection — this tiny little pinhole of light. River has kept her going, in a sense. Even if they didn’t really get to know each other that well, whatever she’s projected onto River, and the reason why she seeks him out, is because there is something there that has been fizzing for a very, very long time. Especially in the absence. I think those things only get bigger when they’re unresolved, and she’s been so adrift for so long.
I was devastated by the cliffhanger. I can’t believe I have to wait an entire year to find out what happened.
Are you someone who reads the books, both to find out what happens with your character and maybe see what happens down the road?

In the interim, I hadn’t read the books, but I read for the season that is about to come out, just because I was like, “Surely I’m coming back!” But [Mick Herron] is such a brilliant writer, and he’s so acerbic, and sometimes it’s not faithfully adapted, but they’re really good companions to each other.

Obviously, you can’t tell me anything too specific about the future on the show, but the one thing I was very bummed out by is that we actually don’t get you and Diana face to face in this season. Do we think that might happen in the future?

I hope so! I want a showdown. With Kristin Scott Thomas, I think she’s a wonderful actor. I could watch her endlessly. So selfishly, I want that for me, for my dear diary. But yes, it feels like that is a very cathartic thing that must happen.
You’re heading into the final season of “House of the Dragon.” Do you have any goals or plans for the other side of that, when there’s gonna be some free time in your schedule?

God, I want to do so much. I really want to do theater. I really, really desperately want to do theater. I am trying. I’ve been trying for years to find the right thing, and maybe I’m just being a bit too picky, and I just need to do it.

But theater, and I’d like to be on the other side of the camera a bit more. I’ve been doing this for 14 years now, which doesn’t sound like a lot, but it feels like a lot. And I think I want to find new avenues to go down because I’m getting a bit sick of myself.
This interview has been edited and condensed.

items.title: Poison Ivy DC Series in the Works at HBO With ‘The Penguin’ Exec Lauren LeFranc
items.description: Another Batman villain may be getting their own TV series.
items.author: Jordan Moreau
paragraphs: Another Batman villain may be getting their own TV series.
A Poison Ivy TV show is in the works at HBO with “The Penguin” showrunner Lauren LeFranc as a producer, Variety has confirmed.

LeFranc’s “The Penguin” marked the first live-action spinoff from a Batman movie, after Colin Farrell originated his villain in Matt Reeves’ “The Batman” in 2022. It aired on HBO in 2024 and became a hit with critics and fans for its gritty, gangster story. Farrell won an Emmy and Golden Globe for his lead performance, and the show nabbed several best limited series nominations.

Poison Ivy, the green femme fatale from the Batman comics, has never been the main focus of a movie or TV show, but she’s appeared in several live-action and animated DC titles. The classic villain has the ability to control plants and often controls people’s minds using seductive pheromones. She first arrived on the big screen in 1997’s “Batman & Robin” and was played by Uma Thurman. In live-action TV, she also appeared in “Gotham” and “Batwoman,” and she’s popped up in several animated shows like “Batman: The Brave and the Bold,” “The New Batman Adventures,” “Young Justice” and more. Recently, she was voiced by Lake Bell in “Harley Quinn” and played the titular character’s girlfriend.

The DC Universe is expanding this weekend with “Clayface,” focused on the shape-shifting Batman villain. It’s unconnected to Robert Pattinson and Reeves’ world, which is continuing in 2028 with “The Batman Part 2.” HBO will also air “The People vs. Gorilla Grodd,” a comedic, villain-focused spinoff from James Gunn’s “Superman” movie, sometime in 2027.

items.title: Electronic Arts Laying Off 3% of Employees in Studios Restructuring: BioWare Shutting Down, Respawn and DICE to Team on ‘Star Wars: Battlefront 3’
items.description: Videogame giant Electronic Arts, in its first major move since going private this summer, is restructuring its studios business — which will result in layoffs of about 3% of global workforce.
items.author: Todd Spangler
paragraphs: Videogame giant Electronic Arts, in its first major move since going private this summer, is restructuring its studios business — which will result in layoffs of about 3% of global workforce.

The updates to EA’s studios operations were outlined in a memo to EA employees Wednesday from Cam Weber, president and chief studios officer, and David Tinson, president and COO. “Over the past several months, we’ve taken a hard look at our business, how we operate, and what it will take to lead in this next era of interactive entertainment,” the execs said. (Read the full memo below.)

Among the big changes: Games studio BioWare is shutting down after EA decided to pull the plug on its development of a new “Mass Effect” title. The company will close BioWare’s Canadian office in Edmonton. “BioWare is a legendary studio that helped define the role-playing genre, and we do not take this decision lightly,” Weber and Tinson said.
EA last reported 14,500 employees, meaning the layoffs affect around 400 staffers.

In a social media post Wednesday, the BioWare team said: “For more than 30 years, BioWare has been more than a studio. It has been a home for storytellers, developers, and the players who brought our worlds to life. Baldur’s Gate. Neverwinter Nights. Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic. Dragon Age. Mass Effect. Anthem. Now, after more than three decades of shared adventures, BioWare is closing and early development on the next Mass Effect project is ending.”

The message from BioWare continued: “There is nothing easy about writing those words. Our focus right now is on our incredibly talented team who put their hearts into these games, and supporting one another through this transition. What generations of BioWare built together is something to celebrate and remember. These games became so much more because you played them, debated your choices, fell in love with the characters, and made these worlds your own. From all of us at BioWare, thank you for being the most meaningful part of our story.”

In more upbeat news, EA’s Weber and Tinson touted first-person shooter “Battlefield 6” as “a great success, and we learned a lot from the launch and the live service.” Going forward, in addition to future “Battlefield” titles, the execs said “we’ll be bringing together our Respawn and DICE studios to collaborate on a future project.” While they did not identify the project, multiple sources confirmed that this is “Star Wars: Battlefront 3″ for Lucasfilm.
EA also will continue to “invest heavily” in the “Apex Legends” franchise over the next few years, with plans to introduce new gameplay modes in multiplayer, along with other new experiences.
Elsewhere in the action-adventure segment, EA remains committed to delivering on “our two huge launches coming up,” the execs said: “Marvel’s Iron Man” and the next “Star Wars Jedi” game.

At EA Sports, there are two new projects in development that will be revealed over the next few months, including a new, “social-first open-world experience for our American Football team that we call ‘Project Gridiron,'” the execs said. The studio also is in pre-production to bring back fan-favorite boxing game “Fight Night” after a 15-year hiatus.

Finally, in the lifestyle category, “we’re focusing on the long-term potential” of “The Sims” and skateboarding title “Skate.”, the EA execs wrote. “We’re going to prioritize our efforts on ‘Project Evergreen’ for The Sims to give the team more time to reach the full potential and vision for the game, and to help make this possible, we’re pausing development on ‘Project Lotus,’” they said. For “Skate.”, EA is “making changes to the studio to have a more focused, smaller team to deliver on a very clear roadmap for our community that we believe will build a healthier and more sustainable business,” the execs wrote.
On Aug. 4, EA closed the announced private-equity deal with Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, Silver Lake and Jared Kushner’s Affinity Partners in an all-cash transaction valued at $55 billion.
Read the memo from Weber and Tinson:

Through every major moment we’ve faced as a company, your commitment to creating awesome games and experiences for our players continues to be impressive. Together, we’ve built epic worlds and global communities that are part of the lives of hundreds of millions of people.

Today, we’re the number one publisher in Western HD gaming. That’s an extraordinary position to lead from, and one we should be proud of. Yet our industry is changing quickly. Players have more choices than ever for their time and attention, competition is intensifying, and some of our biggest opportunities for growth are beyond the markets, platforms, and business models where EA has traditionally been the strongest.

That’s why, over the past several months, we’ve taken a hard look at our business, how we operate, and what it will take to lead in this next era of interactive entertainment. We’ve challenged assumptions, confronted hard realities, imagined new possibilities, and made deliberate choices in order to deliver exceptional experiences for our players and to drive sustained growth.

We believe our best creative work happens when we’re clear about what matters most for our players and give our teams the freedom to move quickly. So, we’re concentrating our teams, technology, and investment behind these three strategic priorities.

- Deepen Our Core: Our greatest opportunity starts with our franchises and global communities that have made EA a leader in interactive entertainment. This is where we’ve had to make our hardest choices. Saying no to some things we’re passionate about allows us to focus our teams and resources so we give our biggest opportunities everything they need to succeed.

- Expand Our Reach: The strength of our core business creates an enormous opportunity to reach more players across new platforms, markets, and business models. As one example, in regions as dynamic as Asia, success means building experiences that reflect local players, cultures, and expectations.

- Transform Our Business: We believe we can use our experience building interactive entertainment, together with our relationships in sports, to create entirely new ways for fans to engage with the teams, athletes and sports they love. These will be disciplined investments that only scale when they demonstrate real potential.

These priorities will bring clarity and focus to your work every day, and so will the way we work. We’ve spent time listening to teams about what’s working, what’s getting in the way, and what you need to do your best work. The feedback was consistent: you want clearer priorities, faster decisions, and teams that work more closely together. We’ve already begun simplifying how we work so we can spend more time creating and innovating for our players.
Across our portfolio, we’re making deliberate choices to align talent and investments where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth.

In our Shooters business, Battlefield 6 was a great success, and we learned a lot from the launch and the live service. We’re going to take those learnings, balance our resources, and leverage the technology to deliver a shooter portfolio that unlocks growth. In addition to our future Battlefield titles, we’ll be bringing together our Respawn and DICE studios to collaborate on a future project that will help us achieve that ambition. We can’t wait to share more when the time comes. We’re also continuing to invest heavily in Apex over the next few years by introducing brand new gameplay modes in multiplayer, and other new experiences, to expand the universe.

Action-adventure is one of the most competitive and high-stakes genres in the industry, where every game needs our full weight behind it. We’re continuing to deliver on our two huge launches coming up with Marvel’s Iron Man and the next Star Wars Jedi game. Beyond that, we will concentrate our efforts on fewer simultaneous, large-scale projects, ensuring that every game we build in this space is fully set up for success.

As we focus on these larger opportunities, we’ve had a small team at BioWare working on early-development for Mass Effect. We’ve made the decision not to move forward with this development, which means we’re closing the studio and our Edmonton workspace. BioWare is a legendary studio that helped define the role-playing genre, and we do not take this decision lightly.

EA SPORTS continues to operate from a position of strength. We are fully committed and investing in the global growth of our FC franchise and across the full EA SPORTS portfolio. We have two new projects in development you’ll hear about over the next few months, including a brand-new, social-first open-world experience for our American Football team that we call “Project Gridiron,” and we are also in pre-production to bring back a beloved, fan-favorite in Fight Night, leveraging capabilities from our simulation fighting team.

In Lifestyle, we’re focusing on the long-term potential of The Sims and skate. We’re going to prioritize our efforts on “Project Evergreen” for The Sims to give the team more time to reach the full potential and vision for the game, and to help make this possible, we’re pausing development on “Project Lotus.” For skate., we’ve had a lot of success in bringing players into the game, and we need to create an experience that keeps them engaged over the long-term. To do that, we are making changes to the studio to have a more focused, smaller team to deliver on a very clear roadmap for our community that we believe will build a healthier and more sustainable business.
Building the EA We Believe In

The decisions we’re making in our priorities, how we work, and with our portfolio reflect our belief in EA’s future. Some open exciting new possibilities. Others are difficult, especially for the people and teams across the company who are directly affected. In those cases, we will support impacted employees in exploring other opportunities within EA, and we’re committed to treating impacted colleagues with care and respect.

We’re sure there will be questions about what these changes mean for individual teams and for EA more broadly. You can speak directly with your leaders to hear more on that, and we’ll make sure to spend time discussing our direction and the work ahead at our next Global Town Hall in November.

The past several months have strengthened our belief in what EA can become. We have extraordinary people, franchises that matter to millions of players, and opportunities to build experiences we’ve only begun to imagine.

Our responsibility is to make the choices, provide the clarity, and create the conditions for our teams to do their best work. We also want to give every game we choose to build its best chance to succeed for our players and fans around the world.
We look forward to building more great games and experiences together.

items.title: Lea Michele Returning for ‘Glee’ Reboot as Rachel Berry (EXCLUSIVE)
items.description: You can’t rain on her parade.
items.author: Marc Malkin; Selome Hailu
paragraphs: You can’t rain on her parade.

Lea Michele is returning to the role that launched her career in Disney+ and Hulu’s reboot of “Glee,” the Ryan Murphy-created musical dramedy series. Variety has confirmed the news with multiple sources.
“She’s in,” one source said. “It’s still early-ish days, but it feels good and we’re happy to get the band back together,” said another.
Reps for Michele and Murphy did not comment for this story.

So far, two of Michele’s “Glee” castmates have made social media posts that seem to confirm theiy will also return: Heather Morris, who plays Brittany Pierce, and Chord Overstreet, who plays Sam Evans.

For six seasons on Fox from 2009 to 2015, Michele led the cast of “Glee” as the precocious, arrogant and mega-talented Rachel Berry, one of the original members of the McKinley High School glee club. Over the course of the series, Rachel frequently alienated her peers with her ambition; while she stopped at nothing to pursue her dreams on Broadway and beyond, she privately struggled with her reputation and personal relationships. She was in and on-and-off relationship with football player and glee club peer Finn Hudson — played by Cory Monteith, whom Michele dated in real life — before the actor’s death.

Michele was already a seasoned Broadway performer before “Glee,” having appeared in “Les Misérables,” “Ragtime,” “Fiddler on the Roof” and most notably “Spring Awakening” opposite Jonathan Groff. After “Glee,” she had smaller roles in several film and TV projects, including another Murphy collaboration in Fox’s “Scream Queens” (2015-2016). She has enjoyed a career renaissance since 2022, when she joined the cast of Broadway’s “Funny Girl” revival as Fanny Brice — which garnered widespread attention not only for her acclaimed performance but for its resonance with her “Glee” character, who dreamed of playing Fanny for years before finally nabbing the role and later leaving it behind.
Michele was nominated for an Emmy and two Golden Globes for her work on “Glee.”

“I’ve been in touch with around 10 of the original cast members,” Murphy recently said in recent interview with “Entertainment Tonight,” in which he confirmed that he’d just written a “Glee” reboot script with collaborators Brad Falchuk and Ian Brennan. “It’s very sweet, and they all had a lot of questions, but they all were very enthusiastic about the idea.”

Just weeks earlier, Michele told “E! News” that she’d be happy to join a “Glee” reboot. “I love ‘Glee.’ I will always love ‘Glee,’” she said. “I love Ryan Murphy. It just holds such a special place in my heart for me… I will follow Ryan wherever he goes.”

In the series finale, which aired March 20, 2015, Rachel wins a Tony, marries Jesse St. James (played by Michele’s real-life best friend Groff) and becomes a surrogate mother for Kurt Hummel (Chris Colfer) and Blaine Anderson (Darren Criss).

items.title: The Creator A-List: The 25 Influencers Who Matter Most to Hollywood
items.description: This is not, we gather, the first creator power list you have read this year. Nor will it likely be the last. Like pivoting to video or starting a side gig on Substack, influencer power rankings are a media trend du jour. And it’s not shocking: The creator eco
items.author: Seija Rankin
paragraphs: This is not, we gather, the first creator power list you have read this year. Nor will it likely be the last. Like pivoting to video or starting a side gig on Substack, influencer power rankings are a media trend du jour. And it’s not shocking: The creator economy — projected to hit $310 billion this year, up 23 percent from 2025 — has totally reshaped entertainment. At first, they were outside disrupters; now they are part of the industry itself. So this year, for The Hollywood Reporter’s third annual foray into the fray, we wanted to do something different. We’ve culled our Creators A-list into a hyper-specific guide to the influencers who are the most important to Hollywood. These are the comedians, sketch writers and actors who are booking roles and selling scripts, as well as the TikTokers and YouTubers that studios and streamers consider their press tour secret weapons. They’re the creators (both current and former) who are vying for the attention not only of the public at large but the power players right here in town. If you’ve got a series to cast or a movie to promote, these are the people we think you should call — because your competition already has.

Though she got her start posting Get Ready With Me videos on TikTok and then recording the Hot Mess podcast for Alex Cooper’s Unwell Network, Earle has since turned her talents to the reality television space. She competed on season 34 of Dancing With the Stars (earning second place alongside pro Valentin Chmerkovskiy), and this fall she let viewers into her New Jersey manse with Earle Meets World. The series gets a boost thanks to her specific family drama — Earle’s stepmother is Ashley Dupré, the escort at the center of Eliot Spitzer’s fall from grace — and coverage of her rumored fling with Tom Brady, and it’s one of Netflix’s better-performing reality shows (it slid into the streamer’s top 10 during its first week).
THE THING I WOULD MISS ABOUT CREATOR LIFE IF I WENT FULL-TIME HOLLYWOOD “That I could stand next to a male without sparking a dating rumor.”
THE BIGGEST ROOKIE MISTAKE I MADE ONLINE “Going on live without realizing people would screen record it.”
THE PERSON WHOSE SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNT I’D LIKE TO RUN FOR A DAY “My stepmother Ashley Earle] because it would save me from holding my breath every time I refresh my social media.”

After more than a decade, Dimoldenberg will be eating her final chicken nugget as she prepares to wind down her fast food-centric interview series. But she’s not abandoning the form entirely — instead, the YouTuber will be starring in and producing a romantic comedy set up at Amazon MGM Studios’ Orion Pictures. Dimoldenberg will play a journalist who finds love during a seemingly routine celebrity interview; a conceit that will ring familiar to those who kept a close eye on her chemistry with former Chicken Shop Date guest Andrew Garfield.

As the creator and star of Overcompensating, Prime Video’s high-performing campus comedy based on his own life as a closeted college student, Skinner is the north star for creators hoping to break into Hollywood. The comedian, who also hosts a podcast with Overcompensating co-star and longtime friend Mary Beth Barone, spent years posting sketches to his Instagram account and then developing the series with A24 and Amazon Studios. Season two is expected soon, with stars like Kyle MacLachlan and Connie Britton set to return as well. “I spend less time in wigs,” Skinner says of his life on the other side of online sketches. “But I wrote some into Overcompensating season two to fill the void.”
THE BIGGEST ROOKIE MISTAKE I MADE ONLINE “Thinking all gay people would be nice because I’m gay. My boys take me DOWN sometimes holy fuck.”
MY DAILY MEDIA DIET CONSISTS OF … “Makeup reviews, gays dancing to Slayyyter, The O.C. or PEN15 fan cams, raccoons as pets and Disney adults ♥ I’m healthy!”
THE PERSON WHOSE SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNT I’D LIKE TO RUN FOR A DAY Ben Shapiro. “I’d wipe everything!”

Broski’s YouTube chat show Royal Court continues to reign supreme as a place for actors to do just that — chat. This year alone, the likes of Matt Damon, Anne Hathaway, Nicole Kidman, Sandra Bullock, Keke Palmer and Bob Odenkirk have all been lured in by the chance to trade a little bit of dignity (guests must dress up in medieval costumery) for a guaranteed-friendly interview. “I used to post videos of me being horny for celebrities I now have to sit opposite from and interview about their careers,” jokes Broski. There are no gotcha moments on Royal Court, but A-listers still have a high likelihood of virality thanks to the way the interview clips circulate across Instagram and TikTok.
CELEBRITY GUEST WHO MOST SURPRISED ME “I LOVE Riz Ahmed. I missed him the second he left the studio.”
THE BIGGEST ROOKIE MISTAKE I MADE ONLINE “Assuming the general public will operate in good faith, or ever offer you the benefit of the doubt.”
THE PERSON WHOSE SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNT I’D LIKE TO RUN FOR A DAY Alix Earle. “No further comment.”

Earlier this fall, Morales launched the Bri So for Real show on Instagram and TikTok, an interview series in which she asks guests to tell her their personal lore. As for her own lore? She gained fame as the host of NowThis Media’s Are You Okay? show, where she set a high — and, more importantly, cringe-free — bar for the sort of man-on-the-street interview concepts that are now taking over TikTok. She played herself on the newest season of FX’s hangout sitcom Adults, interviewing Jack Innanen’s Paul Baker.

CELEBRITY GUEST WHO MOST SURPRISED ME “The Rock was amazing. He seems nice online, but it’s true he really is one of the kindest people. Our interview got interrupted, and he went out of his way to come back and finish it.”

Charli D‘Amelio — the reigning queen of TikTok — loves to dance. Whenever a new song comes on at this photography studio in L.A., Charli is shimmying her shoulders, shaking her hips. Now she stamps and turns like a flamenco dancer, swishing the skirt of her ruffly black gown. “So pretty, stunning,” says Emman Montalvan, the photographer snapping her. “Gorg!”

With her glossy black hair and sparkly smile, Charli is gorg. She’s the girl next door drawn by Disney; she’s the bright and shiny face of social media, making it all seem benign. “This is her before she becomes jaded,” Montalvan observes. “Nothing calculated. Natural. She reminds me of when Britney Spears was young.”
Rihanna’s “Breakin’ Dishes” begins to play. Charli mouths the words: “I don’t know who you think I am —”

“Are you having fun?” I ask, finding myself smiling. Because when Charli is happy, you feel happy — which is no doubt part of her appeal. You want to believe that a life spent dancing around in fabulous clothes and opening yourself up to a dizzying 160 million-plus followers (the second most on TikTok) really is as wonderful as it looks.

But a flicker of annoyance crosses Charli’s brow, as if the question touches a nerve. Maybe that’s because of how the algorithms are always demanding she offer up the semblance of a perfect life, the performance of joy, no matter the reality. Read the full profile by Nancy Jo Sales.

Colin Rosenblum and Samir Chaudry have built a large following — and a lucrative business — as creators catering to other creators. They host a video series breaking down the influencer economy and offering industry analysis, and this year they hosted a sold-out summit on the Fox lot dedicated to the intersection of creators and Hollywood. They’re also starting to set up their own EP business, with (still secretive) projects in development with both Lionsgate and A24.

As the owner of Dhar Mann Studios, the creator makes inspirational scripted and unscripted short- and longform videos — popular topics include unlikely romances and overprotective parents — for an audience of 170 million followers globally. Now, thanks to a new content deal, he’ll be producing 20 episodes of his signature shortforms exclusively for Disney. (The company recently launched a new vertical video product and struck a separate deal with TikTok, all part of a push to make its streaming platform more comprehensive.) “Some of my biggest breakthroughs came when I stopped worrying about production quality and started focusing on the story,” says Mann of his early learnings. “Turns out, people connect with authenticity, not perfection.”
THE THING I WOULD MISS ABOUT CREATOR LIFE IF I WENT FULL-TIME HOLLYWOOD

“Being able to wake up with an idea, film it in my apartment and post it that night. Now an idea can involve five soundstages, hundreds of people and a lot of meetings. Sometimes I miss when my biggest production problem was convincing a friend to hold the camera.”

Best known for her appearances on The Bachelor, The Bachelorette and The Traitors, and for the way she harnessed her reality TV stardom to build a dedicated online following, Windey is now turning to the big screen. She’ll appear in next year’s Peaked, an A24 comedy directed by and starring Molly Gordon that is said to revolve around a high school reunion as two former mean girls attempt to relive their glory days. Windey will also play the coach of a Catholic girls’ school dance team that experiences a mass hysteria event in Netflix’s series The Body, which bows Nov. 11. Her comedic sensibility has been compared to that of Jennifer Coolidge, and it seems Hollywood is finally giving her the chance to prove it.
THE BIGGEST ROOKIE MISTAKE I MADE ONLINE “Big of you to think I live life with regret.”
THE PERSON WHOSE SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNT I’D LIKE TO RUN FOR A DAY “I would never give away my creativity to another.”

Reiter started her own mass hysteria event — online — when her SNL season 52 announcement went live. The comedian built a faithful-slash-rabid following on TikTok and YouTube and as part of the American High sketch troupe. She cut her TV teeth during the first season of Tim Robinson’s delightfully wacky The Chair Company (she played Robinson’s soon-to-be daughter-in-law and nemesis) and is already set to take up the sketch show’s resident weirdo position. But to her OG fans, she promises she’ll never leave content creating completely: “I’m Hannah Montana, I get the best of both worlds.”
THE BIGGEST ROOKIE MISTAKE I MADE ONLINE “I went on Omegle on TikTok live and got banned.”
MY DAILY MEDIA DIET CONSISTS OF …. “I’m trying to train my fyp to only show me pug videos and videos with only four likes. Those videos inspire me.”

Coyne’s social media show Track Star* started as a simple on-the-street contest; if you stopped to listen to a track and could name the artist, you won $5. Now, it’s a name-that-tune quiz game meets interview format and a must-stop on global press tours for actors looking to show off a little of their own version of street cred. Like Maya Rudolph sharing iconic stories from her childhood or Andrew Garfield making his plea to star in a Cat Stevens biopic.
THE THING I WOULD MISS ABOUT CREATOR LIFE IF I WENT FULL-TIME HOLLYWOOD “The magic of being a creator is being firmly in control of your creative work. I’d hate to give up that creative control.”

This year, the TikToker and podcaster made his Broadway debut as part of the cast of All Out, did a guest role on the second season of Adults and is developing a half-hour comedy series with Hulu. He’s also worked hard to continue to crank out the digital content that his followers connect to, be it for his quirkiness on TikTok and Instagram (he takes requests for impressions of things like “a USB being flipped around a whole bunch when you try to plug it in” and “the iceberg getting hit”) or his extreme relatability on his podcast (asking Troye Sivan to explain what “the bush” is).
THE BIGGEST ROOKIE MISTAKE I MADE ONLINE “Asking Kacey Musgraves what the line ‘in Beijing they’re heading out to work’ meant.”
THE PERSON WHOSE SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNT I’D LIKE TO RUN FOR A DAY Kylie Jenner

She first burst onto the scene during the sixth season of Love Island USA and quickly pivoted her reality TV notoriety into internet stardom, doing collabs with brands like Truly, Maybelline and Venmo. Now she’s turning her sights on entertainment, with a cameo in All for Love, a film produced by Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star Whitney Leavitt and a still-highly secretive lead role in a vertical series from Issa Rae’s production company. (In the meantime, you can find her at the Traitors US mansion filming season six, which is expected to hit Peacock in early 2027.)
THE BIGGEST ROOKIE MISTAKE I MADE ONLINE “Going on Snapchat rants and posting a man before getting a ring. I will never post a man again until I get a ring on my finger.”

Woods has been on screens of all kinds for years, first on the original Keeping Up With the Kardashians and then Life of Kylie, and then she came to our phones as she started building her career as a content creator. But it was this year that she truly became a star thanks to her courtside appearances and her now-husband Karl-Anthony Towns’ historic run with the New York Knicks. Her lucky bag, a faux-ostrich purse in Knickerbocker orange, became a viral sensation in and of itself — and now sits in a glass case in the hallowed halls of the Guggenheim Museum.

THE THING I WOULD MISS ABOUT CREATOR LIFE IF I WENT FULL-TIME HOLLYWOOD “The freedom to create and connect with people on my own terms. I’ve grown up in this industry, and my audience has grown with me. There’s something special about being able to share different chapters of my life while also building something of my own.”

THE BIGGEST ROOKIE MISTAKE I MADE ONLINE “I’ve been on social media since I was 15, and honestly, I don’t really look back at anything as a mistake. We were all figuring it out together, and back then, social media was just fun. There wasn’t the same pressure to be perfect or turn every moment into a business opportunity.”

What started as a heartwarming web series about a 20-something guy interviewing elementary school children for life advice has now evolved into a sought-after press stop — like doing a guest role on Sesame Street. Shapiro-Barnum still hosts Recess Therapy (guests have included Olivia Rodrigo and Matt Damon, and he’s also taken the series to awards show red carpets) and he’s since expanded his online oeuvre with Celebrity Substitute and the recently launched Outside Tonight, the first digital late night show, in partnership with YouTube.
THE BIGGEST ROOKIE MISTAKE I MADE ONLINE “I posted the back of my credit card on main … lesson learned …”
THE PERSON WHOSE SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNT I’D LIKE TO RUN FOR A DAY “Let me try and run Elmo’s socials. That guy’s got potential. I can make him a star!”

The media entrepreneur’s Subway Takes series (in which celebs share their hot takes in front of a car full of straphangers) has become an all-out sensation, even earning an Emmy nomination this year for outstanding short form comedy, drama or variety series. But Rahma’s real superpower lies in longform programming: He recently relaunched Keep the Meter Running, mini-docs that follow Rahma as he hops into the back of a taxi and asks the driver to take him to their favorite place in the city. Where Subway Takes trades in virality, Meter is all heart; as he follows drivers through far-flung corners of New York, Cairo and even Damascus, he asks poignant questions about life, love and loss. If comparisons to Anthony Bourdain were still au courant, we’d use one here.
CELEBRITY GUEST WHO MOST SURPRISED ME “I had a ton of fun with Colin Jost. He’s more buff than I thought he would be!”
MY DAILY MEDIA DIET CONSISTS OF … “Emily Sundberg’s Feed Me, Matthew Belloni’s The Town, a quick scroll of X (10 minutes max) and then lots and lots of Instagram and YouTube.”
THE BIGGEST ROOKIE MISTAKE I MADE ONLINE “Posting a selfie. Men should never post selfies. I’m only sending you a selfie because it is required.”
THE PERSON WHOSE SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNT I’D LIKE TO RUN FOR A DAY Donald Trump

Le became known for posting thoughtful and researched commentary on both newly released and upcoming movies and TV shows — like her deep dive on blondes in the wake of FX’s Love Story. Now, she’s quickly becoming Hollywood’s right-hand woman for marketing campaigns and has paid partnerships ranging from Apple TV, HBO and Netflix to Mubi and YouTube’s Oscars programming. A role in a yet-to-be-announced major series is next.
